title: I was arrested protesting Netanyahu’s New York visit. Here’s why we took a stand | Darializa Avila Chevalier | The Guardian
description: I refuse to play host to a man who has overseen the slaughter or injury of more than 64,000 children in Gaza with American taxpayer dollars. I refuse to be complicit in genocide
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I refuse to play host to a man who has overseen the slaughter or injury of more than 64,000 children in Gaza with American taxpayer dollars. I refuse to be complicit in genocide
Content: ‘That is why I was arrested today outside of the United Nations alongside hundreds of my fellow New Yorkers.’Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘That is why I was arrested today outside of the United Nations alongside hundreds of my fellow New Yorkers.’Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty ImagesOpinionBenjamin NetanyahuI was arrested protesting Netanyahu’s New York visit. Here’s why we took a standDarializa Avila ChevalierI refuse to play host to a man who has overseen the slaughter or injury of more than 64,000 children in Gaza with American taxpayer dollars. I refuse to be complicit in genocideThu 24 Sep 2026 17.20 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.27 EDTShareBenjamin Netanyahu belongs at The Hague; not in the streets of New York City, and certainly not before the United Nations general assembly. The international criminal court has a warrant out for his arrest for war crimes and crimes against humanity. The UN’s own commission of inquiry has found that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza and named Netanyahu as its chief architect.As the Democratic nominee for New York’s 13th congressional district, I refuse to allow a war criminal to roam the streets of our city unchallenged. I refuse to play host to a man who has overseen the slaughter or injury of more than64,000 children in Gazawith American taxpayer dollars. I refuse to be complicit in genocide.That is why I was arrested today outside of theUnited Nationsalongside hundreds of my fellow New Yorkers.Israel has killed more than73,000 people in Gaza. It has bombed hospitals, schools, places of worship, fishing boats, and refugee tents. It hascollectively starvedan entire population as a tool in its genocide.It has subjected men, women and children to systematic sexual torture and imprisonment. It hasthreatened to kill people for flying kites, killed more than1,000 people since its so-called ceasefire, andfired 335 bulletsinto a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab.And when it comes to consequences, world leaders offer carefully worded statements that don’t even amount to a slap on the wrist.Here in the US, establishmentDemocratsand Republicans alike have shielded Netanyahu from prosecution for his crimes and sent over$21bn of our tax dollarsin just two years to fund Israeli bombs.TheBidenandTrumpadministrations both obscured evidence, lied about what Israel was doing in Gaza, funded the carnage, and isolated and arrested people that spoke out against it. Just last week, the Trump administrationproposed a $2.8bn weapons saleto Israel including 2,000lb bombs.New Yorkers refuse to be silent. That’s why today’s civil disobedience, led by Jewish Voice for Peace, NYC-DSA, Sunrise Movement, CAAAV, Palestinian Youth Movement, Adalah Justice Project, the US Campaign for Palestinian Rights and more had 400 participants including more than 100 people arrested to demand an end to this injustice.Netanyahu’s speech at UN spurs protests in New York City: ‘Let Gaza live’Read moreAnd NY-13, and New York City, is with us. This summer, Harlem, Washington Heights, Inwood and the West Bronx unseated a five-term, Aipac-backed incumbent. Their message was clear: invest in their babies here at home, not in bombs dropped abroad.They made me their Democratic nominee with a mandate to pass legislation like theBlock the Bombs Actand fight back against our country’s insatiable war machine. Across this city, New Yorkers elected candidates to Congress and the state assembly who’ll fight to stop the bombs, divest from death, and invest in a politics of life.Families inPalestine, Lebanon and Iran are not our enemies.Our enemy is a system where billionaires get rich from stoking hatred and war while our own communities go without. Tonight, shelters across uptown and the Bronxwill be full. This past year, more than100,000 childrenin New York City’s public schools have experienced homelessness. And right now, families are feeling the physical toll of cuts to Snap and Medicaid, and New York City Housing Authority residents are once again forced to sleep in inadequate housing.I ran for Congress because I am done being told that there is never enough money for our communities while watching our government write blank checks to enact atrocities. Every dollar spent on slaughtering communities abroad is a dollar stolen from our communities here at home.In 1967, Dr Martin Luther King Jrstood at the pulpit of Riverside churchin my district and warned that a country that spends more on war than “on programs of social uplift is approaching spiritual death”.Members of Congress have a responsibility to act with courage in the face of grave injustice, not to continue funding it. Unfortunately, nearly 60 years later, not much has changed.Palestinians are facing unthinkable conditions every single day under an Israeli apartheid regime that that disappears men, women and children intomilitary prisons knownfor their physical, sexual and psychological torture.And here at home, families in my district have to endure their schools, clinics and food assistance being cut to pay for war, and ICE kidnapping our neighbors for speaking up for Palestinians, while nearly 40% of the babies in my district are growing up inpoverty.From NY-13 to Palestine, all children, and all people, deserve the safety and the resources to live dignified lives. That’s why I take to the streets, and that’s why I’m headed to Congress: to stop sending our tax dollars to arm genocide, to end senseless wars, and to build a government accountable to the working people of this country.Our communities deserve leaders with an unwavering moral compass, who understand that our shared humanity is sacred, and that fights to build a politics of life even when it is politically costly. If that requires my arrest, so be it.Darializa Avila Chevalier is the Democratic nominee for New York’s 13th congressional districtExplore more on these topicsBenjamin NetanyahuOpinionIsraelGazaMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineNew YorkUnited NationscommentShareReuse this content

title: Why is the UK’s suppressed climate national security report significant? | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Warnings about the catastrophic effects of vital ecosystems collapsing were not published under previous prime minister
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: Warnings about the catastrophic effects of vital ecosystems collapsing were not published under previous prime minister
Content: A satellite image of Hurricane Lowell, left, Hurricane Karina, centre, and Hurricane Marie, right, over the Pacific Ocean earlier this month.Photograph: NOAA/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA satellite image of Hurricane Lowell, left, Hurricane Karina, centre, and Hurricane Marie, right, over the Pacific Ocean earlier this month.Photograph: NOAA/AFP/Getty ImagesClimate crisisExplainerWhy is the UK’s suppressed climate national security report significant?Warnings about the catastrophic effects of vital ecosystems collapsing were not published under previous PMUK shares findings of damning climate crisis national security report suppressed under StarmerFiona HarveyEnvironment editorThu 24 Sep 2026 14.27 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 14.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUK spy chiefs warned government ministers of the catastrophic impacts on national security from the collapse of vital ecosystems around the world, driven by the climate crisis and the overexploitation of nature. But their report, which was supposed to be published almost a year ago, was suppressed under Keir Starmer. Now the government isbriefing foreign ministers from other countries on the findings, with a view to gathering global support for more concerted action on the risks.What is the report?In the first report of its kind, the UK’s spy chiefs set out stark warnings of the catastrophic risks to the UK from thecollapse of vital ecosystems around the world, driven by the climate crisis and our failures to protect nature. The Guardian has seen part of the report and has spoken to a large number of people familiar with its contents, which warn of food shortages, conflicts, mass migration and other threats to the UK’s national security, including going as far as the risk of nuclear war or the breakdown of society. These threats are not regarded as some far-off or remote contingency: disastrous impacts, for instance on the UK’s food supply, could be expected as soon as 2030, it warns.What did they find?The report, which was originally commissioned under the previous Tory government, looked at the potential consequences of a range of scenarios such as the collapse of the Amazon rainforest, which scientists have warned could beclose to switching from a rainforest to a savannah-like system under the impact of heating and deforestation. The authors found these could result in food shortages in the UK, which imports about 40% of its food. The report also reviewed the development of new pandemics from areas deforested and overexploited, border disputes among countries affected by the climate crisis, increased Russian and Chinese influence over critical mineral supply chains, and civil tensions within the UK as these impacts play out.Collapsing ecosystems overseas – the Congo basin was also a focus – could result in mass migration as people are forced to leave areas no longer habitable, triggering potential unrest and “more polarised and populist politics in the UK and its allies”, along with “more strain on national infrastructure”, and conflict could result from countries fighting over scarce food supplies. While the risk of nuclear war is still regarded as small, it is a potential impact.One person who had seen the whole report described it to the Guardian as “apocalyptic”.How was the report suppressed?The report wassupposed to be published in full last October, before theCop30 climate summit in held in Belém, in the Brazilian Amazon. But Downing Street officials intervened at the last moment to prevent its publication. The Guardian revealed the report’s key findings at the time through leaks, as subsequently did other media, but nothing was officially forthcoming until January, when, after several refused attempts under the Freedom of Information Act, apartial summary of parts of the report was released to the Green Alliance thinktank.We’ve been reading for years about the impacts of the climate and biodiversity crises – what is different about this?Scientists have issuednumerous stark warnings of a future of droughts, floods, storms and severe heatwaves, if global heating exceeds 1.5C above preindustrial levels.This report is different, however, because it comes from the UK’s joint intelligence committee, the cross-government ministerial advisory body that oversees the work of the UK’s spy agencies and is tasked with monitoring national security. It examined the climate and nature crises for their potential to damage the UK’s security and defence, and found the UK underprepared for the impacts.What has the government done about these risks?The government has not issued a formal response. The fact that the report has not been published means ministers can hide from its implications, according to Adrian Ramsay, the Green party MP for Waveney Valley, who has called repeatedly for its publication and led a parliamentary debate on it earlier this year. A parliamentary committee has also tried to persuade ministers to disclose the findings, and their response to them.View image in fullscreenEd Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, made a presentation on the findings at a private meeting with some of his foreign counterparts on Wednesday night.Photograph: Stefan Jeremiah/APMoreover, while the report warns of what will happen if ecosystems break down, the UK hasslashed its overseas development aid, hurting the vulnerable countries where many of these ecosystems are located. International climate finance has been reduced from £11.6bn in total over the five years 2021 to 2026, to about £2bn a year for the next two years, and the previous ringfencing of spending on nature and forests within that budget has been dropped. Manynature conservation projects in vulnerable countries were among those cut, the Guardian previously revealed.However, this week the government has taken the first steps towards acting on the report’s findings, under the guidance of the foreign secretary, and former energy and climate secretary, Ed Miliband, with the backing of the prime minister, Andy Burnham.What has he done?On Wednesday,Miliband led a briefing about the report’s findings to foreign ministries from around the world, including those of the EU, Kenya and Australia, which is in charge of the negotiations at thenext UN climate summit, Cop31 in November. Ministers were not given full copies of the report at the closed-door meeting at the UN general assembly in New York, but were given verbal summaries of its findings.What impact will this have?Miliband, whotold the Guardian he would put the climate at the heart of foreign policy, also announced £330m for the Global Environment Fund (GEF), one of the principal vehicles for funding nature protection in the developing world. The UK will also provide £400m for Brazil’s Tropical Forests Forever Facility (TFFF).Jonathan Hall, managing director of Conservation International UK, told the Guardian: “The Starmer administration’s decision to drop the longstanding precedent to spend a significant proportion of our international climate aid on nature and forests was totally unjustified. This [spending] is both scientifically essential and very popular with the UK public, according to polling, so Miliband now needs to build on the contributions to the TFFF and GEF and reintroduce a clear target for at least a third of UK climate aid to be dedicated to natural ecosystems and tropical forests.”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisEd MilibandexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Price hikes, ads and lower quality: has ‘streamflation’ ruined the TV experience? | Television | The Guardian
description: US consumers are starting to opt out of the streaming world as several services raise prices without offering many perks
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: US consumers are starting to opt out of the streaming world as several services raise prices without offering many perks
Content: A still from Toy Story 5.Photograph: Disney/PAView image in fullscreenA still from Toy Story 5.Photograph: Disney/PATelevisionPrice hikes, ads and lower quality: has ‘streamflation’ ruined the TV experience?US consumers are starting to opt out of the streaming world as several services raise prices without offering many perksJesse HassengerThu 24 Sep 2026 10.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 10.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt may not be quite as politically buzzy as the price of gasoline or eggs, but another household expense is going up for millions of people. Disney has brought the price-gouging experience of its theme park home again by raising the prices of most iterations and bundles of its Disney+ and Hulu streaming services. Whether you pay to watch them with or without ads, separately or bundled together, you’re probably getting a price hike of a couple of bucks per month. The few bundles that will remain the same price feature ad-supported versions of both services (plus ESPN). Don’t worry, though; paying extra to avoid the ad-supported versions of those services won’t mean that you’re missing out on some cross-promotional opportunities. Disney’s terms of service note that they reserve the right to insert ads before and after programming on whatever subscription tier they want, regardless of what you’re paying for. True magic!Kim Kardashian’s Team Moms highlights the ridiculous excess of the US youth-sports industryRead moreThis particular magic isn’t reserved for Disney, though. Price hikes among streaming services have become so common that The Verge has adedicated pageaggregating the news of them, which tends to arrive every few months. Apple, apparently high on Emmy fumes, has raised its prices four times in four years, keeping pace with many of its competitors despite a vastly smaller dedicated catalog. Depending on which version of Peacock subscribers use, they’ve seen their bills padded by five or six dollars a month just since the summer of 2025, including another increase last month. Netflix, meanwhile, hasn’t gone up since March 2026. That’s not a reprieve; that’s a sign another hike must be around the corner.Consumers have noticed. Reportedlyan estimated 39% of Americanscanceled a streaming service in the past six months due to what’s been dubbed “streamflation”. Anothersurveyindicates that a majority of people subscribe to at least three such services, which is consistent with estimates of streaming households spending about $70 per month. Access to the six big streaming services (Netflix, Disney+/Hulu, HBO Max, Paramount+, Apple TV, Peacock) will boost that number somewhere in the neighborhood of $120, on top of which subscribers need broadband internet for the services to actually work. For the total price, you might as well call the whole thing Cable+, in that it’s like your old cable bill, only there’s more of it. No wonder cancellations are rampant.To retain subscribers without putting the screws directly to them, it might be viable for streaming companies to stabilize annual prices – typically a discounted lump-sum payment covering a full year of a service – even when raising monthly costs. Some, like Netflix, don’t offer this option. While those that do have kept annual subscriptions cheaper than the a year’s worth of month-to-month, companies don’t seem interested in maintaining bargain levels. The annual price for Disney+ at launch was $70. Now it’s $190, an increase of 170% – presumably to stay competitive with eggs. Amazon Prime, whose streaming service began as a perk for members already paying an annual membership fee for unlimited shipping and other benefits, has also risen while inserting more ads into its programming and downgrading the picture quality. You want higher resolution and fewer ads? That’s another $50 a year.View image in fullscreenMatthew Rhys in Widow’s Bay, a big hit for Apple.Photograph: Robert Clark/AppleThe reasons for all this shameless gauging are pretty simple: Wall Street doesn’t just demand profits (though those have sometimes been scarce in the streaming world) but endless growth, and some services don’t have all that much more room, realistically, to sign up more users any more. Netflix has 325 million subscribers worldwide. What’s their reach goal? 500 million? Three billion? What happens when everyone on Earth with an internet connection and a credit card already has Netflix?Not every service is so close to a saturation point (unless you count electricity as a streaming service). But it’s notable that even a supposedly lower-tier streamer like Peacock commands over 40 million monthly subscribers, equivalent to more than 10% of the United States population. (It’s a heavily US-skewing service, so unlike Netflix those users aren’t especially global.) By comparison, the biggest magazine in the US has a subscriber base of around half that (and that’s the AARP magazine, an outlier in that it’s distributed to paying members). The New York Times, considered an especially successful recent example of the subscription model, has 13 million subscribers. The AMC Stubs A-List program that allows moviegoers to see four films a week has about 1 million.That’s all to say that streaming has unprecedented reach, which means the only realistic way to boost profits is to either raise subscription prices, or make less stuff. The latter might sound ridiculous, especially given that we’ve been living in the post-boom age for streaming shows for a while now. Then again, that’s worked out well for the catalog-basedTubi, whose original works are lower-profile and lower-budget than its competitors. One of several free streaming services, Tubi outstrips some of those paid competitors in market share and turns a profit based only on its ads.Watching a movie or a show on a free service isn’t exactly an optimal experience; there are those ad breaks, sometimes the transfers aren’t top-notch, and the content churn tends to be a little faster than the subscription streamers. It’s definitely not a place where you can catch much of anything nominated for an Emmy in the past five or six years (though some Oscar movies or second-tier popular hits from that period might turn up). On the other hand, free streamers often manage to under-promise and over-deliver; at a time when paid subscriptions seem eager to offer less than ever, especially in the quite broad field of films made before 1995, Tubi, PlutoTV and their ilk always have at least a couple dozen stone-cold classics on hand that more than make up for not including the latest big-name time-wasters (looking at you,Matthew McConaughey/Woody Harrelson sitcomwhere they play themselves!). And the price always stays the same.View image in fullscreenTubi’s original works are lower-profile and lower-budget than its competitors.Photograph: TubiStill, some free streaming services with surprisingly robust and shifting catalogs aren’t exactly the dream of cord-cutting that was fed to consumers throughout the 2010s. The initial idea was to shed the bloat from all-or-nothing cable services that hold monopolies, or something close to it, in plenty of geographic areas. Competition for subscribers would keep good deals in the offing. Instead, what’s been happening over the past five years or so is a redistribution of that money from one set of giant companies to another. There’s slightly more consumer control over the size of the bills, in the sense that, yes, it’s possible to cancel a couple of services in a way that picking and choosing individual cable channels wasn’t possible outsidea few premium subscriptions. But there’s also far less clarity about how to catch the best shows and movies of any given year. For ages, it was mostly a simple formulation: have cable, add HBO. Now even the prestige of HBO seems a little more niche – a Game of Thrones spin-off; a well-liked Green Lantern show – than in the past.There’s also a strange sense that this scramble of greed isn’t paying off as well as it should; many streaming services feel like they’re in far more precarious financial positions than most cable companies or channels were at their peak. It’s a dystopian development: corporations still want consumers on the hook for endless subscription payments, but also seem to want them to share in the nervous stock-checking of a shareholder, without any particular upside. Each month, you check your streaming holdings and see if you’re about to be charged even more, and whether you need to pick one to divest (cancel, whether for good or for now). You can toggle some of them on and off timed to the occasional appearance of a major series like Severance or The Pitt, but the onus for keeping track of erratic streaming schedules is on the subscriber. None of these shows are as necessary as basic groceries. But the ability to relax and watch TV after a long day is still in danger of becoming another budget-related stressor – an unholy combination of cable bloat and the endless doomscroll.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionUS televisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Toxic bosses: why do companies protect managers who make working life hell? | Work & careers | The Guardian
description: Bullying, manipulation and intimidation can destroy lives, yet abusive authoritarians continue to rise to the top. How do they get away with it – and can they be brought to heel?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Bullying, manipulation and intimidation can destroy lives, yet abusive authoritarians continue to rise to the top. How do they get away with it – and can they be brought to heel?
Content: ‘The leaders who do the most psychological damage rarely arrive as tyrants.’Composite: Guardian design; Bojan89; Antonio_Diaz/Getty Images (posed by models)View image in fullscreen‘The leaders who do the most psychological damage rarely arrive as tyrants.’Composite: Guardian design; Bojan89; Antonio_Diaz/Getty Images (posed by models)Work & careersToxic bosses: why do companies protect managers who make working life hell?Bullying, manipulation and intimidation can destroy lives, yet abusive authoritarians continue to rise to the top. How do they get away with it – and can they be brought to heel?Kathleen SaxtonThu 24 Sep 2026 09.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Andrea finally resigned, her colleagues told her the truth they had always known about her boss. Some apologised. Others admitted they had watched what happened to her and said nothing. One offered the sentence I have been unable to forget: “You’ve been an emotional stab vest for us. You protected us.”Andrea was a senior legal executive with decades of credibility when she began reporting to a powerful new colleague. Within months, something was wrong. Expectations shifted without warning and feedback contradicted itself. He spoke over her in public and undermined her in private. Slowly she began questioning not just him but herself, her competence, even her grip on reality.What disturbed Andrea most was the gradual discovery that everybody already knew. Colleagues confessed that when they heard this executive was returning to the organisation, they had cried. When Andrea approached HR, a senior executive told her: “People work longer at McDonald’s than they work for him.” That was acknowledgment, not discovery. And there is something brutally revealing in the stab-vest description. Andrea had become the organisation’s psychological shock absorber. While she took the blows, everybody around her was safer.Stories like Andrea’s are usually told as stories about monsters: the bullying boss, the narcissistic founder who finally, spectacularly, falls. I have come to think of such framing as the least useful way to tell them. Instead, I’m interested in how such people keep acquiring power and why, once their behaviour is visible to almost everyone, nobody stops them.I have encountered power through three lenses. For 20 years, I was an executive-level headhunter, spending thousands of hours assessing the people organisations were preparing to entrust with authority. I then held that authority myself, as a global chief marketing officer in New York. Now, as a psychotherapist, I meet power from the opposite side, through people trying to understand what happened to them when somebody wielded it badly. The industries differ; the consequences rarely do. Brilliant people become convinced they are incompetent. Experienced professionals stop trusting their own judgment. Good leadership enlarges people. Bad leadership, at its darkest, persuades a person, slowly, to disappear.View image in fullscreen‘The qualities needed to win a job are not necessarily the qualities required to do it.’Photograph: Weiquan Lin/Getty Images (posed by a model)It never begins that way. The leaders who do the most psychological damage rarely arrive as tyrants. They arrive as answers, wrapped in charm and certainty, mirroring your values back to you. That first meeting can feel like the best of your professional life. Clinically, this can create a rapid sense of attachment, in which trust and emotional closeness develop before the relationship has had time to be tested. What follows – withdrawing warmth and then restoring it just often enough – is the logic of the slot machine: intermittent reward keeps people hopeful and vigilant, working ever harder to recover the golden beginning. By the time the storm breaks, the job has been accepted and the mortgage signed – leaving feels unthinkable.Some of this starts at selection. Consider the language of the senior job specification: bold, decisive, resilient, charismatic, comfortable under pressure, possessed of “executive presence”. There is nothing wrong with any of it. The problem is that a healthy leader and a dangerous one can look almost identical at interview. One candidate is decisive because they have experience and a secure enough ego to make the difficult call; another because doubt itself is intolerable. One is resilient through self-regulation, another through emotional detachment. Both interview beautifully. Corporate language launders the difference: low empathy is repackaged as decisiveness, ruthlessness as “high standards”, emotional detachment as resilience, manipulation as influence.In 2015, a meta-analysis led by the psychologist Emily Grijalva found that narcissism meaningfully predicts leadership emergence, which is to say getting the job, but has almost no relationship with leadership effectiveness. People high in the so-called dark triad traits – narcissism, machiavellianism and psychopathy – are disproportionately skilled at impression management, and although psychopathic traits appear in roughly 1% of the general population, studies of corporate samples suggest markedly higher concentrations among business leaders.As a therapist, I am also interested in what forms such leaders. Research published in the Leadership Quarterly found an association between supervisors’ experiences of family undermining during childhood and abusive supervisory behaviour in adulthood, particularly among those with lower self-control. This demands careful interpretation. Trauma in itself does not create toxic leaders and disqualifies nobody from leadership. Many remarkable leaders have transformed painful experience into empathy and wisdom.View image in fullscreen‘Good leadership enlarges people.’Photograph: Thomas Barwick/Getty Images (posed by models)The distinction that matters is between trauma and unprocessed trauma. There is a profound difference between a leader who has made sense of their lived experience and one whose unexamined wounds continue to seep into the way they use power. The child who survived chaos by monitoring everything can become the executive who must control everything. Somebody who once felt profoundly powerless may spend an adult lifetime making sure they never feel powerless again.The survival mechanisms do not necessarily disappear. They can professionalise. Hypervigilance becomes “strategic oversight”. The inability to trust becomes “strong leadership”. Emotional suppression becomes “composure under pressure”. What once protected a person from vulnerability can become, under the authority of office, the very thing that makes everybody around them unsafe.The psychoanalyst and organisational psychologist Manfred FR Kets de Vries has spent decades examining the psychological forces beneath executive ambition, and in conversations I had with him about narcissism, his warning about what happens when personality meets authority has always stayed with me. “When people get into a situation of power, unfortunately, narcissism is a very heavy drug and many people cannot handle it,” he said in a2025 interview. The corporate world can compound that risk because it often rewards the very behaviours it produces: intensity, certainty, relentless drive and control.But explanation is not exoneration, and an explanation of the leader must never become an alibi for the institution. The facts of each case vary, but what is most striking about the public cases is not what the leader did but how many people knew. The CBI’s implosion under misconduct allegations, the Ted Baker staff petition against their founder’s culture of“forced hugging”,Harvey Weinsteinas Hollywood’s open secret: in account after account, the recurring detail was that none of it was hidden. The Ethics & Compliance Initiativereports that about three-quarters of employeeswho witness wrongdoing do report it, either internally or externally. The signals arrive, yet too often they fail to prompt meaningful action, particularly when the person involved is judged too valuable to lose.View image in fullscreen‘NDAs are at the foundation of the architecture of silence’ … Zelda Perkins, a former assistant to Harvey Weinstein.Photograph: Geoff Pugh/ShutterstockAround a destructive leader grows what I think of as an architecture of accommodation: colleagues who privately disapprove, boards that soften the language, investors who admire the numbers, and employees who decide, entirely understandably, that their mortgage matters more than becoming the next target. Nobody has to intend to protect abuse. Each person simply has to make the safest decision available to them.Inside a hierarchy, these forces compound. We doubt what we are seeing because nobody else appears alarmed, we assume somebody senior must know more than we do, and we watch what happens to the first person who speaks before quietly deciding not to become the second.The silence is expensive. When MIT Sloan researchers analysed 34m employee profiles, toxic culture proved 10 times more powerful than pay in predicting who quit. Britain’sHealthand Safety Executive identifies the way managers manage staff as a major cause of work-related stress, and Stanford’s Jeffrey Pfeffer, studying workplace mortality, concluded that harmful management practices are “literally killing people”. We banned smoking in offices, so why do we still tolerate this?Curiously, we govern almost everything except behaviour. A serious company has audit committees, risk registers, compliance functions and external auditors, because financial integrity is never entrusted to goodwill. Yet when the issue is the conduct of the most powerful person in the building, we become oddly informal. It’s a “leadership style”, a “personality clash”, a HR matter, something sensitive to be mediated quietly. And HR is structurally the weakest player. Research I conducted across the media industry in 2022 found that HR ranked as the least respected function by senior executives, which means the people charged with guarding behaviour are marginalised precisely where power most needs guarding.This is the point at which personality becomes organisational. One person’s personality can become policy. One person’s psychology can become culture. One person’s appetite can become the company’s strategy. Personality, when combined with authority, can become a system.So what would behavioural governance look like in practice? Boards could independently test whether people can safely disagree with senior leaders. They could look for patterns in attrition rather than treating every departure as a separate event, connect complaints, settlements and confidentiality agreements rather than letting organisational memory reset with each exit, and assess a leader at three, six and 12 months in, once the interview performance is over and the experience of working beneath that person has begun.View image in fullscreen‘Toxic leadership survives through repetition’ … Weinstein in court in New York, 2026.Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/AFP/Getty ImagesAbove all, such mechanisms must be independent, because asking a function embedded within a hierarchy to investigate the most powerful person in that hierarchy is an obvious conflict. If we insist on independent governance for finance, why do we accept its absence for people?The law, at least, is beginning to evolve. Since October 2025, new NDAs in England and Wales cannot prevent victims, or those who reasonably believe they are victims, from making specified disclosures about criminal conduct. The Employment Rights Act 2025 will go further: when its NDA provisions take effect, contractual clauses will be void insofar as they prevent workers speaking about harassment or discrimination, or about how an employer handled their complaint.Zelda Perkins, the former Weinstein assistant whose Can’t Buy My Silence campaign has been at the forefront of this reform, described NDAs to me as sitting “at the foundation of that architecture of silence”, concealing patterns of behaviour and preventing organisations from recognising the risk. It is a striking description because secrecy does more than protect one individual. Left unchallenged, one person’s pathology can become an organisation’s dysfunction.Workplace bullying itself, though, is not a stand-alone criminal offence, and Britain still has no specific law against it. Legislation is beginning to tackle the secrecy surrounding workplace abuse. But protection against bullying still lags behind.Toxic leadership survives through repetition. One generation learns to tolerate it and quietly teaches the next how to survive it: keep your head down, toughen up, don’t become difficult, protect your income, guard your reputation, learn to manage the boss. That inheritance can be refused by the board member who asks the harder question, the colleague who declines to join the whispering afterwards, the investor who asks how the numbers were achieved, the organisation that protects the person telling the truth rather than the person holding the power.The people who have benefited from our silence are counting on us to keep it that way. We should give them reason to think again. Through structured governance, yes, but more than anything by treating our colleagues with something far less onerous – simple humanity.Andrea is a pseudonymSly & Mighty: How to Recognise, Resist and Rise Above Toxic Power by Kathleen Saxton is published by Sheldon Press, £16.99. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com.
