title: ‘I get lost going to the bathroom’: John Hannah on world travel, stealing props and being ‘the Scottish Eminem’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Four Weddings and a Funeral actor answers your questions on inspiring Eminem, nicking props and having a new perspective after turning 60
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The Four Weddings and a Funeral actor answers your questions on inspiring Eminem, nicking props and having a new perspective after turning 60
Content: ‘It’s good if people think I’m Jimmy Nesbitt, because I can be rude and he gets the blame’ … John Hannah.Photograph: Valéry Hache/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It’s good if people think I’m Jimmy Nesbitt, because I can be rude and he gets the blame’ … John Hannah.Photograph: Valéry Hache/AFP/Getty ImagesFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesInterview‘I get lost going to the bathroom’: John Hannah on world travel, stealing props and being ‘the Scottish Eminem’As told toRich PelleyThe Four Weddings and a Funeral actor answers your questions on being confused with James Nesbitt, his own Sliding Doors moment and a new perspective since turning 60Thu 24 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow often do you get asked to recite thatWH Audenpoem fromFour Weddings and a Funeral, and can you do it from memory right now?mattyjjandsimoitNot for a long time. I could probably do the first couple of lines: Stop all the clocks, cut off the telephone / Prevent the dog from barking with a juicy bone / Turn out the lights? And with muffled drums / Something, something … let the mourners come. There you go. Terrible!View image in fullscreenHannah in Four Weddings and a Funeral, 1994.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyInSteve Coogan’s Paul Calf’s Video Diary, your character praisesOrson Welles’ The Trialfor its “tremendous energy”, while Paul says he would “rather watch Dave Lee Travis playing Macbeth”. What’s your actual opinion of The Trial [by Franz Kafka]?AdrianH1God, it’s a long time since I’ve read that. I read a lot of those books in my younger days, but probably, like a lot of people, even those who are graduates of English literature, I’d be hard pushed these days to tell you what it was about, other than the persecution of some minor character.As a popular jobbing actor, you have a massive list of credits. Has anyone ever come up to you to express their appreciation for a certain role and you had no idea what they were on about?KevcoeNo. It’s always heartwarming when somebody comes up and offers their congratulations on something a little bit lower down the pecking order. Fortunately, people rarely ever come up to tell me that they thought I was shit in something. I quite often get Paul Calf’s Video Diary, and that Macbeth line. To be frank, I can’t quite remember the context.ShouldEminembe thanking you forStan, rather thanDido, given that he first heard Thank You on the Sliding Doors soundtrack?vammypIt’s strange how Sliding Doors and Four Weddings have travelled the world. It’s certainly cool to think that somebody as far out of left field as Eminem has actually even seen something you’ve done. Although, the story I heard was he was so sickened by the sweetness that he decided to counterpoint it with an obsessed fan trying to murder his girlfriend.What’s your Sliding Doors moment?MurdomaniaIt’s interesting that “sliding doors” as an expression has become such common parlance, hasn’t it? I certainly don’t run for trains any more.View image in fullscreen‘I don’t run for trains any more’ … with Gwyneth Paltrow in Sliding Doors.Photograph: Alex Bailey/Paramount/Miramax/Intermedia/Kobal/REX/ShutterstockI was so traumatised by your characters inTruth or DareandCarnivàlethat whenever I see you in anything else, I think: “Oh no, it’s that horrible man.”Do you enjoy playing characters like that?FioreSebekThere you go: a prime example of something coming from left field. I do think that old cliche is true about bad guys always being more fun. I also get to play a lot of scientists or doctors, because for some reason, my Scottish accent makes me sound educated.Which was most fun: filmingCharlie Brooker’s police procedural parodyA Touch of Cloth, or appearing in an episode of Black Mirror?MrMustardA Touch of Cloth was great fun. We certainly had to do a lot of takes for all the laughing. Black Mirror felt more like a 1980s dark BBC late-night psychopath drama. Working with Charlie was quite high-concept in Black Mirror, but high camp in Cloth.Apparently, you nicked some props from The Mummy to decorate your then-new home. What have you pinched since?LuddersIt’s like the old joke: you shag one sheep … You nick one prop. It was this fibreglass, spray-painted gold, Egyptian dog head with arms all going in different directions. I had a tiny garden at the time, and thought it would be something to look at other than a wall. But Brendan [Fraser] took the piss out of me, and constantly said I nick stuff. I can imagine Ridley Scott’s allowed to steal Aliens and put them in his vineyard. Richard E Grant’s a bit of a klepto too – he’s got shitloads in his garden. And Alan Cumming is a bit sticky-fingered.If you took part in Celebrity Race Across the World, would you still narrate it in the third person?AngryTomatoWell, the bottom line is I wouldn’t be doing Race Across the World. I get lost going to the bathroom. I’ve missed planes, turned up on the wrong day, got off the train at the wrong stop … I’m no good at stuff. So I’d be terrible.Have you ever had more fun on a set than onSpartacus– thundering great big lines of fruity dialogue about “Thracianwhores” while lounging about in various states of distress withLucy Lawless?mikebhoyIt was pretty spectacular. As we mentioned earlier, it’s always fun playing the villain. You only got the scripts as you were shooting, so you never knew what was coming next. Some of the stuff, you could not believe. I think in episode two, I come into our chamber with Lucy Lawless. We’re about to have a bit of how’s-your-father, but it’s been a stressful day, so she gets one of the servants to get me going by fellating me, so I had to deliver all this dialogue, while pretending to be fellated. If I had to live in Roman times, I know where I’d like to be. I’d definitely want to be upstairs.View image in fullscreen‘Pretty spectacular’ … with Lucy Lawless in Spartacus.Photograph: AlamyDid the Co-op employ you to do their voiceovers becauseyou have the perfect Scottish accent to rhyme “good” with “food”?OnTheEdgeOfEuropeNo, I think that was one of those happy coincidences. I don’t think they realised that it could possibly rhyme. It’s like when Eminem rhymes all these things with “orange”. I’m the Scottish Eminem!InAgents of SHIELD, you created Life Model Decoys of people. If you could make one of anyone in real life, who would you choose?NotCEEFAUXhonestMy dad. He died 11 years ago. My mum, too. It’s funny, you still miss them. I wish I could phone them up and tell them what was happening, what was going on. As a parent, my kids are never off their phones, but you never hear from them unless they want money. I think back to when I left home at 16 and, if I wanted to phone my parents, I’d have to grab a handful of coins and head across the street to the phone box, which I probably did once a month. Recognising how things are now as a parent, I sort of wish I’d got to know my parents better. If you asked me who I could have dinner with, alive or dead, I’d speak to my mum and dad. I’d ask them all this shit I wish I could have asked them before.You’ve had a really diverse career, despite some people’s attempts to pigeonhole you as a Scottish mummy’s boy. What’s left on the bucket list?AmongstTheWavesWell, when I turned 60, I joked with my kids that I was retiring. What that meant was I felt comfortable with what I’d achieved. Maybe there were sort of gaps, maybe it wasn’t quite as great a career as I would have liked, but I was going to step back from trying tohavea career. I think I spent too long seeing jobs as a step to the next job, and didn’t really appreciate the moment. So turning 60 I thought: “Bollocks to this, I’m just going to do stuff that I like, that’s filming somewhere nice, or is especially well paid. If it’s got two out of three of those things, I’ll do it.”View image in fullscreen‘I’ve never been busier’ … in Bad Day at the Office.The reality is that I’ve probably never been busier. Stuff like Bad Day at the Office comes out of left field. After decades of complaining about playing cops and being a Scottish mummy’s boy it was nice to do something that was so ridiculous, strange and experimental that, at 64, you could never have imagined it.Do you andJames Nesbittever go out for a pint together just to watch the confusion on people’s faces?RobinGoodfellowWe used to play five-a-side back in the 90s. The last time I bumped into him was when his daughter and my son graduated from Manchester uni, last summer. It’s good if people think I’m Jimmy Nesbitt, because I can then swear at them and be rude and he gets the blame.When did you last use the expression“by Jupiter’s cock”?wellywearer2This morning, funnily enough.Bad Day at the Office is in UK and Irish cinemas from 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmFilm & Music reader interviewFour Weddings and a FuneralJames NesbittinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: NHS bodies in England impose two-year minimum wait for ADHD and autism assessments | NHS | The Guardian
description: Patient groups decry ‘scandalous’ delays as four integrated care boards take step due to soaring demand for diagnoses
Author: Anna Bawden
Headline: Patient groups decry ‘scandalous’ delays as four integrated care boards take step due to soaring demand for diagnoses
Content: A government-commissioned report due to be published next month will highlight up to 24-fold rises in the prevalence of neurodiversity in boys since 2000.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAView image in fullscreenA government-commissioned report due to be published next month will highlight up to 24-fold rises in the prevalence of neurodiversity in boys since 2000.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PANHSNHS bodies in England impose two-year minimum wait for ADHD and autism assessmentsPatient groups decry ‘scandalous’ delays as four integrated care boards take step due to soaring demand for diagnosesAnna BawdenandDenis CampbellThu 24 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 19.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNHS bodies are forcing people with suspected attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism to wait at least two years before they can be assessed as they struggle to meet surging demand for diagnoses of neurodiversity.Four NHS integrated care boards (ICBs) covering large regions ofEnglandhave adopted the approach because they cannot afford the cost of the number of assessments that people are seeking.Patient groups are warning that the “scandalous” delays such policies involve may damage children’s chances of succeeding at school, deny people the help they need to manage their lives, and increase the risk of suicide. The charity ADHD UK denounced minimum waits as “heartless and dangerous”.In all, 15 ICBs, which between them cover 19 million people, have brought in various ways of rationing assessments for ADHD and autism to try to balance their books. These include limiting the number of assessments the ICBs will pay for in any given year and using “clinical prioritisation” criteria to restrict assessment to those with the most serious signs of neurodiversity.Disclosure of the NHS’s widespread efforts to delay and deny access to assessments comes before the publication of a major government-commissioned review of the colossal increases in diagnoses of mental illness, as well as ADHD and autism, in recent years. It was ordered last year by Wes Streeting, the then health secretary, amid concern that the weight of requests for assessment, diagnosis and care was overwhelming the health service’s ability to meet demand.The 700-page report of the review, led by Prof Peter Fonagy, was due to be published on Thursday but was unexpectedly postponed until early next month.Sources familiar with the document told the Guardian that it painted a detailed picture of how the fast-rising demand for help with mental illness conditions, ADHD and autism has left those affected struggling to get rapid access to NHS care and increasingly reliant on private providers.Fonagy’s report raises serious concerns about the sector, especially about the consistency and quality of the assessments it provides and the fact that there are “financial incentives associated with assessment activity”.It also lays bare the scale of the challenge that the increasing number of diagnoses of mental illness, ADHD and autism pose for the NHS, as well as schools, employers and families, by highlighting up to 24-fold rises in the prevalence of neurodiversity in boys since 2000.It reveals that the percentage of seven- to 18-year-old boys with autism rose from 0.2% in 2000 to 4.7% in 2025. Prevalence among boys aged six to 11 rose from 0.4% to 6.3% over the same period – a 16-fold jump.Similarly, the percentage of seven to 18-year-old boys diagnosed with ADHD rose from 0.4% to 5.1% between 2000 and 2025 – an almost 13-fold leap – and from 0.7% to 3.8% – up five-fold – among boys aged six to 11, according to figures provided by the Clinical Practice Research Datalink.Graphic for rise in autism diagnoses“Minimum waits” after referral by a GP mean people in the areas affected cannot seek an assessment by a private sector provider. That is even though private clinics now undertake half of NHS-funded assessments of ADHD and a third of those for autism, because many patients exercise their legal right to choose non-NHS care, given the NHS’s own limited capacity to do the assessments.Such curbs by the NHS are likely to force those who can afford it to pay a private provider for an assessment for themselves or their child, which can cost several thousand pounds. They are being implemented at a time when there are 960,000 people in England waiting for an ADHD assessment and another 295,000 awaiting one for autism.West Yorkshire NHS integrated care board hasintroduced a minimum waiting timeof two years from referral for anyone seeking an ADHD or autism assessment with an independent provider. That was in response to its bill for such assessments soaring from £7m in 2023-24 to £21m last year, it said.The West Yorkshire ICB’s decision applies to the 2.4 million people for whom it commissions and pays for care in Leeds, Bradford, Kirklees, Calderdale and Wakefield. Its area includes the constituency of Pontefract, Castleford and Knottingley – the parliamentary seat of the health secretary Yvette Cooper.Private providers that the North East and North Cumbria ICB funds to assess people “are working to an approximately 78-week minimum waiting time for an initial assessment”,it says.Somerset ICB is operating a minimum wait of 52 weeks, while the equivalent in Devon is a lot lower, at 14 weeks. Kent and Medway ICB has also decided to impose a minimum wait.This month, in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, assessment for ADHD and autism has been restricted to those patients who meet the ICB’s priority criteria.“It’s scandalous that any NHS body should impose a two-year minimum wait for ADHD and autism assessments,” said Henry Shelford, the chief executive of ADHD UK.“This is the health service denying people care they need, and care that is available, and slamming the door shut on people who need an assessment of their symptoms to give them a diagnosis and unlock essential care that helps people hold down jobs, stay in education and stay out of crisis services.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“A minimum wait is heartless and dangerous. It is institutionalised cruelty.’A spokesperson for Finally Seen,which tracks NHS restrictionson the right to choose, said: “A two-year minimum wait is not a waiting list. It is a locked door with a date on it.“The right to choose still exists on paper. In practice it is being rationed by the calendar, which is a blunt and bleak way to treat a legal right.”The British Medical Journalrecently revealedthat 17 of the 36 ICBs had introduced minimum waits of 12 to 16 weeks before patients could have a new hip or knee fitted or cataract removed, even though the NHS is meant to give 92% of patients planned hospital care within 18 weeks.Mel Merritt, the head of policy and influencing at the National Autistic Society, said: “Restricting access to autism assessments denies people support because, while it shouldn’t be the case, a diagnosis is needed to get help. For children, this can mean years of wasted school while they wait for an assessment and further waits to get a plan for support and adjustments to be put into place.“A diagnosis doesn’t only confirm if people are autistic or not, but also their needs and what adjustments could make a massive difference to being able to participate and enjoy life. Longer waiting times and restricting access to assessments will only worsen challenges for autistic people, pushing them into crisis and increasing the number of people with urgent needs.”‘Her mental health deteriorated’: family forced to wait years for autism diagnosisRead moreThe Independent Healthcare Providers Network, which represents many independent assessment services, urged the NHS to let private clinics offer as many appointments as were available.Sean Phillips, its head of policy, said: “For someone struggling with suspected ADHD or autism, those extra months or years without diagnosis and support can have a profound impact on their mental health, education, work and family life.“With more than a million people already waiting, we should be using all available capacity to get people the support and treatment they need as well as ensuring that their legal right to choose the best provider for them is being upheld.”Rebecca Gray, the director of the NHS Alliance’s mental health network, said local NHS leaders were “keenly aware of the deep frustration caused by long delays and are doing all they can to address them.“But the need to balance budgets and the pressures of soaring demand have – in some places – led to ‘minimum waits’ or even the closure of some waiting lists.“The current situation is unsustainable and delivers a bad deal for patients and taxpayers.”Explore more on these topicsNHSAttention deficit hyperactivity disorderAutismNeurodiversityMental healthHealthEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Far-right activist Daniel Thomas charged over alleged dinghy slashing in Channel | UK news | The Guardian
description: Thirty-seven-year-old in custody on suspicion of crimes including criminal damage with intent to endanger life
Author: Amelia Gentleman
Headline: Thirty-seven-year-old in custody on suspicion of crimes including criminal damage with intent to endanger life
Content: Daniel Thomas on a small boat appearing to point a sharp object at another dinghy at sea. Photograph: Danny Tommo/YouTubePhotograph: Danny Tommo/YoutubeView image in fullscreenDaniel Thomas on a small boat appearing to point a sharp object at another dinghy at sea. Photograph: Danny Tommo/YouTubePhotograph: Danny Tommo/YoutubeUK newsFar-right activist Daniel Thomas charged over alleged dinghy slashing in ChannelThirty-seven-year-old charged with one count of criminal damage and failing to disclose his phone pin to policeAmelia GentlemanandDiane TaylorThu 24 Sep 2026 17.20 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 04.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been charged with criminal damage and failing to disclose his phone pin to police following an incident in the Channel on Tuesday, where he allegedly slashed a dinghy while a French rescuer was on board.Thomas, 37, of no fixed abode, has been charged with one count of criminal damage along with an offence under section 53 of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (Ripa), for allegedly failing to comply with a notice to disclose a phone pin to police.He has been remanded in custody to appear via videolink at Basingstoke magistrates court on Friday.The charge came as the Home Office recorded 781 arrivals in 10 boats on Wednesday, the highest number for a single day so far this year. Responding to the figures, the government said it would “push further and harder” to crack down on the people organising the crossings.View image in fullscreenDaniel Thomas in London this month.Photograph: Carl Court/Getty ImagesChris Derrick, of the Crown Prosecution Service, said: “The CPS has decided to prosecute Daniel Thomas following an investigation by Hampshire constabulary into an incident on Tuesday 22 September.“Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue criminal proceedings.“We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial.”Hundreds of people gathered outside Basingstoke investigation centre, where Thomas was believed to be held, on Thursday evening.They included scores of mainly men dressed all in black, though the vast majority were not covering their faces. One person said he had come from Manchester to take part in the protest.Some chanted: “Free DT” and “Oh, Danny, Danny”. One person had brought a sign reading: “Get Danny out.”Extra police were drafted in from forces as far away as Kent, and a police drone hovered above the protest.View image in fullscreenPeople gather outside Basingstoke police station in support of Daniel Thomas after his arrest.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesThomas’s livestreamed footage appeared to show him approaching one of the dinghies, which was empty, shouting: “Let’s get rid of that boat.” After the rescue worker got onboard, Thomas shouted: “Get off the boat. You’ve got time to get off the boat.” His footage shows his boat speeding away before the rescue worker climbed back on to a larger boat.Thomas, who goes by the name Danny Tommo, had spent the afternoon in a boat, filming himself as he tracked two dinghies carrying asylum seekers from France to the UK. The livestreamed footage was watched by more than 200,000 people.A longtime associate of fellow far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, AKA Tommy Robinson, Thomas this summer gathered dozens of nationalist protest groups under the umbrella anti-immigration movement Patriot Platform.The organisation was behind marches this month in Dover and Portsmouth, when masked men in black gathered and protested over immigration and asylum policy. Thomas repeatedly told his followers they should march silently, without violence, and avoid doing anything that could lead to arrests.Thomas apparently managed to film and upload footage of his own arrest before police were able to stop him. On Wednesday night a 56-second clip was uploaded to his YouTube platform showing a police officer telling him he was being arrested on suspicion of criminal damage and “recklessly endangering someone’s life”.Thomas said: “I understand. I knew this was coming.”The latest Home Office figures put renewed focus on the government’s handling of small boat arrivals in the UK. A government spokesperson said: “Our progress this year in tackling small boats is indisputable, with crossings down by 42% and the lowest recorded over the summer months since 2020.“But this week’s events show that while the peaks we are seeing are far below those of previous years, we need to push further and harder in order to eradicate this vile trade.”Wednesday’s arrivals take the provisional total for Channel crossings for the year so far to 18,565. Home Office data indicates this is down 42% on this time last year (32,188) and 26% below the figure at this stage in 2024 (25,165).This week ministers have also been concerned by two uncontrolled landings from the Channel in two days. Most small boats carrying asylum seekers to the UK are escorted to shore by rescue services or Border Force vessels, and no unescorted small boats had been recorded since 6 September 2025.The education secretary, Lucy Powell, said: “You can’t stop everything all of the time,” after 21 people were detained when a boat evaded Border Force to reach the beach of Samphire Hoe in Dover on Wednesday. Another dinghy made an uncontrolled landing in Folkestone on Monday morning.The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has ordered an urgent review by Border Security Command, describing the failure to intercept the two boats as “not acceptable”.Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Powell said: “Of course, it’s a concern. That’s why the home secretary has demanded and ordered this urgent review, because this is not what we want to see. This is not acceptable.”View image in fullscreenDel Somerville.Photograph: Hampshire Constabulary/PAOn Thursday a 42-year-old man was jailed after throwing a plastic bottle at a police line and swearing at officers during an anti-migrant protest in Portsmouth.Del Somerville, of Paulsgrove, was sentenced at Portsmouth crown court to two years in prison, having previously pleaded guilty to the charge of violent disorder. He is the first to be sentenced over violence that erupted after the arrival of a small boat in the Hampshire city on 6 September.Judge Daniel Sawyer told him his sentence would act as a deterrent to others after subsequent protests in the area. Describing Somerville as a “thug”, he told the defendant: “Police officers dedicate their lives to the protection of the public regardless of their own views, the very least they can expect is that those who engage in protests treat them with respect and the courts punish those who assault them.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: At Trump meeting, Xi Jinping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflict | US news | The Guardian
description: Chinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and trade
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: Chinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and trade
Content: Xi Jinping, Peng Liyuan and Donald Trump at the White House in Washington DC on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAView image in fullscreenXi Jinping, Peng Liyuan and Donald Trump at the White House in Washington DC on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAUS newsAt Trump meeting, Xi Jinping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflictChinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and tradeRobert Taitin WashingtonThu 24 Sep 2026 19.58 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleXi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan.At the start of his summit meeting withDonald Trumpin the White House, the Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could steer the two competing superpowers away from future military conflict and on to a road of mutual gain.Rather than confrontation, conditions for “achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again go hand in hand” and should be the goal, Xi said, citing Trump’s political catchphrase.“We should strengthen communication.Chinaand the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” said Xi, with Trump looking on.“We should coexist in peace. China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.”With such conditions in place, Xi said, “the Thucydides trap can be overcome”, refering to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power.Xi invoked the phrase in his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it.His proposals for lessening tensions – which also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges – come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other.Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit occurred in 2015, when Barack Obama was president.“President Xi and Madame Peng arrive at an important moment for America, the 250th anniversary of our founding,” he said.Trump said he had forged “a truly great friendship” with Xi. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” he said. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balances trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.”He said the current visit would include discussion overs security, technology and AI – which he called “super intelligence”, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday.Xi also extolled his personal relationship with his American counterpart, saying: “President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.”Addressing Trump directly, he said: “During your visit to China this year, we agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability. I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course towards the future.”The White House welcome ceremony came after Trump had taken the unusual step of going to Andrews air force base in Maryland the evening before to greet the Chinese leader and his wife on the tarmac.Much of the same pageantry was repeated in Thursday’s ceremony, with both countries’ national anthems being played. Trump was flanked by his wife, Melania, while members of his cabinet and senior aides – including Natalie Harp, Trump’s dedicated assistant nicknamed “the human printer” by fellow staffers – looked on.Trump and Xi held bilateral talks after the ceremony and the welcoming speeches.Later on Thursday, Trump hosted Xi at the White House for a state dinner. Notable invited guests from the tech world included Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Apple chair Tim Cook, SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.Trump gestured to the titans of the industry in his remarks to the dinner, recounting when Chinese diplomats first arrived in the US 158 years ago, meeting American intellectuals like Henry David Thoreau and prominent political figures.“Tonight, we revive the spirit of that first encounter here on American soil as we are joined by some of the top leaders in business, culture and government from our own time,” he said. “On one side, China draws on thousands of years of history and tradition from Sun Tzu to Sun Yat-sen. For Americans, we inherit a legacy of faith from Jerusalem to Rome, democracy of ancient Athens, the triumphs of Sparta and the freedom proclaimed in Philadelphia 250 years ago.”Trump also touted his relationship with the Chinese leader.“President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better,” he said.Xi also addressed the dinner, saying talks with Trump during the visit had yielded “common understanding on many issues”, and suggesting the US and China find a new approach to working together.“China ⁠and the United States must act as responsible major countries,” he said.Despite the harmonious tone adopted by both leaders, analysts have voiced scepticism about the possibility of longstanding stable arrangements being arrived at over a host of issues.In the race for AI, the US has placed strict export controls on microchips, semiconductors, software and chip-making equipment in a bid to slow China’s development.A truce agreed between Trump and Xi in South Korea last year aimed at keeping tariffs lower had been due to expire in November but has now been extended until February, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent said.Analysts believe the extension suggests Trump continues to be dissatisfied with Xi’s concession offers on trade and wants to keep the pressure on in the hope of getting a better deal if the two meet again at the G20 summit scheduled to be held in Miami in December.Despite the trade war between the two countries, Chinese imports have continue to surge into the US. China is on course to run a $1tn trade deficit for the second year running.Uwa Ede-Osifo contributed reportingThe headline and text of this article were amended on 24 September 2026 to correct a misspelling of Xi Jinping.Explore more on these topicsUS newsXi JinpingDonald TrumpChinaUS politicsUS foreign policyTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Netanyahu calls Israel’s war in Gaza ‘opposite of genocide’ in UN speech | United Nations | The Guardian
description: Israeli PM attacks critics and calls New York mayor Zohran Mamdani ‘antisemitic’ in inflammatory address
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Israeli PM attacks critics and calls New York mayor Zohran Mamdani ‘antisemitic’ in inflammatory address
Content: Benjamin Netanyahu addresses the UN general assembly in New York on Thursday.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersView image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu addresses the UN general assembly in New York on Thursday.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersUnited NationsNetanyahu calls Israel’s war in Gaza ‘opposite of genocide’ in UN speechIsraeli PM attacks critics and calls New York mayor Zohran Mamdani ‘antisemitic’ in inflammatory addressAndrew Rothin New YorkThu 24 Sep 2026 15.28 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBenjamin Netanyahu delivered an inflammatory address to the United Nations on Thursday, decrying what he said was a global anti-Jewish conspiracy and swatting aside criticism of Israel’s war in Gaza, as he faces down international isolation and a fight for political survival in upcoming elections in Israel.As planned protests erupted on the streets ofNew YorkCity, Netanyahu took aim at critics of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, the international media, regional leaders such as Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, the leftwing commentator Hasan Piker and the New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani in an address that doubled as a stump speech to ignite his rightwing base for the elections.Invoking his late brother Yonatan Netanyahu, a commando killed in a 1976 raid to free Israeli hostages from a hijacked airliner in Entebbe, Uganda, he repeated the lines: “We are going to win. We have no other choice.”Dozens of delegates, inspired by a Palestinian call, walked out of the General Assembly Hall of the UN headquarters as Netanyahu took the stage, leading a speaker to pound his gavel and announce: “I’m calling for order in the hall.”Palestinian representatives organising diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech said they wanted to “send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end”.“If there are any other moral cowards in the audience, I urge them to walk out,” Netanyahu said before launching into his prepared remarks.UN delegates walk out as Benjamin Netanyahu prepares to address general assemblyThe speech revealed little new in terms of Israeli policy over the war inGaza, militant settler violence in the West Bank, or Israel’s plans to end other regional conflicts including its joint war with the United States against Iran.But he argued that the world faced an existential threat from Iran, suggesting that several missiles from Tehran could have destroyed the UN, and cited quiet support from world leaders for Israel’s actions that could not be aired in public.“Devastating Iran’s nuclear facilities was … very hard to do,” he said of launching joint US-Israeli strikes in February. “But for me, it was one of the easiest decisions I’ve ever had to make as prime minister. Because if we hadn’t done it, we’d all be dead.”He branded Turkey’s Erdoğan as a “tyrant” who “hosts Hamas terrorists”, decried Mamdani as the “antisemitic mayor of New York”, and declared that Israel’s war in Gaza is not genocide – “it’s the opposite of genocide”.“So, to all those spreading these lies about my country and about our brave soldiers, whether they sit in this hall or in the office of the antisemitic mayor of New York, I say this: shame on you!” he said.Netanyahu delivered the controversial address to theUnited Nationson Thursday just hours after Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas said his delegation was “unlawfully” denied visas by the Trump administration to attend the meeting of world leaders.Netanyahu’s speech at UN spurs protests in New York City: ‘Let Gaza live’Read moreIn a video address from Ramallah, broadcast in the General Assembly Hall, Abbas condemned Israel’s policies in Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem as a “malicious colonial plan” to establish a “‘Greater Israel’ and erase the Palestinian presence”.Citing the humanitarian crisis in Gaza and the violent expansion of settlements in the West Bank, Abbas said that the Israeli government “now threatens the very life and existence of the Palestinian people in their homeland”.“Do not allow another Nakba and further massacres like those of 1948 to continue taking place,” he added, referring to the expulsion of Palestinians upon the founding of Israel.For the second year in a row, the US state department denied visas to Abbas and the Palestinian Authority delegation, arguing that they had failed to live up to their commitments to seek peace with Israel.“As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,” the state department said last week in a statement.In his speech, Abbas said his delegation “[rejects] these unlawful punitive measures, as well as the accusations and justifications on which they were based”.He said: “Preventing the Palestinian delegation from reaching United Nations headquarters is inconsistent with the obligations of the United States as the host country.”As he spoke, protests were forming on the streets of New York near the United Nations headquarters in advance of Netanyahu’s arrival.Hundreds of demonstrators crowded into the street on Manhattan’s east side in midtown and held signs that said “End the Genocide” and wore shirts reading “Fund people not bombs”. By the end of Netanyahu’s speech, more than 100 demonstrators, including several local elected officials, had been arrested by New York City police.Earlier this summer, the mayor, Zohran Mamdani, had said that Netanyahu was “not welcome” in New York, and said he was reviewing whether Netanyahu could be arrested by city police under an international criminal court warrant for his arrest.He has since tempered that stance, saying this week that he wouldn’t attend the protests but promising to protect their “right to [protest] in this city”.Netanyahu is not expected to meet Donald Trump, who is in Washington to host the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, nor with other senior US officials, as he faces growing international condemnation over his hardline stance. Netanyahu has said that he needs to return to Israel quickly because of the election campaign and the holiday of Sukkot, which begins on Friday.Explore more on these topicsUnited NationsBenjamin NetanyahuNew YorkMahmoud AbbasPalestineIsraelUS-Israel war on IrannewsShareReuse this content

title: UK food and drink trade deficit largest since 2000 at £21bn | Food & drink industry | The Guardian
description: Industry leaders call on government to protect homegrown produce in the interest of national security
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Industry leaders call on government to protect homegrown produce in the interest of national security
Content: Brexit, war in the Middle East and US tariffs have all dented deliveries overseas while imports of food and drink have soared.Photograph: Martin Lee/AlamyView image in fullscreenBrexit, war in the Middle East and US tariffs have all dented deliveries overseas while imports of food and drink have soared.Photograph: Martin Lee/AlamyFood & drink industryUK food and drink trade deficit largest since 2000 at £21bnIndustry leaders call on government to protect homegrown produce in the interest of national securitySarah ButlerThu 24 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe gap between Britain’s food and drink exports and imports has neared its highest this century, as a combination ofBrexit, war in the Middle East and US tariffs dented deliveries overseas while imports soared.The UK’s food and drink trade deficit has risen to more than £21bn – the largest since 2000 – in what industry leaders said was a “wake-up call” for the government to protect homegrown produce in the interest of national security.UK food and drink export volumes fell by more than a tenth (11.7%) in the first half of 2026 to 4bn kg, only marginally above levels at the height of the Covid pandemic and in the aftermath of the 2001 foot-and-mouth disease outbreak, according to analysis by the Food & Drink Federation (FDF).Exports to the EU continued to fall – down 0.9% in value – amid the additional costs and complexity of trading since Brexit.The FDF recorded an even larger fall in exports beyond the EU – down 6.9% in value terms. That was partly driven by disruption in sales to the Middle East, with exports to the UAE down by almost a quarter as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran. The US’s introduction of a 10% import tariff hit cross-Atlantic sales by 16.5%.Food and drink imports were 19.1bn kg in the first half of this year, the second highest ever, only beaten by the same period last year. Imports from outside the EU are up more than a fifth since 2023 as restrictions have been eased through trade deals, particularly with Australia which now sends 25% more in value terms to the UK than a year ago including meat, oils, vegetables and even whisky.Thesuspension of tariffson a range of manufactured foods, including chocolate and biscuits, this year as part of the former chancellor Rachel Reeves’s package to ease the cost of living has also raised import levels. In addition, EU food producers increased deliveries to the UK in value terms – up 0.8% year-on-year – having recovered in volume terms since Brexit.Tom Bradshaw, the president of the National Farmers’ Union of England and Wales, said: “These figures should be a wake-up call. At a time of growing geopolitical uncertainty, we cannot afford to take our food production capacity for granted.”He said the widening trade deficit underlined the need for a long-term plan to support British production and recognise “a simple truth that food security is national security”.“The pressures facing farm businesses are immense, from rising costs and regulatory burdens to extreme weather and global market volatility,” said Bradshaw. “If government is serious about food security, economic growth and national resilience, it must create the conditions that give businesses the confidence to invest, innovate and grow.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe FDF, which represents hundreds of food and beverage producers, said pressures on manufacturers were “significant and growing” as the cost of energy, ingredients, transport, packaging and labour continued to rise. It said changing regulation also added to pressures on the industry.Karen Betts, the chief executive of the trade body, said: “Our food and drink trade deficit is growing and is now the largest it’s been in over 25 years. In a world beset by conflict and the ever-increasing impacts of climate change, this poses some stark questions about our food security.“When the government then chooses to remove tariffs on, for example, biscuits imported from China, it’s not surprising that they’ll be sold more cheaply here than biscuits made in the UK.”Explore more on these topicsFood & drink industryInternational tradeEuropean UnionBrexitBritish food and drinkTrade policyTariffsnewsShareReuse this content

title: France says EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ law should not include the UK | European Union | The Guardian
description: ‘If you’re not in the internal market, you don’t get the same protection,’ says French minister of policy designed to curb Chinese competition
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: ‘If you’re not in the internal market, you don’t get the same protection,’ says French minister of policy designed to curb Chinese competition
Content: A Mini Cooper on the production line at Germany-headquartered BMW’s Cowley plant near Oxford. New EU laws could hit the British car industry.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Mini Cooper on the production line at Germany-headquartered BMW’s Cowley plant near Oxford. New EU laws could hit the British car industry.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesEuropean UnionFrance says EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ law should not include the UK‘If you’re not in the internal market, you don’t get the same protection,’ says French minister of policy designed to curb Chinese competitionJennifer Rankinin BrusselsThu 24 Sep 2026 13.42 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrance is leading a push to exclude the UK from the EU’s “Made in Europe” policy that could result in British companies losing out in the race to supply European countries with low-carbon technologies and electric cars.The plans wereraised by Andy Burnham when he met the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen,on the sidelines of the UN general assembly earlier this week.The policy, still under negotiation, aims to protect European companies from intense and “unfair” state-subsidised competition fromChina. But the government fears British companies risk being collateral damage and resolving the issue has become one of Burnham’s top priorities for the EU-UK relationship.One key EU proposal is the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), which would require authorities spending public money – awarding subsidies or public contracts –to favour European products in sectors such as renewable technologies and electric cars.But there is an intense debate inside the EU on how to define “made in Europe” and how far to include countries such as the UK, Canada and Japan.UK ‘losing up to £6.5bn a year in EU trade’ without post-Brexit product dealRead moreAt a meeting of EU industry ministers in Brussels on Thursday, France pushed for a narrow definition, starting with the EU27.“European taxpayers’ money should support [European] workers and European factories,” the French industry minister, Sébastien Martin, told reporters.Asked about the UK, he said: “The United Kingdom made a choice a few years ago to leave theEuropean Union.“That doesn’t mean that we don’t discuss things or that we don’t trade, it doesn’t mean that there can’t be agreements in certain sectors, but fundamentally there are those who have chosen the European project and those who have decided to leave.”France’s Europe minister, Benjamin Haddad, speaking in London, had few assurances to offer the Burnham government either.Asked about the risks of pushing the EU’s like-minded trading partners away, Haddad said: “At the end of the day, if you are not part of the internal market and if you are not contributing to the financial capacity of the internal market, you don’t get the same kind of protection.”Germany wants a broader “Made with Europe” policy that would include the UK and other allies. Germany’s economic affairs minister, Katherina Reiche, told her counterparts: “We must reduce unilateral and critical dependencies, but we must not isolate ourselves from the rest of the world. This means that partner countries must be included in the union-origin principle, in general and on the condition of reciprocity.”This position gets broad support from Nordic countries, which traditionally favour open trade.Sweden’s outgoing deputy prime minister, Ebba Busch, who leads on business policy, said “we always miss the Brits”. Sweden wanted “a good solution where there is balance, given that some European countries are not members of the European Union but still completely essential for a functioning European market”, she added.The charged internal EU27 debate on Made in Europe raises questions about thetiming of the EU-UK reset summit, which was postponedwhen Keir Starmer stood down as prime minister. Since Burnham took office, no date has been fixed for the talks which are meant to happen in 2026.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBritish officials expect the summit will take place in November, although an earlier 6 November date has been scratched out. By December the EU is expected to be embroiled in deeply difficult internal negotiations on the bloc’s next seven-year budget, which are likely to consume the political bandwidth of EU leaders.EU insiders believe that a Made in Europe agreement is a top priority for the UK, but have cautioned this cannot happen before the union has finalised its own position.One EU diplomat said it was a “big risk” if the UK government were to insist on a deal at an autumn summit. “It puts [the UK] in a corner, because this [Made in Europe criteria] is a process that is very difficult for the EU27 [to agree internally].”The Republic of Ireland, which is chairing EU ministerial negotiations, hopes for an agreement in December on the IAA, including the Made in Europe provisions, between the EU Council and the European parliament. “There are a divergence of views on the Industrial Accelerator Act, on European preference, on working with trusted partners and third countries,” said Ireland’s enterprise minister, Peter Burke. “It is difficult, but we have a pathway in sight.”Poland’s economic development minister, Michał Baranowski, said it was too early to say whether countries such as Switzerland, the UK, Japan, Australia and Canada would be in or out, adding: “All these countries are in the mix of the discussion.”The UK, he said, should have clarity on its status when the EU act is passed, he said, adding: “We are in the last stretch, but this last stretch might take a while.”A UK government spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and trusted European partner, committed to our shared security and economic cooperation.“We will continue to engage with the EU on Made in Europe and work together, as like-minded partners, to boost growth and open up trade.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionIndustrial policyChinaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran awaiting response from Trump on proposal to open strait of Hormuz in six days | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Country says US must lift sanctions on its oil exports and end the war on all fronts, including in Lebanon
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Country says US must lift sanctions on its oil exports and end the war on all fronts, including in Lebanon
Content: The strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on 31 August.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenThe strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on 31 August.Photograph: ReutersUS-Israel war on IranIran awaiting response from Trump on proposal to open strait of Hormuz in six daysCountry says US must lift sanctions on its oil exports and end the war on all fronts, including in LebanonPatrick Wintourin New YorkThu 24 Sep 2026 17.57 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 15.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran said it has told Donald Trump it is willing to open the strait of Hormuz in six days, and to start talks on its nuclear program the day after, so long as the US lifts sanctions on Iran’s oil exports in return, ends the war on all fronts – including in Lebanon – and releases some of Iran’s frozen assets.The proposal is designed to accelerate the steps first laid down in the memorandum of understanding signed by the US and Iran in June, particularly by helping the talks on Iran’s nuclear program start much more quickly than previously agreed.Iran says a deal on the temporary route through the strait of Hormuz has been agreed with Oman, describing it as a done deal, and is ready to register the details with the International Maritime Organisation.Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, said he was waiting to hear a response from the Americans to the proposal. He added that he had consulted on the plan with China, which fully supported the proposal.Saudi Arabia had been expected to endorse the Oman-Iran route through the strait last week, but pulled back partly due to anger that Iranian-backed Houthis had started attacking Saudi Arabia as part of their dispute over the future of Yemen.Iran claims it has urged the Houthis to cease the attacks on Saudi Arabia but that it does not have control over Houthi decision-making.Araghchi, speaking to reporters in New York, said: “We have introduced a plan to the US through the mediators that if certain conditions are met, the strait will be open within seven days and talks will start.”He said the Iranian preconditions were not new, and were contained in the Islamabad memorandum of understanding that was signed by Trump.The advantage of the proposal, apart from opening the strait and lifting the chokehold on the world economy, would be bringing the US to the talks on Iran’s nuclear program much more quickly. Talks on the nuclear program under the MoU would not have started for 60 days. Araghchi said he was staying in New York over the weekend to await an American response, but added he was not in a hurry.Privately, Iranian officials believe they could reach a deal with the Americans, and the Saudi hurdle over aspects of the route could be overcome, but fear Israel will use its influence to pull the US president away from the proposal.Araghchi added he would like the deal to go through before the midterm elections, by which he meant that the strait of Hormuz could be opened and energy prices thereby reduced, something Trump badly needs for the Republican party to survive a political mauling.For the US, there are difficulties in the plan related to forcing Israel to end the war in Lebanon. Israel may object to giving Iran such clear control over the route through which ships would travel through the strait of Hormuz. Iran also wants to retain control of shipping to prevent some US military shipping going through the strait.Issues such as whether tolls or navigational fees could be imposed by the littoral states Oman and Iran would be settled later in the process.View image in fullscreenThe Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi (left), speaks with his Jordanian counterpart, Ayman Safadi, at the UN in New York City.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesEarlier in the day, the UK foreign secretary,Ed Miliband, met Araghchi, his Iranian counterpart, for the first time in New York.It was also the first meeting between UK and Iranian ministers for a year, and the first exchange since the UK in July proscribed the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organisation, a move that has worsened the already sour relations between the two countries.Miliband made clear that the UK was committed to freedom of navigation in the strait and wanted a diplomatic solution, also stressing support for Saudi Arabia, a UK ally in Yemen.He warned Iran about its behaviour in the UK, including threats to Jewish communities, and called for the UK to be given consular access to theBritish couple sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonmentin Tehran.Araghchi and the US’s special envoy Steve Witkoff also met earlier this week on the sidelines of the general assembly to discuss Iran’s terms for reopening the strait and the speed at which that may happen, as well as the time the US had been given to respond.Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talkRead moreA faction inside Iran is arguing that Tehran should seek to escalate the conflict with a vulnerable US president, rather than let the crisis drift in its current deadlock. Brent crude was trading at about $107 (£81) a barrel on Thursday.Some IRGC officers have also linked the strait of Hormuz issue to the closure of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway close to the south-west of Yemen now under control of Iranian-backed Houthis.Maj Gen Rahim Safavi, a senior Iranian military figure, said: “If the Americans start a new war, a new front centred on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab strait may open before their eyes. Are they ready to enter the battle on this front? This is a question that they should pay more attention to.”Domestically, Pezeshkian’s defiant message to the UN general assembly on Wednesday was deemed a success overall in that it balanced a refusal to bend the knee to “the US bully” with a willingness to seek diplomatic talks.He also proposed a new security architecture for the future in partnership with Gulf states, including those it has been bombarding in an effort to dislodge the US from its military bases.Maj Gen Ahmad Vahidi, commander-in-chief of the IRGC, praised Pezeshkian’s speech, saying: “We are not afraid of war. It is the loud and firm call of the Iranian nation – a call that resonated from theUnited Nationspodium, through the words of the esteemed president, and reached the ears of the world.”Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranEd MilibandIranStrait of HormuzUS foreign policyTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The eyes have it: Rory Stewart’s ‘magnificently strange’ Newsnight moment goes viral | Rory Stewart | The Guardian
description: Clip of the former Tory MP staring intently at fellow panellist is shared widely online
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Clip of the former Tory MP staring intently at fellow panellist is shared widely online
Content: Rory Stewart watches his fellow panellist, the journalist Ailbhe Rea, speak on the BBC’s Newsnight.Photograph: BBC NewsnightView image in fullscreenRory Stewart watches his fellow panellist, the journalist Ailbhe Rea, speak on the BBC’s Newsnight.Photograph: BBC NewsnightRory StewartThe eyes have it: Rory Stewart’s ‘magnificently strange’ Newsnight moment goes viralClip of the former Tory MP staring intently at fellow panellist is shared widely onlineRachel HallThu 24 Sep 2026 10.39 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 12.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRory Stewart has been an Afghan NGO leader, a Conservative leadership candidate, a Harvard professor, a popular podcaster, and the deputy governor of an Iraqi province.This week, he created a moment that drew wider attention than any of them: he fixed a beady gaze on a fellowNewsnightpanellist for the longest four seconds in television history.Stewart, who now co-presents The Rest Is Politics podcast with Alastair Campbell, appeared on theBBCprogramme on 18 September – but in the last few days, a clip of the moment in question has taken on a life of its own on social media.Stewart appeared alongside the former Labour leader Neil Kinnock and the New Statesman’s political editor, Ailbhe Rea, to discuss the day’s main news stories, including the race between China and the US to develop artificial intelligence (AI).Rory Stewart on NewsnightAfter Stewart made his comments, the presenter Matt Chorley asked Rea what Westminster could do about the development of AI. Stewart then swivelled around in his chair and stared directly at the journalist with an expression – and posture – of absolute focus.Chorley told the Guardian the behaviour had not appeared overly strange in person: “I didn’t notice Rory looking particularly intently at anyone during the course of the programme,” he said.He only became aware of what had happened when several friends texted him. “You know a moment from Newsnight has cut through when friends and family who don’t normally watch it are suddenly sending me clips,” he said. “But it is just quite a funny moment.”He added that as it was the first Newsnight episode to move to the programme’s new earlier slot at 7pm, it had been “quite manic” in the runup. He had even joked to the panellists: “Anything that can be used to go viral, maybe a punchup or whatever, a tiff at the table, if you want to do that, that’d be great.”Chorley observed that Stewart was “used to this”, after another clip of him taking his tie off during a Tory leadership debate had gone viral in 2019.“It’s not the first time that something he’s done has gone wild online. I think he was genuinely probably just intently listening to what Ailbhe had to say. But there was something about the camera angle and his very direct look,” he said.Many behaviours that appear normal in person can look strange on screen, Chorley added.He said he had learned to “remember you’re always on” and to control his naturally emphatic hand movements, which can “look crazy” on screen. He also recalled an early Newsnight episode which had surprised viewers when Tim Stanley, a columnist at the Telegraph,winked at the camera.“This is just the beauty of live telly,” he said. “It’s a reminder that even when the camera is on the person who’s talking, you might be in shot.”Rea, who was on the receiving end of the stare, posted the clip on X to joke that she would “please like attention levels like this on my latest interview” after sharing a link to her most recent reporting.The clip has turned into a meme online, with commenters imagining situations in which the stare could have taken place.The Larry the Cat social media account posted: “When HR tells you that you need to listen better to female colleagues.”Total Politics Group’s chief executive, Mark Wallace, compared Stewart’s behaviour to the comedian Kevin Eldon’s surreal style, writing: “There’s a high degree of Kevin Eldon energy to this. Magnificently strange.”Explore more on these topicsRory StewartNewsnightBBCnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘First there’s the gruelling task of trying to charge my laptop’: a day in the life of a university lecturer in Gaza | Global development | The Guardian
description: As the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each tells the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the conflict. Overcoming internet cuts and power outages, Mahmoud battles to provide his students an education
Author: Seham Tantesh
Headline: As the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each tells the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the conflict. Overcoming internet cuts and power outages, Mahmoud battles to provide his students an education
Content: Mahmood. Art direction by Guardian DesignGaza: a week in the lifeGlobal development‘First there’s the gruelling task of trying to charge my laptop’: a day in the life of a university lecturer in GazaAs the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, the Guardianfollows five ordinary Palestiniansas they go about their lives. Each tells the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the conflict. Overcoming internet cuts and power outages, Mahmoud battles to provide his students an educationSupported byAbout this contentSeham Tanteshin Gaza andHoda OsmanThu 24 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 07.03 EDTShareIt is time for Mahmoud Seydam’s online lecture on museum architecture. He squats in front of the step he calls a table and opens his laptop.“Is Mohammed the only one here?” He pulls out his phone and types into the students’ chat group that the lecture is about to start. There are two students now. Mahmoud decides to wait a little for the others to join.“Today, we have a simple presentation: an overview of museum design.” He asks his students to imagine the museum as honey in a glass. “The museum is a beautiful interior space. It becomes an element that attracts people.”The internet connection drops out and halts the lecture.Mahmoud gives an online lecture on a laptop in his tentMahmoud, head of engineering sciences and applied arts at the University College of Science and Technology in Khan Younis and a lecturer at al-Aqsa University, does not seem frustrated. He is used to this.In his usual calm and professional tone, he records a voice message to his students: “Hello everyone … There seems to be an internet problem, so I will record the lecture, upload it to YouTube and send you the link.”This is what a day in the life of a university lecturer inGazalooks like.Daybreakdouble quotation markSleep itself is a struggle. Sleeping isn’t easy while living in tents. Anxiety dominates everything … because there’s no sense of stability.You compare how your life was before the war to your current life and, psychologically, you’re unable to accept this reality. You’re living in a tent, which doesn’t protect you from anything and doesn’t provide any privacy. You can’t even do your work peacefully because of the noise.Not to mention the anxiety about an emergency occurring. There was a strike on the tents around us before. There’s fear for the children, of harm to any member of the family. There’s anxiety about being displaced again. We were displaced more than 15 times, including from a place thatwas uncomfortable, unstable anddidn’t support humanlife, to one that was even worse, sometimes abandoning all our belongings just to save our lives. We slept for three or four nights on the street, on the pavement.You feel anxious at night. I wake up around dawn, pray and open my mobile phone. I make a cup of coffee and sit outside the tent to respond to messages from students and colleagues that came overnight. I preserve some of my phone’s battery specifically for this task. It’s easier for me to send them voice notes than to type. This is how I start my day.MorningThe first task of Mahmoud’s day is to fetch waterThe morning tasks begin with fetching water. Mahmoud grabs a plastic container and walks to where the water truck stops. His children – three sons and a daughter, studying engineering, nursing and computer science – often help out. He brings the water back to the tent and pours it into their tank, then into buckets of different sizes and colours in front of their tent.double quotation markWe use these buckets to store some of the water for daily use to make it last as long as possible, because the tank only holds 200 litres.We don’t have any other tanks. They were all destroyed when our house was bombed. And the water doesn’t reach us every day.In displacement, we face things we didn’t expect in life. The tent constantly needs repairs. Plus, there is the gruelling task of trying to charge my mobile phone and laptop to start my day and do my work.Sometimes we have breakfast; sometimes we don’t. Currently, there is flour and we knead and bake in the tent, but the bread spoils from the heat and then thereis no breakfast. Meals are not regular, but if I get absorbed in work, I forget about food.AfternoonMahmoud starts to set up for the day’s lecture. As soon as he plugs his laptop into the power strip, the system shuts down. He has learned basic solar energy technology to manage these recurring breakdowns. He grabs the broom, steps on to a plastic chair and cleans the dust off the solar panels on top of the tent. He records the museum design lecture and then it is time to set off for theScholars Without Bordersoffices, the college’s temporary headquarters.Top: Mahmoud cleans the dust off his tent’s solar panels; above: the power system he uses to record his lecturesdouble quotation markNot everything is online; there are meetings and student issues for which you need to be present. The distance to Scholars Without Borders is about 6km.I usually go on foot because of how difficult transportation is: the roads are rough and everything is packed with tents and carts.Today, I useda cart pulled by an old car–it’s the kind that is usually pulled by a horse or a donkey – and then a rundowntuk-tuk. It takes me an hour to get there.Being in these circumstances and still being able to carry on, to give my all– frankly, I find it incredibly difficult. The basic necessities of life must be in place for a person to be able to excel in their work. People don’t even have the bare minimum for life right now.The application and practical side of learning has become extremely difficult. Most sessions are online. Most of the basic tools and materials needed for the learning process have become difficult to access or simply unavailable.From the early stages of the war, we noticed that the universities were deliberately targeted. The university has a certain symbolic significance. It brings together all the future talent and potential, whether among students or the teaching staff.At one point, we were displaced in an area between Rafah andKhan Younis, where my university was visible from a distance. I saw with my own eyes the military strikes against the university buildings and facilities.When the ceasefire was broken, a video emerged showing the demolition of all of the university buildings,a complete levelling of the site.We continue with a certain degree of patience and perseverance.Video footage shows the university buildings being bombedEveningdouble quotation markBefore the war you could take your family out to eat in arestaurant.As an architect, I was also quite interested in archaeological and heritage sites, and I’d pop into some of the shops selling antiques to have a look around.All of this is lost now. There is no time for leisure; we can barely secure the bare necessities. Our life runs like a machine. Every day is just like the next.My parents and two siblings live in tents nearby, a10-minute walk. My parents– because of the war, illnesses and old age – have been really affected. It’s a responsibility, so almost every dayI visit them to see if they need anything.I sometimes sit outside my tent and talk with others to unwind after the long day. Then I resume my communications with students. This doesn’t stop until I sleep.From the moment you wake up until you go to sleep, you’re barely able to keep up with anything other than the tasks you have to do.CreditsVideo: Tantesh Media ServicesArt direction: Harry Fischer, Anaïs Mims, Barry Ainslie and Alessia AmitrianoVideo editor/producer: Joshua JacobVideo executive producers: Temujin Doran and Augusta AnthonyAdditional reporting and research: Aseel Mousa and Harriet Barber

title: ‘Her mental health deteriorated’: family forced to wait years for autism diagnosis  | Society | The Guardian
description: A mother describes the frustration of endless waiting lists and difficulties getting appointments so her teenage daughter can get the help she requires
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: A mother describes the frustration of endless waiting lists and difficulties getting appointments so her teenage daughter can get the help she requires
Content: Rosalyn, left, and daughter Imogen have waited years for an autism diagnosis.View image in fullscreenRosalyn, left, and daughter Imogen have waited years for an autism diagnosis.Society‘Her mental health deteriorated’: family forced to wait years for autism diagnosisA mother describes the frustration of endless waiting lists and difficulties getting appointments so her teenage daughter can get the help she requiresCaroline DaviesThu 24 Sep 2026 17.08 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor Rosalyn, the battle for an official autism diagnosis for her 14-year-old daughter, Imogen, has been intense, deeply frustrating and has lasted five and a half years.That Rosalyn has three other children who have autism diagnoses meant she was acutely aware of the signs.Rosalyn, 53, from Trafford, Greater Manchester, who works in the medical profession, was diagnosed aged 39. She noticed her youngest child’s problems with socialising and sensory issues at about the age of eight. “It wasn’t going to be unusual that she might also be autistic. We have a very strong family history of it,” Rosalyn said.The school had noticed issues and agreed to start collecting information for a referral, which took about 18 months. It was sent off in the hope a diagnosis would be made before Imogen started high school.TraffordAutismand Social Communication Pathway then “sat on the referral for a while”, said Rosalyn. There were multidisciplinary meetings to decide if they would accept the referral – which took months. Finally, two years later – on 27 March 2023 – Imogen was accepted on to the waiting list.NHS bodies in England impose two-year minimum wait for ADHD and autism assessmentsRead more“And we waited. And we waited. I kept emailing every few months to say ‘Where is she?’ And they would say ‘Oh, it’s a 12-month waiting list’. And then after a year: ‘It’s an 18-month waiting list’. And then: ‘It’s a 24-month waiting list’.“In this time, her mental health deteriorated. She started struggling with a lot of issues that she wasn’t struggling with at the time she was referred.“I kept writing. The GP wrote several times. Nothing. The school wrote. Nothing. Eventually, about six months ago, I wrote a very strongly worded email.” Rosalyn then listed all the mental health problems her daughter had developed “particularly in the last 12 months”.“They eventually agreed to expedite her, after three and a half years. They finally saw her about a week-and-a-half ago. But we haven’t got a result yet,” Rosalyn said.Getting a diagnosis is important, she said. “It is helpful to understand who you are,” Rosalyn said. It also affects the support her daughter can access. “Quite a lot of doors are shut to you if you don’t have a diagnosis,” she added.In school, Imogen does not have an education health and care plan (EHCP) used to access certain support in school. “If you don’t have a diagnosis, that undermines your evidence,” said Rosalyn. “It’s a catch-22.”Without a diagnosis, she will not qualify for a disabled students’ allowance, which she will need if she goes to university. Or, should she require it, a personal independence payment. Some support groups “want evidence – the evidence is the diagnosis”, Rosalyn said.“There is a lot of self-diagnosis now, and I think that is because people cannot access diagnosis. You are simply driving people towards self-diagnosis, which is then creating a health inequality.“You’ve got wealthy people who can access [private] diagnosis. Great. And they are opening the door to all that diagnosis means. And you have people who can’t afford that never getting a diagnosis.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOf her daughter, Rosalyn added: “She’s into her GCSEs now. Her mental health has massively deteriorated.” They have a “complex family situation”, she said, and Imogen is dealing with a lot of things “perhaps other kids aren’t dealing with”.Young people’s Pip claims for ADHD and autism ‘rising fastest in affluent areas’Read more“There’s the circumstances around our family life, I accept that. But I think not having a diagnosis for her, she feels like a fraud. People go ‘Well. Do you have a diagnosis? No? Oh right. OK!’ Some people are very critical of self-diagnosis.“Most people seeking an autism assessment are doing so because they’ve had years of wondering why they don’t feel like other people. Not because it’s trendy. Nobody wants to be autistic. I don’t want to be; I just am,” Rosalyn said.Imogen’s siblings were diagnosed far more swiftly, partly because of the way referrals are now dealt with and partly to do with waiting times, Rosalyn said.“With Imogen – six years younger – it’s become such a battle.“It’s very distressing. She has a lot of issues around her behaviour, her sensory needs, her inability to socialise. She doesn’t leave the house. She’s 14. She should be out living her best life and she isn’t. And that makes me mad.”Explore more on these topicsSocietyAutismHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rogue AI hacks government system for first time - The Latest | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: A government database has been hacked for the first time by a rogue OpenAI agent, which infiltrated part of the Australian healthcare scheme. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s UK technology editor Robert Booth
Author: Zoe Hitch
Headline: A government database has been hacked for the first time by a rogue OpenAI agent, which infiltrated part of the Australian healthcare scheme. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s UK technology editor Robert Booth
Content: 12:23Today in Focus: The LatestOpenAIRogue AI hacks government system for first time - The LatestA government database has been hacked for the first time by a rogue OpenAI agent, which infiltrated part of the Australian healthcare scheme in June. OpenAI became aware of the hack in August, but only informed the government in September. Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has expressed his ‘extreme concern’ about the hack, which raises serious AI security concerns for governments around the world.
