title: From idealists to struggling sceptics: how Labour’s majority depends on five progressive voter types – in charts | Labour | The Guardian
description: Analysis reveals groups with sharply contrasting priorities – and who has drifted the most from Labour towards Greens and Reform
Author: Ashley Kirk
Headline: Analysis reveals groups with sharply contrasting priorities – and who has drifted the most from Labour towards Greens and Reform
Content: Composite: Prina Shah for the Guardian / Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Prina Shah for the Guardian / Getty ImagesLabourFrom idealists to struggling sceptics: how Labour’s majority depends on five progressive voter types – in chartsAnalysis reveals groups with sharply contrasting priorities – and who has drifted the most from Labour towards Greens and ReformTactical voting at next election could push Reform into fourth place, poll findsAshley KirkandJessica Elgot. Illustrations byPrina ShahThu 24 Sep 2026 05.15 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA new MRP poll suggestsLabour would remain the largest partyif a general election were held now, but would fall well short of an overall majority as Reform surged into second place.Behind those headline figures, research from Survation and 38 Degrees casts new light on five distinct voter groups who are collectively defined as the “progressive majority”. These people share concerns about living costs and theNHS, but differ over immigration, the environment, political trust and the pace of change needed to address the UK’s policies.Tactical voting at next election could push Reform into fourth place, poll findsRead moreTo build a parliamentary majority,Labourmust hold on to the groups that have remained relatively loyal, while winning back voters drifting towards the Greens, Reform or political disengagement. In short, they need enough of this “progressive majority” to stay within the fold.Labour strategists – including Keir Starmer’s former chief of staff Morgan McSweeney – have often been wary of a tactic that seeks only to unite the progressive bloc. But while it would result in Labour losing huge swathes of seats that it won in 2024, it may be enough to lock Nigel Farage out of No 10 if there were significant tactical voting.It also gives a clue to howAndy Burnhammight seek to structure his priorities – and why the cost of living will be at the heart of the prime minister’s policy platform at the Labour conference, one with salience for voters considering either the Greens or Reform.The charts below, which are based on polling of more than 8,000 voters, show how Labour’s support cuts across age, class and geography – and reveal five distinct voter groups with contrasting priorities.The five groups in the ‘progressive majority’The researchers identified five groups of people who collectively make up what they call the “progressive majority”.It is a key group of voters who they argue the Labour government should be targeting if they want to win an overall majority at the next general election.The five groups are described as:View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/GettyRootedtraditionalists: Older, economically left-leaning voters who are highly concerned about immigration and less interested in environmental issues. Many moved from theConservativesto Labour but could shift again, including towards Reform. Cost of living pressures and NHS access provide the strongest common ground with other progressive voters.View image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian design / GettyOpen-heartedidealists: Affluent, highly educated and the most socially liberal, pro-immigration and politically engaged group. They lean strongly towards Labour, the Greens and Lib Dems and are particularly open to tactical voting. Bills, NHS access and progressive taxation matter most, while tougher immigration policies risk alienating them.View image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian design / GettyQuietpersuadables: The youngest and least politically committed segment, often holding centrist or uncertain views. Their support is spread widely across the parties and they are the most likely to vote tactically. They are potentially winnable, but need a compelling reason to engage with politics.View image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian design / GettyTrustingoptimists: Young, affluent, urban and highly educated, with strong confidence in their finances, the government and the country’s future. Most support Labour and economically progressive policies, but they are also the most socially authoritarian group. Their political loyalty could weaken if their circumstances deteriorate.View image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian design / GettyStrugglingsceptics: The least financially secure, trusting and electorally engaged group, with many believing voting changes little. Although economically left-leaning, their support is divided between Labour, the Greens and Reform. Winning them back could depend on tangible improvements to bills, wages and living standards rather than political messaging alone.There are clear demographic differences between the groups.Quiet persuadables are the youngest-leaning group, while very few rooted traditionalists are young; more than a third of them are over 65.Age groups chartTrusting optimists are twice as likely as voters overall to live in London, while rooted traditionalists are half as likely.Regional chartStruggling sceptics are most likely to have no or low-level qualifications. Meanwhile, almost two-thirds of trusting optimists are graduates.Education chartWhile nearly a third of struggling sceptics are in lower-income households, trusting optimists and open-hearted idealists are the most affluent groups, with most households earning more than £40,000.Income chartRooted traditionalists are overwhelmingly white, while trusting optimists are by far the most ethnically diverse group.Ethnic groups chartRooted traditionalists and struggling sceptics contain the most leave voters, while open-hearted idealists are overwhelmingly remain-aligned.Brexit chartHow the ‘progressive majority’ is intending to voteThese five constituent groups collectively account for nine in 10 current Labour voters.This is up from eight in 10 at the 2024 general election, showing that Labour’s support has become more concentrated among progressive voters in the last two years.Open-hearted idealists provide the largest share of Labour’s support at 28%, followed by quiet persuadables at 21%. Trusting optimists have recorded the largest increase, rising four percentage points in the last two years.2024 election chartAt the time of polling, Labour led among all five progressive voter groups – although support ranged from 25% among struggling sceptics to 57% among trusting optimists.Open-hearted idealists lean heavily towards progressive parties, with the Greens being supported by 23% of this group.Struggling sceptics are the most fragmented group: Labour leads on 25%, but the Greens and Reform both attract substantial support. Thirteen per cent remain undecided – the highest rate of any group.Reform performed relatively strongly among rooted traditionalists, whereas the Conservatives reached their highest level among quiet persuadables.Voting intention chartThe shifts since 2024 are often down to the fact that, while Labour has lost support across the board, some of these groups are more likely to have found another political home – despite the government switching prime minister.The Greens have gained the most support among open-hearted idealists, while Reform’s rise is most concentrated among struggling sceptics and rooted traditionalists.The struggling sceptics are the group among which Labour has lost the most support, falling from 39% to 28%. Both the Greens and Reform have gained among these people, rising to 21% and 18% respectively.Greens and Reform gainsThe quiet persuadables and trusting optimists are the groups that have stuck with Labour the most, recording only small drops in support since the general election.While this is probably due to the stronger financial position of the trusting optimists, who are more likely to trust progressive politicians, the quiet persuadables are less committed to politics and generally don’t hold stronger political views.Conflicting policy priorities – but ‘manageable’ dividesLooking at the concerns of these five groups reveals conflicting priorities which could be hard for Burnham to bridge.The cost of living is the dominant concern across every progressive voter group, cited by between 54% and 77%.Health and the NHS generally ranks second, peaking at 56% among open-hearted idealists, while the economy is a significant but less prominent concern across all groups.Issues chartThe sharpest divide is over immigration: it is cited by 34% of rooted traditionalists and 28% of struggling sceptics, but just 5% of pen-hearted idealists.The climate crisis shows a reverse pattern, reaching 29% among open-hearted idealists but only 10% among rooted traditionalists.Rooted traditionalists are also notably more concerned about pensions, while housing and jobs feature more strongly among trusting optimists and quiet persuadables.Clashes in opinion chartWhen looking at the salience of different issues among voters as a whole, the research concluded that immigration is the area where Labour is least trusted – but also that this might not be a significant vulnerability.It is named as a vote-deciding issue by 40% of voters – level with the NHS and second only to the cost of living – but Reform leads Labour on it by 10 points. Thirty-one per cent of the public trust Reform on this issue, compared with 21% trusting Labour.But the researchers point to the fact that these figures are population-wide, and that immigration is not a driving factor in the votes of most people within the progressive majority. Instead, the cost of living and the economy are bigger drivers of people’s votes.Across the public as a whole, Labour led Reform on every other major issue, including the NHS, by 12 points, and the cost of living, by six.Trust chartDamian Lyons Lowe, the founder and chief executive of Survation, said: “Labour’s potential coalition is best understood as five distinct segments making up a ‘progressive majority’ – those voters that strongly consider voting for one or more of Lib Dems, Labour, the Greens, Plaid and the SNP. They have very different views on social and economic policy – the balancing act is real – but our data suggests it’s more manageable than the conventional wisdom implies.“The issues that divide these groups, immigration above all, are largely ones where Labour isn’t trusted and where the voters it could win are already spoken for. The issues that unite them – the cost of living, energy, food and housing bills, and cleaning up politics – are exactly where even the most sceptical parts of the coalition trust Labour more than anyone else. The way to build such a winning coalition isn’t to referee their disagreements. It’s to deliver visibly on the concerns every one of them shares.”Explore more on these topicsLabourReform UKGreen partyConservativesUK cost of living crisisNHSEconomic policyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ready to knock? Play School returns as BBC pushes quality children’s programming | Children's TV | The Guardian
description: TV heads hope the revamped show – back after four decades – will win over parents seeking quality shows amid concerns about addictive online content
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: TV heads hope the revamped show – back after four decades – will win over parents seeking quality shows amid concerns about addictive online content
Content: Presenters assemble: John Craven (Newsround), Sarah Greene (Blue Peter), Johnny Ball and Floella Benjamin (Play School), and Tony Hart (Take Hart) in 1980.Photograph: PAView image in fullscreenPresenters assemble: John Craven (Newsround), Sarah Greene (Blue Peter), Johnny Ball and Floella Benjamin (Play School), and Tony Hart (Take Hart) in 1980.Photograph: PAChildren's TVReady to knock? Play School returns as BBC pushes quality children’s programmingTV heads hope the revamped show – back after four decades – will win over parents seeking quality shows amid concerns about addictive online contentMichael SavageMedia editorThu 24 Sep 2026 11.13 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the generations who grew up watching Humpty, Jemima and Big Ted, the mere mention of the BBC’s Play School evokes a pang of childhood nostalgia.The show, which featured much-loved presenters such as Floella Benjamin and Johnny Ball, became synonymous with wholesome children’s television during its run of more than 20 years on air.After a 38-year break, the BBC has announced plans to bring back the programme as it tries to win over parents desperately seeking quality children’s programming amid a torrent of online content.The programme will be revamped for the digital age and will include content for the BBC’s new CBeebies Parenting YouTube channel. It is a sign that the corporation is doubling down on its drive to create more for the digital platform, where children’s content of varying quality has been booming for years.The BBC said the companion YouTube content would provide “practical play ideas, expert guidance and resources for parents and carers”.Its decision to revamp Play School comes amid continuing concerns over online children’s content, with complaints of low-quality and addictive slop. The issue is being examined by MPs on the culture, media and sport select committee.However, Play School’s return also fits with the BBC’s search for its own standout brands that can hold their own in the increasingly global market for children’s TV.View image in fullscreenSarah Greene and Floella Benjamin promote children’s programming on the BBC in 1980.Photograph: Geoffrey White/ANL/ShutterstockThe announcement coincides with the launch of the BBC’s “parenting promise”, touted as a commitment to “help every child learn through play”.The original Play School, which first aired in 1964, was designed as a way of recreating the nursery experience at home. The new series will also be live-action.Producers are being invited to pitch their vision for the show, with the BBC envisaging a traditional blend of songs, stories, movement, music, poetry and imaginative play.Potential producers have been told the aim is to retain “the values that made it one of the BBC’s most enduring children’s programmes”.Patricia Hidalgo, the director of BBC Children’s and Education, said: “Parents and carers place enormous trust in CBeebies and that is a responsibility we never take for granted. Behind every programme is a team of experts, programme makers and storytellers committed to creating content that helps children learn, grow and thrive.“In a changing media landscape, we believe trusted, high-quality children’s content has never been more important.”She added: “Play School has always embodied so much of what CBeebies stands for: creativity, curiosity, imagination and learning through play. Bringing it back for a new generation is a meaningful opportunity to build on that legacy, while continuing to support parents and carers through CBeebies Parenting and the wider commitment set out in our parenting promise.”Hidalgo is one of the most senior people in the media world raising concerns about children’s content and the need to retain quality. Earlier this year, she told MPs there had been an alarming decline in shows for younger audiences among British broadcasters.CBeebies presenter George Webster looks back: ‘Aside from Mr Tumble and Dave Benson Phillips, my dad is my hero’Read moreWith broadcasting budgets under huge pressure, she said investment into the sector by the BBC, ITV, Channel 4 and Channel 5 fell by 40%, to below £80m, over the 14 years to 2024.Over the same period, the amount of original content halved to less than 400 hours. Meanwhile, online, scrollable content aimed at children has proliferated.Last year, Hidalgotold the Guardianthe amount of American content children were consuming onYouTuberisked weakening their connection to British culture and language.Pre-production for the reinvented Play School show is expected to begin in February 2027, with the first episodes airing in the 2027-28 financial year.Explore more on these topicsChildren's TVCBBCBBCTelevision industryTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: I love my life and my cup is full but I’m drowning in shame for things left undone. How can I balance it all? | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: You are not the only one, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. It will help to ask whether you have a time problem or a bandwidth problem
Author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith
Headline: You are not the only one, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. It will help to ask whether you have a time problem or a bandwidth problem
Content: ‘There should be an amnesty each year when we confess our administrative stuff-ups so we wouldn’t feel so alone,’ Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. Painting: Girl at a Window to St Mark’s Square, Feeding Pigeons by Anton Romako.Photograph: Peter Horree/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘There should be an amnesty each year when we confess our administrative stuff-ups so we wouldn’t feel so alone,’ Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. Painting: Girl at a Window to St Mark’s Square, Feeding Pigeons by Anton Romako.Photograph: Peter Horree/AlamyLeading questionsAustralian lifestyleI love my life and my cup is full but I’m drowning in shame for things left undone. How can I balance it all?You are not the only one, advice columnistEleanor Gordon-Smithwrites. It will help to ask whether you have a time problem or a bandwidth problemRead moreLeading questionsEleanor Gordon-SmithThu 24 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 20.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI love my life in so many ways. I have a rewarding job, I’m making stellar progress towards a graduate degree, I have incredible friends and community, plus I’m even reconnecting with estranged family. My cup is very full but I still feel grief and shame for how much falls to the wayside.I have missed countless doctors’ appointments. My vehicle’slicenseplates have been expired for almost a year. I often apologise to angry friends and acquaintances after they confront me for not seeing them in months. My significant other says she doesn’t see me enough. So do my parents. I clock out of work and shudder at the thought of facing my growing avalanche of text messages. I panic whenever I receive an email that demands I arrange yet another appointment or submit to a lengthy phone call. The stack of forms I’m overdue to submit makes me feel so irresponsible,as if I’m the only adult alive who can’t seem to take care of business.I cannot imagine how anyone stays afloat in this world. When I divulge a little bit about these struggles – such as sneaking away from police cars on my daily commute because I keep running out of time to go to the DMV [Department of Motor Vehicles] – people seem to react with utter shock. Am I really the only one drowning in modern bureaucracy and relationships? How can I balance it all? Or, at least, navigate it with some more grace?Eleanor says:I think there’s an important clue in the fact that requests from people you love go in the same mental bucket as the DMV.But I want to start by saying: you are not the only one.I’m so sorry you hear incredulity when you divulge this. There should be an amnesty each year when we confess our administrative stuff-ups so we wouldn’t feel so alone; you wouldn’tbelievewhat’s out there.Some of us are at the more ultraviolet end of the spectrum, admittedly. But there are leagues upon leagues of us who understand this feeling all too painfully well. Ask any tax agent.You might want to look into the possibility ofADHD.I’m nearly 30, a virgin and feel lonely. The manosphere is trying to draw me in – where else can I seek assurance? | Leading questionsRead moreYou don’t have to be totally sold on a hypothesis of what ADHDisto know that management can be life-changing. That doesn’t have to just mean medication. It can also be astonishingly helpful to offload executive function on to yourphysical(not digital!) environment;making timevisually very salient,externalising things you need to remember.As a more general strategy for “balancing it all”, I think it helps to ask whether you have a timeproblem, or a bandwidthproblem.If you need more time,you need more time. You need your tasks to chew up less of it – outsource, batch, ban perfectionism, insist on a timer, usethis email charter, say no. And you need the people who want more time from you to understand how little you have. If you’re the only one who knows how many plates you’re spinning, you’re the only one who knows how fair or unfair these requests are.However, it’salsopossible that there is time but it isn’t usable, because you just don’t have the bandwidth.If you end every day exhausted and pulled in dozens of directions, and if each call or request feels so heavy and hard to “do right” that it requires self-steeling and psychic warm-up and you’re completely exhausted afterwards, then having the minutes technically available isn’t useful. You might as well tell me, as I collapse across the triathlon finish, that there’stimeto run another 10km. Yeah, sure. But I can’t. I’m in no condition to use that time to that end.Bandwidth problems show up as mismatches between how we experience things and how other people do. They think: “Why haven’t you ticked off those to-do list items, it would take 20 minutes?” But because each one is so emotionally expensive, they may as well ask why you haven’t yet called an estranged lover to bury the hatchet, or confronted your childhood bully, given it would take 20 minutes. The time is not the issue, the effect on my nervous system is.I suspect for most of us, overwhelm is at least partly a bandwidth issue. (One way to check: keep atime audit.) To be clear, I am not saying this could be solved by working harder or “making time”.It’s precisely the opposite. If time itselfdoesn’thelp, what you ultimately need are ways for these things to feel less like horrific burdens, so there’s less reason to avoid them and less exhaustion from encountering them.How you dothatdepends on why they feel so horrible to start with.We can make such thickets of shame.It could be about competence; “I’m not sure I can do this, and I hate how it feels to be bumbling.” It could be about the fear that people will always want more, no matter how much you can or want to give them: so “I’d like to see you!” hits the ear like “I want something from you, and after that I’ll want more” – a request for your time can feel like the threat of being consumed. (Are there any unsatisfiable parents in your past?) It could be perfectionism; I’d rather not do this at all than do it only to the level it can be done quickly. It could be screen overload, if workandadminanda lot of your socialising all happens through the same demand-communicating device.How to make these things feel less like running another 10km depends on why they exhaustyou,particularly – on why exactly your loved ones and the DMV can feel somehow the same. Understanding the specifics of your overwhelm may feel like yet another task but, once you do, the rest may come easier.Ask Eleanor a questionShare your questionTell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.NameWhat is your question for Eleanor?Email addressYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.By submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreExplore more on these topicsAustralian lifestyleLeading questionsHealth & wellbeingFriendshipAttention deficit hyperactivity disorderMental healthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tom Watson’s move to Palantir is the latest sign of how far the rot has spread in UK politics | Clive Lewis | The Guardian
description: When a former Labour deputy leader joins a firm built on surveillance and military targeting, it deepens public cynicism – and democracy depends on trust, says Labour MP Clive Lewis
Author: Clive Lewis
Headline: When a former Labour deputy leader joins a firm built on surveillance and military targeting, it deepens public cynicism – and democracy depends on trust, says Labour MP Clive Lewis
Content: ‘Palantir probably doesn’t hire a former deputy leader for his coding skills. But does it hire access?’ Tom Watson in London, January 2025.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Palantir probably doesn’t hire a former deputy leader for his coding skills. But does it hire access?’ Tom Watson in London, January 2025.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersOpinionPalantirTom Watson’s move to Palantir is the latest sign of how far the rot has spread in UK politicsClive LewisWhen a former Labour deputy leader joins a firm built on surveillance and military targeting, it deepens public cynicism – and democracy depends on trustThu 24 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 09.25 EDTShareWhatever is said about Tom Watson, the former deputy leader of the Labour party has a knack for landing headlines. In the past he did it at the expense of the rich and powerful – from News International,over phone hacking, to the Home Office,over its mass surveillance of our data. But his latest headline – that he has joined Palantir as a senior vice-president – has been at the expense of public confidence in the political class.Hisnew appointmentis more than just a private career choice. It sends yet another signal to a weary public about just how far the rot in our democracy has spread.Now, the former scourge of mass surveillance finds a surveillance company “the most interesting … on the planet”. It’s quite a journey, and one not many of us will want to take with him. Palantir does do work of real consequence. That’s rather the point. Watson says some criticism of Palantiris propaganda. Some of it is also true, which is the part he will find harder to square.Palantir is a company built on surveillance and military targeting. Its co-founder Peter Thielwrote in 2009that he no longer believed freedom and democracy were compatible. He sees technology as an alternative to politics, a way to change the world without having to persuade voters, andbacks private “startup cities”run by chief executives. This attitude runs through the company’s DNA. Palantir’s co-founder and chief executive, Alex Karp,has boastedthat its work is there “to scare enemies and on occasion kill them”. Its software is used totarget people for ICE raidsin the US, andcivilians in Gaza. This isn’t just another global corporation with some unsavoury corners to its business.I can’t parse Watson’s mind or motivation. Palantir probably doesn’t hire a former deputy leader for his coding skills. But does it hire access? Access to networks across party and government, and to the doors behind which Palantir would fight to keep a£330m NHS England contractand legally challengeSadiq Khan’s blockon a £50m Metropolitan police contract?Watson won’t be alone. He will joinmore than 30former UK officials at a company that Peter Mandelson’s former lobbying firm, Global Counsel, counted as a client. Mandelson accompanied Keir Starmerto Palantir’s Washington officein 2025, while still retaining a stake in Global Counsel.The MoD has since signed amajor partnershipwith Palantir. And none of this will have broken a single law. The rules on jobs for former ministers last only two years and have no legal force. Therein lies the problem.Whether it’s Tony Blair and his relationship with Oracle, Mandelson and Global Counsel or Nick Clegg and his time at Meta, the section of the political class meant to oppose vested interests and promote public service appears to have switched sides.According to the Institute for Public Policy Research’slatest findings, the main political parties, including Labour and the Liberal Democrats, have been accepting donations from wealthy individuals at an accelerating pace. The research found 72% of all £1m-plus donations from individuals since records began in 2001 had come since 2019. Sadly, none of this can be described as an aberration. Rather, it’s how the system increasingly works. Now politicians’ proximity to wealth and the “elites” who own it has fostered a growing public mistrust. One need only listen toDanny Dyer at a rally last week, calling for public ownership of water, to get a feel for that sentiment. These examples are all symptoms of the growing proximity between political power and the wealth it is supposed to hold to account.In the recentRobin Cook memorial lectureI gave, I termed this malaise the “integrity gap”: the widening gulf between what governments and politicians say and what people believe. Every flagrant act deepens public cynicism about politics, and about the democracy that depends on public trust. This is a fact of which those around Trump are well aware. They know every allegation of presidential corruption erodes people’s willingness to defend democracy.Thiel understands this implicitly. His vision for our society is simply not compatible with a progressive worldview. That is why a former Labour deputy leader lending his name toPalantirmatters so much.The integrity gap will not close with better messaging. It will close only when politicians show whose side they are on. That means revolving-door rules with the force of law, and a regulator with teeth. It means capping political donations and ending second jobs in the House of Commons, while abolishing the House of Lords altogether. And it means public ownership and democratic control of the things firms such as Palantir want to run, from our health data to our water.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThose who sell access to power have made their choice. Those who oppose Thiel’s vision need to make theirs, and act on it. It’s time to pick a side.Clive Lewis is theLabourMP for Norwich SouthDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Abandoned, dismissed and gaslighted: there is no excuse for the way ME sufferers have been betrayed | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: Changes in guidance and science seem to have little impact on millions of devastated lives. It’s a social crisis playing out behind closed doors, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: Changes in guidance and science seem to have little impact on millions of devastated lives. It’s a social crisis playing out behind closed doors, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: Illustration: Bill Bragg/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Bill Bragg/The GuardianOpinionME / Chronic fatigue syndromeAbandoned, dismissed and gaslighted: there is no excuse for the way ME sufferers have been betrayedGeorge MonbiotChanges in guidance and science seem to have little impact on millions of devastated lives. It’s a shocking social crisis playing out behind closed doorsThu 24 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTShareI’ve spent my working life covering neglected issues. But few are neglected like the devastating chronic condition ME/CFS (myalgic encephalomyelitis, or chronic fatigue syndrome). In severe cases, the illness shuts down people’s lives almost entirely, causing an extreme loss of energy and a wide range of physical and cognitive symptoms that can prevent patients from working, socialising and, sometimes, even moving or eating. Yet these people have been more or less airbrushed from our minds.To find out what this neglect looks like in practice, this week I putout a call on Blueskyasking people with ME/CFS about their recent experiences of treatment. I was immediately inundated with horrifying testimonies. “I’ve just been completely abandoned”; “a 10-year waiting list for treatment”; “we’ve given up seeking medical support”; “stuck in limbo”; “I just felt utterly unheard, invalidated”. I’ve been sent hundreds of shocking and heart-rending accounts.Exact numbers are hard to establish, but in the UK alone, anestimated 400,000 peoplelive with the condition.It affects women far more than men, by a ratio of about 4:1, according to a study in England. The number of people with long Covid, some of whom meet the diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS,was estimated in 2024at 2 million in England and Scotland.You might have imagined politicians and the media would be all over it. Instead, this great social crisis is met with silence or worse. Some outlets, despite the overwhelming weight of evidence, havemockedortrivialisedthese conditions.There’s along, dark history here, rooted in centuries of dismissal of predominantly female illnesses as “hysterical”, and amplified in recent decades by government attempts to reduce the benefits bill and insurers’ attempts to reduce payouts. If you can establish that a condition is caused by malingering, poor self-care or a negative attitude, you won’t have to cough up.Official guidance in many countries was informed by a series of deeply flawedstudiesthat purported to show these illnesses could be treated with cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), or graded exercise therapy (GET). In 2020, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice)foundthat the quality ofallthe research promoting these therapies as curative treatments for ME/CFS was either “low” or, in most cases, “very low”. In 2021,it stopped recommending these therapiesas primary treatments. We now know CBT cannot treat the condition (though it can sometimes help patients to come to terms with it), while GET is not only useless but actively dangerous, as exercise can trigger one of the most devastating ME/CFS symptoms: post-exertional malaise (PEM). PEM robs people of their remaining energy, rendering many patients bedbound, sometimes incapable of almost all movement.Since then, two other things have happened. At the inquest into the death of a young ME/CFS patient, thecoroner ruledthat provision in the health service for patients with severe ME “was and is nonexistent”. Something would have to be done. And a number of seemingscientific breakthroughs, somevery recent, havebegun inching towards identifyingpossible biological causes of both ME/CFS and long Covid. Now, or so we should hope, it’s undeniable.So what has changed as a result of these shifts? Alongside the horror and heartbreak in the testimonies of the people who emailed me, I was struck by the sense of sheer relief that someone, anyone, was asking the question.Many said they arestillbeing treated as if they have a psychological illness, andstillbeing pushed into GET and CBT. One patient told me: “I’ve gone from relatively mild to now mostly house- and bedbound, largely thanks to repeated attempts at graded exercise and ‘pushing through’.” A few days ago, anNHSclinic told another patient to undertake “graded exercise” and “simply to walk, despite the fact I’m a wheelchair user”.One mother told me “the consultant cardiologist recommended a graded exercise programme” and “a treadmill test” for her bedbound son. When she told him this contradicted Nice guidelines, he replied: “Well, what do you want me to do?” Another made the same challenge to her GP, but the doctor “denied this strongly and reiterated to my daughter that she should do the exercises”. This is very common: many doctors, I’m told, seem unaware of the new guidelines and react defensively when challenged. In many practices, GET has simply been rebranded as “building tolerance” or “pacing up” or “a little more activity each day”.Patients report being treated with “contempt and derision”. Loads are still being offered CBT. Some have been propelled by NHS doctors towards quack private “cures”, now offered by a growing industry that preys on people’s desperation.Others tell me they’ve not been pushed into inappropriate treatments, but “that’s only because I receive no treatment for it whatsoever”. Some have had to explain to their doctors what ME/CFS is. And it gets worse. I’ve been contacted by parents who have been accused of fabricating and inducing illness and even referred to social services, because doctors who seem to know nothing about ME/CFS believe they are making up their children’s symptoms.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt’s as if nothing has been learned. Perhaps that’s not surprising. A freedom of information requestto NHS Englandfound that, of the tens of thousands of practitioners who would benefit from it, after a year, only 74 had completed the new learning module on ME/CFS guidance. Meanwhile, as recently as last summer, the Department for Work and Pensions wasstill teaching its traineeselements of the old, discredited view of the condition. And, as the Liberal Democrat MP Tessa Munt, a hero of this story, tells me: “The piecemeal offerings in thegovernment’s final delivery planare not going to touch the system-wide failings.”It’s not only the UK. I’ve been contacted by patients from around the world. InSwedenandAustralia, official guidance still recommends GET and CBT. In Switzerland, I’m told, treatment is spiralling backwards, with a new wave of psychologisation. Norway, Finland and the Netherlands, despite their progressive medical reputations, sound like a waking nightmare for ME/CFS patients.Of course, as there is no effective treatment, it’s a difficult situation for doctors as well as patients. But even worse than no solutions is false solutions, and a dangerous, gaslighting, even punitive approach to a terrible disease.Across the decades, millions of people have been neglected, dismissed and mistreated, and still it goes on. We need to ask why so many patients have been abandoned, why discredited and dangerous treatments continue to be prescribed and why ignorance and neglect still dominate, in the health system and beyond. In other words, there has seldom been a stronger case for a public inquiry.George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsME / Chronic fatigue syndromeOpinionNHSHospitalsHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: Vistry is the laggard in a housebuilding sector full of cracks | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: Group shrinks ambitions from 20,000 to just 12,000 homes a year in an attempt to balance the books
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Group shrinks ambitions from 20,000 to just 12,000 homes a year in an attempt to balance the books
Content: A newbuild housing development by Countryside, part of the Vistry group, in Hertfordshire.Photograph: Colin Palmer Photography/AlamyView image in fullscreenA newbuild housing development by Countryside, part of the Vistry group, in Hertfordshire.Photograph: Colin Palmer Photography/AlamyNils Pratley on financeVistry GroupVistry is the laggard in a housebuilding sector full of cracksNils PratleyGroup shrinks ambitions from 20,000 to just 12,000 homes a year in an attempt to balance the booksThu 24 Sep 2026 12.19 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.38 EDTShareThe entire housebuilding sector is in a funk, grumbling about energy prices, the cost of labour, regulation, planning delays, taxes and more, but few have messed up a bad hand quite like Vistry. Three years ago this mashup of the Bovis, Linden and Countryside brands aspired to build 20,000 houses a year, and made itself the darling of the incoming Labour government by betting big on “affordable mixed-tenure housing” in partnership with councils, housing associations and institutional landlords.The City, too, fell for former executive chair Greg Fitzgerald’s promise that a “capital light” approach of pre-selling homes via a partnership model would yield oodles of cash. The share price doubled to almost £14 between October 2023 and August 2024.Fitzgerald departed in May after too many profit warnings and now, with the shares down to the bare foundations of 262p, it’s time for newchief executive Adam Daniels’ review of what happened. Short version: the logic of the partnership stuff wasn’t so silly, but the execution was horrible, especially in the south of England.“The pace of change meant that the operating model, controls and culture did not scale consistently with the group’s volumes [of construction],” he said, a polite summary of a growth strategy gone awry. For good measure, a proportion of the land bank would not be acquired “under the investment approval criteria that will be applied in the future”, which read as a confession that Vistry simply overpaid for plots.The good news, of a sort, for shareholders is that the damage to the balance is not deemed so severe that fresh equity is required. Daniels’ prescription for recovery, however, is a long exercise in getting smaller and living with shrunken ambitions.The aim is to build 12,000 houses a year, rather than the 20,000-plus imagined by Fitzgerald. A greater proportion of those homes will be in the north of England. As for return on capital employed – a critical metric for housebuilders – the old idea was 40%. That’s been cut to 30%, and only by 2031.It all sounds perfectly reasonable: keep things simple, fix the balance sheet by eating into the land bank, and concentrate on the parts of the country where market prices (which still matter for a mixed-tenure model) are holding up better.In Vistry’s favour is the fact that, for all its financial troubles, it’s still in the government’s good books. Last month, the company received a £350m direct grant to construct 3,000 affordable homes under the £39bn social and affordable homes programme. If you take the long view, there is a possibility of a turnaround if Daniels can live up to the promise of better execution. At the age of 35, he has time on his side – and may need it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe wider message for the government’s target to build 1.5m homes in England during this parliament, however, is as discouraging as ever. Vistry is an extreme example but virtually everybody is reining in ambitions in the name of financial discipline and cash generation. Even Barratt Redrow, the biggest of the lot, said in April itwould be scaling back its land purchases. Angela Rayner, the housing secretary,has taken to calling the 1.5m figure a “stretch target”. Indeed, the only real question is by how much it will be missed. By an embarrassing margin, on current form.Explore more on these topicsVistry GroupNils Pratley on financeConstruction industryHousingcommentShareReuse this content

title: The west is in freefall – and the worst part is that we were warned, but chose not to listen | Owen Jones | The Guardian
description: Endless pursuit of wealth and power by western leaders led us here. What strikes me most is how many saw what was coming, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Author: Owen Jones
Headline: Endless pursuit of wealth and power by western leaders led us here. What strikes me most is how many saw what was coming, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Content: US soldiers in Zangabad, Afghanistan, 2012. A US envoy said he had warned in 1988 that Washington’s Afghan policy was ‘going very, very badly’.Photograph: Tony Karumba/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUS soldiers in Zangabad, Afghanistan, 2012. A US envoy said he had warned in 1988 that Washington’s Afghan policy was ‘going very, very badly’.Photograph: Tony Karumba/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionForeign policyThe west is in freefall – and the worst part is that we were warned, but chose not to listenOwen JonesEndless pursuit of wealth and power by western leaders led us here. What strikes me most is how many saw what was comingThu 24 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 16.59 EDTShareThe symptoms of decline are everywhere you look. On Sunday, Germany’s far rightwon another state election, taking nearly 40% of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. France is preparing a €54bn fiscal squeeze, which could turn the screw still further on a foundering so-called European social model. At the UN general assembly, Donald Trump once again threatened to “annihilate” Iran, even as the fourth failed western war on a Muslim nation this century hasadded more than $100bnto Americans’ fuel bills.There is little dispute over the symptoms. The great fight of our age is over the diagnosis, and the right has been winning it for years. Its story is simple and, as the latest German state election underlines, effective: the west is dying because of migrants, Muslims, trans people, “woke” and the “deep state”. So when I told friends I was writing a book called The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost It, they worried I had shape-shifted into Liz Truss, who, after being outlasted in officeby a lettuce, produced Ten Years to Save the West.My diagnosis is rather different. The west is in decline because after the cold war, its elites declared a victory from which they have never recovered. They proclaimed an economic model that channelled wealth upwards as the inevitable future, while treating an apparently invincible military as free to reshape the Muslim world. Both convictions were terribly convenient for those who benefited from them. The result has been catastrophic: an economy that no longer delivers sustained improvements in living standards or public services, and western military interventions humiliated in Kabul, Baghdad, Tripoli and now the strait of Hormuz.Abroad, the west’s claims of moral superiority have been incinerated, not least by Israel’s genocide of the Palestinian people in Gaza. At home, the disillusionment and despair spawned by these overlapping disasters have fuelled the rise of the far right, threatening democracy itself.What struck me while researching the book was how often people had seen what was coming – and how little difference their warnings had made.In the spring of 1994, one of the most senior political officers at the US embassy in Moscow sent Washington a long dissenting cable. Its argument was stark enough to make its author an outcast within the foreign-policy establishment.Wayne Merry is nobody’s idea of a radical. He grew up in a wheat-country settlement in Oklahoma called – no joke – Kremlin, and admired the then Russian president, Boris Yeltsin. But he had spent two years witnessing “shock therapy” – the overnight conversion of a planned economy into a casino – being imposed on the wreckage of the Soviet economy by Washington, Harvard economists and the IMF. He had taken to stuffing his pockets with cash for old women begging in the streets, “because,” he told me simply, “they were starving”.Russia was ruled by westernisers, butMerry’s cablewarned that “democratic forces in Russia are in serious trouble” and that “there is no reason to believe the Russian economy is capable of rapid market reform”. If the US chose “the role of economic missionary rather than true partner”, he predicted, it would strengthen extremists and revive an “adversarial relationship between Russia and the west”.As Merry told me: “We’re gutting working-class living standards, and then expecting people to vote for us.” Washington’s answer was to make him persona non grata. The cable remained classified for three decades, quietly released only at the end of 2024. By then, one study estimated there had been12.2 million excess deathsin Russia during the transition. Meanwhile the strongman who rose from the wreckage was nearly three years into his murderous full-scale invasion of Ukraine.View image in fullscreenUkrainian firefighters searching the rubble for civilians after a Russian airstrike on a residential building in Oleksandrivka, Donetsk.Photograph: Diego Herrera Carcedo/Anadolu/Getty ImagesThe men who ignored Merry were not coy about their assumptions. Russia had to move towards “our way of doing things,”said Strobe Talbott, President Bill Clinton’s main Russia adviser. If that sounded like “an obnoxious confirmation of our doctrine of exceptionalism”, his answer was simple: “Well, tough. That’s us; that’s the US. We are exceptional.”This was the basic structural problem of the post-cold war order. It has never gone away. However strong the evidence behind a warning, when it collided with the interests of western power, the warning gave way.I spent two years travelling from Baghdad to Pittsburgh, and Nairobi to Ramallah, for the book, and Merry’s experience turned out to be less the exception than the rule. In a 2005 interview, the US envoy Edmund McWilliamssaid he had warned in 1988 thatWashington’s Afghan policy was “going very, very badly”, as US weaponry flowed to Islamist fundamentalists. But the overriding objective was defeating the Soviet Union. McWilliams said he was frozen out, smeared as mentally ill, alcoholic and gay, and reassigned. CIA analysts themselves had warned in 1987 that a victorious Islamist regime might inherit a “mountain of weapons” and use them to arm or train Islamist guerrillas elsewhere. The weapons kept flowing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe same triumphalism took hold at home. Western economies were not starved of wealth: they were increasingly organised to extract it rather than invest it. As the economist Mariana Mazzucato told me, 80% of British finance now flows back into finance, insurance and real estate. Western economies became increasingly good at rewarding ownership, but increasingly bad at building the productive foundations on which prosperity depends.In early 2007, an executive director of the World Bank told his friend, the economist Ha-Joon Chang, that a huge crisis was coming. His evidence was his cleaner, who he suspected was undocumented: she had a $300,000 mortgage. Stagnant wages had been papered over with cheap credit – “let them eat credit,” as one economist summed up the model – and the paper was about to tear. When it did, the crash should have finished off this failed economic model. Instead, ordinary people were forced to pay to save it, through shredded social provision.Where this chaotic fall could lead is frightening. Israel’s genocide has normalised limitless depravity. Trumpism has repurposed the rhetoric and institutions of the “war on terror”, now used to target domestic dissent. Authoritarianism and barbarism are entirely plausible futures.There is another possibility: the left makes a different case. That it was the endless, unchecked pursuit of wealth and power by western elites, at home and abroad, that brought us here, and that the task is to rebuild what Margaret Thatcher sought to destroy – society – by investing the wealth we collectively produce. Or, as the man who wrote that buried cable put it to me: stop gutting people’s living standards and then expecting them to vote for you.Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost It, is published on 1 October. title: We’re in a crisis of loneliness – but is buying friends on an app likely to help solve it? | Elle Hunt | The Guardian
description: Shortcuts work against the rewards of friendship: authentic relationships can surely only be forged when you’re not expecting a return on your money, says journalist Elle Hunt
Author: Elle Hunt
Headline: Shortcuts work against the rewards of friendship: authentic relationships can surely only be forged when you’re not expecting a return on your money, says journalist Elle Hunt
Content: People meeting at a party.Photograph: Thomas Barwick/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople meeting at a party.Photograph: Thomas Barwick/Getty ImagesOpinionFriendshipWe’re in a crisis of loneliness – but is buying friends on an app likely to help solve it?Elle HuntShortcuts work against the rewards of friendship: authentic relationships can surely only be forged when you’re not expecting a return on your moneyThu 24 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 14.59 EDTShareWhat price would you put on friendship? In these hyper-capitalistic times, where nothing is beyond being given a monetary value, perhaps even Mastercard wouldn’t dare to claim that it’s priceless. AYouGov surveyfound that 15% of Britons say they have no close friends, while nearly one in 10 (8%) have no friends at all. The numbersare similarly dismalin the US. As we face this contemporary crisis of connection, it is little wonder that friendship, or at least the possibility of it, is increasingly being marketed for sale.There has been a striking increase in online platforms and apps that promise to introduce you – algorithmically, through social mixers or a combination – to your next BFF. There’sCliq,PLY, standing for “People Like You”, andRealRootswhich promises user satisfaction with the tagline: “Make new friends. Guaranteed”. Meanwhile,222boldly declares it is “not a friend-making service”, but a means to “explore serendipity” through social experiences with compatible people.And this new sweep of pay-to-play friendships doesn’t stop at apps and algorithmic matchmaking. It is accompanied by supper clubs, book clubs, running clubs and other opportunities for you to mingle with people in your area – for a fee, of course.CircleUp, for example, holds regular social mixers across the UK for paying members, so that you can “keep seeing the same faces”. Others cultivate a more exclusive crowd.Gathering Tableshosts dinners for a “curated mix of guests”, united by their willingness to pay £145 a head.These initiatives dangle community, but whether this trumps their commercial reason for being is debatable. The price of these apps and events is sometimes framed as a means of securing commitment, not just covering costs. “When you do things for free, people often don’t turn up,” PLY’s foundertold the Guardian. But the effort becomes less civic-minded when you consider the desire for friendship is what makes these services valuable in the first place. These friend-making apps and paid-for gatherings may well offer opportunities for social connection – they are at least a date in the diary. But make no mistake, they exist primarily to encourage investment in a brand and even create opportunities to spend. Of course it is possible to make genuine connections in commercial spaces – many of us have made close bonds at work – but paying for introductions feels antithetical to the spirit of true friendship.This new commercial interest in facilitating “gathering” speaks to the sense of collective untethering from community. Many of us understand we are lacking community, perhaps even more than friendship. It is unsettlingly common to hear people complaining of their current social network, as though a more suitable or nourishing one already exists, just waiting for you to slot into it. No wonder brands are attempting to package them up.Cliq claims the first step to “start your community” is to download its app. But real community is built, not bought (and certainly not downloaded). It takes time, shared investment and oftensome weathering on both sides. It is certainly possible that meaningful, enduring ties can begin at a paid-for meet-up. But while the payment can create the conditions for friendship, it can’t manufacture the friendship itself.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hill I will die on: Private karaoke is the death of socialism – only a pub singalong is good enough for the people | Kelli BlanchettRead moreTellingly, ease is often central to the offering: Cliq claims “finding your people shouldn’t be difficult”. Shouldn’t it? No matter how you meet, it takes time and effort to turn an acquaintance into a friend; that same process, multiplied and sustained, is what creates a community. Seeking shortcuts or higher-quality connections is not only beside the point, it works against the rewards: authentic relationships can only be forged without expectation of a return on investment.That’s not to say we don’t need more places and opportunities to meet new people; the very existence of these services at least demonstrates that we do. But before entrusting our need for greater intimacy and affection to a third party, we might ask ourselves if we could be doing more to put ourselves out there socially. Could we extend an invitation to friendly strangers, or introduce our mutuals and turn acquaintances into friends?The best community-building exercise I’ve heard of lately was before a performance of Austentatious – the Jane Austen comedy play – where all solo ticket-holders were invited to come early and mingle before the show. The event was free, organised around a preexisting commitment and people could opt in. There was the opportunity to meet people; the work, and potential reward, of making a new friend was left to you.Elle Hunt is a freelance journalistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: #NotAllLesbians – we can’t let the Massachusetts bar drama turn us all into a punchline | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The Last Ditch Bar saga is a case of ridiculous lefty infighting. But well-meaning people often have to tolerate nonsense
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The Last Ditch Bar saga is a case of ridiculous lefty infighting. But well-meaning people often have to tolerate nonsense
Content: Jackie Matellian (left), the owner of Last Ditch Bar and Arts Venue, talks with a patron at the bar in Greenfield, Massachusetts, last week.Photograph: Sophie ParkView image in fullscreenJackie Matellian (left), the owner of Last Ditch Bar and Arts Venue, talks with a patron at the bar in Greenfield, Massachusetts, last week.Photograph: Sophie ParkOpinionMassachusetts#NotAllLesbians – we can’t let the Massachusetts bar drama turn us all into a punchlineArwa MahdawiThe Last Ditch Bar saga is a case of ridiculous lefty infighting. But well-meaning people often have to tolerate nonsenseThu 24 Sep 2026 14.48 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.35 EDTShareI have just wrapped up an emergency meeting with the International Office of Homosexual Affairs and would like to share a statement regarding therecent incidentin Greenfield, Massachusetts.Here we go: those shenanigans, reported in a viral story by the Boston Globe, don’t represent us all. #NotAllLesbians.But, of course, I shouldn’t be centering myself here. Nor should I be assuming knowledge in a way which reinforces oppressive hegemonic structures. So let me hold space to share the details of everything that has transpired with all you folx reading who have not had the privilege of devouring every detail of the drama already.The story begins at the Last Ditch Bar and Arts Venue, which opened up last year as a place for “dykes, transsexuals, gender freaks, workers, and their friends”. One of the bar’s key selling points was that it required KN-95 masks (“or better”) at all times, to accommodate the immunocompromised and the Covid-conscious. Well I say “selling points”, but a big issue with Last Ditch is it didn’t do much selling. In keeping with its values, it had an open-door policy, stating that nobody would be turned away if they couldn’t pay the cover charge, including “unhoused people”. This was very generous of them, but also a formula for losing money.double quotation markI think it’s worth stressing that [the Last Ditch saga] is still ultimately a story about a woman who tried to create an inclusive spaceIn order to try to stop hemorrhaging cash so they could continue to pay rent, the venue eventually decided to move to a mask-optional policy. This caused an uproar. A sample comment on Instagram: “I hope your venue gets firebombed for robbing my fellow immunocompromised people of their Saturday plans just to scrape extra revenue from ablists [sic].”And from there the story wades deeper and deeper into “surely this isn’t real, surely this is a psyop by rightwingers who want to make the queer community look unhinged” territory. An emergency Zoom meeting was declared and lasted over three hours. A performer called Soe Noire accused Jackie Matellian, the last remaining operator of the venue (the other founders left; one so they could enrol in clown school), of shedding “WHITE THEY THEM TEARS”.The bar was not “a safe environment nor interested in revolutionary praxis”, Noire added. Matellian, who is working four different jobs in a desperate attempt to pay off the $50,000 loan for the business, was contrite. “There’s conflict, but we just hope that there’s more repair than conflict,” she told the Globe.Alas, it’s the conflict (and the lesbians) which has made this story go so viral. It fits squarely into a genre I will call “moderately ridiculous lefty infighting”, which is beloved by sensible centrist authors and the rightwing press. Stories of progressives leaning into all the most extreme stereotypes are guaranteed to be turned into parables of why leftists are self-absorbed drama queens who can’t get anything done. Fox News is already all over the Last Ditch drama, and Bari Weiss’s Free Press jumped on it with glee. Meanwhile, Newsweek is drawing parallelswith a storyabout a white Jewish Philadelphia teacher who spent yearspresenting herselfas Black and Palestinian. “The stories are different but their respective absurdity rhymes,” Newsweek writes. And by “rhymes” they mean: they are both good opportunities to attack progressives.But while there is a lot of absurdity in the Last Ditch saga, I think it’s worth stressing that it is still ultimately a story about a woman who tried to create an inclusive space where some of the most vulnerable people in society could feel accepted. It’s easy to laugh at all the shenanigans, but the world would be a lot better if it had more people like Jackie Matellian in it: kind, well-meaning people who try to live their values. Of course, the problem with people like Matellian is that, because they are kind and well-meaning, they can sometimes tolerate too much nonsense. Narcissists who use a marginalized identity as cover for bad behaviour can find themselves drawn to places like Last Ditch because it’s the only space in which they will be indulged.The flag culture wars have come to an unlikely place: progressive Iceland | Alexander HurstRead moreI don’t know whether going viral is going to be a boon for Last Ditch, but it’s certainly been good for the Boston Globe. The (masterfully written) piece is responsible for asurge in subscriptionsthis week. According to its editor, it’s the best performing story of the year and is “on pace to shatter all sorts of Globe records”.And I think that takes us to the real moral of this story. If you want to save local news you can forget all about adopting AI or pivoting to video, the secret is pivoting to lesbians.Explore more on these topicsMassachusettsOpinionLGBTQ+ rightsCoronavirusBars, pubs and clubscommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m an avid fan of chard – but you can have too much of a good thing | Adrian Chiles | The Guardian
description: My veg patch has turned into a chard jungle and now it’s chard for breakfast, lunch and supper, writes Adrian Chiles
Author: Adrian Chiles
Headline: My veg patch has turned into a chard jungle and now it’s chard for breakfast, lunch and supper, writes Adrian Chiles
Content: Leave it out … chard of many colours.Photograph: merc67/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenLeave it out … chard of many colours.Photograph: merc67/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionGardensI’m an avid fan of chard – but you can have too much of a good thingAdrian ChilesMy veg patch has turned into a chard jungle and now it’s chard for breakfast, lunch and supperThu 24 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.38 EDTShareChard. It’s hard with so much chard. As Jennifer Lopez might put it if she were in my gardening shoes, I used to have a little, now I have a lot. There was too little last year, for whatever reason. I probably did something wrong. This year, I sowed more. Come summer, the crop underwhelmed me again. So I sowed still more, throwing around seeds of as many varieties as I could get hold of. Then I went off to Croatia for most of August, where there is chard aplenty. That’s not why I go there, incidentally, but it suits me because I really like it, which is just as well because on the Adriatic coast it comes with every meal.If you have not tried chard, I’d describe it as like spinach, but more substantial. In Croatian it’s called blitva, which oddly enough is the sound my belly starts making when I eat too much of it, as I do every summer there. It can get too much. In Split, I met a woman who was so sick of chard she got rather angry at the very mention of it. She was the cousin of the wife of a famous Serbian footballer I know. She wrote pop songs for a living, but she won’t be penning a love song to blitva any time soon, I can tell you that. As she started forking it off her plate on to mine, she spat out the word blitva as if it were a profanity rather than the sound of a stomach-gurgle. And now I, too, am taking its name in vain.While I was away, my neighbour kindly watered my garden. I almost wish she hadn’t. My chard patch is now a chard jungle, featuring stems of many colours and leaves of all shades of green. Some of the leaves are so big that if I was naked they would cover not just my bits, but my whole lower half. Strip the leaves and I’m left with stems thick enough to do service as lethal weapons.And it’s chard for breakfast, chard for lunch and chard for dinner. Chard for the freezer, chard for friends and more for enemies. Chard, chard, chard. I do love chard, but too much chard is hard.Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
