title: The Guardian view on a supersized El Niño: a natural phenomenon and human folly are a lethal combination | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Hundreds of thousands are expected to die, millions to go hungry. This is not just about weather patterns, but about injustice
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Hundreds of thousands are expected to die, millions to go hungry. This is not just about weather patterns, but about injustice
Content: A dried-up field in Jonggol, Indonesia. El Niño increases drought risk in a large swathe of the world.Photograph: Mast Irham/EPAView image in fullscreenA dried-up field in Jonggol, Indonesia. El Niño increases drought risk in a large swathe of the world.Photograph: Mast Irham/EPAOpinionEl Niño southern oscillationThe Guardian view on a supersized El Niño: a natural phenomenon and human folly are a lethal combinationEditorialHundreds of thousands are expected to die, millions to go hungry. This is not just about weather patterns, but about injusticeThu 24 Sep 2026 13.37 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTShareSome warnings are so grave that it is almost impossible to fully comprehend them. The descriptions ofa super-sized, “Godzilla-level” El Niñoalready heating our planet would sound hyperbolic were they not issuing from eminent scientists. They say that the weather pattern, which occurs roughly every two to seven years, may be the strongest in at least a millennium. With its peak yet to come, the temperature rise in the Pacific Ocean has already surpassed the previous high.The consequence will be huge amounts of heat in an atmosphere already experiencing frighteningly higher temperatures due to the human-caused climate crisis. Next year is almost certain to be the hottest on record globally, breaking this year’s record. The World Food Programme has warned that 50 million people are likely to bepushed into acute hunger. Others estimate that the extra heat from El Niño alone will cause thedeaths of 450,000 people by February, from Nigeria and Indonesia to the US. That extraordinary toll is in addition to those killed by the wildfires, droughts and floods it is likely to bring – and also to deaths caused by global heating.While the weather system develops in the Pacific Ocean, its knock-on effects will be felt far away. It increases drought risk in a large swathe of the world, while increasing rainfall elsewhere. Indiahas already experienceda 50% shortfall in essential monsoon rains this month, affecting crops. In Sri Lanka, reservoirs for drinking water are running dry. European countries may be indirectly affected, with a stormier autumn, but the primary impact for them islikely to be on food supplies.View image in fullscreenEd Miliband, the UK foreign secretary.Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/GettyWhile there is ongoing debate aboutthe impact of global heating on the pattern itself, a major study published last monthfoundthat strong El Niños in recent decades have been supercharged by the overheating of the planet due to fossil fuels. It is beyond doubt that the effects of this natural phenomenon are compounded by human-made folly and injustice. Domestically and internationally, the poorest will be worst hit, due to factors such as living conditions and underlying health, while being the least able to pay their way out of trouble. At the same time, the wealthy few will continue to enrich themselves from an economic system built on pumping out more emissions. Defenders of the status quo will continue to insist that we cannot afford to clean up our act. It is more than ever evident that we cannot afford not to do so.The UK foreign secretary’s warning to other countries at the UN on Wednesday that El Niño and the climate and nature crises threatentheir national security and defencewas welcome. Andy Burnham, as well as Ed Miliband, should be seizing the opportunity to make the political case for tough action on emissions, and accelerating efforts to prepare the UK for increasingly extreme weather. The Climate Change Committee, which advises the government, warned in alandmark report in Maythat the country is “built for a climate that no longer exists”.Globally, boosting the loss and damage fund to ensure support for developing countries, which have contributed the least to the climate crisis but are likely to suffer most, should be a priority. ThisunprecedentedEl Niño poses an immense threat. It could also be a spur to action against global heating and its associated injustices, which otherwise will only deepen.Explore more on these topicsEl Niño southern oscillationOpinionClimate Change CommitteeGreenhouse gas emissionsClimate crisisPovertyeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on vocational GCSEs: why now? | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Ministers’ commitment to cutting youth unemployment is admirable, but how new qualifications will help is unclear
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Ministers’ commitment to cutting youth unemployment is admirable, but how new qualifications will help is unclear
Content: ‘It is not clear where a workforce for teaching 14- to 16-year-olds building skills would come from.’Photograph: Getty/Image Source/Posed by modelsView image in fullscreen‘It is not clear where a workforce for teaching 14- to 16-year-olds building skills would come from.’Photograph: Getty/Image Source/Posed by modelsOpinionGCSEsThe Guardian view on vocational GCSEs: why now?EditorialMinisters’ commitment to cutting youth unemployment is admirable, but how new qualifications will help is unclearThu 24 Sep 2026 13.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 18.48 EDTShareThe first question that should be asked about plans to launch abatch of vocational GCSEsis: how will these differ from the roughly 50 similar courses that already exist? Is this primarily a rebadging exercise, aimed at boosting the qualifications’ status and name recognition, while signalling how seriously non-academic education is taken by Andy Burnham and his education secretary, Lucy Powell? Or is there something the matter with the existing courses that they want to put right?The independent curriculumreviewcompleted last year recommended a moratorium on new technical  awards, except where there is an “exceptionally compelling” case for change. It also proposed that the Department for Education analyse existing ones, including how well they prepare pupils for 16-19 education; no such research has appeared.Last year, around 170,000 16-year-olds in England and Walestook a level 2 BTec qualificationalongside GCSEs – the two most popular being health and sport and leisure. They are also studied by post-16 students at further education colleges. While the number of entries is dwarfed by the overall annual total of 5.7m GCSEs, it is not the case that all individual GCSEs have higher take-up. In 2024, for example, just6,723 pupils took a GCSE in dance.View image in fullscreenLucy Powell.Photograph: Thomas Krych/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockThe fact that technical awards are not on the radar of many pupils and parents does not mean that they lack value. Thelow awarenessof vocational options is widely recognised as a problem and was cited by Pepe Di’Iasio, the general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, in response to this week’s announcement. Clearer signposting is expected to be among the recommendations of a review chaired by Charles Clarke, a former education secretary, when it is published later this autumn.The second question about vocational GCSEs is how they will relate to the plans for new V-levels (level 3 qualifications like A-levels), to which the government is already committed. V-levels are due to replace all existing vocational level 3s apart from T-levels, after ministers rejected acampaignaimed at saving some older courses. Will vocational GCSEs be viewed as stepping stones to the new V-level courses? If not, how will duplication and repetition be avoided?For schools, the key issues will be practical. Construction is one of the new GCSEs promised. But there are alreadymany vacanciesfor construction‑related college teaching positions and it is not clear where a workforce for teaching 14- to 16-year-olds building skills would come from – or whether training teachers for new subjects should take priority overexisting shortages.The government’s commitment to getting more young people into jobs is admirable, and ministers are right to push for more work‑experience opportunities. But given the difficulties in this area encountered byT-level students– which led to a watering down of the initial requirement for a placement – it is doubtful whether the aim of getting large numbers of14- to 16-year-olds into workplacesis realistic.There is nothing wrong with rebranding level 2 technical awards and reshaping them if they are shown to be deficient. But given their ambitious reboot of post-16 options, as well as hugely challengingreforms of the special educational needs system, ministers should beware of new GCSEs becoming a distraction. If they are serious about boosting vocational learning, it is the overlooked further education sector that needs attention.Explore more on these topicsGCSEsOpinionVocational educationEducation policyExamsFurther educationDepartment for EducationYoung peopleeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: How Labour could solve the youth jobs crisis | Youth unemployment | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an editorial on creating opportunities for today’s young people to build future careers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an editorial on creating opportunities for today’s young people to build future careers
Content: Labour should become the employer directly, says one reader.Photograph: UK Stock Images Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreenLabour should become the employer directly, says one reader.Photograph: UK Stock Images Ltd/AlamyYouth unemploymentLettersHow Labour could solve the youth jobs crisisReaders respond to an editorial on creating opportunities for today’s young people to build future careersThu 24 Sep 2026 13.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.31 EDTShareYour youth unemployment editorial (18 September) sees the crisis clearly, but reaches for the wrong tools. Placements, apprenticeships and work coaches cannot conjure jobs that do not exist. We need macro solutions to macro problems. Youth unemployment is not a crisis of skills or geography. It is insufficient government deficit spending. There is not enough money circulating to employ everyone who wants to work and that is a policy choice, not an accident.Macroeconomists divide the economy into three sectors: government, households and businesses, and the rest of the world. One sector’s spending is another sector’s income. Put simply, government spending is income for the non-government sectors.All transactions across these three sectors add to zero. With the UK running a persistent current account deficit, money flows continuously abroad. Unless the government runs a deficit large enough to offset that outflow, households and businesses cannot accumulate financial assets. So jobs vanish, wages stagnate, and young people bear the brunt.Indeed, unemployment has long been used deliberately as an inflation management tool. As the US economist Stephanie Kelton notes, orthodox economic policy assumes that a certain amount of unemployment is necessary. When the Bank of England raises rates, it intends to slow activity, and the inexperienced young are always first out of the door.So what should Labour do? Notpay employers £3,000to hire someone that the market won’t touch (an admission that demand is absent), but become the employer directly. A job guarantee, publicly funded and locally administered, would offer anyone a job at a living wage doing socially useful work. It expands in downturns and shrinks in booms, stabilising wages precisely when the economy needs it. It is not welfare. It is work.As a currency issuer, the UK is not constrained like a household. The question is never “can we afford it?”, but “do we have the real resources?” On youth unemployment, we plainly do.Simon RiptonCo-founder, Resilient Economy CICIt doesn’t take a graduate qualification in economics to see that Rachel Reeves’s increase in employers’ national insurance contributions has reduced their ability to take on new people. She has also created a timebomb – as, by reducing the number of new people getting jobs, she has also reduced the number of people able to start paying into pensions.What will happen if young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) never get jobs and so those not on benefits don’t get pensions? I believe the government pays the pension contributions of those on benefits, so surely they could reduce costs by putting money into creating more jobs?How does one stop being a Neet at 24 when jobs don’t magically appear just by getting older? My son is 27 and did what he was supposed to do and got a first-class degree in a Stem subject, but now I support him on my pension. He was unable to do a placement for his degree because of Covid, and 6% compound interest means that his student loan is now a third more than when he graduated.He has applied for almost 500 jobs, temporary and part-time roles, graduate training schemes and apprenticeships. He has even done a government-funded data technician digital skills boot camp, and is now close to giving up.Susan WestQuorn, LeicestershireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Apprenticeships need to be made more accessible | Apprenticeships | The Guardian
description: Letters: Dr Gillian McIver and Don Macdonald respond to an article on the low uptake of apprenticeship schemes
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Dr Gillian McIver and Don Macdonald respond to an article on the low uptake of apprenticeship schemes
Content: ‘We need far more apprenticeships in all fields, but especially in technical ones, and expanding provision would benefit employers as well as young people.’Photograph: Stockbroker/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘We need far more apprenticeships in all fields, but especially in technical ones, and expanding provision would benefit employers as well as young people.’Photograph: Stockbroker/AlamyApprenticeshipsLettersApprenticeships need to be made more accessibleDr Gillian McIverandDon Macdonaldrespond to an article on the low uptake of apprenticeship schemesThu 24 Sep 2026 13.02 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.55 EDTShareI agree with the Fabian Society’s finding that many people struggle to access apprenticeships because the system is so confusing (Only 160 apprenticeship starts in eight months on Labour’s flagship scheme, 21 September).In my work in youth employment, students often tell me that they do not want to go to university and want to pursue an apprenticeship instead. But finding suitable opportunities is extremely difficult.Even with specialist staff available to help them, navigating the process remains challenging, so it is hard to see how young people are expected to manage it independently.Apprenticeships are extremely important. We need far more of them in all fields, but especially in technical ones, and expanding provision would benefit employers as well as young people.Yet the system is labyrinthine and many employers do not appear to be fully up to speed with how it works or what support is available. How can we simplify the process and make apprenticeships accessible?Dr Gillian McIverLondonWhat politicians and civil servants fail to understand about the low take-up of apprenticeships is how bad the situation became under the Conservatives.Youth services were decimated, young people’s work opportunities and expectations were squeezed, and the voluntary sector was allowed to wither.What is needed is something like theFuture Jobs Fund, which created real jobs in community organisations, provided positive work experience and developed relevant skills.It was not cheap, but between 2009 and 2011, the scheme generated a net societal benefit of around £7,750 per participant.Don MacdonaldLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Thank you, Phil Gates, for nearly 40 years of country diaries | The Guardian | The Guardian
description: Letters: Jim McManners says Phil’s columns have inspired his teaching, while Ann MacAskill says she intends to follow his marvelling method
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Jim McManners says Phil’s columns have inspired his teaching, while Ann MacAskill says she intends to follow his marvelling method
Content: Phil Gates pictured in 2007 at an event to celebrate 100 years of the Guardian’s country diary.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhil Gates pictured in 2007 at an event to celebrate 100 years of the Guardian’s country diary.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianThe GuardianLettersThank you, Phil Gates, for nearly 40 years of country diariesJim McMannerssays Phil’s columns have inspired his teaching, whileAnn MacAskillsays she intends to follow his marvelling methodThu 24 Sep 2026 13.02 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.55 EDTShareI was with great sadness that I read that Phil Gates’s country diary piece was to be his last (Country diary: A lesson from my final diary after nearly 40 years – keep looking closely, 19 September). It has become my habit to check the column as soon as I get my hands on the paper to see if it was a “Phil Gates diary day”, then to savour it.This is partly, perhaps, because his diaries are from my own county, but mainly because I have never failed to learn something new and interesting about some overlooked or unspectacular species in the natural world, despite this being my subject.The information in his column would usually find its way into my teaching. I well remember my class of 10-year-olds calculating and measuring their jumps after learning fromPhil’s piecethat a springtail can use its furcula to jump many times its own body length.Jim McMannersTrimdon Grange, County DurhamI do not know anything about Phil Gates, but I must have read and enjoyed countless country diaries by him over the years. These became especially important during a long period of being unable to get outside independently or walk at all. Country diary became my news from the world outside – not news about the never-ending machinations of humankind but of the world I really missed: the sights, sounds and backstories of the wild flower and the calling bird.Now that I am taking my first slow steps into local woods, I intend to follow the Phil Gates method and marvel at what I can find at my feet. There is indeed much marvelling there to carry me on into my 70s as I get back on my feet. Thank you, Phil Gates, whoever you are.Ann MacAskillSheffieldHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: João Félix strike for Portugal enough to sink Wales but Ronaldo fever falls flat | Nations League | The Guardian
description: João Félix’s first-half goal gave Portugal a 1-0 win against a resilient Wales in their Nations League opener
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: João Félix’s first-half goal gave Portugal a 1-0 win against a resilient Wales in their Nations League opener
Content: João Félix of Portugal celebrates with teammates after scoring.Photograph: Gualter Fatia/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJoão Félix of Portugal celebrates with teammates after scoring.Photograph: Gualter Fatia/Getty ImagesNations LeagueJoão Félix strike for Portugal enough to sink Wales but Ronaldo fever falls flatBen Fisherat the José Alvalade StadiumThu 24 Sep 2026 16.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 19.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was a comic-strip feel to another eventful evening in the kingdom of Cristiano Ronaldo. Where to start? It was the 67th minute when his No 7 went up on the fourth official’s board, the cue to remove the captain’s armband from his left bicep before departing to a universal ovation, but for the pocket ofWalessupporters.The referee, Donatas Rumsas, hurried him off the pitch but Ronaldo, his hair glazed copper, was presumably ruminating on a series of missed chances, a sitter from a few yards at the start of the second half, and his disallowed goal, after skating offside to latch on to a Bruno Fernandes pass. The grandiose “Siu” celebration went to waste, though try telling that to the locals who worship him.Gakpo denies Klopp perfect start as Xavi’s Netherlands rescue draw against GermanyRead moreIn the end, Portugal began theirdefence of the Nations Leaguewith a narrow victory courtesy of another Al-Nassr forward, João Felix’s deflected first-half strike from the edge of the box beating Danny Ward in goal.Many of the Wales squad have been lightly raced of late, but they could have snatched a late equaliser when Brennan Johnson hit the crossbar and Rúben Dias desperately denied Lewis Koumas, who again impressed Craig Bellamy. For Wales, this was an exhaustive physical effort and afterwards the head coach, citing his own experiences as a player, referenced how mentally sapping games against elite opposition can prove. “I needed an ice pack on my head,” Bellamy said.All eyes were on Ronaldo, back playing in Lisbon for the first time since last October, at the José Alvalade Stadium where he made his name as a teenager. The 41-year-old started, as Jorge Jesus promised he would, and despite Ronaldo talking of a new era, different tactics and even a different language, alluding to Jesus’s predecessor Roberto Martínez, this all felt rather run of the mill.Rúben Neves, another player in Saudi, replacing João Neves in Portugal’s three-man midfield was the only change from theirWorld Cup last-16 exitby Spain in Dallas.Ronaldo finished with 27 touches, the fewest of any of Portugal’s outfield starters, and looked to the heavens after fluffing the best of the hosts’ chances to extend their lead four minutes into the second half.View image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo sends a shot wide on a night when good fortune in front of goal eluded him.Photograph: Miguel Lemos/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty ImagesNeves put in a delicious cross from the right flank but Ronaldo, unmarked and alone with his thoughts in the six-yard box, shanked the ball over off his left shin. Sunday’s visit to Norway is his next opportunity to edge towards his 1,000 goals target. “I took him out 25 minutes before the end, because I thought it was important to have a fresh player on the pitch,” Jesus said. “I knew that Cris could stay a little longer, five or 10 minutes, but I was going to take him out anyway, I had planned it.” In a previous answer, he added: “Some players who are important were not up to their quality.”Jesus, who twice managed Benfica and spent three years here in charge of Sporting, knows all about Ronaldo, having spent last season coaching him at Al-Nassr and defended the striker on the eve of this game, describing him as a symbol of Portugal. It is hard to disagree on that front. Ronaldo-mania is omnipresent in Lisbon, chiefly inside the official Portugal stores in Praça da Figueira, the city’s downtown, where you can buy CR7-branded briefs, face masks, action figures, lanyards, Lego, and even a Ronaldo boxset celebrating his time at Sporting.Bellamy accepted Wales would suffer against a starting XI boasting five Champions League winners and three Ballon d’Or nominees, but began confidently. Bellamy does not have the same quality at his disposal, with Harry Wilson, Wales’s best performer in recent years, and Karl Darlow, these days the undisputed No 1, among those absent through injury. A harmless Ben Cabango header was Wales’s sole effort at goal in the first half and they did not trouble Diogo Costa. “He practically didn’t have to touch the ball,” Jesus said of his goalkeeper.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIsrael’s Saied Abu Farchi sent off for gun gesture celebration in defeat by AustriaRead moreRonaldo spurned four decent chances in the first half alone, the best of which was from about 12 yards and left him scuffing his boots in frustration. Then, after a predictably excitable buildup, there was a free-kick flighted into Wales’s yellow wall. He should have done better when Fernandes presented him with his first opening amid huge cheers from the locals, but his touch was rusty and the ball bobbled off his left foot, and he later volleyed wide from an awkward angle.Wales were valiant. Jay Dasilva was excellent at left-back. Ben Davies, a Wales centurion and always a dependable performer for his country, marshalled the defence on his second appearance of the season, his only minutes for Tottenham coming against a Charlton B team in the Carabao Cup. Ward’s sole appearance was in the same competition for Wrexham six weeks ago.Portugal racked up 23 shots but recorded only five on target and Wales will take plenty of confidence from this slender defeat. “I’m fully aware of who we were playing and what their value is,” Bellamy said, claiming the value of Portugal’s squad totals £1.4bn. “But the positive I’m coming away with is: I think there’s more [to come from us]. I’m beyond proud. We showed a big heart.”Explore more on these topicsNations LeaguePortugalWalesmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Jos Buttler injury and Kusal Mendis century derail England as Sri Lanka level ODI series | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: The hosts fell short by 16 runs at Headingley after Sri Lanka made 321 for six with their captain Kusal Mendis scoring 121
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: The hosts fell short by 16 runs at Headingley after Sri Lanka made 321 for six with their captain Kusal Mendis scoring 121
Content: England’s Jos Buttler drops to the floor in pain after sustaining an injury against Sri Lanka.Photograph: Allan McKenzie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEngland’s Jos Buttler drops to the floor in pain after sustaining an injury against Sri Lanka.Photograph: Allan McKenzie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockEngland cricket teamJos Buttler injury and Kusal Mendis century derail England as Sri Lanka level ODI seriesWicketkeeper sustains hamstring injury while taking runSeries goes to a decider at the Oval on SundayAli Martinat HeadingleyThu 24 Sep 2026 16.19 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 18.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA beautiful batting surface and a greased lightning outfield made this second one-day international wildly different from the first 48 hours earlier. Unfortunately for England, on the wrong end of a thriller, the result was wildly different too.Set 322 to win, and boosted by a rapid-fire 143-run opening stand between Ben Duckett and Tom Banton, England had appeared on course to wrap up the series with a match to spare. But Sri Lanka refused to give up, delivering a famous shutout and profiting from an injury to Jos Buttler to win by 16 runs.Sri Lanka beat England by 16 runs: second men’s one-day cricket international – liveRead moreIt was agony for Buttler, who had earlier pulled up with a hamstring problem on 66 when the equation was 68 to win off 75 balls. Re-emerging when this became 27 needed off 14, the 36-year-old was unable to run singles, watched Will Jacks hole out for 52, and then eventually perished himself in the final over.As it is, the series now heads to a decider at the Oval on Sunday that Buttler will miss and where Sri Lanka will be buoyant. Their captain, Kusal Mendis, had delivered a sparkling 121 from 100 balls, before Dunith Wellalage’s three-wicket haul and a fine display of death bowling brought a run of four defeats on tour to a juddering halt.“It is always disappointing when you lose,” said Harry Brook, having seen England stumble to 305 for nine. “I thought Sri Lanka played exceptionally well, especially the last 10-15 overs. They were electric in the field. They nailed every ball.“Jos being the player he is, getting injured at that moment isn’t ideal. You can’t dwell on that too much. I don’t think he ever had any doubt in his mind. It was a matter of when we were going to send him out really.“Tight games are always good games to watch and good games to be a part of. Having the opportunity to play in a decider will only benefit us.”Headingley may have been bathed in sunshine for much of the day but half-full stands perhaps said something about the appetite for September internationals in this part of the world. Although try telling that to the Sri Lankan supporters, who outnumbered those of Pakistan during the recent Tests and loved every minute.Their afternoon was lit up by Kusal Mendis and was aided by a string of useful cameos from his teammates. Plenty was loaded in the favour of the batters but the right-hander’s innings was no less thrilling, with 14 fours and three sixes pinging sweetly off the bat to seal his first international century on English soil.View image in fullscreenSri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis scored 121 as his side levelled the ODI series against England.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAOne crucial chance came and went for England, however, when a top-edge off Jamie Overton sent one high into the sky on 17, Gus Atkinson misjudged the ball’s trajectory in the deep and it spilled out of his hands. Had it stuck, England’s task with the bat would probably have been far more straightforward.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAtkinson was the pick of the England bowlers, at least, finishing with two for 55 from his 10 overs and his removal of Kamindu Mendis for 54 – Brook clinical under another high ball – broke a 137-run stand for the second wicket. Rehan Ahmed, who saw his first ball disappear for six, came back well to pick up two for 48 from eight overs.It was tough going in the main, however, with hard length the order of the day for the quicks but the margin for error minimal. Overton saw two chances go down off his bowling and Kusal Mendis successfully review a phantom nick behind on 99. Jofra Archer and Josh Tongue likewise leaked runs, while Jacks was no doubt yearning for the assistance he had enjoyed48 hours earlier.Things were no less tricky when it was Sri Lanka’s turn in the field and Duckett and Banton tucked into some wayward new-ball bowling. But the introduction of Wellalage’s left-arm spin flipped the script, inducing a collapse of three for 14 in 23 balls that sent something of a pleasure cruise into far choppier waters.Duckett was bowled through the gate for 67, Banton was stumped for 73 trying to launch a fourth six, and Brook was pinned lbw for one on review. When Joe Root chipped Sachindu Colombage to cover for 15 – the leg-spinner having otherwise endured a difficult second album following that eye-catching debut on Tuesday – England were suddenly 203 for four in the 29th over.Buttler responded in incendiary fashion. But when his hamstring popped and was followed by Ahmed gloving behind for a five-ball duck, Sri Lanka believed once more. In the end an excellent display of yorkers from their quicks that starved England’s lower order of boundaries proved the difference.Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamSri Lanka cricket teamCricketmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Russell vows to ‘keep fighting’ in F1 title race despite Antonelli’s advantage | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: The Briton said: ‘I want to try and win every single race. That’s my goal’ after  finishing quickest in practice for Saturday’s Azerbaijan Grand Prix
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: The Briton said: ‘I want to try and win every single race. That’s my goal’ after finishing quickest in practice for Saturday’s Azerbaijan Grand Prix
Content: George Russell is 81 points behind his Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli going into the race in Baku.Photograph: Pavel Bednyakov/APView image in fullscreenGeorge Russell is 81 points behind his Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli going into the race in Baku.Photograph: Pavel Bednyakov/APFormula One 2026Russell vows to ‘keep fighting’ in F1 title race despite Antonelli’s advantage‘I want to try and win every single race. That’s my goal’Briton quickest in practice for Azerbaijan Grand PrixGiles RichardsThu 24 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGeorge Russell has insisted he will keep fighting for the Formula One world championship until it is mathematically gone but while he made an encouraging start to his efforts by going quickest in practice for this weekend’s Azerbaijan Grand Prix the makeup of said numbers remains somewhat in limbo.Russell is 81 points behind his Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli going into the race in Baku which is taking place on Saturday to avoid clashing with Azerbaijan’s national remembrance day. The Italian has eight victories this season including the past two in a row, coming through towin from 19thon the grid in Monza and thentaking the flag in Madrid.‘I want to go’: Lewis Hamilton hopes F1 is able to end season in Middle EastRead moreDespite having a mountain to climb Russell has maintained the stoical and determined attitude he has demonstrated all season.“I’m going to keep fighting at every single race until it’s mathematically impossible,” he said in Baku. “I want to try and win every single race and put it on pole at every single race. That’s my goal and that’s what I’m working towards every single weekend.“There’s obviously a huge [points] deficit but it’s not even really a consideration right now. I’m in this position because the performance hasn’t been strong enough.”As things stand nine meetings remain with a potential 233 points still on the table. However, with the races that close the season inQatar and Abu Dhabi still under threatof cancellation because of the war in the Middle East, that number may come down. If both races are cancelled it is understood they will be replaced by one round at Imola, reducing the total by 25 points.F1’s current position is that the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi will go ahead, with a final decision now expected in mid-October after the current triple header of races in Baku, Malaysia and Singapore.Mattia Binotto, the Audi team principal, confirmed that this was the latest the sport could leave it for logistical reasons. “As we discussed during the F1 Commission last Monday, mid-October is the last call for such a decision,” he said. “The main challenges are more organisation and logistics.”After the decision the mathematics will at least be clear. If all nine remaining races take place Antonelli would still take the title if he is 100 points ahead in Mexico or 75 clear in Brazil.On track Russell opened well in Azerbaijan, quickest in first practice in a session where Antonelli lost half his run time with a hydraulic problem. In the afternoon Mercedes were once more on top, looking ominously quick on the street circuit which is energy-starved and plays to their car’s strengths in energy harvesting and deployment. Russell was quickest again, a full half a second up on Antonelli with their nearest competitor, Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, eight-tenths back in third.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026George RussellMercedes GPFormula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK Football Police Unit accused of ‘bringing Hillsborough’ into alcohol debate | Soccer | The Guardian
description: English football’s leading fans’ group has criticised the UK Football Policing Unit for ‘bringing Hillsborough into the debate’ around drinking in sight of the pitch
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: English football’s leading fans’ group has criticised the UK Football Policing Unit for ‘bringing Hillsborough into the debate’ around drinking in sight of the pitch
Content: Andy Burnham’s comments about drinking alcohol in stands met a wary response from police.Photograph: Peter Powell/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham’s comments about drinking alcohol in stands met a wary response from police.Photograph: Peter Powell/AFP/Getty ImagesSoccerUK Football Police Unit accused of ‘bringing Hillsborough’ into alcohol debate‘The disaster was not caused by alcohol,’ says fan groupPolice say they had not intended to make such a linkPress AssociationThu 24 Sep 2026 14.07 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 12.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEnglish football’s leading fans’ group has criticised the UK Football Policing Unit for “bringing Hillsborough into the debate” around drinking in sight of the pitch.Talk of changing the law to allow fans to drink at their seat or in the stands has resurfaced after Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said the rules wereoutdated and discriminatory and should be scrapped.The Football Supporters’ Association (FSA) immediately backed his call but the UKFPU urged caution, stating: “Following a number of football-related tragedies, changes in legislation were implemented after the Taylor Report for good reason and we are currently in the longest ever period without a significant football-related disaster.”Archive, 1985: Alcohol banned from football grounds in England and WalesRead moreThe UKFPU added it would be “incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence”.“The UKFPU would welcome a meeting with the prime minister to discuss his views and explain the challenges these proposed changes would bring to policing and the safety of staff and fans at football games.“Other sports simply don’t see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour. It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games.”The Taylor Report referenced by the UKFPU was commissioned in the wake of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster, which resulted in the deaths of 97 Liverpool fans.The FSApublished a thread on its X accountsetting out its position on drinking in the stands, which began: “Arguably the most important point is that the UK Football Policing Unit’s comments bringing Hillsborough into this debate have to be corrected. The disaster was not caused by alcohol. Full stop. Fans were ‘unlawfully killed and a catalogue of failings by police and the ambulance services contributed to their deaths’.”A spokesperson for the UKFPU said: “It was not our intention to link the issue of alcohol with the Hillsborough tragedy. The laws around alcohol, which we acknowledge were first introduced in 1985, are one of a range of measures in addition to the subsequent Taylor Report recommendations that have contributed to making football much safer for fans in this country.”Burnham’s comments have sparked social media debate in which differing views have been expressed by match-going fans.The FSA’s post on Thursday added: “It’s unfair to criminalise fans for having a pint – especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league. We are fundamentally sceptical of any law which is only targeted at football supporters.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“That doesn’t mean every club should be forced to serve alcohol to every seat! A club should have the choice to do what is right for its fans. Consultation is critical, some stadiums or stands might not be suitable (eg family areas) whereas it might be popular elsewhere.“Ultimately, we think clubs, in liaison with their supporters, should be able to determine what is best for themselves, rather than relying on legislation which is decades old and was written through the prism of viewing all football fans as potential hooligans.”The Sporting Events (Control of Alcohol) Act 1985 prohibits drinking in sight of the pitch in England and Wales in the top five men’s leagues.Burnham said on Wednesday: “I don’t think it’s fair for football fans to be singled out in that way and I made that point. I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different. And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done, perhaps on a trial basis.“But I’m not going to back away from what’s been a long-held view of mine. I don’t see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently from others.”Explore more on these topicsFootballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Raphinha: ‘In my head I was leaving Barça, but a few small words can change you’ | Barcelona | The Guardian
description: The Brazilian had thought his time at Barcelona was ending but now, he tells Sid Lowe, he is thriving as captain and the most potent No 9 in Europe
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: The Brazilian had thought his time at Barcelona was ending but now, he tells Sid Lowe, he is thriving as captain and the most potent No 9 in Europe
Content: Raphinha, the Barcelona and Brazil forward, has relished the twin responsibilities of leading the line and leading the team.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRaphinha, the Barcelona and Brazil forward, has relished the twin responsibilities of leading the line and leading the team.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianBarcelonaInterviewRaphinha: ‘In my head I was leaving Barça, but a few small words can change you’Sid Lowein BarcelonaTwo years ago the Brazilian thought his time at Barcelona was ending but, two La Liga titles later, he is now captain and the most potent No 9 in EuropeThu 24 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor once, Raphael Dias Belloli puts the brakes on. The man who seems to be in perpetual motion, a footballer forever on fast forward, pauses, goes quiet for a moment and then, softly, utters something that says so much: “I think maybe people saw in me something I didn’t realise was there.” He did not know he was a leader, but he likes it. He did not know he was a captain, but according to his manager he is the “perfect captain”. And he did not know he was a No 9 either, but right now he is the best No 9 there is. InBarcelonaor anywhere.There was a time when Raphinha did not know whether he would be in Barcelona, when, feeling unwanted, he had accepted it was over, but this week he extended his contract to 2030. He will be 33 then: he would like to retire here and they would like him to retire here, too, a legend built on empathy and affection. “This is the best decision the club has made,” said Hansi Flick, the head coach Raphinha says changed his life. Sometimes you cannot get what you want so you have to settle for the best.Paper trail of protests: José Mourinho plays the hits in Madrid derby defeat | Sid LoweRead moreThe first word Raphinha uses when training has finished and the tape starts rolling at Sant Joan Despí, when he is addressed as the world’s top No 9, is “false”. It comes with a smile; turns out there is nothingfalseabout this 9. Seven games into the league season, the man filling in at centre-forward has scored 12 goals, plus two in the Champions League. The scorers leading the way in Europe’s other top leagues are five behind. No one in Barcelona’s history has started a season like this. And, no, Raphinha says, he has never played there before: “Even as a kid I wasn’t a 9.”As if it is even about the goals. There may be no one as enjoyable to watch as Raphinha; no one as admirable or important either. The touch at speed is astonishing and there is a wild intensity about everything he does, only it is not wild, he says; it is worked upon, the entire system depending on him. The press defines Barcelona’s identity and it is, Raphinha says, “mechanised”. No, he is not going to reveal how but it begins with him. “As captain, he goes and everyone follows,” Flick says. “We always start with the No 9 and he has that incredible hunger and intensity, the mentality and attitude we need.”Yet this is not what Raphinha or anyone expected. This summer Robert Lewandowski, Ferran Torres and Marcus Rashford departed, having contributed 38 league goals between them last season. They were supposed to be replaced by Julián Álvarez butAtlético Madrid refused to sell, leaving Barcelona with no striker. “There was a moment of need,” Raphinha says. “There was no No 9 for the [friendly] against Basel, so I played there.”Raphinha backs Lamine Yamal to win Ballon d’Or – videoIt was not supposed to be permanent, although Flick suspected it might be and was warming to the idea: Barcelona had not given up on Álvarez yet and the coach considered other solutions, including Anthony Gordon. This was better. Raphinha did not score but Barça got five.“In pre-season we did a few tests: the manager liked what he saw and after Basel he told me a bit about his idea,” Raphinha says. “The adaptation came over the last two years, getting used to coming inside, closer to goal. But we tested [me as] an actual No 9 and it went well. There’s the occasional detail that has to be explained, but I’m OK. Before Elche [on the opening day], he asked if I was comfortable there or wanted to go back to my position. I said it was fine, see how it goes, we can always change back.”Raphinha scored two against Elche, one against Athletic, two against Rayo andanother at Valencia.Against Racing there was a hat-trickand another against Sevilla: right foot, left foot, header. Raphinha showed his old qualities and new, less expected ones: the movement, timing and clinical finishing of a classic No 9, efficiency to go with the intensity. Only one La Liga player has a better shot conversion rate. Against Feyenoord came two more.View image in fullscreenRaphinha (right) is joined by Lamine Yamal – the player he says he is a ‘big brother to’ – after scoring during the Champions League match against Feyenoord.Photograph: Judit Cartiel/Uefa/Getty ImagesNor is it just about him. The point of Raphinha is that it is notevenabout him. Only once this season has he not scored, and against Levante he created the first two, then handed over the penalty for Lamine Yamal to add the third. Barcelona have scored five, two, five, five, five, four, seven and three, respectively in winning their first eight games.Flick had done it again. “I always have and always will say that he changed my mentality, changed me as a person,” Raphinha says.By 2024, Raphinha was convinced he had no future at Barcelona. His numbers were good: 10 goals and 12 assists in his first season, 10 goals and 13 assists in his second. ButLamine Yamal was emergingand, more importantly, Raphinha did not feel backed, completing 90 minutes seven times in 60 games under Xavi Hernández. It had not escaped his attention that Barcelona thought about selling him; it had not escaped anyone’s attention that they wanted to buy Nico Williams, publicly keen to reunite thepair that tore up the Euros.Barcelonafailed twice, and were all the better for it. A Photoshopped image of Williams in his No 11 shirton social media hurt, Raphinha admitted. But Flick had arrived and if there is something even more powerful than the desire to prove people wrong, it is the desire to prove people right.View image in fullscreenRaphinha fires in his team’s fourth goal in the 5-2 win against Rayo Vallecano.Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images“In my head, I knew I was leaving,” Raphinha says. “That was [mentally] done, that’s the truth. I was in Brazil and Flick called. He said come talk to him before taking a final decision. I met him and he said he trusted in me, that I was going to be important, that the team[’s play] would be good for me. In a moment like that, a few small words can change you. I felt a lot of faith in me. He gave me the confidence to play my football. I got an idea into my head: give everything, your life, regardless of the personal moment you’re in.”Love won out, even if Raphinha is swift to add: “If you get results people are going to love you; if not, they’re not.” Feeling supported and valued changed everything. His success is a human story, his qualities human ones. He led Barcelonato the league. Flying in from the left, Raphinha scored 34 goals and provided 26 assists in 57 games.Another titlefollowed in 2025-26 and although injuries reduced his contribution, there were 21 goals and eight assists in 33, Flick’s faith gratefully repaid.His teammates’ faith, too. The dressing room had voted Raphinha as a club captain, third in line. He had not expected it and was genuinely touched. There was something in that moment, in the realisation of how they felt about him, how much they believed in him, that was transformative. Now Flick has named him his first choice.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA jubilant Raphinha with the trophy after winning the Spanish Super Cup against Real Madrid.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesThat moment brings pause, thought. “When I saw people had voted for me, it was like a switch had been flipped, a shift in mindset,” he says. “People could see something in me I didn’t realise was there, and that’s changed me. Before being captain, I didn’t know how much I would like it. Having that responsibility has also changed my mentality, helped me. I never thought I’d like being Barcelona captain so much. You feel you matter. It’s an honour. It’s not just wearing the armband.”He is a natural, as pure a captain as there has been since Carles Puyol – even if he did need to be told. It is there in the relentless example he sets: Raphinha has sprinted the second-furthest distance in La Liga andGradient Sportshas measured only three players with more final-third pressures per 30 minutes out of possession. Raphinha says: “I talk less than most captains but I know people are watching. They think: ‘If this guy’s running like an animal, I have to follow.’. If you talk too much and then don’t do what you have to, people aren’t going to listen.”Yet what teammates saw in him went deeper, to his very being. Leadership is there in the empathy, kindness and understanding too, in Raphinha returning the support that was good for him, an approach at once collective and individual. He says he can see when Lamine Yamal is drifting from games and how to reconnect him, every celebration shared with the teenager. A clip went round recently in which he quietly tells Gordon not to be afraid. And no clip was more powerful, more eloquent, than the moment when Flick sat on the bench, alone, lost in his thoughts andRaphinha consoled him, drawing him out of his dark place, roles reversed.View image in fullscreenFermín López, Raphinha, Lamine Yamal and Anthony Gordon celebrate their team’s third goal against Valencia.Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images“The coach-player relationship is the most important in football,” Raphinha says. “From the moment [Flick] arrived, we could talk to him about anything – and anything isanything. That time, I saw him, head down. At first, I didn’t really understand why. I asked what was wrong. He said he felt the team wasn’t playing well. From what I remember, I told him it was OK, we’d won and we would play well again. I prefer a thousand times to win playing badly than lose playing well. Win games, confidence and the football comes.“What kind of leader [I am] depends on the moment. If I have to be slightly tougher, I can. But I prefer nicer moments, jokes. The last two years have been spectacular so I haven’t had to be thepesado[pain in the arse] often. I know that annoys people but someone has to do it sometimes.”With a squad like this, especially? Four of Barcelona’s first team were born in 2007. “Buah!” Raphinha says, laughing. “That hurts: it shows I’m closer to the end than starting out at 18, 19, like them. But I’m in spectacular physical shape so [retirement] is some way off. It’s very easy with them. There are young players but they’re very responsible about their career, their lives. Once in a while, you have to [be paternal] because they’re kids. But they understand. If they get told off, they know it’s for their own good. I’ll tell them.”View image in fullscreenRaphinha, pictured at the Barcelona training complex, is thriving in the role of captain.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianIs there something of the father figure in him with Lamine Yamal in particular? “No, no,” Raphinha jumps in. “Big brother, that’s better.” And Lamine Yamal is the star who should win the Ballon d’Or, he says: for his “individual numbers, collective titles, and the magic on the pitch, charisma. There’s no doubt. For me, he has to take the prize, no matter what. Even if I wasn’t Lamine’s teammate, for what he does, the numbers, the titles – and I think titles are important – he’sthecandidate. One of one. Of three trophies, he won two with Barcelona. He won the World Cup with Spain.”Only the Champions League escaped them; for two years Barcelona have come close, and it is their obsession now. “Thesemi-final against Inter[in 2025] hurt the most,” Raphinha says. “Against Atlético[in the quarter-final in 2026] we could have gone through, we could talk about things that could have gone differently, decisions. But against Inter, we had one foot in the final and to lose that way was hard. We’re a young team – that’s not an excuse – and sometimes you lack the maturity to manage key moments. This season we’re more mature, better prepared. If we carry on like this, with this mentality, we can compete for it all. We have everything.”Starting from the front with the captain, the leader and the No 9.Explore more on these topicsBarcelonafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Alcaraz tops the bill as the Laver Cup returns to London still aiming to prove its worth | Tennis | The Guardian
description: The Ryder Cup-style event has struggled financially since its legendary founder, Roger Federer, retired but still offers a spectacle unlike any other in tennis
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: The Ryder Cup-style event has struggled financially since its legendary founder, Roger Federer, retired but still offers a spectacle unlike any other in tennis
Content: A fit-again Carlos Alcaraz is the leading light for Team Europe at the Laver Cup.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA fit-again Carlos Alcaraz is the leading light for Team Europe at the Laver Cup.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianTennisAlcaraz tops the bill as the Laver Cup returns to London still aiming to prove its worthThe Ryder Cup-style event has struggled financially since its legendary founder, Roger Federer, retired but still offers a spectacle unlike any other in tennisTumaini CarayolThu 24 Sep 2026 13.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe sight of a tennis player marching to the bathroom between sets has become increasingly common in modern tennis but Alexander Zverev’s journey back to the locker room in Prague nine years ago remains particularly remarkable. On this occasion, Zverev happened to be sandwiched between two of the greatest male players of all time. Neither legend was happy.To his right, an incensed Roger Federer spent their walk back to the locker room brutally laying down the law: “I want a fist pump or a ‘Let’s go!’ every fucking point you win,” he said. “And every point you lose, you fucking take it like a man. Because the problem is, when you don’t have the [result] you want, it’s like:‘Ah, I knew it.Fuck, shit.’I don’t want … honestly!”‘I hope it works’: Tim Henman on Raducanu’s coach and vice-captain duties at Laver CupRead moreAs Federer mercilessly told Zverev off, cursing, shaking his head and even mocking the then-20-year-old’s negative body language until they disappeared into the locker room, his message was amusingly ad-libbed to Zverev’s left by Rafael Nadal, the good cop: “Not one negative face,” he ordered.Prague 2017 marked the first year of the Laver Cup, an event masterminded by Federer and his longtime manager Tony Godsick. If ever there was an image that validated and underlined the value of the competition, a Ryder Cup-style event that pits Team World and Team Europe against each other, it was this one.Catching such an unfiltered glimpse into Federer’s demeanour away from the cameras was rare enough, but this was even more remarkable considering the recipient of Federer’s passion and ire happened to be the fast rising world No 4, one of the players hoping to end his reign at the top of the sport.Nine years on, the Laver Cup returns to London at an interesting point in its development. After initiallybeing viewed as an adversaryto the Davis Cup and ATP events, it is now an official part of the calendar and has firmed up its place in the tennis ecosystem. The event has allowed the likes of Federer, Nadal, Novak Djokovic and Andy Murray to compete alongside each other as well as a score of other top players. Although there is naturallyfar less star poweron the tour today, its current iteration is clearly led byits one global star: Carlos Alcaraz.The tournament’s organisers have long held visions of this event attaining a similar status within tennis as the Ryder Cup; one of the most important events on the calendar. It is difficult to imagine that happening for various reasons, starting with the decision to return to London. While it has always presented a good spectacle, a glance over the Laver Cup’s company accounts suggests a more complicated story.View image in fullscreenTeam World, which includes the world No10 Taylor Fritz (left), are captained by Andre Agassi (right).Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThe tournament made operating losses of £1.8m in Vancouver in 2023, and on the face of it a much healthier £2,000 in 2024, when the event was held in Berlin. However, this includes “non-tournament revenue”, in other words an injection of cash. Without that additional money, Berlin 2024 would have lost £1.5m.By far its best performing events were Boston in 2021, which made an operating profit of £4.9m, and London, which delivered £4.1m in 2022. This is surely a significant reason why the organisers were willing to return four years later. The accounts of San Francisco 2025 have not yet been published. At the moment, it appears that there are a limited number of markets where this event can truly be profitable.Every year since 2017, arguments have raged about whether the Laver Cup should be described as an exhibition, a word that many view as a filthy phrase that describes an unserious hit-and-giggle affair. These arguments seem quite irrelevant. This is obviously, at the very least, a special event considering some of the invitations are arbitrary, its rules are convoluted and there are no ranking points on offer.However, one of the common characteristics of a top tennis player is their intense competitiveness. This event has produced plenty of high-quality tennis and tightly contested matches between players trying their hardest to win.View image in fullscreenThere are no British players in the main lineup for Team Europe, but Arthur Fery is the team’s alternate.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianBut there are limits to the competitive nature of these events. It is hard to imagine the Laver Cup generating the emotions, negative and positive, that some of the biggest events will do. Alcaraz is never going to sit down with his team at the end of the season and anguish over how he let the Laver Cup get away, nor will he put his body on the line and prioritise this event over more important tournaments.That’s fine. The Laver Cup doesn’t have to be enormous or massively meaningful to add great value to the sport. Since its inception, it has been a slick, well-run event that has been willing to innovate and present the sport in a different light. The sight of longtime rivals suddenly working together is incomparable to anything else in the sport and it has been fascinating to see the players’ competitiveness come alive under different circumstances.In the final stretchof a gruelling season, when most players are tired and diehard fans have spent the past nine months watching tennis in the exact same format every week, the Laver Cup also represents a nice interlude before the final run-in to the ATP and Davis Cup Finals. Perhaps most of all, it has repeatedly delivered on what should be the most important aspect of all sporting events: entertainment. It will do so this weekend as tennis returns to the O2 Arena once more.Explore more on these topicsTennisCarlos AlcarazfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fury v Joshua fight confirmed for December at Cardiff’s Principality Stadium | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Tyson Fury will face Anthony Joshua in Cardiff on 11 December after one of the biggest bouts in British boxing history was finally agreed
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: Tyson Fury will face Anthony Joshua in Cardiff on 11 December after one of the biggest bouts in British boxing history was finally agreed
Content: Tyson Fury (left) exchanges words with Anthony Joshua after his fight with Arslanbek Makhmudov in April.Photograph: Mark Robinson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTyson Fury (left) exchanges words with Anthony Joshua after his fight with Arslanbek Makhmudov in April.Photograph: Mark Robinson/Getty ImagesBoxingFury v Joshua fight confirmed for December at Cardiff’s Principality StadiumFight on 11 December will start in UK Saturday small hoursNon-title all-British bout to be streamed globally on NetflixBryan Armen Grahamin New YorkThu 24 Sep 2026 08.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Battle of Britain is officially fixed for Wales. Tyson Fury andAnthony Joshuawill stage their long-awaited heavyweight blockbuster in Cardiff on 11 December after an 11th-hour standoff over the venue that threatened to derail the encounter.The agreement ends years of false starts between the former world champions and clears the way for one of the biggest all-British fights in boxing history. The undercard will take place on a Friday night, with the main-event ringwalks at the Principality Stadium expected in the small hours of Saturday morning – widely reported to be around 2am.That is to accommodate a prime-time American audience for Netflix, which will broadcast it globally after its preferred plan to stage the fight at New York’s Madison Square Garden was scuppered.‘I had a headache for days’: Hrgovic reveals brutal toll of Itauma world title fightRead moreThe non-title bout will represent the culmination of a rivalry that has played out in fits and starts and largely from afar for nearly a decade, but securing the necessary signatures required one final round of brinksmanship between the parties.While both fighters had initially agreed to a November date following their respective July tune-up bouts, the original contract stipulated that the fight would take place in the UK.But Netflix, backed by the Saudi power brokerTurki al-Sheikhand Zuffa Boxing executives, pushed for New York after expressing disappointment with the audience for Fury’s July fight in a UK-friendly time slot, according to a source familiar with the negotiations.That preference became the ultimate impasse in the final negotiations. Eddie Hearn, Joshua’s promoter, resisted the proposed move to New York, seeking a contractual addendum to account for the heavier US tax burden. On Thursday, Hearnsaidthe UK provision had proved decisive.“If we hadn’t put that in the contract, which was a request fromAnthony Joshuathat the fight must be in the UK, we wouldn’t have had a leg to stand on,” he said. “This fight would have been in America.”The dispute also drew in the UFC chief executive,Dana White. Fury welcomed White’s involvement, while Hearn opposed him serving as lead promoter, prompting an expletive-laden broadside from Fury. Thursday’s announcement said Al-Sheikh’s The Ring and White “will collaborate to promote” the fight, while making no mention of Hearn, Frank Warren, Matchroom or Queensberry.Tale of the tape: Fury v JoshuaFury, 38, and Joshua, 36, remained on course for the lucrative meetingafter winningagainst limited opponents on successive nights in July. While Joshuasurvived a scarein Saudi Arabia, Fury stopped the 46-year-old Mariusz Wachinside seven rounds in Thailand.Both men are attempting to return to the summit of boxing’s prestige division after suffering two defeats apiece against Oleksandr Usyk, the unbeaten former undisputed heavyweight champion from Ukraine whorelinquished his remaining world title beltsin June but insists he has not retired. Fury has won twice since returning to the ring, while Joshua has spent the year rebuilding afterhis devastating knockout by Daniel Duboisin 2024.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJoshua (30-4-0, 27 KOs) held the IBF’s version of the heavyweight title across two stints from 2016 to 2019 and 2019 to 2021, making seven successful defences while also winning the WBA and WBO belts.Fury (36-2-1, 25 KOs) first became the lineal and unified world championy dethroning Wladimir Klitschkoin 2015, beforebeing stripped of the IBF titleand later relinquishing his remaining belts during a 31-month layoff that saw him swell to nearly 28st amid public battles with addiction and bipolar disorder. The Manchester nativecompleted an extraordinary comebackto hold the WBC title from 2020 to 2024, defending it three times successfully afterending Deontay Wilder’s five-year reign.The rivals came closest to meeting for the undisputed championship in 2021, but the fight collapsed aftera US arbitrator ruledFury was contractually obligatedto face Wilder for a third time.Joshua subsequentlylost his titles to Usyk, with several attempts to revive the Fury contest falling apart in the years since.The bloom is inevitably off the rose. A fight that once promised to determine the world’s best heavyweight will instead bring together two former champions in their late 30s, each twice beaten by Usyk and closer to the end of his career than the peak. Incredibly, boxing’s long-suffering fansdidn’tget it before GTA 6, yet the many years of thwarted negotiations and mutual ill will between Fury and Joshua have endowed the matchup with an aura compelling enough to eclipse its diminished stakes.There was always something incongruous about an all-British affair of this magnitude finally playing out in New York rather than on UK soil, in front of the supporters whose loyalty and spending helped make both men global stars. Only months after hostingTaylor Swift’s weddingand theKnicks’ drought-busting NBA title run, the Garden appeared to have saved its least likely spectacle for last. But after myriad twists and turns, the biggest British fight that can be made today found its way back to where many felt it always belonged.Explore more on these topicsBoxingTyson FuryAnthony JoshuanewsShareReuse this content

title: Northampton lead Prem charge but history shows title defence will be no simple task | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: Boosted by retaining Henry Pollock, champions are eager to keep improving but a revitalised Saracens and Exeter should push them all the way
Author: Robert Kitson
Headline: Boosted by retaining Henry Pollock, champions are eager to keep improving but a revitalised Saracens and Exeter should push them all the way
Content: Northampton celebrate their title in June. Now comes the harder part – retaining their crown.Photograph: Steve Paston/PAView image in fullscreenNorthampton celebrate their title in June. Now comes the harder part – retaining their crown.Photograph: Steve Paston/PAPrem RugbyAnalysisNorthampton lead Prem charge but history shows title defence will be no simple taskRobert KitsonBoosted by retaining Henry Pollock, champions are eager to keep improving but a revitalised Saracens and Exeter should push them all the wayThu 24 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 16.57 EDTShareIt used to be simple. Win the Prem once and people would assume it was just the beginning. At various times no one could dethrone Bath, Leicester or Saracens, serial winners by fair means or foul. And now? It is so long since any club defended their English domestic title that “doubling up” feels almost as quaint as reading a physical newspaper or chatting up a complete stranger in the pub.Which explains why Northampton’s Phil Dowson, whose side are chasing a third title in four years, is keen to draw a distinct line under what happened last season. Yes, the Saints were unplayably good on occasions and deservedlyclaimed the trophy in June. But that was then. The last team to win two in a row were Saracens in 2019, shortly before the salary cap small print intervened.Three leading Prem clubs in talks with overseas investors on eve of rugby union seasonRead moreThree of the past six champions, as highlighted by the keen-eyed stats guru Russ Petty, did so having finished sixth or lower the previous season. Northampton, for example, finished a lowly eighth in 2024-25. Dowson, accordingly, is wary of assuming anything. He says: “We have to be mindful of complacency and saying: ‘We won the league last year doing this, all we need to do is do this again.’ When actually the key is: ‘What do we have to develop?’”Watching Saints train recently was to sense they will be absolutely fine, early-season injuries permitting. Dowson and his coaching partner, Sam Vesty – rapidly becoming the East Midlands’ answer to Starsky & Hutch – are impressively smart and have been liaising closely with the club’s performance psychologist, Oli Dixon. And, of course, there is Henry Pollock, strutting around the paddock like a thoroughbred racehorse and visibly hungry for more. We’ll forgive him, this time, for all the agent-driven hot air just priorto re-signing for Northampton, the biggest load of Pollocks since Jackson was in his prime.The truth, either way, is that Saints are nicely placed to go back to back, unless the rest can locate another gear. Bath should be right up there, albeit with one or two caveats. The biggest is the departure of Thomas du Toit, their set-piece colossus. Also gone is Alfie Barbeary, who did not start every game but was unfailingly good for squad morale. Nor is it ideal that, if they do make the playoffs, they will not be able to host a semi-final at the soon-to-be-redeveloped Rec. They will be reliably competitive but maybe not impregnable.View image in fullscreenHenry Pollock opting to stay at Northampton was a major boost for the defending champions.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesBehind them in the queue are plenty of other rejuvenated contenders, led by Barbeary’s new employers, Saracens. Brendan Venter, back at the helm in place of Mark McCall, knows only one way and it has never been backwards. Add in the power of George Martin and Barbeary, the class of Tomos Williams and some of the most exciting young backs in the land and, even without the departed Tom Willis, Sarries could be rather more than just makeweights.It is equally hard to imagine Exeter fading quietly away having made last year’s final. On the subject of forceful back-row forwards who love a hard carry, how about Greg Fisilau, Ethan Roots and Kane James, potentially among the league’s fastest-rising talents? Not to mention Tom Hooper, the yet-to-arrive Kiwi centre Dallas McLeod and the irresistible Immanuel Feyi-Waboso. Keep that lot fit and Rob Baxter’s squad will be top-four material again.Leicester? They remain perhaps the trickiest side in the league to assess, not least because Ollie Chessum, Joe Heyes and the rest of the Tigers’ international contingent will have so much on their plates between now and next year’s World Cup. If they finish fifth – one place lower than last year – it will be further proof of the league’s increasing depth.View image in fullscreenExeter’s promising young talent Kane James.Photograph: Matt Impey/ShutterstockA 10-team Prem without relegation also leaves little margin for error, particularly for those who start sluggishly. Which makes this a massive season for Sale Sharks, underachievers last year but bolstered by the arrival of Courtney Lawes, Joe Marchant and Alex Lozowski. They will be desperate to improve on last season’s seventh-place finish but there may be slicker teams out there in a league that quickens in pace by the year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat trend might suit Gloucester who look better organised and more focused than has mostly been the case in recent seasons. No side with Chris Boyd involved lacks for strategic nous and they are not overly constrained by expectation. Again injuries will be crucial but their pre-season form has been positive and the arrival of Dewi Lake and Jac Morgan should deliver the kind of forward dynamism the Shed can get right behind.View image in fullscreenThe Wales international Dewi Lake should give Gloucester added forward energy.Photograph: Chris Fairweather/Huw Evans/ShutterstockIt is even possible they could finish ahead of Bristol Bears for the first time since 2022. At their best the Bears attack as slickly as anyone but memories oftheir sobering 94-33 lossto Northampton at Franklin’s Gardens last season have not entirely faded. Keeping AJ MacGinty and the lock Pedro Rubiolo fit – they won seven of the eight league games in which the latter started last year – will be pivotal if they are to prosper.All of which leaves Newcastle Red Bulls and Harlequins eyeing each other nervously. Both have reshuffled coaching staffs and can be relied upon to be better in a year’s time. As things stand, though, they have a lot to prove, all the more so if they stumble on the season’s opening night. Newcastle are at Franklin’s Gardens while a slightly depleted Quins entertain Bath; start sluggishly and it could be another long, hard winter.The collective big picture, though, is tantalising. It is entirely possible that, by Christmas, the makeup of Steve Borthwick’s 2027 Rugby World Cup squad will also have altered significantly. While Northampton and their chatty man Pollock are in pole position to defend their crown, the modern-day Prem is rarely that straightforward.Explore more on these topicsPrem RugbyRugby unionanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Shaun Edwards inspired by mum’s memory as he beds in with Red Roses | England women's rugby union team | The Guardian
description: Shaun Edwards has proven to the Red Roses he ‘wants to be there and make the players better’ rather than using the women’s game as a stepping stone, according to England’s Jess Breach
Author: Sarah Rendell
Headline: Shaun Edwards has proven to the Red Roses he ‘wants to be there and make the players better’ rather than using the women’s game as a stepping stone, according to England’s Jess Breach
Content: Shaun Edwards with his fellow coach Sarah Hunter and the forward Alex Matthews as England prepare for the Black Ferns.Photograph: Matt Impey/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenShaun Edwards with his fellow coach Sarah Hunter and the forward Alex Matthews as England prepare for the Black Ferns.Photograph: Matt Impey/ShutterstockEngland women's rugby union teamShaun Edwards inspired by mum’s memory as he beds in with Red RosesCoach ‘not just bunny hopping’ says Jess BreachCrowd of nearly 60,000 expected against New ZealandSarah RendellThu 24 Sep 2026 12.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 18.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShaun Edwards has proven to the Red Roses he “wants to be there and to make the players better” rather than using the women’s game as a stepping stone, according to the England wing Jess Breach.Edwards, a rugby league legend and hugely decorated defence coach in union, joined England on a consultancy basis this week and will be with the squad until the end of the WXV Global Series in October. The 59-year-old, who left the France men’s team this summer, has been helping England prepare to take on New Zealand at Twickenham on Saturday in front of almost 60,000.Shaun Edwards finally lands England coaching role after joining Red RosesRead more“I think probably our biggest question around him coming into the programme was why?” Breach, who starts on the wing against the Black Ferns, said. “I think a lot of coaches come into women’s teams to potentially bunny-hop and progress into male teams. Not that we don’t like that, but we want people to be here because they want to be here and they want to make the programme better and they want us to be better.“I think he does want that. He explained the story about his mum and I think it is important and it touched a lot of us, like you do want to be here and you do want to make us better.”At the start of the week Marlie Packer disclosed that Edwards stood in front of the squad and told them one of the reasons he wanted to coach the Red Roses was that his mum, Phyllis, who died in 2021, did not have the opportunity to play rugby. He added it was something his mum thought was “incredible” and she “would have loved to have done it”. Edwards also stated he wanted an insight into the women’s game having never coached in women’s rugby before.England’s head coach, John Mitchell, said on Thursday that before Edwards came into camp he wanted to learn all the players’ names and wanted to see success in the Red Roses’ defensive system.View image in fullscreenJess Breach said Shaun Edwards ‘wanted to be here’ and had demonstrated his commitment to the Red Roses.Photograph: Steve Bardens/RFU/The RFU Collection/Getty ImagesMitchell said he was learning from Edwards, adding: “I am dragging plenty out of him and I am sure he is stealing a few things as well, which is great. As coaches we always want to find something a little bit different that can grow the players or refreshes how you go about things. We are very, very fortunate to have a person of his ability.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMitchell added Edwards has brought his “no nonsense” personality into the team and while he is “highly honoured” to be a part of the England camp, Edwards does not want the limelightEngland are on a 40-game unbeaten streak but will be looking to bounce back after their consecutive-win record ended last Saturday with a26-26 draw against Canada.Explore more on these topicsEngland women's rugby union teamRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rick Wakeman performs piano concert to 150 rescued moon bears in Vietnam | Animal welfare | The Guardian
