description: Former Yes musician plays at sanctuary to raise awareness of animals that remain stuck in cages at ‘bile farms’
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Former Yes musician plays at sanctuary to raise awareness of animals that remain stuck in cages at ‘bile farms’
Content: Rick Wakeman at the piano at the bear sanctuary in Vietnam.Photograph: hson/Animals AsiaView image in fullscreenRick Wakeman at the piano at the bear sanctuary in Vietnam.Photograph: hson/Animals AsiaAnimal welfareRick Wakeman performs piano concert to 150 rescued moon bears in VietnamFormer Yes musician plays at sanctuary to raise awareness of animals that remain stuck in cages at ‘bile farms’Helena HortonThu 24 Sep 2026 11.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRick Wakeman has played to all kinds of people around the globe, but he has now performed to an audience he had never encountered before – an enclosure of 150 bears.The former Yes musician, who has gone on to have a prolific solo career, played the piano at a Vietnamese bear sanctuary.“Before you ask, I won’t be playing the teddy bear’s picnic,” he joked ahead of the performance. Wakeman, who is a supporter of animal welfare causes and has rescue dogs and cats of his own, is conducting the concert to raise awareness of moon bears kept in cruel conditions for the extraction of their bile.He said he was a bit worried about how hot it is going to be. “You know the heatwave we had in England? It’s double that,” he said. “They offered to rig up a fan for me, but I figured that will just blow more hot air around.”View image in fullscreenA moon bear at the bear sanctuary in Tam Dao national park, Vietnam.Photograph: Luong Thai Linh/EPAHis concert was performed live on a Yamaha grand piano positioned inAnimalsAsia’s bear sanctuary in the Tam Dao national park, and Wakeman had written some new compositions especially for rescued bears.Asked whether the bears would enjoy the music, he said: “They’ve not got much choice, really. It’s a well-known fact that all animals react to music, especially gentle melodic music. So what I am going to do is piano music that is melodic, and I can only hope that they will come up to the perimeter of the sanctuary and have a listen.”Rick Wakeman plays piano at bear sanctuaryWakeman has been sponsoring rescue bears since 2016 and recently adopted a new one: “He’s only 20 months old, a big fella, I went to see him today. He came out right to the edge and stood on his back legs and just stared at me, it was brilliant.”Bile is extracted from bears for traditional Chinese medicine by putting a needle into their gall bladder and drawing it out. The bears are kept in poor conditions in countries including China and in Vietnam, where it has just been banned, but where some bears are still in captivity in cramped enclosures. It is the fourth-biggest market in the illegal wildlife trade in east Asia, resulting in a dramatic decline in the Asiatic black bear populations in Vietnam, with nearly a third of their numbers lost around the world in just 30 years.1:04Rick Wakeman plays piano at bear sanctuary – videoOf the sanctuary, which he has been visiting this week, Wakeman said: “To see the bears be rehabilitated, having a life they never had before, some have never put their feet on grass before. They are so wonderful, that we can do such horrendous things to animals is beyond belief. Before this, they were chained in cages sometimes for 10 or 20 years in conditions where they couldn’t even turn around.”He is playing to raise awareness for the bears still stuck in cages in Vietnam and tourge the governmentto get them released: “We have 150 bears at the sanctuary, but there are 125 bears left in cages in the old bear bile farms, and there are four dying a month. We have to get them out quick and into the sanctuary.”He treats his rescue dogs and cats to music back at home in Suffolk. “I had one cat who used to jump on the grand piano, and if I stopped playing he would put his paw in the strings and rattle them until I played again. I know if my dogs don’t like it, they will get up and walk out, and my cats don’t like metal, grunge or rap. They want a melody.”View image in fullscreenBears playing at the sanctuary.Photograph: Luong Thai Linh/EPAWakeman spends hours watching the bears. “If you see these bears it is hard to put into words, they are almost human the way they look at you,” he said. “If you see them, you can’t help but be moved. They aren’t tame but they are very safe, very happy, they play, they romp. I witnessed two today jumping in a bubble bath and playing. They’ve got a life back.”Dr Jill Robinson, the founder and CEO of Animals Asia, said: “We are beyond blessed to have Rick’s support for Animals Asia and the bears. His love for them is immeasurable and can be heard in the beautifully haunting music he has written for them. We’re all so excited to hear his performance in the open air at our sanctuary in the stunning setting of Tam Dao national park. I can’t wait to see how the bears respond.”Wakeman added: “I hope they lay down and have a listen, that would make my day. I would have a big grin on my face.”Explore more on these topicsAnimal welfareAnimalsWildlifeVietnamRick WakemanEndangered habitatsConservationnewsShareReuse this content

title: BBC ‘risks entering inescapable doom spiral’ as further cuts hit TV and radio | BBC | The Guardian
description: Warning from union comes as corporation cuts local specialist correspondent roles as part of plan to save £500m
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Warning from union comes as corporation cuts local specialist correspondent roles as part of plan to save £500m
Content: BBC staff are expecting announcements over the closure of programmes to follow next week.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APView image in fullscreenBBC staff are expecting announcements over the closure of programmes to follow next week.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APBBCBBC ‘risks entering inescapable doom spiral’ as further cuts hit TV and radioWarning from union comes as corporation cuts local specialist correspondent roles as part of plan to save £500mMichael SavageMedia editorThu 24 Sep 2026 12.59 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheBBChas been warned it risks entering a “doom spiral” of endless cuts and weaker public support for its services, as insiders anticipate the imminent closure of some TV and radio services.Morale at the corporation is said to be extremely low as a series of cutsare slowly revealed to staff. In the latest announcement, the BBC said it would be reducing the number of local specialist correspondent roles.It immediately triggered concerns about the loss of expert, local knowledge. The cuts are part of a plan to save £500m and shed up to 2,000 jobs.Staff are now expecting announcements over the closure of programmes to follow next week.Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, has been open with staff for several months that popular shows would have to go, to ease the broadcaster’s mounting financial pressures.There has been speculation that the BBC Three channel could be closed for the second time in its short history. BBC Three, which launched shows includingFleabagandThis Country, was moved online in 2016 before the decision to take it off television was reversed in 2022.BBC radio output is also likely to be affected. Between 350 and 400 hours of audio content will be cut by the end of the next financial year.BBC boss concedes real prospect of strikes over pay and job cutsRead moreBBC Local staff have now been told the corporation would be reducing the number of specialist correspondent roles. Instead, there will be “two dedicated, multi-platform correspondents in every BBC region”.Earlier this week,staff at BBC Sportwere told that 36 more jobs were going, including some senior production journalists.Staff morale had already been hit by a series of cuts announcements this year. In June, it said there would be 550 job cuts in news, nations and TV and radio content. It included theend of Radio 4’s The World Tonightafter more than 50 years.Brittin is making the cuts at the same time asbattling staff over pay– and holding weekly meetings with the government over the BBC’s future funding model.In a comprehensive statement on the cuts, theNational Union of Journalistssaid they risked locking the BBC into producing worse content and lower public support for the licence fee that funds it.“The BBC’s ongoing campaign of cuts is devastating and demoralising for our members and severely undermines the broadcaster’s ability to serve audiences across the UK,” said Laura Davison, general secretary of the National Union of Journalists. “The latest wave of cuts piles on the misery already being felt.“The more cuts the BBC makes, the more its services suffer. This makes it more difficult for the broadcaster to justify public spending, which in turn leads to further cuts. The BBC is at risk of entering an inescapable doom spiral if it continues in this direction.“This is where the UK government must step in. The BBC has been undermined by years of underinvestment and interference.”At the TUC conferencelast week, delegatespasseda motion instructing the body to press the government to intervene over cuts to public service broadcasters.Senior management roles are also being reduced, with 10% of “senior leaders” going. About 700 roles are expected to go across the BBC’s corporate divisions.Explore more on these topicsBBCMedia businessPublic service broadcastingMatt BrittinTelevision industryNational Union of JournalistsMedia unionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Macklemore announces Free Palestine tour to benefit humanitarian aid organisations | Macklemore | The Guardian
description: The US rapper, removed from Ed Sheeran’s US stadium tour after voicing support of Palestine, has convened a charity show that will visit Dublin, Paris and London, with a North American run to be announced
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: The US rapper, removed from Ed Sheeran’s US stadium tour after voicing support of Palestine, has convened a charity show that will visit Dublin, Paris and London, with a North American run to be announced
Content: Macklemore performing in Switzerland in 2025.Photograph: Anthony Anex/Keystone/APView image in fullscreenMacklemore performing in Switzerland in 2025.Photograph: Anthony Anex/Keystone/APMacklemoreMacklemore announces Free Palestine tour to benefit humanitarian aid organisationsThe US rapper, removed from Ed Sheeran’s US stadium tour after voicing support of Palestine, has convened a charity show that will visit Dublin, Paris and London, with a North American run to be announcedLaura SnapesThu 24 Sep 2026 12.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 18.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMacklemore has announced a “Free Palestine” tour, a series of live shows that will feature the US rapper performing alongside musicians and friends to raise funds for humanitarian causes in Palestine.The news comes after Macklemore (AKA Benjamin Haggerty) was removed from Ed Sheeran’s US stadium tour after he called for a “free Palestine” onstage and said he wanted the people of Gaza and “the occupied West Bank” to know “we have not forgotten about them”.The speech, made on 4 September, prompted venue owners to refuse to allow any concerts featuring Macklemore to take place on their property.Sheeran respondedto the backlash over Macklemore’s removal with a written statement in which he declined responsibility for the decision and said: “I am not complicit.”View image in fullscreenA poster for the London date of Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour.All Sheeran’s remaining support acts subsequently dropped out of the tour – Irish songwriter Aaron Rowe, Billie Eilish’s older brother Finneas and Danish band Lukas Graham – alongside the Irish trad group Beoga, who were to accompany Sheeran for portions of the show.Macklemore posted on Instagram alongside his tour announcement: “If these last couple of weeks have shown us anything, it’s that something has shifted over the last three years. There has been a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now.“It’s 2026. Being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work anymore. People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community. To use the stage for more than entertainment. To push back when the call for a FreePalestineis met with attempts to silence it.“What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage. When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention.”On his solo return to the stage in Philadelphia on 19 September, Sheeran read an apology about “making mistakes” from a teleprompter. “I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet,” he said.Small groups of fans protested outside the venue, with some of them having sold their tickets in protest. Other concertgoers said they were sticking by the musician. A tearful Sheeran told the crowd: “Everyone is telling me to cancel, and I’m feeling all of my friends and family and people I know abandon me and I look at the end of the week and I see 50,000 people who haven’t abandoned.”In the days since the controversy kicked off, Sheeran is estimated to have lost almost half a million followers across social media, according todata from Social Blade reported by the Independent.3:09Ed Sheeran sorry for ‘mistakes’ as tour resumes – videoMacklemore’s statement continued: “So, as you all know, my schedule freed up a bit.” He said he had been using his time to contacts “artists who have shown up and used their stages to stand in solidarity with the Palestinian people, regardless of the consequences. Artists who understand that our platforms mean very little if we’re only willing to use them when it’s safe.”No further lineup details have yet been released for Macklemore’s tour.“Because of how quickly all of this has come together, a lot of the conversations, schedules and details are still being worked out,” he wrote. “But this is a moment of momentum, and there is work to be done.”Macklemore’s tour will begin in Dublin on 26 October. Two of Sheeran’s former support acts are Irish and many Irish musicians have been outspoken in their support for the Palestinian people, citing their own country’s history of occupation and oppression, asRowe did in his statementexplaining his departure from Sheeran’s tour:“As Irish people, we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation,” Rowe wrote. “I need to be true to myself and my ancestors who resisted colonisation, and fought for a freedom that I enjoy today in Ireland.”The list of organisations to benefit from the concerts has been shared: Anera, Glia, Gaza Soup Kitchen, Taawon, Heal Palestine, Palestinian Youth Movement, Middle East Children’s Alliance, Jewish Voice for Peace, Medical Aid for Palestinians. Institute for Middle East Understanding, Palestine Children’s Relief Fund and UNRWA USA.A press release said that these organisations “represent the array of work in support of Palestinian people. That includes medical care, humanitarian assistance, education, community support, advocacy, organising and media work connected to Palestinians.”Further dates in Paris (29 October) and London (30 October) have been announced, with North American dates to follow. Fans hoping to get tickets are encouraged to sign up for presale access at macklemore.com.Explore more on these topicsMacklemoreEd SheeranPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukrainians in UK fear homelessness over host scheme funding cuts | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Monthly ‘thank you’ payments for people hosting refugees to be cut from £350 to £100 from next year
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Monthly ‘thank you’ payments for people hosting refugees to be cut from £350 to £100 from next year
Content: Nataliya Rumyantseva, right, is hosting her mother, Valentyna Klymova. She said it would be ‘cruel’ if hosting changed to become a more commercial rental arrangement.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNataliya Rumyantseva, right, is hosting her mother, Valentyna Klymova. She said it would be ‘cruel’ if hosting changed to become a more commercial rental arrangement.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianImmigration and asylumUkrainians in UK fear homelessness over host scheme funding cutsMonthly ‘thank you’ payments for people hosting refugees to be cut from £350 to £100 from next yearDiane TaylorThu 24 Sep 2026 13.45 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkrainian refugees in the UK fear they could be left homeless after the government quietly axed 70% of funding for hosts of theHomes for Ukrainescheme, reducing monthly “thank you” payments to them from £350 to £100.The scheme was launched after Russia’s invasion ofUkrainein February 2022 and has provided support for 181,000 of the 234,000 Ukrainians who have since sought sanctuary in the UK.Now the government has said it will cut the hosting payments and reduce contributions to local authorities, which are paid a sum for each arrival to meet the costs associated with delivering the programme.A writtenstatement to parliamentfrom the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) on 15 September said funding would be reduced from £5,900 to £3,300. The changes will come into effect from 1 January 2027.Tetiana, a 73-year-old Ukrainian refugee who has been hosted for two years and four months, said she was devastated to read the government’s letter circulated to hosts in the last few days informing them of the changes.She said: “I feel that this financial change could impact on my host’s ability to host me. If the hosting comes to an end, I don’t know where I will go and how I can start again. I can’t work because of my age and because I have mobility problems.“I fled from Kharkiv, which is close to the Russia frontline, so I can’t go back to Ukraine. I don’t know what I will do. I’m at a loss about what my options will be. This change has created a lot of uncertainty for me. I don’t know how I would be able to pay rent if hosting finishes for me.”Nataliya Rumyantseva is hosting her mother, the first Ukrainian to arrive in the UK after the war started. She said the changes were likely to have a significant impact. “When refugees arrive here from Ukraine, they are shellshocked and need time to adapt and learn the language. If hosting changes to become a more commercial rental arrangement, I think that’s cruel.”One host who lives in Greenwich said he did not know if he would be able to continue hosting because of the drop in payments. “I’ve been a sponsor since May 2022. I was dismayed to learn that thank you payments are reducing to just £100,” he said. “I lost my job within months of becoming a sponsor and these payments have become an absolute lifeline even though I did not volunteer for this scheme for the money. I genuinely worry about the consequences of this change for Ukrainians in the UK.”One option the government proposes is that hosts can switch to landlord status and charge refugees rent.A host who lives in Cardiff and is hosting a Ukrainian who has enrolled on a course of study said: “The situation feels like a cheap shot from the government. We, in good faith, opened our home to someone in need. That person, in good faith, planned for a life in the UK. And the government, in what seems like very bad faith, saw an easy way to claw money back from people who aren’t in a position to stop them.”The government says it has so far provided more than £1.81bn for the scheme.An MHCLG spokesperson said: “The UK’s commitment to supporting Ukrainians is unwavering and the Homes for Ukraine scheme remains open. As the scheme has evolved from an initial emergency response into a more established programme, these changes are designed to secure the scheme’s long-term future while maintaining support for sponsors, guests and councils.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumUkraineRefugeesHome OfficeEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia could attack a Nato country within months, Danish intelligence says | Nato | The Guardian
description: Warning comes hours after Poland says fire at Starlink satellite station was ‘act of sabotage’
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Warning comes hours after Poland says fire at Starlink satellite station was ‘act of sabotage’
Content: Left to right: Thomas Ahrenkiel, the head of the Danish defence intelligence service; Jeppe Bruus, the defence minister, and Michael Hyldgaard, the chief of defence, at the release of the intelligence report in Copenhagen.Photograph: Ida Marie Odgaard/ReutersView image in fullscreenLeft to right: Thomas Ahrenkiel, the head of the Danish defence intelligence service; Jeppe Bruus, the defence minister, and Michael Hyldgaard, the chief of defence, at the release of the intelligence report in Copenhagen.Photograph: Ida Marie Odgaard/ReutersNatoRussia could attack a Nato country within months, Danish intelligence saysWarning comes hours after Poland says fire at Starlink satellite station was ‘act of sabotage’Pjotr Sauerin KyivThu 24 Sep 2026 12.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia could launch a limited military attack against a Nato country in the coming months, Danish intelligence said, in one of the starkest warnings yet by western security services.In a report published on Thursday, the Danish defence intelligence service warned of a “low but growing risk” that Russia could launch long-range strikes on Nato infrastructure supportingUkraine, or carry out a limited incursion into a neighbouring country with a small number of troops, potentially operating without insignia.The report came hours after a fire at a Starlink satellite station in centralPolandthat local authorities described as an “act of sabotage”.Krzysztof Gawkowski, the deputy prime minister of Poland, said the blaze, which broke out overnight in the Masovian voivodeship, had been “deliberately designed to disable the station”, disrupting internet access for a number of institutions, including the Ukrainian military.View image in fullscreenThe Starlink station in Wola Krobowska, Poland, April 2026.Photograph: Pleiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/ReutersGawkowski said it had not been established who ​was responsible for the fire, but that “many signs suggest this aligns with Russia’s new ‌doctrine ⁠of attack.“While everything is operational today, we must recognise, as prime minister [Donald] Tusk recently noted, that this is an element of hybrid warfare,” he said.Starlink has become a key part of Ukraine’s military communications, and the incident comes amid a spate of suspected Russian sabotage operations across European infrastructure supporting Ukraine.Earlier this month, Germanypublicly blamed Russiafor an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle airport, while a series of other incidents – including fires at drone factories and sabotage targeting rail infrastructure – have also been investigated for possible links to Moscow. Russia has denied involvement in such attacks.European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against NatoRead moreIn recent weeks, several European intelligence chiefs have warned that Russia may bepreparingmore assertive actions to test Nato countries’ commitment to supporting Ukraine, though officials differ over how imminent such a move may be.Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid attacks against European countries with “greater consequences” for those targeted in the coming months, the Danes warned, including “destructive cyber-attacks that cripple societal functions as well as sabotage attacks that carry a high risk of casualties”.A source familiar with Moscow’s thinking agreed that Russia was likely to step up its hybrid attacks.“Russian military top command is convinced someNatocountries are directly involved in the war against Russia – not just by supplying Ukraine with weapons and intelligence, but by helping to guide missiles and drones,” the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity.“They therefore believe Nato is already waging a hybrid war against Russia, and that Russia has the right to respond in kind,” the source added.“Hybrid attacks” are broad terms generally used to describe non-military tactics aimed at pressuring or destabilising an adversary, including cyber-attacks, sabotage and disinformation.The aim of Russia’s actions would be to divert European resources away from supporting Ukraine, and deepen divisions within Nato if the alliance failed to agree on a collective response, the report added.The service believes it remained “highly unlikely” that Russia would launch an outright invasion of a Nato country, but notably said it “cannot be ruled out”.The Danish services said Russia could seek to test Nato’s article 5, which commits members to collective defence. They warned there was “a risk that Russia assesses that the Nato countries will not respond collectively”, particularly if Moscow believes the US is unable or unwilling to support its European allies in a potential war with Russia.There have been ongoing jitters among Nato members over whether the alliance’s most powerful member, the US, would come to Europe’s defence under Donald Trump in the event of a Russian attack.Questions over unity within Europe are also growing. Last week, Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, who has maintained close ties with the Kremlin, cast doubt on his country’s commitment to Nato’s collective defence principle, saying he did not want Slovakia drawn into a military conflict “because of some article 5”.Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia continued to threaten countries beyond Ukraine, including Moldova, Poland and the Baltic states, while showing “no respect” for the sovereignty of countries in the south Caucasus and central Asia.“The more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else,” he said.Explore more on these topicsNatoRussiaDenmarkPolandUkraineEspionageEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Backlash as Indian oil heir made professor of sustainability by Newcastle University | Newcastle University | The Guardian
description: Role for Anant Ambani, son of India’s richest person, who also runs a controversial mega-zoo, met with incredulity
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Role for Anant Ambani, son of India’s richest person, who also runs a controversial mega-zoo, met with incredulity
Content: Anant Amabani, 31, is worth an estimated £90bn.Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/ReutersView image in fullscreenAnant Amabani, 31, is worth an estimated £90bn.Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/ReutersNewcastle UniversityBacklash as Indian oil heir made professor of sustainability by Newcastle UniversityRole for Anant Ambani, son of India’s richest person, who also runs a controversial mega-zoo, met with incredulityRachel HallandPatrick GreenfieldThu 24 Sep 2026 06.26 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNewcastle University is facing a backlash from conservationists over the appointment of the heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune who runs a controversial mega-zoo as a professor of sustainability.The university announced that Anant Ambani had been given a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship” and “significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”.Ambani is the son of India’s richest person, Mukesh Ambani, who made his fortune primarily in oil and gas, owns the world’s largest oil refinery and has close ties with the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Mukesh Ambani has enthusiastically praised BJP policies, and firms linked to his Reliance conglomerate have recently made significant donations to the party. The prime minister, Narendra Modi, attended Anant Ambani’s lavish 2024 wedding in Mumbai.Anant Amabani, 31, who is leads on renewable energy on the Reliance Group’s executive board and is worth an estimated £90bn, has set up Vantara, a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near the family’s oil refining facilities in Gujarat, which reportedly has more than 150,000 animals including 200 lions, 250 leopards and 900 crocodiles, and where he hosted his opulent pre-wedding celebrations attended by celebrity guests and politicians.Conservation groups have previously raised questions about how some of the animals were sourced, given many were endangered species. Vantara has never been found guilty of any wrongdoing.View image in fullscreenThe Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, visiting the Vantara zoo in Gujarat in March 2025.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesThe university’s announcement was met with incredulity and derision from academic staff and Indian and international conservationists and environmentalists.Ramachandra Guha, a leading Indian public intellectual and the author of the book Speaking With Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism, said: “I must say that it is a rather mystifying choice. As a scholar of Indian and global environmentalism, I can name at least 50 – perhaps 100 – individuals who are far better qualified to be thus honoured. They include soil scientists, energy scientists, water conservation experts, community forest workers, ecologists, pollution abatement experts etc who have made real and tangible contributions to a more sustainable future for India and Indians.“I wonder on whose adviceNewcastleUniversity has acted, and whether it did due diligence on what has and has not been done in these fields. Its appointment of Mr Ambani is puzzling in the extreme, and is likely to adversely affect the university’s institutional credibility and intellectual standing.”View image in fullscreenA Newcastle University spokesperson said the professorship ‘recognises Mr Ambani’s contributions to conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship’.Photograph: Washington Imaging/AlamyBhuvan Mangalore, an Indian investigator into illegal wildlife trade who is completing a dissertation on Vantara at Anglia Ruskin University, asked: “Is this a joke?”Prof Matt Perry, the chair of the University and College Union branch at Newcastle University, said staff members had objected to the appointment citing environmental concerns.Prof Lyla Mehta, the head of the climate, environment and sustainability department at the University of Sussex’s Institute of Development Studies, shared concerns that “as public funding for universities falls, there is a real danger that billionaire and corporate money begins to shape academia”.She said: “Universities are supposed to be places that question power and hold corporations to account, not give them academic legitimacy.”In April, AnantAmbani launched Vantara University, billed as the world’s first global university dedicated to wildlife conservation and veterinary science.Lorne Stockman, a research co-director at Oil Change International, said: “At a time when the climate crisis demands an urgent phaseout of oil and gas, we must demand our publicly funded institutions do better.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn 2025, aninvestigation by the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitungfound that many animals delivered to Vantara arrived through countries with opaque wildlife trading networks such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United Arab Emirates, raising concerns that endangered species may have been illegally trafficked.In August last year, an investigation by India’s supreme court, which lasted less than three weeks, cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing. A subsequentfact-finding missioninto the zooby Cites, the UN body that regulates the trade of endangered species, found that some of the permits used to bring animals to Vantara were probably forged.Itsreport said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”Cites recommended restrictions on India’s imports of endangered wild animals. However, it subsequently reversed its decision after objections from India, the US and Japan at a Cites meeting after they argued there was not enough proof of illegal imports.In August, the zoo launched a “reset” in its operations by appointing a former Cites head to oversee its operations and said it would voluntarily pause all wildlife imports until June next year.View image in fullscreenAn employee watching news related to Vantara on a website at his office in Bengaluru.Photograph: Idrees Mohammed/AFP/Getty ImagesVantara has declined to comment. The Ambani family and Vantara have previously denied the allegations of wildlife trafficking. They have said: “Our mission and focus continues to be the rescue, rehabilitation and care of animals.”A Newcastle University spokesperson said: “The award of a professorship of practice recognises Mr Ambani’s contributions to conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship through his work with Vantara, a wildlife rescue and conservation initiative, and as the executive lead for the Reliance Group’s transition toward a green energy future.”Explore more on these topicsNewcastle UniversitySustainabilityConservationZoosIndiaSouth and central AsiaUniversitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The eels were climbing out of the water to die’: why did every fish in this idyllic lake perish overnight? | Pollution | The Guardian
description: Furnace Brook in East Sussex was home to carp, tench, bream, roach and trout – and 15 trailer-loads had to be buried. The mystery led to a neighbouring farm, and a story of waste, pollution and dirty rivers that reveals a lot about Britain today
Author: Steve Rose
Headline: Furnace Brook in East Sussex was home to carp, tench, bream, roach and trout – and 15 trailer-loads had to be buried. The mystery led to a neighbouring farm, and a story of waste, pollution and dirty rivers that reveals a lot about Britain today
Content: ‘It’s so beautiful’ … Diane and Alistair Gould by the lake at Furnace Brook.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It’s so beautiful’ … Diane and Alistair Gould by the lake at Furnace Brook.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianPollution‘The eels were climbing out of the water to die’: why did every fish in this idyllic lake perish overnight?Furnace Brook in East Sussex was home to carp, tench, bream, roach and trout – and 15 trailer-loads had to be buried. The mystery led to a neighbouring farm, and a story of waste, pollution and dirty rivers that reveals a lot about Britain todaySteve RoseThu 24 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 06.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Alistair and Diane Gould bought Furnace Brook in 2013, they had big plans. It was an idyllic spot: a stream-fed fishing lake nestled in a secluded valley in the High Weald, East Sussex, surrounded by woodland and fields. “People loved to come fishing here because it’s so beautiful,” says Diane. “Some of them had been coming for so many years that they got to know the individual fish.”Diane moved here from Kent in 2000, whenFurnace Brookwas owned by a distant relative. Her two younger sons, then 10 and 14, flourished. They would chat to the anglers about the fish they were catching and throwing back in, and sell them bacon sandwiches. Her elder son, Simon, moved from London to join them in 2006 and became a keen angler himself, and then the fishing manager, or bailiff, looking after the fish and the landscape around the lake.View image in fullscreenEd, a local angler, at Furnace Brook.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianDiane, who is 68, and Alistair, 69, met in 2008. After Diane’s relative died, they decided to buy the property. Alistair, an ecological consultant witha background in low-carbon design, had drawn up a plan to restore the entire ecosystem of the eight-hectare (20-acre) site.But two years ago, their plans were blown out of the water.On the morning of 20 June 2024, Alistair and Simon walked down to the lake and noticed dead fish floating on the surface. “We looked at it and thought: ‘This is a bit odd,’” says Alistair. On further inspection, almost everything in the 2.4-hectare lake was dead. “It brings tears to my eyes,” says Diane. There were at least 15 species of fish in the lake, she adds: carp, tench, bream, roach, trout and some large eels. “You get a sort of relationship with them, as living beings.” The larger fish even had names.“It was very traumatic for us all,” Alistair continues. “Obviously for nature directly, but also seeing all these fish on the surface and the fact that Simon has been a fishery bailiff here for 15-plus years and these are his babies, and he’s just seeing them all curl up and die.”View image in fullscreenMassacre … 15 trailer-loads of dead fish were removed from the lake.Photograph: Courtesy of Furnace BrookDiane continues: “More than 2,000 fish were dead. Plus, the ones we don’t know about that sank to the bottom. The eels were climbing out of the lake to die.” Eels are pretty hardy, says Alistair; they can even travel over land if they need to. To see them gasping and dying on the banks was heartbreaking. “It was apocalyptic.”At first, the Goulds thought it must be their fault, that they had mismanaged the fish stocks somehow. But when Alistair walked to the top of the lake, he saw that Clippenham stream, which feeds the lake, was also full of dead fish. “That’s when I twigged: ‘This isn’t us. There’s something else going on.’” It seemed clear to him that pollution was coming from somewhere upstream. “All down the stream, our friends were finding dead fish: lamprey, brown trout, freshwater mussels,” says Diane. The stream runs to the Pevensey Levels on the south coast, where water is extracted for drinking and agriculture.View image in fullscreen‘The eels were climbing out of the lake to die.’Photograph: Courtesy of Furnace BrookThey immediately called the Environment Agency (EA), the body responsible for the “protection and enhancement” of the environment in England, which visited two days later and declared it aCategory 1 incident, the most severe kind, meaning it had “a serious, extensive or persistent impact on the environment, people or property”. The Goulds and their team removed 15 trailer loads of dead fish from the lake, which the EA advised them to bury. Their angling business was gone overnight. They estimate they have lost £500,000 in income so far. A biologist later estimated that the lake would take 10 to 15 years to recover. “It’s not just the loss of money,” says Alistair. “It’s the loss of the ecological function.”The story of Furnace Brook could be Britain in microcosm. We take pride in our rural heritage, in the natural beauty of our countryside, but the illusion that it is an unspoilt, unchanging idyll is becoming ever harder to maintain.River pollution has become a national scandal. The release of sewage by privatised water companies – illegal but persistent and apparently unpoliced – has devastated landscapes throughout England. Often, we register this in terms of how picturesque our rivers are or how safe they are to swim in – how the pollution affects us directly – but beneath the surface, decades of pollution have decimated how much life they can support. According togovernment statisticsfrom 2025, just 14% of England’s rivers and lakes have a “good ecological status” and every one of them is polluted with chemicals.Illegal dumping has become a separate scandal, the scale and effects of which also seem beyond authorities’ control. In the past 12 months, there have been high-profile cases such as the 150-metre-longmountain of rubbish“discovered” in Kidlington, Oxfordshire, or the 35,000 tonnes of rubbish dumpedin Hoad’s Wood, Kent, the latter of which cost an estimated £15m to clean up.In August, Andy Burnham visited another huge, foul-smelling illegal dump, in Midland Road, Bradford, where he vowed to take action, declaring: “The days of making easy money out of waste are over.” He has a (waste) mountain to climb. Over the past two decades, successive governments have loosened environmental regulations and removed protections – not least by neutering the EA.View image in fullscreenThe aftermath … Simon Dole, Furnace Brook angling coordinator and coach, holds one of the dead fish.Photograph: Courtesy of Furnace BrookThe fact that this is happening in the countryside, sometimes in isolated areas, makes it hard to monitor or police. Furnace Brook is a symptom of all these problems, although it could also become a model for how to overcome them. The Goulds are working on a plan not only to restore the landscape, but also to show how we could reset our relationship to it in a more sustainable, nature-friendly, community-oriented way.In the case of Furnace Brook, the water companies were not to blame. So the Goulds set out to discover what was. “I thought: ‘I bet I know exactly where that’s come from,’” says Jack (not his real name),Furnace Brook’s former ecological consultant, who has worked in the area for decades and knows the landscape intimately. He remembers walking up Clippenham stream two days after the pollution event. “It was hot weather and the whole of the valley stank. It smelled of dead fish and aquatic life. I thought: ‘It’s probably something that’s come off another property. And if any of the properties around here are likely to be doing something unpleasant like that, I’ll put money on it that I know which one it was.”He headed about half a mile up the valley to a tributary joining the stream from a neighbouring property named Morgans Farm. “You could clearly see the water upstream [of the tributary] was totally normal, a sandy colour with clay silt in it, and what was below it had gone a blue-black colour. You could see dead brook trout, wild eels, and there was a dead crow or raven, which may well have eaten something poisonous from the river.” In some places, he says, there was a thick layer of blue-grey scum on the water, which he later learned is sometimes called “bacterial cheese”. “There’s so much nutrient [sic] in the water that it allows for a bacterial colonisation explosion.” The bacteria take up all the oxygen, which causes most of the fish, especially the older, larger ones, to die.Jack followed the polluted tributary up through Ann Wood, a small pocket of ancient woodland on Morgans Farm. The source of the tributary seemed to be a large hole or pit at the north-west corner of the wood, in a cleared area, accessible by heavy vehicle. In one council document, it is referred to as a “slurry lagoon”. Shortly after the pollution incident, this hole was filled in and covered with waste soil. When I visited in September 2025, the area where the hole had been was obscured beneath a stack of hundreds of plastic-wrapped hay bales.When EA officers visited in the days after the pollution event, they were shown the devastation and the suspected source of the pollution. They took water samples from various locations. One officer also visited Morgans Farm. The EA has the power to investigate and prosecute those in breach of environmental protection laws, which can result in fines or even imprisonment for offenders, but the process is notoriously slow. Investigations can take years and rarely result in meaningful penalties. More than two years later, the EA has yet to take action over the incident at Furnace Brook.View image in fullscreen‘Bacterial cheese’ … the fishing lake at Furnace Brook with scum from pollution on its surface.Photograph: Courtesy of Furnace BrookIn the interim, Alistair and his team took matters into their own hands. They bought equipment to test the water for factors such as dissolved oxygen, dissolved solids and conductivity. They also tested for heavy metals, such as lead, cadmium, arsenic and mercury, which are usually a byproduct of industrial, rather than agricultural, processes. You can do crude tests for them with a paper strip that changes colour from orange through to dark purple. When they tested the water coming from Morgans Farm, it was “off the chart”, says Jack. “This went about as deep into the purple as you possibly could go.”A year later, in July 2025, Furnace Brook sent samples of water collected from the lake to an independent testing lab. The results still found unusually high levels of heavy metals, ammonia levels that were “well outside acceptable limits for any freshwater life” and nitrogen levels that were “toxic to all aquatic life”.What was going on at Morgans Farm? Quite a lot, according to its neighbours. Going by planning statements submitted by Morgans Farm, the owners farmed “a mix of cattle and sheep spread out over 243 hectares throughout Sussex”. Several large agricultural barns and other buildings have been constructed on the property, with planning permission. In 2022, the owners also applied for planning permission to extend an existing forestry track down one edge of Ann Wood, parallel to the suspected tributary. Permission was withheld – the woods are classified as “ancient and semi-natural woodland” and an “irreplaceable habitat” – but a 300-metre surfaced track was built anyway.View image in fullscreenVolunteers carrying out a monthly water test on the river.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianOver the years, Furnace Brook and other neighbours have seen a steady succession of tipper trucks arriving at Morgans Farm and depositing material on the land, some travelling down the new surfaced track and on to the lower part of the farm, closest to Clippenham stream. This activity preceded the pollution incident, but increased afterwards and has continued since.Some days, trucks arrived every 10 minutes, says Jack. They would queue up, he says, pointing across the valley to the main road that passes Morgans Farm, before “travelling down and going into various different meadows and just tipping these heaps”. They have also observed material from the trucks being tipped into dug trenches in the fields, before soil is spread over the top. There is a mechanical excavator and a bulldozer on the site, says Jack: “They were using both of those flat-out, day after day, week after week, month after month, piling individual piles up into huge single piles.“Then we noticed other activity: the excavator was making enormous, deep holes in the ground and they were bringing lorries in and emptying stuff into the holes, then using other soil from the site to cover the holes over. We were like: ‘What are they putting in? What are they digging and burying and then covering over?’ Because that’s, I believe, how the original spill took place.”On my first visit to Furnace Book, in April 2025, large heaps of what looked like soil and manure were clearly visible on the lower fields of Morgans Farm. Jack has seen them up close. “The heaps were a very, very low grade of kind of compressed clay topsoil, sort of slag mixed with chunks of ceramic, red brick, tarmac scalpings – which are toxic to aquatic life and have to be controlled and licensed in their storage and their implementation on farmland, according to the government’s own laws. There was a lot of plastic refuse in there, plasterboard, all sorts of foreign objects, which I would not consider to be a clean, acceptable level to be putting all over permanent pasture in a protected landscape.”View image in fullscreenA digger on neighbouring land at Furnace Brook.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianWhen I returned in September 2025, there were even more signs of activity: previously green pastures now appeared to be barren brown fields, with soil or construction waste spread across them. “When it rains, that leaches huge amounts of very negative ammonia and nitrates into the watercourses,” Jack says. He and the Furnace Brook team have been testing the water continually since the pollution event. They have continued to find high levels of heavy metals, ammonia and long-chain hydrocarbons – compounds associated with industrial processes.Other neighbours also say they have witnessed the trucks, sometimes as many as 30 to 40 a day, and into the night, arriving full at Morgans Farm and leaving empty. Material is now being deposited on the upper part of Morgans Farm as well. Where once there were pastures and ponds, now it is mostly bare soil and rubble. “England’s green and pleasant land,” the neighbour says sarcastically.One of the neighbours shows me drone footage they took in March 2022 that appears to confirm Jack’s observations. It clearly shows a deep hole on Morgans Farm – about four metres in diameter and 10 metres deep – in a different location from the suspected source of the pollution incident. A large mechanical digger is scooping material out of the hole, as a truck full of an unknown substance reverses towards it.Almost all the trucks seen bringing materials to Morgans Farm have come from one company: Robins of Herstmonceux, a family-run waste transfer company and supplier of topsoils and building materials, which has operated in the area for more than 60 years. Its vehicles are a familiar sight in the area. Thecompany’s websiteclaims it is “able to recycle 100% of inert waste received” and to produce and deliver “recycled materials such as crushed concrete … and screened soils”.View image in fullscreenThe river that runs into the fishing lake.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianThere are complex rules concerning what materials can and can’t be put on farmland, in what quantities and for what uses. In March 2024, three months before the pollution incident, Robins of Herstmonceux and Morgans Farm obtained what is known as aU1 exemptionfrom the EA. This means they were permitted to use a limited amount of “suitable waste for construction projects and maintenance work” on the site: up to 5,000 tonnes of non-hazardous waste from construction over three years, for example. By Furnace Brook’s estimate, in 2025 alone, counting the number of trucks that have come into the farm, more than 15,000 tonnes of material was deposited at Morgans Farm.Even so, this activity may not have been illegal. As well as the U1 exemption, there is another route landowners can take to import materials on to their land, known as CL:AIRE, which stands for Contaminated Land: Applications in Real Environments. The CL:AIRE scheme, a registered charity, enables the reuse of excavated material “without the need for traditional waste regulatory controls such as permits and exemptions”, according to itsintroductory video.Essentially, it connects people generating large amounts of such material (construction sites, say) with people who might have a use for that soil “in a pre-identified place for a pre-identified purpose”. This makes sense from a sustainability perspective – the waste soil would otherwise go into a landfill. According to CL:AIRE, the process has plenty of checks and balances: each project requires a detailed “materials management plan” and a “qualified person” (such as the landowner) who must submit a declaration to the EA, as well as a verification report after the work is completed to confirm that it was done properly.However, the CL:AIRE code of practice is apparently self-regulated and details of its extent or participants are opaque. Morgans Farm was mentioned as being part of the CL:AIRE scheme in a letter from the EA, but in response to requests for more details, CL:AIRE replied that “we cannot share any scheme-specific or participant-level information with you” and that “managed schemes are treated as strictly confidential”. That leaves a great many questions unanswered. How much material was Morgans Farm permitted to import under this scheme? How well was it being monitored? Where was all this material coming from? How many other properties are operating under similar conditions?Morgans Farm and Robins of Herstmonceux were approached for comment regarding these issues, but neither responded.View image in fullscreenNew material deposited on neighbouring land at Furnace Brook.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianEnvironmental groups, politicians and employees from government agencies all told me of their frustration at how powerless they are to act over what is happening at Furnace Brook and in many other cases like it, locally and nationally.“It brought me down to earth with a bump to discover how little power a district council appears to have over such things,” saysGreg Collins, a Green party councillor for Wealden district council, in which Furnace Brook is situated. Wealden is one of five district and borough councils within the county of East Sussex and at present it is under joint Green and Liberal Democrat control. (Diane Gould has been a Green party councillor for Wealden since July 2025.)Collins continues: “My understanding is – and I am satisfied that I’ve kicked the tyres hard on this – that the district council has no effective powers in respect of the event that damaged the ecology of Furnace Brook. That is an EA matter. They own the regulatory regime that would deal with that and my understanding is that they’ve effectively gone: ‘Nothing to see here. Move along. Hey-ho, life’s a bit shit sometimes.’”The EA investigation is showing little apparent progress, nearly two years later. In a letter last July, the EA wrote that it had visited Morgans Farm in late 2024 and early 2025, alongside other district and county council officials. “Having regard to all the circumstances, and in consultation with other agencies, we, theEnvironment Agency, have not found any evidence of the illegal importation of waste to Morgans Farm,” it wrote.The EA was approached for comment and responded: “We take the incident at Furnace Brook Fishery very seriously and are progressing with our investigation. As this is an ongoing case, further details cannot be provided at this time.”In the recent Channel 4 seriesDirty Business, a docudrama that exposed water companies’ role in river pollution, the EA is portrayed as under-resourced, reluctant to take action and unhealthily close to the corporations it is supposed to police. There is evidence to support this. In January 2022, three EA officerstold the Guardianthe agency was increasingly unable to hold polluters to account or to improve the environment as a result of the body’s policies. Government grants to the EA have grown from£800m in 2016-17to£1.8bn in 2024-25, but its powers apparently continue to diminish.“Should a polluter be caught, any tools that were at [the EA’s] disposal to take action have been systematically removed,” a whistleblower said in 2022. “Officers are actively encouraged not to take enforcement action.” Another whistleblowerlast year revealedthat the EA did not send investigators to nearly a third of reported water industry incidents in 2024. In July 2025,the EA admittedthat, due to staff shortages, thousands of water samples from pollution incidents had not yet been tested, or never would be.While water and river pollution are ostensibly the EA’s domain, matters of waste, dumping and contaminated land ought to be policed by local government. But, again, a lack of funding and resources has hampered this, says Rachel Millward, the leader of Wealden district council and the deputy leader of the Green Party in England and Wales. She says: “The basic issue is that the policy is there, but it has no teeth, because it doesn’t have funding so that the authorities who are meant to do it can do it, and then there’s no real threat of prosecution.”Millward and other councillors point to the contaminated land regime, laid out in part 2A of theEnvironmental Protection Act, which requires local authorities to identify and monitor contaminated sites in their district.According to Wealden district council’s website, “there are no formally determined contaminated land sites in the Wealden District” and, owing to lack of funding, “the council is not currently pursuing strategic site inspections”. In other words, says Millward: “Councils have stopped making contaminated land registers and stopped updating them because they can’t afford to do it.”View image in fullscreenA holiday cottage on the lake at Furnace Brook.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianContaminated land is often identified only when a developer comes along and wants to build on it. Then the developer must pay for removing those contaminants; it becomes a planning matter, rather than an environmental one. But the planning system is also underfunded and incapable of monitoring such issues, according to insiders. “The planning system is designed toencouragedevelopment; it’s not designed to prevent it,” says Collins. “The rules are there to create the impression in the minds of the public that there is some sort of jeopardy if you break the rules. They are not there so that you actually experience that jeopardy.”The pressure to build new homes only puts more strain on rural areas. To meet government targets, Wealden district council is expected to addmore than 1,400 new homes a yearto its housing stock. According to one planning expert, the town of Hailsham, five miles from Furnace Brook, has more than doubled in size in the past decade. Several sources wondered if there were connections between this scale of construction and the materials arriving at Morgans Farm.A spokesperson for Wealden district council responded: “The council does not accept the assertion that planning enforcement is weak. Our planning enforcement team investigates reported breaches and takes proportionate action in line with national policy, legislation and the council’s adopted enforcement approach. Planning enforcement is intended to remedy unacceptable harm caused by breaches of planning control; it is not a mechanism for preventing development that has planning permission.”‘Small changes can make a big difference’: how getting farmers, fishers and beavers together could save a Cornish riverRead moreIn terms of illegal dumping, the local picture is also bleak, says Collins. “Anybody who drives around the district sees so much casual fly-tipping. If they stopped to think about it, it would be hard for them not to come to the conclusion that there is a large-scale problem.”Other sources close to local government in East Sussex, who did not wish to be identified, are in despair at the situation. “There is so much to do with illegal waste disposal, organised criminality and the failure of agencies to apprehend these issues that it’s just depressing and extraordinary,” one insider says. “It’s so expensive to dispose of waste legally that many people attempt to do it illegally. And there are plenty of dubious arrangements to be arrived at between operators and landowners which are financially beneficial to both. It’s very difficult with our resources to keep up with those.”Wealden district council responded that it has “one of the lowest reported levels of fly-tipping in East Sussex” and that “the number of recorded incidents in the district has fallen over the past five years”.A report shared with the Guardian in November 2025 found that there wereat least 8,000 illegal dumping sitesin the UK, containing approximately 13m tonnes of rubbish. When Air & Space Evidence, the satellite company that helped compile the report, presented its findings to the EA, it said there was little interest at the management level. “From the outside, this looks like a fear of finding out. If the Environment Agency finds more illegal waste sites, then they feel they will have to do something about them. So, they would rather not know.” The EA has said itstopped activity at 743 illegal waste sitesin 2024-25. Itreceived 10,238 reportsof suspected waste crime in 2025.This March, the House of Commons’ public accounts select committee issued areport on environmental regulationin England. It concluded that the system needs to be overhauled. It stated: “We are concerned about the recent rise of illegal waste dumping. Gaps in the Environment Agency’s powers and intelligence have led to delays in responding to a problem that is out of control.”If Furnace Brook is Britain’s polluted countryside in microcosm, it could also become a model for how to fix it. The pollution event was “a huge lag at one level, but a huge opportunity at another”, says Alistair Gould. Before the events of June 2024, his plan was to establish Furnace Brook as a “living laboratory”, a showcase for how to transform a landscape degraded by industrial farming into something richer and more resilient on every level: soil and water quality, biodiversity, food security, sustainable energy, community participation. That is still the plan, he says. They are starting several steps further back, but with a broader canvas: the Goulds recently acquired a neighbouring farm, quadrupling the size of the Furnace Brook site.Much of Gould’s career as an environmental consultant was spent thinking about and researching these problems: clean technologies, decarbonising the environment, permaculture principles. He is plugged into what has become a global network of people pursuing similar goals and he has gathered a team of colleagues, volunteers and like-minded experts to help at Furnace Brook.The immediate challenge is restoring the fishing lake. The emphasis is on “bioremediation”: removing pollutants and toxins using natural materials and processes – everything from plants to fungi, bacteria to rocks, explains Cassandra Shaffer, an ecological consultant from Oregon who is leading Furnace Brook’s restoration. For example, the team has been testing floating islands of straw and reeds in the lake, which use biochar – a form of charcoal – and fungi-based “mycorrhizal filtration systems” to trap sediment and encourage the proliferation of micro-organisms that digest the pollution and clean the water.The area upstream from the lake will be a “constructed wetland” – a managed landscape of reeds, wildflowers and other plants. Particular plants have been found to be good at absorbing particular pollutants, says Shaffer. For example, species ofJuncushave proved to be particularly effective atremoving cadmium. “You plant specifically to the qualities of chemicals or pollutants that you find in your system.”View image in fullscreenCommunity support may be the key to restoring Furnace Brook.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianIt sounds highly experimental, but these low-tech methods are tried and tested, says Bryan Spooner, a former colleague of Gould’s and an adviser on the project. “This is exactly how mother nature keeps our water clean. If you look at what beavers do, if you look at how an estuary works, if you look at how waterfalls operate, nature is full of examples.” If all goes to plan, these techniques should accelerate the healing of Furnace Brook’s damaged ecosystem. “You should see a very near complete remediation within 18 months,” says Shaffer.The project is also envisioned as a teaching resource for students and organisations. That is the ethos of the “living lab” – to show other people what can be done and to give them a role in it. “We hope that the community members around us would be able to come and help us on volunteer days, and that way they get some hands-on experience,” says Shaffer.She has worked on similar projects in the US and elsewhere in Europe and has seen how approaches benefit people as well as the landscape. “They’re faced with looking at the news and seeing everything that’s happening with these heatwaves, climate catastrophe, huge pollution spills, and it seems so out of our control and so much bigger than us.” When people are able to participate and see results such as water quality improving within a few weeks, she says: “It makes a huge difference in their mental aspect, in the way they communicate, in the way they make friends.”Beyond the restoration, Alistair Gould sees Furnace Brook as a model for a new kind of rural community, where people jointly own and manage their landscape, to cater to local needs. “At the heart of the model is the idea that land should function as a shared foundation for regenerative activity, rather than as a commodity,” he says. “The land is bought so that aligned farmers, entrepreneurs, educators and families can steward it together, generate real value from it and use that value over time to repay the original purchase, enabling ownership to move into more permanent, community‑anchored forms and allowing the original capital to support similar projects elsewhere.”He lays out aspects of the bigger plan: care for elderly people; cohousing projects; reconditioning dilapidated farm buildings; supporting local businesses. Food is a big part of it, including community farming, food storage and food resilience – as in preserving produce locally to feed the community in the event of an emergency, rather than growing it to sell to large, centralised suppliers.This is effectively a reversal of the corporatised industrial model that has done so much to degrade our rural landscape, whether that be industrial farming, privatised water companies mismanaging rivers or operators dumping waste in the countryside. “It extracts from the rural areas and it doesn’t really reinvest in them,” says Spooner. “If you turn that around and start looking at the opportunities to build local community resilience, food resilience, and then looking at what that means in terms of new skills, new employment, new supply chain lines, and localising things again, the economic opportunities are massive.”Illegal dump becomes ‘symbol of north-south divide’ at heart of Makerfield byelectionRead moreThe community engagement aspect of the plan is already under way, with some help from Maarten Klop, a Dutch organiser who has developed similar initiatives in the Netherlands, organising events, bringing people together, “thinking about how to make these eco-social topics something fun and include everyone”. On a small scale, they are developing locally produced wares such as a “Clean the Lake” lager (Diane already runs acraft breweryat Furnace Brook) and a “cookie of resilience”, the profits from which will go towards the restoration, to draw people deeper into the story of the project.There are plans for beekeeping, forest schooling, market gardening for local restaurants and community fridges and pantries. The soil consultant Michael Kennard has set up a“community compost club”, which collects food waste and turns it into nutrient-rich compost. “You don’t have much room for trying new things if you’re running a commercial farm. We have the space here to experiment and exemplify,” says Klop.Amid a global crisis, all this may sound like a drop in the ocean, but “locally is the only place where we can fix ecological or social challenges”, says Klop. “We can plant a tree, harvest a vegetable, experience community, but if we want to change to a new system, then it needs to happen everywhere all at once. And, luckily, it’s been happening all over the world for decades already.”In the meantime, the prospect of the Goulds receiving any compensation for the damage done to their land remains as remote as ever – they continue to await action by the EA while the truck deliveries continue to roll into Morgans Farm. But the Goulds are focusing on the future, rather than anger or despair. As much as they want to restore the land and model a sustainable rural future, they also want to see the return of the community that made Furnace Brook what it was, says Diane. “The ones who really valued this place, the ones who were really touched by it,” she says. “I really would like to see it open for them. It would be again a place of peace, tranquillity and healing.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘Cash to trash’ levy on house developers too low to offset damage to Norfolk Broads, say critics | Environment policy | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Levy that allows almost 16,000 houses to be built on Norfolk Broads will not cover cost of mitigating environmental damage, critics say
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: Exclusive: Levy that allows almost 16,000 houses to be built on Norfolk Broads will not cover cost of mitigating environmental damage, critics say
Content: The Norfolk Broads are a heavily protected wetland network of 60 shallow lakes and winding rivers, home to some of England’s rarest species.Photograph: SPK/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Norfolk Broads are a heavily protected wetland network of 60 shallow lakes and winding rivers, home to some of England’s rarest species.Photograph: SPK/AlamyEnvironment policy‘Cash to trash’ levy on house developers too low to offset damage to Norfolk Broads, say criticsExclusive: Levy that allows almost 16,000 houses to be built on Norfolk Broads will not cover cost of mitigating environmental damage, critics saySandra LavilleThu 24 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA new levy on developers to allow almost 16,000 homes to be built in the environmentally protectedNorfolkBroads has been cut by tens of thousands of pounds per house, the Guardian can reveal.Ministers say the government’s environmental delivery plans (EDPs) were created to unblock housing growth across the country and are a “win-win” for development and nature.They allow environmental damage to protected habitats and species to be overlooked as long as developers pay into a nature restoration fund, which is used for conservation actions at a later date designed to address the impacts. Once the first instalment of the fee is paid, work can start immediately.Labelled by critics as“cash to trash”, the first EDP was published last week by the government’s nature adviser, Natural England. It allows 15,780 houses to be built within the Norfolk Broads, a heavily protected wetland network of 60 shallow lakes and winding rivers that is home to some of England’s rarest species.View image in fullscreenThe development is expected to cause increased nutrient pollution from a rise in sewage pollution and urban run-off into protected chalk stream rivers.Photograph: Tim CochraneThe published plan, which isopen for consultation for 28 days, states that the developer will pay £2,675 per house – £42m in total – into the nature restoration fund to cover compensatory actions including fenland creation and restoration, a change in use of agricultural land to semi-natural habitat, catch-dyke restoration and deer management.But a previous draft of the EDP, seen by the Guardian, set the levy much higher. Ecologists said this was to properly reflect the realistic costs of mitigating the increased nutrient pollution from increased sewage pollution and urban run-off into protected chalk stream rivers – the Wensum, Bure and Yare – caused by the development.The fee was to be between £5,400 and £60,500 per house, depending on the scale of total nutrient pollution that the development would cause.MapThe fenlands, marshes, bogs and mires of the Broads are a biodiversity hotspot, home to more than a quarter of the rarest wildlife in the UK such as the otter, cuckoo and fen orchid.Natural England acknowledges that the new homes will cause environmental harm in the form of physical, chemical, hydrological and biological damage to the habitats and rare species in the Broads from increased nitrogen and phosphorus pollution.But the EDP states that the payment of the levy and the conservation actions it funds “will materially outweigh the negative effect of the maximum amount of development on the conservation status of each identified environmental feature”.Critics point out that NaturalEnglandis being funded by the developer’s £42m levy to carry out the works, raising concerns of a conflict of interest.Environmental lawyers, ecologists and environmental professionals say the levy is too low. They say none of the conservation actions created by Natural England address reducing the nutrient pollution coming from the development.Analysis of the figures in the EDP reveal that an extra 7,695kg a year of nitrogen will enter the protected waterways, amounting to 83% of the development’s pollution load, and up to 435kg a year of extra phosphorus, according Alexa Culver, legal counsel atRSK Wilding.View image in fullscreenAll the actions in the EDP compensate rather than mitigate or avoid environment harm: not one avoidance measure has been included.Photograph: Chris Herring/Alamy“Developers will be paying a levy that green-lights more pollution rather than solves the problem – quite literally the definition of ‘pay to pollute’ or ‘cash to trash’,” Culver said.The Norfolk Broads EDP is the first since the Planning and Infrastructure Act came into force. Others will be rolled out to allow development alongside and within some of the UK’s most protected sites.Sally Hayns, the chief executive of the Chartered Institute of Ecology and Environmental Management (CIEEM), said: “It is important to get this right because this first EDP is effectively the blueprint for all the other EDPs targeting nutrient pollution that are going to follow: these are already in preparation and will be coming thick and fast.“This EDP is an articulation of the government’s ambition to deliver a win-win for development and nature through the Planning and Infrastructure Act. We finally get to see what that looks like in practice – and there is real concern.”View image in fullscreenThe Norfolk Broads are already so polluted by nitrogen and phosphorus from sewage, agriculture and run off that they are on the red list of concern and severely depleted.Photograph: Tim CochraneHayns said the levy seemed low. “I think there has been a very conservative estimate of how much things are going to cost, with minimal contingency built in.”Not one avoidance measure has been included in the EDP.Hayns said she was at a loss to understand why recognised solutions to strip out nutrient pollution before it enters waterways, including sustainable drainage systems, and integrated constructed wetlands – pools and marshes to filter out nutrient pollution – had not been included.The Broads are already so polluted by nitrogen and phosphorus from sewage, agriculture and run off that they are on the red list of concern and severely depleted.“If nutrient pollution gets worse we will end up with choked, poisoned waterways and we will lose some of our most vulnerable and rarest species,” Hayns said.Dr Justin Neal, the head of legal at WildFish, said the delivery plan was full of holes and set up a worrying “pay to pollute” system that was being used to sacrifice countryside for concrete.View image in fullscreenThe banks of the River Yare, which is home to white clawed crayfish and lamprey.Photograph: Tim Cochrane“Norfolk’s chalk streams and wetlands are protected for a good reason,” he said. “The Yare and Wensum, for instance, hold white clawed crayfish and lamprey. They shouldn’t be sacrificed on the altar of growth.”Bradley Tooze, the nature restoration fund director at Natural England, said: “The environment delivery plan aims to deliver better outcomes to protect the precious habitats of the Norfolk Broads while enabling sustainable development, including through river restoration measures and wetland habitat creation.“The consultation on this first plan is now open. We welcome all views on our proposals and encourage stakeholders to share their expertise to help shape this new approach to nature restoration.”Explore more on these topicsEnvironment policyPlanning policyNatural EnglandConservationWildlifeWetlandsRiversnewsShareReuse this content

title: Big-eyed bugs and praying mantises: climate crisis drives new visitors to UK shores  | Insects | The Guardian
description: Britain has seen an explosion of migrating insects – in some cases from as far as northern Africa
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Britain has seen an explosion of migrating insects – in some cases from as far as northern Africa
Content: Hummingbird hawk-moth (Macroglossum stellatarum) hovering and feeding on pink flowers, showing its long proboscis and distinctive orange wings.Photograph: Ian Mears/AlamyView image in fullscreenHummingbird hawk-moth (Macroglossum stellatarum) hovering and feeding on pink flowers, showing its long proboscis and distinctive orange wings.Photograph: Ian Mears/AlamyInsectsBig-eyed bugs and praying mantises: climate crisis drives new visitors to UK shoresBritain has seen an explosion of migrating insects – in some cases from as far as northern AfricaAisling IrwinThu 24 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 10.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a stifling evening in July and Matt Phelps was out for a stroll, when a piercing, whirring noise stopped him in his tracks. As an ecologist, Phelps knows his fauna – and he could think of no UK creature that could emit such a sound.“It was like the classic sound effect of a cricket in a film, a beeping sort of little trilling sound,” said Phelps, who works at Knepp Estate in West Sussex. He returned with entomologist Graeme Lyons to track it down. But the sound, though incredibly loud, “seemed to be all around us … it was very ventriloquial”.The duo hunted for three hours. Night fell before they realised their quarry was, said Phelps, “literally below the ground where we stood”.View image in fullscreenA female Verge cricket.Photograph: Frederic Grimaitre/AlamySure enough, in a crack in the parched clay they made the first identification of a Verge (or Bordeaux) cricket (Eumodicogryllus bordigalensis)in the British Isles.Once they announced it, other reports poured in. “It turns out there’s been this wave of them right at the moment when there was an enormous wildfire in Bordeaux,” said Phelps. “And it made you think: have some of these things fled the flames of southern Europe?”Verge crickets are just one of many “first sightings” of insects on the UK mainland this summer. It’s been an “extraordinary flood”, he said. And it’s not just the professionals who are finding them.Jackie Harmer, a retired secretary from North Cheshire, was one week into her new hobby of moth-trapping when she found an odd-looking creature native to the Iberian peninsula,Odice pergrata– a first for the UK.And David Cousins, a city trader who collects moths by night at his home in north Essex, opened his box one June dawn to find a white moth with bluish markings.View image in fullscreenSpotted-seal enolmis moth (Enolmis acanthella).Photograph: piemags/nature/Alamy“I just knew it was something really unusual,” he said. It turned out to be not just a new moth but “a completely undiscovered genus in Britain”. In north Africa and southern Europe it’s known as a spotted seal moth (Enolmis acanthella).Then there’s Olly McKeown, 18, in Truro, who didn’t even leave his room to discover what were pronounced in August to be the UK mainland’s first breeding praying mantises.View image in fullscreenA praying mantis.
