Mantises are the only insects capable of turning their heads from side to side without moving the rest of its body, which is a key advantage when hunting, allowing for minimal movement as it sneaks up on prey.Photograph: Robin Loznak/ZUMA Press Wire/REX/Shutterstock“I sat at my table doing some work and then one was crawling across my keyboard – and then I saw one on top of the chair and then I just started spotting loads all around the tables, chairs and then some on the walls as well,” he said.McKeown’s sighting has subsequently been trumped by reports of others that predate his, in places such as the New Forest. The CornwallWildlifeTrust said: “There are a few sites now where experts agree that the species has likely bred.”Liam Crowley, a fellow of the Royal Entomological Society and entomologist at Oxford University, said that the simplest explanation of these shifts is that the world is warming up and insects are moving northwards.. But, he added, “there’s a lot of different dynamics going on and it’s hard to know the true cause”.For example, insects that inhabited the UK a century ago may have gone locally extinct because of habitat destruction – only to return now if nature is restored, or if the climate crisis makes it the least-worst option.Some arrivals may even be part of events unfolding since the ice age ended 11,700 years ago, said Crowley. “As humans, we tend to obsess and focus on our own timescales.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe said there was also an explosion of migrating insects this summer.“Every year there are trillions of insects arriving in the UK, migrating up from the continent and in some cases even northern Africa. They fly up high into the air streams and they use that as a bit of a lift.View image in fullscreenA long hoverfly (Sphaerophoria scripta) hovering on approach to ragwort wildflowers to feed.Photograph: Gillian Pullinger/Alamy“With the record-breaking heat, it’s been an absolutely bumper year [for migrating insects], particularly for very noticeable species.” Crowley highlighted hummingbird hawk moths and hoverflies, while others point to vast numbers of cicadas, striped hawkmoths, painted lady butterflies and clouded yellow butterflies.“Some of these species are starting to breed and establish and potentially survive through the winter in the south,” he said.Harry Witts, who discovered two new species in July, said he had mixed feelings about them. The excitement of discovery is balanced by the knowledge that “it’s only occurring because of climate change – a symptom of a very damaging force in our world”.View image in fullscreenA slender blue-winged grasshopper (Sphingonotus caerulans).Photograph: imageBROKER.com/AlamyWitts, who works at the Essex Wildlife Trust, described the moment at Colne Point, Essex, when “this grasshopper with blue wings jumped out in front of me”. It was bigger than most UK grasshoppers, with much broader wings, which helped him identify it as a blue, slender-winged grasshopper(Sphingonotus caerulans). He thinks he was the first witness of its “natural arrival” on the mainland: other specimens found in Kent this summer were probably Channel tunnel stowaways, he said.A few days later he and colleague Joss Carr found a new species of big-eyed bug (Geocoris megacephalus) in the same place, lurking on a piece of driftwood.Crowley said that most of these arrivals, if they survive the winter and settle, will find their niche and get on with life and may even enhance the ecosystems.“Occasionally,” added Phelps, “you’ll get something that becomes more problematic because it’s out-competing other species. But generally a lot of the ones that turn up by themselves don’t tend to do that.”Explore more on these topicsInsectsAnimalsWildlifeInvertebratesBiodiversityClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Former England player Andy Carroll reveals he was sexually assaulted in 2021 | Andy Carroll | The Guardian
description: Andy Carroll has said in his autobiography he was sexually assaulted by a man at his home during his second spell at Newcastle in 2021
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Andy Carroll has said in his autobiography he was sexually assaulted by a man at his home during his second spell at Newcastle in 2021
Content: ‘What happened to me affected every facet of my life,’ said Andy Carroll, who is now a player and co-owner at Dagenham & Redbridge.Photograph: Gavin Ellis/TGS Photo/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘What happened to me affected every facet of my life,’ said Andy Carroll, who is now a player and co-owner at Dagenham & Redbridge.Photograph: Gavin Ellis/TGS Photo/ShutterstockAndy CarrollFormer England player Andy Carroll reveals he was sexually assaulted in 2021Carroll was assaulted by a man at his home while he sleptAttacker found guilty of sexual offences after player testifiedPress AssociationThu 24 Sep 2026 13.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former England forwardAndy Carrollhas revealed in his autobiography he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021. The 37-year-old included the details in his book, Owning It. As a victim of sexual assault, Carroll was automatically granted anonymity.Carroll revealed the incident took place at his home during a second spell at Newcastle. The offender – a friend of his former partner, who was staying away at the time – was later jailed for three years, with Carroll having testified in court.The former Liverpool and West Ham striker, who is now a player/co-owner of the National League South club Dagenham & Redbridge, said the incident happened when he was sleeping. He then threw the man out of the house, then knocked him unconscious when he attempted to get back inside.“I was sexually assaulted, there I said it. Scary to even think about and only a few people knew about it before now,” wrote Carroll, who had decided to include the incident in his book “at the very last minute” after discussing it with his partner, Lou Teasdale.“Me and Lou spent a lot of time discussing whether to mention it in this book or not. I avoided my publisher for so long that they probably suspected I got cold feet.“Scary to talk about but it’s made [me] the person I am today as much as any of the good stuff. And if me talking about it helps just one person then good, it will have been worth it.”Carroll said testifying in court, where the attacker was found guilty of sexual offences and placed on the sex offenders register, was “humiliating and embarrassing and absolutely horrendous”.The 37-year-old said: “What happened to me affected every facet of my life. I’d think about it every day, making it difficult to focus on anything else, including football … The trauma of what happened to me hasn’t gone away.”Explore more on these topicsAndy CarrollnewsShareReuse this content

title: Launch of UK’s ‘largest AI supercomputer’ delayed by power supply problems | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Datacentre hailed by government was supposed to start operating next year but may be held back into mid-2030s
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Datacentre hailed by government was supposed to start operating next year but may be held back into mid-2030s
Content: An artist’s impression of Nscale’s planned supercomputer in Loughton, Essex.Illustration: NscaleView image in fullscreenAn artist’s impression of Nscale’s planned supercomputer in Loughton, Essex.Illustration: NscaleAI (artificial intelligence)Launch of UK’s ‘largest AI supercomputer’ delayed by power supply problemsDatacentre hailed by government was supposed to start operating next year but may be held back into mid-2030sDan MilmoGlobal technology editorThu 24 Sep 2026 13.26 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA huge datacentre project hailed by the UK government will miss its launch date next year and could be delayed into the mid-2030s.The site in Loughton,Essex, was described as the country’s largest AI supercomputer when it was announced in 2025, but power supply problems mean it now faces a lengthy wait before coming online.Doubts had already emerged about the scheme after the Guardianrevealed in Marchthat the planned location was still an operational scaffolding yard.Now there are further concerns about the project due to its inability to obtain enough power before its planned 2027 debut. The Loughton supercomputer is being built by Nscale, a UK-based startup seeking a $35bn (£26bn) flotation this year.UK Power Networks (UKPN), the company that will connect the site to the local power grid, has reportedly told Nscale the grid will not be able to supply sufficient power to the datacentre until the early to mid-2030s.The power delay was first reported by Morning Intelligence, an AI industry newsletter.Nscale said it was “committed to the project” but the failure tofind a quick fix to the power supply issue underlines how much energy has become a hindrance to datacentre development. The scaffolding yard site has now been cleared by Nscale, however. The company is also investigating whether it can generate power onsite and whether it can speed up the connection process.Keir Starmer’s government cited the Loughton project when announcing theUK’s AI strategy in 2025, describing the site as the “largest UK sovereign AI datacentre”. Datacentres are the central nervous system of AI technology such as chatbots.View image in fullscreenThe scaffolding company, which was operating on the site.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianOfgem, the energy industry regulator, has warned of alogjam in applications for electricity connections. In June, it revealed there were 315 datacentres queueing to connect to the National Grid, representing 73GW of demand – compared with the peak energy demand for the entire country of 45GW.The Loughton site is seeking up to 90MW of capacity, equivalent to the energy consumption of about 315,000 homes.UKPN said it could not comment on an individual project. Schemes with large energy demand also require work to be done at a National Grid level, in order to ensure that energy demands can be met properly.“In general, many datacentres, whilst they will connect to our distribution network, are awaiting works on the wider national electricity transmission network before they can begin operation,” said a UKPN spokesperson.National Grid said: “We’re continuing to work closely with NESO [the government-owned NationalEnergySystem Operator], distribution network operators and customers to identify opportunities to accelerate connections where possible and support economic growth.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingEssexDatacentres - UKInfrastructurenewsShareReuse this content

title: Reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways rise by fifth in a year | Rail transport | The Guardian
description: Unions say record high of nearly 25,000, including assaults on rail workers and public, shows need for more staff and policing
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Unions say record high of nearly 25,000, including assaults on rail workers and public, shows need for more staff and policing
Content: British Transport Police funding cuts ‘have been disastrous’, said the general secretary of the RMT union, Eddie Dempsey.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBritish Transport Police funding cuts ‘have been disastrous’, said the general secretary of the RMT union, Eddie Dempsey.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianRail transportReported assaults on Great Britain’s railways rise by fifth in a yearUnions say record high of nearly 25,000, including assaults on rail workers and public, shows need for more staff and policingTell us: have you been assaulted on Great Britain’s railways?Gwyn TophamTransport correspondentThu 24 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 08.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe number of reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways has risen by a fifth to a record high of almost 25,000 incidents in a year.Unions said the “horrendous” figures showed the need for more staff and policing, as the Office of Rail and Road (ORR) revealed a sharp increase in assaults on the travelling public and on railway staff last year.There were 13,464 reported assaults against passengers and members of the public on the mainline railway in 2025-26, up 36% on the previous year and the highest number recorded by the ORR since it started tracking the figures in 2004.Assaults on rail staff were up 12% in a year to 11,289 reported incidents, mainly verbal abuse but including nearly 2,500 physical assaults – an average of about seven every day.The assaults on members of the public included startling rises in cases of harassment, up 52% year on year, and common assault, up by 30%.Tell us: have you been assaulted on Great Britain’s railways?Read moreThe figures partly reflect increased reporting and zero-tolerance campaigns on public transport, but also underline concerns flagged by unions about the threats to frontline workers as well as passengers, and theavailability of transport police.TheRMTgeneral secretary, Eddie Dempsey, said the numbers were horrendous but chimed with the union’s own surveys showing two-thirds of its members had experienced some form of violence at work in the past year.He said: “We are calling for a significant increase in staffing across public transport, including an end to lone working. We also clearly need stronger legal protections for public transport workers against assaults at work.“BritishTransportPolice funding cuts have also been disastrous which has undermined a proper policing presence on all public transport.”The TSSA union’s general secretary, Maryam Eslamdoust, said: “These new figures are shocking but not surprising because we have been warning for many months that violence on the railways is spiralling out of control.”The government said it was increasing police funding and taking the issue “extremely seriously”.A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “The rise in assaults on the railway is deeply concerning and completely unacceptable. No passenger or rail worker should face violence, threats or abuse, and we encourage anyone affected to report incidents to the police.“The government and rail industry are taking this extremely seriously, with a £63m increase in British TransportPolicefunding by 2028-29, which will see over 200 additional officers recruited.”New measures called railway behaviour notices were introduced in June 2026, strengthening the railway’s ability to exclude repeat offenders from stations.BTP said they had been encouraging greater reporting of all types of assault by staff and passengers, including record use of the 61016 discreet text-to-report number, which partly explained the growing numbers.Nonetheless, the BTP assistant chief constable said: “These figures are a stark reminder of the violence and abuse rail workers face simply for doing their jobs. We will never tolerate violence or abuse directed at passengers or staff on the railway, and anyone committing these crimes can expect a robust response from us.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We remain committed to driving down these offences and ensuring the network is safe for everyone.”The chief inspector of railways, the ORR’s Richard Hines, said the increase in reported assaults was concerning, adding: “No one on the railway should be subjected to violence, threats or abuse.”He said the ORR had set out guidance for employers on the risks, effective controls and encouraging staff to report incidents.View image in fullscreenThe RMT is calling for increased rail staffing, including an end to lone working, and stronger legal protections for public transport workers.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianA spokesperson for Network Rail and train operators said: “Violence, abuse and intimidation directed at passengers or staff are completely unacceptable. The rail industry works closely with British Transport Police to investigate incidents, support victims and bring offenders to justice.”They said the numbers also reflected greater intelligence sharing, improved reporting processes, and more CCTV and body-worn cameras for frontline staff.The ORR report noted that the headline numbers of reported assaults can include multiple counts in a single incident, for example for both harassment and common assault, while workforce assaults are now recorded even if no physical injury occurs. On the London Underground, where there is single counting, the number of assaults on the workforce fell slightly last year.The chief executive of the Rail Safety and Standards Board, Mark Phillips, said the rail industry was taking action to better protect staff, but the figures “underline the need for a change in public behaviour and greater respect for the people who keep the railway running safely every day”.Reports in recent years have highlighted thatwomen and girls were at particular risk, while thegrowing number of assaults year on yearsince the pandemic has coincided with pressure on British Transport Police numbers.The abuse and intimidation faced by frontline staff on the railways has also been seen in sectors including retail and in the NHS. The British Retail Consortium warned over“endemic” violence towards shop workersearlier this year, while the number of reports of violence against NHS staff by patientssurpassed 100,000 in 2025.Explore more on these topicsRail transportPublic transportRail industryCrimeRMTTrade unionsPolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Met chief criticises court system after paedophile granted bail | London | The Guardian
description: Officers left feeling ‘hamstrung’, says Mark Rowley after offender allowed to return to flat overlooking playground
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Officers left feeling ‘hamstrung’, says Mark Rowley after offender allowed to return to flat overlooking playground
Content: Zafer Dogan was jailed for two years and four months after he was convicted of taking thousands of pictures of women and girls before using AI technology to turn them into nude images.Photograph: Metropolitan Police/PAZafer Dogan was jailed for two years and four months after he was convicted of taking thousands of pictures of women and girls before using AI technology to turn them into nude images.Photograph: Metropolitan Police/PALondonMet chief criticises court system after paedophile granted bailOfficers left feeling ‘hamstrung’, says Mark Rowley after offender allowed to return to flat overlooking playgroundPA MediaThu 24 Sep 2026 15.57 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 16.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePressure to cut the number of prisoners on remand has led to “dangerous and prolific offenders” being granted bail, the country’s most senior police officer said after a paedophile was allowed to return to his flat that overlooked a children’s playground.Zafer Dogan was jailed on Thursday for two years and four months after he was convicted of taking thousands of pictures of women and girls before using AI technology to turn them into nude images for his sexual gratification.But despite protests from the police and prosecutors, he was bailed to his flat in Enfield, northLondon, forcing one family who had fallen victim to his crimes to move into temporary accommodation.After the 32-year-old’s sentencing at Wood Green crown court,Metropolitan policecommissioner Sir Mark Rowley took the unusual step of publicly criticising the justice system.He said it was leaving his officers feeling “hamstrung” by making “unfathomable decisions” to grant the most prolific offenders bail.Speaking outside the court after he attended the sentencing, he said: “The children should be put first, not the paedophile.“The pressure to reduce the remand population has contributed to more dangerous and prolific offenders being granted bail routinely despite strong submissions from the police and CPS.“Victims are left fearful, and communities are left feeling less safe, and confidence in the justice system is undermined.”Earlier, the court had heard how Dogan, who worked as a mechanic, took photos of adults and children going about their “daily business” without their knowledge before using AI software to digitally alter them into sexually explicit images.He had previously pleaded guilty to several image offences, including making indecent images of children, having been arrested on 16 July on suspicion of offences involving indecent images of children.Prosecutor Sarah Gabay said investigators discovered “thousands of images of women and children which seem to have been taken without their consent or their knowledge”.She said they were “going about their daily business” in the photographs, which included pictures of children on climbing frames.According to the police, Dogan had taken more than 5,000 images, many of which were from his bedroom window which overlooked a playground.The court was told photos of 33 adult women and two children, aged seven and 13, were “digitally altered” using AI software to create sexualised content.Dogan was arrested again on 4 August and the following day he was charged and remanded by police. The defendant appeared at Highbury Corner magistrates court on 6 August and accepted all the charges against him. According to the prosecutor, Dogan had “been on conditional bail throughout these proceedings”.Dogan gave no-comment interviews after both arrests, the court heard.The court heard victim impact statements from the mothers of Dogan’s two child victims, who have been kept anonymous for legal reasons.The mother of the 13-year-old victim described feeling as if she had been “punched in the gut” when police officers told her what had happened. She added: “I’m really worried that my daughter’s photos are online and other paedophiles have them.”The mother of the seven-year-old victim described feeling “helpless”, adding: “Our lives will never be the same again and I can’t do anything about it all because one man exploited my child.”Joseph Carr, mitigating, said the defendant “recognises the profound seriousness” of his offending. He said Dogan separated from his long-term partner in 2025 and subsequently “spiralled into depression”.The lawyer said he “fell down the rabbit hole and was unable to find his way out”, but added there is no excuse for his actions.The judge described Dogan as a “Jekyll and Hyde” character during the hearing, having read several character references, which, Carr said, “speak to positive character”.Dogan pleaded guilty to three counts of making indecent images of a child, which included 900 category C images, 294 category B images and 653 category A images – which are the most severe.He also admitted possessing extreme pornography, possessing a prohibited image of a child, creating purported intimate images of an adult, obstructing a constable in the execution of their duty and a further two counts of making indecent photographs of a child.Rowley also criticised the AI companies for being “grossly irresponsible” in the way they developed technology.He said: “This is another example of how some grossly irresponsible technology and AI companies must do more to prevent their platforms and tools from being used to facilitate sexual offending and harm.“Innovation cannot come at the expense of public safety, and industry has a clear responsibility to help prevent these technologies being exploited by predators.“Victims, in this case extremely young children and their families, deserve better from both the tech companies and the criminal justice system.”Sentencing , Judge Jacobs said: “The offences are so serious that in my judgment only a custodial sentence is justified.”He commended the “bravery” of the mothers who gave victim impact statements, adding: “As they rightly say, whatever sentence I impose, it will not undo what you did. No sentence can give those families back what you stole from them through your depraved actions.”He said all of Dogan’s offending was “completely sexually motivated”.The Met police said that alongside the CPS, it had opposed Dogan’s bail on three occasions but their attempts were unsuccessful and the offender was allowed to return to his flat.Explore more on these topicsLondonMark RowleyEnglandMetropolitan policenewsShareReuse this content

title: Democratic lawmakers accuse Trump administration of interference in Brazilian elections | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Legislators sent letter to Marco Rubio saying US interference is weakening Brazil’s democratic institutions
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Legislators sent letter to Marco Rubio saying US interference is weakening Brazil’s democratic institutions
Content: Brazil’s president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, attends a rally in São Gonçalo, Brazil, on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Tita Barros/ReutersView image in fullscreenBrazil’s president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, attends a rally in São Gonçalo, Brazil, on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Tita Barros/ReutersBrazilDemocratic lawmakers accuse Trump administration of interference in Brazilian electionsLegislators sent letter to Marco Rubio saying US interference is weakening Brazil’s democratic institutionsUS politics live – latest updatesTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroThu 24 Sep 2026 13.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA group of 31 Democratic members of theUS Congresshas sent a letter to the secretary of state,Marco Rubio, criticising theTrump administrationover “an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine”Brazil’s elections.Latin America’s largest country will hold the first round of its presidential election on 4 October, with polls showing atechnical tiebetween the incumbent leftist president,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and the far-right senatorFlávio Bolsonaro.In the letter sent to Rubio on Thursday, 30 members of the House of Representatives and the senator Bernie Sanders listed aseries of measuresthe US government took that they interpret as attempts to secure a victory for Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former presidentJair Bolsonaro.Brazil’s Lula announces higher welfare payments and free weight-loss jabs ahead of electionRead moreThey wrote that those actions “reflect a broader and deeply troubling pattern of interference by the Trump administration in recent electoral processes across Latin America”, citing the recent midterm elections inArgentinaand presidential elections inHondurasandColombia.In July, a group of 11 Democratic members of Congress sent a similar letter arguing that Trump was trying to interfere in Colombia’s election in favour of the far-right millionaire and former lawyerAbelardo de la Espriella, who went on towin the second round.In Thursday’s letter, the lawmakers wrote that US officials under Trump have engaged in a “sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilization in Brazil”.They noted that when Trump imposed his first tariffs on Brazil last year, he made clear that one reason was Bolsonaro’s trial over hisattempt to stage a coupafter losing the 2022 election to Lula. The former president wasultimately convictedand, unable to run because he is under house arrest, named his son to take his place.They also citednew tariffs that Trump imposedon Brazil in July under section 301 of US trade law, as well asplans by the US governmentto send two officials to Brazil to “cast doubt on the integrity of the country’s voting system, considered by many experts to be among the most reliable in the world”. The Lula administration ultimately denied the US delegation visas.The Brazilian president has repeatedlycomplainedthat Trump is trying to interfere in Brazil’s elections and, in his speech opening the UN general assembly this week, said, without naming anyone: “We will not allow the enemies of democracy, internal or external, to act against the will of the people.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the letter sent to Rubio on Friday, the Democratic lawmakers wrote that “rather than helping defend Brazilian democracy”, the US is “acting as an agent of interference and destabilization – using diplomatic, economic and political pressure in ways that risk weakening the country’s democratic institutions, undermining confidence in Brazil’s electoral process, and inflicting further damage on our relationship with a strategic US ally and trading partner”.They asked Rubio if Trump’s administration would commit to respecting Brazil’s electoral process and requested a response by 1 October.The state department has not yet responded to a request for comment.Explore more on these topicsBrazilTrump administrationMarco RubioLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaJair BolsonaroDonald TrumpTrump tariffsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Germany investigates 105-year-old suspected former Nazi prison camp guard | Germany | The Guardian
description: Man accused of being accessory to murders at Stalag 326 VI K amid race to prosecute suspects before they die
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: Man accused of being accessory to murders at Stalag 326 VI K amid race to prosecute suspects before they die
Content: Russian prisoners celebrate being released by US soldiers from the German camp Stalag 326 VI K in February 1945.Photograph: FPG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRussian prisoners celebrate being released by US soldiers from the German camp Stalag 326 VI K in February 1945.Photograph: FPG/Getty ImagesGermanyGermany investigates 105-year-old suspected former Nazi prison camp guardMan accused of being accessory to murders at Stalag 326 VI K amid race to prosecute suspects before they dieKate Connollyin BerlinThu 24 Sep 2026 10.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 105-year-old man is under investigation on suspicion of being an accessory to multiple murders at a Nazi prisoner of war camp, German prosecutors have said.The case, which is being handled by the public prosecutor’s office in Dortmund, centres on the Stalag 326 VI K camp in westernGermany, in what is now the state of North Rhine-Westphalia.“The 105-year-old suspect is thought to have been a guard at the prisoner of war camp Stalag 326 VI K in the Senne region of western Germany,” prosecutors said in a statement. The man is “accused of being an accessory to multiple murders owing to his activities there”, they said.The Senne camp housed between 180,000 and 200,000 Soviet prisoners of war between 1941 and April 1945, when it was liberated by American troops.The investigation is the result of an urgent last-minute scramble by the judiciary to prosecute alleged participants in the Nazi killing machine before they die. The judicial efforts stem in part from a recognition that many of the suspects who have escaped prosecution in the eight decades since the end of the second world war on the grounds that they were considered to have played an insignificant role were in fact integral to the implementation of the Hitler regime’s murderous aims.A judicial precedent was set by the court case of John Demjanjuk, a former guard at the Nazi Sobibór death camp in occupied Poland, who wasconvicted in 2011of being an accomplice to the murders of more than 28,000 Jews that took place in the time he worked there.Prosecutors had sought Ukraine-born Demjanjuk’s extradition from his Ohio home to Germany for years, arguing that he was complicit in the crimes committed at Sobibór despite a lack of evidence that he had directly killed anyone.Demjanjuk died aged 91 in March 2012 awaiting an appeal due to his age and frailty, which meant he did not go to prison.View image in fullscreenJohn Demjanjuk, a former guard at the Sobibór death camp, died without going to prison.Photograph: David Rubinger/Getty ImagesThe Demjanjuk case lowered the bar for proof of complicity, paving the way for other nonagenarians and more recently centenarians to stand trial.The most prominent trial of recent years, and representative of what Hannah Arendt, a political theorist, described as aSchreibtischtäter(desk perpetrator, or bureaucratic mediator), was that ofIrmgard Furchner, who worked at the Stutthof concentration camp between 1943 and 1945 as a secretary to the camp commandant. She was given a two-year suspended sentence for her role as an accessory to murder.Her trial was, contrary to normal rules, filmed for historical purposes. Furchner made headlines afterrunning awayfrom her retirement home on the scheduled opening day of her trial.Josef Schütz, a former guard at the Sachsenhausen concentration camp north of Berlin, was sentenced for being an accomplice to murder to five years in prison in June 2022. He died the following year, aged 102.In April last year an alleged former guard at Sachsenhausen died before he was able to face trial over charges of complicity in the murder of more than 3,300 people.A separate investigation was opened last year by Dortmund prosecutors into a 100-year-old former guard at a PoW camp in Hemer, North Rhine-Westphalia, which also held mainly Soviet prisoners. He is suspected of participating in executions of prisoners between December 1943 and September 1944.The new investigation was initiated by the Central Office for the Investigation of National Socialist Crimes in Ludwigsburg, in the southern state of Baden-Württemberg, which passed its preliminary investigation into the man to public prosecutors along with that of another former guard. The other suspect has since died, according to German media.If the trial goes ahead, like other recent cases it is expected to throw light on the Stalag system in general and on Senne in particular, drawing survivors and historians to give evidence. Up to 5.7 million Soviet prisoners were held captivity in Germany. More than half did not survive.Explore more on these topicsGermanyNazismEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Rebel offensive against Ethiopian army stokes fears of return to civil war | Ethiopia | The Guardian
description: Fighting escalates after Tigrayan rebels form new coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed government
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: Fighting escalates after Tigrayan rebels form new coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed government
Content: Members of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) walk along a main road in Mekelle on 23 September, as tensions intensify in northern Ethiopia.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMembers of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) walk along a main road in Mekelle on 23 September, as tensions intensify in northern Ethiopia.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesEthiopiaRebel offensive against Ethiopian army stokes fears of return to civil warFighting escalates after Tigrayan rebels form new coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed governmentCarlos Mureithiin Nairobi and agenciesThu 24 Sep 2026 11.29 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 09.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are growing fears of a return to civil war inEthiopiaafter an offensive by fighters from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara and the formation of a new rebel alliance aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed.About 600,000 people died between 2020 and 2022 duringa devastating warbetween the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict.On Sunday, seven armed groups from around the country, including the TPLF, announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at deposing the government in Addis Ababa. Then, on Wednesday, the TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police. The state-owned carrier, Ethiopian Airlines, said it had suspended flights to the region “due to the current situation”.The TPLF also launched attacks into Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told Agence France-Presse there were heavy artillery attacks by the group on Thursday as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the Tigrayan border.Flights to the historic Ethiopian town of Lalibela were also suspended on Thursday because of nearby fighting, while people in Tigray stocked up ⁠on food and cash, with one resident telling Reuters that people there feared they could face siege conditions similar to those during the previous war.A resident of Adigrat, a city close to the Eritrean border, ‌described panic-buying and shops emptying. “Food shortages are worsening as market shelves sit empty … Essential medicines remain scarce and astronomically expensive,” he told Reuters. “Daily survival has become a constant calculation.”Graphic – Ethiopia mapThe TPLF’s vice-president, Amanuel Assefa, told AFP: “We are in the situation of full-blown war now.” He confirmed Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara.The group took control of Abala, also on the Tigray-Afar border, on Wednesday, a foreign security source based in Ethiopia told AFP, while a TPLF source said they had seized several other towns in Afar. The foreign security source also said there was fighting around the Amhara town of Weldiya – one of the few routes to the capital.In its first public comments on the fighting, Ethiopia’s army said on ⁠Thursday it had foiled the attacks and killed, wounded or captured more than 500 enemy fighters.Analysts say the TPLF has support from Ethiopia’s​ neighbour and historic adversary Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade its territory to gain access to the Red Sea. The TPLF’s Assefa told AFP “we have no information about Eritrea’s plan”. Asked if they would request Eritrean intervention, he said: “Not yet.”The current fighting reflects shifting dynamics from the civil war, whenEritreaand Fano, an insurgent group that is now part of the new alliance, both fought with the government against the Tigrayans.Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, the Ethiopian president, Taye Atske-Selassie Amde, decried “the forces of destruction and mayhem” and “interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements”. He said Ethiopia had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours.Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, said members of the alliance had been collaborating for a while ​with the financial backing of Eritrea. Eritrea ​has repeatedly denied similar accusations.The TPLF ruled Ethiopiafrom 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, eventually triggering the civil war.The renewed fighting marks the most serious challenge ​yet tothe 2022 Pretoria agreement, which ended the civil war and maintained an uneasy calm until late last year, when clashes resumed.It raises fears of a broader regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across and further destabilise a region already strained by war in neighbouring Sudan and tensions along the Red Sea.On Wednesday, the African Union chair, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf,urged“utmost restraint” from the warring parties and resumption of direct talks. An EU spokespersoncalled for“immediate de-escalation” and a recommitment to the Pretoria agreement.In the 2020-22 war, Tigray was largely cut off from the outside world as communications were severed, and access to food, cash and medicines was severely restricted, pushing hundreds of thousands of people into famine-like conditions.AFP and Reuters contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsEthiopiaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Family of Iranian twins sentenced to death and decades in jail ask UN for help | Iran | The Guardian
description: Taraneh and Romina Rahimi were charged with ‘waging war against God’ after joining protests against Tehran regime
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Taraneh and Romina Rahimi were charged with ‘waging war against God’ after joining protests against Tehran regime
Content: Taraneh and Romina were taken from their beds by men from the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps eight months ago.View image in fullscreenTaraneh and Romina were taken from their beds by men from the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps eight months ago.IranFamily of Iranian twins sentenced to death and decades in jail ask UN for helpTaraneh and Romina Rahimi were charged with ‘waging war against God’ after joining protests against Tehran regimeSupported byAbout this contentDaniel BoffeyChief reporterThu 24 Sep 2026 09.15 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 14.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe family of 21-year-old twins who have been sentenced respectively todeath and decades in jailfor protesting against the Iranian regime have appealed to the United Nations for help.A formal “submission of information” relating to the case of Taraneh and Romina Rahimi has been submitted by British human right lawyers on their family’s behalf.The move could lead to the UN’s human rights council opening talks with the Iranian regime about resolving the case if it is found to involve human rights violations.Broken feet, ripped-out hair and now a death sentence: the fate of twin sisters jailed over Iran protestsRead moreThe president of Iran, Masoud Pezeshkian, told the UN’s general assembly in New York this week that the country was “ready for dialogue and diplomacy”.Taraneh and Romina Rahimi were taken from their beds by men from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps eight months ago after they joined nationwide protests against the regime.They were tried over charges that includedmoharebeh(waging war against God) for taking to the streets of Isfahan, in central Iran, on 8 and 9 January.At the end of August, Taraneh, along with nine others, was sentenced to death. Romina received a 25-year prison sentence.The girls’ family are seeking to appeal against the sentences but human rights groups have raised concerns that Taraneh’s execution could be fast-tracked.The women are being held in Dowlatabad prison in Isfahan, where the twins’ family claim that Taraneh was threatened with being forced to watch the rape of her sister if she failed to sign a confession to her alleged crimes.The sisters have been held in isolation but are said to have been able to hear each other’s screams as torture was inflicted upon them.Neither of the women have been seen by their mother, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, or other members of the family since their sentencing.After the Guardianhighlighted the case, the women’s cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, an IT engineer who lives in the US state of Utah, said Taraneh was told she would only be allowed to eat leftovers of other prisoners’ meals as punishment.Nourmohammadi, 43, said he had turned to the UN out of desperation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTaraneh is said to be in need of surgery due to injuries inflicted during interrogation.Nourmohammadi said: “Turning to theUnited Nationsis not something I ever wanted to have to do. I am simply asking the international community to help ensure that Taraneh and Romina receive the basic rights that every human being is entitled to: a fair process, protection from torture and abuse, access to medical care and legal counsel, and the right to have their cases genuinely reviewed.“Taraneh is facing the death penalty, and Romina is facing decades in prison. They are young women who should be thinking about their futures, not whether one sister will be executed and the other will spend the best years of her life behind bars.“They are my family and I will continue to use every peaceful and legal avenue available. I ask the United Nations to stand with them before it is too late – especially for Taraneh.”A submission to the UN through its “special procedures” can lead to a formal request by the international organisation to a member state for an explanation and action.Iran hasexecuted more than 500 people this year, including at least 16 women. Hundreds of protesters have been sentenced to death or are facing charges which could carry the death penalty, including more than 70 in Isfahan.Explore more on these topicsIranMiddle East and north AfricaUnited NationsTortureViolence against women and girlsHuman rightsWomen's rights and gender equalitynewsShareReuse this content

title: TikTok drops appeal against £12.7m fine for not keeping under-13s off platform  | TikTok | The Guardian
description: UK watchdog fined video app in 2023 for failing to enforce minimum age limit and remove underage users
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: UK watchdog fined video app in 2023 for failing to enforce minimum age limit and remove underage users
Content: Chinese-owned TikTok said it disagreed with the ruling but decided to pay the fine because it related to a period after which it had implemented ‘many youth safety measures’.Photograph: Matt Cardy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChinese-owned TikTok said it disagreed with the ruling but decided to pay the fine because it related to a period after which it had implemented ‘many youth safety measures’.Photograph: Matt Cardy/Getty ImagesTikTokTikTok drops appeal against £12.7m fine for not keeping under-13s off platformUK watchdog fined video app in 2023 for failing to enforce minimum age limit and remove underage usersDan MilmoGlobal technology editorThu 24 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTikTok will pay a £12.7m fine to the UK’s data watchdog after dropping an appeal against a ruling that it did not do enough to keep children below the age of 13 off the platform.The video app waspunished by the Information Commissioner’s Office in 2023for inadequate checks of who was using the platform, and failing to remove underage users.When issuing the fine the ICO said TikTok had done “very little, if anything” to address underage use of its service.TikTok has a minimum user age of 13 but failure to enforce that limit resulted in up to 1.75 million UK children under 13 using the service in 2020, the ICO said. TikTok also failed to provide users with information about how their data was being collected and used, and neglected to obtain parental consent.Emily Keaney, the ICO’s deputy commissioner, said: “Our successful action against TikTok shows how important it is for companies to have the right protections in place, including to prevent access by children who are not old enough to be using their services.”Chinese-owned TikTok said it disagreed with the ruling but had decided to pay the fine because it related to a period between 2018 and 2020, after which it had implemented “many youth safety measures and policies”.TikTok, which has more than 30m users in the UK, has also withdrawn an appeal against an ICO request for information about how its algorithm processes teenagers’ personal data – and how it serves potentially harmful content. The ICO said it would now resume the investigation.At the time the fine was issued, the then information commissioner, John Edwards, told the Guardian that TikTok was “not doing enough” on multiple fronts.“Our findings were that TikTok were not doing enough to prevent under-13s accessing their platform, they were not doing enough when they became aware of under-13s to get rid of them, and they were not doing enough to detect under-13s on there,” he said.Age-checking measures at tech platforms will be at the vanguard of the government’snew under-16 age limitfor accessing social media platforms, which comes into force next year.The UK’s communications watchdog, Ofcom, has said “more action from the tech industry is needed” on enforcing age limits as the ban approaches. In Australia, which introduced a social media ban for under-16s last December, theeSafety commissionerhas said a “substantial proportion” of under-16s in the country have kept their accounts, managed to create new ones or bypassed age-gating systems.Explore more on these topicsTikTokSocial mediaChildrenDigital mediaInternet safetyData protectionAppsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Oil price rise creates more pressure on UK policymakers before budget | Economics | The Guardian
description: Treasury sources concede ‘less room’ for manoeuvre as global bond selloff also hikes government’s borrowing costs
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Treasury sources concede ‘less room’ for manoeuvre as global bond selloff also hikes government’s borrowing costs
Content: Oil prices remain elevated as a result of the Iran war, with severe knock-on effects for consumers.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenOil prices remain elevated as a result of the Iran war, with severe knock-on effects for consumers.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA/ShutterstockEconomicsOil price rise creates more pressure on UK policymakers before budgetTreasury sources concede ‘less room’ for manoeuvre as global bond selloff also hikes government’s borrowing costsInternational bodies warn of rising debt and borrowing risksBurnham stands by claim UK is ‘in hock’ to bond marketsHeather StewartandGraeme WeardenThu 24 Sep 2026 07.41 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOil prices lurched upwards again on Thursday, creating a growing headache for UK policymakers ahead of John Healey’s budget next month.While Healey has been keen to present an upbeat picture of the UK’s economic prospects, Treasury sources concede the sharp jump in oil and gas prices means they have “less room” than a month ago.Officials are working “at pace” on a range of possible options for supporting consumers, particularly if high prices persist, feeding through into a sharp rise in the quarterly energy price cap in January.But any package is expected to fall far short of the costly across-the-board subsidies announced by Liz Truss in 2022, with the Treasury mindful of the measures already taken, including Andy Burnham’s VAT cut on electricity bills.Options are believed to include shifting more green subsidies into general taxation, echoing the approach taken by Rachel Reeves, or targeting help at the poorest households – though some officials are sceptical about how effectively this can be achieved.The price of a barrel of Brent crude was up almost 5% at $108 on Thursday after reports of more military clashes between Saudi Arabia and Houthi forces.Donald Trump has given little indication of how, or when, the wider US-Israeli war on Iran could be brought to a close, despite the impact on gasoline prices in the US before crucial midterm elections.Senior UK government figures are also increasingly concerned about the prospect of interest rate rises, which could push up the cost of a mortgage just as Burnham has promised voters “breathing space”.After leaving interest rates on hold at 3.75% last week, the Bank of England said it expected the energy price cap to rise by as much as 24% in the new year.The Bank’s chief economist, Clare Lombardelli, said in a speech on Thursday that the longer oil prices remained elevated as a result of the war, the more likely it was that rates would have to rise.“The longer higher energy prices persist, the greater the risk that indirect effects build and that inflation expectations, wage bargaining and price-setting behaviour begin to adjust in response,” she told an economic conference in Warsaw, Poland. “On that basis, policy is increasingly likely to need to tighten if elevated energy prices persist, absent clear evidence of disinflation or weaker activity.”Lombardelli’s warning was echoed by another member of the Bank’s monetary policy committee, the deputy governor Sarah Breeden, who told a conference at Imperial College London: “The larger and longer the shock, the more likely it is that we’ll see the material second-round effects that policy needs to respond [to].”Expectations of higher inflation and interest rates caused by rising energy prices are a key factor driving the global selloff in government bond markets – raising the cost of borrowing for the UK, alongside other economies.The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds, known as gilts, rose to 5.39% on Thursday, approaching the 19-year high set last week.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHigher interest rates raise the upfront cost of government investment and feed through into Office forBudgetResponsibility forecasts of whether the chancellor is on course to meet Labour’s fiscal rules.Analysts believe recent increases in yields have wiped out more than half of the £24bn “headroom” against the rules that Reeves had built up at the time of the spring statement in March.The perilous economic conditions facing the UK can be traced back to Trump | Richard PartingtonRead moreHealey has repeatedly promised to meet the rules with a “buffer against uncertainty” but this is widely expected to be significantly lower than £24bn. Rebuilding it to that level would be likely to require large tax increases or spending cuts, but Treasury sources insist the budget will be narrowly focused.Investors across the main markets have beenditching bonds in recent weeksin a wave of selling, as the conflict in the Middle East rumbles on. As the bond sell-off continued to worsen on Thursday, yields on 10-year US treasury bonds surged to 5.17%, the highest level since 2007.Alongside higher inflation, investors appear to be concerned about the risks of uncontrolled US government spending. Some analysts also suggest large-scale bond issuance by AI firms is undermining demand for treasuries.Explore more on these topicsEconomicsOilGiltsBondsInterest ratesBudget 2026Government borrowingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Housebuilder Vistry slashes profit forecasts as losses balloon | Vistry Group | The Guardian
description: Firm unveils further cost-cutting plan including job losses, blaming poor summer sales of private homes
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Firm unveils further cost-cutting plan including job losses, blaming poor summer sales of private homes
Content: Construction work on former farmland at the Bovis Homes Windsor Arch site in Berkshire, southern England.Photograph: Maureen McLean/AlamyView image in fullscreenConstruction work on former farmland at the Bovis Homes Windsor Arch site in Berkshire, southern England.Photograph: Maureen McLean/AlamyVistry GroupHousebuilder Vistry slashes profit forecasts as losses balloonFirm unveils further cost-cutting plan including job losses, blaming poor summer sales of private homesJulia KolleweThu 24 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 12.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVistry Group, one of Britain’s biggest housebuilders, has cut its annual profit expectations after half-year losses ballooned as it grappled with a £600m pile of unsold homes.Adam Daniel, the new chief executive of theBovis Homes and Countrysideowner, insisted “the issues can be fixed” as he set out a detailed turnaround plan that involves pulling out of private sales in south-east England and slimming operations to turn Vistry into a more focused, 12,000-homes-a-year builder.Further job losses loom, however, after Vistry announced new cost savings of £50m, on top of a £25m voluntary redundancy programme and hiring freeze earlier this year. It said it reduced its workforce to 4,150 at the end of July, with 350 people leaving since the summer, according to PA. The company is closing some regional offices, moving from 25 to 12 regions.Housebuilder Crest Nicholson warns of annual loss in ‘subdued’ property marketRead moreVistry reported a loss before tax of £661.3m for the first six months of the year, versus a profit of £40.9m the year before, dragged back by a £475m writedown and a £73m provision for building safety works.For the year as a whole, it now expects to post an adjusted profit before tax of £165m, after making an adjusted loss of £83.3m in the first half,far worse than expected.The company completed 6,304 homes, down by 8% from a year earlier. Afterresorting to steep discountsto sell a £600m pile of houses, it is now left with £220m of unsold properties. In July it said the average discount offered to homebuyers was 7.1%. Half-year revenues fell by 9% to £1.7bn while Vistry’s debt jumped from £293.1m to £468.8m.Vistry blamed “disappointing summer sales of private homes” and withdrawals or renegotiation of deals to build affordable homes. It has also been hit by cost inflation of 3% to 4% as a result of the Iran war, which has driven fuel prices sharply higher.In August, the company received £350m funding from the government to construct 3,000 affordable homes, the largest slice awarded under the £39bn social and affordable homes programme, and it is one of 33 strategic partners that take part. Vistry said it had already started building those homes.Daniels, who took the helm in April, laid out measures such as reducing the land bank from 51,000 to 36,000 plots and a reorganisation of the business, simplification of product range, brands and operating processes, and greater exposure to the north, Midlands and west of England.Daniels said: “We have made substantial progress in refocusing the business and delivering on our immediate priority to improve cash generation. In parallel, we have now completed an extensive review of our business and operating model including how best to position the group for future success.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Vistry share price plunged more than 8% in early trading.Victoria Scholar, the head of investment at Interactive Investor, said: “The housebuilder has been faced with macro headwinds from this year’s energy shock leading to cost pressures, weaker affordability and consumer confidence amid the higher-for-longer interest rate backdrop.“Shares had already had a painful run lately, shedding close to 60% year-to-date before this morning’s further sharp slide, underscoring the challenges at hand for its boss and the need for a drastic turnaround.”Explore more on these topicsVistry GroupConstruction industryHousing marketReal estateJob lossesnewsShareReuse this content

title: EU says Trump plan to ban US diesel exports would ‘negatively impact both sides’ | Oil | The Guardian
description: US president’s suggested 90-day export ban before midterm elections could bring even higher fuel prices across Europe
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: US president’s suggested 90-day export ban before midterm elections could bring even higher fuel prices across Europe
Content: Trump is reportedly considering a 90-day export ban on diesel fuel to ease high pump prices for US households.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrump is reportedly considering a 90-day export ban on diesel fuel to ease high pump prices for US households.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesOilEU says Trump plan to ban US diesel exports would ‘negatively impact both sides’US president’s suggested 90-day export ban before midterm elections could bring even higher fuel prices across EuropeJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentThu 24 Sep 2026 10.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EU has warned Donald Trump against plans to ban US diesel exports to the global market, saying the move would negatively affectEuropeand the US.The European Commission has reacted with “concern” toreportsthis week that the US president could prevent diesel from reaching the global market.Trump is reportedly considering a 90-day export ban to provide a temporary respite from high pump prices for US households before the midterm elections, after US diesel reached a record average of $6.52 (£4.93) a gallon. “I’ve ​said let’s not send ‌out the diesel. ‌We make a lot of diesel … I’ve called for it. ‌I’ve called for it within my people,” he said.Olof Gill, a spokesperson for the EU’s executive arm, said on Thursday “any disruption would risk negatively impacting both sides” and the EU expected “close partners to consult each other before taking measures that affect shared markets”.The EU made the diplomatic intervention as experts said that the potential export ban could be “devastating” for Europe, and traders scrambled to assess the continent’s reliance on imports from the US.The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, has warned that banning exports was a “blunt tool” that could harm US fuel supplies in the long term.For Europe, the ban could be far more damaging. US diesel exports have made up a third of the continent’s imports this year, as supplies from war-damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia have plummeted. By August, the US supplied about half of Europe’s diesel imports.Pump prices have already climbed to record highs across Germany and the Netherlands, leading to calls for political leaders toprotect households from rising costs.In the UK, motorists may be only days away from fresh all-time highs, raising concerns over the economic impact of further price hikes for hard-pressed households. The RAC said the average cost of diesel was 197.75p a litre on Thursday, up from 142.38p before the start of the Iran war.“A US export ban would be devastating for diesel supply in Europe, which would struggle to replace supply,” said Josh Michalowski, the head of European diesel pricing at Argus Media, a commodities data provider.View image in fullscreenDiesel prices in some parts of the UK have passed £2 a litre  – and reached £2.17 a litre at BP Kinross Services in Perthshire, Scotland.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianFuel stations across Europe are unlikely to run dry, because Europe produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries. It also stores fuels in reserve. But experts fear that competing for cargoes on the global market would lead to higher market prices.So far the market for diesel cargoes has remained relatively quiet since reports of a potential US diesel ban emerged this week, according to Benedict George, the head of European products at Argus. He said traders were still weighing up the degree to which the White House might limit US exports.“If this prospect became even relatively serious [in the White House], it would be very serious for European markets. There would be some degree of panic given how reliant buyers have become on US cargoes,” George said. “There’s enough European diesel production to ensure that we wouldn’t run out, but losing US cargoes would mean buyers would have to compete with buyers in Asia for the few available cargoes from the Middle East and India, in what is already a very competitive global market.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe price of diesel has outpaced the rising price of global oil markets due to severe disruption to refineries in the Gulf and in Russia. The price difference – known as the “crack spread” – reached a record high earlier this month and could climb further still.“A US ban on diesel exports would pose a significant challenge for the UK, given the country’s growing reliance on American refined fuel,” said Thomas Pugh, the chief economist at the audit, tax and consulting firm RSM UK.View image in fullscreenThe Fawley oil refinery in Hampshire is one of only four remaining refineries in the UK.Photograph: Graham Mulrooney/AlamyThe UK has only four operating oil refineries after the closures of Grangemouth and Lindsey last year. Both produced diesel for the UK market. Pugh warned that losing almost 90,000 barrels a day of US distillate, or 18% of the country’s total consumption, would leave the UK even more exposed to global diesel prices. He added that, while shortages of fuel were unlikely immediately, a longer-term ban would make them a “real possibility”.Although the number of motorists driving diesel passenger vehicles has fallen, it remains the lifeblood of the UK’s agricultural and logistics sectors by fuelling heavy machinery,lorries and vans.The European Commission spokesperson said: “High-level contacts between theEuropean Unionand the US administration are ongoing.”A UK government spokesperson said: “Forecourts in the UK are being supplied with petrol and diesel as normal and we have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry.”Explore more on these topicsOilEuropean UnionPetrol pricesEuropeCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Beverly Buchanan review – ramshackle mini barns and shanties bursting with brutal history  | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Inspired by the shacks and sheds of the American south, Buchanan’s exceptional sculptures combine folk art and minimalism to memorialise the survival of enslaved people
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: Inspired by the shacks and sheds of the American south, Buchanan’s exceptional sculptures combine folk art and minimalism to memorialise the survival of enslaved people
Content: The weathering effect of injustice … Miss Flossie's Shack, 1989.Photograph: Andrew Judd/collection of Lorenzo Legarda Leviste and Fahad MayetView image in fullscreenThe weathering effect of injustice … Miss Flossie's Shack, 1989.Photograph: Andrew Judd/collection of Lorenzo Legarda Leviste and Fahad MayetArt and designReviewBeverly Buchanan review – ramshackle mini barns and shanties bursting with brutal historySpike Island, BristolInspired by the shacks and sheds of the American south, Buchanan’s exceptional sculptures combine folk art and minimalism to memorialise the survival of enslaved peopleEddy FrankelThu 24 Sep 2026 10.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 10.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen she was a kid, Beverly Buchanan visited tenant farmers and sharecroppers across the American south-east with her dad. There in the fields she saw shacks and sheds, shanties and shotgun houses. More than 100 years after the abolition of slavery, she saw in this rough improvised architecture a symbol of survival and perseverance, of a people making their own way against the odds.Buchanan spent the rest of her life – a life marked by multiple chronic illnesses before she died in 2015 – translating that architectural heft into art. This show at Spike Island is filled with ramshackle, half-broken, semi-dilapidated little sculptures, each one based on the buildings of the south. There are houses made of scrap wood, churches made of cardboard, tiny barns hammered together and splashed with paint or covered with buttons. The one large sculpture here is great, a shed seemingly on the verge of collapse, but Buchanan’s physical condition forced her to work on a smaller scale as she was often stuck at home for long periods.They’re improvised sculptures, just like the shacks of the south are improvised buildings. And each one is filled to the brim with history, bursting at the seams with the past. In every shack sculpture you see an echo of slavery, a memorial to the people who survived it, a paean to the endurance of the enslaved.View image in fullscreenArchitecture as a symbol of perseverance … Lamar County. CA, 2003.Photograph: courtesy of the Estate of Beverly Buchanan and Andrew Edlin Gallery, New YorkThe sculptures sit neatly between folk art and minimalism. You can see them as modernist geometric forms or slapdash DIY craft; both are true, and that’s what makes them so compelling. But Buchanan was keen to reject any idea that her art was nostalgic. She saw her work as an attempt to make sure these symbols of grim history weren’t erased. Lots of her best stuff remains in the fields and marshes where it was installed, almost as much a part of nature as the trees and tide. She experimented with concrete and tabby, a material made from oyster shells, sand and ash historically formed into bricks by the enslaved people of the deep south. Buchanan made her own tabby bricks – a filthy, dangerous process – then stacked them up and left them outside where they could be eroded slowly by nature.This idea of weathering is everywhere in Buchanan’s work, symbolising the way people, bodies, could be worn away by injustice. A handful of these works – which she called Frustulas – sit on plinths here, pockmarked and weather-beaten, like someone left a modernist sculpture out in the rain. Each one, again, is a fragment of a violent past, an object weighed down by the history implied in its material, its shape.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLike modernist sculptures left out in the rain … Untitled (Maquette), c1970s.Photograph: Andrew Judd/collection of Lorenzo Legarda Leviste and Fahad MayetNot everything here is that emotionally heavy. A lot of Buchanan’s work is serious and formal and societal, but plenty of it is more personal too. She spent a lot of time in her local pharmacy, a place she could get her meds, but also one where she could meet friends, have some lunch. She made the pharmacy a promo T-shirt, drew out her favourite lunch menu. They’re fun objects that show you a lighter side to Buchanan but they’re not particularly interesting as artworks. The same goes for a lot of her drawings of flowers and chickens and angels, though her self-portraits tell a bit more of a story.The show is also a bit hamstrung by some overthought curation, which pulls the work into a bunch of barely discernible thematic groupings. And there’s no part of me that understands the inclusion of new work by young English artist Phoebe Collings-James – a sound piece and a film of her cousins playing with a sculpture – which has zero relation to Buchanan or her work.But the good stuff here – the shacks and Frustulas – is exceptional. It’s not just morose memorialising of brutal history: it’s a joyful celebration of ingenuity and survival in a world of inequality. As rickety as they look, these shacks tell a story that’s built to endure.AtSpike Island, Bristol, 26 September-31 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designSculptureArtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Global release announced for acclaimed Gaza documentary NAZA | NAZA | The Guardian
description: Theatrical rollout across 56 territories planned for documentary about Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza before film will stream on Guardian website
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: Theatrical rollout across 56 territories planned for documentary about Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza before film will stream on Guardian website
Content: ‘The death threats will not stop the film’ … a scene from NAZA.Photograph: The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The death threats will not stop the film’ … a scene from NAZA.Photograph: The GuardianNAZAGlobal release announced for acclaimed Gaza documentary NAZATheatrical rollout across 56 territories planned for documentary about Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza before film will stream on Guardian websiteCatherine ShoardandLorenzo TondoThu 24 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNAZA, the award-winning documentary from Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, is set to be released in cinemas inmore than 50 countries before a digital global release on theguardian.com.The film, which the Guardian produced, premiered at the Venice film festival earlier this month, where it was met with a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went onto win the special jury prize.‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligenceRead moreAfter screenings in Bologna and at the San Sebastián film festival, the film will receive its North American premiere on Saturday at the New York film festival before opening four days later at the IFC Center in New York City. On 9 October it will expand to Los Angeles and other key US cities before a national rollout.A theatrical release in partnership with MK2 Films is also planned in 55 other territories, including the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Canada, Hong Kong, Brazil, Turkey, Thailand, France, Spain, Germany, Turkey, Central America and the Middle East.After its run in cinemas, the film will stream in late November on the Guardian’s website, for free, as part of the news organisation’s commitment to the dissemination of independent journalism.“NAZA is grounded in rigorous journalism published over the past three years,” said Harry Davies, a Guardian investigations correspondent and one of NAZA’s producers. “But it is also a powerful piece of cinema that will soon be available on screens, large and small, around the world.”Documentary NAZA gets 25-minute standing ovation at Venice film festival premiere – videoA number of distributors and cinemas in Israel have been offered the film, and the Guardian is exploring ways by which NAZA can be seen in the occupied Palestinian territories.From ovations in Venice to death threats in Israel: the extreme responses to NAZA documentaryRead moreThe documentaryreveals the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. NAZA is a military acronym euphemistically used by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians that it expects will be killed in an airstrike.Shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, the film features interviews with 24 members of Israeli intelligence and military, granted on the condition of anonymity. The film builds on journalism first published by the Guardian, +972 Magazine, an Israeli-Palestinian publication, and Hebrew-language outlet Local Call between 2023 and 2025.In 2024, Abraham and Szorwon the best documentary Oscarfor No Other Land, along with their two Palestinian co-directors, Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal. Jonathan Glazer, the Oscar-winning film-maker of The Zone of Interest and Under the Skin, has executive produced, while his longtime collaborator, James Wilson of JW Films, also produced the film.The film won unanimously positive reviews at its premiere, but last week Benjamin Netanyahu and a number of senior military and far-right political figures called for the directors’ citizenship to be revoked, and accused them of“treason against the state”.The Israeli prime minister said he would seek new laws allowing the country to strip citizenship from people who “smear” Israeli soldiers and “defame” the state of Israel. Alongside the announcement,dozens of rightwing activists gathered outside Szor’s parents’ home.Police and border police officers were deployed at the scene. One protester called for the “death penalty for traitors” and demanded that the homes of the film-makers’ families be demolished.Speaking on Thursday, Abraham and Szor said: “We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israelis to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible.“The threats from the Israeli government to revoke our citizenship and the death threats do not change that and will not stop the film. We thank our colleagues for the solidarity and look forward to sharing NAZA all over the world very soon.”‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directorsRead moreLast week, 43 local human rights organisations issued ajoint statementurging Israeli authorities to stop what they described as incitement and threats against the film-makers, and not to prosecute either them or their sources.More than 1,500 Israeli film-makershave also signed a petition defending “freedom of expression and creation” and expressing solidarity with Szor and Abraham.Their sentiments have been echoed by a number of leading film-makers around the world, including Ken Loach, Joshua Oppenheimer, Paul Laverty, Laura Poitras, Nan Goldin, Richard Eyre and Hanif Kureishi. Oppenheimer, the US director of Oscar-nominated documentaries The Act of Killing and The Look of Silence, said, “The Israeli government is waging a full-scale intimidation campaign against film directors. I am appalled and enraged.”Explore more on these topicsNAZAFilm industryVenice film festivalGazaJonathan GlazerNo Other LandPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Cracking auction, Gromit!’ Original Aardman puppets go under the hammer  | Aardman | The Guardian
description: Wallace and Gromit stop-motion models and other beloved creations raise money to train new generations of animators
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Wallace and Gromit stop-motion models and other beloved creations raise money to train new generations of animators
Content: Wallace and Gromit stop-motion puppets from the film Vengeance Most Fowl are displayed during a preview of the Propstore auction of Aardman memorabilia.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAView image in fullscreenWallace and Gromit stop-motion puppets from the film Vengeance Most Fowl are displayed during a preview of the Propstore auction of Aardman memorabilia.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAAardman‘Cracking auction, Gromit!’ Original Aardman puppets go under the hammerWallace and Gromit stop-motion models and other beloved creations raise money to train new generations of animatorsSteven MorrisThu 24 Sep 2026 17.41 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWallace’s reaction as the auction got into full swing might have been a trademark “good grief!” – and the enthusiasm of some of the bidding could have caused even the phlegmatic Gromit to show surprise.Fans of Wallace and Gromit and other beloved creations of Aardman Animations seized the chance to grab souvenirs when more than 200 pieces – including Wallace, Gromit, Shaun the Sheep and Chicken Run puppets fromAardmanproductions – went under the hammeron Thursday.Wallace’s dog Gromit was nearly a cat, reveals creator as Aardman turns 50Read moreSought-after items included Wallace and Gromit stop-motion models from the Bristol studio’s hugely popular 2024 filmVengeance Most Fowl.Lot 216, for example, was Wallace in his traditional outfit of a knitted green tank top, red tie and brown trousers. The catalogue said he was in “smashing condition”, and gave details of his construction: “Wallace’s head is moulded from clay; while his body is made of silicone to facilitate smooth repositioning by the animators.“He has a skeleton, just like every salt-of-the-earth lad, it’s just that his happens to be made of metal.
