His teeth, shirt collar, tie, pen, and pencil are fast-cast resin and his eyes are plastic.” It sold for an eye-popping £50,400.A puppet of Gromit on all fours from the same film was “crafted over a fully jointed internal metal armature, allowing him to be held in his most natural pose”. It fetched £31,500.The catalogue made it clear these were not toys but pieces of art needing special packaging, shipping and careful handling. “Please also be aware that exposure to extreme temperatures may cause damage,” it said.View image in fullscreenFeathers McGraw alongside CI Mackintosh. A Feathers puppet, with the villain wearing his red rubber glove disguise, sold for almost £57,000.Photograph: Richard Gardner/ShutterstockAnother eye-catching lot was number 219 – Wallace and Gromit’s nemesis, Feathers McGraw, disguised as a nun. The catalogue reminded bidders of one of the best Wallace and Gromit lines: “Feathers McGraw? Don’t be ridiculous. That’s just an innocent nun, out for a pleasure cruise.”It went for more than £30,000 while a second Feathers puppet – with the villain wearing his red rubber glove disguise to make out he was a chicken rather than a sinister penguin – did even better, selling for almost £57,000. Crime, it appears, does pay.It was not only Wallace, Gromit and Feathers that proved popular.Aardmanaficionados snapped up pieces related to the studio’s early days, including clay puppets of Morph and his pal Chas.Every lot started at £100 but as bidding got under way at teatime in London, it was clear they were not going to stay low for long.The Morph and Chas puppets, made from plasticine by Aardman co-founder Peter Lord and accompanied by handwritten care instructions, one of the first lots to be auctioned, sold for £3,780.View image in fullscreenChas (left) and Morph sold for £3,780.Photograph: PropstoreMischievous Morph first appeared in 1977 as part of Take Hart, before starring in his own series of adventures. Another lot – lunch for six with Lord in Bristol – was bought by someone for more than £11,000. A stop-motion masterclass with an Aardman animator sold for just over £20,000.Storyboards fromWallace & Gromit: the Wrong Trouserssigned by another Aardman grandee, Nick Park, went for almost £4,000. A 9cm-tall clay rabbit that appeared inThe Curse of the Were-Rabbitcost almost £10,000.Bidders whose budget could not stretch to a Wallace or Gromit puppet could buy more modest souvenirs such as lot 89 – dry stone walls and gate from the Shaun the Sheep TV series. That came with “adhesive remnants from where the pieces were secured to the set”. It sold for a more affordable £567.The sale, run bythe memorabilia auction house Propstore, marked the 50th anniversary of the studio, with the profits to be used to train new generations of animators.Ngaio Harding-Hill, the director of attractions and live experiences and archive at Aardman, described it as an “unprecedented opportunity” to own a part of the studio’s 50-year history.Harding-Hill said the collection had been carefully curated by the Aardman team to make sure the studio’s five decades were reflected in the auction.She said: “Proceeds from the auction will be invested in talent development initiatives across Aardman, including bursaries at our world-class training facility, the Aardman Academy, meaning every sale is contributing to nurturing the next generation of animation talent.”Explore more on these topicsAardmanWallace & GromitAnimation on TVTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Greek epics, gory obsessions and awkward invites: where does this year’s Oscars race stand? | Oscars | The Guardian
description: Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey might be the one to beat but a crop of competitors is starting to materialise
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey might be the one to beat but a crop of competitors is starting to materialise
Content: Top: Olivia Wilde in The Invite, Anne Hathaway in The Odyssey Bottom: Inde Navarrette in Obsession, Andrew Scott in Elsinore.Composite: AlamyView image in fullscreenTop: Olivia Wilde in The Invite, Anne Hathaway in The Odyssey Bottom: Inde Navarrette in Obsession, Andrew Scott in Elsinore.Composite: AlamyOscarsGreek epics, gory obsessions and awkward invites: where does this year’s Oscars race stand?Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey might be the one to beat but a crop of competitors is starting to materialiseBenjamin LeeThu 24 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReporting from fall film festivals used to be a more streamlined process – what’s good, what’s bad, what’s being sold, what hasOscarschances – but with each year, the season arrives with larger, more existential questions.The 2025 run, from Venice to Telluride to Toronto, was notably underwhelming and took place months after Sinners went from box-office hit tolegitimate contenderand at the same time as One Battle After Another skipped festivals and went on towin best picture. The pipeline that had once birthed winners such as Birdman, Spotlight, 12 Years a Slave and The King’s Speech had no longer played as big of a part with Covid-affectedNomadlandbeing the last fall festival film to win the top prize. Even without an awards hat on, there has been a more general lack of buzz, an excitement of something new that much harder to find as more films of considerably lower quality took up underserved space. If the trades are to be believed, a lot of it is down to studios choosing against the risk of bad buzz and potential embarrassment to A-listers because for every The Shape of Water or Poor Things, there’s a White Noise or Joker: Folie à Deux. So while this season might see new films starring Tom Cruise, Timothée Chalamet, Anne Hathaway, Christian Bale, Amy Adams, Daisy Edgar-Jones, Ben Affleck and Mikey Madison, none of them are braving a festival premiere.La Bola Negra wins Toronto film festival people’s choice awardRead moreAs Oscar nominations were being announced back in January of this year, the next crop of contenders started revealing themselves over in Park City where Utah hosted its finalSundance film festival. The biggest story was the return and reinvention of Olivia Wilde, who was the best part of Gregg Araki’s comedyI Want Your Sexand finally announced herself as a serious director with chamber comedyThe Invite, a remake of the Spanish film The People Upstairs. It was the buzziest title of the festival and after a rapturous premiere, a heated auction led to A24buyingthe rights and a summer release scored solid box office and sustained word of mouth. It didn’t automatically seem like an obvious Academy pick even if it might have been viewed as such years prior – a talky, human comedyabout sex and relationshipswithout much of a recent precedent – but it slowly seemed like a surer thing. Wilde could become the first woman ever to receive nominations for acting and directing while, as it stands, it seems like A24’s strongest contender.There was also support for John Turturro’s turn in simple, old-fashioned crime dramaThe Only Living Pickpocket in New York, a film that was purchased by Sony Pictures Classics, an Oscar campaign clearly in mind. Turturro has yet to receive an Oscar nomination and with a rare every-scene performance here, he could sneak into the best actor five.The festival’s big prize isn’t usually a predictor of Oscar success (recent winners have includedClemency,Atropia,Nannyand In the Summers), yet films such as Coda, Minari and Whiplash have managed to use this early win as the start of fruitful Oscar campaign. This year’s winner wasJosephine, an acclaimed drama starring Channing Tatum that seemed like one of the bigger breakouts. But its uncomfortable subject matter – an eight-year-old girl spirals after witnessing a graphic sexual assault – made it a difficult watch for some (there were walkouts) and an even more difficult purchase for buyers, ultimatelygoing toa small and untested new company called Sumerian Pictures. Tatum gives arguably his greatest performance yet (I would hand him the best supporting actor Oscar now if I could) and the film is thoughtfully made by writer-director Beth de Araújo, but it’s a steeper hill to climb due to its backers and content and it might have to unfairly settle for some critics circle prizes.Josephine review – Channing Tatum is a knockout in shattering drama of lost innocenceRead moreTheBerlin film festivalhasn’t tended to produce many Academy-friendly movies over the years (Ethan Hawke in Blue Moon, Charlotte Rampling in 45 Years, four wins for The Grand Budapest Hotel) but with more doors open for international films at the Oscars, it’s become more present in the race. This year most eyes were on Sandra Hüller and her gender-switching turn in black-and-white dramaRose, which could find her on the outskirts of the best actress race. It helps that she’s also inthreeotheracclaimedfilms of the year, one of which premiered soon after the festival finished …No one was quite sure what to expect of March’s sci-fi adventureProject Hail Mary, with starRyan Goslingproving to be an unreliable box-office draw and directors Phil Lord and Chris Miller having not made a live-action film since 2014’s 22 Jump Street. But the film was a considerable win, both critically and commercially, and many believe it could follow in the footsteps of The Martian, also from author Andy Weir, a film that nabbed seven Oscar nominations. Amazon doesn’t have the best track record with the Academy but since the Academy seems to be once again favouring blockbuster fare (ifF1couldget in…) this could easily become one of the final 10.Next came Cannes and a notablelack of many American movies, with most studios and stars choosing not to make the journey over. James Gray’sPaper Tiger, starring Adam Driver and Scarlett Johansson, was well-received but like his other similarly well-received films, such as Armageddon Time and The Lost City of Z, it might not be to the Academy’s tastes (he has yet to score a single nomination). The biggest American breakout was Jordan Firstman’s Club Kid, a fairly conventional comedy about a gay man dealing with a son he didn’t know about, which scored strong reviews and interest from buyers, leading to an A24pickup. It’s continued to play well at fall festivals but could be another beloved smaller indie from the company that appeals more to critic circles than the Academy (see also:Sorry Baby, Uncut Gems, The Souvenir and I Saw the TV Glow). The buzziest breakouts came from outside the US – from Spain to Japan to Romania.Fjord review - Cristian Mungiu at sea with strange child abuse drama starring Renate Reinsve and Sebastian StanRead moreThe Palme d’Or winner was Cristian Mungiu’sFjord, a divisive culture wars drama starring Oscar nominees Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve. It was picked up by Neon, a company that knows a thing a two about turning this into Oscar success (they have previously secured noms and wins for previous Palme d’Or picks Anora, It Was Just an Accident, Parasite, Anatomy of a Fall and Triangle of Sadness). But Fjord has its fair share of hurdles (it went downpoorlyat Toronto, some have accused it of being too rightwing and Mungiu previously saw his last Palme d’Or honoree – 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days – snubbed by the Academy). A farsafer betwould be the ambitious Spanish epicLa Bola Negra, which tells the story of interconnected gay men across three different timelines. It had a 20-minute standing ovation and was snapped up for the US byNetflix, who are giving it an unusually generous theatrical window later this year. It also features a cameo fromPenélope Cruz, having quite the year with this and an Oscar-tipped supporting turn in The Invite. Elsewhere, there were thumbs up (and somewavering) for Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s care home dramaAll of a Suddenthat might not have the support that pushed his breakoutDrive My Carto Oscar glory, but its star Virginie Efira could find her way into the best actress category. She’ll face competition from another performance by Hüller, who turned up again in her second black-and-white drama of the year, this time in Paweł Pawlikowski’sFatherland, a 1940s-set father-daughter tale.Back in the US, an unlikely contender took shape at the start of the summer season. At last year’s Toronto film festival, micro-budget horrorObsessionturned midnight madness screams into a $15m purchase by Focus Features, 20 times what it was made for. It became asmash hitin May, breaking multiple box-office records and energising gen Z audiences – and while none of this immediately screams Oscars, the ongoing acclaim for breakout star Inde Navarrette caused many to ask, well why not? The Academy’s slow appreciation for horror – with The Substance and Weapons recently breaking through – shows that the genre has finally scared voters into submission and with Focus behind it, who know a thing or two about FYC campaigns, it seems like at least Navarrette is in the race, with the film itself possibly joining her. A more traditional challenger came soon after,Christopher Nolan’s epicThe Odyssey, which also became a box-office titan and, like previous best picture-winningOppenheimer, it appealed to critics as much as it did with audiences. It’s by far the strongest across-the-board option we have at this stage with likely acting noms for Hathaway andMatt Damonas well as a range of craft nods. Even though Nolan did win director and picture so recently, it’s hard to see who can stop him from doing it again at this moment.Possible Love review – a tale of two couples is finely judged study of exploitation and friendshipRead moreIt was then time for the fall festivals withVeniceemerging, a little light on the bigger titles many had expected. It kicked off with Danny Boyle’s tabloid taleInk, which received decent notices but not quite decent enough for the film to be deemed a major player, with Netflix unlikely to prioritise it over La Bola Negra and a more substantial Venice breakout, Lee Chang-dong’sPossible Love. Lee’s last film,Burning, might not have made the cut (it was, however, the first Korean film to make it to the final nine-film shortlist) but rapturous reviews for his latest, along with timely themes of class and power as well as the might of Netflix behind it, could turn it into one of the year’s best international feature nominees.The major English language success story came from Martin McDonagh, who has previously used the festival as a springboard for Oscar nominations or wins for films such as Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri and The Banshees of Inisherin. His latest,Wild Horse Nine, might not have quite the same amount of universal acclaim but it’s hard not to see it picking up multiple nominations. Its most likely win would be forJohn Malkovich, who has two nods under his belt but is yet to take an Oscar home. There was also the world premiere ofPrimetime, the thriller that seesRobert Pattinsonplay To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen, but it felt more curio than contender, the only real thing anyone could agree on being the surprisingly effective supporting performance from Skyler Gisondo, who could factor into the race.The Golden Lion, again not always a predictor of Oscar success (winners have included Father Mother Sister Brother, Roma, The Room Next Door and Nomadland), wasawardedtoWoman Unknown, a well-regarded Danish thriller that will likely be an international feature competitor but might not break into other major categories.‘He’s simply astonishing’: will Andrew Scott become the first out gay man to win the best actor Oscar?Read moreNext wasTelluridewith a more stacked lineup than Venice, led by two films that might well feature the season’s two lead acting winners. First wasElsinore, a drama starringAndrew Scottas the Chariots of Fire actor Ian Charleson as he plays Hamlet while dealing with the devastation of the Aids crisis. While some were sniffier about what was perceived as “Oscarbait” storytelling, virtually all agreed that Scott had acted his way to the front of the pack for best actor. Notably the film did go down well enough at Toronto towinthe people’s choice award for international film, suggesting it may also receive some other high-profile nods. Meanwhile the best actress race found itself suddenly led by Julianne Moore for her all-in performance in Jesse Eisenberg’s offbeat theatre comedyThe Debut. While it’s unusual for a turn quite so wildly comedic and devoid of much recognisable humanity to win (Emma Stone in Poor Things might be a recent example but that character did have some pathos), Moore is beloved by the Academy (one win and another four nominations) and whileA Real Painwasn’t embraced by the Academy as much as some expected (awinfor Kieran Culkin and just one other nod), the film’s focus on acting will appeal to a lot of voters.The long weekend also saw the premiere ofTender Loving Care, what might well beMike Leigh’s final film. It’s another humane, textured and universally adored comedy drama about the lives of recognisably real people and while critics circles will likely shower it, the Academy hasn’t gravitated towards his films for a while.Hard Truthswas snubbed, Another Year had just one nod for screenplay (and criminally nothing for Lesley Manville), Peterloo received no noms, while his only winning film is Topsy-Turvy and that was for below-the-line craft. What might lift this one slightly for voters is both the fact that Leighsaid it could likely behis swan song and the presence of Kate O’Flynn, still riding high after her Emmystriumphfor Apple’s hit horror comedyWidow’s Bay. She may well see herself in the supporting actress category. Elsewhere,Carrie Coonimpressed in cult dramaThe Liberationbut the film had mixed notices. There was also a last-minute surprise screening of You Can See Everything,Nathan Fielder’s unconventional, almost three-hour Elizabeth Holmes documentary, which some are claiming could be an unlikely best picture nominee, though this would be a first in the category. A documentary nod seems more likely, although that branch has mostly favoured international films of late.Misty Green review – Chris Rock’s jumbled LA drama saved by fiery Rosalind EleazarRead moreTorontocame next with alineupstacked with films but of a noticeably lower wattage than what once was. On the ground, it was mostly repeats of films that had premiered elsewhere that received the most attention, with The Debut, Elsinore and La Bola Negra in particular getting a substantial boost, the first foreign language winner of the people’s choice award since 2011. Of the festival’s world premieres, the biggest hit seemed to be Peter Farrelly’s making-of dramaI Play Rocky, which had a standing ovation and was the runner-up for people’s choice. Farrelly previously saw his crowd-pleasing comedy Green Book go from Toronto hit to best picture winner, and while his Stallone biopic might not feel quite as primed with fewer social issues in its corner, its ability to energise audiences could see it land a nomination at the least. There were a number of failed best actress bids from Cynthia Erivo with a mostly loathed adaptation of award-winning playPrima Facie, Sarah Paulson with buzz-free dame v dame dramaClosing Nightand Naomi Watts with misfiring Nazi thrillerThe Housewife, none of which have found a US buyer as yet. Far more convincing was British Slow Horses star Rosalind Eleazar, who rose above Chris Rock’s otherwise patchy Hollywood sagaMisty Greento impress with a turn that could see her sneak in, especially given how weak that category is this year.This week sees the kick-off of the New York film festival with more world premieres than usual. Andrew Garfield will be hoping his Sam Altman impression in OpenAI sagaArtificialis good enough to reintroduce directorLuca Guadagninointo the Academy’s good books, Tom McCarthy will be aiming to repeat his Spotlight glory with talky, 80s-set climate change drama A Statement, and Tony Gilroy’s music drama Behemoth! will try to launchPedro Pascalas a late best actor challenger. Outside of festivals, two-time best director winner Alejandro González Iñárritu is dragging Tom Cruiseout of his comfort zonein the darkly comedic satire Digger (which some are suggesting will be bigger for supporting actorJohn Goodmanthan its lead) the week before Aaron Sorkin tries to copy The Social Network’s success with follow-upThe Social Reckoningled by best actress winner Mikey Madison. Soon we’ll also see one-time Oscar mainstay David O Russell return with the sports biopic Madden, starring Oscar winners Nicolas Cage and Christian Bale, his first film since 2022’s disastrousAmsterdam;Robert EggersfollowingNosferatu, which surprised with four nominations, with another gothic horror called Werwulf; and thereturn of Dune, a franchise that has so far won eight Oscars, with the third and “final” chapter. Could we have a best picture-winning Return of the King on our hands?Seven safe-ish nominee betsChristopher Nolan – best director, The OdysseyJulianne Moore – best actress, The DebutAndrew Scott – best actor, ElsinoreInde Navarrette – best actress, ObsessionJohn Malkovich – best actor, Wild Horse NineRashida Jones and Will McCormack – best adapted screenplay, The InviteJohn Goodman – best supporting actor, DiggerExplore more on these topicsOscarsAwards and prizesOlivia WildeThe OdysseyChristopher NolanRyan GoslingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kim Kardashian’s Team Moms highlights the ridiculous excess of the US youth-sports industry | Baseball | The Guardian
description: A new Paramount+ series premiering Thursday turns pushy sports parents into glossy entertainment – with the children largely ushered off stage
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: A new Paramount+ series premiering Thursday turns pushy sports parents into glossy entertainment – with the children largely ushered off stage
Content: The cast of Team Moms, a new reality series following a group of mothers whose children play competitive youth baseball.Photograph: Paramount+View image in fullscreenThe cast of Team Moms, a new reality series following a group of mothers whose children play competitive youth baseball.Photograph: Paramount+BaseballKim Kardashian’s Team Moms highlights the ridiculous excess of the US youth-sports industryA new Paramount+ series premiering Thursday turns pushy sports parents into glossy entertainment – with the children largely ushered off stageAndrew LawrenceThu 24 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 09.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRemember when pushy sports parents were deserving objects of our collective scorn? WhenMarv MarinovichandJim Piercewere bywords for abusive fatherhood, Sarah Palin made the overbearing hockey mom a global punchline, and grim stories of pushy parentsassaulting officials, kids and one another grabbed headlines and traineda harsh spotlight on youth sports? Well, the rebrand is in full swing.Team Moms: Baseball is a glossy new reality series premiering Thursday that aims to recast the pushy sports parent as something well worth coveting, a sexy black hat with a designer label. From the makers of Love Island (ITV America), forHollywood’s most rapacious studio(Paramount Skydance), with none other thanbasketball mom Kim Kardashianattached as executive producer, the Paramount+ series follows a cluster of parents whose sons attend Legendary Prep Academy –a Scottsdale, Arizona baseball hothousewith an intense focus on cultivating diamond gems. Anyone coming to this expecting genuine insights on a $40bn industry that’s nowunder siege from private equity, swallowing ever larger chunks of hard-earned family budgets along the way, should know up front: this is a closer cousin to Bravo’s Real Housewives franchise than ESPN’s 30 for 30.The title alone – a deliberate play on Teen Mom,MTV’s train-wreck young-mothers series– gives the game away. It makes abundantly clear that the focus of Team Moms’ eight hour-ish episodes isn’t the 13- and 14-year-olds chasing their field of dreams. It’s the middle-aged parents chasing vicarious glory, proximal clout and social validation. The tone is reinforced at the start of the show, in an around-the-horn-style opening title sequence that punctuates family portraits with the kids’ heroic glove work before landing on baseball cards of the individual moms fanned out over home plate. Never mind that the moms are set up to be the fall guys for the real drama queens: the dads.View image in fullscreenParents watch from the sidelines as their children compete in the high-pressure world of travel baseball featured in Team Moms.Photograph: Paramount+The Kardashian-meets-Love Island alchemy is undeniable in the way Team Moms presents staggering opulence as wholly incidental: the luxury car fleets, the giga-mansions, the immaculate show kitchens that provide the backdrop for daily routines and gossip. The kids move through this world as you’d expect of kids who essentially have baseball for a job, zombieing themselves from bed to a hot cup ofcoffeebefore shuffling off into the predawn for another shift at the ballpark salt mines. For inspiration, the kids only need look to the writing on the walls:Prefer pain. Comfort is a slow death. Die growing, pledge growth to the grave. Upton Sinclair,eat your heart out.It’s a five-days-a-week grind before you even get to weekend games – many of which demand hours of commuting – or the additional baseball “tutoring” many of these families seek out in hopes of keeping their kids on a steady development curve or outpacing their peers. The same can hardly be said of the academic side of this equation, which doesn’t appear to take up more than a few hours of the training day if the players even have energy left to get it at all. Producers can barely be bothered to ask about the obvious toll of this grind in the gratuitous kiddie confessionals, much less get them to consider the prospect of taking up other sports – something many great athletes do, as my former Sports Illustrated colleague David Epstein explores inhis 2019 book Range.View image in fullscreenYoung players from the Legendary Performance Academy arrive at the ballpark ahead of a game.Photograph: Paramount+Of course none of this athletic hothousing comes cheap. Legendary Prep doesn’t publicize its tuition costs, but I suppose you’re already in trouble if you even have to ask. Similar academies charge anywhere from $12,000 to more than $20,000 annually for the same basic bundle of high-level athletic training, sports science analytics, team travel and a hybrid or supervised online academic curriculum. There was no explicit mention of tuition costs in the three-ish episodes of Team Moms that I watched, but one mom did let slip that she bought her 16-year-old daughter aPorsche Macanto somewhat offset the money the family spends on her brother’s baseball prospects.While this same mom – we’ll call her Pilates Mom because the names on this show aren’t as important as the archetypes – bankrolls her boy’s dream despite her keen awareness of his having “a 0.02% chance” of making it to the MLB, the other parents in the series are quite convinced they have the next Aaron Judge or Bryce Harper on their hands. (With names like Jett and Stryker, how could these kids miss?) All the families are white, and the irony of their sons of privilege chasing an MLB dream that so many less-resourced Latin American kids pursue,with relatively outsized success, is completely lost on them (even though that pipelinehas its leaky bits, too).We’re meant to view Pilates Mom as the villain because she swans around in athleisure wear that accentuates her curves and draws snide remarks. Pilates Mom sets tongues wagging after offhandedly calling one boy “a little bitch” during one of her Pilates sessions with the kids – the same boy had told her son he watches Pilates Mom on OnlyFans, prompting a schoolyard dustup.View image in fullscreenPlayers from the Legendary Performance Academy warm up before a game, one casually tossing a baseball as teammates look on.Photograph: Paramount+Team Mom fault lines are drawn in hair dye. On one side, there’s the cliquey blondes: Martha Stewart Mom, the type-A who leaves her husband a “How to Be Me” memo when she steps away from the house; Party Mom, living her best life in retirement with streaks; and Trophy Mom, a Nascar wife who cites marriage and motherhood as her biggest accomplishments. On the other, the slightly more self-aware brunettes: Pilates Mom, often shot inside her empty studio; Wine Mom, the wary wife of a hobby vintner; and Friends Mom, a Courteney Cox lookalike whose coming-out story and enduring friendship with her fogey ex-husband frustrate the parent group into making crude jokes about her “returning to the other side of the pond”.Travel baseball: a world where eight-year-olds are treated like prosRead moreBut the women and their drama just provide cover for their pushy sports spouses. A group spring break trip has Wine Dad torn over whether to let his son, a flashy teen who seems better at branding than baseball, join his friends on a kayaking excursion or drive him an hour away for some extra hitting. (So as a compromise, they do both.) Party Dad can’t stop touting Pilates Mom’s body in mixed company. Only Nascar Dad sets a halfway decent example because Casey Mears,motor racing royalty, has actually been there, done that and ismoving merch.But the worst is Egg Dad – the Humpty Dumpty who can’t let a moment pass without mentioning he played professional hockey, even though he was no better thana minor-minor leaguerin his day. Ever irascible, he’s always threatening to drop the gloves and throw down with the moms and dads at the first sign of a funny look. Egg Dad’s son, a U14 pitcher, is relegated to the fringes of the production after breaking his forearm in a fielding collision. After Egg Mom carts him home from a hospital visit to have the surgical pins removed from his arm, Egg Dad pushes him to get back on the ball.“I don’t even know if I could put on a glove right now,” the kid says.“The doc says it’s up to you, but I want to see you play,” Egg Dad says.View image in fullscreenTensions flare among parents during a gathering in Team Moms, the reality series set in the world of competitive youth baseball.Photograph: Paramount+On spring break, Egg Dad organizes a game of Plant the Flag on the gravel driveway of their Italianate resort compound –Great idea, Wine Dad says, with an eye roll – and his son winds up hurting his armagain. Egg Dad puts his poor kid on the kayak without a thought and then booze-bonds with Party Dad over how soft their two kids are. “[They’ve] got to understand the difference between a real injury and [pain] and just go,” Party Dad says. It seems no amount of Hollywood high gloss can make the stigma of the pushy sports parent disappear, even if it’s buffed and contoured by Kim K.Likely, this won’t be the last Team Mom installment if the titular colon is any indication. You can just picture spinoffs into soccer, tennis and perhaps even the southern California youth basketball scene – where Kardashian already features prominently. Really, the fact that youth sports in the US can so easily be spun into idle entertainment tells you everything that’s wrong with a homegrown approach to athletic development that favors the paying parents over the toiling kids, or even the major college and professional clubs who have a financial incentive to turn a catch-as-catch-can approach to talent scouting into a halfway dependable,European-style conveyor belt.And the fact that Kardashian and her producing partners intuitively know that parents would rather watch richer, better-looking versions of themselves than watch kids like theirs crash and burn while pursuing their dreams is just proof that pushy sports parents haven’t softened. They’re just reaping the benefits of softer lighting now.Explore more on these topicsBaseballUS sportsReality TVTelevisionKim KardashianUS televisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: U2 announce new album Carnaval de Luz, featuring final recording by Dolly Parton | U2 | The Guardian
description: Irish rock legends’ 16th studio album, described by the Edge as ‘a messy, provocative, sacred collection of songs’, to arrive in November
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Irish rock legends’ 16th studio album, described by the Edge as ‘a messy, provocative, sacred collection of songs’, to arrive in November
Content: Riding the crest of an industrious spell … U2, who have announced new album Carnaval de Luz.Photograph: Viviane SassenView image in fullscreenRiding the crest of an industrious spell … U2, who have announced new album Carnaval de Luz.Photograph: Viviane SassenU2U2 announce new album Carnaval de Luz, featuring final recording by Dolly PartonIrish rock legends’ 16th studio album, described by the Edge as ‘a messy, provocative, sacred collection of songs’, to arrive in NovemberBen Beaumont-ThomasThu 24 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleU2 have officially announced their first album of new material in nearly a decade, entitled Carnaval de Luz, to be released on 13 November.Closing out the album’s 12 tracks is Torn, the final recorded performance byDolly Parton, who duets with Bono on a song described in press materials as “a tender country song detailing broken family ties, that holds wider resonances”. Parton died aged 80 on 25 August.Guitarist the Edge described Carnaval de Luz, U2’s 16th studio album, as “a messy, provocative, sacred collection of songs”, whileBonopromised “loud guitars, deep bass, some ecstatic rhythms … the same imagination that brings us our creativity can also bring us monsters. So we make the drums louder. We build a bigger fire. We make our stories wilder and funnier. We make the melodies sweeter and the songs, they better shine, because if the world is in darkness we better not be.”The album caps an industrious spell for the Irish rock legends, who have already released two EPs this year: Days of Ash and Easter Lily.Speaking as Days of Ash was released in February, Bono trailed the release of the new album, saying it would have “a carnival vibe … a more defiantly joyful feel” than the vexed political songwriting of that EP, which reflected on ICE, Iran, Ukraine and the Israel-Palestine conflict.Days of Ash was praised by the Guardian’s Alexis Petridis, who said the “zeal, purpose and belief” of the band’s peak years “has been recaptured here”.U2: Days of Ash review – six new tracks reaffirm the band as a vital political voiceRead moreThe new album announcement comes 50 years, to the week, after drummer Larry Mullen Jr, then aged 14, pinned a message to the noticeboard of Dublin’s Mount Temple Comprehensive School which read “drummer seeks musicians to form band”.The quartet, rounded out with bassist Adam Clayton, were all there from the very first meeting, and went on to become arguably the defining rock band of the late 20th century thanks to critically acclaimed and commercially successful albums such as The Joshua Tree and Achtung Baby.They extended their success into the new millennium, with a trio of back to back UK No 1 albums: All That You Can’t Leave Behind, How to Dismantle an Atomic Bomb and No Line on the Horizon. Their most recent albums are a loosely connected trilogy between 2014 and 2023: Songs of Innocence, Songs of Experience and Songs of Surrender, the latter a collection of reworked versions of material from their back catalogue.Carnaval de Luz reunites the band with Brian Eno and Daniel Lanois, the duo who produced The Unforgettable Fire, The Joshua Tree and Achtung Baby. Eno co-writes and plays synths on three tracks, while Lanois plays pedal steel on the Parton duet. More contemporary names also feature in the form of EDM megastar Martin Garrix, co-writer of Glorify, and pop star and producer Ryan Tedder, co-producer of Silencio.The latter track, a raucous rock’n’roll song, has been released alongside the album announcement. The first track from the album, Street of Dreams, was released in July.Explore more on these topicsU2Pop and rockIrelandDolly PartonBononewsShareReuse this content

title: George Bush, murder and nautical infidelity: the Chicks’ 20 greatest songs – ranked! | The Chicks | The Guardian
description: As the country trio once known as Dixie Chicks celebrate 20 years of their album Taking the Long Way, we count down the best of their catchy, sometimes controversial catalogue
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: As the country trio once known as Dixie Chicks celebrate 20 years of their album Taking the Long Way, we count down the best of their catchy, sometimes controversial catalogue
Content: The former Dixie Chicks …(from left)Martie Maguire, Natalie Maines and Emily Strayer in 2002.Photograph: Harry Langdon/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe former Dixie Chicks …(from left)Martie Maguire, Natalie Maines and Emily Strayer in 2002.Photograph: Harry Langdon/Getty ImagesRankedThe ChicksGeorge Bush, murder and nautical infidelity: the Chicks’ 20 greatest songs – ranked!As the country trio once known as Dixie Chicks celebrate 20 years of their album Taking the Long Way, we count down the best of their catchy, sometimes controversial catalogueAlexis PetridisThu 24 Sep 2026 08.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 09.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. If I Fall You’re Going Down With Me (2001)One of eight singles released from the album Fly. Amazement at the sheer number should be matched by astonishment at their consistency. If I Fall … is just great. Organ-driven rock lent a Nashville twang by the fiddle, it barrels along, rich with the confidence of a band who know they can’t put a foot wrong.19. Tights on My Boat (2020)You don’t want for dirt dished about Natalie Maines’ divorce on Gaslighter, the band’s eighth album, but this accusation of nautical infidelity stands out. It’s ferociously angry and very funny – plus its understated, live-in the-studio sound only compounds the sense that you’re eavesdropping on tea being spilled among friends.18. You Were Mine (1998)A great country weeper in its own right, You Were Mine is also part of the Chicks’ origin story. It was written by the sisters Emily Strayer and Martie Maguire about their parents’ divorce; they then invited Maines, the daughter of the producer Lloyd Maines, to sing on the demo, rather than the then Chicks vocalist Laura Lynch. A lineup change and vast success ensued.17. The Long Way Around (2006)The chief theme of the Taking the Long Way album – being celebrated soon with a 20th anniversary reissue and tour – was the Chicks’ war of words with President George W Bush and Nashville conservatives. The musically sweet-toned opening track suggests that attitude was par for the course – of a piece with a longstanding disinclination to “kiss all the asses” and “do it like everybody else”.View image in fullscreenThe Chicks performing in 2003.Photograph: Pictorial Press/Alamy16. Julianna Calm Down (2020)Over a soft organ backing and something approaching a dancefloor pulse, the Chicks offer hard-won advice to the recently dumped: “Put on your best shoes and strut the fuck around like you’ve got nothing to lose.” Its slow build to a euphoric climax – elevated by Maguire’s fiddle – is great.15. Ready to Run (1999)You could suggest the Celtic motifs on Ready to Run are an acknowledgment of Irish folk’s seminal influence on country; equally, they may have something to do with the Corrs’ late-90s success. Either way, Ready to Run’s breezy mood carries a witty lyric that offers a middle finger to marriage and commitment.View image in fullscreenThe band during their world tour in Cincinnati, Ohio, in June 2016.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for PMK14. Texas Man (2020)Marooned in California post-divorce, Maines pines for the more rough-hewn gents of her home county. But the beauty of Texas Man is really about the music’s experimental bent: a tight, close-miked, new-wave-leaning sound replete with fuzzed-out guitar that’s completely unlike anything the Chicks had released before, but still somehow sounds like them.13. Cold Day in July (1999)Five minutes of inconsolable misery. “The moon is full, and my arms are empty / All night long, I’ve pleaded and cried,” it opens, with Maines’ voice at its most angst-ridden. The guitar-driven arrangement is simple, but spot-on: it doesn’t need anything more to work its sob-inducing magic.12. Sin Wagon (1999)In the early 80s, there was talk of a subgenre called cowpunk. It never crossed over into the mainstream, but the title perfectly fits Sin Wagon, named after a line in Grease. A thrilling blend of speedy bluegrass with raw, growling energy, its lyrics are home to a splendid celebration of “mattress dancin”.11. Sleep at Night (2020)There’s a pleasing circularity about Sleep at Night, which bears the distinct influence of the noted Chicks fan Taylor Swift; you can almost hear her delivering the line: “My husband’s girlfriend’s husband just called me up – how messed up is that?” An extra point for the slapping rhythm track, the perfect accompaniment to the punches landed in the lyrics.10. Easy Silence (2006)The negative image of Taking the Long Way’s two-fisted lead single Not Ready to Make Nice, Easy Silence details the downside of being the centre of a media storm. It sounds utterly, affectingly weary – “everyone is running” it notes, before evincing a longing to “keep the world at bay”.9. There’s Your Trouble (1998)The Chicks’ biggest UK chart hit offers the perfect example of why their fourth album, Wide Open Spaces, catapulted the former bluegrass/western-swing combo to superstardom: beautifully turned songwriting, a fresh pop sheen that didn’t overwhelm their audible country bona fides, impressively tough and salty lyrics and – in their new vocalist Maines – the ideal voice to deliver them.8. Landslide (2002)This version of the Stevie Nicks song is bold – the original is a classic – and ahead of the curve, arriving years before Fleetwood Mac became a hip name for leftfield musicians to drop. Stripped down to country basics, in keeping with the rest of the album Home, the song shines, highlighting the trio’s impeccable harmonies.7. Long Time Gone (2002)The back-to-the-land saga of Darrell Scott’s Long Time Gone comes complete with a critique of modern Nashville – “they got money, but they don’t have Cash” – and the Chicks’ version is suitably old-fashioned, with no drums and a distinct bluegrass influence about the banjo and fiddle. The lyrics are biting, but it still sounds like a party.6. Gaslighter (2020)The title track of the first Chicks album in 14 years pulled no punches. Its subject, Natalie Maines’ ex-husband Adrian Pasdar, had reportedly been concerned that the group’s unreleased material would violate a confidentiality clause in their prenuptial agreement. Gaslighter was released after the couple finalised their divorce, but it is almost unsettlingly brutal in its frankness – and insanely catchy.5. Wide Open Spaces (1998)Wide Open Spaces started life as a student’s poem about returning to Texas from university in Montana and ended up a kind of Stetson-cladShe’s Leaving Home. A huge hit – and the kind of Chicks song that one suspects sunk in deep with the young Swift.View image in fullscreenStrayer, Maines and Maguire on the set of a video shoot for Goodbye Earl in 2000.Photograph: Paul Natkin/WireImage4. Travelin’ Soldier (2002)This is destined to be remembered as the track Maines was introducing in London when she criticised Bush, but the ensuing furore shouldn’t overshadow how fantastic Travelin’ Soldier is. Stark and moving, never mawkish, it isn’t a protest song so much as a heartbreaking story entwined with the Vietnam war.Big hits, massive ballads and titanic emotions: Céline Dion’s greatest songs – ranked!Read more3. Cowboy Take Me Away (1999)A song based on the slogan of a US advert – for Calgon bath and beauty products! – should be a novelty. Cowboy Take Me Away is anything but. Instead, it’s a wistful paean to escape, lent a tear-jerking quality by the sense said escape may never happen. Balanced between uplift and melancholy, the music fits perfectly.2. Not Ready to Make Nice (2006)The Chicks’ best-known musical response to the Bush incident is a thing of snarling, screw-the-lot-of-you wonder: “It’s too late to make it right / I probably wouldn’t if I could.” The ensuing album slightly belaboured the point, but as a short, sharp burst of bitterness and bile, Not Ready to Make Nice is a triumph.1. Goodbye Earl (1999)Long before controversy engulfed their career, the Chicks were entirely capable of causing it. Twenty country stations refused to play Goodbye Earl, apparently horrified by the lyric: high school friends Mary-Anne and Wanda successfully plot to murder Wanda’s abusive husband after he breaches a restraining order and leaves her in intensive care. It still sold a million copies – deservedly so. The chorus is a singalong monster, the lyric is gripping and superbly written and the Chicks’ reading of it is perfect. The vocals switch from cold rage to gleeful celebration over music that is taut and explosive. Tongues firmly in cheek, they stuck a cover of Stand By Your Man on the B-side.Listen to the playlist.SpotifyTaking the Long Way: 20th Anniversary Edition is released on 3 October via Legacy Recordings. The Chicks’ anniversary tour begins on 30 September, at Fox theatre, Detroit.Explore more on these topicsThe ChicksRankedPop and rockCountryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gilla Band: Pugnello review – furious originality fuelled by cathartic aggression and absurdist confessions | Music | The Guardian
description: Your favourite band’s favourite band unleash a thrilling and relentless 42 minutes of monstrous noise whose precise instrumental source always remains discomfitingly unclear
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Your favourite band’s favourite band unleash a thrilling and relentless 42 minutes of monstrous noise whose precise instrumental source always remains discomfitingly unclear
Content: Punishing … (from left) Alan Duggan Borges, Adam Faulkner, Dara Kiely and Daniel Fox of Gilla Band.Photograph: El HardwickView image in fullscreenPunishing … (from left) Alan Duggan Borges, Adam Faulkner, Dara Kiely and Daniel Fox of Gilla Band.Photograph: El HardwickAlexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewGilla Band: Pugnello review – furious originality fuelled by cathartic aggression and absurdist confessions(Rough Trade)Your favourite band’s favourite band unleash a thrilling and relentless 42 minutes of monstrous noise whose precise instrumental source always remains discomfitingly unclearAlexis PetridisThu 24 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGilla Band have attracted some impressive plaudits since announcing their fourth album this summer. Afeature in Pitchforkheralding its arrival described them as “Ireland’s most influential band sinceMy Bloody Valentine”. Should any readers feel this was a classic example of music journalism hyperbole, it was followed up with a succession of quotes from the Dublin quartet’s musical peers, all eager to attest to their importance, originality and impact. One of them, Selin Macieira-Boşgelmez – one half of Brighton-based punk duoLambrini Girls– went so far as to say precisely the kind of thing about Gilla Band that people said about My Bloody Valentine 35 years ago: “They basically reinvented guitar music.”View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Pugnello.Under the circumstances, there’s something faintly disappointing about the fact that Pugnello opens with a very prosaic and familiar sound indeed: that of someone striking a power chord on a distorted electric guitar. But then something disconcertingly odd happens. The power chord doesn’t fade away. It just … keeps going, for the best part of two and half minutes. That grinding drone underpins a track called The Angelus, punctuated by frantic bursts of warp-speed rhythm that would sound like drum’n’bass breakbeats were it not for the fact that they appear to be played live on a drum kit consisting entirely of snares. The drone is eventually replaced by a series of ferocious, shuddering bass explosions, overlaid with a sound that could, theoretically, be feedback, but most evokes a dial-up modem.Throughout, frontman Dara Kiely keeps up a torrent of spoken-word vocals. Sometimes he seems utterly anguished, his voice a raw-throated scream. At other points, he appears to reference the theme tune of the old cartoon Top Cat – “his close friends get to call him TC” – and the kids’ TV show Bananas in Pyjamas. The sense of WTF? is overwhelming.Indeed, the sense of WTF? doesn’t abate until Pugnello finally draws to a close 42 minutes later. In the interim, the listener is confronted with the kind of music that leaves you casting about for something to compare it to and coming up with only the vaguest suggestions – not a regular occurrence when dealing with alternative rock in 2026, which tends to wear its influences very much on its sleeve. You can see why people keep mentioning My Bloody Valentine in relation to Gilla Band – the contents of Pugnello certainly invoke the jarring, exhilarating experience of hearing Loveless or the Tremolo EP in 1991, and boggling at the idea that it’s actuallysupposedto sound like that.Gilla Band: Alogia – videoGilla Band’s is a resolutely contemporary sound, glitching and juddering like a faulty signal, less interested in melody than it is in texture. There’s nothing in the way of a hummable tune: Pugnello’s power comes from the way it drags the listener headlong through sudden shifts in tone and volume, as when the weird electronically treated vocals of At the Gallop are shelled by eruptions of noise, or when Computer Sadness’s racing heartbeat pulse is disrupted by blasts of atonal guitar. The album’s closest musical relation might be found not in alt-rock but the punishing, industrial-flecked techno of Regis or Surgeon. You catch an echo of it inPlaceholder’s monstrous distorted bass line, the machine rhythms of The Megazord and especiallyAlogia, where a particularly urgent brand of funk is overlaid with blaring klaxon-like tones.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘We’ve got to release the dead hand of the past’: how Ireland created the world’s best alternative music sceneRead moreMeanwhile, if your vocal style involves barking out a stream of spoken word lyrics at turns acerbic and absurd, you’re inevitably going to get compared to the Fall, and so it proves. There’s a definite hint of Mark E Smith about some of Kiely’s cadences and indeed about his way with a put-down: “I’m injecting a lethal amount of nothing,” he sings on Placeholder, “I’m blaring a dangerous amount of Coldplay.” But abstract as they are, you can’t miss a certain confessional cast to Kiely’s lyrics, which frequently touch on both the singer’s mental health – he’s been diagnosed with schizophrenia – and his fractured relationship with his late father. Amid the torrent of imagery he spews forth on Jacobsons, there’s an affecting depiction of trying and failing to summon the requisite emotions around his dad’s death: “I should,” he bellows frantically, “be more sad”.Clearly, Pugnello is the dictionary definition of “not for everyone”, although, like a lot of extreme music, it feels fitting in the context of 2026. You could view it as a suitably anxious, unpredictable soundtrack to anxious, unpredictable times; you might equally find it exhilaratingly cathartic. What you would definitely struggle to do is set it in any kind of complementary musical context: Pugnello is the work of a band audibly – and thrillingly – out on their own.This week Alexis listened toBonnie “Prince” Billy – I See a Darkness (Live in the City of Ghosts)Some gentle respite from the album of the week: the old BPB classic beautifully reimagined on his albumGhosts of American Psychonauts.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekPunkExperimental musicPop and rockElectronic musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Julia Jacklin: The Gem review – tender, emotional storytelling of hope and hopelessness  | Australian music | The Guardian
description: The Australian musician’s fourth album blends mystery and intimacy with luscious pop-rock, bright, upbeat jangle and stripped-back acoustics
Author: Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen
Headline: The Australian musician’s fourth album blends mystery and intimacy with luscious pop-rock, bright, upbeat jangle and stripped-back acoustics
Content: Julia Jacklin: her ‘gentle, startlingly controlled voice is her superpower’.Photograph: Izzie AustinView image in fullscreenJulia Jacklin: her ‘gentle, startlingly controlled voice is her superpower’.Photograph: Izzie AustinAustralian musicReviewJulia Jacklin: The Gem review – tender, emotional storytelling of hope and hopelessness(4AD/Remote Control Records)The Australian musician’s fourth album blends mystery and intimacy with luscious pop-rock, bright, upbeat jangle and stripped-back acousticsGiselle Au-Nhien NguyenThu 24 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJulia Jacklin is an artist of dualities. Over her decade-plus career, the Melbourne singer-songwriter has examined the question of how to be both vulnerable but protected, spiritual but grounded.Her second studio album and commercial breakthrough, 2019’sCrushing, introduced her to an international audience as an introspective storyteller. Rich in detail, Crushing delivered tales of heartbreak and betrayal with a kind of quiet impassivity, setting the scene for her own duality as an artist – at once open and reserved.In 2022 Jacklin turned even more inward withPre Pleasure, examining the impact of childhood religion on her sexuality. The sound often contrasted these complicated ponderings: these were big, bold songs more obviously influenced by modern pop, chimes and all.Gang of Youths are back: ‘Does it sound like a cynical gesture towards pop radio stardom?’Read moreThe musician’s fourth album, The Gem, finds its place between these musical and thematic worlds. God is, again, a recurring theme – Jacklin grapples with the tension of “how to feel free with someone watching over me”, as she sings on track five, Angel Vision. She shifts the perspective by imagining herself, or a loved one, in the almighty role.The second track on the 10-song album, God Sometimes, describes the necessity of taking control of your own destiny, whereas If I Had the Hand of God takes the opposite approach, with Jacklin wondering if being all-knowing would actually change anything at all. Hope and hopelessness blur into a singular kind of surrender.View image in fullscreen‘The Gem offers a window into the contradictions and confusions of Jacklin’s smart, sensitive mind.’Photograph: John McDermott/James J RobinsonJacklin’s eye remains sharply observational throughout, as she imbues life’s ordinary scenes with contemplative weight – whether watching a neighbour eat a peach over their kitchen sink, calling her dad or forgetting to water a friend’s plants. “Can’t afford to have an inner life,” she sings on the album opener, Brand New – but everyday moments do seem to awaken her rich internal monologue across the record.Julia Jacklin finds the light: ‘I’ve wasted a lot of energy in my life trying to be cool’Read moreSonically, The Gem balances luscious pop-rock (God Sometimes, The Hardest Thing) with bright, upbeat jangle – such as in the lead single, Get Away From Me (I Think I’ll Love You Soon) – and stripped-back acoustics (Angel Vision, the piano-led You Turned On the Tap). At the album’s halfway mark, Real Life finely straddles the line between lo-fi and more dense arrangements, beginning with a tinny drum machine before building to something more quietly complex.Jacklin’s gentle, startlingly controlled voice is her superpower, bringing stories to life with tenderness and emotion. She accompanies herself on Brand New, singing the title phrase over and over as it’s layered with a defiant statement: “I’m free now, let me be brand new.” Elsewhere, sumptuous harmonies come courtesy of her bandmate and collaborator Jacob Diamond; the album closer, I Wish, features the Melbourne folk duo the Maes, bringing to mind another Melbourne band, Folk Bitch Trio, and their melting three-part harmonies.The vocals are especially affecting on Walk On Me, which sounds as though it could be a cut from Crushing. Downbeat guitar and drums back a vignette of a doomed, unequal relationship: “When the band begins to play / I say, ‘I know this song’ / you say, ‘Everyone knows this one’ / so why am I the only person singing along?” Jacklin sings plaintively, before the music takes over. Her voice transforms into an instrument for the rest of the song, soaring over thick sonic layers. There are no words but the pained strength in her vocalisations says it all.Blending mystery and intimacy, The Gem offers a window into the contradictions and confusions of Jacklin’s smart, sensitive mind. The album cover shows a triptych of lockets, all containing Jacklin’s face: in two circular frames, she smiles, but in a rectangular one, her expression is inscrutable. It’s an apt visualisation of Jacklin’s genius duality, continuing her trajectory as one of Australia’s finest contemporary songwriters.The Gem is out nowExplore more on these topicsAustralian musicPop and rockFolk musicIndiealbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Exit Party by Emily St John Mandel review – alternate visions of post-crisis America | Science fiction books | The Guardian
description: Is the price of stability necessarily the loss of freedom? Two possible future worlds are linked in the new novel from the author of Station Eleven
Author: Nina Allan
Headline: Is the price of stability necessarily the loss of freedom? Two possible future worlds are linked in the new novel from the author of Station Eleven
Content: Superlative storytelling … Emily St John Mandel.Photograph: Laura Barisonzi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSuperlative storytelling … Emily St John Mandel.Photograph: Laura Barisonzi/The GuardianBook of the dayScience fiction booksReviewExit Party by Emily St John Mandel review – alternate visions of post-crisis AmericaIs the price of stability necessarily the loss of freedom? Two possible future worlds are linked in the new novel from the author of Station ElevenNina AllanThu 24 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 02.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn her second novel, 2009’s The Singer’s Gun, Emily St John Mandel tells the story of Anton Waker, a young man desperate to make a break from his criminal family. His plans are thwarted by his cousin Ari, whose hard-nosed talent for operating outside the law has become a way of life. A decade later inThe Glass Hotel, a painting called Swan Dive that hangs in the lobby of the luxury retreat stands as a symbol of escape from a trap that is closing. You will not need to have read either of these earlier novels to enjoy Mandel’s seventh, Exit Party, though their loose intertwining of narrative threads will provide extra pleasure and a sense of homecoming for those who have. It is also interesting to observe Mandel’s evolution from a writer of quirky tales of offbeat protagonists to a novelist whose world-spanning, politically resonant narratives now attract a wide and devoted following.Exit Party begins five years into our future, in 2031. Ari Waker has just come out of prison after serving an 18-year sentence for the attempted murder by contract killing of her cousin Anton. Much has changed while she has been inside: a second civil war has devastated lives and blighted the economy, and the United States as such has ceased to exist.As the novel opens, the newly inaugurated independent State of California is celebrating the end of violence and the lifting of curfews. Ari and her flatmate Gloria have been invited to a party at the home of Gloria’s friend, Kareem. Ari has the feeling that she is meant to be there; she has experienced such premonitions before, and learned to trust them. Arriving at Kareem’s home, she has the sense that something strange is happening. A woman she’s never met before addresses her as Ibari – the name that is legally hers but never used. A painting disappears from the wall. Someone else talks of “extra people” and of the party being “a door that swings both ways”. “There’s something wrong with this party,” mumbles Kareem, before stepping out into the night and walking away.double quotation markMandel’s landscapes are intricately constructed, an elegant dance in which plot, character and idea appear effortlessly matchedKareem never returns. But Ari does not have time to dwell on the incident. Forced back on her own resources, she spends the next few years working menial jobs, all the time with the underlying sense that there is a different future waiting for her, if she can only reach it: “It wasn’t that she thought she deserved more than what she had … it was just that she’d once had a considerable amount of money, her own business, and a beautiful apartment in a tower in New York City”. Old habits die hard, and it is not long before Ari falls back into criminal company. She is offered a surveillance job – she has always been attracted to detective work – but when the woman she is spying on turns out to be the doppelganger of Gloria, her former flatmate, Ari can no longer ignore the sense of deja vu that has begun to plague her life.Ari’s world is fractious and chaotic, characterised by scarcity, systemic instability and the ravages of climate change. While her ability to adapt to every situation has enabled her to survive, it has also prevented her from making lasting attachments, a fact she recognises but cannot bring herself to regret. Gloria’s doppelganger Nico speaks of a different world, in which Ari’s own doppelganger Ibari is a high-ranking detective in a government secret police force known as Service.In this other world, Nico was a physicist, part of a team conducting experiments into teleportation. She was also a dissident. In the novel’s second half, B-Side, we enter a United States where environmental catastrophe has been averted and resources are equitably distributed. It is also a society ruled by universal surveillance, in which the presidency is passed from father to son and where anyone veering from the established order is quietly disappeared.This is a peaceful dystopia, its glittering streetscapes and self-styled progressivism more reminiscent of Huxley’s Brave New World than Orwell’s concrete-and-jackboots Nineteen Eighty-Four. It is an eerie place, nonetheless. “I studied History before I came to Service,” Ibari says when asked why she decided to serve the lawmakers. “It made me terrified of discord.” While Ibari – reticent, calculating, a loyal arm of Service – might seem to be the polar opposite of the fiercely driven, anarchic Ari, the two women ultimately prove themselves capable of similar acts of recklessness and similar loyalty.Is the price of stability necessarily the loss of freedom? The question plays out daily in our political reality, its fictional possibilities providing inspiration for writers from Plato’s time onwards. The “upbeat-downbeat” ending Mandel chooses for her novel is not new in science fiction; indeed, it bears comparison to her own earlier take on the post-catastrophe novel, the 2014 blockbusterStation Eleven. What makes Exit Party a superlative example of the form is its structural cohesiveness, its expert play of signs and symbols, its psychological realism. Mandel’s imaginative landscapes have from the first been intricately constructed, an elegant dance in which plot, character and idea appear effortlessly matched. In Exit Party, her ability to handle a complex array of material while never once allowing her focus to drift from the human story reaches new heights.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat does the stolen painting Swan Dive represent? Freedom? Risk? A doomed plunge towards self-destruction? In one particular, irrecoverable moment, Mandel memorably demonstrates how by the end of this extraordinary novel it will have come to mean all three.Exit Party by Emily St John Mandel is published by Picador (£18.99).
