title: Meet the real-life Pokémon professors, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battling | Games | The Guardian
description: They offer advice, referee card games and manage players’ tantrums – we caught up with some of the volunteer profs who keep the competitive game going at this year’s world championships
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: They offer advice, referee card games and manage players’ tantrums – we caught up with some of the volunteer profs who keep the competitive game going at this year’s world championships
Content: Let the battles begin … people attend the 2026 Pokemon world championships in San Francisco, California.Photograph: Frederic J Brown/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLet the battles begin … people attend the 2026 Pokemon world championships in San Francisco, California.Photograph: Frederic J Brown/AFP/Getty ImagesGamesMeet the real-life Pokémon professors, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battlingThey offer advice, referee card games and manage players’ tantrums – we caught up with some of the volunteer profs who keep the competitive game going at this year’s world championshipsAna DiazThu 24 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProfessors may be the most revered characters in the fictional world ofPokémon(apart from perhaps the Gym Leaders). In Pokémon Red and Blue, Professor Oak greets the player in a pixelated lab coat, and later provides trainers with their first battle partner; since then, each successive generation of games has introduced another professor to aid and guide trainers through their journeys. If you’ve ever played a Pokémon game, they are often the first people that you meet, apart from your in-game mom.But you may not know that there are also real-world Pokémon professors – volunteers who help organise the game’s competitive communities around the world. Instead of lab coats, they can be seen at events wearing red Pikachu-mascot shirts labelled “staff”, paired with black trousers and shoes.I spoke with several of these profs at the 2026 Pokémon world championships in San Francisco, California. Not only do they happily distribute their knowledge about Pokémon, but they also serve as vital staff at the tournament, working as referees and teachers, as well as event managers.Theofficial Pokémon websitedescribes the Pokémon Professor Program as a “global network of passionate and knowledgable fans” who volunteer their time to help run official Pokémon events. There were roughly 300 Pokémon professors present at the 2026 Pokémon world championships, according to a representative of the Pokémon Company International. A professor’s responsibilities depend on the game they work with and their assigned role at the event. A Pokémon professor officiating a game such as Pokémon Unite might be hyper-focused on wrangling players and providing technical support, whereas a judge for a trading card game tournament might provide competitors with hands-on guidance as they navigate their first live competitive event.View image in fullscreenThe OG Pokémon prof … Professor Oak in Pokémon: Let’s Go, Pikachu!Photograph: The Pokémon Company/NintendoGemma Byard, a head judge in charge of making the final call on any decisions or questions that arise, became a Pokémon professor after her son started competing in the trading card game. She says that she and the other professors help ensure the integrity of the tournament, describing what goes into the day-to-day work at worlds – such as ensuring that event officials record the results of competitions correctly.“We’ve got to make sure that all of the match slips have the correct results on them and are signed by the players to ensure, you know, that we get the right results,” Byard said. “We have to make sure that the venue is safe for everybody that’s around. We’re constantly looking out for anything that may be unsafe, or anybody that shouldn’t be in the venue. There’s a lot to think about on top of the rulings.”Professors often juggle multiple responsibilities on the competition floor and will travel across the world to staff an event such as the world championships. When asked about how the Pokémon Company International compensates its professors, however, most people I spoke to declined to disclose details. One Pokémon professor said that the European professors are compensated with goodies, such as a special staff kit with merchandise, whereas the professors at regional tournaments in the US are paid wages; the same professor said that the Pokémon Company International helped with travel, room and board for the event. (When asked for an official statement explaining how Pokémon professors are paid, a representative from the Pokémon Company International declined to comment.)Evelyne de Groot travelled from the Netherlands to staff this year’s championships. Like the other Pokémon professors I spoke to, de Groot worked her way up to staffing worlds after organising local competitions in her home region. Before we spoke, she was helping usher players out of the Moscone Center after the main convention hall closed for the evening. This year, she worked at a trading card game side event called Pokémon Sisterhood League, dedicated to giving women and non-binary people a chance to compete and connect.View image in fullscreenPassionate and knowledgeable …about 300 professors were working at this year’s Pokémon world championships in San Francisco.Photograph: San Francisco Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesFor her, a good Pokémon professor must balance enforcing the rules with giving competitors the tools they need to enjoy the game itself. She compared the position to working in “customer service”.“[Players] make friendships. You see them smile. You see them have a good time, but you’re part of that,” de Groot said. “If you’re not organising it properly, if you don’t give them clear instructions, then you see some failure […] You will sometimes get questions. You need to make sure you’re knowledgable regarding that. If you don’t know what you’re doing, if you don’t know how the card game works, then you can’t help them.”De Groot’s experience as a professor has been relatively relaxed. However, some professors must serve as referees and make contentious calls throughout the competition. For Byard, that means she sometimes needs to deal with upset players. At one point during the tournament, she had to manage a player who was upset with a ruling that didn’t go his way.“I got called over to the table, and I said to him: ‘Look, I need you just to keep your voice down and be respectful, and we’ll talk through what’s happened.’ And he was like: ‘I don’t need to talk to you. I need to talk to the head judge,’” Byard said, chuckling. “Well, buddy, you are talking to the head judge. That’s the kind of sass that we deal with a lot.”View image in fullscreenTough calls … a judge surveys the scene at a previous Pokémon event.Photograph: PokémonA difficult call can lead to controversy. Earlier this year, a ruling from a different judge at another tournament made headlines when a competitive Pokémon Go player who goes by the name Firestar73 was disqualified after winning the final at thePokémon Orlando regional championships. Many, including the competitor himself ina statement, conceded that the decision was a “good-faith mistake”.I asked Byard about what it’s like to make tough calls at the tournament. She said that the professors are often seen as “the bad guys”. What does she wish competitors and viewers understood about the role?“What they don’t understand is that they’re seeing a picture, but we’re getting the entire story, and we’re making the decisions based upon that story,” she said. “That can make a real difference. And we’re the ones putting ourselves out there to right a situation that’s been broken by players. We haven’t caused any distress. We’re there just to try and put it back together again.”Interviews for this feature took place at the Pokémon world championships in San Francisco. The writer’s travel and accommodation expenses were met bythe Pokémon Company.Explore more on these topicsGamesPokémonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nicole Eisenman review – ICE-like goons clash with sublime stargazing as America’s magical magpie returns | Art | The Guardian
description: Abstract, humorous yet deeply unsettling, the painter’s dazzling exhibition sees her caught between distant skies and the ugly reality on the ground
Author: Ben Eastham
Headline: Abstract, humorous yet deeply unsettling, the painter’s dazzling exhibition sees her caught between distant skies and the ugly reality on the ground
Content: ‘Dazzling variety of tones and textures’ … The Waiter by Nicole Eisenman.Photograph: © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy the Artist and Sadie Coles HQ, LondonView image in fullscreen‘Dazzling variety of tones and textures’ … The Waiter by Nicole Eisenman.Photograph: © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy the Artist and Sadie Coles HQ, LondonArtReviewNicole Eisenman review – ICE-like goons clash with sublime stargazing as America’s magical magpie returnsSadie Coles HQ, LondonAbstract, humorous yet deeply unsettling, the painter’s dazzling exhibition sees her caught between distant skies and the ugly reality on the groundBen EasthamThu 24 Sep 2026 10.14 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 12.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNicole Eisenman’s2023 exhibition at the Whitechapel Gallerytook its title from Hillary Clinton’s account of the 2016 US presidential election: “What happened.” With its absurdist riffs on contemporary American life, the show confirmed that Eisenman is among the most important artists of her time and that “what happened” was a disaster. So her return to London might be thought of as a sequel, with the working title: “So what do we do now?”Eisenman is justly celebrated for her rambunctious, magpie and irreverent subversions of the conventional histories of art and society. A painter who has lately (and successfully) turned to sculpture, her work often places people in situations – ranging from crowded bars to town squares flooded with mud – that match broad humour to sharp technique in reflecting on how our identities are shaped by the company we keep. And yet my first thought on entering Sadie Coles’ gallery was the artist had turned her back on the world.View image in fullscreenNever allows the eye to settle … The Orgy.Photograph: © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy the Artist and Sadie Coles HQ, LondonThe ground floor is dominated by a vast painting of a solitary figure standing alone amid the ruins of Stonehenge. Identified by the title as The Waiter, he looks up to a night sky teeming with the wonders of the universe and holds a drum but does not play it. The painting is overwhelming, not only for its scale but also for its dazzling variety of tones and textures, from the schematic design of the planets to its impasto treatment of the moss on the stones, which blooms from the surface of the canvas in wild green clumps. The effect is sublime.Yet this image of a musician struck dumb by nature is also unsettling. Has Eisenman retreated from the public arena to wait things out in cosmic speculations? Is she the latest artist to join the flight from reason, seeking refuge in the dubious consolations of New Age mysticism? The neighbouring canvas shows an astronomer alone beneath a sky through which the Milky Way slices a star-studded diagonal. Behind her are low-rise apartments through the illuminated windows of which cartoon figures can be seen eating, embracing, squabbling. Again the impression is of a woman who has averted her gaze from the mess of humanity to make beautiful pictures of the more trustworthy heavens.View image in fullscreenBack to earth with Parking Lot of Violent Forces and Depressive Positions.Photograph: © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy the Artist and Sadie Coles HQ, LondonI was happy to be brought back to earth. In the upstairs gallery, Parking Lot of Violent Forces and Depressive Positions, the title of which saves me some descriptive labour, riffs onPhilip Guston’s 1969 painting City Limits. Where Guston shows his hooded clowns roaming around in an absurdly small car in search of somebody to lynch, Eisenman has replaced them with goons in the military fatigues and wraparound shades beloved of ICE agents, pimpled white arses riding up out of their trousers. If the comment on contemporary US society is clear, then British viewers might also be reminded of the recent images of paunchy men standing in ragged formation as some ex-private schoolboy exhorts them to avenge their feelings of inadequacy on those who cannot defend themselves.Set in an apocalyptic landscape overseen by a comic-book monster, the painting proposes righteous anger as an alternative response to “what happened”. Hedonism is another, and one long associated with the end of empire. Unfurling across six conjoined canvases, The Orgy is a remarkable compositional achievement, transforming a writhe of limbs, feet and breasts into interlocking planes of colour that never allow the eye to settle. Like a stubbornly physical take on the more lyrical visions of mid-century painters such as Lee Krasner, it conjures the momentary escape (from the world, from the self) that sexual ecstasy affords.Hands at the edges of this orgy clutch at the rippling bedsheet as if preparing to draw a veil over the scene, and it is notable that the only other direct depiction of human companionship (Me and G under the J) is also framed by a painted curtain. The device reminds the viewer that the artist retains the right to block their gaze into the lives of others. That feels consistent with a more general ambivalence about the function of images in a surveillance society, in which to be visible is to be vulnerable (a fact not lost on Eisenman, whosuffered a substantial backlashafter speaking out about Israel’s assault on Gaza).View image in fullscreen‘Bleakest and best form of comedy’ … Stack by Nicole Eisenman at the Royal Academy.Photograph: Peter Nicholls/Getty ImagesAnother response to the predicament, hinted at by two sculptural installations on the theme of dance and a jangling cubist portrait, is to embrace abstraction. There would be a certain irony if Eisenman, who emerged when socially conscious figurative painting was widely accepted to be dead, should take that path now that the wheel has turned. But abstraction might offer some relief from the market’s demand that artists today produce easily legible expressions of their own (and their communities’) identity, not to mention their ideological commitments. When artists are being blacklisted, you can understand the appeal.If this show finds the artist at a crossroads, uncertain of what road to take next, then who doesn’t feel that way? A couple of hundred yards down the street, a sculpture by Eisenman has been unveiled in the courtyard of the Royal Academy. It shows the bent-backed artist carrying the world on her shoulders. Unlike Atlas, however, her world comprises a gigantic barrel of wine, an oversized potato, the artist’s leaping cat and, on top of it all, the late British sculptor Phyllida Barlow. The artist staggers forward, one hand wrapped around a stick, the other holding out a glass in the faint hope of catching a drip of wine from the barrel. This is the bleakest and best form of comedy. The artist can’t go on, she’ll go on.Nicole Eisenman is at Sadie Coles HQ, Savile Row, London until 21 Novemberandthe courtyard of the Royal Academy until 5 FebruaryExplore more on these topicsArtRoyal Academy of ArtsSculpturePaintingExhibitionsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Kneebone review – who knew porcelain could be so edgy, nerve-wracking and marvellous? | Art | The Guardian
description: The British sculptor’s delicate, intimate and ready-to-pop creations feel right at home among Hertford House’s rococo masterpieces
Author: Chloë Ashby
Headline: The British sculptor’s delicate, intimate and ready-to-pop creations feel right at home among Hertford House’s rococo masterpieces
Content: Hanging in the balance … Pull, 2023.Photograph: White Cube (Theo Christelis)/© the artistView image in fullscreenHanging in the balance … Pull, 2023.Photograph: White Cube (Theo Christelis)/© the artistArtReviewRachel Kneebone review – who knew porcelain could be so edgy, nerve-wracking and marvellous?Wallace Collection, LondonThe British sculptor’s delicate, intimate and ready-to-pop creations feel right at home among Hertford House’s rococo masterpiecesChloë AshbyThu 24 Sep 2026 11.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaybe it was that wine glass I broke this morning while unloading the dishwasher, but seeing a Rachel Kneebone porcelain sculpture suspended makes me nervous. Can those skinny wires really hold the weight? Should there perhaps be a soft landing just in case? Emerging from a tangled clump of ribbons and roses are a couple of bone-white bubbles, ready to pop. This is art that quite literally hangs in the balance; a sense of peril is what makes it so marvellous.Born in 1973, the British sculptor is the latest contemporary artist to be invited to show her workat the Wallace Collection. Following in the footsteps of Damien Hirst, Flora Yukhnovich and Grayson Perry, Kneebone has positioned nine milky sculptures made between 2017 and 2026 throughout Hertford House. So this display, titled Metamorphoses, is an intervention – that’s the art world lingo. Except it feels different, like the contrast has been turned down. Sure, there are collisions as well as similarities, but seeing sculpted heaps of human and floral forms alongside the prized masterpieces for which the London gallery is best known feels … right.View image in fullscreenDecoration meets high drama … Temple, 2026.Photograph: White Cube (Theo Christelis)/© the artistKneebone was studying at the Royal College ofArtin 2004 when she started working with porcelain, a medium more commonly associated with the types of cups and saucers safely stowed away behind glass in Manchester Square. Instead, Kneebone gives us strangely intimate pileups that recall art historical sources from the sculptural fragments of Auguste Rodin to the erotic figures of Jake and Dinos Chapman. Among the fleshly folds are glimpses of Ovid and Dante. While distinctly modern, they also nod to classical friezes, baroque fountains and, as is about to become abundantly clear, rococo canvases.One of two works that have been created specially for the show, Temple, is presented on a plinth at the top of the stairs. Sandwiched between Boucher’sThe Rising of the Sun(1753) andThe Setting of the Sun(1752), it’s a lustrous, solid take on the churning waves the 18th-century French master conjures in paint. Emerging from the surf are three columns and a jumble of gnarly barnacles and tendrils, plus a gleaming scallop shell containing a pearl – a reference to Boucher’s bejewelled water nymphs. Just like those vast mythological scenes, it’s a mashup of decoration and high drama, pleasure and peril.Challenging preconceived notions of domesticity, Kneebone embraces instability, finding beauty in the blisters and cracks that can emerge when her chosen material is fired in the kiln. Look closely and you’ll notice distortions and fissures among her graceful twisting forms. In the billiards room, Dance (2017) is perfectly imperfect, a throng of protruding legs and toes – some pointed, others flexed – sprouting from a hulking mass with deep fractures at the base.Which is where the metamorphosis part comes in. Like heated clay, Kneebone’s figures are undergoing a transformation, their limbs buckling and splaying. They’re also playfully sensual. Either side of Boucher’sJupiter and Callisto(1769), Pearl IV (2025) and Pearl II (2025) lunge towards one another like lovers, just as the god disguised as Diana springs towards the nymph. Elsewhere, rounded porcelain forms might resemble bubbles and pearls, but here there’s no mistaking the resemblance to Callisto’s creamy breasts.View image in fullscreenRewards slow looking … Dance, 2017.Photograph: White Cube (Stephen White)/© the artistShape-shifting art rewards slow looking, and at the Wallace you can walk around it (as well as under it), watching it change and morph from different points of view. What makes the pairing of Kneebone’s contemporary creations and the treasures in the collection so delightful is that it makes you look at well-known works afresh, too.It’s only seeing Bower (2026) in front ofThe Swing(c1767-68) that I notice the silvery quality of Fragonard’s palette, complemented by the porcelain, a dazzling white. Guided by Kneebone’s twisting forms and knots, my eyes aren’t drawn to the young woman wearing the frothy pink frock, as is usually the case, but to the knotted rope wound around the bulky branches above. As for the cracks: well, they may be a fortuitous byproduct of the kiln, but they do provide a nice nod to the fractured relationship between the lady and her elderly husband, who’s playing tug of war with a much younger man.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSurrounded by amorous scenes and opulent paintings of fruit and flowers, you might expect porcelain to feel cold and austere. Instead, it’s titillating and decadent – just wait until you see the two pieces positioned at either end of the great gallery, seductively pale beside the red damask walls and flashy gilt frames. I’d wondered whether nine works – or eight, depending on the fate of that suspended one – would get lost among the infinite riches of the Wallace Collection. No chance. The beauty of even a single Kneebone sculpture is the way its parts merge and multiply before your eyes.At theWallace Collection, London, until 25 AprilExplore more on these topicsArtSculptureCeramicsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Three Men in a Boat review – quirky novella makes for perky, fun-forward theatre | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A rag puppet Montmorency, a fake moustache and an aria for reeking cheese add to the mischief of Jerome K Jerome’s very English story
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: A rag puppet Montmorency, a fake moustache and an aria for reeking cheese add to the mischief of Jerome K Jerome’s very English story
Content: Slapstick … Jonny Weldon, Bronté Barbé and Richard David-Caine in Three Men in a Boat.Photograph: Helen MurrayView image in fullscreenSlapstick … Jonny Weldon, Bronté Barbé and Richard David-Caine in Three Men in a Boat.Photograph: Helen MurrayTheatreReviewThree Men in a Boat review – quirky novella makes for perky, fun-forward theatreRose theatre, Kingston upon ThamesA rag puppet Montmorency, a fake moustache and an aria for reeking cheese add to the mischief of Jerome K Jerome’s very English storyMark LawsonThu 24 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBack from Lib Dem conference, Ed Davey watched this adaptation in his Kingston constituency ofJerome K Jerome’s novellaabout a trio of late Victorian gents rowing the Thames accompanied by fox terrier Montmorency. Might the up-for-fun politician suddenly drop on to the stage in a Scooby-Doo suit?He didn’t, although Christopher Haydon’s perky production features one actor making an applause-winning entrance from an improbable location. This version is also certainly more liberal and democratic than the 1889 text whose language has often dated in meaning or propriety.View image in fullscreenMind your ankles … Calum Donald-Bruce with Montmorency.Photograph: Helen MurrayBronté Barbé plays, with false moustache and lower voice notes, the eccentric Harris who, with lugubrious George (Richard David-Caine), joins pompous hypochondriac Jerome (Jonny Weldon) on a river trip that starts from Kingston. As with all quirky, discursive books, the challenge of adaptation is imposing momentum and tension. Al Smith’s dramatisation neatly juggles chronology (the sixth chapter is his first scene) and anchors the book’s best set pieces (swan attack, putrid cheese, a murder investigation) in a new narrative where the blokes are heading to Oxford for Harris’s wedding, his choice of best man a bugbear.Three Men in a Boat has come to represent an idyllic, witty lost England.Tom Stoppard, an immigrant ecstatic to have landed here, wrote a 1975 BBC adaptation in that spirit. But the book has darker meditations on religion, society and death. Smith makes George, originally a bachelor banker, a doctor who has been recently widowed, with a boldly bleak monologue about bereavement that is presumably a tonal surrogate for an incident in the original, not dramatised, where the boaters spot a floating corpse.Otherwise, the show foregrounds jauntiness. Montmorency, a menace to ankles, cats and other dogs in the book, is here a charming puppy rag puppet (animated by Calum Donald-Bruce), a theatrical device now so familiar that it prompts in-jokes: “We’ll have to eat the puppeteer!”View image in fullscreenJaunty … Three Men in a Boat.Photograph: Helen MurrayThe 135-minute show is punctuated by eight musical numbers and, though it is now almost obligatory for classic literature to be sung and danced (the most recent victimJane Eyre), this is a logical candidate. The book includes references to Gilbert and Sullivan, opera, music hall, banjos, bagpipes and accordions. Grant Olding’s songs incorporate all, including a biographical patter number about Jerome, an Italianate aria for the reeking cheese and a Tchaikovsky ballet pastiche (choreographed by Simon Hardwick) when the journey reaches swan river.That sequence and others justify the poster for the show which, referencing Magritte and Dalí, suggests the story is surrealist. But slapstick dominates in an engaging evening that smooths the jagged oddness of the book.AtRose theatre, Kingston upon Thames, until 10 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)MusicalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Stranger Things was a train you can’t jump off’: Gaten Matarazzo on his return to the stage | Musicals | The Guardian
description: The actor we know as Dustin was a ‘theatre kid’ from age 11. Now he’s starring in a new staging of Rent. He discusses why the musical is as relevant as ever – and what it’s like being a child star in the internet age
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: The actor we know as Dustin was a ‘theatre kid’ from age 11. Now he’s starring in a new staging of Rent. He discusses why the musical is as relevant as ever – and what it’s like being a child star in the internet age
Content: Paid in full … Matarazzo and the cast of Rent in rehearsal.Photograph: Pamela RaithView image in fullscreenPaid in full … Matarazzo and the cast of Rent in rehearsal.Photograph: Pamela RaithMusicalsInterview‘Stranger Things was a train you can’t jump off’: Gaten Matarazzo on his return to the stageHannah J DaviesThe actor we know as Dustin was a ‘theatre kid’ from age 11. Now he’s starring in a new staging of Rent. He discusses why the musical is as relevant as ever – and what it’s like being a child star in the internet ageThu 24 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRent is a study in both joy and despair. The 90s rock opera spawned the kinds of irrepressible musical numbers – Seasons of Love, Take Me Or Leave Me – that would become Broadway standards, mastered and massacred in choir auditions and high schools across the world. Jonathan Larson’s self-described attempt “to bring musical theatre to the MTV generation” is also a capitalist critique: a drama about a bohemian coterie of penniless creatives sticking it to the man, all while their circle is ravaged by HIV and Aids. It still feels highly relevant today; see: What You Own – sample lyric “And when you’re living in America / At the end of the millennium / You’re what you own”.Gaten Matarazzo says “that song may arguably be more impactfulnowthan in 1996, considering what we know about what American media and world media would become, and our access to constant mind-numbing noise …” This autumn, he makes his West End debut as Mark, the struggling film-maker who chronicles the lives of his friends in New York’s East Village, and serves as the show’s de facto narrator.It’s something of a musical theatre-themed year for the 24-year-old, best known for playing lovable super-geek Dustin in Netflix’s Spielbergian smashStranger Things. Earlier this year, he filmed Octet, an upcoming Lin-Manuel Miranda a cappella film about phone addiction, based on a play by Dave Malloy. Of course, when a TV star makes the transition to musical theatre – or just theatre full stop – there are often accusations of stunt casting. “I understand that the work I’ve done leading up to this has influenced my ability to do these fun things,” says Matarazzo. “I will acknowledge fully that that probably has played a big role.”View image in fullscreenStager things … Gaten Matarazzo with Danielle Fiamanya in rehearsals for Rent.Photograph: Pamela RaithExcept that, well, if anyone is getting stunt-casting accusations it probably shouldn’t be him. After years of auditions, Matarazzo made his Broadway debut aged just nine, in the antipodean jukebox musical Priscilla, Queen of the Desert. A dive into the depths of Google unearths a video of him – in Les Misérables, aged 11 – giving a tour of the theatre to camera (“We use alotof fog in the show,” he explains). He cringes a little at the mention. “I hate watching those,” he laughs. He left Les Mis in March 2015 and booked Stranger Things in June of the same year. (“Bananas!” he says.) But before the show had finished airing, he had already found his way back to the stage, appearing in Dear Evan Hansen and Sweeney Todd on Broadway in 2022 and 2023 respectively. It was around this time that many of his TV fans discovered his background in musicals (one YouTube comment reads: “The day I found out he could sing was a beautiful day indeed”).double quotation markAll of these characters are perfect representations of people who are imperfect – and strugglingWe meet at a fancy bar in central London, close to where the Rent rehearsals are taking place, Matarazzo arriving with a heavy-looking rucksack slung over his shoulder and a smattering of brown curls poking up messily from under a baseball cap. Stranger Things may have finally ended on 1 January 2026, but it still looms large over his professional and personal life. The show that was “expected to probably only be one season” went on for five, with Covid and the Hollywood writers’ strikes stretching its run to almost 10 years.Matarazzo tries a couple of metaphors – catapults, snowballs – before settling on one to describe the feeling of going from being an average kid to a TV star. It was, he says, “a train you can’t really jump off. Not that we really would havewantedto, but it would become stressful every now and again.”Up until that point, his life – blossoming Broadway career aside – had indeed been quite normal. Raised in Little Egg Harbor Township, New Jersey (population: 22,000), Matarazzo and his two siblings always sang at home, though he’s keen to point out that his sister Sabrina was “the real singer in the camp”. His parents worked “nights, and several jobs” to support his ambitions, before his mum was laid off and decided to pivot to being her son’s chaperone. Then at13 came the chance to join a new Netflix series, originally scheduled to film in Long Island but later relocated to Atlanta. He decides not to give too many details about where he lived, “because I’ll probably go back a ton – a lot of us lived in one neighbourhood because we loved it so much”.View image in fullscreenWorld changing … Gaten Matarazzo (third from left) in season four of Stranger Things.Photograph: Tina Rowden/NetflixYou get the sense with Matarazzo that it’s especially important for him to have some boundaries. In the early days of the show, he says he carefully tracked how many followers he was amassing, and how many likes his posts attracted. “And I was too damn young to be doing that.” He says he was encouraged to have a public account, to reply to DMs from fans and to post videos. “It wasn’t like there were people in the wings orchestrating some malicious idea,” he explains. “But I think in retrospect, it would have been very reasonable to say: ‘Maybe it’s not OK for [users of] big public spacesto know intimate details about the lives of children?’”While he’s keen to stress that “nothing really bad happened”, understandably he has qualms about young stars growing up in the glare of 24/7 publicity. Earlier this year a news story resurfaced about a fortysomething woman who told Matarazzo that she had had a crush on him since he was 13.While some interpreted it as #MeToo-adjacent, Matarazzo thinks that it “wasn’t as malicious as it may have been presented as afterwards. It wasn’t very scary, more just inappropriate and icky.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSure shot … Travis Ross and Gaten Matarazzo in rehearsal for Rent.Photograph: Pamela RaithMatarazzo, who describes his interactions with most fans as “the greatest pleasure and honour in the world”, has an understated nice-guy aura about him. We segue to the nonprofit he founded, CCD Smiles, which supports people who have the same condition as him, cleidocranial dysplasia, which affects the growth of teeth and bones (although he describes himself as having a “mild case” he has undergone multiple surgeries, while the Stranger Things writers, the Duffer Brothers, wrote his condition into the show). Does he find that he’s a role model to people he meets with CCD? “I look up to them probably more than they look up to me,” he says. “I guess I can’t generalise, but I’ve met several hundred people now with the condition, and they are some of the most positive people I’ve ever met, and a lot of them are dealing with a lot more physical issues than I am.” Creating a community has been, he says, “really damn cool … I’m really honoured to do it.” Matarazzo grew up with a family who “encouraged me to brag about [my condition]. Others were raised in families who either felt pretty indifferent or negatively about it. That breaks my heart.”Much like Mark in Rent – who hails from upstate New York – Matarazzo is a transplant to NYC. He remembers watching the pro-shot (that is, the professionally filmed version) of Rent on Broadway as a child, “and being like, ‘Oh, this is the real fucking deal!’” Growing up, he says people told him that “you should do Mark one day. And as a theatre kid, any time somebody tells you you’d be really good at a part it becomes your life’s obsession.”The mix of tragedy and elation that powers Rent is also somewhat central to its DNA. Jonathan Larson died from an aortic dissection of the heart just hours before the first off-Broadway previews; it was, says Matarazzo, “the most horrifyingly bad luck in the world”. He thinks part of Rent’s charm may stem from this genesis, though, and the feeling that Larson wasn’t totally finished with his creation. “What I think is so brilliant about this show – and I mean this as a compliment – is that it feels incomplete and unpolished. All of these characters are perfect representations of people who are imperfect, and struggling.”‘It was pretty depressing when Stranger Things ended’: Finn Wolfhard on growing up on TV – and his new life in musicRead moreHow does he think it will resonate not only with a West End audience, but a 2026 one? “I mean, it’s a show about people living in a city where the cost of living is astronomical and unfathomable, as well as living through a pandemic that is killing people very rapidly, and no one knows how to fix it or what the proper steps are moving forward.” He doesn’t want to negate the specificity of HIV/Aids, though. “I think we can forget how truly terrifying and up in the air the idea of that diagnosis was. At the time, there really wasnopossibility of knowing whether you’re going to live another 20 years or 20 months.”TV may well come calling again soon but – for now – Matarazzo seems more than comfortable with his return to the stage. Some lucky audience members will be up there with him, too, thanks to some onstage seating; he’s excited about people seeing the show “without a hint of a barrier. I think that’s just how Rent was supposed to be experienced.” Not stunt casting, then, but certainly in your face.Rent is at the Tom Stoppard theatre, London, 26 September to 27 March 2027.Explore more on these topicsMusicalsStranger ThingsTheatreTelevisioninterviewsShareReuse this content
