title: Greek PM: deal to return Parthenon marbles could still be reached with ‘political will and courage’ | Parthenon marbles | The Guardian
description: But Kyriakos Mitsotakis says he cannot accept any arrangement that recognises British Museum’s ownership of the sculptures
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: But Kyriakos Mitsotakis says he cannot accept any arrangement that recognises British Museum’s ownership of the sculptures
Content: The Greek PM wrote in the Guardian that the reunification of the marbles could become ‘the foundation of a broad and enduring cultural partnership between our countries’.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Greek PM wrote in the Guardian that the reunification of the marbles could become ‘the foundation of a broad and enduring cultural partnership between our countries’.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianParthenon marblesGreek PM: deal to return Parthenon marbles could still be reached with ‘political will and courage’But Kyriakos Mitsotakis says he cannot accept any arrangement that recognises British Museum’s ownership of the sculpturesKyriakos Mitsotakis: Britain would not cut up the Bayeux tapestry. So seize this moment and reunite the Parthenon sculptures in GreeceRowena MasonandNadia KhomamiThu 24 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Greek prime minister has said a deal can still be reached to return theParthenon marbleswith “political will” but his country will not accept a loan in the style of the Bayeux tapestry’s visit from France.Writing for the Guardian, Kyriakos Mitsotakis said Greece “cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum’s ownership of the sculptures,or a scheme that would mean we ‘borrow’ parts of our own monument”.He made the intervention weeks after theBritish Museumdirector, Nicholas Cullinan, told the Financial Times that France’s 10-month loan of the Bayeux tapestry to the British Museum could provide a model for a deal. The director said there was “no cookie-cutter template” but the exchange was an example of a successful international partnership.In his article, Mitsotakis says the situation with the Parthenon marbles was completely different as half of the frieze is in Athens – and no one would suggest cutting the Bayeux tapestry in two.Pointing out that Andy Burnham once backed returning the marbles, the Greek prime minister said “political will and courage” would be needed butGreecewould not accept anything less than “reunification” of the marbles in Athens.He said this could become “the foundation of a broad and enduring cultural partnership between our countries, creating new opportunities for exhibitions, scholarship, conservation and exchanges between Greek and British museums” which was “the prize”.It comes amid speculation about the status of talks between the British Museum and the Greek government about the return of the antiquities, with the Telegraph reporting they were on the brink of collapse.Sources close to the talks disputed that characterisation but acknowledged there was a large gap to bridge in the long running dialogues.Burnham, who once said the marbles should be given back to Greece, said more recently it was a matter for the British Museum.The Parthenon marbles are also known as the Elgin marbles after the British peer Lord Elgin, who removed them from Athens more than 200 years ago.Carved 2,500 years ago by Phidias, a master sculptor, the antiquities embellished the Parthenon’s monumental frieze before their removal in highly contentious circumstances by Elgin, who was Britain’s ambassador to the Ottoman empire. Bankrupted by his endeavours, Elgin then sold them to the British government in 1816.It has been a decades-long cultural dispute between the UK, which prevents the British Museum from returning items from its collection, and Greece, which considers the objects to have been plundered.George Osborne, the former chancellor and current chair of the British Museum, confirmed in 2023 he was in talks with Greece about a deal but also that he was not attempting to change the law – a reference to the British Museum Act 1963, which prohibits the museum from permanently removing objects from its collection.At the time, it was proposed it could involve the sculptures being inLondonand Athens at different times and Britain receiving “Greek treasures” in return.The British Museum said its position and openness to a deal was unchanged.Explore more on these topicsParthenon marblesBritish MuseumLondonGreeceEuropeHeritagenewsShareReuse this content

title: Pete Byrne, frontman of British new wave band Naked Eyes, dies aged 74 | Music | The Guardian
description: Duo had US hits with their cover of Always Something There to Remind Me as well as Promises, Promises and more
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Duo had US hits with their cover of Always Something There to Remind Me as well as Promises, Promises and more
Content: Pete Byrne performing in 2014.Photograph: Randy Miramontez/AlamyView image in fullscreenPete Byrne performing in 2014.Photograph: Randy Miramontez/AlamyMusicPete Byrne, frontman of British new wave band Naked Eyes, dies aged 74Duo had US hits with their cover of Always Something There to Remind Me as well as Promises, Promises and moreBen Beaumont-ThomasThu 24 Sep 2026 05.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 05.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePete Byrne, the frontman of British new wave group Naked Eyes who carried them to repeated chart successes in the US, has died aged 74.The news was announced on the band’s website and social media on Wednesday, stating that Byrne died peacefully in Los Angeles on 14 September after a brief illness.Byrne was part of the “second British invasion” when synthpop and new wave bands from the UK, powered in part by the rise of MTV, swept into the US, with peers including Duran Duran, A Flock of Seagulls and more.He formed Naked Eyes in the late 1970s after the failure of his groups Studio and Neon, with Neon featuring future Tears for Fears members Curt Smith and Roland Orzabal as well as his future Naked Eyes bandmate Rob Fisher and others. “Rob and I found that running a band was not as interesting as writing and recording,” Byrne said. “We decided to go back to square one.”View image in fullscreenNaked Eyes in 1983, with Byrne, left.Photograph: Ron Wolfson/Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesThey split off as a duo, renamed themselves and signed to EMI. Their debut single became their biggest hit: a cover of the Burt Bacharach-penned Always Something There to Remind Me, powered by Byrne’s earnest boyish croon, which reached the Top 10 in the US, Canada and Australia.Though Naked Eyes never hit the Top 40 in their native UK, they continued a run of US successes with three more Top 40 hits there: Promises, Promises (which reached No 11 and featured Madonna on unreleased remixes), When the Lights Go Out and (What) In the Name of Love (which was remixed by Arthur Baker).The group weren’t able to replicate their synth-heavy studio setup on tour, and they split after their second album, 1984’s Fuel for the Fire. Byrne later blamed the split on him and Fisher living in Los Angeles and London respectively, and on EMI losing faith in the project.Byrne retreated, writing and producing with other artists – later including a song for Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen – and recorded backing vocals for Stevie Wonder’s 1985 US No 1 Part-Time Lover. He released a solo album, The Real Illusion, in 2001, and began working with Fisher again, rebooting Naked Eyes as a solo project after Fisher’s death in 1999. Byrne released two further albums under that name and became a familiar face on 80s revue tours, alongside the likes of the Go-Go’s and the Human League.Speaking in 2017, Byrne said music has been “the main focus of my life since I was 18. Nothing has changed really. I still get up in the morning, make coffee, fiddle around on the guitar and scribble down some nonsense. And I eventually look back and say: ‘There might be something there.’”He is survived by three children, Merlin, Dylan and Chloe, from his marriage to ex-wife Elena, as well as his siblings Eileen, Sandy, Carol and Steve.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rocknewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m a writer but then nobody’s perfect’: how Billy Wilder conquered Hollywood | Movies | The Guardian
description: From émigré roots to a titan of modern cinema, penning classics such as Double Indemnity, Some Like It Hot and The Apartment, a new retrospective celebrates the father of film noir’s incredible career
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From émigré roots to a titan of modern cinema, penning classics such as Double Indemnity, Some Like It Hot and The Apartment, a new retrospective celebrates the father of film noir’s incredible career
Content: An inveterate self-mythologiser … Billy Wilder.Photograph: BFIView image in fullscreenAn inveterate self-mythologiser … Billy Wilder.Photograph: BFIMovies‘I’m a writer but then nobody’s perfect’: how Billy Wilder conquered HollywoodFrom émigré roots to a titan of modern cinema, penning classics such as Double Indemnity, Some Like It Hot and The Apartment, a new retrospective celebrates the father of film noir’s incredible careerDarren RichmanThu 24 Sep 2026 04.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 21.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLike all survivors,Billy Wildernever forgot where he came from or what he had left behind. He was born at the start of the 20th century in Austria-Hungary and died at the start of the 21st in California, the inscription on his gravestone a nod to his most famous line: “I’m a writer but then nobody’s perfect.” Wilder, though, had a habit of of making flawless films throughout his career, a point proved by Almost Perfect, a comprehensive retrospective of his work, running at the BFI Southbank from 19 October until the end of the year.Wilder was an inveterate self-mythologiser, a film-maker with a brand long before there were opportunities for promotion through Instagram accounts and chicken shop dates. He told a story of living in Berlin during his fledgling years in show business and being kept awake all night by “a toilet that was on the blink”.“I would lie there and listen to it, and since I was young and romantic, I’d imagine it was a beautiful waterfall – just to get my mind off the monotony of it and the thought of it being a can.”Most of us would have called a plumber but the aspiring young film-maker chose instead to use the incident as fuel for perhaps the greatest body of work in cinema’s golden age. This is the man who made Double Indemnity, the archetypal film noir and the genre’s zenith, a film often imitated but never equalled. He was responsible forSome Like It Hot, a movie routinely voted the greatest comedy ever made, while his Sunset Boulevard is generally acknowledged as the best film about show business. The Apartment, arguably his magnum opus, is rightly considered one of the greatest films in the history of the medium.View image in fullscreenFilm noir’s zenith … Barbara Stanwyck and Fred MacMurry in Double Indemnity.Photograph: BFILike Stanley Kubrick, Wilder mastered a variety of genres and displayed a range rarely seen in the profession. Ace in the Hole was a scathing satire of the newspaper industry, Witness for the Prosecution a hugely influential courtroom drama and The Lost Weekend dealt with alcoholism in a way that was unprecedented in the 1940s. Even a lesser work like The Seven Year Itch contains one of the century’s defining images: that of Marilyn Monroe standing on a subway grate as her dress is blown upwards. Wilder was undeniably an egotist but he had much to be egotistical about.He was born Samuel Wilder in 1906 to a Jewish family but the name change in this case was not an attempt at assimilation. His mother nicknamed the young Wilder “Billie”, having been inspired by Buffalo Bill’s Wild West shows, an entertainment she experienced during a brief spell living in New York. Wilder worked as journalist andtaxi dancerearly in his career, jobs that seem to foreshadow an almost pathological desire to observe people in all their complexity, as well as a love of the limelight.His screenwriting career began in Berlin during the silent era, most notably collaborating with Robert Siodmak and Edgar G Ulmer for People on Sunday. All three men would end up in Hollywood having fled their home countries due to the rise of nazism and are among the most significant players in shaping the film noir movement, the fatalism of the genre surely a byproduct of the fates of their families.View image in fullscreenA fatalism inspired by the fate of his family … Mauvaise Graine.Photograph: BFIWhen Adolf Hitler came to power, Wilder fled to France. With some understatement, he said: “It seemed like the wise thing for a Jew to do.” He made his directorial debut there in 1934 with Mauvaise Graine although nothing about that film suggested what was to come once he arrived in Hollywood later in the same year.Wilder teamed up with Charles Brackett and penned films for the great and the good of Hollywood, writing screenplays for the likes of Howard Hawks, Mitchell Leisen and Ernst Lubitsch. The last was Wilder’s hero and he hung a sign above his desk for ease of reference while working. It read simply: “What would Lubitsch do?”Wilder made a couple of minor American films beforeDouble Indemnity– but this was the movie that made his name, the most influential crime picture in the annals of cinema. The Holocaust hangs over Double Indemnity like the smoke from Phyllis Dietrichson’s cigarette and it is worth noting that Wilder was working on the project as his family perished in the camps thousands of miles away. It was as though he used all his creativity and negativity about the human condition to do something worthwhile with the survivor’s guilt. Tellingly, in an alternative ending that has never made its way out of the Paramount vaults, Fred MacMurray’s Walter is executed in a gas chamber.Early in those Hollywood days, Wilder was summoned to the consulate and it looked as though he might be deported. It was not just his febrile imagination that led Wilder to conclude he would ultimately end up “shipped off to Dachau” unless he could convince this interlocutor of his worth. The American on duty asked Wilder what he did for a living and the answer was succinct: “I write movies.” The official paced back and forth in the office before stamping the young man’s passport and saying: “Write some good ones.”View image in fullscreenWilder’s magnum opus … Shirley MacLaine and Jack Lemmon in The Apartment.Photograph: BFIHe certainly did that, from early gems such as an adaptation of Erich Kästner’s Emil and the Detectives in the Berlin years to underappreciated work at the end of his career such as the superlative The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes, via one of cinema’s great runs from the 1940s to the 1960s. He never forgot that interrogation and maintained, to the end, that he “did not want to disappoint that dear man in Mexicali”.Wilder’s final few films suggested a man out of time, although Fedora at least inspired Jonathan Coe’s terrific 2020 novel Mr Wilder & Me. The latter is being adapted for the screen by Christopher Hampton with Stephen Frears set to direct, yet raising the funds has proved difficult. This feels somewhat apt since Fedora concerns an ageing film star bemoaning the New Hollywood film-makers of the 1970s, dismissing them as “kids with beards”.Fluctuating between obscurity and acclaim feels right for a film-maker who expertly blended darkness with light. Twenty-five years after being kept awake by the toilet, Wilder made it to an Austrian spa and an actual waterfall, “the most beautiful in the world”.“There I am in bed, listening to the waterfall. And after all I have been through, all the trouble and all the money I’ve made, all the awards and everything else, there I am in that resort, and all I can think of is that goddamned toilet. That, like the man says, is the story of my life.”Almost Perfect: The Films of Billy Wilder is at theBFI Southbank, London, from 19 October until 31 DecemberExplore more on these topicsFilmBilly WilderFilm industryCrime filmsComedy filmsDrama filmsRomance filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bob Mackie obituary | Fashion | The Guardian
description: American fashion designer and costumier who clothed glamorous showbiz celebrities, especially Cher
Author: Veronica Horwell
Headline: American fashion designer and costumier who clothed glamorous showbiz celebrities, especially Cher
Content: Bob Mackie with some of his memorabilia at his home in Palm Springs, California, 2021.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/APView image in fullscreenBob Mackie with some of his memorabilia at his home in Palm Springs, California, 2021.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/APFashionObituaryBob Mackie obituaryAmerican fashion designer and costumier who clothed glamorous showbiz celebrities, especially CherVeronica HorwellThu 24 Sep 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 12.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost costume designers are novelists, supplying character, back stories, social placement and history, done in cloth.Bob Mackiewas also a genius cartoonist, assembling details into an image, memorable on sight, that could hold anything from a small 1960s television screen to a concert arena.Mackie, who has died aged 87, was master of the showbiz sartorial aesthetic that evolved on stage and in films to entertain in itself as well as project performers.Rhinestones, sequins, beads, plaques, plumes, plush,le tout ensemble. An audience got a big kick from a Mackie costume before a word was spoken or a note was sung, and performers had total confidence in him, as he studied their bodies, movements and personality before designing.He did that with divas from Judy Garland through Diana Ross, Barbra Streisand, Bette Midler,Whitney Houston, Madonna and, especially, Cher.View image in fullscreenCher in a Bob Mackie creation at the 1986 Oscars.Photograph: Alamy/PATheirs was an interactive relationship from Cher’s television appearances in the 70s, when he guided her out of hippiedom and into minimal material spectacularly styled. He and she plotted the crest ofblack feathers she wore to the 1986 Academy Awards, atop an outfit that linked back to the extreme exoticism of early movie stars such as Gloria Swanson. What little there was of it was perfectly executed; Mackie costumes were made to couture standards – even his reworkings of second-hand gowns for a brokeTina Turner.That Cher ensemble was also funny. Mackie’s sharp but not unkind wit shaped performers’ personas as much through humour as glamour. When he dressedElton John as Donald Duck for a Central Park concert, Elton could barely sing for laughing; he later said Mackie liberated him, let him expand into performance space.Mackie loved parody, and could crack terrific jokes directly in fabric. His best was one of the thousands of garments he created for Carol Burnett’s TV show though the 60s and 70s. She was playing a spoof Scarlett O’Hara from Gone With the Wind, who had famously sewn a gown from her mother’s curtains. Burnett suggested she could just be draped in curtains, uncut, unsewn. Mackie had her enter wearing the curtain pole across her shoulders as well. The costume is now in the Smithsonian’s collection.The idea depended on Mackie’s passionate film knowledge. He was born in Monterey Park, on the outer rim of Los Angeles, where cinema was the local industry, the child of Robert Mackie, who worked in a bank, and Mildred (nee Smith). After they divorced, Mildred parked the boy with his grandmother Bessie. Weekdays, he drew. Weekends, he went with his visiting mother and elder sister, Patricia, to the cinema, to watch the many Technicolor musicals that studios confected during the second world war and postwar era from elaborate costumes loosely joined by plot.Mackie’s favourite stars were Carmen Miranda, the definition of camp from her fruit-crowned head through bare midriff to high platform soles, and Betty Grable, who was kitsch layered in fur and satin, also bare-midriffed. When he noticed there were credits for “costumes designed by” on the 1951 movie An American in Paris, he set out to make that his job.Mackie attended Pasadena City College and got into Chouinard Art Institute, but dropped out to sell his skills and sketch for LA costumiers. FromJean Louis, who createdMarlene Dietrich’s stage costumes, he learned the power of nude soufflé, a sheer silk almost invisible when cleverly lit, yet strong enough to bear heavy beading. Mackie sketched the dress made of it that Louis made forMarilyn Monroe at President John Kennedy’s 1961 birthday bash, and went on using it, in new stretch forms, notably forCher’s “naked but for the glitter” 1974 Met Gala gown.View image in fullscreenBarbra Streisand wearing a Bob Mackie gown in 1975.Photograph: Screen Archives/GettyHe also sketched for the celebrated Edith Head at Paramount. She was dabbling in television, and Mackie turned there too, working as assistant to the talentedRay Aghayan, designing for Garland’s TV shows in 1963-64. They became personal and professional partners, campaigning for an Emmy for costume design.They won the first one in 1967 for their joint work on a production of Alice Through the Looking Glass, and picked up Oscar nominations for Lady Sings the Blues (Ross as Billie Holiday, 1972) and Funny Lady (Streisand as Fanny Brice, 1975).Mackie was offered the 1974 adaptation of The Great Gatsby, in part because of the evident research behind his pastiche period clothes for Burnett’s show, but his input into a wide variety of design for weekly, starry TV comedy and music shows was respected, and they drew huge audiences; he turned the offer down.Mackie received his own Oscar nomination for the movie of Dennis Potter’s Pennies from Heaven (1981), recreating 30s dreamworld lamé and Depression drab; he dressed the film’s ordinary people with great affection.Disintegrating studios had closed their workrooms of craftspeople, so Mackie and Aghayan had set up their own Californian atelier in 1968 to custom-make for industry clients, and even civilians. At the height of his showbiz fame, Mackie decided to produce actual fashion, and showed ready-to-wear at New York Fashion Week from 1982.View image in fullscreenThe V&A’s Diva exhibition, 2023, which included costumes designed by Bob Mackie.Photograph: Guy Bell/ShutterstockBy then, mainstream international couture had already left the salon for theatrical parades of often fantastical garments, yet fashion critics treated Mackie as a vulgar intruder, Mr Hollywood, Barnum Bob. His fashion project lapsed by the end of the decade, except for profitable licensed accessories and a long-running outlet on QVC TV shopping channel. Meanwhile, celebrities began to appear on the new red carpet scene in loaned couture gowns, advertising labels rather than themselves.Mackie still had faithful clients, especially Mattel’s Barbie. Mattel made at his request a custom Barbie face, without her eager smile, and from 1990 he dressed more than 50 dolls as stately miniatures of his style, some with handsewn embellishment. He had also become, he said, “the patron saint of drag queens”, many of whom had first understood the possibilities of self-fashioning through clothes when viewing his 70s shows. RuPaul proudly wore original Mackie and invited him as a guest judge on the very first episode of RuPaul’sDragRace in 2009.View image in fullscreenDick Van Dyke, left, with Carol Burnett and Bob Mackie in 2024.Photograph: Giles Harrison/London Entertainment/ShutterstockThough semi-retired, Mackie remained a pop-culture name, and young showbiz, including Beyoncé, Miley Cyrus and Zendaya, pressed him to borrow archive pieces. He noticed amusedly that European couture had been freely stealing tropes from his oeuvre since the late 90s, but as a guest at the Met Museum’s 2019 camp-themed ball, was amazed that Alessandro Michele, then of Gucci, and John Galliano approached him, moreover tearfully, to tell him he was their idol.Mackie won seven Emmys, the Council of Fashion Designers lifetime achievement award, and a Tony for the 600 costumes of TheCherShow on Broadway in 2018.Aghayan died in 2011, as did Mackie’s sister. A son, Robin, from a brief youthful marriage to the actor Lulu Porter (born Marianne Wolford), died in 1993. He is survived by a granddaughter and two great-granddaughters.Bob (Robert Gordon) Mackie, designer, born 24 March 1939; died 14 September 2026Explore more on these topicsFashionCherDiana RossBarbra StreisandTelevisionUS televisionBette MidlerobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Check the men’s rail – and embrace imperfection: a stylist’s guide to shopping secondhand | Vintage fashion | The Guardian
description: Buying preloved always feels that bit cooler, says celebrity stylist Bay Garnett, but how do you find a gem in charity shops or online? She reveals her top tips
Author: Bay Garnett
Headline: Buying preloved always feels that bit cooler, says celebrity stylist Bay Garnett, but how do you find a gem in charity shops or online? She reveals her top tips
Content: Secondhand is the first choice for many a savvy shopper.Photograph: Jonas Gratzer/LightRocket/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSecondhand is the first choice for many a savvy shopper.Photograph: Jonas Gratzer/LightRocket/Getty ImagesGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterVintage fashionCheck the men’s rail – and embrace imperfection: a stylist’s guide to shopping secondhandBuying preloved always feels that bit cooler, says celebrity stylist Bay Garnett, but how do you find a gem in charity shops or online? She reveals her top tipsYour favourite secondhand findsBay GarnettThu 24 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve been championing secondhand shopping for decades. For my debut shoot for British Vogue in 2003, I dressed Kate Moss entirely in pieces I’d found in New York charity shops – including a banana-print top that cost $5 and a gold sequin jacket I found in the Salvation Army for $7.I think every shoot I have done has had secondhand in it – vintage jeans, blazers, coats, belts, boots – and they are always the pieces the people I am dressing exclaim over and want. So, often they just look and feel cooler.But wearing secondhand isn’t just a style choice. There is the pure thrill of the hunt – finding that unique, one-off piece that tells a story – and every time you give a garment a second life, you keep it out of landfill and turn the simple act of getting dressed into a beautiful form of climate activism.Want to do a bit of your own secondhand shopping? Here are my tips for hunting and styling secondhand – from the charity shop rail to online.How to shop secondhandView image in fullscreenBay Garnett has dressed many a celebrity in secondhand clothing.Photograph: Amber Ahmad/OxfamStart with accessoriesIf you’re new to secondhand, an accessory is often the easiest way to introduce something distinctive into a wardrobe. I once bought a preloved belt in New York after saving up and bartering with the shop. It has brass punk studs and has weathered beautifully – it looked like it was owned by one of the Ramones or Debbie Harry. I put this belt on Sophie Dahl when I styled her as Debbie Harry for British Vogue, as well as Chloë Sevigny and many others. I still wear it often – with a silk shirt, a vintage blouse, a roll-neck cashmere sweater, you name it. It gives any outfit a vibe.Push outside your comfort zoneSometimes I’ll buy high-street clothes in a charity shop–always basics such as a long-sleeved Cos, New Look or Zara T-shirt or vest to go with my existing wardrobe – but on the whole, I find it’s best to look for pieces that feel original and outside the norm – whether that’s a colour, fabric or a shape I’m drawn to. If something catches your eye immediately, it’s worth trying it on, even if it’s not your usual style.Check out the men’s railView image in fullscreenSearching the men’s sections of charity shops and vintage stores can unearth gems.Photograph: Anadolu/Anadolu Agency/Getty ImagesI’m not precious about sticking to womenswear. I once spotted a shirt I loved that cost £1,200 new – then went to the men’s rail of a charity shop and found it. It’s a habit worth adopting even if you’re not shopping for a man: some of the best finds are sitting in the men’s section. There is nothing cooler than men’s button-down shirts. Oxford or poplin are gorgeous with a stiff structure. Find one in a classic sky blue or a faded banker stripe, roll the sleeves right up to your elbows, and tuck into something unexpected like a silk slip skirt or some old jeans.Hunt for the lovely soft jumperI don’t get too hung up on fabrics, but I’ll always look out for a cashmere sweater or anything that’s beautiful cotton. Older cashmere can feel noticeably thicker, and natural fibres are, in some cases, biodegradable. They can also be circular – when you rescue a pure cotton shirt or knit, you are keeping a high-quality material in rotation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDon’t be afraid of a little imperfectionWear and tear isn’t necessarily a reason to put something back. I once bought a brilliant secondhand 1970s sweatshirt despite its faded fabric because this ruggedness suited the piece.I’m all for a little patina and wear, particularly on something like a leather bag; a new handbag is, in my view, less good than one that has lived a little. That said, stains are where I draw the line – if you can see one, don’t buy it.A piece also doesn’t need to fit perfectly off the rail to be worth buying; I’ll buy something then get it altered by a tailor – whether that’s adjusting a hem or removing shoulder pads to make it feel more up to date.Mix old and newView image in fullscreenIn with the old: clever styling can give new life to preloved clothing.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesA great secondhand piece can make something you already own feel different. A preloved belt can change the silhouette and energy of a dress, and I love wearing vintage shirts with jeans. Before buying something new, try finding one preloved find and styling it with three pieces already hanging in your wardrobe. It’s often the quickest way to make old favourites feel fresh again – and stops you from buying new clothes you don’t need.Know where to look online – and search creativelyOnline secondhand shopping can be overwhelming simply because there’s so much out there. Though I always prefer a physical shop, I love Etsy for deep-diving into particular styles, while eBay works well for specific searches. Vinted is great too for the sheer volume and variety of clothes on offer, and I’ve got a lot from Oxfam’s online shop over the years.Start with an idea of what you’re looking for, then refine the search. A good rule of thumb is to combine a decade, a style and an item, for example,70s bohemian boots. Also, try searching for colours, fabrics or even specific collar shapes instead of broad terms such as dress or jacket.Shoppingfor vintage online is like a good haircut – the more detail you can give the hairdresser, the better the result.For more, readreaders’ favourite secondhand findsandhow to make your leather last a lifetimeBay Garnett is supportingOxfam’s Second Hand September, which encourages people to make more sustainable shopping choices by buying preloved fashion and donating unwanted clothesExplore more on these topicsVintage fashionThe FilterWomen's dressesWomen's coats and jacketsAccessoriesShoppingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Do any coffee-flavoured drinks come close to the real thing? | Food | The Guardian
description: Our drinks columnist – a UK coffee lover – explore the world of canned lattes and flavoured protein drinks
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Our drinks columnist – a UK coffee lover – explore the world of canned lattes and flavoured protein drinks
Content: Coffee-flavoured drinks, from lattes to cold brews, are having a bit of a moment right now.Photograph: amenic181/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCoffee-flavoured drinks, from lattes to cold brews, are having a bit of a moment right now.Photograph: amenic181/Getty ImagesFoodDo any coffee-flavoured drinks come close to the real thing?In which a UK coffee lover, long devoted to her moka pot, tiptoes gingerly into the world of coffee-derived drink productsMina HollandThu 24 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy family has benefited hugely fromcharities that support healthcare, so it is with extra zeal that I’ll be drinking coffee with a slice of cake tomorrow to mark this year’sMacmillan Coffee Morning. In anticipation, I’ve been tasting some coffee-flavoured drinks.I should preface this by saying that, when it comes to coffee, I am a creature of habit and, almost 30 years into my relationship with the stuff, I know what I like: short-ish, strong, preferably made in a moka pot and only a tiny splash of milk. I’m less faithful to brands, though I do rateUnion’s House Roast, which is bold, crowdpleasing, not too bitter and sold in most big supermarkets. Much as my partner has tried to seduce me to the trendy charms of filter coffee, this leopard can’t seem to change her spots.So imagine my feelings when I lined up the cast of products to taste for this column. Canned lattes! Coffee-flavoured protein drinks! Instant coffee 2.0! I’ll start with the first group, because the market is now teeming with examples (many of them in extra-unsustainable packaging). All the big players are there – Starbucks, Nescafé, Califia Farms – and all with the three-quarters (or more) milk to one quarter (or less) coffee ratio typical of a latte. The difference is that these drinks all have added sugar or sweeteners, thereby turning your morning coffee into a liquid pudding. If they contain dairy milk, it tends to be UHT (not a taste I like), although some use lactose-free or plant-based milks. The best of the bunch wasGrind’s Iced Vanilla Oat Latte: less milk (57%), more coffee (40%) and less sugar, too.As far as I could tell,Emmi’s Caffe Latte High Proteinis no higher in protein than any of the rest, so it strikes me that the brand may simply be jumping on what’s becoming a rather hackneyed bandwagon catering to a health-anxious and possibly appetite-suppressed crowd.Yfood’s This Is Food, meanwhile, made me quickly wonder: “Is it?” This ready-to-drink, coffee-flavoured “complete meal” with 30g protein per bottle and more than 20 ingredients is a sorry substitute for a food, and it certainly isn’t coffee.Cold brew – that is, coffee that has been steeped in cold water for an extended period for a softer, more naturally sweet result – takes a fair while to make, so I can see the point in buying it off the shelf: Tesco and Nescafé both make inoffensive unsweetened cold-brew concentrates that are a good option for an Indian summer. And, much to my surprise, I rather enjoyed the next-gen flavoured instant coffees by Little’s andBeanies, especially the former’sglazed cinnamon number. But as much as Union from my moka? Come off it.Four coffee drinks worth your attentionGrind Iced Vanilla Oat Latte£2.25 (250ml) Ocado. The best example of this dubious genre: a not-too-sweet, good-quality cold brew blended with oat milk.Tesco Finest Cold Brew Coffee£4.50 (500ml). A cold brew concentrate to which you just add water. Would be nice with a slice of citrus.Little’s Glazed Cinnamon£4 (50g) Ocado. The doughnut vibes are more in the aroma than the taste, but it’s a scent that could seduce non-coffee drinkers.UnionHouse Roast£7.50 (200g) Ocado. You can’t beat a home brew, and this balanced, slightly chocolatey all-rounder is my food shop stalwart.Explore more on these topicsFoodCoffeeSoft drinksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: What to cook when summer meets autumn | Food | The Guardian
description: The weather is in transition, so here are some dishes to bridge the gap between crisp salads and hearty stews
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The weather is in transition, so here are some dishes to bridge the gap between crisp salads and hearty stews
Content: For that awkward stretch between salads and stew, Rachel Roddy's fusilli with roast vegetables and gorgonzola.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFor that awkward stretch between salads and stew, Rachel Roddy's fusilli with roast vegetables and gorgonzola.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The GuardianFeastFoodWhat to cook when summer meets autumnThe weather is in transition, so here are some dishes to bridge the gap between crisp salads and hearty stewsSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastItamar Srulovich and Sarit PackerThu 24 Sep 2026 07.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 07.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe weather in London can’t quite make up its mind. You leave the house in the morning and immediately wish you’d brought gloves, but by lunchtime you’re carrying your jacket under your arm, and by dinner you’re closing the windows again. Summer hasn’t exactly gone, but winter has started sending little reminders that it knows where we live.We love this time of year. The air feels fresh from the occasional shower, the days are still long enough to make something of, the light is perhaps the most beautiful it will be all year, and, for cycling, it is perfect. There are days when London seems to contain two seasons at once: summer in a sunny spot at lunchtime, winter the moment the sun disappears.For the cook, however, this time of year can be confusing. A bowl of cold salad no longer feels quite enough, but we’re not yet ready for the great pots of soup, beans and stews that will soon take up permanent residence on the hob. We want something cooked, but not necessarily piping hot; substantial, but still bright.Foodthat acknowledges the chill in the evening without surrendering completely to it.View image in fullscreenSweet, sour and spicy … Yotam Ottolenghi’s aubergine and red pepper pahi.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianOur solution is to live in the territory between salad and supper. Roast vegetables, grains, rice and pasta are particularly good here: dishes that can be eaten warm from the oven or sit happily on the table until everyone is ready to eat, with plenty of lemon, herbs, vinegar, chilli or yoghurt to keep things lively. Rachel Roddy’srice salad with red peppers, celery, herbs and eggis exactly that sort of thing, especially eaten at room temperature rather than fridge-cold. Rukmini Iyer’sroast red pepper orecchiette with pistachios and ricottatakes the last of the peppers somewhere warmer without turning them into winter food, while another Rachel dish,fusilli with roast squash, gorgonzola and sage, pushes us a little farther into autumn. Nigel Slater’sbraised aubergines, courgettes, preserved lemon and olivesare perhaps even better at room temperature than hot, which is exactly where we want to be. Then there’s Yotam Ottolenghi’saubergine and red pepper pahi with fenugreek and curry-leaf oil, which has that combination we crave now: something cooked and substantial, but also sweet, sour and spicy. Finally, and staying with Yotam, hisblack rice with fennel and butternut squashfeels made for this time of year: roast vegetables, rice, chilli and a sharp dressing.This is how we want to eat now, with one foot in each season. A tray comes out of the oven, something sharp gets squeezed over it, a handful of herbs goes on top, and dinner can wait while we take one last bike ride before dark. In the coming months, the days will get shorter and colder, and our food will get darker and browner, so we will take this opportunity to get as much colour and zest as possible out of every meal.Our month in foodView image in fullscreenSome of the best food in London … The Kerfield Arms.Photograph: Joe Howard/The Kerfield ArmsLocal heroes|Our new favourite London street is Grove Lane in Camberwell. Turn down it from Camberwell Church Street and you will first seeLala Books, surely London’s most charismatic bookshop thanks to the consistently excellent selection, the coffee and the neighbourhood feel. A few shops down isTheo’s pizzeria, which we have long loved, while even further down the road is the gloriousKerfield Arms, which offers some of the best food in the city right now, including an incredible Sunday lunch and what has to be the best lunch deal in town: a plate and a glass of wine for £15. They even have a Michelin star.Happy place|Wildflowersis a restaurant nestled in a Pimlico back yard and it’s easy to miss – but it really shouldn’t be, because it’s where we want to spend every birthday and anniversary for the foreseeable future. The menu is very seasonal, so we will spend the next 12 months praying they’ll bring back the heavenly sweetcorn and truffle agnolotti.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGo west|We are heading back to the US – and before you ask, no, it’s not just to get more ofTrader Joe’s pickle mustard, though we certainly will stock up. Instead, we’re setting out on the west-coast leg of our book tour, so if you’re reading this and are in the area, do come say hi! And if you have any recommendations – and we mean food recs, obviously – do drop us a line.If you want to read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive Feast in your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastSaladDessertVegetablesRicenewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Pumpkin, pecan, quince, apple or plum: Adriann Ramirez’s autumn pie recipes | Autumn food and drink | The Guardian
description: The pastry chef gives autumn’s best ingredients a golden glow-up
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The pastry chef gives autumn’s best ingredients a golden glow-up
Content: Adriann Ramirez’s piloncillo pumpkin pie.Photograph: Laura Edwards/The Guardian. Food styling: Joss Herd. Prop styling: Tabitha Hawkins.View image in fullscreenAdriann Ramirez’s piloncillo pumpkin pie.Photograph: Laura Edwards/The Guardian. Food styling: Joss Herd. Prop styling: Tabitha Hawkins.Autumn food and drinkPumpkin, pecan, quince, apple or plum: Adriann Ramirez’s autumn pie recipesThe pastry chef gives autumn’s best ingredients a golden glow-upAdriann RamirezThu 24 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 07.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhave come to adore what the British autumn brings: beautiful apples, pumpkins, plums and quince galore. These pies not only sing the praises of this bounty, but put them front and centre. I also use ingredients such aspiloncillo(a Mexican raw cane sugar), tonka bean (which adds a beautiful fig-leaf flavour) and buckwheat flour (for a wonderfully nutty taste). These aren’t always easy to find, but they are worth the extra effort, taking these bakes to the next level.Piloncillo pumpkin pie (pictured top)Prep10 minChill/Freeze1 hr 30 minCook2 hrServes8-12For the pie dough90g cold water30g apple cider vinegar375g plain flour, plus extra for dusting50g caster sugar5g table salt250g cold butter,cut into 6 chunks1 egg,beaten, for brushingDouble cream,lightly whipped, to serveFor the filling200g double cream115g whole milk3 medium-sized eggs (170g)300g gratedpilconcillo(panela),or brown sugar50g maple syrup425gtinned pumpkin1 tbsp vanilla extract1 tbsp rum2 tsp ground cinnamon2 tsp mixed spiceA few gratingsfresh nutmegA few gratingstonka beanCombine the water and vinegar in a container and put in the freezerfor about 10 minutes, until cold.Meanwhile, put the dry ingredients for the dough in the bowl of a stand mixer and whisk to combine. Add the butter and, using the paddle attachment, mix on slow until it has broken down but some medium-large (flattened) pieces remain. (To do this by hand, use your fingertips to rub the butter into the flour.)Add the water/vinegar and mix again until it just comes together into a shaggy dough. Turn out on to a floured surface and bring the last bits together with your hands.Using a rolling pin, flatten into a rough rectangle, cut into four equal pieces and stack the pieces on top of each other. Flatten into a rectangle again and repeat this process once more. Chill for one hour.Once chilled, flour the work surface and dough, and roll it into a 25cm circle, roughly 3mm thick . Gently press the dough into a 23cm loose-bottomed pie tin, folding the overhang under itself to create a small edge. Using two fingers, push the edge in the opposite direction to crimp. Freeze for 15 minutes.Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5. Line the pastry with scrunched up baking paper, fill with rice or baking beans, then bake for 15 minutes. Remove the rice/baking beans and parchment paper, and return to the oven for a further 10 minutes. Brush with the beaten egg and bake for a further five minutes to seal.Turn the oven down to 150C (130C fan)/300F/gas 2. To make the filling, mix all the ingredients in a bowl with a whisk, until combined. Pour into the pie crust and bake for 45-50 minutes, until there is only a slight wobble to the filling.Let the pie cool completely in the tin, then transfer to the fridge to chill. Serve cold with lightly whipped double cream.Pecan, buckwheat and chocolate pieView image in fullscreenPrep10 minChill/Freeze1 hr 15 minCook1 hr 30 minMakes8-12For the dough140g unsalted butter,softened85g icing sugar1 medium-sized egg45g buckwheat flour175g plain flour,sieved (plus extra for dusting)30g ground almond15g cocoa powderFor the filling150g granulated sugar155g maple syrup165g golden syrup2tbsp rum1tbsp sea salt1tsp vanilla extract1tsp ground cinnamonZest of½ orange55g cold unsalted butter3 medium eggs (170g),lightly beaten300g pecan halvesIn a stand mixer with the paddle attachment, beat the butter and icing sugar for three minutes, or until light in colour. Add the egg and beat until combined.In a separate bowl, whisk together the buckwheat and plain flour, ground almond and cocoa powder, then combine with the egg mixture.Pat the dough into a round disc,wrap in clingfilm and refrigerate for at least an hour.Lightly flour the work surface and dough, then roll out the dough to about 2.5cm larger than a 20cm loose-bottomed tart tin. Gently fold the dough in half, then fold in half again and place it in your tin. Gently unfold it and begin to press the dough into your tin – if it tears, just gently push it back together. Freeze for 15 minutes.Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4.Fill the tart shell with crumpled baking paper and baking beans, and bake for 15 minutes. Remove the paper and beans, and bake for another five minutes. Leave to cool.Meanwhile, make the filling: combine the sugar, syrups, rum and salt in a saucepan, and cook over a medium heat until it begins to boil. Continue cooking for another minute.Take off the heat and add the vanilla, cinnamon, orange zest and butter, stirring until just combined. Let it come to room temperature, then whisk in the eggs.Spread the pecans in an even layer in the pie shell, then pour over the filling. (If you like things on the salty side, sprinkle a bit more sea salt over the top.) Bake the pie for 40-45 minutes, until the filling is just set. If the pecans are beginning to brown too quickly, gently put some foil on top and continue cooking. Serve cooled with some creme fraiche.Quince and apple crumble pieView image in fullscreenPrep15 minChill/Freeze1 hr 15 minCook1 hr 45 minServes8-10For the pie dough90g cold water30g apple cider vinegar375g plain flour, plus extra for dusting50g caster sugar5g table salt250g cold butter,cut into 6 chunks1 egg,beaten, for brushingFor the filling500g crisp apples,likeRosette,DiscoveryorJazz200g quince50g caster sugar1 tbsp vanilla extract2 tsp ground cinnamon2 tbsp plain flourA sprinkle of sea saltJuice of 1 lemonA few gratings of nutmegFor the crumble200g plain flour175g dark brown sugar25g demerara sugar1 tbsp ground cinnamon1 tsp table salt150g unsalted butter,cold and cubed100g pecans,roughly choppedCombine the water and vinegar for the dough in a container and put in the freezerfor about 10 minutes, until cold.Put the dry ingredients in the bowl of a stand mixer and whisk to combine. Add the butter and, using the paddle attachment, mix on slow until it has broken down but some medium-large (flattened) pieces remain. (To do this by hand, use your fingertips to rub the butter into the flour.)Add the water/vinegar and mix again until it just comes together into a shaggy dough. Turn out on to a floured surface and bring the last bits together with your hands.Using a rolling pin, flatten the dough into a rough rectangle, cut into four equal pieces and stack the pieces on top of each other. Flatten into a rectangle again and repeat this once more. Chill for one hour.Flour the work surface and dough, and roll it out into a 25cm circle, roughly 3mm thick. Press the dough gently into a 23cm loose-bottomed pie tin, and with the overhang, fold it under itself to create an edge. Using two fingers, push it in the opposite direction to create a crimped edge, then freeze for 15 minutes.Heat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5. Line the pastry with scrunched up baking paper, fill with baking beans and blind bake for 15 minutes . Remove the parchment and beans, and bake for a further 10 minutes; leave to cool.Meanwhile, peel and core the apples and quince. Cut the apples in quarters then thinly slice them; grate the quince. Toss the fruits in a bowl with the remaining filling ingredients, and leave to macerate while you make the crumble topping.Using a stand mixer with the paddle attachment, mix all the dry crumble ingredients. Add the cubed butter and mix until it just begins to clump – do not overmix or it will become a solid dough. Toss in the pecans and mix by hand.Spread the fruit mix evenly on the baked dough, then top with the crumble mix. Bake at 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 for 40-45 minutes, until the crumble is firm and the fruit slowly bubbles underneath. Serve hot with freshly whipped cream or ice-cream, and custard, too, if you’re nasty like me.Spiced plum slab pieView image in fullscreenPrep10 minChill1 hr 30 minMacerate30 minCook2 hrServes8-10For the pie dough180g cold water60g apple cider vinegar750g plain flour100g caster sugar10g table salt500g cold butter,cut into 12 chunksFor the filling1kg plums,your favourite variety (I lovepluots).100g caster sugar¼ tsp ground cinnamon¼ tsp ground gingerA pinch of ground clovesA pinch of ground nutmeg1 vanilla pod,split in half and the seeds scraped outJuice of1lemonA pinch of salt3 tbsp cornflourDouble cream,for glazing and servingDemerara sugar,for sprinklingCombine the water and vinegar in a container and put in the freezerfor about 10 minutes, until cold.Put the dry ingredients for the dough in the bowl of a stand mixer and whisk to combine. Add the butter and, using the paddle attachment, mix on slow until it has broken down but some medium-large (flattened) pieces remain. (To do this by hand, use your fingertips to rub the butter into the flour.)Add the water/vinegar and mix again until it just comes together into a shaggy dough. Turn out on to a floured surface and bring the last bits together with your hands.Using a rolling pin, flatten the dough into a rough rectangle, cut into four equal pieces and stack the pieces on top of each other. Flatten into a rectangle again and repeat this once more. Chill for one hour.Macerate the plums by cutting them into quarters (if they’re large plums, cut into eighths) and putting in a bowl with the sugar, spices, vanilla, lemon juice, salt and cornflour. Combine and leave for 30 minutes.Drain the plums, putting the liquid in a saucepan over a medium heat. Whisk until it begins to boil, then continue cooking, stirring, for a further minute. The liquid will be very thick and glossy.Add the now-thickened liquid back to the plums and mix gently. Taste and add more sugar, lemon or spice, if needed; set aside to cool completely.Roll out the two separate pieces of dough to the shape of your baking tray (I use a 25cm x 20cm one, with at least 3cm height) with at least 2.5cm excess on the sides. Chill in the fridge for 30 minutes.Take one piece of dough and line the tray with it, pressing the dough firmly into the sides of the tray, then lightly prick the base with a fork. Crumple up a piece of baking paper to make it more pliable, flatten it, then use this to line the dough, and use this to line the dough, adding baking beans on top. Blind bake at 190C (170C fan)/gas 5 for 15 minutes, then remove the beans and parchment, and continue baking for another eight minutes. Set aside to cool.Tip in the filling and spread evenly. Using a pastry brush, brush the edges of the cooked pastry with cream, then top with the second piece of dough, gently crimping your edges. Brush the lid with more double cream and sprinkle with demerara sugar. Make two slits in the lid and bake for 40-45 minutes, until the top is golden brown and the filling slow bubbling. Serve hot with creme fraiche, ice-cream or whipped cream.Adriann Ramirez is head of pastry atFinks, in north London.Explore more on these topicsAutumn food and drinkPieFoodDessertFruitNuts and seedsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for tomatoes stuffed with breadcrumbs, chickpeas and herbs | Food | The Guardian
description: A well-seasoned and comforting meal to ease you into the autumn months
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: A well-seasoned and comforting meal to ease you into the autumn months
Content: Rachel Roddy’s tomatoes stuffed with breadcrumbs, chickpeas and herbs.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenRachel Roddy’s tomatoes stuffed with breadcrumbs, chickpeas and herbs.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The Guardian.A kitchen in RomeFoodRachel Roddy’s recipe for tomatoes stuffed with breadcrumbs, chickpeas and herbsA well-seasoned and comforting meal to ease you into the autumn monthsRachel RoddyThu 24 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt this time of year, baked tomatoes stuffed with rice and surrounded by a packing-chip sea of potatoes are typical all over central and southern Italy, and in many other places besides. So much so that when I see a tray of those wrinkled red caps in a bakery or canteen-liketavola calda(literally, “hot table”), it doesn’t cross my mind that the hollowed-out tomatoes underneath might be filled with something other than rice. It was only when the woman behind the counter was wrapping my two portions of cannelloni and four slices of margherita pizza that another person’s order alerted me to the fact that these tomatoes were in fact filled with breadcrumbs, chickpeas, sausage, cheese and herbs. Suddenly, the tomatoes were the most appealing item behind the steamed-up glass, and the only thing I could want. We were inTavola Calda in Latina, just south of Rome, during the lunchtime rush, which is why I didn’t feel able to add to my order, but then I was dissatisfied with my lunch.But dissatisfaction gave me a reason to pullClaudia Roden’s A Book of Middle Eastern Foodfrom the shelf, for her chapter dedicated to stuffed vegetables, which draws inspiration from Turkish, Uzbekistani, Azerbaijani, Armenian, Greek, Egyptian, Persian, Syrian, Lebanese, Saudi Arabian and north African recipes. Having noted that almost any vegetable can be stuffed, Roden adds that the most common filling for a hollowed-out vegetable is a well-seasoned mix of chopped onion, minced meat, rice, chopped parsley, and maybe chopped tomato; and she then goes on to give seven filling variations – some with rice, some with meat (no pork), and with various herbs and spices. She also provides a not disappointing filling including chickpeas, which is what I have adapted, also with inspiration from the busy Tavola Calda, for this week’s recipe.I haven’t included sausagemeat in my version, but if you wish to, squeeze the meat from a couple of pork sausages and crumble it in at the same time as the chickpeas. Seasoning is fundamental here – salt, obviously (a small amount at various stages is better than all at once), as well as a little minced garlic and herbs. While my instinct here is for parsley and either rosemary or sage, dried mint also works wonderfully, as does cinnamon, whose warm, woody sweetness works beautifully with tomatoes, as it does in tomato sauce, but that’s another column.How long the tomatoes take to bake will depend very much on their ripeness; harder ones need 10-20 minutes more than those with softer shells, but keep an eye on them and leave them to rest for a while before serving. I also think tomatoes stuffed this way benefit from being baked close together in a ceramic oven dish, which is why I baked cubed potatoes separately; some salted yoghurt or mashed courgettes or aubergine are also good accompaniments. As in the best and busiest tavole calde, serve the wrinkled tomatoes just hotter than room temperature.Tomatoes stuffed with breadcrumbs, chickpeas and herbs or spicesServes48 tennis ball-sized tomatoesSalt and black pepper½ garlic clove, minced1 red onion, peeled and dicedOlive oil1 tbspminced flat-leaf parsley1 tspminced rosemary, or mint, or ground cinnamon200gcooked chickpeas,and/or the meat squeezed from two pork sausages100g soft white breadcrumbs (from two-day-old bread)2-3 tbspgrated cheese(whatever you have)Cut the caps off the tomatoes, then use a teaspoon (and knife, if necessary) to scoop the pulp and seeds into a bowl, in order to hollow out the tomatoes.Sprinkle the insides of the tomato shells with salt, and keep the caps. Remove any hard, white bits from the pulp/seeds, then mash the rest, seasoning with a little salt and the garlic.In a frying pan on a medium-low heat, soften the onion in four teaspoons of olive oil with a pinch of salt. Add the herbs and chickpeas (and sausages, if using), then add the breadcrumbs, grated cheese and enough of the tomato pulp to make a soft stuffing.Arrange the empty tomato shells in an oiled ovenproof dish, then fill them with the chickpea and breadcrumb mix. Put on the lids and bake for 30-45 minutes, or until the tomatoes are baked through, a little wrinkled and the stuffing cooked.Explore more on these topicsFoodA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkTomatoesMain courseBeans, pulses and legumesBreadHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: You be the judge: should my partner dial down the heat when he cooks?  | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Rhonda believes Ned turns the heat up too high and ruins woks. He reckons he has famous chefs on his side. You decide whose argument is in flames
Author: Georgina Lawton
Headline: Rhonda believes Ned turns the heat up too high and ruins woks. He reckons he has famous chefs on his side. You decide whose argument is in flames
Content: Illustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianYou be the judgeLife and styleYou be the judge: should my partner dial down the heat when he cooks?Rhonda believes Ned ruins woks. He reckons he has famous chefs on his side. You decide whose argument is in flamesFind out how to get a disagreement settled or become a jurorInterviews byGeorgina LawtonThu 24 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 05.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheprosecution: Rhondadouble quotation markHe whacks the heat right up, which stains our wok and makes it really hard to wash upMy partner, Ned, does most of the cooking in our house and he’s really good at it. I help prep and I usually do the washing up, which is how this issue arose. We had an old wok that became so encrusted with burnt stir-fry it was difficult to clean. Eventually, I said we needed to buy a new wok. We bought an expensive stainless steel one, but we’ve only had it three weeks and it’s stained already.double quotation markI was annoyed because I have had a sore shoulder and knew I would be the one scrubbing the wok afterwardsNed cooks with the heat turned up as high as possible. I know with a wok you turn the heat up high initially before you put in the meat or vegetables, but you’re supposed to turn it down before you add the sauces. Otherwise, they burn on to the wok and make it difficult to clean. Once you get stainless steel to a certain temperature, it maintains that heat, so you don’t need to keep the flame on maximum. The point of stainless steel is that it stays stainless. If you stain it, you’re overheating it.Once, when Ned was cooking, I turned the heat down myself. He objected and there was a bit of argy-bargy in the kitchen. I was annoyed because I knew I would be the one scrubbing the wok later, and I had a sore shoulder.Ned can also get distracted while cooking. He might put the rice on and then walk out of the kitchen, start reading or listening to a podcast, and forget that he needs to turn something off in five minutes. He has left the gas on before. There have even been occasions when, if I hadn’t turned the knobs down, I reckon we could have had a fire.Ned admits he has become distracted in the past, but he won’t accept my argument about the wok. He likes to have the heat up the whole time when stir-frying and says that is the proper way to cook with a wok. I love that he does the cooking, but I’d like to avoid being burned in a fire and stay alive to eat the food – and not have to scrub the pots so hard afterward. Since I’m doing the washing up, I don’t think it’s unreasonable to ask him to turn the heat down.Thedefence: Neddouble quotation markThe person doing the cooking is in charge of the temperature – plus a wok is supposed to blackenI do most of the cooking and occasionally we have a stir-fry. A chef once told me that the key to making one is that you’ve got to be fast and the pan has to be “scary hot”. I also learned how to make a stir-fry from my brother-in-law, who is a chef. Preparation is essential: everything should be chopped beforehand and then added to the wok in sequence. The oil goes in, then the vegetables – we don’t eat much meat these days – and the sauces go in last. It all happens quickly and on a very high heat. It’s quite a dramatic way of cooking.Rhonda doesn’t complain about the quality of my cooking. I don’t burn the food or the sauces, although I acknowledge we get some residue left on the pan. I think that’s an acceptable part of cooking with a wok. For me, the marks left on a wok are part of its character. They’re a testament to the cooking you’ve done. I’ve also heard Australian chefKylie Kwongsay your wok is supposed to blacken.double quotation markI accept that I have occasionally left other things cooking on a low heat and become distractedI’m happy to wash the wok, but I don’t think it needs to remain as shiny as it was when we bought it. And I don’t want anyone touching the knobs while I’m cooking. The person cooking has to be in charge of the temperature. If someone comes in halfway through and changes the temperature, it interferes with what I’m doing.I accept that I have occasionally left other things cooking on a low heat and become distracted. My preferred cuisines are Italian and Indian. Indian food can cook slowly for a long time, and with Italian food I might make a sauce or ragu and let it reduce. But stir-frying is different. It’s fast and intense, and you need complete focus because it happens so quickly. To say I’m nearly burning things down is a gross exaggeration. I’m fixated on the task at hand and I like to keep the heat high. Maybe I am too focused on speed and heat sometimes, but I maintain that a wok needs to remain hot. A lightly stained wok doesn’t mean I’m cooking incorrectly.Names have been changedThe jury of Guardian readersSome food staining is normal. But Ned should get his head in the game and focus on the frying pan, lest they all end up in the fire.Pablo, 35skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI’m not a chef, but growing up I was told three things about cooking. First, if you aren’t the one cooking, don’t interfere unless something is on fire (but not if they are flambéeing). Second, the person not cooking does the washing up. And finally, stainless steel rarely stays stainless.Nathan, 44While professional chefs with seasoned carbon steel woks stir fry at speed on a high heat, it doesn’t sound like that is what Ned is doing. Staining from frequent use and stains from burned-on food are different. Maybe leaving it to soak immediately after use could resolve this issue.Jess, 37I’m not sure having a brother-in-law who is a chef qualifies Ned as a culinarian, and staining a stainless steel pan is a waste of time (scrubbing) and money (when they eventually need to replace it). Perhaps he would benefit from taking a class – cooking, fire safety or, preferably, both.Isabella, 31If Ned is the one who does the cooking, he should decide on the heat and the how the food is made – but Rhonda shouldn’t have to clean the wok if he makes a real mess of it. As a compromise, how about letting Ned use the wok however he chooses, as long as he also cleans it and buys the replacements?Ivy, 18Now you be the judgeIn our online poll, tell us: is Ned getting too hot under the collar?Last week’s resultsWe asked whether Ahmed wasright to use the moneyhe borrowed from his sister to go on holiday.96% of you said no – Ahmed is guilty.4% of you said yes – Ahmed is innocent.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleYou be the judgeFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Going places with panache’: Max Mara channels audacious women for Milan show | Max Mara | The Guardian
description: Chore jackets and loose-fit trousers nod to ‘nonconformist glamour’ of Amelia Earhart and other pioneers
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Chore jackets and loose-fit trousers nod to ‘nonconformist glamour’ of Amelia Earhart and other pioneers
Content: A model walks the runway during the Max Mara show as part of the women's spring/summer 2027 collection at Milan fashion week.Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA model walks the runway during the Max Mara show as part of the women's spring/summer 2027 collection at Milan fashion week.Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/AFP/Getty ImagesMax Mara‘Going places with panache’: Max Mara channels audacious women for Milan showChore jackets and loose-fit trousers nod to ‘nonconformist glamour’ of Amelia Earhart and other pioneersJess Cartner-Morleyin MilanThu 24 Sep 2026 07.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 09.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Max Mara catwalk atMilan fashion weekhad well-cut coats, sturdy block-heeled boots, crisp white shirts and capacious suede handbags. What it quite deliberately did not have was shock value. “I hope everyone watching this show can recognise something of themselves in what they see,” said Ian Griffiths, the British designer who has been at this Italian house since 1987. “I think that’s really important. Without being critical of other brands or designers, so much of fashion alienates people and makes them feel that they aren’t good enough or thin enough or young enough to wear what’s being represented.”Models for Max Mara spring/Summer 2027 fashion show in Milan. Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/GettyTrousers were pleated and roomy, skirts long enough to be elegant but not long enough to trip you up. In shades of sand and chalk, grey and black, every piece was designed to work with everything else, and to blend into an existing wardrobe. The styling gestures – a popped collar here, a knotted belt there – stopped short of gimmick. The models could have walked off the runway and on to the Milan street – which, Griffiths said backstage, was the point. “The catwalk show is only the prelude to what to me is the real presentation, which is when I see women walking down the street in my clothes.”Recently, even this most adult and sensible of brands has sometimes been unable to resist the temptation to chase the youth vote. This season,Max Marawent back to doing what it does best, which is fashion for grownups. (Nothing here for wearing in da club.) Griffiths said: “We were founded on the simple mantra of real clothes for real women, back in the 1960s, and when we stick to that idea, we never go wrong. So more than ever, I wanted to focus on real life chic.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMax Mara has gone back to doing what it does best, which is fashion for grownups.Composite: Giovanni Giannoni Credit WWD/Getty ImagesThe beauty of practical clothes is that they allow you to live an exciting life. On Griffiths’s moodboard for this season were portraits of aviatorsAmelia EarhartandBeryl Markham, explorer Freya Stark, wildlife photographer Osa Johnson and cross-continental driver Eva Dickson, audacious women of the 1930s and 1940s whose “nonconformist glamour” Griffiths wanted to channel for the modern wardrobe. Some models wore their hair swept up and away at the temples, a tousled take on the victory roll, but nothing looked twee or retro. Griffiths said: “I’m not suggesting for a minute that women fill the pockets of their organza cargo vests with notepads and compasses and explorer’s instruments. It’s the idea of getting up in the morning and going places with a certain amount of panache.”Chore jackets, loose-fit trousers, cross-body bags and shirting are a modern uniform in cities all over the world. This collection was a glossy, Milanese take on how many women already dress. Overshirts, with four patch pockets, took the chore jacket principle and added a dash of safari-jacket exoticism. Stretchy halter tops were cinched with D-rings; while double-breasted silhouettes made for dashing blazers.Explore more on these topicsMax MaraMilan fashion weekFashion weeksItalynewsShareReuse this content

title: Taking a deep dive in Helsinki’s subterranean city | Helsinki holidays | The Guardian
description: Under the Finnish capital lies a world of swimming pools, go-karting tracks, playgrounds – and even an art gallery
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Under the Finnish capital lies a world of swimming pools, go-karting tracks, playgrounds – and even an art gallery
Content: Itäkeskus swimming hall, excavated from granite bedrock, could accommodate almost 4,000 people in an emergency.Photograph: Maarit HohteriView image in fullscreenItäkeskus swimming hall, excavated from granite bedrock, could accommodate almost 4,000 people in an emergency.Photograph: Maarit HohteriHelsinki holidaysTaking a deep dive in Helsinki’s subterranean cityUnder the Finnish capital lies a world of swimming pools, go-karting tracks, playgrounds – and even an art galleryGabriella BennettThu 24 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 02.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe moon is an impostor.Swimmingbackstroke beneath its surface, I look up at craggy hollows in close relief. White rock undulates in all directions, a forest of peaks rising next to a desert of craters. Every time I trick myself into thinking I’m somewhere celestial, the sound of children splashing brings me back to earth.This is no lunar landscape but Helsinki’s underground swimming hall, excavated from granite bedrock and officially opened in 1993. These days,Itäkeskusuimahalliis one of the Finnish capital’s most visited leisure facilities, welcoming 400,000 people a year. Local people mingle with tourists, I will discover, during a week exploring Helsinki’s subterranean metropolis.My visit was one of 12 research trips I made over three years to better understand how cities are being reimagined. It turned into a book,How to Build a City, for which I travelled to locations that are testing the frontiers of urban living in response to an increasingly uncertain world.Many global cities feature a version below ground, but Helsinki’s is thought to be the only one transformed for peace. As urbanisation increased the population, a more efficient solution was needed for heating plants and telecoms cables. You could scatter them around in expensive pockets of land, digging up the streets and sacrificing parks. Or you could tuck them away beneath ground level, by adding to bomb shelters first carved out during the second world war.And that’s what Helsinki did. By 2010, its city council approved the world’s first officially masterplanned underground city, home to hundreds of vast human-made caves and tunnels up to 90 metres deep. Itäkeskus pool was opened 17 years before this space allocation plan was approved.In peacetime, the caves function as shopping malls, playgrounds, a go-karting track and subway stations, all connected by almost 200 miles (293km) of tunnels. In the event of war, however, each can be transformed into a bomb shelter, part of a network capable of accommodating 900,000 Finns.View image in fullscreenTourists explore the roof of Helsinki’s underground art museum, Amos Rex.Photograph: Paavo Turtiainen/AlamyItäkeskus swimming hall alone could house almost 4,000 people. In less than 48 hours it can be drained and fitted with decontamination showers. For the rest of the time, there are no clues as to its defence nature. Only the comforting hallmarks of the public pool: the tang of chlorine in my nose and the warmth that cloaked my skin.I arrived in Helsinki on the morning of the spring solstice, although the ground was still dusted with greying snow and I was grateful for the heated carriages on my 25-minute Metro ride from the city centre. At Itäkeskus station, past a school surrounded by Soviet-style tower blocks, silver birches trailed bare branches over cars. From the outside, a municipal glass building gave an uninspiring welcome, but inside, I found a different world entirely.A broad staircase swept me down steeply, framed by rocky, whitewashed walls. After paying (entry to all four of Helsinki’s public swimming halls is €6 for adults and €3.30 for children, making it popular with families as well as budget-conscious travellers), I disrobed in changing rooms spun off from a cathedral-tall granite core. Signs were in Finnish, but the space was easy for non-natives to navigate. Staff spoke excellent English.double quotation markA postmodern dreamscape was revealed, a large pool lined in lavender, canary yellow and burgundy tilesAt one side of the colossal hangar, men grimaced as they lowered themselves into a triangle of freezing water. On the other, a postmodern dreamscape was revealed, a large pool lined in lavender, canary yellow and burgundy tiles, with huge plastic triangles in cerulean and lilac suspended overhead. The only windows were set into a lifeguard’s tower next to a waterfall that filled the air with the roar of water in motion.Swimming under the ersatz moon was an otherworldly experience. After 50 lengths, I’d earned my reward. Included in the entry fee is access to a gym, which I did not visit, plus a hot tub, steam room and two saunas, which I did. A graphic on the door showed a swimming costume crossed out in red and I gingerly removed mine, sliding into place on the bench and reminding myself that prudishness is a uniquely British affliction. Inside, it was so dark I could barely make out other bodies. The low light created the effect of a confession booth.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenTemppeliaukio church is half-buried in the Töölö neighbourhood.Photograph: Danny Lehman/Getty ImagesAround me, conversations bubbled in Finnish, American English and German. The quotidian details of living emerged. I joined in, asking a stranger for dinner recommendations and whether I should brave the plunge pool. If you don’t dwell on it, you could forget the true purpose of this place.It was something I kept returning to over the following days as I wandered through experimental installations at Helsinki’s underground art museumAmos Rex(from €20; children go free), whose antennae-like skylights popped up on concrete stalks from the pavement near the chichi shopping district of Kluuvi. And in the Töölö neighbourhood’s exquisiteTemppeliaukio church(€8; children go free), half-buried in a giant mound of rock.All were examples of a supremely responsive city. All were bomb shelters, too. Evidence that you can design for the future with verve and beauty. Helsinki shows it is possible to do it all.How to Build a City: Journeys into the Urban Future by Gabriella Bennettis published byHeadline(£25). To support the Guardian buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsHelsinki holidaysFinland holidaysCity breaksEurope holidaysScandinavia holidaysCultural tripsSwimmingfeaturesShareReuse this content

Content: One of the many cats of Istanbul, and they have a lot of questions for you.Photograph: Martin Belam/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOne of the many cats of Istanbul, and they have a lot of questions for you.Photograph: Martin Belam/The GuardianThursday quizLife and styleThursday news quiz: Long-haul flights, changing lights and a lot of Turkish catsTest yourself on topical news trivia, pop culture and general knowledge every Thursday.
