title: ‘That’s so AI!’ What gen Alpha’s biggest insult tells us | Young people | The Guardian
description: The year’s most popular slang reveals what young people think about artificial intelligence – and it’s not positive
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The year’s most popular slang reveals what young people think about artificial intelligence – and it’s not positive
Content: ‘OMG my mum and dad aresoAI.’Photograph: Posed by models; Iuliia Bondar/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘OMG my mum and dad aresoAI.’Photograph: Posed by models; Iuliia Bondar/Getty ImagesPass notesYoung people‘That’s so AI!’ What gen Alpha’s biggest insult tells usThe year’s most popular slang reveals what young people think about artificial intelligence – and it’s not positiveThu 24 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:“That’s AI!”Age:Brand new.Appearance:Primary schools everywhere.What’s AI?It’s just a thing the kids are saying now: “That’s AI!” or “That’s so AI!”But what is?Something inauthentic, unbelievable or rubbish.Whichwas made by AI?No. Artificial intelligence has very little to do with this.But isn’tartificial intelligence poised to destroy humankind?Very possibly, but that doesn’t concern us right now.It doesn’t?No. The kids – gen Alpha – have noticed that certain qualities of AI-generated slop, such as the way it’s superficially convincing but ultimately cheap and of dubious value, can be found in lots of other things: knock-off merchandise, exaggerated claims, excuses your parents make. If something is considered somehow suspect, then it is also, by definition, AI.Is “That’s AI” the new “six-seven”?No, this bit of slang means something: the young people have simply broadened the definition of AI to make it equivalent to “bullshit”.So it’s always deployed as an insult?Always.But aren’t things more complicated than that? Couldn’t AI also be our saviour, as long as goodjudgmentis used and the right guardrails are in place?While the rest of us are having that debate, gen Alpha has already made up its mind: AI is so AI.What will happen when AI finds out it’s AI? Will it get trapped in a logical feedbackloop until all thedatacentres start exploding?You’re not a very scientific person, are you?Anyway, didn’t Donald Trump just change the name of artificial intelligence to“super intelligence”, or SI?SI is so AI. And Donald Trump is AI.Not for the first time this year, I feel like dumping all my tech stocks.Tech stocks are AI.What about driverless taxis?Driverless taxis are AI, especially the ones that havehumans in the driver’s seat.My job in marketing was certainly AI, which is probably why AI took it.I’m sorry.Do say:“That’s so AI!”Don’t say:“No, that’s Al – Al Gordon. He’s in my year, and he’s actually OK. But his shoes are AI.”Explore more on these topicsYoung peoplePass notesAI (artificial intelligence)featuresShareReuse this content

title: After so long in Trump’s sights, hopeful Greenlanders breathe a collective sigh of relief | Greenland | The Guardian
description: Locals hope agreement signed this week is step towards independence and end to US threats to annex island
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Locals hope agreement signed this week is step towards independence and end to US threats to annex island
Content: Picture shows Aqqalukkuluk Fontain, his girlfriend, Stella, and their three-year-old daughter, Aura.Photograph: Family handoutView image in fullscreenPicture shows Aqqalukkuluk Fontain, his girlfriend, Stella, and their three-year-old daughter, Aura.Photograph: Family handoutGreenlandAfter so long in Trump’s sights, hopeful Greenlanders breathe a collective sigh of reliefLocals hope agreement signed this week is step towards independence and end to US threats to annex islandMiranda BryantNordic correspondentThu 24 Sep 2026 10.27 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 14.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreenland’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and Múte B Egede, the foreign minister, received a hero’s welcome when they landed back in Nuuk from New York on Wednesday night – and a nation took a collective sigh of relief.Colleagues, friends and members of the public turned out to greet them at an airport where, just 20 months ago, the landing of a Trump-branded planecontaining Donald Trump Jrhad kickstarted a geopolitical crisis that the people of Greenland now hope is over.To cheers and applause, and waving red and white Erfalasorput flags, the politicians were credited with saving the nation thanks to anew defence agreementbetween Greenland, Denmark and the US signed this week at the UN in New York. It comes after an unprecedented period of turbulence in which Donald Trumprepeatedly threatenedto invade the Arctic island and almost tore apart Nato in the process.1:09Greenland leaders receive hero's welcome after signing security pact with US and Denmark – video“Welcome home,” the speaker of Inatsisartut, the Greenlandic parliament, Kim Kielsen, said. “Welcome to a country that we were about to lose. You have ensured that we have a future here.” Like many Greenlanders, for the last year-and-a-half he said he had been holding his breath.Nielsen, who became prime minister last year in the middle of the crisis, told the crowd: “We can be calm. Our land will not be taken. Our land will not be bought. The road has been long, and it has been very difficult and dangerous.”Hundreds then attended a celebratory coffee party at Katuaq, the Greenlandic capital’s cultural centre. Aqqalukkuluk Fontain, 38, who was there with his girlfriend, Stella, and their youngest daughter, Aura, who is three, said the collective release of tension was palpable. “It was a joyous moment. It’s going to linger for a while,” said the IT manager, who earlier this yearorganised a protestoutside the new US embassy in Nuuk.He cautioned he could not entirely relax – concerned that, after the midterms, Trump could change his mind and relations could “take a turn for the worse” – but hailed the deal with the US as a moment of pride for Greenland and a stroke of “strategy genius” from Greenlandic and Danish negotiators. “Trump is trying to angle it that he made a great deal. But he wanted total control, ownership of Greenland. He didn’t get that,” he said.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump, Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister of Denmark; and Jens-Frederik Nielsen, the prime minister of Greenland, at the UN headquarters this week.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APIts full text contains some key differences from the 1951 defence agreement it is intended to update – for example, the US gets underwater access to Greenland and specific permission to construct a missile defence system – but is a far cry from Donald Trump’s originalthreat to annexthe Arctic island. And in terms of tangible outcomes, the biggest winner is arguably Greenland, where it is seen as a potential stepping stone to future independence.When the 1951 agreement was signed, Greenland was still a colony ofDenmark. Now, it is a largely autonomous territory that has signed an agreement alongside Denmark with the US that it played a central role in negotiating.A big question hanging over Greenland independence was what would happen to its status withinNatoand relationship with the US.The new agreement answers that question. It stipulates that if it did become independent, the governments of Greenland and Denmark would “together ensure that the independent Greenlandic state will agree to remain in Nato, including by applying to become a member if necessary”.View image in fullscreenTrump, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio; Lars Løkke Rasmussen, the Danish foreign minister; Frederiksen, Nielsen and Egede.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesThe centrality of Nato to the agreement is also seen as a boost for an alliance that was creaking under US claims against one of its fellow members’ territory.Greenlandic politician Qarsoq Høegh-Dam, who earlier this yearbecame the first memberof the pro-independence party Naleraq to be elected to the Danish parliament, said there was still considerable work to do in terms of gaining independence but that “a lot of what ifs” have now gone.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDenmark reportedly flew blood bags to Greenland in preparation for a US attackRead more“It’s a point of relief for Greenlanders,” he said. “They can lower their shoulders a bit, so we can talk about domestic issues, the road to independence more freely, instead of the search of what if?”Much of the agreement already existed in practice, he said, but now “it is written in ink” with Greenland’s explicit involvement. “It’s a continuation of an agreement since the 1950s. The difference is now that Greenland has some say in it. They want to agree for themselves instead of a country overseas agreeing on behalf of them,” he said. “That’s the difference first and foremost and it is significant.”View image in fullscreenPeople protesting against Trump’s policy towards Greenland at the US consulate in Nuuk, Greenland, in January.Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/APHe said, however, there were still questions about what the words will equate to in practice, for example on investment. “It’s a good foundation, but the details are missing,” he said.View image in fullscreenAviaja Fontain: ‘We don’t have to think about getting attacked and just live our peaceful life again.’Photograph: Inesa Matuliauskaite/The GuardianGiven that just a few months ago Trump was threatening to invade Greenland, and a few weeks since he posted a map of Greenland covered with the US flag to social media, in many ways the very fact that a diplomatic agreement has been reached is a victory in itself.Ulrik Pram Gad, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS), said: “For Danes and Greenlanders, it’s a win to be able to force Trump into doing something diplomatically. And if this actually puts the Greenland crisis to rest, it will be felt as a win for Greenland, Denmark andEuropebecause then we can concentrate on real problems and trying to find ways to work with the US on that.”Aviaja Fontain, 41, a student from Nuuk, said the agreement puts to rest months of anxiety. At one point, amid government warnings about preparedness, she thought Nuuk was being attacked by the US during what turned out to be a power cut caused by a storm. “Many of us have been afraid that Trump will use force, but now I can feel relief,” she said. Now she feels she can finally relax. “We don’t have to think about getting attacked and just live our peaceful life again.”Explore more on these topicsGreenlandTrump administrationDenmarkUS foreign policyEuropeDonald TrumpNatofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The long-range drone war: Ukraine and Russia scramble for supremacy in the skies | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: A conflict that began with tanks and then artillery is now pivoting around a new generation of drones focused on military, industrial, economic and civilian targets
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: A conflict that began with tanks and then artillery is now pivoting around a new generation of drones focused on military, industrial, economic and civilian targets
Content: A pilot from Ukraine’s 413 Raid drone regiment waiting to launch mid-range attack drones in eastern Ukraine. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianA conflict that began with tanks and then artillery is now pivoting around a new generation of drones focused on military, industrial, economic and civilian targetsByDan Sabbaghin eastern Ukraine. With photographs byJulia KochetovaThu 24 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFinally, in the dead of night, the threat above has passed. The rain has eased and the Ukrainian drones are ready, prepared by a ground crew shrouded in hard-to-detect green and red lights. A small succession of Ukrainian Fire Point FP-2 craft, miniature monoplanes with a 6-metre wingspan and more than 100kg of explosive, line up for an attack mission into occupied Luhansk, over 200 miles away.The drone’s main piston engine is a familiar scooter’s buzz, but its launch booster is something else. The jet sound reverberates, almost painfully. A burst of fire lurches into the distance, the last of which signifies it is time for Ukraine’s 413 Raid drone regiment to pack and go.View image in fullscreenThe launch of an FP-2 drone during the mission into occupied LuhanskIt is a scene that is now played out nightly by dozens of Ukrainian crews, reflecting a fast-changing conflict that began with tanks, then artillery, but is now pivoting beyond a first generation of drones. Death and destruction are delivered by new weapons in growing volumes, hundreds of miles beyond the frontline, and at targets that are military, industrial and economic but that affect civilians too.But just as Ukraine has developed its drone and missile capability to almost match Russia’s – after its cities were subject at times to hundreds of drone strikes a day – Moscow has transformed its drone arsenal with a jet-powered revolution. The balance of power remains uncertain.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenPilots of the 413 Raid drone regiment preparing an FP-2 for launchRaid is a specialist drone unit, created two years ago, and has been operating Ukrainian-designed and -built FP-2 attack drones since last autumn, according to Skipper, a former corporate IT worker with a master’s in computer science who is now one of its commanders. If, he says, there was only one crew that could run two missions a week when they started, today he says “we can do 10 times more, or even more”.Speaking in a car as the rain pelts down, Skipper cautions there is “a flipside” when asked if long-distance wars are easier to fight because nobody has to be killed visibly. “They can do it as well,” he says – Raid’s crew are targets too. “Maybe you don’t see the enemy with your own eyes, but still it’s a very dangerous game,” he adds.The FP-2 was only first publicly acknowledged by Ukraine last September. It is designed to attack hardened targets at a mid-range, to disrupt Russian logistics to the frontline. The success of Raid and others engaged in mid-strike bombing has helped grind the pace of the invaders’ advance to a near halt. Russia gained a modest 90 square kilometres of Ukraine in August, compared with 505 sq km a year earlier, and western officials estimate it is losing 6,000 more soldiers a month than it can recruit.Ukrainian drones and missiles chartIn Ukraine’s sprawling military, the specialist drone units of the Unmanned System Forces, including Raid regiment, work and overlap with army units working closer to the frontline and special forces. A major attack, such as the attack thatdisabled the Moscow refineryabout 300 miles from the border on 20 September, involves several working at once.A long-range attack could involve launching up to 300 drones, though the target is to be able to launch 1,000 a night, in what soldiers describe as an “orchestra”, where cheap drones identify an air corridor towards the final target.View image in fullscreenAn employee walks past a plume of smoke rising from a fire at the Russian e-commerce firm Wildberries’ logistics complex near the town of Podolsk, outside Moscow, on 16 August. Photograph: Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP/Getty ImagesThelong-range, $75,000 FP-1, sister to the FP-2, has been used to repeatedly attack warehouses, refineries and other military-economic sites at a depth of 1,800 miles inside Russia, causing the country’s crude oil production to fall by 7.7% in a year, according to figures from the International Energy Agency, and interest rates to remain at 14%. “Both sides are getting better at translating deep strikes into economic effects,” says Sidharth Kaushal, of the Royal United Services Institute.View image in fullscreenA refinery burning in Moscow after Ukrainian drones strikes, 21 September. Photograph: EyePress News/ShutterstockMission planning is rarely shown, but a short-range drone unit operating in the eastern Donetsk front – Unit 17, Special Operations Centre – is happy to show their war work from their dacha. Znakhar, 33, a software coder before the full Russian invasion, is one of a squad of English-speaking men in their early 30s. During the day, he clicks on fresh, static targets – artillery, electronic jamming systems – that have been added to a common system from western satellites or Ukrainian reconnaissance drones, studying their pictures for extra information.View image in fullscreenPilots of Unit 17, Special Operations Centre, posing for a portrait next to a Sych mid-strike droneView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenThe temporary base of pilots of Unit 17, Special Operations Centre. Right: the ‘drop bombs’ Unit 17 used for middle strikesAt night, the crew use a $25,000 Sych drone, which looks like a large model aeroplane. If the rain holds off, they can fly two to six bombing runs, dozens of miles behind enemy lines. Znakhar, whose call sign means healer or herbalist, draws up an initial flight path in seconds with a few clicks on a map, then adjusts the route to avoid population centres, high ground and known interceptor drone launch sites. What’s changed recently? “More drones,” he says. “Russian drones.”Colleagues such as Ananas, 30, head out at night, taking more precautions than they did when the unit started drone work two years ago, preparing launches underground where once they could work in a field. He studied architecture, then worked as a 3D artist in a video game studio. “I play a lot of video games,” he says, “so I’m good with a gamepad. It’s a big plus because now I’m a pilot.” It’s a narrowing of the gap between fiction and reality.On the other side, Moscow always has ballistic and cruise missiles available, allowing it to bomb anywhere inside Ukraine since February 2022. It imported delta-winged Shahed drones from Iran in the war’s first year to boost its long-range attack numbers, and developed a family of cheap battlefield drones plus its own version of the Shahed. But since May there has been a notable set of upgrades, allowing Russian forces to strike Ukraine more effectively with fast, jet-engined drones, allied with a new ruthlessness of targeting.View image in fullscreenFirefighters working at the site of a Russian drone strike on Kyiv business centre on 23 September“Russia never stops,” Serhii Beskrestnov, Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s defence technology adviser, saidduring an interview in Kyivpunctuated by an air raid and explosions in the distance. The original Iranian delta wing Shahed (known by Russia as the Geran-2) has been redesigned and a jet engine added.The new Geran-4, with more aerodynamic wings, flies at anywhere from 300km/h (186mph) to 550km/h, while the cigar-shaped Geran-5 is even faster, at closer to 600km/h. It is similar in speed to a new light cruise missile, the Banderol. The prediction is that Russia will make 36,000 jet Shaheds in 2027, a further 10,000 Banderols, plus a similar number of cheap cruise missiles, the Dan-T. All could be used to bomb Ukraine’s strained electricity, heating and water systems this winter.Russian drones and missiles chartThe new weapons, whose Telefly engines are made in China, are faster than the Ukrainian interceptors, designed to stop the old piston-engined Shahed Geran-2s. Shahed interception rates, once over 90%, are down to 60% against Russia’s newer models, with predictable results.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenThe aftermath of a Russian attack on ammunition storage in Myla village, Kyiv region, in AugustA mix of jet- and traditional-engined drones made a rare morning attack into the centre of Kyiv on Wednesday, bombing a market near the central railway station and business centre, killing two people and injuring 41. At the end of August, a Geran-4 hit an ammunition dump atMyla, outside Kyiv,killing 38 and destroying homes nearby.Another struck Ukraine’s SBU domestic intelligence agency in the centre of Kyiv, though it may have been controlled in its final phase by a Russian agent on the ground. Food supplies in Kyiv supermarkets are uneven after sustained attacks on warehouses in August;petrol stations in the capitalwere targeted in early September.View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of a Russian Geran-5-type jet-powered drone strike on an Ukrnafta petrol station in the Holosiivskyi district of Kyiv, 15 September. Photograph: Libkos/Getty ImagesUkrainian military propaganda is excellent at highlighting successful missions on social media, but the wider picture of the impact of its drone strikes on Russia is harder to discern. “This spring we had a really nice time and almost every night we could see one, two, three, four systems destroyed,” Skipper says. “Since June, July, they are just hiding.” Other Ukrainian military sources emphasise that Russia has improved its jamming capabilities, and cheap strike drones are simply not as accurate now.In this long-distance war, civilian casualties are climbing. New UN figures show 2,222 killed in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026, more than in all of 2025. In August, 368 were killed in Ukraine and a further 113 reported dead in Russia. Warehouses owned by Ukrainian supermarkets, its Nova Poshta postal service and e-commerce groups were hit at least 32 times. Wildberries and Ozon warehouses in Russia were bombed 17 times by Ukraine.View image in fullscreenFirefighters at a warehouse in the Kyiv region after a Russian attackThe impact could be harder for Ukraine. “Russia has advantages that Ukraine does not,” says Kaushal. “A more diversified range of long-range weapons, more of an air defence network and more slack as a society, because its people have not faced so much pressure for so long.” Ukraine, meanwhile, faces economic pressure at a time when its war budget is overspent and needs to find £40bn more next year.Yet, though war is escalating as the technology changes, neither side is close to defeat or a crisis. Tests will come if Russiatries to mobiliseup to 300,000 men after parliamentary elections – and as Ukraine tries again to refinance and, most urgently, get through the winter.Back in their soldiers’ dacha, Ananas and Znakhar wonder if the war will ever end. “Sometimes I catch this feeling,” Ananas admits, then Znakhar comes in: “We just need to hang on one more day than them.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaDrones (military)EuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘My first screen kiss was in a cowshed!’ Lesley Manville on her greatest roles – and why sex scenes for over-50s are booming | Television | The Guardian
description: In the last 15 years, she has gone from respected actor to stratospheric, garlanded star. Now she is back on TV as a chic sleuth in a racy car – despite being terrible at guessing whodunnit
Author: Gabriel Tate
Headline: In the last 15 years, she has gone from respected actor to stratospheric, garlanded star. Now she is back on TV as a chic sleuth in a racy car – despite being terrible at guessing whodunnit
Content: ‘I’m glad I was never flavour of the month’ … Manville.Photograph: Clara Molden/Camera Press/TelegraphView image in fullscreen‘I’m glad I was never flavour of the month’ … Manville.Photograph: Clara Molden/Camera Press/TelegraphTelevisionInterview‘My first screen kiss was in a cowshed!’ Lesley Manville on her greatest roles – and why sex scenes for over-50s are boomingGabriel TateIn the last 15 years, she has gone from respected actor to stratospheric, garlanded star. Now she is back on TV as a chic sleuth in a racy car – despite being terrible at guessing whodunnitThu 24 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 04.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is high summer and, while Lesley Manville may be suffering a bit with hay fever and the heat (“I’m so white, all I do is burn”), she doesn’t do wilting. Soon to head outside to tend to the ailing garden of her London home, she is enjoying a rare period of rest after six almost unbroken months ofOedipuson Broadway and thenLes Liaisons Dangereusesat the National. She keeps, incidentally, the Tony she won for playing Jocasta in Oedipus on a shelf by the computer, “next to its friend, Larry Olivier” – an Olivier awarded for the same role.“You don’t go into a job thinking about awards,” she says, before grinning conspiratorially. “Listen, you don’t say to an Olympian, ‘Oh, is it OK that you didn’t win?’ Yes, you like to win!”double quotation markOedipus and Les Liaisons Dangereuses were both highly sexualised pieces of theatre and I love thatManville has done a fair bit of winning recently, and not before time. The last 15 years have seen her graduate from widely respected actor to garlanded star: since 2011 there has been that Tony, two Oliviers, an Oscar nomination for Paul Thomas Anderson’s Phantom Thread, Emmy and Golden Globe nominations and seven Bafta nominations. Her cinematic collaborators have included not only PTA but Luca Guadagnino, Alfonso Cuarón and Joel Coen. This relatively late blooming has come as a relief.View image in fullscreen‘You’d like to win!’ … Manville was Oscar-nominated for Phantom Thread, directed by Paul Thomas Anderson, in 2017.Photograph: Focus Features/Zuma Press/PA Images“I’m so glad I was never flavour of the month,” she says, “because it’s so hard to maintain. No one went to LA for pilot season when I was young – we were just interested in doing the work. But you’re right, there has been a shift. Winning the Olivier forIbsen’s Ghostsin 2014 took me somewhere else, theatre-wise. An Oscar nomination makes a difference. A whole sequence of high-profile television, not least The Crown, which obviously wasn’t all about Princess Margaret but boy did Peter Morgan write me two astonishing episodes. Mrs Harris Goes to Paris brought me to a new audience, andMumis the thing I still get stopped about most.”These are just some of the most recent projects from an amazing body of work, one of which Manville – whose combination of wry wit, warm intelligence and stern savvy keeps me on my toes throughout our conversation – is rightly proud. Marble Hall Murders, her new TV series, starting on BBC One this week, completes Anthony Horowitz’s trilogy of ingenious Susan Ryeland mysteries. It may be one of her lighter pieces, but it’s no less satisfying for that.Manville was willingly cajoled into returning as publisher-cum-crimebuster Ryeland by Horowitz, who offered to write a third book if she’d do a third series. Susan is back being single, back in London and back in publishing – albeit reluctantly – when a young writer proposes to conclude the bestselling saga of fictional detective Atticus Pünd. As before, many of the cast take dual roles as fact and fiction intertwine, and Pünd’s investigation into the murder of a publicly beloved, privately monstrous children’s author in Corfu is reflected by events in Susan’s world, where her sparring partners include Mark Bonnar and Rupert Penry Jones. If it is indeed the end, Manville will miss Susan immensely.“She feels closer to me than a lot of other parts I’ve played. I like to think I don’t conform to a received notion of how one should be when one reaches a certain age. I love the fact that she wears these fabulous clothes, drives an open-top red sports car – I used to drive an MG in my 20s, although it broke down all the time – and doesn’t put up with any shit. Like her, I’m very clear about who I am. I’ve found myself at this point in my life. And although I’m absolutely terrible at guessing whodunnit, I’ve caught out a few boyfriends in the past, so my detective work hasn’t been all bad.”Manville, now 70, grew up on a council estate in Hove, a seaside town in East Sussex, one of three daughters of lifelong Labour supporters. “Those principles stay with you. My early influences were very leftwing, working at the Royal Court with actors and playwrights who felt the same way.” These included Andrea Dunbar and Caryl Churchill. “I really want the Labour party to be everything it could be, and under Andy Burnham, we might have a glimmer of hope that happens. I’ve got a lot of time for him.”Manville was a gifted performer from a young age, albeit not in the art form she would go on to conquer. “I had a really good, classically trained voice when I was young,” she says. “I could have been an opera singer, but something about it felt formal and stiff, so my 15-year-old brain went, ‘OK, I’ll go and do musicals.’”View image in fullscreen‘Like an extreme sport’ … with Aidan Turner in a publicity shot for Les Liaisons Dangereuses.Photograph: Alexandre BlossardThanks to a council grant she commuted daily to London’sItalia Conti stage school, and, after O-levels, studied dance, singing and drama. “From my first job in a musical when I was 16 until I was 22, I did every job I was offered. I was a presenter. I did two pantomimes, a musical, a telly play, everything, but I never thought about playing characters. I just played me. Meeting Mike Leigh was the lightbulb moment, not just because he told me I was good but because I played someone a million miles from me. And I thought, ‘This is what I want to do.’”That was in 1979, and Manville has now worked with Leigh more than any other actor, their eight films together producing what were, for years, her defining screen roles. Lonely daytime drinker Mary inAnother Year, and the nervy, vulnerable breadwinner Penny inAll or Nothing, in particular, condensed so much of what makes her great: the precision of characterisation, the deep dredging of despair, the dogged resilience. She still values Leigh’s opinion more than almost anyone else’s.She even turned down an offer to joinArlene Phillips’dancing troupe Hot Gossip. When I suggest she could resurrect her dancing on Strictly, she gently corrects me, explaining that she never really let it die. I should have guessed from her enviably upright deportment. “I’ve spent every night of the last three months dancing with professionals in Les Liaisons Dangereuses,” she says. “It felt like an extreme sport and it’s been wonderful!”View image in fullscreen‘Meeting Mike Leigh was the lightbulb moment’ … Manville with David Bradley in Another Year.Photograph: Cinematic Collection/AlamyShe pauses before taking a brief, impassioned detour. “Thank God, just because we’re over 50, we don’t have to have walking sticks – or not be thought of as sexual any more. We are! Oedipus and Les Liaisons were both highly sexualised pieces of theatre and I love that. Anyway, if I’d been asked to do Strictly 15 years ago, I might have said yes. Now, I’m not available much.”She has been busy ever since her breakthrough TV role back in 1975, in ITV’s then new daytime soap Emmerdale Farm. “My first screen kiss was in a cowshed!” she says, hooting with laughter. “My character was younger and adored an older man. It was more affectionate than passionate. I’ve been kissed in more glamorous locations since.”As with so many actors, soap opera gave her an “amazing grounding” in the technique and discipline of screen acting. “But I knew it was time to go. I remember a lot of the cast saying, ‘Oh, you shouldn’t leave. It’s great money. You’ve got security.’ I just thought, ‘I know, I hear you, I’ve learned a lot, it’s been amazing. But I’m off.’”View image in fullscreen‘I learned a lot’ … Manville as Rosemary Kendall, with Frazer Hines as Joe Sugden, in Emmerdale Farm in 1975.Photograph: ITV/REX/ShutterstockAt times, her work rate frankly boggles the mind. For 10 weeks in 2018, for instance, she spent her days filming the costume drama Harlots in Watford and her evenings on the West End stage for Long Day’s Journey into Night. Where did this all come from?“I just want to keep going. You’re either that person or you’re not. I’m very good at looking after myself. Just crack on with it is very much my philosophy and not a lot fazes me. If there was an Olympic event for multitasking, I’d win! When I was a single mum, I went back to work because I had to.” Gary Oldman, her first husband, left her, and the UK, three months after their son Alfie was born in 1989. “When I had too much to do, a play to learn and a baby who needed feeding and bathing and stories, I allocated my time much better.”Alfie is now a father of three and a cameraman who has worked on projects with both his parents. “My friend Alan Rickman was on Harry Potter,” Manville remembers, “and he said, ‘Alfie, I’ll get you through the door [as a runner], but the rest is up to you,’ which was exactly right. Now if I see Alfie at work I’ll think, ‘What are you doing here?’ What a privilege. And he likes me. I like him. So it’s a win-win.”Manville’s work ethic and eye for quality endure: days after we speak, it is announced that she will star with Anna Maxwell Martin in a new production of the American tragicomedyAugust: Osage County, and she is currently filming a new Prime series called Escorted, playing a Manhattan nightclub singer opposite Brett Goldstein as her son. There will be no slowing down for this formidable performer.“I’ve got as much energy as all of those dancers I’ve just finished working with,” she says matter-of-factly. “I really am a bit like Susan Ryeland. I couldn’t give a fuck how old I am!”Marble Hall Murders is on BBC One on 26 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTelevisionLesley ManvilleActingTheatreDramaMike LeighThe CrownfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rebel offensive against Ethiopian army stokes fears of return to civil war | Ethiopia | The Guardian
description: Fighting escalates after Tigrayan rebels form new coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed government
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: Fighting escalates after Tigrayan rebels form new coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed government
Content: Members of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) walk along a main road in Mekelle on 23 September, as tensions intensify in northern Ethiopia.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMembers of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) walk along a main road in Mekelle on 23 September, as tensions intensify in northern Ethiopia.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesEthiopiaRebel offensive against Ethiopian army stokes fears of return to civil warFighting escalates after Tigrayan rebels form new coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed governmentCarlos Mureithiin Nairobi and agenciesThu 24 Sep 2026 11.29 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 09.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are growing fears of a return to civil war inEthiopiaafter an offensive by fighters from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara and the formation of a new rebel alliance aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed.About 600,000 people died between 2020 and 2022 duringa devastating warbetween the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict.On Sunday, seven armed groups from around the country, including the TPLF, announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at deposing the government in Addis Ababa. Then, on Wednesday, the TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police. The state-owned carrier, Ethiopian Airlines, said it had suspended flights to the region “due to the current situation”.The TPLF also launched attacks into Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told Agence France-Presse there were heavy artillery attacks by the group on Thursday as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the Tigrayan border.Flights to the historic Ethiopian town of Lalibela were also suspended on Thursday because of nearby fighting, while people in Tigray stocked up ⁠on food and cash, with one resident telling Reuters that people there feared they could face siege conditions similar to those during the previous war.A resident of Adigrat, a city close to the Eritrean border, ‌described panic-buying and shops emptying. “Food shortages are worsening as market shelves sit empty … Essential medicines remain scarce and astronomically expensive,” he told Reuters. “Daily survival has become a constant calculation.”Graphic – Ethiopia mapThe TPLF’s vice-president, Amanuel Assefa, told AFP: “We are in the situation of full-blown war now.” He confirmed Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara.The group took control of Abala, also on the Tigray-Afar border, on Wednesday, a foreign security source based in Ethiopia told AFP, while a TPLF source said they had seized several other towns in Afar. The foreign security source also said there was fighting around the Amhara town of Weldiya – one of the few routes to the capital.In its first public comments on the fighting, Ethiopia’s army said on ⁠Thursday it had foiled the attacks and killed, wounded or captured more than 500 enemy fighters.Analysts say the TPLF has support from Ethiopia’s​ neighbour and historic adversary Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade its territory to gain access to the Red Sea. The TPLF’s Assefa told AFP “we have no information about Eritrea’s plan”. Asked if they would request Eritrean intervention, he said: “Not yet.”The current fighting reflects shifting dynamics from the civil war, whenEritreaand Fano, an insurgent group that is now part of the new alliance, both fought with the government against the Tigrayans.Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, the Ethiopian president, Taye Atske-Selassie Amde, decried “the forces of destruction and mayhem” and “interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements”. He said Ethiopia had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours.Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, said members of the alliance had been collaborating for a while ​with the financial backing of Eritrea. Eritrea ​has repeatedly denied similar accusations.The TPLF ruled Ethiopiafrom 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, eventually triggering the civil war.The renewed fighting marks the most serious challenge ​yet tothe 2022 Pretoria agreement, which ended the civil war and maintained an uneasy calm until late last year, when clashes resumed.It raises fears of a broader regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across and further destabilise a region already strained by war in neighbouring Sudan and tensions along the Red Sea.On Wednesday, the African Union chair, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf,urged“utmost restraint” from the warring parties and resumption of direct talks. An EU spokespersoncalled for“immediate de-escalation” and a recommitment to the Pretoria agreement.In the 2020-22 war, Tigray was largely cut off from the outside world as communications were severed, and access to food, cash and medicines was severely restricted, pushing hundreds of thousands of people into famine-like conditions.AFP and Reuters contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsEthiopiaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Democratic lawmakers accuse Trump administration of interference in Brazilian elections | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Legislators sent letter to Marco Rubio saying US interference is weakening Brazil’s democratic institutions
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Legislators sent letter to Marco Rubio saying US interference is weakening Brazil’s democratic institutions
Content: Brazil’s president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, attends a rally in São Gonçalo, Brazil, on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Tita Barros/ReutersView image in fullscreenBrazil’s president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, attends a rally in São Gonçalo, Brazil, on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Tita Barros/ReutersBrazilDemocratic lawmakers accuse Trump administration of interference in Brazilian electionsLegislators sent letter to Marco Rubio saying US interference is weakening Brazil’s democratic institutionsUS politics live – latest updatesTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroThu 24 Sep 2026 13.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA group of 31 Democratic members of theUS Congresshas sent a letter to the secretary of state,Marco Rubio, criticising theTrump administrationover “an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine”Brazil’s elections.Latin America’s largest country will hold the first round of its presidential election on 4 October, with polls showing atechnical tiebetween the incumbent leftist president,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and the far-right senatorFlávio Bolsonaro.In the letter sent to Rubio on Thursday, 30 members of the House of Representatives and the senator Bernie Sanders listed aseries of measuresthe US government took that they interpret as attempts to secure a victory for Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former presidentJair Bolsonaro.Brazil’s Lula announces higher welfare payments and free weight-loss jabs ahead of electionRead moreThey wrote that those actions “reflect a broader and deeply troubling pattern of interference by the Trump administration in recent electoral processes across Latin America”, citing the recent midterm elections inArgentinaand presidential elections inHondurasandColombia.In July, a group of 11 Democratic members of Congress sent a similar letter arguing that Trump was trying to interfere in Colombia’s election in favour of the far-right millionaire and former lawyerAbelardo de la Espriella, who went on towin the second round.In Thursday’s letter, the lawmakers wrote that US officials under Trump have engaged in a “sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilization in Brazil”.They noted that when Trump imposed his first tariffs on Brazil last year, he made clear that one reason was Bolsonaro’s trial over hisattempt to stage a coupafter losing the 2022 election to Lula. The former president wasultimately convictedand, unable to run because he is under house arrest, named his son to take his place.They also citednew tariffs that Trump imposedon Brazil in July under section 301 of US trade law, as well asplans by the US governmentto send two officials to Brazil to “cast doubt on the integrity of the country’s voting system, considered by many experts to be among the most reliable in the world”. The Lula administration ultimately denied the US delegation visas.The Brazilian president has repeatedlycomplainedthat Trump is trying to interfere in Brazil’s elections and, in his speech opening the UN general assembly this week, said, without naming anyone: “We will not allow the enemies of democracy, internal or external, to act against the will of the people.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the letter sent to Rubio on Friday, the Democratic lawmakers wrote that “rather than helping defend Brazilian democracy”, the US is “acting as an agent of interference and destabilization – using diplomatic, economic and political pressure in ways that risk weakening the country’s democratic institutions, undermining confidence in Brazil’s electoral process, and inflicting further damage on our relationship with a strategic US ally and trading partner”.They asked Rubio if Trump’s administration would commit to respecting Brazil’s electoral process and requested a response by 1 October.The state department has not yet responded to a request for comment.Explore more on these topicsBrazilTrump administrationMarco RubioLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaJair BolsonaroDonald TrumpTrump tariffsnewsShareReuse this content

title: At Trump meeting, Xi Jinping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflict | US news | The Guardian
description: Chinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and trade
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: Chinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and trade
Content: Xi Jinping, Peng Liyuan and Donald Trump at the White House in Washington DC on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAView image in fullscreenXi Jinping, Peng Liyuan and Donald Trump at the White House in Washington DC on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAUS newsAt Trump meeting, Xi Jinping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflictChinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and tradeRobert Taitin WashingtonThu 24 Sep 2026 19.58 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleXi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan.At the start of his summit meeting withDonald Trumpin the White House, the Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could steer the two competing superpowers away from future military conflict and on to a road of mutual gain.Rather than confrontation, conditions for “achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again go hand in hand” and should be the goal, Xi said, citing Trump’s political catchphrase.“We should strengthen communication.Chinaand the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” said Xi, with Trump looking on.“We should coexist in peace. China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.”With such conditions in place, Xi said, “the Thucydides trap can be overcome”, refering to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power.Xi invoked the phrase in his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it.His proposals for lessening tensions – which also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges – come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other.Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit occurred in 2015, when Barack Obama was president.“President Xi and Madame Peng arrive at an important moment for America, the 250th anniversary of our founding,” he said.Trump said he had forged “a truly great friendship” with Xi. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” he said. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balances trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.”He said the current visit would include discussion overs security, technology and AI – which he called “super intelligence”, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday.Xi also extolled his personal relationship with his American counterpart, saying: “President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.”Addressing Trump directly, he said: “During your visit to China this year, we agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability. I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course towards the future.”The White House welcome ceremony came after Trump had taken the unusual step of going to Andrews air force base in Maryland the evening before to greet the Chinese leader and his wife on the tarmac.Much of the same pageantry was repeated in Thursday’s ceremony, with both countries’ national anthems being played. Trump was flanked by his wife, Melania, while members of his cabinet and senior aides – including Natalie Harp, Trump’s dedicated assistant nicknamed “the human printer” by fellow staffers – looked on.Trump and Xi held bilateral talks after the ceremony and the welcoming speeches.Later on Thursday, Trump hosted Xi at the White House for a state dinner. Notable invited guests from the tech world included Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Apple chair Tim Cook, SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.Trump gestured to the titans of the industry in his remarks to the dinner, recounting when Chinese diplomats first arrived in the US 158 years ago, meeting American intellectuals like Henry David Thoreau and prominent political figures.“Tonight, we revive the spirit of that first encounter here on American soil as we are joined by some of the top leaders in business, culture and government from our own time,” he said. “On one side, China draws on thousands of years of history and tradition from Sun Tzu to Sun Yat-sen. For Americans, we inherit a legacy of faith from Jerusalem to Rome, democracy of ancient Athens, the triumphs of Sparta and the freedom proclaimed in Philadelphia 250 years ago.”Trump also touted his relationship with the Chinese leader.“President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better,” he said.Xi also addressed the dinner, saying talks with Trump during the visit had yielded “common understanding on many issues”, and suggesting the US and China find a new approach to working together.“China ⁠and the United States must act as responsible major countries,” he said.Despite the harmonious tone adopted by both leaders, analysts have voiced scepticism about the possibility of longstanding stable arrangements being arrived at over a host of issues.In the race for AI, the US has placed strict export controls on microchips, semiconductors, software and chip-making equipment in a bid to slow China’s development.A truce agreed between Trump and Xi in South Korea last year aimed at keeping tariffs lower had been due to expire in November but has now been extended until February, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent said.Analysts believe the extension suggests Trump continues to be dissatisfied with Xi’s concession offers on trade and wants to keep the pressure on in the hope of getting a better deal if the two meet again at the G20 summit scheduled to be held in Miami in December.Despite the trade war between the two countries, Chinese imports have continue to surge into the US. China is on course to run a $1tn trade deficit for the second year running.Uwa Ede-Osifo contributed reportingThe headline and text of this article were amended on 24 September 2026 to correct a misspelling of Xi Jinping.Explore more on these topicsUS newsXi JinpingDonald TrumpChinaUS politicsUS foreign policyTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump swoons over strongman soulmate Xi – are you feeling jealous, Vladimir? | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Deference was deafening as US president rolled out red carpet for world’s biggest jailer of journalists – perhaps he was seeking tips
Author: David Smith
Headline: Deference was deafening as US president rolled out red carpet for world’s biggest jailer of journalists – perhaps he was seeking tips
Content: Trump with President Xi Jinping at the White House on Thursday.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAView image in fullscreenTrump with President Xi Jinping at the White House on Thursday.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAThe US politics sketchDonald TrumpTrump swoons over strongman soulmate Xi – are you feeling jealous, Vladimir?Deference was deafening as US president rolled out red carpet for world’s biggest jailer of journalists – perhaps he was seeking tipsDavid Smithin WashingtonThu 24 Sep 2026 14.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 18.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne is an authoritarian who represses the media with a strong allergy to democratic elections. The other is head of the Chinese Communist party.Donald Trump welcomed the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, to the White House on Thursday, setting the stage for a scene quite unlike anything the august old building has seen over more than two centuries.“Remarkably,” observed the US president, “this is our first time meeting together here at the White House, and as President Xi has already seen, a lot has changed since he was last here.”At Trump meeting, Xi Jinping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflictRead moreWhile Xi remained poker-faced, only a brief look around a grand foyer bedecked with American and Chinese flags would have verified Trump’s statement. On one wall, where an official portrait of Barack Obama once hung, was the dramatic image of a bloodied Trump with fist raised urging his supporters to “fight!” after a failed assassination attempt.And while Chinese state media had been welcomed onto the White House grounds, many US journalists had not, thanks to Trump’s ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico. Michael McFaul, a former US diplomat,described the vivid contrastas “wrong and embarrassing”.That was hard to deny, given thatChinaranks 178th in Reporters Without Borders’ press freedom index, ahead of only North Korea and Eritrea (the US, for the record, is down to 64th). But it also made perfect sense because, whereas past presidents sought to make China more like the US, Trump evidently aspires to make the US more like China.View image in fullscreenTrump and Xi walk along the Colonnade at the White House.Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/Abaca/ShutterstockThe deference was deafening. On Wednesday night he and his wife, Melania, travelled to Joint Base Andrews in Maryland to greet Xi off his plane – a schlep that US presidents rarely make for foreign leaders – and rolled out a literal red carpet for his strongman soulmate.Chuck Schumer, the Democratic minority leader,observed on X: “If you’re a foreign authoritarian, Trump won’t just invite you to visit America, he’ll roll out the red carpet for you…”Vladimir, are you feeling jealous yet?“I met President Xi at the plane (Airport!) yesterday and he looks strong, vibrant, and fit — Better than ever,” a gooey-eyed Trump gushed on his Truth Social patform. “Madam Xi, of course, BEAUTIFUL!”Protocol error! Protocol error! When the president wrote “Madam Xi”, referring to Xi’s wife Peng Liyuan, he should have said “Madame Peng”, which is how she is recognised.Xi is such a star that he got two welcomes. On Thursday morning, there were more flags, more trumpet blasts, and another red carpet as the Trumps emerged from the White House south portico to greet Xi and Peng.Then it was on to the grand foyer for statements – with no reporter questions allowed, of course – before the two delegations, including Vice-President JD Vance and wife Usha, sitting in neat rows. Trump went first. You can tell when he’s on his best behaviour because he (mostly) sticks to the teleprompter. The interpreter must have been relieved that he did not have to match Trump, weave for weave.View image in fullscreenThe presidents meet with their delegations at the Oval Office.Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/APTrump touted his “truly ⁠great friendship” with Xi and claimed the two countries ⁠had made strides on trade since his trip ​to China in May. “During this visit, we will also discuss pressing issues concerning security, technology, and ‘super intelligence,’” he said, using his alternative name for artificial intelligence. If Xi felt like rolling his eyes at that, he managed to resist.The president, ever nostalgic for the 20th century, suggested that the second world war offers a lesson on how the competitors can work together. “Brave American pilots volunteered to come to China and fight for the very survival of the legendary country,” he said, referring to the Flying Tigers air corps that helped defend China against Japanese invasion. “They were just unbelievable.”He added that it was US marines’ interactions with Chinese citizens that inspired them “to adopt a Chinese phrase that they still use today: gung ho”.Rarely does Trump appear at an event and not end up behind the microphone for longer than any other speaker on the bill.But it was Xi, speaking more substantially, who looked like he owned the place. Trump, sitting behind with hands clasped together, had the appearance of junior partner. Xi said he was ready to work with the president to “steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course toward the future”.Damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead!Xi had a charm offensive of his own. “President Trump and I have respect for each other,” he said. “We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.”He announced Thursday that 100,000 young American students would be invited to study in China over the next five years. Better still, he revealed China will sent two giant pandas – Ping Ping and Fuchuan – to a zoo in Atlanta.Then he got to the meat in the sandwich, insisting that the countries can “co-exist in peace” and their competition “should be a healthy one”. “The Thucydides trap can be overcome,” Xi declared, in a tacit acknowledgement that China is threatening to displace the US as the world’s superpower.View image in fullscreenTrump speaks to reporters after walking with Xi to show him Marine One at the White House.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesBut with more flattery, he added: “Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand.”Next up was a military ceremony including a flyover at the Rose Garden, with Chinese flags waving from the Oval Office roof alongside US flags. A marching band dressed in the garb of the Revolutionary War era – tricorn hats, white wigs, red tunics – paraded in the paved over Rose Garden (another change since Xi’s last visit).None of this was covered by the usual cable news networks because they were boycotting shared coverage, in solidarity with the banned outlets. If a tree falls in a forest and no one is around to hear it, does it make a sound? If a democracy falls and no one is around to film it, does it make a yelp?Trump then sat down with the world’s biggest jailer of journalists for bilateral talks. Perhaps he was seeking tips.When they met face to face, was this a Reagan-Gorbachev style summit of great historical import, discussing guardrails on AI and other ways not to destroy the world? Maybe not.Showing off the Marine One helicopter and his new helipad on the south lawn,Trump reported: “We had a great meeting - and he has a great interest in granite. He likes granite. He’s an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite.”Not even Xi had been spared the dreaded tour of Trump’s architectural follies.By the afternoon, some of the banned reporters had been allowed back on to the White House campus after a judge found Trump’s action to be unconstitutional. It must have been a tricky one to explain to Xi. He remains the master of repression; Trump is merely The Apprentice.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpThe US politics sketchUS politicsXi JinpingChinaAsia PacificUS foreign policyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rick Wakeman performs piano concert to 150 rescued moon bears in Vietnam | Animal welfare | The Guardian
description: Former Yes musician plays at sanctuary to raise awareness of animals that remain stuck in cages at ‘bile farms’
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Former Yes musician plays at sanctuary to raise awareness of animals that remain stuck in cages at ‘bile farms’
Content: Rick Wakeman at the piano at the bear sanctuary in Vietnam.Photograph: hson/Animals AsiaView image in fullscreenRick Wakeman at the piano at the bear sanctuary in Vietnam.Photograph: hson/Animals AsiaAnimal welfareRick Wakeman performs piano concert to 150 rescued moon bears in VietnamFormer Yes musician plays at sanctuary to raise awareness of animals that remain stuck in cages at ‘bile farms’Helena HortonThu 24 Sep 2026 11.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRick Wakeman has played to all kinds of people around the globe, but he has now performed to an audience he had never encountered before – an enclosure of 150 bears.The former Yes musician, who has gone on to have a prolific solo career, played the piano at a Vietnamese bear sanctuary.“Before you ask, I won’t be playing the teddy bear’s picnic,” he joked ahead of the performance. Wakeman, who is a supporter of animal welfare causes and has rescue dogs and cats of his own, is conducting the concert to raise awareness of moon bears kept in cruel conditions for the extraction of their bile.He said he was a bit worried about how hot it is going to be. “You know the heatwave we had in England? It’s double that,” he said. “They offered to rig up a fan for me, but I figured that will just blow more hot air around.”View image in fullscreenA moon bear at the bear sanctuary in Tam Dao national park, Vietnam.Photograph: Luong Thai Linh/EPAHis concert was performed live on a Yamaha grand piano positioned inAnimalsAsia’s bear sanctuary in the Tam Dao national park, and Wakeman had written some new compositions especially for rescued bears.Asked whether the bears would enjoy the music, he said: “They’ve not got much choice, really. It’s a well-known fact that all animals react to music, especially gentle melodic music. So what I am going to do is piano music that is melodic, and I can only hope that they will come up to the perimeter of the sanctuary and have a listen.”Rick Wakeman plays piano at bear sanctuaryWakeman has been sponsoring rescue bears since 2016 and recently adopted a new one: “He’s only 20 months old, a big fella, I went to see him today. He came out right to the edge and stood on his back legs and just stared at me, it was brilliant.”Bile is extracted from bears for traditional Chinese medicine by putting a needle into their gall bladder and drawing it out. The bears are kept in poor conditions in countries including China and in Vietnam, where it has just been banned, but where some bears are still in captivity in cramped enclosures. It is the fourth-biggest market in the illegal wildlife trade in east Asia, resulting in a dramatic decline in the Asiatic black bear populations in Vietnam, with nearly a third of their numbers lost around the world in just 30 years.1:04Rick Wakeman plays piano at bear sanctuary – videoOf the sanctuary, which he has been visiting this week, Wakeman said: “To see the bears be rehabilitated, having a life they never had before, some have never put their feet on grass before. They are so wonderful, that we can do such horrendous things to animals is beyond belief. Before this, they were chained in cages sometimes for 10 or 20 years in conditions where they couldn’t even turn around.”He is playing to raise awareness for the bears still stuck in cages in Vietnam and tourge the governmentto get them released: “We have 150 bears at the sanctuary, but there are 125 bears left in cages in the old bear bile farms, and there are four dying a month. We have to get them out quick and into the sanctuary.”He treats his rescue dogs and cats to music back at home in Suffolk. “I had one cat who used to jump on the grand piano, and if I stopped playing he would put his paw in the strings and rattle them until I played again. I know if my dogs don’t like it, they will get up and walk out, and my cats don’t like metal, grunge or rap. They want a melody.”View image in fullscreenBears playing at the sanctuary.Photograph: Luong Thai Linh/EPAWakeman spends hours watching the bears. “If you see these bears it is hard to put into words, they are almost human the way they look at you,” he said. “If you see them, you can’t help but be moved. They aren’t tame but they are very safe, very happy, they play, they romp. I witnessed two today jumping in a bubble bath and playing. They’ve got a life back.”Dr Jill Robinson, the founder and CEO of Animals Asia, said: “We are beyond blessed to have Rick’s support for Animals Asia and the bears. His love for them is immeasurable and can be heard in the beautifully haunting music he has written for them. We’re all so excited to hear his performance in the open air at our sanctuary in the stunning setting of Tam Dao national park. I can’t wait to see how the bears respond.”Wakeman added: “I hope they lay down and have a listen, that would make my day. I would have a big grin on my face.”Explore more on these topicsAnimal welfareAnimalsWildlifeVietnamRick WakemanEndangered habitatsConservationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alarm bells sound in Brussels as EU sales of Chinese hybrid cars rocket | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Explosive growth in imported vehicles omitted from EV tariffs fuels concern for future of European carmakers
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Explosive growth in imported vehicles omitted from EV tariffs fuels concern for future of European carmakers
Content: Chinese-made BYD passenger battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles await distribution at the docks.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAView image in fullscreenChinese-made BYD passenger battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles await distribution at the docks.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAAutomotive industryAlarm bells sound in Brussels as EU sales of Chinese hybrid cars rocketExplosive growth in imported vehicles omitted from EV tariffs fuels concern for future of European carmakersEU imports three times more from China than bloc exports thereLisa O’CarrollThu 24 Sep 2026 04.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 12.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSales of Chinese hybrid cars have rocketed in the EU in the past four and a half years, data shows, underlining growing concerns in Brussels over the future of the European car industry.In 2022, just 659 Chinese-made fully hybrid cars (vehicles in which the petrol or diesel engine charge the motor and battery) were sold in the EU. However, after Brussels imposedanti-subsidy tariffs on fully electric cars from Chinain 2024, sales of hybrids have shot up to 160,662 in the first seven months of this year.Eurostat figures show that sales of Chinese-made plug-in hybrid vehicles – models popular for longer driving distances that can recharge via both the fuel engine and an external power source – have also soared, rising from 56,706 sold in 2022 to 217,764 from January to July this year.The volume of Chinese hybrids on the roads is now spooking the car industry and Brussels, which has askedChinato voluntarily reduce its hybrid exports to the EU or face safeguards, likely to be quotas.On Thursday the German car industry for the first time indicated it would be willing to consider tariffs on Chinese hybrids specifically.High-mileage electric cars are more reliable than petrol ones, study findsRead moreThe German Association of the Automotive Industry, VDA, called on the European Commission to carry out a comprehensive assessment of the impact of any trade safeguards, which can range from quotas to price floors and tariffs.It said: “The EU must also have an effective and up-to-date set of trade defence instruments at its disposal. Where unfair conduct is proven, the use of WTO-compliant trade defence instruments must be considered; these are legitimate and tried-and-tested means of achieving a level playing field and safeguarding fair conditions of competition.”According to new figures released by the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), hybrid cars now account for almost 37% of the overall market, with electric cars making up just over 21% of the market.The ACEA figures show three Chinese manufacturers – BYD, Chery and Leapmotor – making significant inroads with triple-digit growth in the EU.A fourth firm, Geely, has had a steady 8% increase in the first eight months of the year and remains the most popular Chinese brand in the EU, with 205,000 cars sold in the first eight months of the year. Its brands include Sweden’s Volvo and Polestar, the EU’s only all-electric car manufacturer.BYD is catching up with Geely, with sales rocketing by 163% year on year with 177,000 units sold.Both firms, along with a fifth Chinese manufacturer, SAIC, are now firmly ahead of Elon Musk’s Tesla, which sold 142,000 cars across the bloc in the first seven months of the year.European car manufacturers still dominate, with the Volkswagen group selling 2m cars in the first eight months of the year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSales of electric cars are also growing fast in parts of Europe including Germany, up 75% to 69,000 units in August, and in France, where sales are up by 112%. In Slovenia, sales have increased by 266%. This compares with the UK, up 27% in August to 28,000 EVs sold, and Ireland, up just 7% to 2,200 units.Earlier this month, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, described the now€1.18bn-a-day trade deficitbetween the bloc and China as having reached an unsustainable “tipping point”.The EU’s trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao will meet on 8 and 9 October to try to build a truce.Also hoping for a trade truce are Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, who meet in theirthird summit in 12 monthsin Washington on Thursday.Trump agreed in South Korea last October to drop tariffs on certain Chinese imports in exchange for a suspension of China’s export restriction on rare earths, critical to the car industry across the US, EU and the UK.Some believe a deal may not have been reached yet and the suspension may not be announced until the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference next month.Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryEuropeEuropean UnionChinese economyChinaAsia PacificInternational tradenewsShareReuse this content

title: Boy, 11, shot in the face and neck in Sydney dies from his injuries | Sydney | The Guardian
description: The 11-year-old died at Westmead children’s hospital three days after incident at a unit in Norwest
Author: Martin Farrer
Headline: The 11-year-old died at Westmead children’s hospital three days after incident at a unit in Norwest
Content: A police car outside the building in Norwest, Sydney, where the 11-year-old boy suffered his fatal injuries.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPView image in fullscreenA police car outside the building in Norwest, Sydney, where the 11-year-old boy suffered his fatal injuries.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPSydneyBoy, 11, shot in the face and neck in Sydney dies from his injuriesThe 11-year-old died at Westmead children’s hospital three days after incident at a unit in NorwestFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastMartin FarrerThu 24 Sep 2026 19.11 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 08.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA boy who was allegedly shot at a home in Sydney’s north-west earlier this week has died.Police said that the boy, who had been in a critical condition since being found with a gunshot wound at a unit in Norwest on Monday, died in hospital at about 8pm on Thursday.Friends and family paid tribute to the boy, who was a member of Sydney’s Maronite community. “Rip my baby,” his father wrote on social media. “Rest in peace little cuz … Heart broken,” another family member posted.Police had been called to the unit in Fairway Drive at about 5pm on Mondayafter reports of a shooting.Officers found the 11-year-old boy had sustained a gunshot wound to his face and neck.He was treated at the scene by NSW Ambulance paramedics before being taken to at Westmead Children’s hospital in a critical condition.Five other people who were in the home at the time of the incident were not injured.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThree men, all aged 18, were arrested. Two were taken to the Hills police station and later released pending further inquiries.One of the men, Isaac Bechara, was charged with concealing a serious indictable offence, while two of the other men were arrested and released pending further inquiries.He appeared at Blacktown local court on Tuesday morning, where he made no application for bail, which was refused.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDet Supt Naomi Moore told reporters on Tuesday afternoon that police were “aware” of the unit where the shooting had occurred and had “engaged with the occupants previously”.“This shooting at this stage does not appear to be linked directly to current conflicts however a number of individuals who were inside the unit at the time are well known to NSW police,” she said. “Their association with organised crime is being considered by investigators.”Police said the investigation was continuing.Explore more on these topicsSydneynewsShareReuse this content

title: Australia’s newest chicken factory looks like a modern art gallery – but will it improve animal welfare? | Animal welfare | The Guardian
description: Three million chickens a week will be processed at the state-of-the-art facility in Tamworth – a fifth of all those eaten nationwide
Author: Nick Visser
Headline: Three million chickens a week will be processed at the state-of-the-art facility in Tamworth – a fifth of all those eaten nationwide
Content: Jeff Budd, the deputy mayor of Tamworth regional council, says the facility’s unusual design creates a gem for the city and will attract the skilled workers it needs.Photograph: BaiadaView image in fullscreenJeff Budd, the deputy mayor of Tamworth regional council, says the facility’s unusual design creates a gem for the city and will attract the skilled workers it needs.Photograph: BaiadaAnimal welfareAustralia’s newest chicken factory looks like a modern art gallery – but will it improve animal welfare?Three million chickens a week will be processed at the state-of-the-art facility in Tamworth – a fifth of all those eaten nationwideFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastNick VisserThu 24 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 19.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs it for birds? Is it for planes?The sleek, rust-coloured saucer settles into the earth, mirroring the surrounding hills. It looks like an art gallery or a high-end conference centre – an architectural masterpiece designed to sit lightly on the land.Until you see the shed behind it.The sweeping lines are the gateway to a $600m poultry processing plant that will, at full capacity, process 3 million chickens a week.Located in Tamworth, 300km north of Sydney, the new facility is owned by Baiada, one of Australia’s two largest chicken producers and the owner of household brand names Steggles and Lilydale Free Range.View image in fullscreenWorkers at the new plant can spend their lunch breaks at an on-site cafeteria, at a gym or in landscaped gardens.Photograph: BaiadaAt its height, two lines will process 15,000 birds an hour as chickens fly through state-of-the-art chilling systems and automated packing machines en route to supermarkets across the state. The new plant will support more than 1,000 jobs, with workers able to spend their lunch breaks at an on-site cafeteria, at a gym or in landscaped gardens.Jeff Budd, the deputy mayor of Tamworth regional council, has toured the facility, which opened last week. He says the unusual design creates a gem for the city and will attract the skilled workers and technicians needed to run kilometres’ worth of conveyor belts and systems.“I think it’s massive for the entire region,” he said. “The Baiada company … certainly made it look that way. Once you’re inside that main building at the front, it’s like a five-star hotel.”Australians are voracious chicken eaters, consuming an average of 55kg of chicken meat per person per year. Almost half of all meat eaten in Australia is chicken, and consumption has doubled in the past 30 years. More than 800 million chickens will be slaughtered this financial year to meet the demand.Once fully operational, the Oakburn facility will account for almost 20% of that.“We’re happy to see a commitment from a Sydney-based company to one of their regional hubs, to put in such a sophisticated [facility],” says Prof Stephen Walkden-Brown, the interim director of Poultry Hub Australia at the University of New England. “It’s a pretty big development, one of the most modern plants in the world.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailIn a media release, Baiada said the company had “grown alongside” the Tamworth community for six decades, and the facility reflected the company’s commitment to the city.“This is a long-term investment in Tamworth and the people who have supported Baiada for generations,” the managing director, Simon Camilleri, says. “Our history in this region stretches back to the 1960s, when Charlie Baiada first established operations here, and this facility reflects our confidence in the future of Tamworth.”But it did not answer questions about whether the new facility would also deliver improvedanimal welfareoutcomes.Jed Goodfellow, the director of policy and government relations at the Australian Alliance forAnimals, said while the Baiada building may be state of the art, he believes “the welfare model behind it is anything but”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA chart showing more than 800 million chickens are set to be slaughtered in Australia over the span of this year.Slowing the growthA leading welfare issue, Goodfellow says, is the speed at which meat chickens grow.“Chickens are still being selectively bred to grow at extraordinary speeds, with their bodies paying the price for ever greater efficiency,” he said. “Healthier, slower-growing breeds are now being used in many parts of the world, particularly Europe, with Norway, the Netherlands and France producing higher welfare breeds at scale.”“It may cost slightly more but, as their experience shows, the increase is not prohibitive, as European consumers increasingly opt for the healthier option.”Melina Tensen, the senior scientific officer for farm animals at the RSPCA, said about 97% ofchicken meat sold in Australiaabides by the organisation’s welfare standards.“It’s a pretty big deal to have most of industry achieving standards to go well above the legal minimum,” Tensen says. “Wherever animals are farmed for food – and they’re going to be farmed for food for a long time to come – we want to be in there making sure that animals are raised and handled and transported and slaughtered in ways we
