find acceptable.”Free-range, organic and ‘hormone-free’: what do Australian supermarket chicken labels mean?Read moreWelfare standards were updated this month to promote lower stocking density, variable light intensity in sheds – to allow chickens to choose between brighter and darker areas – and the phasing out of a slaughtering method called electrical water bath stunning. Those changes must be enacted by 1 January 2031 for businesses to keep their RSPCA certification.At the same time, the RSPCA has released a new category of “enhanced” welfare standards, which are primarily focused on encouraging producers to rear slower-growing breeds. Most of Australia’s commercial chickens are two fast-growing breeds, the Ross 308 and the Cobb 500, which reach slaughter weight at between four and six weeks of age.Tensen said the RSPCA would ultimately like to see chicken meat producers replace fast-growing breeds with slower-growing breeds but consumers would have to help achieve that transition.“The longer it takes to grow, the greater cost,” she said. “We definitely encourage consumers to be vocal about supporting this transition … because every dollar you spend is a message to the retailer.”Explore more on these topicsAnimal welfareAnimalsChickenMeat industryBusinessnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI hack of Medicare exposes Australia’s vulnerabilities and experts warn ‘there is more of this to come’ | Medicare Australia | The Guardian
description: Council on AI Strategy chief says incident unlikely to be isolated and country should enhance capability to detect and report incidents
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: Council on AI Strategy chief says incident unlikely to be isolated and country should enhance capability to detect and report incidents
Content: Anthony Albanese, left, challenged the OpenAI boss, Sam Altman, after the company’s agent infiltrated systems run by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Victoria’s Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAnthony Albanese, left, challenged the OpenAI boss, Sam Altman, after the company’s agent infiltrated systems run by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Victoria’s Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia.Photograph: Getty ImagesMedicare AustraliaAI hack of Medicare exposes Australia’s vulnerabilities and experts warn ‘there is more of this to come’Council on AI Strategy chief says incident unlikely to be isolated and country should enhance capability to detect and report incidentsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTom McIlroyandKrishani DhanjiThu 24 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 18.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTechnology experts have warned revelations anartificial intelligence agent hacked Medicare’s internal systemswill not be the only dangerous breach of government data and have called for Australia to boost its protections against the growing risk.The prime minister,Anthony Albanese, challenged the OpenAI boss, Sam Altman, on Thursday after the company’s agent infiltrated systems run by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Victoria’s Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia.An OpenAI agent infiltrated Medicare – and Australia only found out months later. Here’s what we know so farRead moreOpenAI alerted the government earlier this month to theJune hackingvia an email to a public-facing address, a situation Albanese called “obviously unacceptable”.But the Australian Council on AI Strategy chief executive, Anna-Maria Arabia, said the case was unlikely to be an isolated incident.“All of the evidence shows that our operating systems are vulnerable,” she told Guardian Australia.“Frontier AI now has capability to expose those vulnerabilities at a rate quicker than we can keep up, quicker than we can patch them.“When the companies are undertaking tests in what they think are secure environments, and when there are breaches of those environments and these incidences do happen, whether it’s accidental or not, what we’re seeing is the frontier AI capability exposing these vulnerabilities.“All evidence suggests that there is more of this to come.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailArabia said Australia needed to quickly enhance capability to detect and report incidents, and the country should host AI training labs here.Johanna Weaver, Australia’s former chief cyber negotiator at the United Nations, agreed more incidents were inevitable.Weaver is a member of the advisory board to the minister for government services, Katy Gallagher, and the executive director of the Tech Policy Design Institute.“Cybersecurity experts have been warning that frontier models and AI agents could expose vulnerabilities in critical systems. What we are seeing now is the tip of the iceberg,” she said.“Governments need to draw a clear line: if companies cannot control their AI systems, they should not release them publicly.”The US Studies Centre expert Olivia Shen warned AI companies should not be allowed to decide on their own disclosure obligations for hacks and breaches.“We just don’t know how big the problem is. It could be the tip of the iceberg but, either way, we can’t be ignoring the risk,” Shen said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s all happening at a time when Australia is designing our national standards on AI. It hasn’t been entirely clear if those national standards were going to be very hyper-focused on datacentres and leave governance questions as a bit of a bolt-on.“This strengthens the argument that you need to have some pretty clear standards, even just based on mandatory incident reporting, built in.”Intelligence agency the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) is reviewing how prepared the government is to block and respond to hacking by AI. Officials will look at policies around how AI companies should report cyber-incidents to the government, and how cooperative companies should be during and after an attack.It will also investigate whether the current laws and systems are adequate to stop AI and how government systems can be strengthened.12:23Rogue AI hacks government system for first time - The LatestThe shadow industry minister, Andrew Hastie, called for Australia to develop its own domestic AI capability, instead of relying on the US.“If there’s rogue AI agents out there, we need to have our own defensive AI agents protecting Australian government data, our private sector and other things that are important to us,” he said.The Greens demanded Labor call in the new US ambassador, David Brat, to establish what the president, Donald Trump, knew about the attack.“This breach by a foreign AI company on an Australian government database is deeply alarming and brings home the risks that these out-of-control tech corporations pose,” the Greens’ acting leader, Mehreen Faruqi, said.“The fact that the government did not even know it happened is disturbing.”Explore more on these topicsMedicare AustraliaAnthony AlbaneseAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIHackingAustralian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Boy, 16, held in ‘cramped’ prison cell alone for 22 hours a day for weeks, Victorian ombudsman finds | Victoria | The Guardian
description: Ombudsman finds government breached teen’s human rights, saying the conditions ‘bordered on solitary confinement’
Author: Benita Kolovos
Headline: Ombudsman finds government breached teen’s human rights, saying the conditions ‘bordered on solitary confinement’
Content: A cell at Melbourne Assessment Prison, where the boy was held.Photograph: Victorian ombudsmanView image in fullscreenA cell at Melbourne Assessment Prison, where the boy was held.Photograph: Victorian ombudsmanVictoriaBoy, 16, held in ‘cramped’ prison cell alone for 22 hours a day for weeks, Victorian ombudsman findsOmbudsman finds government breached teen’s human rights, saying the conditions ‘bordered on solitary confinement’Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastBenita KolovosandBertin HuynhThu 24 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 18.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 16-year-old boy was held in conditions akin to solitary confinement in adult prison for 22 hours a day, leading him to have suicidal thoughts, a Victorian ombudsman report has revealed.The report,tabled in parliament on Thursday, found the Department of Justice and Community Safety breached the teenager’s human rights when transferring him from the Parkville Youth Justice Precinct to the maximum-security Melbourne Assessment Prison in early 2025.The teenager was transferred after he attacked staff, following two formal warnings he would be moved to an adult prison if his “violent behaviour” continued.Shackling prisoners giving birth should be a last resort – but it’s happening around Australia anywayRead moreWhen he arrived at the adult prison he was separated from others due to his age, with records showing he spent an average of more than 22 hours in his cell each day for six weeks.The ombudsman, Marlo Baragwanath, said the conditions “bordered on solitary confinement”.The report described the cell as “cramped and worn”, with the boy telling the ombudsman he couldn’t see out of the window.“I was shocked … if you’re in some type of environment like that, I guess you have no hope,” he said. “After a while, it starts playing with your mind.”Even during his outside hours, he was confined to what the ombudsman described as “effectively a room that is open to the sky” and handcuffed due to his history of violence.View image in fullscreenThe designated outdoor area at the prison unit.Photograph: Victorian ombudsmanHe ate his meals in his cell and drank straight from the tap, because a guard would not provide a cup.“I was like … ‘I’m not a dog,’ you know. [The guard] was like, ‘Huh, you are, mate,’” the teenager said.He also had no in-person visits from family for the six weeks, telling the ombudsman he was told he would not be able to touch them: “If I see them, I want to touch them ‘cause, you know, that’s my family.”The experience led him to suffer “dark, dark thoughts”.“My cell was always dark. I can’t see anything,” he said. “It was playing with my mind. Started thinking stuff I’ve never thought before … a lot of self-harm … Suicidal stuff.”Under Victorian law, a child aged 15 or older can be transferred to an adult prison as a last resort. However, the ombudsman found proper consideration was not given to the child’s human rights in making the transfer application.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I know many people will find it difficult to sympathise with a child who has been repeatedly violent towards youth justice staff. But human rights apply to everyone, including people accused or convicted of a crime,” Baragwanath said.Tracy Beaton, Victoria’s principal commissioner at the Commission for Children and Young People, said “children’s human rights should never be an afterthought” and welcomed the ombudsman’s eight recommendations, including to ban the transfer of children into adult prisons, though it was rejected by the government.Mindy Sotiri, the executive director of the Justice Reform Initiative, said the report was “indicative of a system that is failing”.“Quite aside from the harm that is caused to children in these circumstances, this approach does absolutely nothing to rehabilitate that child or reduce the risk of them reoffending,” Sotiri said.Victoria’s proposed ‘adult time’ plan to impose life sentences on children condemned by advocatesRead moreThe Victorian senator Lidia Thorpe said: “Children need love and care and support. When we know that it costs over a million dollars to lock up a child, that money could be better in the wraparound services that actually make a child well.”The Victorian Greens’ justice spokesperson, Katherine Copsey, described the report as an “indictment” of the Labor government, who last year introduced“adult time for violent crime” lawsin response to rising youth offending.The Victorian Liberal spokesperson for youth justice, Renee Heath, said Labor was “failing at both ends of the youth justice system” – pointing toan audit released on Wednesdaythat found there was no evidence the government’s $40m crime prevention program was working.According to the ombudsman, the teenager was transferred back to an adult prison after he turned 18 and was no longer separated for safety.Explore more on these topicsVictoriaPrisonsYouth justicenewsShareReuse this content

title: UK food and drink trade deficit largest since 2000 at £21bn | Food & drink industry | The Guardian
description: Industry leaders call on government to protect homegrown produce in the interest of national security
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Industry leaders call on government to protect homegrown produce in the interest of national security
Content: Brexit, war in the Middle East and US tariffs have all dented deliveries overseas while imports of food and drink have soared.Photograph: Martin Lee/AlamyView image in fullscreenBrexit, war in the Middle East and US tariffs have all dented deliveries overseas while imports of food and drink have soared.Photograph: Martin Lee/AlamyFood & drink industryUK food and drink trade deficit largest since 2000 at £21bnIndustry leaders call on government to protect homegrown produce in the interest of national securitySarah ButlerThu 24 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe gap between Britain’s food and drink exports and imports has neared its highest this century, as a combination ofBrexit, war in the Middle East and US tariffs dented deliveries overseas while imports soared.The UK’s food and drink trade deficit has risen to more than £21bn – the largest since 2000 – in what industry leaders said was a “wake-up call” for the government to protect homegrown produce in the interest of national security.UK food and drink export volumes fell by more than a tenth (11.7%) in the first half of 2026 to 4bn kg, only marginally above levels at the height of the Covid pandemic and in the aftermath of the 2001 foot-and-mouth disease outbreak, according to analysis by the Food & Drink Federation (FDF).Exports to the EU continued to fall – down 0.9% in value – amid the additional costs and complexity of trading since Brexit.The FDF recorded an even larger fall in exports beyond the EU – down 6.9% in value terms. That was partly driven by disruption in sales to the Middle East, with exports to the UAE down by almost a quarter as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran. The US’s introduction of a 10% import tariff hit cross-Atlantic sales by 16.5%.Food and drink imports were 19.1bn kg in the first half of this year, the second highest ever, only beaten by the same period last year. Imports from outside the EU are up more than a fifth since 2023 as restrictions have been eased through trade deals, particularly with Australia which now sends 25% more in value terms to the UK than a year ago including meat, oils, vegetables and even whisky.Thesuspension of tariffson a range of manufactured foods, including chocolate and biscuits, this year as part of the former chancellor Rachel Reeves’s package to ease the cost of living has also raised import levels. In addition, EU food producers increased deliveries to the UK in value terms – up 0.8% year-on-year – having recovered in volume terms since Brexit.Tom Bradshaw, the president of the National Farmers’ Union of England and Wales, said: “These figures should be a wake-up call. At a time of growing geopolitical uncertainty, we cannot afford to take our food production capacity for granted.”He said the widening trade deficit underlined the need for a long-term plan to support British production and recognise “a simple truth that food security is national security”.“The pressures facing farm businesses are immense, from rising costs and regulatory burdens to extreme weather and global market volatility,” said Bradshaw. “If government is serious about food security, economic growth and national resilience, it must create the conditions that give businesses the confidence to invest, innovate and grow.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe FDF, which represents hundreds of food and beverage producers, said pressures on manufacturers were “significant and growing” as the cost of energy, ingredients, transport, packaging and labour continued to rise. It said changing regulation also added to pressures on the industry.Karen Betts, the chief executive of the trade body, said: “Our food and drink trade deficit is growing and is now the largest it’s been in over 25 years. In a world beset by conflict and the ever-increasing impacts of climate change, this poses some stark questions about our food security.“When the government then chooses to remove tariffs on, for example, biscuits imported from China, it’s not surprising that they’ll be sold more cheaply here than biscuits made in the UK.”Explore more on these topicsFood & drink industryInternational tradeEuropean UnionBrexitBritish food and drinkTrade policyTariffsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukrainians in UK fear homelessness over host scheme funding cuts | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Monthly ‘thank you’ payments for people hosting refugees to be cut from £350 to £100 from next year
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Monthly ‘thank you’ payments for people hosting refugees to be cut from £350 to £100 from next year
Content: Nataliya Rumyantseva, right, is hosting her mother, Valentyna Klymova. She said it would be ‘cruel’ if hosting changed to become a more commercial rental arrangement.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNataliya Rumyantseva, right, is hosting her mother, Valentyna Klymova. She said it would be ‘cruel’ if hosting changed to become a more commercial rental arrangement.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianImmigration and asylumUkrainians in UK fear homelessness over host scheme funding cutsMonthly ‘thank you’ payments for people hosting refugees to be cut from £350 to £100 from next yearDiane TaylorThu 24 Sep 2026 13.45 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkrainian refugees in the UK fear they could be left homeless after the government quietly axed 70% of funding for hosts of theHomes for Ukrainescheme, reducing monthly “thank you” payments to them from £350 to £100.The scheme was launched after Russia’s invasion ofUkrainein February 2022 and has provided support for 181,000 of the 234,000 Ukrainians who have since sought sanctuary in the UK.Now the government has said it will cut the hosting payments and reduce contributions to local authorities, which are paid a sum for each arrival to meet the costs associated with delivering the programme.A writtenstatement to parliamentfrom the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) on 15 September said funding would be reduced from £5,900 to £3,300. The changes will come into effect from 1 January 2027.Tetiana, a 73-year-old Ukrainian refugee who has been hosted for two years and four months, said she was devastated to read the government’s letter circulated to hosts in the last few days informing them of the changes.She said: “I feel that this financial change could impact on my host’s ability to host me. If the hosting comes to an end, I don’t know where I will go and how I can start again. I can’t work because of my age and because I have mobility problems.“I fled from Kharkiv, which is close to the Russia frontline, so I can’t go back to Ukraine. I don’t know what I will do. I’m at a loss about what my options will be. This change has created a lot of uncertainty for me. I don’t know how I would be able to pay rent if hosting finishes for me.”Nataliya Rumyantseva is hosting her mother, the first Ukrainian to arrive in the UK after the war started. She said the changes were likely to have a significant impact. “When refugees arrive here from Ukraine, they are shellshocked and need time to adapt and learn the language. If hosting changes to become a more commercial rental arrangement, I think that’s cruel.”One host who lives in Greenwich said he did not know if he would be able to continue hosting because of the drop in payments. “I’ve been a sponsor since May 2022. I was dismayed to learn that thank you payments are reducing to just £100,” he said. “I lost my job within months of becoming a sponsor and these payments have become an absolute lifeline even though I did not volunteer for this scheme for the money. I genuinely worry about the consequences of this change for Ukrainians in the UK.”One option the government proposes is that hosts can switch to landlord status and charge refugees rent.A host who lives in Cardiff and is hosting a Ukrainian who has enrolled on a course of study said: “The situation feels like a cheap shot from the government. We, in good faith, opened our home to someone in need. That person, in good faith, planned for a life in the UK. And the government, in what seems like very bad faith, saw an easy way to claw money back from people who aren’t in a position to stop them.”The government says it has so far provided more than £1.81bn for the scheme.An MHCLG spokesperson said: “The UK’s commitment to supporting Ukrainians is unwavering and the Homes for Ukraine scheme remains open. As the scheme has evolved from an initial emergency response into a more established programme, these changes are designed to secure the scheme’s long-term future while maintaining support for sponsors, guests and councils.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumUkraineRefugeesHome OfficeEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: France says EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ law should not include the UK | European Union | The Guardian
description: ‘If you’re not in the internal market, you don’t get the same protection,’ says French minister of policy designed to curb Chinese competition
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: ‘If you’re not in the internal market, you don’t get the same protection,’ says French minister of policy designed to curb Chinese competition
Content: A Mini Cooper on the production line at Germany-headquartered BMW’s Cowley plant near Oxford. New EU laws could hit the British car industry.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Mini Cooper on the production line at Germany-headquartered BMW’s Cowley plant near Oxford. New EU laws could hit the British car industry.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesEuropean UnionFrance says EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ law should not include the UK‘If you’re not in the internal market, you don’t get the same protection,’ says French minister of policy designed to curb Chinese competitionJennifer Rankinin BrusselsThu 24 Sep 2026 13.42 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrance is leading a push to exclude the UK from the EU’s “Made in Europe” policy that could result in British companies losing out in the race to supply European countries with low-carbon technologies and electric cars.The plans wereraised by Andy Burnham when he met the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen,on the sidelines of the UN general assembly earlier this week.The policy, still under negotiation, aims to protect European companies from intense and “unfair” state-subsidised competition fromChina. But the government fears British companies risk being collateral damage and resolving the issue has become one of Burnham’s top priorities for the EU-UK relationship.One key EU proposal is the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), which would require authorities spending public money – awarding subsidies or public contracts –to favour European products in sectors such as renewable technologies and electric cars.But there is an intense debate inside the EU on how to define “made in Europe” and how far to include countries such as the UK, Canada and Japan.UK ‘losing up to £6.5bn a year in EU trade’ without post-Brexit product dealRead moreAt a meeting of EU industry ministers in Brussels on Thursday, France pushed for a narrow definition, starting with the EU27.“European taxpayers’ money should support [European] workers and European factories,” the French industry minister, Sébastien Martin, told reporters.Asked about the UK, he said: “The United Kingdom made a choice a few years ago to leave theEuropean Union.“That doesn’t mean that we don’t discuss things or that we don’t trade, it doesn’t mean that there can’t be agreements in certain sectors, but fundamentally there are those who have chosen the European project and those who have decided to leave.”France’s Europe minister, Benjamin Haddad, speaking in London, had few assurances to offer the Burnham government either.Asked about the risks of pushing the EU’s like-minded trading partners away, Haddad said: “At the end of the day, if you are not part of the internal market and if you are not contributing to the financial capacity of the internal market, you don’t get the same kind of protection.”Germany wants a broader “Made with Europe” policy that would include the UK and other allies. Germany’s economic affairs minister, Katherina Reiche, told her counterparts: “We must reduce unilateral and critical dependencies, but we must not isolate ourselves from the rest of the world. This means that partner countries must be included in the union-origin principle, in general and on the condition of reciprocity.”This position gets broad support from Nordic countries, which traditionally favour open trade.Sweden’s outgoing deputy prime minister, Ebba Busch, who leads on business policy, said “we always miss the Brits”. Sweden wanted “a good solution where there is balance, given that some European countries are not members of the European Union but still completely essential for a functioning European market”, she added.The charged internal EU27 debate on Made in Europe raises questions about thetiming of the EU-UK reset summit, which was postponedwhen Keir Starmer stood down as prime minister. Since Burnham took office, no date has been fixed for the talks which are meant to happen in 2026.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBritish officials expect the summit will take place in November, although an earlier 6 November date has been scratched out. By December the EU is expected to be embroiled in deeply difficult internal negotiations on the bloc’s next seven-year budget, which are likely to consume the political bandwidth of EU leaders.EU insiders believe that a Made in Europe agreement is a top priority for the UK, but have cautioned this cannot happen before the union has finalised its own position.One EU diplomat said it was a “big risk” if the UK government were to insist on a deal at an autumn summit. “It puts [the UK] in a corner, because this [Made in Europe criteria] is a process that is very difficult for the EU27 [to agree internally].”The Republic of Ireland, which is chairing EU ministerial negotiations, hopes for an agreement in December on the IAA, including the Made in Europe provisions, between the EU Council and the European parliament. “There are a divergence of views on the Industrial Accelerator Act, on European preference, on working with trusted partners and third countries,” said Ireland’s enterprise minister, Peter Burke. “It is difficult, but we have a pathway in sight.”Poland’s economic development minister, Michał Baranowski, said it was too early to say whether countries such as Switzerland, the UK, Japan, Australia and Canada would be in or out, adding: “All these countries are in the mix of the discussion.”The UK, he said, should have clarity on its status when the EU act is passed, he said, adding: “We are in the last stretch, but this last stretch might take a while.”A UK government spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and trusted European partner, committed to our shared security and economic cooperation.“We will continue to engage with the EU on Made in Europe and work together, as like-minded partners, to boost growth and open up trade.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionIndustrial policyChinaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia could attack a Nato country within months, Danish intelligence says | Nato | The Guardian
description: Warning comes hours after Poland says fire at Starlink satellite station was ‘act of sabotage’
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Warning comes hours after Poland says fire at Starlink satellite station was ‘act of sabotage’
Content: Left to right: Thomas Ahrenkiel, the head of the Danish defence intelligence service; Jeppe Bruus, the defence minister, and Michael Hyldgaard, the chief of defence, at the release of the intelligence report in Copenhagen.Photograph: Ida Marie Odgaard/ReutersView image in fullscreenLeft to right: Thomas Ahrenkiel, the head of the Danish defence intelligence service; Jeppe Bruus, the defence minister, and Michael Hyldgaard, the chief of defence, at the release of the intelligence report in Copenhagen.Photograph: Ida Marie Odgaard/ReutersNatoRussia could attack a Nato country within months, Danish intelligence saysWarning comes hours after Poland says fire at Starlink satellite station was ‘act of sabotage’Pjotr Sauerin KyivThu 24 Sep 2026 12.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia could launch a limited military attack against a Nato country in the coming months, Danish intelligence said, in one of the starkest warnings yet by western security services.In a report published on Thursday, the Danish defence intelligence service warned of a “low but growing risk” that Russia could launch long-range strikes on Nato infrastructure supportingUkraine, or carry out a limited incursion into a neighbouring country with a small number of troops, potentially operating without insignia.The report came hours after a fire at a Starlink satellite station in centralPolandthat local authorities described as an “act of sabotage”.Krzysztof Gawkowski, the deputy prime minister of Poland, said the blaze, which broke out overnight in the Masovian voivodeship, had been “deliberately designed to disable the station”, disrupting internet access for a number of institutions, including the Ukrainian military.View image in fullscreenThe Starlink station in Wola Krobowska, Poland, April 2026.Photograph: Pleiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/ReutersGawkowski said it had not been established who ​was responsible for the fire, but that “many signs suggest this aligns with Russia’s new ‌doctrine ⁠of attack.“While everything is operational today, we must recognise, as prime minister [Donald] Tusk recently noted, that this is an element of hybrid warfare,” he said.Starlink has become a key part of Ukraine’s military communications, and the incident comes amid a spate of suspected Russian sabotage operations across European infrastructure supporting Ukraine.Earlier this month, Germanypublicly blamed Russiafor an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle airport, while a series of other incidents – including fires at drone factories and sabotage targeting rail infrastructure – have also been investigated for possible links to Moscow. Russia has denied involvement in such attacks.European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against NatoRead moreIn recent weeks, several European intelligence chiefs have warned that Russia may bepreparingmore assertive actions to test Nato countries’ commitment to supporting Ukraine, though officials differ over how imminent such a move may be.Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid attacks against European countries with “greater consequences” for those targeted in the coming months, the Danes warned, including “destructive cyber-attacks that cripple societal functions as well as sabotage attacks that carry a high risk of casualties”.A source familiar with Moscow’s thinking agreed that Russia was likely to step up its hybrid attacks.“Russian military top command is convinced someNatocountries are directly involved in the war against Russia – not just by supplying Ukraine with weapons and intelligence, but by helping to guide missiles and drones,” the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity.“They therefore believe Nato is already waging a hybrid war against Russia, and that Russia has the right to respond in kind,” the source added.“Hybrid attacks” are broad terms generally used to describe non-military tactics aimed at pressuring or destabilising an adversary, including cyber-attacks, sabotage and disinformation.The aim of Russia’s actions would be to divert European resources away from supporting Ukraine, and deepen divisions within Nato if the alliance failed to agree on a collective response, the report added.The service believes it remained “highly unlikely” that Russia would launch an outright invasion of a Nato country, but notably said it “cannot be ruled out”.The Danish services said Russia could seek to test Nato’s article 5, which commits members to collective defence. They warned there was “a risk that Russia assesses that the Nato countries will not respond collectively”, particularly if Moscow believes the US is unable or unwilling to support its European allies in a potential war with Russia.There have been ongoing jitters among Nato members over whether the alliance’s most powerful member, the US, would come to Europe’s defence under Donald Trump in the event of a Russian attack.Questions over unity within Europe are also growing. Last week, Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, who has maintained close ties with the Kremlin, cast doubt on his country’s commitment to Nato’s collective defence principle, saying he did not want Slovakia drawn into a military conflict “because of some article 5”.Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia continued to threaten countries beyond Ukraine, including Moldova, Poland and the Baltic states, while showing “no respect” for the sovereignty of countries in the south Caucasus and central Asia.“The more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else,” he said.Explore more on these topicsNatoRussiaDenmarkPolandUkraineEspionageEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Germany investigates 105-year-old suspected former Nazi prison camp guard | Germany | The Guardian
description: Man accused of being accessory to murders at Stalag 326 VI K amid race to prosecute suspects before they die
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: Man accused of being accessory to murders at Stalag 326 VI K amid race to prosecute suspects before they die
Content: Russian prisoners celebrate being released by US soldiers from the German camp Stalag 326 VI K in February 1945.Photograph: FPG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRussian prisoners celebrate being released by US soldiers from the German camp Stalag 326 VI K in February 1945.Photograph: FPG/Getty ImagesGermanyGermany investigates 105-year-old suspected former Nazi prison camp guardMan accused of being accessory to murders at Stalag 326 VI K amid race to prosecute suspects before they dieKate Connollyin BerlinThu 24 Sep 2026 10.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 105-year-old man is under investigation on suspicion of being an accessory to multiple murders at a Nazi prisoner of war camp, German prosecutors have said.The case, which is being handled by the public prosecutor’s office in Dortmund, centres on the Stalag 326 VI K camp in westernGermany, in what is now the state of North Rhine-Westphalia.“The 105-year-old suspect is thought to have been a guard at the prisoner of war camp Stalag 326 VI K in the Senne region of western Germany,” prosecutors said in a statement. The man is “accused of being an accessory to multiple murders owing to his activities there”, they said.The Senne camp housed between 180,000 and 200,000 Soviet prisoners of war between 1941 and April 1945, when it was liberated by American troops.The investigation is the result of an urgent last-minute scramble by the judiciary to prosecute alleged participants in the Nazi killing machine before they die. The judicial efforts stem in part from a recognition that many of the suspects who have escaped prosecution in the eight decades since the end of the second world war on the grounds that they were considered to have played an insignificant role were in fact integral to the implementation of the Hitler regime’s murderous aims.A judicial precedent was set by the court case of John Demjanjuk, a former guard at the Nazi Sobibór death camp in occupied Poland, who wasconvicted in 2011of being an accomplice to the murders of more than 28,000 Jews that took place in the time he worked there.Prosecutors had sought Ukraine-born Demjanjuk’s extradition from his Ohio home to Germany for years, arguing that he was complicit in the crimes committed at Sobibór despite a lack of evidence that he had directly killed anyone.Demjanjuk died aged 91 in March 2012 awaiting an appeal due to his age and frailty, which meant he did not go to prison.View image in fullscreenJohn Demjanjuk, a former guard at the Sobibór death camp, died without going to prison.Photograph: David Rubinger/Getty ImagesThe Demjanjuk case lowered the bar for proof of complicity, paving the way for other nonagenarians and more recently centenarians to stand trial.The most prominent trial of recent years, and representative of what Hannah Arendt, a political theorist, described as aSchreibtischtäter(desk perpetrator, or bureaucratic mediator), was that ofIrmgard Furchner, who worked at the Stutthof concentration camp between 1943 and 1945 as a secretary to the camp commandant. She was given a two-year suspended sentence for her role as an accessory to murder.Her trial was, contrary to normal rules, filmed for historical purposes. Furchner made headlines afterrunning awayfrom her retirement home on the scheduled opening day of her trial.Josef Schütz, a former guard at the Sachsenhausen concentration camp north of Berlin, was sentenced for being an accomplice to murder to five years in prison in June 2022. He died the following year, aged 102.In April last year an alleged former guard at Sachsenhausen died before he was able to face trial over charges of complicity in the murder of more than 3,300 people.A separate investigation was opened last year by Dortmund prosecutors into a 100-year-old former guard at a PoW camp in Hemer, North Rhine-Westphalia, which also held mainly Soviet prisoners. He is suspected of participating in executions of prisoners between December 1943 and September 1944.The new investigation was initiated by the Central Office for the Investigation of National Socialist Crimes in Ludwigsburg, in the southern state of Baden-Württemberg, which passed its preliminary investigation into the man to public prosecutors along with that of another former guard. The other suspect has since died, according to German media.If the trial goes ahead, like other recent cases it is expected to throw light on the Stalag system in general and on Senne in particular, drawing survivors and historians to give evidence. Up to 5.7 million Soviet prisoners were held captivity in Germany. More than half did not survive.Explore more on these topicsGermanyNazismEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder arrested at anti-Netanyahu protest in New York | New York | The Guardian
description: Actors detained at Jewish Voice for Peace demonstration against Israeli prime minister’s address to the UN general assembly
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Actors detained at Jewish Voice for Peace demonstration against Israeli prime minister’s address to the UN general assembly
Content: Susan Sarandon (centre) takes part in a protest ahead of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s address to the United Nations general assembly in New York City on Thursday. She was among those arrested at the rally.Photograph: David Dee Delgado/ReutersView image in fullscreenSusan Sarandon (centre) takes part in a protest ahead of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s address to the United Nations general assembly in New York City on Thursday. She was among those arrested at the rally.Photograph: David Dee Delgado/ReutersNew YorkSusan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder arrested at anti-Netanyahu protest in New YorkActors detained at Jewish Voice for Peace demonstration against Israeli prime minister’s address to the UN general assemblyGuardian staff and agenciesThu 24 Sep 2026 19.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOscar-winning actor Susan Sarandon and Hacks star Hannah Einbinder were among people detained by police in New York on Thursday as they moved in to break up a protest againstBenjamin Netanyahu.Agence France-Presse footage shows NYPD officers cuffing Thelma & Louise star Sarandon at the demo in the city as theIsraeli prime minister was readying to address the United Nations general assembly.‘I was born without self-esteem’: Hannah Einbinder on Hacks, her buzzy queer horror – and being Hollywood’s most outspoken starRead moreTheNew YorkPost reported Einbinder had also been marched away from the demonstration organised by Jewish Voice for Peace, where protesters held banners that read “Stop Arming Israel” and “End the Genocide.”A spokesperson for the NYPD said officers had responded to reports of an “unscheduled demonstration” where people were blocking an intersection.View image in fullscreenHannah Einbinder (R) with Saturday Night Live star Sarah Sherman (L) at the protest.Photograph: Eric Cox/Reuters“Members of the NYPD Community Affairs Bureau issued … warnings, advising participants that they should leave,” the spokesperson said.“They continued to block the intersection. Multiple individuals who didn’t comply were taken into custody,” she said, without providing the number of people arrested.Democratic congressional candidateDarializa Avila Chevalierand New York ⁠City council member Chi Ossé were also among those arrested.Inside the general assembly, dozens of envoys from across the worldwalked outas Netanyahu began his speech, where he assailed both enemies and allies that have crossed him in recent months, including Britain and France, which have recently moved to recognise the state of Palestine.1:38UN delegates walk out as Benjamin Netanyahu prepares to address general assembly – videoI was arrested protesting Netanyahu’s New York visit. Here’s why we took a stand | Darializa Avila ChevalierRead more“They accuseIsrael, tiny Israel, of colonialism – some colonialism. And who’s accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God’s sakes, they invented the term,” he told the assembly.Sarandon, whose movie hits also include The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Dead Man Walking and The Witches of Eastwick, is no stranger to protests over Israel’s war in Gaza.The US actor told journalists at the Venice film festival this month she was losing work because of her outspoken views.“I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still. But that’s the power structure,” she said.“I think there has been a change in terms of the understanding of the situation and the general public, but there are still very strongly held positions within my industry that are held by Zionists and who have not relaxed their feelings towards me.“But I found my family, I found my people, and I’m OK,” she added.Einbinder has previously said the cost of not speaking up about Palestine is greater than losing her Hollywood career, citing industry backlash to actors such as Sarandon andMelissa Barrera.“I think what they know is what I know, which is that the cost of not speaking is higher,”she told Cannes film festival earlier this year.“There is a greater toll in not speaking and you’ve just got to have your priorities straight. I am under no impression that my small career could ever measure up in comparison to even one human life. It’s an obligation and I will always do it.”Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsNew YorkHacksSusan SarandonBenjamin NetanyahuProtestIsraelUnited NationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran awaiting response from Trump on proposal to open strait of Hormuz in six days | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Country says US must lift sanctions on its oil exports and end the war on all fronts, including in Lebanon
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Country says US must lift sanctions on its oil exports and end the war on all fronts, including in Lebanon
Content: The strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on 31 August.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenThe strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on 31 August.Photograph: ReutersUS-Israel war on IranIran awaiting response from Trump on proposal to open strait of Hormuz in six daysCountry says US must lift sanctions on its oil exports and end the war on all fronts, including in LebanonPatrick Wintourin New YorkThu 24 Sep 2026 17.57 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 15.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran said it has told Donald Trump it is willing to open the strait of Hormuz in six days, and to start talks on its nuclear program the day after, so long as the US lifts sanctions on Iran’s oil exports in return, ends the war on all fronts – including in Lebanon – and releases some of Iran’s frozen assets.The proposal is designed to accelerate the steps first laid down in the memorandum of understanding signed by the US and Iran in June, particularly by helping the talks on Iran’s nuclear program start much more quickly than previously agreed.Iran says a deal on the temporary route through the strait of Hormuz has been agreed with Oman, describing it as a done deal, and is ready to register the details with the International Maritime Organisation.Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, said he was waiting to hear a response from the Americans to the proposal. He added that he had consulted on the plan with China, which fully supported the proposal.Saudi Arabia had been expected to endorse the Oman-Iran route through the strait last week, but pulled back partly due to anger that Iranian-backed Houthis had started attacking Saudi Arabia as part of their dispute over the future of Yemen.Iran claims it has urged the Houthis to cease the attacks on Saudi Arabia but that it does not have control over Houthi decision-making.Araghchi, speaking to reporters in New York, said: “We have introduced a plan to the US through the mediators that if certain conditions are met, the strait will be open within seven days and talks will start.”He said the Iranian preconditions were not new, and were contained in the Islamabad memorandum of understanding that was signed by Trump.The advantage of the proposal, apart from opening the strait and lifting the chokehold on the world economy, would be bringing the US to the talks on Iran’s nuclear program much more quickly. Talks on the nuclear program under the MoU would not have started for 60 days. Araghchi said he was staying in New York over the weekend to await an American response, but added he was not in a hurry.Privately, Iranian officials believe they could reach a deal with the Americans, and the Saudi hurdle over aspects of the route could be overcome, but fear Israel will use its influence to pull the US president away from the proposal.Araghchi added he would like the deal to go through before the midterm elections, by which he meant that the strait of Hormuz could be opened and energy prices thereby reduced, something Trump badly needs for the Republican party to survive a political mauling.For the US, there are difficulties in the plan related to forcing Israel to end the war in Lebanon. Israel may object to giving Iran such clear control over the route through which ships would travel through the strait of Hormuz. Iran also wants to retain control of shipping to prevent some US military shipping going through the strait.Issues such as whether tolls or navigational fees could be imposed by the littoral states Oman and Iran would be settled later in the process.View image in fullscreenThe Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi (left), speaks with his Jordanian counterpart, Ayman Safadi, at the UN in New York City.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesEarlier in the day, the UK foreign secretary,Ed Miliband, met Araghchi, his Iranian counterpart, for the first time in New York.It was also the first meeting between UK and Iranian ministers for a year, and the first exchange since the UK in July proscribed the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organisation, a move that has worsened the already sour relations between the two countries.Miliband made clear that the UK was committed to freedom of navigation in the strait and wanted a diplomatic solution, also stressing support for Saudi Arabia, a UK ally in Yemen.He warned Iran about its behaviour in the UK, including threats to Jewish communities, and called for the UK to be given consular access to theBritish couple sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonmentin Tehran.Araghchi and the US’s special envoy Steve Witkoff also met earlier this week on the sidelines of the general assembly to discuss Iran’s terms for reopening the strait and the speed at which that may happen, as well as the time the US had been given to respond.Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talkRead moreA faction inside Iran is arguing that Tehran should seek to escalate the conflict with a vulnerable US president, rather than let the crisis drift in its current deadlock. Brent crude was trading at about $107 (£81) a barrel on Thursday.Some IRGC officers have also linked the strait of Hormuz issue to the closure of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway close to the south-west of Yemen now under control of Iranian-backed Houthis.Maj Gen Rahim Safavi, a senior Iranian military figure, said: “If the Americans start a new war, a new front centred on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab strait may open before their eyes. Are they ready to enter the battle on this front? This is a question that they should pay more attention to.”Domestically, Pezeshkian’s defiant message to the UN general assembly on Wednesday was deemed a success overall in that it balanced a refusal to bend the knee to “the US bully” with a willingness to seek diplomatic talks.He also proposed a new security architecture for the future in partnership with Gulf states, including those it has been bombarding in an effort to dislodge the US from its military bases.Maj Gen Ahmad Vahidi, commander-in-chief of the IRGC, praised Pezeshkian’s speech, saying: “We are not afraid of war. It is the loud and firm call of the Iranian nation – a call that resonated from theUnited Nationspodium, through the words of the esteemed president, and reached the ears of the world.”Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranEd MilibandIranStrait of HormuzUS foreign policyTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Family of Iranian twins sentenced to death and decades in jail ask UN for help | Iran | The Guardian
description: Taraneh and Romina Rahimi were charged with ‘waging war against God’ after joining protests against Tehran regime
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Taraneh and Romina Rahimi were charged with ‘waging war against God’ after joining protests against Tehran regime
Content: Taraneh and Romina were taken from their beds by men from the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps eight months ago.View image in fullscreenTaraneh and Romina were taken from their beds by men from the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps eight months ago.IranFamily of Iranian twins sentenced to death and decades in jail ask UN for helpTaraneh and Romina Rahimi were charged with ‘waging war against God’ after joining protests against Tehran regimeSupported byAbout this contentDaniel BoffeyChief reporterThu 24 Sep 2026 09.15 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 14.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe family of 21-year-old twins who have been sentenced respectively todeath and decades in jailfor protesting against the Iranian regime have appealed to the United Nations for help.A formal “submission of information” relating to the case of Taraneh and Romina Rahimi has been submitted by British human right lawyers on their family’s behalf.The move could lead to the UN’s human rights council opening talks with the Iranian regime about resolving the case if it is found to involve human rights violations.Broken feet, ripped-out hair and now a death sentence: the fate of twin sisters jailed over Iran protestsRead moreThe president of Iran, Masoud Pezeshkian, told the UN’s general assembly in New York this week that the country was “ready for dialogue and diplomacy”.Taraneh and Romina Rahimi were taken from their beds by men from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps eight months ago after they joined nationwide protests against the regime.They were tried over charges that includedmoharebeh(waging war against God) for taking to the streets of Isfahan, in central Iran, on 8 and 9 January.At the end of August, Taraneh, along with nine others, was sentenced to death. Romina received a 25-year prison sentence.The girls’ family are seeking to appeal against the sentences but human rights groups have raised concerns that Taraneh’s execution could be fast-tracked.The women are being held in Dowlatabad prison in Isfahan, where the twins’ family claim that Taraneh was threatened with being forced to watch the rape of her sister if she failed to sign a confession to her alleged crimes.The sisters have been held in isolation but are said to have been able to hear each other’s screams as torture was inflicted upon them.Neither of the women have been seen by their mother, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, or other members of the family since their sentencing.After the Guardianhighlighted the case, the women’s cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, an IT engineer who lives in the US state of Utah, said Taraneh was told she would only be allowed to eat leftovers of other prisoners’ meals as punishment.Nourmohammadi, 43, said he had turned to the UN out of desperation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTaraneh is said to be in need of surgery due to injuries inflicted during interrogation.Nourmohammadi said: “Turning to theUnited Nationsis not something I ever wanted to have to do. I am simply asking the international community to help ensure that Taraneh and Romina receive the basic rights that every human being is entitled to: a fair process, protection from torture and abuse, access to medical care and legal counsel, and the right to have their cases genuinely reviewed.“Taraneh is facing the death penalty, and Romina is facing decades in prison. They are young women who should be thinking about their futures, not whether one sister will be executed and the other will spend the best years of her life behind bars.“They are my family and I will continue to use every peaceful and legal avenue available. I ask the United Nations to stand with them before it is too late – especially for Taraneh.”A submission to the UN through its “special procedures” can lead to a formal request by the international organisation to a member state for an explanation and action.Iran hasexecuted more than 500 people this year, including at least 16 women. Hundreds of protesters have been sentenced to death or are facing charges which could carry the death penalty, including more than 70 in Isfahan.Explore more on these topicsIranMiddle East and north AfricaUnited NationsTortureViolence against women and girlsHuman rightsWomen's rights and gender equalitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Global release announced for acclaimed Gaza documentary NAZA | NAZA | The Guardian
description: Theatrical rollout across 56 territories planned for documentary about Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza before film will stream on Guardian website
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: Theatrical rollout across 56 territories planned for documentary about Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza before film will stream on Guardian website
Content: ‘The death threats will not stop the film’ … a scene from NAZA.Photograph: The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The death threats will not stop the film’ … a scene from NAZA.Photograph: The GuardianNAZAGlobal release announced for acclaimed Gaza documentary NAZATheatrical rollout across 56 territories planned for documentary about Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza before film will stream on Guardian websiteCatherine ShoardandLorenzo TondoThu 24 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNAZA, the award-winning documentary from Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, is set to be released in cinemas inmore than 50 countries before a digital global release on theguardian.com.The film, which the Guardian produced, premiered at the Venice film festival earlier this month, where it was met with a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went onto win the special jury prize.‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligenceRead moreAfter screenings in Bologna and at the San Sebastián film festival, the film will receive its North American premiere on Saturday at the New York film festival before opening four days later at the IFC Center in New York City. On 9 October it will expand to Los Angeles and other key US cities before a national rollout.A theatrical release in partnership with MK2 Films is also planned in 55 other territories, including the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Canada, Hong Kong, Brazil, Turkey, Thailand, France, Spain, Germany, Turkey, Central America and the Middle East.After its run in cinemas, the film will stream in late November on the Guardian’s website, for free, as part of the news organisation’s commitment to the dissemination of independent journalism.“NAZA is grounded in rigorous journalism published over the past three years,” said Harry Davies, a Guardian investigations correspondent and one of NAZA’s producers. “But it is also a powerful piece of cinema that will soon be available on screens, large and small, around the world.”Documentary NAZA gets 25-minute standing ovation at Venice film festival premiere – videoA number of distributors and cinemas in Israel have been offered the film, and the Guardian is exploring ways by which NAZA can be seen in the occupied Palestinian territories.From ovations in Venice to death threats in Israel: the extreme responses to NAZA documentaryRead moreThe documentaryreveals the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. NAZA is a military acronym euphemistically used by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians that it expects will be killed in an airstrike.Shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, the film features interviews with 24 members of Israeli intelligence and military, granted on the condition of anonymity. The film builds on journalism first published by the Guardian, +972 Magazine, an Israeli-Palestinian publication, and Hebrew-language outlet Local Call between 2023 and 2025.In 2024, Abraham and Szorwon the best documentary Oscarfor No Other Land, along with their two Palestinian co-directors, Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal. Jonathan Glazer, the Oscar-winning film-maker of The Zone of Interest and Under the Skin, has executive produced, while his longtime collaborator, James Wilson of JW Films, also produced the film.The film won unanimously positive reviews at its premiere, but last week Benjamin Netanyahu and a number of senior military and far-right political figures called for the directors’ citizenship to be revoked, and accused them of“treason against the state”.The Israeli prime minister said he would seek new laws allowing the country to strip citizenship from people who “smear” Israeli soldiers and “defame” the state of Israel. Alongside the announcement,dozens of rightwing activists gathered outside Szor’s parents’ home.Police and border police officers were deployed at the scene. One protester called for the “death penalty for traitors” and demanded that the homes of the film-makers’ families be demolished.Speaking on Thursday, Abraham and Szor said: “We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israelis to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible.“The threats from the Israeli government to revoke our citizenship and the death threats do not change that and will not stop the film. We thank our colleagues for the solidarity and look forward to sharing NAZA all over the world very soon.”‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directorsRead moreLast week, 43 local human rights organisations issued ajoint statementurging Israeli authorities to stop what they described as incitement and threats against the film-makers, and not to prosecute either them or their sources.More than 1,500 Israeli film-makershave also signed a petition defending “freedom of expression and creation” and expressing solidarity with Szor and Abraham.Their sentiments have been echoed by a number of leading film-makers around the world, including Ken Loach, Joshua Oppenheimer, Paul Laverty, Laura Poitras, Nan Goldin, Richard Eyre and Hanif Kureishi. Oppenheimer, the US director of Oscar-nominated documentaries The Act of Killing and The Look of Silence, said, “The Israeli government is waging a full-scale intimidation campaign against film directors. I am appalled and enraged.”Explore more on these topicsNAZAFilm industryVenice film festivalGazaJonathan GlazerNo Other LandPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Benjamin Netanyahu to deliver defiant UN speech while facing protests and political isolation | Benjamin Netanyahu | The Guardian
description: Prime minister will ‘highlight Israel’s achievements’ as he heads towards his toughest re-election challenge
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Prime minister will ‘highlight Israel’s achievements’ as he heads towards his toughest re-election challenge
Content: Benjamin Netanyahu, who is addressing the United Nations on Thursday.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APView image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu, who is addressing the United Nations on Thursday.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APBenjamin NetanyahuBenjamin Netanyahu to deliver defiant UN speech while facing protests and political isolationPrime minister will ‘highlight Israel’s achievements’ as he heads towards his toughest re-election challengeAndrew RothandAlice Speriin New YorkThu 24 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 08.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen he takes the stage at the UN on Thursday,Benjamin Netanyahuwill deliver a familiar message of defiance even as protests and international condemnation leave the Israeli leader in growing isolation.Netanyahu is facing his toughest re-election challenge in a political career spanning decades with three ongoing conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, and a growing campaign of violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank.Internationally, Israel is facing growing condemnation. The UK, France and Canada are planning to sanction Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and the British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has accused Israeli settlers of committing ethnic cleansing of Palestinian communities.And the US is in the midst of a historic shift in public opinion against Israel, with 62% of respondents telling Pew in July they had a negative opinion of Netanyahu’s government, and 60% of American Jews in a poll released this week hoping he is voted out in October.Protests are expected both in the UN’s general assembly hall and on the streets of New York City, where mayor Zohran Mamdani has tempered his earlier promises to arrest Netanyahu as a war criminal to assure demonstrators this week that he would protect their “right to [protest] in this city”.Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, defended Netanyahu’s government in a telephone interview before this week’s speech seeking to cast criticism of Israel’s actions as the product of misinformation and bias.“We are aware of the fact that we had a very challenging three years since October 7,” said Danon. “We accomplished a lot, but we were criticised. We were under the spotlight, and for us, I think, we are proud of our achievements.”“At the same time, we will work harder to improve the image of Israel, and we know there’s a campaign against us,” he added.Anger at Netanyahu will be on full display in New York City on Thursday, where several protests have been scheduled, including one from Bryant Park in midtown Manhattan to the UN headquarters in Turtle Bay to “reject war criminal Benjamin Netanyahu and the genocidal Zionist project”.“Netanyahu is coming to New York amid a political environment that has made it crystal clear that he is not welcome here,” said Beth Miller, the political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action.She described a “mainstreaming” of public opinion that “Americans do not want to be supporting Israel’s genocide. We do not want to be supporting Israel’s apartheid. We do not want to be arming Israel or supporting Israel.”And Palestinian representatives are calling for diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech to “send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end”.But in Danon’s telling, Israel’s problem was largely one of public relations rather than of policy, and he cited a “wave of misinformation” as the reason for the precipitous shift in polling. Netanyahu would use his speech to “highlight Israel’s achievements”, he said, and to lay out “what still should be done, and how should we verify that we actually achieve the goals of the war?”He did not elaborate on those specific measures before the speech, but the White House and US policymakers will be listening as they calibrate their message to voters – as well as the backlash of public anger – ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.Netanyahu is expected to deliver a hardline message aimed not just at world leaders, but also to his own electorate in Israel ahead of the October elections. “I think that he is trying to demonstrate to the Israeli populace that he still maintains some level of control over the situation,” said Miller. “And I think that he is trying to speak to a rightwing audience and a Trump-Maga audience in this country to try to rile up the hatred and Islamophobia.”Donald Trump and top US officials are not expected to meet with Netanyahu, however, during a visit expected to last less than 24 hours.Trump will be in Washington DC to host the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping,and Netanyahu has cited Israel’s electoral campaign and the holiday of Sukkot as his reason to head home quickly after the speech.A Trump administration official said Netanyahu’s delegation had sought a high-level meeting during the visit but none was organised. There are also no plans to meet congressional leaders, Danon said.With criticism from top Republicans, including the vice-president, JD Vance, and leading democratic presidential contenders, Israel could face a 2028 campaign with two candidates who no longer support arms sales to Israel or the broad diplomatic support that it has enjoyed in the past.Evenwithin the Maga base there are fractures, Miller noted, with “more and more people who don’t really want to be sending our tax dollars to support the Israeli government”.Danon said of a potential shift in the US-Israeli security relationship: “I think that we are still sharing the same values, and that’s why I’m sure that we will continue to have the support from the US.”28:23Has Netanyahu lost America? – Stateside with Kai and CarterBut there are multiple flashpoints now for anger from both US political parties, as well as the international community, includingdire humanitarian concerns and the lack of reconstruction in Gaza,the expansion of settlements in the West Bank, and continued conflicts in Lebanon and Iran, where the US has found itself mired in a conflict that has driven up global energy prices.Asked if a controversial $2.8bn (£2.1bn) arms sale indicated that Israel is preparing to resume its offensive in Gaza, Danon said Israel “hopes that we will see [Hamas’s] disarmament without our involvement”, nodding to efforts by the Trump-backed Board of Peace. But he said Israel “will do it ourselves” if that does not change, adding: “We can not leave it forever like that.”He was equally resolute on the West Bank, saying that Israel would not be swayed by recent criticism led by the UK over plans to expand settlements including E1, the planned construction which would sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank.Senate Democrats are also introducing a bill on Wednesday to sanction facilitators of the new settlement, and Senator Chris Coons, a co-sponsor, said in a statement that “as Palestinian civilians face a campaign of devastation and fear from violent extremist settlers, the United States must send a strong message that this behaviour is unacceptable”.The protests began even before Netanyahu arrived in New York.Already on Wednesday, several members of the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York City chapter rallied at the city’s John F Kennedy international airport in protest at weapons and explosive materials destined for the Israeli military being flown out of the airporton commercial aircraft.Aber Kawas, who in November is slated to become the first Palestinian-American elected official in New York state, spoke at the event and later told the Guardian she plans to join many other New Yorkers protesting Nethanyahu’s UN speech on Thursday.“Thousands of people are against his presence in our city,” she said.Even though some had hailed Netanyahu’s decision to cut his visit short as a victory, she added, “the fact that he is coming shows he continues to have a sense of entitlement to be centred on the world stage while being the head architect of a genocide”.Explore more on these topicsBenjamin NetanyahuIsraelUnited NationsMiddle East and north AfricaProtestIsrael-Gaza warProtest (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Backlash as Indian oil heir made professor of sustainability by Newcastle University | Newcastle University | The Guardian
description: Role for Anant Ambani, son of India’s richest person, who also runs a controversial mega-zoo, met with incredulity
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Role for Anant Ambani, son of India’s richest person, who also runs a controversial mega-zoo, met with incredulity
Content: Anant Amabani, 31, is worth an estimated £90bn.Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/ReutersView image in fullscreenAnant Amabani, 31, is worth an estimated £90bn.Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/ReutersNewcastle UniversityBacklash as Indian oil heir made professor of sustainability by Newcastle UniversityRole for Anant Ambani, son of India’s richest person, who also runs a controversial mega-zoo, met with incredulityRachel HallandPatrick GreenfieldThu 24 Sep 2026 06.26 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNewcastle University is facing a backlash from conservationists over the appointment of the heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune who runs a controversial mega-zoo as a professor of sustainability.The university announced that Anant Ambani had been given a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship” and “significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”.Ambani is the son of India’s richest person, Mukesh Ambani, who made his fortune primarily in oil and gas, owns the world’s largest oil refinery and has close ties with the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Mukesh Ambani has enthusiastically praised BJP policies, and firms linked to his Reliance conglomerate have recently made significant donations to the party. The prime minister, Narendra Modi, attended Anant Ambani’s lavish 2024 wedding in Mumbai.Anant Amabani, 31, who is leads on renewable energy on the Reliance Group’s executive board and is worth an estimated £90bn, has set up Vantara, a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near the family’s oil refining facilities in Gujarat, which reportedly has more than 150,000 animals including 200 lions, 250 leopards and 900 crocodiles, and where he hosted his opulent pre-wedding celebrations attended by celebrity guests and politicians.Conservation groups have previously raised questions about how some of the animals were sourced, given many were endangered species. Vantara has never been found guilty of any wrongdoing.View image in fullscreenThe Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, visiting the Vantara zoo in Gujarat in March 2025.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesThe university’s announcement was met with incredulity and derision from academic staff and Indian and international conservationists and environmentalists.Ramachandra Guha, a leading Indian public intellectual and the author of the book Speaking With Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism, said: “I must say that it is a rather mystifying choice. As a scholar of Indian and global environmentalism, I can name at least 50 – perhaps 100 – individuals who are far better qualified to be thus honoured. They include soil scientists, energy scientists, water conservation experts, community forest workers, ecologists, pollution abatement experts etc who have made real and tangible contributions to a more sustainable future for India and Indians.“I wonder on whose adviceNewcastleUniversity has acted, and whether it did due diligence on what has and has not been done in these fields. Its appointment of Mr Ambani is puzzling in the extreme, and is likely to adversely affect the university’s institutional credibility and intellectual standing.”View image in fullscreenA Newcastle University spokesperson said the professorship ‘recognises Mr Ambani’s contributions to conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship’.Photograph: Washington Imaging/AlamyBhuvan Mangalore, an Indian investigator into illegal wildlife trade who is completing a dissertation on Vantara at Anglia Ruskin University, asked: “Is this a joke?”Prof Matt Perry, the chair of the University and College Union branch at Newcastle University, said staff members had objected to the appointment citing environmental concerns.Prof Lyla Mehta, the head of the climate, environment and sustainability department at the University of Sussex’s Institute of Development Studies, shared concerns that “as public funding for universities falls, there is a real danger that billionaire and corporate money begins to shape academia”.She said: “Universities are supposed to be places that question power and hold corporations to account, not give them academic legitimacy.”In April, AnantAmbani launched Vantara University, billed as the world’s first global university dedicated to wildlife conservation and veterinary science.Lorne Stockman, a research co-director at Oil Change International, said: “At a time when the climate crisis demands an urgent phaseout of oil and gas, we must demand our publicly funded institutions do better.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn 2025, aninvestigation by the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitungfound that many animals delivered to Vantara arrived through countries with opaque wildlife trading networks such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United Arab Emirates, raising concerns that endangered species may have been illegally trafficked.In August last year, an investigation by India’s supreme court, which lasted less than three weeks, cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing. A subsequentfact-finding missioninto the zooby Cites, the UN body that regulates the trade of endangered species, found that some of the permits used to bring animals to Vantara were probably forged.Itsreport said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”Cites recommended restrictions on India’s imports of endangered wild animals. However, it subsequently reversed its decision after objections from India, the US and Japan at a Cites meeting after they argued there was not enough proof of illegal imports.In August, the zoo launched a “reset” in its operations by appointing a former Cites head to oversee its operations and said it would voluntarily pause all wildlife imports until June next year.View image in fullscreenAn employee watching news related to Vantara on a website at his office in Bengaluru.Photograph: Idrees Mohammed/AFP/Getty ImagesVantara has declined to comment. The Ambani family and Vantara have previously denied the allegations of wildlife trafficking. They have said: “Our mission and focus continues to be the rescue, rehabilitation and care of animals.”A Newcastle University spokesperson said: “The award of a professorship of practice recognises Mr Ambani’s contributions to conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship through his work with Vantara, a wildlife rescue and conservation initiative, and as the executive lead for the Reliance Group’s transition toward a green energy future.”Explore more on these topicsNewcastle UniversitySustainabilityConservationZoosIndiaSouth and central AsiaUniversitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Cracking auction, Gromit!’ Original Aardman puppets go under the hammer  | Aardman | The Guardian
