When this occurs, the company said, it works “quickly to support our store teams to correct any unintentional pricing errors and ensure prices are accurately reflected across our products and offers”.Repeat violationsLast year, a state inspector in North Carolina named Tripp Foltzresponded to a complaint that the pump price at a Circle K in Hillsborough was significantly higher than the road-facing sign. The sign said $3.459 for cash or credit. The pump said $3.799.After Foltz explained the situation to the manager, she fixed the problem. But when he returned twice more over the next couple of weeks, he noted two more overcharges – 14 cents and then 24 cents a gallon. His agency imposed a $500 penalty. Weeks later, another consumer complaint prompted a return visit.Foltz recorded another 14-cent overcharge.Because of limited staffing, North Carolina only inspects in-store pricing at convenience stores when it receives complaints. Of the 28 failed Circle K inspections between 2023 and 2025, 16 were follow-ups from previous failures. One store in Kernersville failed five times in a row.Repeat pricing violations are also common at other types of retail stores, the Guardian’s reporting has shown. Even wide-ranging investigations and millions of dollars in fines often do not stop big companies from charging customers more than their posted prices.In 2021, state and local prosecutors in California informed Carquest Auto Parts that their investigation had found that the chain’s stores across the state were routinely overcharging customers. Despite the warning, the problem got worse, authorities claimed in a lawsuit. At one point, the suit said, Carquest stores flunked 39 of 43 price inspections across 20 counties, overcharging on 23% of the items pulled by inspectors.The chainpaid $750,000in 2024 to settle the case.In another example, Walmart agreed to stop overcharging customers in a 2008 settlement with California officials, then paid $2.1m in 2012 to settle claims that it had violated that deal by continuing to ring up higher-than-posted prices at checkout. In August 2025, it agreed to pay state authorities another$5.6mto address claims it had once again overcharged customers at checkout as well as selling produce and other groceries with less weight than promised on the label.Carquest andWalmartdid not reply to questions from the Guardian about these settlements.View image in fullscreenAlexander Stout, a retired military reservist, complained to state officials about a gas-price discrepancy at this 7-Eleven in Somerset, Texas.Photograph: Christopher Lee/The GuardianFriedman, the law professor, said that making real progress against rip-offs at checkout counters will require a national commitment.“There are a lot of people who get speeding tickets and the next day they’re speeding again,” he said. “Unless you have the Federal Trade Commission or state attorneys general stepping in aggressively and repeatedly as a strategy and saying, ‘We are going to litigate against all of the retailers that do this, and we’re going to do it on a broad scale,’ the practices are going to continue.”‘Screwing people over’On a Monday evening in August 2024, Alexander Stout, a 43-year-old retired military reservist who lives with five dogs on a six-acre ranch in Somerset, Texas, pulled his Dodge truck into his local 7-Eleven. He had spotted a roadside sign touting regular fuel at $2.859 a gallon.In an email to his state’s department of licensing and regulation, Stout explained that he discovered the price on the pump read $2.999. He offered to share a video of the 14-cent disparity with the agency. “This gas station has done this before,” Stout wrote.Three months later, he got an email informing him the case had been closed for “insufficient evidence”. An agency attorney said he had tried to contact Stout and indicated that, having performed an on-site inspection and determined the marquee had not been “operational”, he “did not feel it was warranted to move forward to a penalty”.View image in fullscreenAlexander Stout filed a complaint about inaccurate gas prices at a 7-Eleven in Texas.Photograph: Christopher Lee/The Guardian“This closing letter is a joke,” wrote Stout, who says his phone did not register any calls, texts or emails from the state at the time. “Imagine my frustration to do something right and this is how investigations are handled.“I’m pissed about this because you keep screwing people over. Fourteen cents doesn’t seem like a lot,” he added, but “for somebody who’s already hurting” that 14 cents could add up to “a meal their kids miss”.During a June visit to the Somerset 7-Eleven where Stout spotted the overcharge, a Guardian reporter brought two 14-ounce bottles of 7-Select cold-pressed juice advertised on the shelf at “2 for $6” to the counter only to have them ring up at $7.78. Presented with the discrepancy, the cashier counted out a $1.78 refund, suggesting that the sale had probably ended but “we just haven’t removed the sign yet”.In fact, the fine print on the sign indicated that the offer was valid for another three weeks.

title: Alarm bells sound in Brussels as EU sales of Chinese hybrid cars rocket | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Explosive growth in imported vehicles omitted from EV tariffs fuels concern for future of European carmakers
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Explosive growth in imported vehicles omitted from EV tariffs fuels concern for future of European carmakers
Content: Chinese-made BYD passenger battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles await distribution at the docks.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAView image in fullscreenChinese-made BYD passenger battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles await distribution at the docks.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAAutomotive industryAlarm bells sound in Brussels as EU sales of Chinese hybrid cars rocketExplosive growth in imported vehicles omitted from EV tariffs fuels concern for future of European carmakersEU imports three times more from China than bloc exports thereLisa O’CarrollThu 24 Sep 2026 04.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 12.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSales of Chinese hybrid cars have rocketed in the EU in the past four and a half years, data shows, underlining growing concerns in Brussels over the future of the European car industry.In 2022, just 659 Chinese-made fully hybrid cars (vehicles in which the petrol or diesel engine charge the motor and battery) were sold in the EU. However, after Brussels imposedanti-subsidy tariffs on fully electric cars from Chinain 2024, sales of hybrids have shot up to 160,662 in the first seven months of this year.Eurostat figures show that sales of Chinese-made plug-in hybrid vehicles – models popular for longer driving distances that can recharge via both the fuel engine and an external power source – have also soared, rising from 56,706 sold in 2022 to 217,764 from January to July this year.The volume of Chinese hybrids on the roads is now spooking the car industry and Brussels, which has askedChinato voluntarily reduce its hybrid exports to the EU or face safeguards, likely to be quotas.On Thursday the German car industry for the first time indicated it would be willing to consider tariffs on Chinese hybrids specifically.High-mileage electric cars are more reliable than petrol ones, study findsRead moreThe German Association of the Automotive Industry, VDA, called on the European Commission to carry out a comprehensive assessment of the impact of any trade safeguards, which can range from quotas to price floors and tariffs.It said: “The EU must also have an effective and up-to-date set of trade defence instruments at its disposal. Where unfair conduct is proven, the use of WTO-compliant trade defence instruments must be considered; these are legitimate and tried-and-tested means of achieving a level playing field and safeguarding fair conditions of competition.”According to new figures released by the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), hybrid cars now account for almost 37% of the overall market, with electric cars making up just over 21% of the market.The ACEA figures show three Chinese manufacturers – BYD, Chery and Leapmotor – making significant inroads with triple-digit growth in the EU.A fourth firm, Geely, has had a steady 8% increase in the first eight months of the year and remains the most popular Chinese brand in the EU, with 205,000 cars sold in the first eight months of the year. Its brands include Sweden’s Volvo and Polestar, the EU’s only all-electric car manufacturer.BYD is catching up with Geely, with sales rocketing by 163% year on year with 177,000 units sold.Both firms, along with a fifth Chinese manufacturer, SAIC, are now firmly ahead of Elon Musk’s Tesla, which sold 142,000 cars across the bloc in the first seven months of the year.European car manufacturers still dominate, with the Volkswagen group selling 2m cars in the first eight months of the year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSales of electric cars are also growing fast in parts of Europe including Germany, up 75% to 69,000 units in August, and in France, where sales are up by 112%. In Slovenia, sales have increased by 266%. This compares with the UK, up 27% in August to 28,000 EVs sold, and Ireland, up just 7% to 2,200 units.Earlier this month, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, described the now€1.18bn-a-day trade deficitbetween the bloc and China as having reached an unsustainable “tipping point”.The EU’s trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao will meet on 8 and 9 October to try to build a truce.Also hoping for a trade truce are Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, who meet in theirthird summit in 12 monthsin Washington on Thursday.Trump agreed in South Korea last October to drop tariffs on certain Chinese imports in exchange for a suspension of China’s export restriction on rare earths, critical to the car industry across the US, EU and the UK.Some believe a deal may not have been reached yet and the suspension may not be announced until the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference next month.Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryEuropeEuropean UnionChinese economyChinaAsia PacificInternational tradenewsShareReuse this content

title: João Félix strike for Portugal enough to sink Wales but Ronaldo fever falls flat | Nations League | The Guardian
description: João Félix’s first-half goal gave Portugal a 1-0 win against a resilient Wales in their Nations League opener
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: João Félix’s first-half goal gave Portugal a 1-0 win against a resilient Wales in their Nations League opener
Content: João Félix of Portugal celebrates with teammates after scoring.Photograph: Gualter Fatia/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJoão Félix of Portugal celebrates with teammates after scoring.Photograph: Gualter Fatia/Getty ImagesNations LeagueJoão Félix strike for Portugal enough to sink Wales but Ronaldo fever falls flatBen Fisherat the José Alvalade StadiumThu 24 Sep 2026 16.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 19.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was a comic-strip feel to another eventful evening in the kingdom of Cristiano Ronaldo. Where to start? It was the 67th minute when his No 7 went up on the fourth official’s board, the cue to remove the captain’s armband from his left bicep before departing to a universal ovation, but for the pocket ofWalessupporters.The referee, Donatas Rumsas, hurried him off the pitch but Ronaldo, his hair glazed copper, was presumably ruminating on a series of missed chances, a sitter from a few yards at the start of the second half, and his disallowed goal, after skating offside to latch on to a Bruno Fernandes pass. The grandiose “Siu” celebration went to waste, though try telling that to the locals who worship him.Gakpo denies Klopp perfect start as Xavi’s Netherlands rescue draw against GermanyRead moreIn the end, Portugal began theirdefence of the Nations Leaguewith a narrow victory courtesy of another Al-Nassr forward, João Felix’s deflected first-half strike from the edge of the box beating Danny Ward in goal.Many of the Wales squad have been lightly raced of late, but they could have snatched a late equaliser when Brennan Johnson hit the crossbar and Rúben Dias desperately denied Lewis Koumas, who again impressed Craig Bellamy. For Wales, this was an exhaustive physical effort and afterwards the head coach, citing his own experiences as a player, referenced how mentally sapping games against elite opposition can prove. “I needed an ice pack on my head,” Bellamy said.All eyes were on Ronaldo, back playing in Lisbon for the first time since last October, at the José Alvalade Stadium where he made his name as a teenager. The 41-year-old started, as Jorge Jesus promised he would, and despite Ronaldo talking of a new era, different tactics and even a different language, alluding to Jesus’s predecessor Roberto Martínez, this all felt rather run of the mill.Rúben Neves, another player in Saudi, replacing João Neves in Portugal’s three-man midfield was the only change from theirWorld Cup last-16 exitby Spain in Dallas.Ronaldo finished with 27 touches, the fewest of any of Portugal’s outfield starters, and looked to the heavens after fluffing the best of the hosts’ chances to extend their lead four minutes into the second half.View image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo sends a shot wide on a night when good fortune in front of goal eluded him.Photograph: Miguel Lemos/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty ImagesNeves put in a delicious cross from the right flank but Ronaldo, unmarked and alone with his thoughts in the six-yard box, shanked the ball over off his left shin. Sunday’s visit to Norway is his next opportunity to edge towards his 1,000 goals target. “I took him out 25 minutes before the end, because I thought it was important to have a fresh player on the pitch,” Jesus said. “I knew that Cris could stay a little longer, five or 10 minutes, but I was going to take him out anyway, I had planned it.” In a previous answer, he added: “Some players who are important were not up to their quality.”Jesus, who twice managed Benfica and spent three years here in charge of Sporting, knows all about Ronaldo, having spent last season coaching him at Al-Nassr and defended the striker on the eve of this game, describing him as a symbol of Portugal. It is hard to disagree on that front. Ronaldo-mania is omnipresent in Lisbon, chiefly inside the official Portugal stores in Praça da Figueira, the city’s downtown, where you can buy CR7-branded briefs, face masks, action figures, lanyards, Lego, and even a Ronaldo boxset celebrating his time at Sporting.Bellamy accepted Wales would suffer against a starting XI boasting five Champions League winners and three Ballon d’Or nominees, but began confidently. Bellamy does not have the same quality at his disposal, with Harry Wilson, Wales’s best performer in recent years, and Karl Darlow, these days the undisputed No 1, among those absent through injury. A harmless Ben Cabango header was Wales’s sole effort at goal in the first half and they did not trouble Diogo Costa. “He practically didn’t have to touch the ball,” Jesus said of his goalkeeper.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIsrael’s Saied Abu Farchi sent off for gun gesture celebration in defeat by AustriaRead moreRonaldo spurned four decent chances in the first half alone, the best of which was from about 12 yards and left him scuffing his boots in frustration. Then, after a predictably excitable buildup, there was a free-kick flighted into Wales’s yellow wall. He should have done better when Fernandes presented him with his first opening amid huge cheers from the locals, but his touch was rusty and the ball bobbled off his left foot, and he later volleyed wide from an awkward angle.Wales were valiant. Jay Dasilva was excellent at left-back. Ben Davies, a Wales centurion and always a dependable performer for his country, marshalled the defence on his second appearance of the season, his only minutes for Tottenham coming against a Charlton B team in the Carabao Cup. Ward’s sole appearance was in the same competition for Wrexham six weeks ago.Portugal racked up 23 shots but recorded only five on target and Wales will take plenty of confidence from this slender defeat. “I’m fully aware of who we were playing and what their value is,” Bellamy said, claiming the value of Portugal’s squad totals £1.4bn. “But the positive I’m coming away with is: I think there’s more [to come from us]. I’m beyond proud. We showed a big heart.”Explore more on these topicsNations LeaguePortugalWalesmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: NHL’s Andrei Kuzmenko steps away from team after father killed in Siberia bear attack | NHL | The Guardian
description: Alexander Kuzmenko, a hockey coach in Russia whose son plays for the Pittsburgh Penguins, suffered fatal injuries when he was attacked on a fishing trip
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Alexander Kuzmenko, a hockey coach in Russia whose son plays for the Pittsburgh Penguins, suffered fatal injuries when he was attacked on a fishing trip
Content: Andrei Kuzmenko joined the Pittsburgh Penguins this summer.Photograph: Jeanine Leech/Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndrei Kuzmenko joined the Pittsburgh Penguins this summer.Photograph: Jeanine Leech/Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesNHLNHL’s Andrei Kuzmenko steps away from team after father killed in Siberia bear attackAlexander Kuzmenko was fatally injured on fishing tripRegion had been flagged as site of recent bear activityForward joined Pittsburgh Penguins this yearGuardian sportThu 24 Sep 2026 13.08 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePittsburgh Penguins forward Andrei Kuzmenko has stepped away from the team after his father, Alexander Kuzmenko, was killed in a bear attack in Siberia this week.REN TVwas the first to report the death of the 62-year-old, who was a well-known hockey coach in Russia.Kuzmenko was with a group on a fishing trip on Tuesday in Tuva, a landlocked region in Siberia near Russia’s southern border with Mongolia, according to REN TV’sreports. The group encountered a bear that attacked Kuzmenko.Ambulances were reportedly delayed in reaching the group because they were in a densely forested area along the Krasnaya River. REN TV said the group traveled down the river for four hours before an ambulance could locate them. Kuzmenko was airlifted to a hospital with severe facial injuries before he was pronounced dead on Wednesday.“The Pittsburgh Penguins organization was deeply saddened this morning to learn of the passing of Andrei Kuzmenko’s father, Alexander,” team president and general manager Kyle Dubas said in a statement on Thursday. “Our deepest thoughts and sympathies are with the Kuzmenko family and their loved ones as they grieve the loss of Alexander. We ask that the privacy of Andrei and the Kuzmenko family be respected at this time.“Andrei chose to be surrounded by his teammates and practice with the team this morning before returning to Moscow to be with his family this afternoon. Andrei and the Kuzmenko family have the full support of the Penguins organization during this time.”REN TV reported that the forested area where the group went had previously been restricted because of bear activity. The outlet said at least 15 people have been killed in bear attacks acrossRussiathis year.Andrei Kuzmenko, 30, signed for the Penguins in July. After breaking out with CSKA Moscow and SKA Saint Petersburg in the Kontinental Hockey League, he made hisNHLdebut in 2022 with the Vancouver Canucks. He also had stints with the Calgary Flames, Philadelphia Flyers and Los Angeles Kings before joining Pittsburgh. He has 85 goals and 97 assists in 271 NHL appearances.After Andrei Kuzmenko left the Canucks in 2023, his father, mother Galina, sister Victoria and a childhood friendwrote a letterto the city’s fans thanking them for their “warm hospitality towards our son” and “for helping him grow professionally”.The NHL season begins on Tuesday.Explore more on these topicsNHLUS sportsRussianewsShareReuse this content

title: Former England player Andy Carroll reveals he was sexually assaulted in 2021 | Andy Carroll | The Guardian
description: Andy Carroll has said in his autobiography he was sexually assaulted by a man at his home during his second spell at Newcastle in 2021
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Andy Carroll has said in his autobiography he was sexually assaulted by a man at his home during his second spell at Newcastle in 2021
Content: ‘What happened to me affected every facet of my life,’ said Andy Carroll, who is now a player and co-owner at Dagenham & Redbridge.Photograph: Gavin Ellis/TGS Photo/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘What happened to me affected every facet of my life,’ said Andy Carroll, who is now a player and co-owner at Dagenham & Redbridge.Photograph: Gavin Ellis/TGS Photo/ShutterstockAndy CarrollFormer England player Andy Carroll reveals he was sexually assaulted in 2021Carroll was assaulted by a man at his home while he sleptAttacker found guilty of sexual offences after player testifiedPress AssociationThu 24 Sep 2026 13.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former England forwardAndy Carrollhas revealed in his autobiography he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021. The 37-year-old included the details in his book, Owning It. As a victim of sexual assault, Carroll was automatically granted anonymity.Carroll revealed the incident took place at his home during a second spell at Newcastle. The offender – a friend of his former partner, who was staying away at the time – was later jailed for three years, with Carroll having testified in court.The former Liverpool and West Ham striker, who is now a player/co-owner of the National League South club Dagenham & Redbridge, said the incident happened when he was sleeping. He then threw the man out of the house, then knocked him unconscious when he attempted to get back inside.“I was sexually assaulted, there I said it. Scary to even think about and only a few people knew about it before now,” wrote Carroll, who had decided to include the incident in his book “at the very last minute” after discussing it with his partner, Lou Teasdale.“Me and Lou spent a lot of time discussing whether to mention it in this book or not. I avoided my publisher for so long that they probably suspected I got cold feet.“Scary to talk about but it’s made [me] the person I am today as much as any of the good stuff. And if me talking about it helps just one person then good, it will have been worth it.”Carroll said testifying in court, where the attacker was found guilty of sexual offences and placed on the sex offenders register, was “humiliating and embarrassing and absolutely horrendous”.The 37-year-old said: “What happened to me affected every facet of my life. I’d think about it every day, making it difficult to focus on anything else, including football … The trauma of what happened to me hasn’t gone away.”Explore more on these topicsAndy CarrollnewsShareReuse this content

title: Japan teenager Shin Ohashi overcomes Covid and fever to smash breaststroke world record | Swimming | The Guardian
description: The Japanese teenager Shin Ohashi said a bout of Covid helped him smash the men’s 200m breaststroke world record
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Japanese teenager Shin Ohashi said a bout of Covid helped him smash the men’s 200m breaststroke world record
Content: Japan’s Shin Ohashi after breaking the men’s 200m breaststroke world record at the Asian Games in Tokyo.Photograph: Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJapan’s Shin Ohashi after breaking the men’s 200m breaststroke world record at the Asian Games in Tokyo.Photograph: Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty ImagesSwimmingJapan teenager Shin Ohashi overcomes Covid and fever to smash breaststroke world recordSwimmer wins 200m gold at Asian GamesSays Covid helped him rest and ‘was a good thing’Agence France-PresseThu 24 Sep 2026 10.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Japanese teenager Shin Ohashi said a bout of Covid helped him smash the men’s 200m breaststroke world record in a time of 2min 4.83sec at the Asian Games on Thursday.The 17-year-old won his second gold of the Games in Tokyo despite running a temperature of about 39C just days before the competition began.Thirteen-year-old swim sensation sets women’s 200m butterfly record at Asian GamesRead moreThe win continued his stunning rise in the sport and marked him out as the man to beat at the Los Angeles Olympics in two years’ time.Ohashi said his illness had been a blessing in disguise after cutting more than half a second off the previous world record, held by China’s Qin Haiyang, which had stood since July 2023. “With the Covid, it made me feel uneasy mentally,” he said. “But on the other hand it meant I was forced to rest my body properly for a while. I think that was a good thing.”Ohashi had already won the 100m breaststroke gold this week in Tokyo after a dead heat with China’s Dong Zhihao. He will try to make it a hat-trick when he swims in Friday’s 50m breaststroke.Ohashi took control from the off in the 200m final and from then it was a race against the clock. He finished 3.84sec faster than the silver medallist Denis Petrashov of Kyrgyzstan.“My next goal is to win gold at next year’s world championships and then go on to win gold at the Olympics,” said Ohashi. “I don’t want to be satisfied and I want to feel these emotions again.”Ohashi’s success has seen him tipped to follow in the footsteps of the Japanese breaststroke great Kosuke Kitajima. The “Frog King” won the 100m-200m double at the 2004 Athens Olympics and repeated the feat four years later in Beijing.Ohashi said he was “watching all the other swimmers and trying to learn from them”. He continued: “I don’t really have any heroes, I think all swimmers are fantastic. But in terms of achievements, Kitajima is the one I would like to emulate most.”Explore more on these topicsSwimmingWorld recordsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kim Kardashian’s Team Moms highlights the ridiculous excess of the US youth-sports industry | Baseball | The Guardian
description: A new Paramount+ series premiering Thursday turns pushy sports parents into glossy entertainment – with the children largely ushered off stage
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: A new Paramount+ series premiering Thursday turns pushy sports parents into glossy entertainment – with the children largely ushered off stage
Content: The cast of Team Moms, a new reality series following a group of mothers whose children play competitive youth baseball.Photograph: Paramount+View image in fullscreenThe cast of Team Moms, a new reality series following a group of mothers whose children play competitive youth baseball.Photograph: Paramount+BaseballKim Kardashian’s Team Moms highlights the ridiculous excess of the US youth-sports industryA new Paramount+ series premiering Thursday turns pushy sports parents into glossy entertainment – with the children largely ushered off stageAndrew LawrenceThu 24 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 09.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRemember when pushy sports parents were deserving objects of our collective scorn? WhenMarv MarinovichandJim Piercewere bywords for abusive fatherhood, Sarah Palin made the overbearing hockey mom a global punchline, and grim stories of pushy parentsassaulting officials, kids and one another grabbed headlines and traineda harsh spotlight on youth sports? Well, the rebrand is in full swing.Team Moms: Baseball is a glossy new reality series premiering Thursday that aims to recast the pushy sports parent as something well worth coveting, a sexy black hat with a designer label. From the makers of Love Island (ITV America), forHollywood’s most rapacious studio(Paramount Skydance), with none other thanbasketball mom Kim Kardashianattached as executive producer, the Paramount+ series follows a cluster of parents whose sons attend Legendary Prep Academy –a Scottsdale, Arizona baseball hothousewith an intense focus on cultivating diamond gems. Anyone coming to this expecting genuine insights on a $40bn industry that’s nowunder siege from private equity, swallowing ever larger chunks of hard-earned family budgets along the way, should know up front: this is a closer cousin to Bravo’s Real Housewives franchise than ESPN’s 30 for 30.The title alone – a deliberate play on Teen Mom,MTV’s train-wreck young-mothers series– gives the game away. It makes abundantly clear that the focus of Team Moms’ eight hour-ish episodes isn’t the 13- and 14-year-olds chasing their field of dreams. It’s the middle-aged parents chasing vicarious glory, proximal clout and social validation. The tone is reinforced at the start of the show, in an around-the-horn-style opening title sequence that punctuates family portraits with the kids’ heroic glove work before landing on baseball cards of the individual moms fanned out over home plate. Never mind that the moms are set up to be the fall guys for the real drama queens: the dads.View image in fullscreenParents watch from the sidelines as their children compete in the high-pressure world of travel baseball featured in Team Moms.Photograph: Paramount+The Kardashian-meets-Love Island alchemy is undeniable in the way Team Moms presents staggering opulence as wholly incidental: the luxury car fleets, the giga-mansions, the immaculate show kitchens that provide the backdrop for daily routines and gossip. The kids move through this world as you’d expect of kids who essentially have baseball for a job, zombieing themselves from bed to a hot cup ofcoffeebefore shuffling off into the predawn for another shift at the ballpark salt mines. For inspiration, the kids only need look to the writing on the walls:Prefer pain. Comfort is a slow death. Die growing, pledge growth to the grave. Upton Sinclair,eat your heart out.It’s a five-days-a-week grind before you even get to weekend games – many of which demand hours of commuting – or the additional baseball “tutoring” many of these families seek out in hopes of keeping their kids on a steady development curve or outpacing their peers. The same can hardly be said of the academic side of this equation, which doesn’t appear to take up more than a few hours of the training day if the players even have energy left to get it at all. Producers can barely be bothered to ask about the obvious toll of this grind in the gratuitous kiddie confessionals, much less get them to consider the prospect of taking up other sports – something many great athletes do, as my former Sports Illustrated colleague David Epstein explores inhis 2019 book Range.View image in fullscreenYoung players from the Legendary Performance Academy arrive at the ballpark ahead of a game.Photograph: Paramount+Of course none of this athletic hothousing comes cheap. Legendary Prep doesn’t publicize its tuition costs, but I suppose you’re already in trouble if you even have to ask. Similar academies charge anywhere from $12,000 to more than $20,000 annually for the same basic bundle of high-level athletic training, sports science analytics, team travel and a hybrid or supervised online academic curriculum. There was no explicit mention of tuition costs in the three-ish episodes of Team Moms that I watched, but one mom did let slip that she bought her 16-year-old daughter aPorsche Macanto somewhat offset the money the family spends on her brother’s baseball prospects.While this same mom – we’ll call her Pilates Mom because the names on this show aren’t as important as the archetypes – bankrolls her boy’s dream despite her keen awareness of his having “a 0.02% chance” of making it to the MLB, the other parents in the series are quite convinced they have the next Aaron Judge or Bryce Harper on their hands. (With names like Jett and Stryker, how could these kids miss?) All the families are white, and the irony of their sons of privilege chasing an MLB dream that so many less-resourced Latin American kids pursue,with relatively outsized success, is completely lost on them (even though that pipelinehas its leaky bits, too).We’re meant to view Pilates Mom as the villain because she swans around in athleisure wear that accentuates her curves and draws snide remarks. Pilates Mom sets tongues wagging after offhandedly calling one boy “a little bitch” during one of her Pilates sessions with the kids – the same boy had told her son he watches Pilates Mom on OnlyFans, prompting a schoolyard dustup.View image in fullscreenPlayers from the Legendary Performance Academy warm up before a game, one casually tossing a baseball as teammates look on.Photograph: Paramount+Team Mom fault lines are drawn in hair dye. On one side, there’s the cliquey blondes: Martha Stewart Mom, the type-A who leaves her husband a “How to Be Me” memo when she steps away from the house; Party Mom, living her best life in retirement with streaks; and Trophy Mom, a Nascar wife who cites marriage and motherhood as her biggest accomplishments. On the other, the slightly more self-aware brunettes: Pilates Mom, often shot inside her empty studio; Wine Mom, the wary wife of a hobby vintner; and Friends Mom, a Courteney Cox lookalike whose coming-out story and enduring friendship with her fogey ex-husband frustrate the parent group into making crude jokes about her “returning to the other side of the pond”.Travel baseball: a world where eight-year-olds are treated like prosRead moreBut the women and their drama just provide cover for their pushy sports spouses. A group spring break trip has Wine Dad torn over whether to let his son, a flashy teen who seems better at branding than baseball, join his friends on a kayaking excursion or drive him an hour away for some extra hitting. (So as a compromise, they do both.) Party Dad can’t stop touting Pilates Mom’s body in mixed company. Only Nascar Dad sets a halfway decent example because Casey Mears,motor racing royalty, has actually been there, done that and ismoving merch.But the worst is Egg Dad – the Humpty Dumpty who can’t let a moment pass without mentioning he played professional hockey, even though he was no better thana minor-minor leaguerin his day. Ever irascible, he’s always threatening to drop the gloves and throw down with the moms and dads at the first sign of a funny look. Egg Dad’s son, a U14 pitcher, is relegated to the fringes of the production after breaking his forearm in a fielding collision. After Egg Mom carts him home from a hospital visit to have the surgical pins removed from his arm, Egg Dad pushes him to get back on the ball.“I don’t even know if I could put on a glove right now,” the kid says.“The doc says it’s up to you, but I want to see you play,” Egg Dad says.View image in fullscreenTensions flare among parents during a gathering in Team Moms, the reality series set in the world of competitive youth baseball.Photograph: Paramount+On spring break, Egg Dad organizes a game of Plant the Flag on the gravel driveway of their Italianate resort compound –Great idea, Wine Dad says, with an eye roll – and his son winds up hurting his armagain. Egg Dad puts his poor kid on the kayak without a thought and then booze-bonds with Party Dad over how soft their two kids are. “[They’ve] got to understand the difference between a real injury and [pain] and just go,” Party Dad says. It seems no amount of Hollywood high gloss can make the stigma of the pushy sports parent disappear, even if it’s buffed and contoured by Kim K.Likely, this won’t be the last Team Mom installment if the titular colon is any indication. You can just picture spinoffs into soccer, tennis and perhaps even the southern California youth basketball scene – where Kardashian already features prominently. Really, the fact that youth sports in the US can so easily be spun into idle entertainment tells you everything that’s wrong with a homegrown approach to athletic development that favors the paying parents over the toiling kids, or even the major college and professional clubs who have a financial incentive to turn a catch-as-catch-can approach to talent scouting into a halfway dependable,European-style conveyor belt.And the fact that Kardashian and her producing partners intuitively know that parents would rather watch richer, better-looking versions of themselves than watch kids like theirs crash and burn while pursuing their dreams is just proof that pushy sports parents haven’t softened. They’re just reaping the benefits of softer lighting now.Explore more on these topicsBaseballUS sportsReality TVTelevisionKim KardashianUS televisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: US Jockey Club orders racehorse Austrian Painter to be renamed due to Hitler reference | Horse racing | The Guardian
description: The US Jockey Club has ordered a racehorse to be renamed due to a reference to Adolf Hitler
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The US Jockey Club has ordered a racehorse to be renamed due to a reference to Adolf Hitler
Content: The horse won a race in Indiana on Monday.Photograph: Mark Evans/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe horse won a race in Indiana on Monday.Photograph: Mark Evans/Getty ImagesHorse racingUS Jockey Club orders racehorse Austrian Painter to be renamed due to Hitler referenceHitler was an artist in Vienna before first world warHorse also has full sister called New OrderGuardian sportThu 24 Sep 2026 08.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 19.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US Jockey Club has ordered a racehorse to be renamed after ruling the animal’s name was a reference to Adolf Hitler.In a story first reported by Horse Racing Nation, Austrian Painter won its debut race at the Horseshoe Indianapolis track on Monday. However, the Jockey Club received a complaint about the name and began an investigation. Hitler, who was born in Austria,was a professional artist in Viennabefore the first world war. People often use the term “Austrian Painter” online to discuss Hitler without naming him in order to avoid content moderation filters.Belmont Park is back: inside New York’s $555m bet on horse racingRead moreScott Herbertson, the two-year-old’s owner and breeder, appeared to suggest on social media that the name was a reference to Austrian artist Gustav Klimt. The Jockey Club said Austrian Painter’s full sister, New Order, must also be renamed. As well as the well-known British rock band, New Order can refer to Nazi Germany’s plan for an occupied Europe. “New order is my favored band you lune,” Herbertson wrote on social media.The Jockey Club said Austrian Painter would now be known as Merrylegs.“Earlier this week, the Registry was notified through a formal complaint that the name was offensive, and we immediately began a review. The Registrar determined that the name is ineligible under Rule 6.F.9.d, which prohibits names that ‘are likely to be offensive or threatening based upon factors including, but not limited to, color, creed, disability, ethnicity, gender, national origin, race, religion, politics, or sexual orientation,’” the Jockey Club said in a statement Wednesday. “We take these matters seriously and appreciate that they were brought to our attention.”The Jockey Club has ordered horses to be renamed before, usually for racist references. In 2019, a horse called Noose was renamed Scabbard after an order from the Jockey Club.Explore more on these topicsHorse racingUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Have Arsenal been figured out? Three big questions after Brighton’s upset | Sport | The Guardian
description: This week, we dive into the big questions surrounding the most surprising result of the Premier League weekend
Author: Graham Ruthven
Headline: This week, we dive into the big questions surrounding the most surprising result of the Premier League weekend
Content: Arsenal were overrun by Brighton in a 3-0 loss this past weekend.Photograph: Simon Dack/TPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenArsenal were overrun by Brighton in a 3-0 loss this past weekend.Photograph: Simon Dack/TPI/ShutterstockSportHave Arsenal been figured out? Three big questions after Brighton’s upsetThis week, we dive into the big questions surrounding the most surprising result of the Premier League weekendGraham RuthvenThu 24 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore this past weekend, Arsenal had not lost in thePremier Leaguesince April. Nine straight league wins had been enough to crown the Gunners as champions at the end of last season and firmly establish them as the team to beat early this season.Against Brighton on Saturday, though, the team to beat were beaten. Thoroughly.Arsenal weren’t justpecked by the Seagulls. They were pressed to death by them. Usually so resilient, even in the face of such opposition exuberance, the Premier League champions fell apart on the south coast, losing a match by three goals for the first time in over three years. It was jarring to see Arsenal so out of sorts.Mikel Arteta agrees contract extension expected to keep him at Arsenal until 2030Read moreWas this simply a Control-Alt-Delete game forArsenal, or has the manner of the Seagulls’ performance provided a template for others to use? Was Saturday merely a blip that the Gunners will quickly recover from or the first crack in their previously impenetrable armour? Let’s tackle those and some other questions from the Premier League’s big upset before the international break.How did Brighton do it?The most effective element of Brighton’s performance was their relentless pressing of Arsenal in periods of settled possession. While the Seagulls still had pressing triggers which prompted them to push high up the pitch at certain moments, Fabian Hürzeler also recognised the need to prevent the champions from getting to the edge of the box. They were in Arsenal’s faces for most of the match.Brighton defensive midfielder Chema Andrés pushed up on to Martin Ødegaard whenever he could, moving Brighton into a man-to-man shape against the ball and limiting the Norwegian whenever he dropped deep. Faced with a four-on-four situation in build-out, Arsenal simply weren’t sharp enough on the ball to get around the press, forcing David Raya to go long more times than he would have liked. From there, Brighton could turn the ball over and attack at speed in the other direction.This made the match a transition-heavy affair which suited Brighton’s attacking players. Focal point Charalampos Kostoulas was an all-round threat while Pascal Gross, Maxim De Cuyper and Diego Gómez were impactful in open space. Hürzeler’s approach never allowed the game state to shift in Arsenal’s favour. He covered all bases.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘They deserved to win’: Mikel Arteta left humbled by Brighton defeatRead moreIs Brighton’s formula replicable?Maybe, but it will be tough. Hürzeler’s team are a physical force of nature. Of the four players that covered the most distance on Saturday, three were Brighton players and it’s these legs and lungs that allows them to press so hard for so long. No Premier League team is averaging more high turnovers per 90 minutes this season. Not every team can do what Brighton do.For all that Brighton’s approach as a team, and a club, epitomises the modern game, there was an old school quality to the way they disrupted Arsenal. “We wanted to win the small battles first,” explained Hürzeler on talkSport, revealing the instructions he gave his players. “Win the first header, win the first tackle, win the first throw-in, win the first corner.”Should Arsenal fans be worried?Probably not, since there were some mitigating factors that explain Arsenal’s underperformance. The trip to Brighton was their fourth away game in just 10 days, and their general lethargy reflected this. Furthermore, many of Arsenal’s best players, including Martin Ødegaard, Declan Rice and Bukayo Saka, were denied a pre-season due to their extended involvement at the World Cup.Two of Brighton’s three goals came from low-xG shots from outside the box. Arsenal were guilty of not closing the space for the shooter quickly enough, but on another day Gross and Kostoulas would have shot over the bar rather than into the top corner. Indeed, Brighton’s three goals came from a total xG of just 1.31, less than Arsenal’s xG of 1.63.Arsenal are also still without the injured William Saliba whose presence next to Gabriel Magalhaes surely would have steadied their defensive line. Without Ben White in the lineup, the Gunners additionally lacked the chemistry down the right wing that has been such a feature of their early-season success. Saka was a non-factor in the game.Many predicted Arsenal would stroll this season’s title race. They still might. While Manchester City are now top of the table, Arsenal are two points better off now than they were at the same stage of last season when they went on to win the title for the first time since the Arsène Wenger era. Until Saturday, they had won seven out of seven in all competitions this season. Mikel Arteta need not panic.You can bet, however, that the tactical analysts and data crunchers employed by Arsenal’s rivals will have closely watched Brighton’s 3-0 win more than a few times by the time club soccer resumes next month.Explore more on these topicsSportPremier LeagueArsenalBrighton & Hove AlbionFootball tacticsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Russell vows to ‘keep fighting’ in F1 title race despite Antonelli’s advantage | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: The Briton said: ‘I want to try and win every single race. That’s my goal’ after  finishing quickest in practice for Saturday’s Azerbaijan Grand Prix
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: The Briton said: ‘I want to try and win every single race. That’s my goal’ after finishing quickest in practice for Saturday’s Azerbaijan Grand Prix
Content: George Russell is 81 points behind his Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli going into the race in Baku.Photograph: Pavel Bednyakov/APView image in fullscreenGeorge Russell is 81 points behind his Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli going into the race in Baku.Photograph: Pavel Bednyakov/APFormula One 2026Russell vows to ‘keep fighting’ in F1 title race despite Antonelli’s advantage‘I want to try and win every single race. That’s my goal’Briton quickest in practice for Azerbaijan Grand PrixGiles RichardsThu 24 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGeorge Russell has insisted he will keep fighting for the Formula One world championship until it is mathematically gone but while he made an encouraging start to his efforts by going quickest in practice for this weekend’s Azerbaijan Grand Prix the makeup of said numbers remains somewhat in limbo.Russell is 81 points behind his Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli going into the race in Baku which is taking place on Saturday to avoid clashing with Azerbaijan’s national remembrance day. The Italian has eight victories this season including the past two in a row, coming through towin from 19thon the grid in Monza and thentaking the flag in Madrid.‘I want to go’: Lewis Hamilton hopes F1 is able to end season in Middle EastRead moreDespite having a mountain to climb Russell has maintained the stoical and determined attitude he has demonstrated all season.“I’m going to keep fighting at every single race until it’s mathematically impossible,” he said in Baku. “I want to try and win every single race and put it on pole at every single race. That’s my goal and that’s what I’m working towards every single weekend.“There’s obviously a huge [points] deficit but it’s not even really a consideration right now. I’m in this position because the performance hasn’t been strong enough.”As things stand nine meetings remain with a potential 233 points still on the table. However, with the races that close the season inQatar and Abu Dhabi still under threatof cancellation because of the war in the Middle East, that number may come down. If both races are cancelled it is understood they will be replaced by one round at Imola, reducing the total by 25 points.F1’s current position is that the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi will go ahead, with a final decision now expected in mid-October after the current triple header of races in Baku, Malaysia and Singapore.Mattia Binotto, the Audi team principal, confirmed that this was the latest the sport could leave it for logistical reasons. “As we discussed during the F1 Commission last Monday, mid-October is the last call for such a decision,” he said. “The main challenges are more organisation and logistics.”After the decision the mathematics will at least be clear. If all nine remaining races take place Antonelli would still take the title if he is 100 points ahead in Mexico or 75 clear in Brazil.On track Russell opened well in Azerbaijan, quickest in first practice in a session where Antonelli lost half his run time with a hydraulic problem. In the afternoon Mercedes were once more on top, looking ominously quick on the street circuit which is energy-starved and plays to their car’s strengths in energy harvesting and deployment. Russell was quickest again, a full half a second up on Antonelli with their nearest competitor, Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, eight-tenths back in third.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026George RussellMercedes GPFormula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fury v Joshua fight confirmed for December at Cardiff’s Principality Stadium | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Tyson Fury will face Anthony Joshua in Cardiff on 11 December after one of the biggest bouts in British boxing history was finally agreed
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: Tyson Fury will face Anthony Joshua in Cardiff on 11 December after one of the biggest bouts in British boxing history was finally agreed
Content: Tyson Fury (left) exchanges words with Anthony Joshua after his fight with Arslanbek Makhmudov in April.Photograph: Mark Robinson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTyson Fury (left) exchanges words with Anthony Joshua after his fight with Arslanbek Makhmudov in April.Photograph: Mark Robinson/Getty ImagesBoxingFury v Joshua fight confirmed for December at Cardiff’s Principality StadiumFight on 11 December will start in UK Saturday small hoursNon-title all-British bout to be streamed globally on NetflixBryan Armen Grahamin New YorkThu 24 Sep 2026 08.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Battle of Britain is officially fixed for Wales. Tyson Fury andAnthony Joshuawill stage their long-awaited heavyweight blockbuster in Cardiff on 11 December after an 11th-hour standoff over the venue that threatened to derail the encounter.The agreement ends years of false starts between the former world champions and clears the way for one of the biggest all-British fights in boxing history. The undercard will take place on a Friday night, with the main-event ringwalks at the Principality Stadium expected in the small hours of Saturday morning – widely reported to be around 2am.That is to accommodate a prime-time American audience for Netflix, which will broadcast it globally after its preferred plan to stage the fight at New York’s Madison Square Garden was scuppered.‘I had a headache for days’: Hrgovic reveals brutal toll of Itauma world title fightRead moreThe non-title bout will represent the culmination of a rivalry that has played out in fits and starts and largely from afar for nearly a decade, but securing the necessary signatures required one final round of brinksmanship between the parties.While both fighters had initially agreed to a November date following their respective July tune-up bouts, the original contract stipulated that the fight would take place in the UK.But Netflix, backed by the Saudi power brokerTurki al-Sheikhand Zuffa Boxing executives, pushed for New York after expressing disappointment with the audience for Fury’s July fight in a UK-friendly time slot, according to a source familiar with the negotiations.That preference became the ultimate impasse in the final negotiations. Eddie Hearn, Joshua’s promoter, resisted the proposed move to New York, seeking a contractual addendum to account for the heavier US tax burden. On Thursday, Hearnsaidthe UK provision had proved decisive.“If we hadn’t put that in the contract, which was a request fromAnthony Joshuathat the fight must be in the UK, we wouldn’t have had a leg to stand on,” he said. “This fight would have been in America.”The dispute also drew in the UFC chief executive,Dana White. Fury welcomed White’s involvement, while Hearn opposed him serving as lead promoter, prompting an expletive-laden broadside from Fury. Thursday’s announcement said Al-Sheikh’s The Ring and White “will collaborate to promote” the fight, while making no mention of Hearn, Frank Warren, Matchroom or Queensberry.Tale of the tape: Fury v JoshuaFury, 38, and Joshua, 36, remained on course for the lucrative meetingafter winningagainst limited opponents on successive nights in July. While Joshuasurvived a scarein Saudi Arabia, Fury stopped the 46-year-old Mariusz Wachinside seven rounds in Thailand.Both men are attempting to return to the summit of boxing’s prestige division after suffering two defeats apiece against Oleksandr Usyk, the unbeaten former undisputed heavyweight champion from Ukraine whorelinquished his remaining world title beltsin June but insists he has not retired. Fury has won twice since returning to the ring, while Joshua has spent the year rebuilding afterhis devastating knockout by Daniel Duboisin 2024.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJoshua (30-4-0, 27 KOs) held the IBF’s version of the heavyweight title across two stints from 2016 to 2019 and 2019 to 2021, making seven successful defences while also winning the WBA and WBO belts.Fury (36-2-1, 25 KOs) first became the lineal and unified world championy dethroning Wladimir Klitschkoin 2015, beforebeing stripped of the IBF titleand later relinquishing his remaining belts during a 31-month layoff that saw him swell to nearly 28st amid public battles with addiction and bipolar disorder. The Manchester nativecompleted an extraordinary comebackto hold the WBC title from 2020 to 2024, defending it three times successfully afterending Deontay Wilder’s five-year reign.The rivals came closest to meeting for the undisputed championship in 2021, but the fight collapsed aftera US arbitrator ruledFury was contractually obligatedto face Wilder for a third time.Joshua subsequentlylost his titles to Usyk, with several attempts to revive the Fury contest falling apart in the years since.The bloom is inevitably off the rose. A fight that once promised to determine the world’s best heavyweight will instead bring together two former champions in their late 30s, each twice beaten by Usyk and closer to the end of his career than the peak. Incredibly, boxing’s long-suffering fansdidn’tget it before GTA 6, yet the many years of thwarted negotiations and mutual ill will between Fury and Joshua have endowed the matchup with an aura compelling enough to eclipse its diminished stakes.There was always something incongruous about an all-British affair of this magnitude finally playing out in New York rather than on UK soil, in front of the supporters whose loyalty and spending helped make both men global stars. Only months after hostingTaylor Swift’s weddingand theKnicks’ drought-busting NBA title run, the Garden appeared to have saved its least likely spectacle for last. But after myriad twists and turns, the biggest British fight that can be made today found its way back to where many felt it always belonged.Explore more on these topicsBoxingTyson FuryAnthony JoshuanewsShareReuse this content

title: Raphinha: ‘In my head I was leaving Barça, but a few small words can change you’ | Barcelona | The Guardian
description: The Brazilian had thought his time at Barcelona was ending but now, he tells Sid Lowe, he is thriving as captain and the most potent No 9 in Europe
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: The Brazilian had thought his time at Barcelona was ending but now, he tells Sid Lowe, he is thriving as captain and the most potent No 9 in Europe
Content: Raphinha, the Barcelona and Brazil forward, has relished the twin responsibilities of leading the line and leading the team.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRaphinha, the Barcelona and Brazil forward, has relished the twin responsibilities of leading the line and leading the team.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianBarcelonaInterviewRaphinha: ‘In my head I was leaving Barça, but a few small words can change you’Sid Lowein BarcelonaTwo years ago the Brazilian thought his time at Barcelona was ending but, two La Liga titles later, he is now captain and the most potent No 9 in EuropeThu 24 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor once, Raphael Dias Belloli puts the brakes on. The man who seems to be in perpetual motion, a footballer forever on fast forward, pauses, goes quiet for a moment and then, softly, utters something that says so much: “I think maybe people saw in me something I didn’t realise was there.” He did not know he was a leader, but he likes it. He did not know he was a captain, but according to his manager he is the “perfect captain”. And he did not know he was a No 9 either, but right now he is the best No 9 there is. InBarcelonaor anywhere.There was a time when Raphinha did not know whether he would be in Barcelona, when, feeling unwanted, he had accepted it was over, but this week he extended his contract to 2030. He will be 33 then: he would like to retire here and they would like him to retire here, too, a legend built on empathy and affection. “This is the best decision the club has made,” said Hansi Flick, the head coach Raphinha says changed his life. Sometimes you cannot get what you want so you have to settle for the best.Paper trail of protests: José Mourinho plays the hits in Madrid derby defeat | Sid LoweRead moreThe first word Raphinha uses when training has finished and the tape starts rolling at Sant Joan Despí, when he is addressed as the world’s top No 9, is “false”. It comes with a smile; turns out there is nothingfalseabout this 9. Seven games into the league season, the man filling in at centre-forward has scored 12 goals, plus two in the Champions League. The scorers leading the way in Europe’s other top leagues are five behind. No one in Barcelona’s history has started a season like this. And, no, Raphinha says, he has never played there before: “Even as a kid I wasn’t a 9.”As if it is even about the goals. There may be no one as enjoyable to watch as Raphinha; no one as admirable or important either. The touch at speed is astonishing and there is a wild intensity about everything he does, only it is not wild, he says; it is worked upon, the entire system depending on him. The press defines Barcelona’s identity and it is, Raphinha says, “mechanised”. No, he is not going to reveal how but it begins with him. “As captain, he goes and everyone follows,” Flick says. “We always start with the No 9 and he has that incredible hunger and intensity, the mentality and attitude we need.”Yet this is not what Raphinha or anyone expected. This summer Robert Lewandowski, Ferran Torres and Marcus Rashford departed, having contributed 38 league goals between them last season. They were supposed to be replaced by Julián Álvarez butAtlético Madrid refused to sell, leaving Barcelona with no striker. “There was a moment of need,” Raphinha says. “There was no No 9 for the [friendly] against Basel, so I played there.”Raphinha backs Lamine Yamal to win Ballon d’Or – videoIt was not supposed to be permanent, although Flick suspected it might be and was warming to the idea: Barcelona had not given up on Álvarez yet and the coach considered other solutions, including Anthony Gordon. This was better. Raphinha did not score but Barça got five.“In pre-season we did a few tests: the manager liked what he saw and after Basel he told me a bit about his idea,” Raphinha says. “The adaptation came over the last two years, getting used to coming inside, closer to goal. But we tested [me as] an actual No 9 and it went well. There’s the occasional detail that has to be explained, but I’m OK. Before Elche [on the opening day], he asked if I was comfortable there or wanted to go back to my position. I said it was fine, see how it goes, we can always change back.”Raphinha scored two against Elche, one against Athletic, two against Rayo andanother at Valencia.Against Racing there was a hat-trickand another against Sevilla: right foot, left foot, header. Raphinha showed his old qualities and new, less expected ones: the movement, timing and clinical finishing of a classic No 9, efficiency to go with the intensity. Only one La Liga player has a better shot conversion rate. Against Feyenoord came two more.View image in fullscreenRaphinha (right) is joined by Lamine Yamal – the player he says he is a ‘big brother to’ – after scoring during the Champions League match against Feyenoord.Photograph: Judit Cartiel/Uefa/Getty ImagesNor is it just about him. The point of Raphinha is that it is notevenabout him. Only once this season has he not scored, and against Levante he created the first two, then handed over the penalty for Lamine Yamal to add the third. Barcelona have scored five, two, five, five, five, four, seven and three, respectively in winning their first eight games.Flick had done it again. “I always have and always will say that he changed my mentality, changed me as a person,” Raphinha says.By 2024, Raphinha was convinced he had no future at Barcelona. His numbers were good: 10 goals and 12 assists in his first season, 10 goals and 13 assists in his second. ButLamine Yamal was emergingand, more importantly, Raphinha did not feel backed, completing 90 minutes seven times in 60 games under Xavi Hernández. It had not escaped his attention that Barcelona thought about selling him; it had not escaped anyone’s attention that they wanted to buy Nico Williams, publicly keen to reunite thepair that tore up the Euros.Barcelonafailed twice, and were all the better for it. A Photoshopped image of Williams in his No 11 shirton social media hurt, Raphinha admitted. But Flick had arrived and if there is something even more powerful than the desire to prove people wrong, it is the desire to prove people right.View image in fullscreenRaphinha fires in his team’s fourth goal in the 5-2 win against Rayo Vallecano.Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images“In my head, I knew I was leaving,” Raphinha says. “That was [mentally] done, that’s the truth. I was in Brazil and Flick called. He said come talk to him before taking a final decision. I met him and he said he trusted in me, that I was going to be important, that the team[’s play] would be good for me. In a moment like that, a few small words can change you. I felt a lot of faith in me. He gave me the confidence to play my football. I got an idea into my head: give everything, your life, regardless of the personal moment you’re in.”Love won out, even if Raphinha is swift to add: “If you get results people are going to love you; if not, they’re not.” Feeling supported and valued changed everything. His success is a human story, his qualities human ones. He led Barcelonato the league. Flying in from the left, Raphinha scored 34 goals and provided 26 assists in 57 games.Another titlefollowed in 2025-26 and although injuries reduced his contribution, there were 21 goals and eight assists in 33, Flick’s faith gratefully repaid.His teammates’ faith, too. The dressing room had voted Raphinha as a club captain, third in line. He had not expected it and was genuinely touched. There was something in that moment, in the realisation of how they felt about him, how much they believed in him, that was transformative. Now Flick has named him his first choice.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA jubilant Raphinha with the trophy after winning the Spanish Super Cup against Real Madrid.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesThat moment brings pause, thought. “When I saw people had voted for me, it was like a switch had been flipped, a shift in mindset,” he says. “People could see something in me I didn’t realise was there, and that’s changed me. Before being captain, I didn’t know how much I would like it. Having that responsibility has also changed my mentality, helped me. I never thought I’d like being Barcelona captain so much. You feel you matter. It’s an honour. It’s not just wearing the armband.”He is a natural, as pure a captain as there has been since Carles Puyol – even if he did need to be told. It is there in the relentless example he sets: Raphinha has sprinted the second-furthest distance in La Liga andGradient Sportshas measured only three players with more final-third pressures per 30 minutes out of possession. Raphinha says: “I talk less than most captains but I know people are watching. They think: ‘If this guy’s running like an animal, I have to follow.’. If you talk too much and then don’t do what you have to, people aren’t going to listen.”Yet what teammates saw in him went deeper, to his very being. Leadership is there in the empathy, kindness and understanding too, in Raphinha returning the support that was good for him, an approach at once collective and individual. He says he can see when Lamine Yamal is drifting from games and how to reconnect him, every celebration shared with the teenager. A clip went round recently in which he quietly tells Gordon not to be afraid. And no clip was more powerful, more eloquent, than the moment when Flick sat on the bench, alone, lost in his thoughts andRaphinha consoled him, drawing him out of his dark place, roles reversed.View image in fullscreenFermín López, Raphinha, Lamine Yamal and Anthony Gordon celebrate their team’s third goal against Valencia.Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images“The coach-player relationship is the most important in football,” Raphinha says. “From the moment [Flick] arrived, we could talk to him about anything – and anything isanything. That time, I saw him, head down. At first, I didn’t really understand why. I asked what was wrong. He said he felt the team wasn’t playing well. From what I remember, I told him it was OK, we’d won and we would play well again. I prefer a thousand times to win playing badly than lose playing well. Win games, confidence and the football comes.“What kind of leader [I am] depends on the moment. If I have to be slightly tougher, I can. But I prefer nicer moments, jokes. The last two years have been spectacular so I haven’t had to be thepesado[pain in the arse] often. I know that annoys people but someone has to do it sometimes.”With a squad like this, especially? Four of Barcelona’s first team were born in 2007. “Buah!” Raphinha says, laughing. “That hurts: it shows I’m closer to the end than starting out at 18, 19, like them. But I’m in spectacular physical shape so [retirement] is some way off. It’s very easy with them. There are young players but they’re very responsible about their career, their lives. Once in a while, you have to [be paternal] because they’re kids. But they understand. If they get told off, they know it’s for their own good. I’ll tell them.”View image in fullscreenRaphinha, pictured at the Barcelona training complex, is thriving in the role of captain.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianIs there something of the father figure in him with Lamine Yamal in particular? “No, no,” Raphinha jumps in. “Big brother, that’s better.” And Lamine Yamal is the star who should win the Ballon d’Or, he says: for his “individual numbers, collective titles, and the magic on the pitch, charisma. There’s no doubt. For me, he has to take the prize, no matter what. Even if I wasn’t Lamine’s teammate, for what he does, the numbers, the titles – and I think titles are important – he’sthecandidate. One of one. Of three trophies, he won two with Barcelona. He won the World Cup with Spain.”Only the Champions League escaped them; for two years Barcelona have come close, and it is their obsession now. “Thesemi-final against Inter[in 2025] hurt the most,” Raphinha says. “Against Atlético[in the quarter-final in 2026] we could have gone through, we could talk about things that could have gone differently, decisions. But against Inter, we had one foot in the final and to lose that way was hard. We’re a young team – that’s not an excuse – and sometimes you lack the maturity to manage key moments. This season we’re more mature, better prepared. If we carry on like this, with this mentality, we can compete for it all. We have everything.”Starting from the front with the captain, the leader and the No 9.Explore more on these topicsBarcelonafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gakpo denies Klopp perfect start as Xavi’s Netherlands rescue draw against Germany | Nations League | The Guardian
description: The forward’s 92nd-minute equaliser secured the Netherlands a 1-1 Nations League draw against Germany in a clash of two new head coaches
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: The forward’s 92nd-minute equaliser secured the Netherlands a 1-1 Nations League draw against Germany in a clash of two new head coaches
Content: Cody Gakpo fires home the Netherlands’ equaliser two minutes into stoppage time.Photograph: Marcel van Dorst/DeFodi Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCody Gakpo fires home the Netherlands’ equaliser two minutes into stoppage time.Photograph: Marcel van Dorst/DeFodi Images/ShutterstockNations LeagueGakpo denies Klopp perfect start as Xavi’s Netherlands rescue draw against GermanyNick Amesat the Johan Cruyff ArenaThu 24 Sep 2026 18.39 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 16.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least Germany can be sure it will not be dull.Jürgen Klopphad predicted his debut as head coach could be wild, a trait he would accept as long as his team were lively enough. Both transpired in a frayed, pinball-like game whose lack of quality could be forgiven on account of its entertainment levels. The Netherlands more than merited a brilliant late equaliser from Cody Gakpo and by the time those present had drawn breath it felt appropriate that, for all the talk of new dawns, everyone finished back where they had started.World domination is a far-off prospect for both of these flailing giants on such scrappy, frenetic evidence. But at least those with a stake in this famous old fixture, largely shorn of the spite and spit that defined it of old, could come away feeling something. Restoring those essential sensations of joy, pain and meaning sits at the very top of Klopp’s priorities.Germanylooked raw and scattergun for long periods, reined in only by their lack of technical aptitude, but there were signs of an energy that had long been missing.Israel’s Saied Abu Farchi sent off for gun gesture celebration in defeat by AustriaRead moreNonetheless it was the more understated Xavi, making his own bow in charge of the hosts, who could punch the air in added time after Gakpo volleyed in a wonderful outside-of-the-boot cross from the substitute Ruben van Bommel. It so happens that the 22-year-old Van Bommel is son of the 79-times capped Mark; his grandfather is the formerNetherlandsmanager Bert van Marwijk. An enthusiastic if largely toothless performance from Xavi’s crop was a reminder that the stardust of Van Bommel senior’s day is largely absent now; the equaliser’s conception, though, left lingering promise that the past can birth a brighter future.“In a parallel world, if someone said you’d get a draw in Holland you’d take that,” Klopp said. “I feel we lost two points because of the time we conceded. But I’m fine with tonight, not more.” His approach to squad management across this four-gameNations Leaguerun had been to unveil a sprawling 44-player squad, a handful only passingly familiar even to some seasoned Bundesliga watchers, that would be split between assignments. His plans, and perhaps those of two club managers he must keep onside, were derailed by concerning injuries to Jamal Musiala and Kai Havertz.The former felt his thigh in the warm-up, Nadiem Amiri taking his place in the starting lineup; Havertz was similarly afflicted early on, departing on the half-hour, and the pair were due to have MRI scans before returning home. “I hope we get the diagnosis tonight, I hope it’s nothing serious,” said Klopp, who expected the pair to at least miss Sunday’s match against Greece.His team had begun with the intensity demanded before riding their luck, Virgil van Dijk unfortunate not to put one over his old boss when his glancing header was ruled out for a soft foul by Brian Brobbey on Marc-André ter Stegen. The Netherlands were further aggrieved when, with Brobbey lying on the floor near halfway requiring treatment, Joshua Kimmich elected to play on and set in train the move that opened Klopp’s account. The debutant right-back Philipp Treu crossed for Karim Adeyemi to attempt a close-range shot and, from the rebound, Felix Nmecha swept in.View image in fullscreenFelix Nmecha finds the back of the net from close range to give Germany the lead.Photograph: Dean Mouhtaropoulos/Getty ImagesVan Dijk led impassioned home protests, which turned into scuffles between the sides on the far touchline, but no laws had been broken. Germany should have doubled their lead when Adeyemi spooned Nathaniel Brown’s pass horribly high, Klopp reduced to grim laughter at the side, but Xavi’s players took charge thereafter.“The second half is the way we must play,” Xavi said. “We want to show this ambition, passion and desire.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJoão Félix strike for Portugal enough to sink Wales but Ronaldo fever falls flatRead moreTer Stegen, playing at his new Ajax home, frustrated his old Barcelona manager with commendable saves on numerous occasions while looking consistently jittery under set pieces. He should have finally been beaten when Max Meerdink, on for the stricken Brobbey, somehow diverted Denzel Dumfries’s centre wide from a matter of feet.Germany were brisk but bereft of control in a scruffy but beguiling second period; much of that could be put down to their new broom but it will surely have irked Klopp that the substitute Serge Gnabry, one of his more experienced call-ups, had presented the ball carelessly to Van Bommel before the leveller.“To develop a way of football you need more than two days,” Klopp said. “We only scratched the surface. We have to go deeper.” For better or worse, this taster was enough to promise a compelling ride ahead.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueNetherlandsGermanyJürgen Kloppmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Israel’s Saied Abu Farchi sent off for gun gesture celebration in defeat by Austria | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Israel’s forward Saied Abu Farchi was ⁠sent off for celebrating his goal by using the corner ⁠flag to simulate a gun in a Nations League loss to Austria
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Israel’s forward Saied Abu Farchi was ⁠sent off for celebrating his goal by using the corner ⁠flag to simulate a gun in a Nations League loss to Austria
Content: Saied Abu Farchi, who had been booked four minutes earlier, is shown a red card after his goal celebration.Photograph: Georg Hochmuth/APA/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSaied Abu Farchi, who had been booked four minutes earlier, is shown a red card after his goal celebration.Photograph: Georg Hochmuth/APA/AFP/Getty ImagesNations LeagueIsrael’s Saied Abu Farchi sent off for gun gesture celebration in defeat by AustriaForward uses corner flag to simulate gun after equaliserNations League match ends in 3-1 loss for IsraelAgenciesThu 24 Sep 2026 17.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 19.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael’s forward Saied Abu Farchi was ⁠sent off for celebrating his goal against Austria in ⁠his side’s 3-1 ​Nations League defeat on Thursday by using the corner ⁠flag to simulate a gun.Abu Farchi headed home in the 55th ⁠minute to bring Israel level after ​Austria had ‌taken the lead ‌through a Romano Schmid penalty before ‌half-time at the Raiffeisen Arena in Linz.The 20-year-old ran to the corner flag, grabbed it and made a gun-firing gesture during his celebration.View image in fullscreenSaied Abu Farchi after scoring his side’s equaliser against Austria.Photograph: Georg Hochmuth/APA/AFP/Getty ImagesThe ‌referee had booked Abu Farchi four minutes earlier and showed ​him a second yellow card for the celebration, leavingIsraelwith 10 players.Austria regained ⁠the lead in the 90th minute through ​Phillipp ​Mwene, who scored via Paul ​Wanner’s cross. ‌Sasa Kalajdzic ​added ​a third in stoppage time with a close-range finish.Gakpo denies Klopp perfect start as Xavi’s Netherlands rescue draw against GermanyRead moreTheRepublic ofIrelandslipped to a 1-0 defeat away atKosovoin their Nations League opener in Pristina. The buildup had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which the Ireland manager, Heimir Hallgrímsson, had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly. The home side saw two shots cleared off the line before the Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhín Kelleher clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson’s side got to the break on level terms.Ireland, who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday, showed plenty of spirit as they dug in for the second half, but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when the Kosovo captain, Vedat Muriqi, bundled the ball in from close range.In a Group A4 match,Norway’s ‌Erling Haaland struck twice, including a 74th-minute winner, to edge his team pastDenmark3-2 in Oslo and earn their first competitive win over their opponents.“It tasted sweet.
