It feels great to beat our neighbours,” the captain, Martin Ødegaard, said. “There is a lot we could have done better, but ​even when we were put under pressure, we found a way back and responded.”View image in fullscreenErling Haaland scores to put Norway 2-0 ahead against DenmarkPhotograph: Ulrik Pedersen/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockThe Danes had powered back from a two-goal deficit and levelled the game on the hour after first-half goals from Oscar Bobb and Haaland had put the hosts 2-0 up. Norway were also left with 10 men in stoppage time after David Møller Wolfe was sent off following a second booking.There was drama in Belgrade where visitorsGreececame from a goal down to snatch a 2-1 victory overSerbiathanks to Tasos Douvikas’s winner deep in stoppage time.Maltacame from behind to beatAndorra2-1 in their League D clash, whileLithuaniawon 2-0 inLichtenstein.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueIsraelAustrianewsShareReuse this content

title: James Garner keen to live up to ‘mini-Valverde’ tag after late England call | England | The Guardian
description: Everton midfielder’s spirit and footballing intelligence have earned him another international chance and he is eager to test himself against Rodri and co in the Nations League on Saturday
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Everton midfielder’s spirit and footballing intelligence have earned him another international chance and he is eager to test himself against Rodri and co in the Nations League on Saturday
Content: James Garner has thrived as a midfielder having started out in defence.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenJames Garner has thrived as a midfielder having started out in defence.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAEnglandJames Garner keen to live up to ‘mini-Valverde’ tag after late England callEverton midfielder’s spirit and intelligence earned him another chance and he is eager to test himself against Spain in the Nations League on SaturdayDavid HytnerThu 24 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 18.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“It’s a very good comparison,” James Garner says, and he is not kidding. It came from Thomas Tuchel in March after the England manager had watched the Everton midfielder impress on hisinternational debut against Uruguay. He was up against Federico Valverde and Tuchel went big with his praise. Garner was a “mini Valverde”, he said after the 1-1 draw at Wembley.It was surely too much, despite the prefix that Tuchel attached, yet it was possible to see where he was coming from. Like Valverde, Garner wants to operate in central midfield but he can play at right-back or on the wing. And like Valverde, who they calledEl Pajarito– or the Little Bird – when he was a kid, Garner can sometimes fly a bit under the radar.‘It’s not in us’: Anthony Gordon backs Tuchel over England’s possession problemRead moreIs Valverde the most underrated player in the game? The more the question is asked, the more the point is lost but there is certainly something there. “You wouldn’t really call him a household name, would you?” Garner says of the Real Madrid player. “But players who have played the game – they know how good he is. I watch a lot of football. I watch all the Champions League games and he always stands out. So yeah, I would go as far as saying that he’s underrated. In my opinion, he’s one of the best midfielders in the world.”The pros know. And within the game, there is a burgeoning appreciation of Garner, who located such outstanding form atEvertonfrom the turn of the year that he won his first England call-up and was considered unlucky to miss out on the World Cup squad. In the end, Tuchel went with Jordan Henderson and Kobbie Mainoo as the midfield back-ups to Declan Rice and Elliot Anderson. Henderson played six minutes as a substitute during the tournament; Mainoo not at all.“It was a tough phone call [from Tuchel] because you don’t know whether it’s a yes or a no,” Garner says. “He just said that he could only take a certain amount of players and I’ve missed out this time. I respect his decision and it just makes you hungrier.”View image in fullscreenJames Garner impressed on debut against Uruguay but missed out on the World Cup.Photograph: Alex Davidson/The FA/Getty ImagesThe 25-year-old is back in the squad for the upcoming Nations League fixtures, albeit as a late call-up after thewithdrawals of Rice and Mainoo. Henderson was not picked on fitness grounds. Tuchel recalled Alex Scott and Myles Lewis-Skelly in his original selection and continues to overlook Adam Wharton. Anderson stands as the most established midfielder as Tuchel prepares for the visit of Spain to Wembley on Saturday night. Thereafter, England play Czechia and Croatia away before returning to Wembley to face Czechia.Garner flew to Bodrum in Turkey on Sunday night for a holiday with his partner and he had just put the key in the hotel room door when he got the call from the Football Association. He flew home on Monday before reporting to St George’s Park on Tuesday. “It was a very short holiday,” he says with a smile. “I’m more than happy to be here now.”Tuchel also gave a late call to Morgan Gibbs-White, who had just got to Dubai for a family holiday. The Nottingham Forest attacking midfielder made a lighthearted TikTok video in which he and his fiancee mimed Gotta Go My Own Way from High School Musical 2 as he packed up and headed back. Was Garner tempted to do something similar? “No. That’s not me,” he replies.Garner is no-nonsense. He is laidback company but there is a toughness to him on the pitch, a warrior spirit to go with the intelligence of his game, the technique and range of his passing. Growing up in the Manchester United academy, he played as a centre-half until the age of 15 and his boyhood hero feels appropriate.“I’ve never actually said this but I used to love Nemanja Vidic,” he says. “I used to love the No 15 [which Vidic wore] and things like that. Then you grow up a little bit more, I became a midfielder and I used to love Lampard, Scholes and Gerrard.”Garner made the move into midfield with United at a junior tournament. “It was the Nike Cup and our midfielder got injured in the first game,” Garner says. “I’ve always been half-decent with the ball at my feet so they thought: ‘We’ll push him into midfield.’ I had a really good tournament and it just went from there. Albeit when I was withEnglandunder-16s and under-17s, I played centre-back.”He is a student of the game. “I watch all matches and also, as mad as it sounds, I played Fifa for so long,” he says. “I’ve been so indulged in football since I was a kid. My brother is five years older than me, he played and I’ve always been around football. I was lucky enough to come through United’s academy, which is one of the best academies in the world, and I learned so much from a lot of good coaches. I’ve just always had that tactical awareness and maybe that helps me playing different positions.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGarner could not see a first-team pathway at United. They loaned him to Watford for six months, then Forest for 18 months. The writing was on the wall for him in the summer of 2022 when United bolstered their midfield with the signings of Casemiro and Christian Eriksen. His move to Everton for a bargain £9m still rankles with a section of the United support.View image in fullscreenJames Garner has no regrets over leaving Manchester United and joining Everton.Photograph: Gary Oakley/Everton FC/Getty Images“It was the perfect thing for me to do – 1,000%,” Garner says. “I’ve never been shy of going into a more uncomfortable place, changing scenery or anything like that. I went on loan. I moved down to London and Nottingham. It was about playing games and Everton was the perfect choice. I didn’t want to fizzle into the background and just sit on the bench. I wanted to go to a team where I felt like I had a chance to fight for my position.“Do I have any regrets about leaving United? No, not really. I am a big believer that everything happens for a reason. Had I stayed I wouldn’t have been where I am today so I am more than happy that I left.”Garner made a statement on the international stage when he starred for the England under-21s in theirEuropean Championship triumph of 2023. He was named in the team of the tournament – as a right-back, which was where he played in the final when England beat Spain 1-0. He hopes to make another against the same nation.“Spain have got the Ballon d’Or winner in their midfield [Rodri] so to play against someone like that is the ultimate test,” Garner says. “You want to go against the best and see how you fare.”Explore more on these topicsEnglandNations LeagueThomas TuchelEvertonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My bad TV history qualifies me to discuss Disney’s women’s football coverage | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: A golden retriever and a game of guess the pasta were unusual inclusions for a Women’s Champions League show on Disney+ – but I understand how the producers arrived there
Author: Max Rushden
Headline: A golden retriever and a game of guess the pasta were unusual inclusions for a Women’s Champions League show on Disney+ – but I understand how the producers arrived there
Content: I feel for Alex Scott, who perpetually finds herself in the middle of some kind of culture war.Photograph: Mike Marsland/Getty Images for Disney+View image in fullscreenI feel for Alex Scott, who perpetually finds herself in the middle of some kind of culture war.Photograph: Mike Marsland/Getty Images for Disney+Women's Champions LeagueMy bad TV history qualifies me to discuss Disney’s women’s football coverageMax RushdenA golden retriever and a game of guess the pasta were unusual to see in a Women’s Champions League show – but I understand how they arrived thereThu 24 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 14.59 EDTShareDisclaimer: I have made a lot of bad TV programmes. I have done quite a few below-average radio shows. Podcasts, there are millions of them – some might say too many – and I’ve done my fair share that won’t go down in history. In between those, I’ve hopefully done some pretty good ones – it’s not for me to say.I have had good ideas and the odd great one that didn’t make it to air (attention the full-size unreferenced post-Keys and Gray elephant in the Soccer AM studio). I’ve had more awful ones. I’ve hosted shows where I’ve had almost complete editorial control, and ones where I could have been replaced by a performing monkey.I’ve had to host TV shows at every possible height – sitting on a sofa, on a normal chair, on a normal chair behind a desk, on a bar stool in a pub, on a bar stool not in a pub, and standing up when there was somewhere comfortable to sit just out of shot. I complained a lot, but standing did actually work, Murray.Disney+ criticised for advert break during Women’s Champions League gameRead moreThe point being, I have some experience when it comes to reviewing the opening night of the Disney+ coverage of the Women’s Champions League. The Hangout was hosted by Alex Scott with her fellow former England international Lianne Sanderson, the content creators Tyra Mills and Alex Bailess, and quite inexplicably a golden retriever called Barley Boy, who at the time of writing has 82,000 more Instagram followers than I have – I must work on my reels.The show included a quiz about Italy, including guess the Italian name for football and what pasta the reporter in Milan is cooking. There’s an incredible still image of the panel staring at a load of farfalle on a big screen normally reserved for team lineups or key match incidents.The immediate reaction was a mix of bewilderment and fury from seasoned lovers of the women’s game. Kathryn Batte wrotean understandable critique for the Telegraph. The broadcaster Flo Lloyd-Hughesposted on X: “Disney’s new UWCL coverage is the closest we’ve seen to CBBC football (derogatory). I wouldn’t be surprised if we see someone gunged for making a wrong prediction or perhaps Raven will make a cameo. Keep stopping to remind myself this isn’t a dream.”Consistent with all the criticism is the truth that the men’s Champions League would never be covered in the same way. It is perhaps interesting to ask how the team arrived at the concept. Why replace former pros with content creators, why replace tactical analysis with asking what’s the biggest city in Italy? Why a dog?The broadcaster Marva Kreel perfectly articulated one of the issuesin her own X post: “I think a lot of the problem with the debates in women’s football broadcasting over analysis and punditry v content creation and gimmicky fun, is that in men’s football you can get both – and in different shows. In women’s football you get one show, and so they try to do it all.”It’s a fair point. I’ve mainly hosted the show before the show – where a dog running around wouldn’t be regarded as a crime against the game. In fact hosting live football is significantly more straightforward than interviewing an indie band about their difficult second album or trying to come up with a three-hour radio show in the middle of the international break. The show Disney tried to make on Wednesday is technically much harder than Super Sunday – but that doesn’t mean it was the right call.I can understand the thinking. I imagine the bosses told the producers they want to bring in a younger audience. I have been told this before. Exactly how to do that is impossible to work out. Should I stop making references to Jossy’s Giants and Aswad? And Disney could probably argue that most of the criticism didn’t come from young people. It came from people who expect the game to be covered in a certain way.(From left) Former England international Lianne Sanderson, content creators Alex Bailess and Tyra Mills, and golden retriever Barley Boy.Photograph: Disney+Disney may be being cynical – people are talking and writing about it. The hardcore will watch anyway. Had they produced more traditional coverage, no one would have said anything. And sometimes you have to try something different. I wouldn’t want to be too critical; Disney may give me a gig one day.Major broadcasters have less money to make the same amount of stuff – and have had a battle over the past 20 years to work out how to harness social media. I saw it at Sky, where a Facebook livestream filmed on an iPhone in the green room would get as many views as the show itself with the costs of studio/lighting/sound/producers etc.As a middle-aged man – whose wife accuses him of being a “boomer” – I really dislike the phrase “content creator”; perhaps I’m nervous that eventually they’ll take all my jobs. From what I saw, Bailess and Mills came across as very personable and fun – which was clearly the brief – and you can’t criticise anyone for taking a job. And they bring a following with them – quite how many followers lead to subscriptions is a different question.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI feel for Scott, who perpetually finds herself in the middle of some sort of culture war. You are entitled to regard her as the greatest or worst broadcaster of her generation – or somewhere in between – as you are with me or anyone else. I know many listeners certainly feel the latter about my abilities.Has the time come to separate home and away fans at WSL games?Read moreI found the discourse aroundthe end of Football Focuspretty troubling – people suggesting the show went woke and lost its way when she was appointed. It’s much more accurate to accuse me of turning Soccer AM woke, with my clarinet, lefty snowflake opinions and inability to flirt on live television. But then I’m not a woman and I’m white; generally people just accuse me of turning it shit.But back to the Hangout. I imagine Scott didn’t suggest having a dog in the studio or having guess the pasta. Perhaps she has a lot of editorial control – I genuinely don’t know. But sometimes as a host you have to do what you’re told and do it with conviction.The reality of live football coverage is that people are watching because they want to watch the game. If people want comedy, they’ll watch Curb Your Enthusiasm. If Liverpool are playing Real Madrid, the fans will watch it – and either enjoy or endure the coverage. But what you can do as a broadcaster is make it as compelling as possible, and there are different ways of being a good host or pundit.Live football coverage hasn’t changed dramatically in 50 years. Welcome, team news, managers, bit of tactics or player focus, throw to commentators. Half-time: what did you make of that? Full time: what did you make of that?The dog did not return for the second night of coverage. I know it would have been a strange and difficult day for everyone involved. They made a show, people didn’t like it and they had to go again the next night. Do you double down, screw the haters, or try to subtly move towards a more traditional setup? It seemed on Wednesday they went for the latter.You can’t magic up an audience, but you can make people feel like you respect the game, you can do it in an entertaining way without introducing animals, and people will come back and watch you again.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueWomen's footballDisney+Sport TVcommentShareReuse this content

title: UK Football Police Unit accused of ‘bringing Hillsborough’ into alcohol debate | Soccer | The Guardian
description: English football’s leading fans’ group has criticised the UK Football Policing Unit for ‘bringing Hillsborough into the debate’ around drinking in sight of the pitch
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: English football’s leading fans’ group has criticised the UK Football Policing Unit for ‘bringing Hillsborough into the debate’ around drinking in sight of the pitch
Content: Andy Burnham’s comments about drinking alcohol in stands met a wary response from police.Photograph: Peter Powell/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham’s comments about drinking alcohol in stands met a wary response from police.Photograph: Peter Powell/AFP/Getty ImagesSoccerUK Football Police Unit accused of ‘bringing Hillsborough’ into alcohol debate‘The disaster was not caused by alcohol,’ says fan groupPolice say they had not intended to make such a linkPress AssociationThu 24 Sep 2026 14.07 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 12.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEnglish football’s leading fans’ group has criticised the UK Football Policing Unit for “bringing Hillsborough into the debate” around drinking in sight of the pitch.Talk of changing the law to allow fans to drink at their seat or in the stands has resurfaced after Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said the rules wereoutdated and discriminatory and should be scrapped.The Football Supporters’ Association (FSA) immediately backed his call but the UKFPU urged caution, stating: “Following a number of football-related tragedies, changes in legislation were implemented after the Taylor Report for good reason and we are currently in the longest ever period without a significant football-related disaster.”Archive, 1985: Alcohol banned from football grounds in England and WalesRead moreThe UKFPU added it would be “incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence”.“The UKFPU would welcome a meeting with the prime minister to discuss his views and explain the challenges these proposed changes would bring to policing and the safety of staff and fans at football games.“Other sports simply don’t see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour. It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games.”The Taylor Report referenced by the UKFPU was commissioned in the wake of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster, which resulted in the deaths of 97 Liverpool fans.The FSApublished a thread on its X accountsetting out its position on drinking in the stands, which began: “Arguably the most important point is that the UK Football Policing Unit’s comments bringing Hillsborough into this debate have to be corrected. The disaster was not caused by alcohol. Full stop. Fans were ‘unlawfully killed and a catalogue of failings by police and the ambulance services contributed to their deaths’.”A spokesperson for the UKFPU said: “It was not our intention to link the issue of alcohol with the Hillsborough tragedy. The laws around alcohol, which we acknowledge were first introduced in 1985, are one of a range of measures in addition to the subsequent Taylor Report recommendations that have contributed to making football much safer for fans in this country.”Burnham’s comments have sparked social media debate in which differing views have been expressed by match-going fans.The FSA’s post on Thursday added: “It’s unfair to criminalise fans for having a pint – especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league. We are fundamentally sceptical of any law which is only targeted at football supporters.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“That doesn’t mean every club should be forced to serve alcohol to every seat! A club should have the choice to do what is right for its fans. Consultation is critical, some stadiums or stands might not be suitable (eg family areas) whereas it might be popular elsewhere.“Ultimately, we think clubs, in liaison with their supporters, should be able to determine what is best for themselves, rather than relying on legislation which is decades old and was written through the prism of viewing all football fans as potential hooligans.”The Sporting Events (Control of Alcohol) Act 1985 prohibits drinking in sight of the pitch in England and Wales in the top five men’s leagues.Burnham said on Wednesday: “I don’t think it’s fair for football fans to be singled out in that way and I made that point. I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different. And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done, perhaps on a trial basis.“But I’m not going to back away from what’s been a long-held view of mine. I don’t see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently from others.”Explore more on these topicsFootballnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s not in us’: Anthony Gordon backs Tuchel over England’s possession problem | England | The Guardian
description: Anthony Gordon has sided with Thomas Tuchel’s assertion that controlling games through possession is not part of English football’s DNA
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Anthony Gordon has sided with Thomas Tuchel’s assertion that controlling games through possession is not part of English football’s DNA
Content: Anthony Gordon (left) and Morgan Gibbs-White battle for possession during an England training session in preparation for the Spain game on Saturday.Photograph: Eddie Keogh/The FA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAnthony Gordon (left) and Morgan Gibbs-White battle for possession during an England training session in preparation for the Spain game on Saturday.Photograph: Eddie Keogh/The FA/Getty ImagesEngland‘It’s not in us’: Anthony Gordon backs Tuchel over England’s possession problemBarcelona winger says England cannot play like SpainGordon: ‘The Mexico game set us up a bit’Jacob SteinbergThu 24 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthony Gordon has sided with Thomas Tuchel’s assertion that controlling games through possession is not part of English football’s DNA. Although Gordon revealed surprise at being substituted when England were 1-0 up in theirWorld Cup semi-final against Argentina, the winger refused to blame the defeat on Tuchel’s decisions and argued that wider cultural issues influenced the side’s collapse.England’s perennial struggle to keep the ball when under pressure flared when a place in the final was within touching distance in July, allowing Argentina to fight back and go through with two late goals. The pain has not gone away and there has been intense scrutiny of Tuchel’s role in Atlanta. The head coach’s tactical choices were criticised and he faced a backlash after saying “ball possession” was not in his team’s DNA.Thomas Tuchel rocked by five key withdrawals from England squadRead moreBut Gordon, who thinks he will always be scarred by losing against Argentina, sided with Tuchel’s observations about England’s style as he looked towards theNations Leaguegame against Spain on Saturday. The 25-year-old admitted the side had an ingrained inability to control games but argued they should stop trying to copy other nations.Gordon has gained an insight into the Spanish understanding of how to use the ball since his move to Barcelona. His view is that England should lean more into their physical strengths.“Culturally it’s not just that tournament or that game where we couldn’t control a game,” Gordon said. “As a nation we don’t have that strength like the Spanish, where we control games like they do. It’s not in us. I’m not sure it’s something that can be taught. Playing in Spain I can speak with an educated view on the way they keep the ball.“It’s much different than I’ve ever experienced in this country, so I’m not sure we can ever get that. We can definitely get better – or maybe go the other way and really play to our strengths, which is play physical, play direct football and on the counterattack.”Tuchel, who has talked about embracing the chaos of English football, is unsure whether his side can play with more control. “It’s not in the English DNA,” Gordon said. “We as English players are educated the same way as the Spanish players, we know how to keep possession, but it’s the decision-making of certain players in Spain. I look at some of the decisions they take on the ball sometimes and think: ‘I’m not sure how you’ve seen that.’”The dilemma is that Tuchel wanted England to play like a Premier League side at the World Cup. It was put to Gordon that fatigue makes it harder to be physical at a tournament. He suggested that England struggled to recover from the emotion of theirlast-16 win against Mexico.Gordon added that Jordan Henderson fracturing a wrist during the celebrations at the Azteca took a toll. The sense is there was little left in the tank for the Argentina game. “That Mexico game, although I said it was the best experience of my life, I think it kind of set us up a little bit,” he said.“I remember it took us four days to recover from all the emotion. It took a lot out of me, the travel was tough. Obviously Jordan Henderson falling, I felt like that was a massive moment in the tournament. The Norway game, I remember feeling really tired, couldn’t perform how I would have liked to.”View image in fullscreenThomas Tuchel tries to get his ideas across in a drinks break during the semi-final against Argentina.Photograph: Simon M Bruty/Getty ImagesGordon opened the scoring against Argentina and was surprised to be replaced by Ezri Konsa when Tuchel made the first of two defensive moves and switched to a back five after the hydration break in the second half.“I’d just scored,” Gordon said. “I’m really good when I play off adrenaline. When I score, I normally don’t have many bad games, because I get into an untouchable mode of confidence.“But as a winger I come off most games. It’s normal, it’s usually the position that’s targeted first for substitutions, because the player on the bench in your position is usually quick, and usually really good.”Gordon defended Tuchel and said England’s performances did not match their level in training. “It makes a lot of sense to me why the manager would then go more safe and more defensive [against Argentina],” he said.“As players we could have done more to take the initiative, to control the game. We had the best team, we had the best players in that semi-final, and in the last 20 minutes we didn’t play the best football. That’s something the manager can’t really affect.”Gordon said his Barça teammates had told him England would have given Spain a tougher game than Argentina in the final. Spain dominated in New Jersey, winning 1-0 in extra time.Explore more on these topicsEnglandThomas TuchelNations LeagueWorld Cup 2026World CupFootball tacticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Warwickshire blow through Leicestershire to hone in on title: County Championship cricket, day one – as it happened | County Championship | The Guardian
description: Warwickshire bowled out Leicestershire for just 125 at Edgbaston, while Surrey racked up runs at Somerset
Author: James Wallace
Headline: Warwickshire bowled out Leicestershire for just 125 at Edgbaston, while Surrey racked up runs at Somerset
Content: 14.52 EDTDay one reportThe champagne is on ice inWarwickshirebut probably not for much longer. Fourteen wickets fell on the opening day in Edgbaston and ten of them belonged to relegation scufflersLeicestershirewho won the toss in late September sunshine and decided to bat first. A couple of hours later and the Foxes were bowled out for just 125. Baby faced assassin Ethan Bamber continued his fine season with the ball, the cherubic 27 year old took 4-42 to go level with Hampshire’s Kyle Abbott as the leading wicket-taker in Division one this year. It was the seventh innings in succession that the Bears have routed their opponents for under 200. They finished the day five runs ahead with six wickets in hand and have at least a few digits on the trophy.Asa Tribe scored his second century in successive innings asGlamorganreached 318-3 againstEssexin Cardiff. The bowling point Essex picked upis likely enough to see Leicestershire relegated. An asterisk comes in the form of the appeal club Chief Executive Emma White confirmed the midlands club had lodged with the independentCricketDiscipline Panel after they were handed a 27 point deduction for a poor pitch in their match against Glamorgan in the ninth round.Any chance of a Mexican standoff in the race for the Division One title was deescalated bySurreyracking up327-4against second placedSomerset.Dan Lawrence going to his sixth century of the campaign with a howitzer six into the stands off Jack Leach. The sun setting along with Somerset’s hopes of a hoodoo breaking Championship title late in the day at Taunton.At Trent Bridge, third placedNottinghamshireslipped from a well-placed 172-4 to finish on 242-9 againstYorkshireand in the battle of the south coast Hampshire slipped to 55-4 in reply toSussex’s 244.In Division Two,Northamptonshire’shopes of promotion were dashed by the decision to bat first at Lord’s,Middlesex’sRyan Higgins taking 4-30 with the ball to skittle the visitors for 103 and then scoring 115 off 124 balls as the home side posted 255 in response.Emilio Gay scored his fourth ton of the season forDurhamas they cruised to 355-5 against a beleagueredLancashireat Old Trafford.WorcestershireleadDerbyshireby 131 runs, Ben Allison pocketing 5-22 to raze Wayne Madsen’s side for 88 in their first innings.Kentare 77-1 replying toGloucestershire’s229 at Canterbury.ShareUpdated at14.58 EDT

title: Shaun Edwards inspired by mum’s memory as he beds in with Red Roses | England women's rugby union team | The Guardian
description: Shaun Edwards has proven to the Red Roses he ‘wants to be there and make the players better’ rather than using the women’s game as a stepping stone, according to England’s Jess Breach
Author: Sarah Rendell
Headline: Shaun Edwards has proven to the Red Roses he ‘wants to be there and make the players better’ rather than using the women’s game as a stepping stone, according to England’s Jess Breach
Content: Shaun Edwards with his fellow coach Sarah Hunter and the forward Alex Matthews as England prepare for the Black Ferns.Photograph: Matt Impey/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenShaun Edwards with his fellow coach Sarah Hunter and the forward Alex Matthews as England prepare for the Black Ferns.Photograph: Matt Impey/ShutterstockEngland women's rugby union teamShaun Edwards inspired by mum’s memory as he beds in with Red RosesCoach ‘not just bunny hopping’ says Jess BreachCrowd of nearly 60,000 expected against New ZealandSarah RendellThu 24 Sep 2026 12.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 18.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShaun Edwards has proven to the Red Roses he “wants to be there and to make the players better” rather than using the women’s game as a stepping stone, according to the England wing Jess Breach.Edwards, a rugby league legend and hugely decorated defence coach in union, joined England on a consultancy basis this week and will be with the squad until the end of the WXV Global Series in October. The 59-year-old, who left the France men’s team this summer, has been helping England prepare to take on New Zealand at Twickenham on Saturday in front of almost 60,000.Shaun Edwards finally lands England coaching role after joining Red RosesRead more“I think probably our biggest question around him coming into the programme was why?” Breach, who starts on the wing against the Black Ferns, said. “I think a lot of coaches come into women’s teams to potentially bunny-hop and progress into male teams. Not that we don’t like that, but we want people to be here because they want to be here and they want to make the programme better and they want us to be better.“I think he does want that. He explained the story about his mum and I think it is important and it touched a lot of us, like you do want to be here and you do want to make us better.”At the start of the week Marlie Packer disclosed that Edwards stood in front of the squad and told them one of the reasons he wanted to coach the Red Roses was that his mum, Phyllis, who died in 2021, did not have the opportunity to play rugby. He added it was something his mum thought was “incredible” and she “would have loved to have done it”. Edwards also stated he wanted an insight into the women’s game having never coached in women’s rugby before.England’s head coach, John Mitchell, said on Thursday that before Edwards came into camp he wanted to learn all the players’ names and wanted to see success in the Red Roses’ defensive system.View image in fullscreenJess Breach said Shaun Edwards ‘wanted to be here’ and had demonstrated his commitment to the Red Roses.Photograph: Steve Bardens/RFU/The RFU Collection/Getty ImagesMitchell said he was learning from Edwards, adding: “I am dragging plenty out of him and I am sure he is stealing a few things as well, which is great. As coaches we always want to find something a little bit different that can grow the players or refreshes how you go about things. We are very, very fortunate to have a person of his ability.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMitchell added Edwards has brought his “no nonsense” personality into the team and while he is “highly honoured” to be a part of the England camp, Edwards does not want the limelightEngland are on a 40-game unbeaten streak but will be looking to bounce back after their consecutive-win record ended last Saturday with a26-26 draw against Canada.Explore more on these topicsEngland women's rugby union teamRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nick Clegg plays down fears ‘godlike’ AI could exterminate humanity | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Former deputy PM now involved in tech industry says many within sector are ‘winding themselves up into a lather’
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Former deputy PM now involved in tech industry says many within sector are ‘winding themselves up into a lather’
Content: Nick Clegg, who stepped down from Meta in 2025, said one person who runs an AI lab told him the current discourse was ‘totally silly’.Photograph: Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNick Clegg, who stepped down from Meta in 2025, said one person who runs an AI lab told him the current discourse was ‘totally silly’.Photograph: Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)Nick Clegg plays down fears ‘godlike’ AI could exterminate humanityFormer deputy PM now involved in tech industry says many within sector are ‘winding themselves up into a lather’Rachel HallThu 24 Sep 2026 05.19 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 19.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNick Clegg has dismissed fears over AI’s “godlike power to exterminate humanity”, calling it a sign that tech bosses are “breathing their own fumes”.The former UK deputy prime minister said that tech bosses should focus on addressing known specific threats such as cybersecurity and bioweapons rather than the “slightly hand-wavy view that this technology is unavoidably going to develop some godlike power which is going to turn on us and exterminate humanity”.Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, he said: “I think it is perhaps accidentally self-serving, because it sort of implies that we can only be made safe by having everything controlled, in effect, by an oligopoly of a small number of companies, and I think it slightly paralyses the political debate.”Clegg, who was formerly the president of global affairs atMetaand owns more than 917,000 shares in Nscale, a UK-based datacentre, and is a cofounder of the AI startup AMI Labs, said he spent “a huge amount of time” with people in the tech industry.“They don’t agree amongst themselves at all. Of course, we hear the most apocalyptic voices,” he said, noting that one person who runs an AI lab said the current discourse was “totally silly”.“There is a culture in Silicon Valley – it’s an odd place for those who haven’t been there. It is in many ways the centre of the universe, or at least claiming to shape it. It’s also an oddly parochial place. It’s a strange sort of culture where the engineers can get quite close to the technology and start slightly breathing their own fumes as they wind themselves up into a lather about these things,” he said.Asked about theautonomous hackconducted by a group of OpenAI agents on a major real-world company, Hugging Face, Clegg said there was a case for “tramlines and greater transparency”.30:27However, he said this would be unlikely to happen under a Trump administration given its competitiveness on AI. He also suspected China’s cooperation would be limited, since the development of AI technologies was viewed as a “national mission” after the country was “cheated out of the Industrial Revolution”.He added: “I think there’s a great potential for the big three techno democracies in the world – India, Europe and the US – to collaborate more.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAsked whether the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, could take a lead on such efforts, Clegg noted the UK was not a world leader on AI: “We need to be realistic about what influence we can and cannot exert.”Clegg also disagreed with other proposed remedies, such as introducing a “kill switch”, which he said would be unworkable; or only producing closed models, where source code is not made public, which he said were no safer than open source models according to the evidence.Instead, he suggested: “There is a lot that can be done both voluntarily and through regulation, to enforce far greater transparency on the way in which these models are concocted and how they operate.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Nick CleggMetaData and computer securityPolitics pastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Launch of UK’s ‘largest AI supercomputer’ delayed by power supply problems | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Datacentre hailed by government was supposed to start operating next year but may be held back into mid-2030s
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Datacentre hailed by government was supposed to start operating next year but may be held back into mid-2030s
Content: An artist’s impression of Nscale’s planned supercomputer in Loughton, Essex.Illustration: NscaleView image in fullscreenAn artist’s impression of Nscale’s planned supercomputer in Loughton, Essex.Illustration: NscaleAI (artificial intelligence)Launch of UK’s ‘largest AI supercomputer’ delayed by power supply problemsDatacentre hailed by government was supposed to start operating next year but may be held back into mid-2030sDan MilmoGlobal technology editorThu 24 Sep 2026 13.26 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA huge datacentre project hailed by the UK government will miss its launch date next year and could be delayed into the mid-2030s.The site in Loughton,Essex, was described as the country’s largest AI supercomputer when it was announced in 2025, but power supply problems mean it now faces a lengthy wait before coming online.Doubts had already emerged about the scheme after the Guardianrevealed in Marchthat the planned location was still an operational scaffolding yard.Now there are further concerns about the project due to its inability to obtain enough power before its planned 2027 debut. The Loughton supercomputer is being built by Nscale, a UK-based startup seeking a $35bn (£26bn) flotation this year.UK Power Networks (UKPN), the company that will connect the site to the local power grid, has reportedly told Nscale the grid will not be able to supply sufficient power to the datacentre until the early to mid-2030s.The power delay was first reported by Morning Intelligence, an AI industry newsletter.Nscale said it was “committed to the project” but the failure tofind a quick fix to the power supply issue underlines how much energy has become a hindrance to datacentre development. The scaffolding yard site has now been cleared by Nscale, however. The company is also investigating whether it can generate power onsite and whether it can speed up the connection process.Keir Starmer’s government cited the Loughton project when announcing theUK’s AI strategy in 2025, describing the site as the “largest UK sovereign AI datacentre”. Datacentres are the central nervous system of AI technology such as chatbots.View image in fullscreenThe scaffolding company, which was operating on the site.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianOfgem, the energy industry regulator, has warned of alogjam in applications for electricity connections. In June, it revealed there were 315 datacentres queueing to connect to the National Grid, representing 73GW of demand – compared with the peak energy demand for the entire country of 45GW.The Loughton site is seeking up to 90MW of capacity, equivalent to the energy consumption of about 315,000 homes.UKPN said it could not comment on an individual project. Schemes with large energy demand also require work to be done at a National Grid level, in order to ensure that energy demands can be met properly.“In general, many datacentres, whilst they will connect to our distribution network, are awaiting works on the wider national electricity transmission network before they can begin operation,” said a UKPN spokesperson.National Grid said: “We’re continuing to work closely with NESO [the government-owned NationalEnergySystem Operator], distribution network operators and customers to identify opportunities to accelerate connections where possible and support economic growth.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingEssexDatacentres - UKInfrastructurenewsShareReuse this content

title: AI hack of Medicare exposes Australia’s vulnerabilities and experts warn ‘there is more of this to come’ | Medicare Australia | The Guardian
description: Council on AI Strategy chief says incident unlikely to be isolated and country should enhance capability to detect and report incidents
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: Council on AI Strategy chief says incident unlikely to be isolated and country should enhance capability to detect and report incidents
Content: Anthony Albanese, left, challenged the OpenAI boss, Sam Altman, after the company’s agent infiltrated systems run by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Victoria’s Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAnthony Albanese, left, challenged the OpenAI boss, Sam Altman, after the company’s agent infiltrated systems run by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Victoria’s Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia.Photograph: Getty ImagesMedicare AustraliaAI hack of Medicare exposes Australia’s vulnerabilities and experts warn ‘there is more of this to come’Council on AI Strategy chief says incident unlikely to be isolated and country should enhance capability to detect and report incidentsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTom McIlroyandKrishani DhanjiThu 24 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 18.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTechnology experts have warned revelations anartificial intelligence agent hacked Medicare’s internal systemswill not be the only dangerous breach of government data and have called for Australia to boost its protections against the growing risk.The prime minister,Anthony Albanese, challenged the OpenAI boss, Sam Altman, on Thursday after the company’s agent infiltrated systems run by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Victoria’s Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia.An OpenAI agent infiltrated Medicare – and Australia only found out months later. Here’s what we know so farRead moreOpenAI alerted the government earlier this month to theJune hackingvia an email to a public-facing address, a situation Albanese called “obviously unacceptable”.But the Australian Council on AI Strategy chief executive, Anna-Maria Arabia, said the case was unlikely to be an isolated incident.“All of the evidence shows that our operating systems are vulnerable,” she told Guardian Australia.“Frontier AI now has capability to expose those vulnerabilities at a rate quicker than we can keep up, quicker than we can patch them.“When the companies are undertaking tests in what they think are secure environments, and when there are breaches of those environments and these incidences do happen, whether it’s accidental or not, what we’re seeing is the frontier AI capability exposing these vulnerabilities.“All evidence suggests that there is more of this to come.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailArabia said Australia needed to quickly enhance capability to detect and report incidents, and the country should host AI training labs here.Johanna Weaver, Australia’s former chief cyber negotiator at the United Nations, agreed more incidents were inevitable.Weaver is a member of the advisory board to the minister for government services, Katy Gallagher, and the executive director of the Tech Policy Design Institute.“Cybersecurity experts have been warning that frontier models and AI agents could expose vulnerabilities in critical systems. What we are seeing now is the tip of the iceberg,” she said.“Governments need to draw a clear line: if companies cannot control their AI systems, they should not release them publicly.”The US Studies Centre expert Olivia Shen warned AI companies should not be allowed to decide on their own disclosure obligations for hacks and breaches.“We just don’t know how big the problem is. It could be the tip of the iceberg but, either way, we can’t be ignoring the risk,” Shen said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s all happening at a time when Australia is designing our national standards on AI. It hasn’t been entirely clear if those national standards were going to be very hyper-focused on datacentres and leave governance questions as a bit of a bolt-on.“This strengthens the argument that you need to have some pretty clear standards, even just based on mandatory incident reporting, built in.”Intelligence agency the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) is reviewing how prepared the government is to block and respond to hacking by AI. Officials will look at policies around how AI companies should report cyber-incidents to the government, and how cooperative companies should be during and after an attack.It will also investigate whether the current laws and systems are adequate to stop AI and how government systems can be strengthened.12:23Rogue AI hacks government system for first time - The LatestThe shadow industry minister, Andrew Hastie, called for Australia to develop its own domestic AI capability, instead of relying on the US.“If there’s rogue AI agents out there, we need to have our own defensive AI agents protecting Australian government data, our private sector and other things that are important to us,” he said.The Greens demanded Labor call in the new US ambassador, David Brat, to establish what the president, Donald Trump, knew about the attack.“This breach by a foreign AI company on an Australian government database is deeply alarming and brings home the risks that these out-of-control tech corporations pose,” the Greens’ acting leader, Mehreen Faruqi, said.“The fact that the government did not even know it happened is disturbing.”Explore more on these topicsMedicare AustraliaAnthony AlbaneseAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIHackingAustralian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Price hikes, ads and lower quality: has ‘streamflation’ ruined the TV experience? | Television | The Guardian
description: US consumers are starting to opt out of the streaming world as several services raise prices without offering many perks
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: US consumers are starting to opt out of the streaming world as several services raise prices without offering many perks
Content: A still from Toy Story 5.Photograph: Disney/PAView image in fullscreenA still from Toy Story 5.Photograph: Disney/PATelevisionPrice hikes, ads and lower quality: has ‘streamflation’ ruined the TV experience?US consumers are starting to opt out of the streaming world as several services raise prices without offering many perksJesse HassengerThu 24 Sep 2026 10.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 10.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt may not be quite as politically buzzy as the price of gasoline or eggs, but another household expense is going up for millions of people. Disney has brought the price-gouging experience of its theme park home again by raising the prices of most iterations and bundles of its Disney+ and Hulu streaming services. Whether you pay to watch them with or without ads, separately or bundled together, you’re probably getting a price hike of a couple of bucks per month. The few bundles that will remain the same price feature ad-supported versions of both services (plus ESPN). Don’t worry, though; paying extra to avoid the ad-supported versions of those services won’t mean that you’re missing out on some cross-promotional opportunities. Disney’s terms of service note that they reserve the right to insert ads before and after programming on whatever subscription tier they want, regardless of what you’re paying for. True magic!Kim Kardashian’s Team Moms highlights the ridiculous excess of the US youth-sports industryRead moreThis particular magic isn’t reserved for Disney, though. Price hikes among streaming services have become so common that The Verge has adedicated pageaggregating the news of them, which tends to arrive every few months. Apple, apparently high on Emmy fumes, has raised its prices four times in four years, keeping pace with many of its competitors despite a vastly smaller dedicated catalog. Depending on which version of Peacock subscribers use, they’ve seen their bills padded by five or six dollars a month just since the summer of 2025, including another increase last month. Netflix, meanwhile, hasn’t gone up since March 2026. That’s not a reprieve; that’s a sign another hike must be around the corner.Consumers have noticed. Reportedlyan estimated 39% of Americanscanceled a streaming service in the past six months due to what’s been dubbed “streamflation”. Anothersurveyindicates that a majority of people subscribe to at least three such services, which is consistent with estimates of streaming households spending about $70 per month. Access to the six big streaming services (Netflix, Disney+/Hulu, HBO Max, Paramount+, Apple TV, Peacock) will boost that number somewhere in the neighborhood of $120, on top of which subscribers need broadband internet for the services to actually work. For the total price, you might as well call the whole thing Cable+, in that it’s like your old cable bill, only there’s more of it. No wonder cancellations are rampant.To retain subscribers without putting the screws directly to them, it might be viable for streaming companies to stabilize annual prices – typically a discounted lump-sum payment covering a full year of a service – even when raising monthly costs. Some, like Netflix, don’t offer this option. While those that do have kept annual subscriptions cheaper than the a year’s worth of month-to-month, companies don’t seem interested in maintaining bargain levels. The annual price for Disney+ at launch was $70. Now it’s $190, an increase of 170% – presumably to stay competitive with eggs. Amazon Prime, whose streaming service began as a perk for members already paying an annual membership fee for unlimited shipping and other benefits, has also risen while inserting more ads into its programming and downgrading the picture quality. You want higher resolution and fewer ads? That’s another $50 a year.View image in fullscreenMatthew Rhys in Widow’s Bay, a big hit for Apple.Photograph: Robert Clark/AppleThe reasons for all this shameless gauging are pretty simple: Wall Street doesn’t just demand profits (though those have sometimes been scarce in the streaming world) but endless growth, and some services don’t have all that much more room, realistically, to sign up more users any more. Netflix has 325 million subscribers worldwide. What’s their reach goal? 500 million? Three billion? What happens when everyone on Earth with an internet connection and a credit card already has Netflix?Not every service is so close to a saturation point (unless you count electricity as a streaming service). But it’s notable that even a supposedly lower-tier streamer like Peacock commands over 40 million monthly subscribers, equivalent to more than 10% of the United States population. (It’s a heavily US-skewing service, so unlike Netflix those users aren’t especially global.) By comparison, the biggest magazine in the US has a subscriber base of around half that (and that’s the AARP magazine, an outlier in that it’s distributed to paying members). The New York Times, considered an especially successful recent example of the subscription model, has 13 million subscribers. The AMC Stubs A-List program that allows moviegoers to see four films a week has about 1 million.That’s all to say that streaming has unprecedented reach, which means the only realistic way to boost profits is to either raise subscription prices, or make less stuff. The latter might sound ridiculous, especially given that we’ve been living in the post-boom age for streaming shows for a while now. Then again, that’s worked out well for the catalog-basedTubi, whose original works are lower-profile and lower-budget than its competitors. One of several free streaming services, Tubi outstrips some of those paid competitors in market share and turns a profit based only on its ads.Watching a movie or a show on a free service isn’t exactly an optimal experience; there are those ad breaks, sometimes the transfers aren’t top-notch, and the content churn tends to be a little faster than the subscription streamers. It’s definitely not a place where you can catch much of anything nominated for an Emmy in the past five or six years (though some Oscar movies or second-tier popular hits from that period might turn up). On the other hand, free streamers often manage to under-promise and over-deliver; at a time when paid subscriptions seem eager to offer less than ever, especially in the quite broad field of films made before 1995, Tubi, PlutoTV and their ilk always have at least a couple dozen stone-cold classics on hand that more than make up for not including the latest big-name time-wasters (looking at you,Matthew McConaughey/Woody Harrelson sitcomwhere they play themselves!). And the price always stays the same.View image in fullscreenTubi’s original works are lower-profile and lower-budget than its competitors.Photograph: TubiStill, some free streaming services with surprisingly robust and shifting catalogs aren’t exactly the dream of cord-cutting that was fed to consumers throughout the 2010s. The initial idea was to shed the bloat from all-or-nothing cable services that hold monopolies, or something close to it, in plenty of geographic areas. Competition for subscribers would keep good deals in the offing. Instead, what’s been happening over the past five years or so is a redistribution of that money from one set of giant companies to another. There’s slightly more consumer control over the size of the bills, in the sense that, yes, it’s possible to cancel a couple of services in a way that picking and choosing individual cable channels wasn’t possible outsidea few premium subscriptions. But there’s also far less clarity about how to catch the best shows and movies of any given year. For ages, it was mostly a simple formulation: have cable, add HBO. Now even the prestige of HBO seems a little more niche – a Game of Thrones spin-off; a well-liked Green Lantern show – than in the past.There’s also a strange sense that this scramble of greed isn’t paying off as well as it should; many streaming services feel like they’re in far more precarious financial positions than most cable companies or channels were at their peak. It’s a dystopian development: corporations still want consumers on the hook for endless subscription payments, but also seem to want them to share in the nervous stock-checking of a shareholder, without any particular upside. Each month, you check your streaming holdings and see if you’re about to be charged even more, and whether you need to pick one to divest (cancel, whether for good or for now). You can toggle some of them on and off timed to the occasional appearance of a major series like Severance or The Pitt, but the onus for keeping track of erratic streaming schedules is on the subscriber. None of these shows are as necessary as basic groceries. But the ability to relax and watch TV after a long day is still in danger of becoming another budget-related stressor – an unholy combination of cable bloat and the endless doomscroll.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionUS televisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Eat the rich, save the planet’: climate protesters call out big tech’s disconnect from reality | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Activists gathered outside the OpenAI offices on Monday during climate week in New York City
Author: Lex McMenamin
Headline: Activists gathered outside the OpenAI offices on Monday during climate week in New York City
Content: Protests come after a former Anthropic employee warned that AI could ‘kill us all’ within a decade.Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The GuardianView image in fullscreenProtests come after a former Anthropic employee warned that AI could ‘kill us all’ within a decade.Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The GuardianBuilding powerAI (artificial intelligence)‘Eat the rich, save the planet’: climate protesters call out big tech’s disconnect from realityActivists gathered outside the OpenAI offices on Monday during climate week in New York CityBuilding power is supported byAbout this contentLex McMenaminin New York City, with photographs byJulius Constantine MotalThu 24 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Monday evening, protesters gathered outside the unmarked Manhattan offices of OpenAI, maker of ChatGPT, holding signs calling to “Eat the rich, save the planet”. Over the next two days, groups also picketed outside the offices of fellow tech giants Google and Amazon; other protesters, including clergy, were arrested whiledisrupting a closed-door AI health summitin the city. Tonight, protesters will target a Brooklyn gas power plant that was set to close – until it was purchased to power AI datacenters.The protests come on the heels of an Anthropic employee quitting his job witha warning that intensifiedan already-growing AI panic: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”Though it wasfar from the first timean AI expert had issued a doomsday message about the threat the tech poses, this time it dominated public attention, arriving as trust in big tech has hitan all-time lowand communities across the country are trying to stop the building of datacenters. From 2024 to 2026,at least $64bn in proposed datacenter buildoutwas blocked by local organizing. Today, bans have been passed in at least18 statesat the local or county level, and New York passed a statewide moratorium this summer.View image in fullscreenPeople protest outside OpenAI’s office in New York.Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The Guardian“They are claiming that they have the power to end humanity, but at the same time can’t get AI to do a lot of major things that they’re pushing for,” said Jonathan Westin of Climate Defenders and the Stop Funding Billionaires campaign, which organized the “unplug AI” week of action.Like Westin, many of the protesters at the anti-AI protests this week were part of climate organizations, in town for New York’s climate week, a global gathering of elected officials, policy experts and advocates timed to the meeting of the United Nations general assembly. Datacenters require significant amounts of water to function and an immense amount of energy to power,often using fossil fuels, bringing pollution into communities. Organizers are calling for more datacenter moratoriums and stronger commitments to protect water access and to block fossil fuels. They say tech companies’ greed is the real threat to the environment.Even Wall Street has warned the AI boom could cause another economicbubble to burst– one that, protesters say, will be carried on the backs of working Americans. “Regular people shouldn’t be left holding the bag for a bunch of billionaires and trillionaires to play Monopoly with our economy,” Westin said.View image in fullscreenDaisy Maldonado (right) of New Mexico at the protest outside OpenAI’s office building in New York City on Monday.Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The GuardianOther groups at this week’s protests, like the anti-war organization Code Pink, called attention to how many big tech corporations work with the US military: the US has used tech made by Palantir, xAI and Anthropic to establish targets and rain down bombs in the war in Iran – all with far-from-perfect accuracy.Alex Hanna, director of research at the Dair Institute, an AI research organization centering communities facing environmental damage and extraction from AI, said the doomsday prophesying from tech companies and former employees are a distraction amid “the climate and ecological crisis, the rising fascism that is borne out of climate politics, the making of climate refugees, and the growing inability of people just to get by from day to day. It’s such a disconnect from what seems to be actually happening.”OpenAI’s Altman and Anthropic’s Amodei address UN security councilRead moreSome protesters outside the OpenAI offices Monday had traveled from New Mexico, where aplanned datacenter threatens the already-sapped Rio Grandeand a community facing a 20-year drought. Oracle’s Project Jupiter, which is contracted to OpenAI, was pitched as a job creator for the community, but organizers say the companies aren’t talking about how it would drain the area’s limited water resources.“There’s just so much misinformation that’s being sold, not only to the elected [officials], but to the community, and I think it’s really a disservice to the people of New Mexico for these companies to come in and just basically lie about what they’re going to do and how these projects are going to benefit communities,” said Daisy Maldonado, a resident of Doña Ana county, the planned site of the datacenter.View image in fullscreenOutside OpenAI’s office in New York on 21 September 2026.Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The GuardianAt an AI sustainability conference elsewhere in the city on Tuesday, five protesters were arrested for disrupting a keynote on using AI to solve the energy grid crisis. Activists called out the conference framing as “greenwashing”, or using misleading descriptions to brand something as eco-friendly or less harmful. “We do not want to greenwash these datacenters that are being built,” said Adrosto de Silva, who also traveled from New Mexico to the OpenAI protest. “There is no way that you can do harm reduction in any sort of datacenter whatsoever.”At Monday’s protest, attendees – including the Tennessee state representative Justin Jones, who dropped in while in town for climate week – emphasized that many of these fights are happening in communities of color and poor communities, where the companies thought they wouldn’t face local backlash.“This building behind me is a danger to humankind,” said Jones, gesturing at the OpenAI offices. “The confluence of this techno oligarchy is a threat to us all. I’m here because if they come for one of us, they’re coming for all of us.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Building powerProtest (US)New YorkActivismDatacenters – USfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘This gap opens up of doubt and scepticism about everything’: Jess and Morgs confront the politics of deepfakes | Dance | The Guardian
description: In the choreographers’ new work, virtuosic movement and some green-screen magic unfurl the theatricality of high-stakes television interviews
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: In the choreographers’ new work, virtuosic movement and some green-screen magic unfurl the theatricality of high-stakes television interviews
Content: ‘It’s really about the strange shifting relationship with the landscape of truth’ … Morgann Runacre-Temple and Jessica Wright.Photograph: Yonathan KellermanView image in fullscreen‘It’s really about the strange shifting relationship with the landscape of truth’ … Morgann Runacre-Temple and Jessica Wright.Photograph: Yonathan KellermanDanceInterview‘This gap opens up of doubt and scepticism about everything’: Jess and Morgs confront the politics of deepfakesLyndsey WinshipIn the choreographers’ new work, virtuosic movement and some green-screen magic unfurl the theatricality of high-stakes television interviewsThu 24 Sep 2026 05.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 09.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt appears the interviewer has got him on the ropes. “For the record, I did not take part in a pagan ceremony with minor members of the royal family in which we daubed ourselves in paint,” states the beleaguered politician, caught outside Buckingham Palace with his flies undone and forced to defend himself. This is a fabrication, of course – I’m watching the scene play out in an east London dance studio – but it doesn’t feel miles away from something that could be true. And how do we know what’s the truth anyway? That’s the question inDeepfake, the latest piece from award-winning dance duo Jessica Wright and Morgann Runacre-Temple, AKAJess and Morgs.The pair tell modern stories with ambitious tech – film and live camera work – and often techy themes, too. “We’ve always been drawn to where there’s a crossover between the theme and the form,” says Runacre-Temple. “What gets us excited is seeing the contemporary world reflected back.” The pair scored a massive hit with their 2022 pieceCoppélia, made for Scottish Ballet, which turned a twee 19th-century ballet about a dancing doll into a cautionary tale of AI automatons and unrestrained tech bro egos. Definitely not one-hit wonders, earlier this year theymade their debut at the highly esteemed Paris Opera Ballet.View image in fullscreenGladiatorial drama in smart tailoring … Deepfake.Photograph: ChewboyDeepfake is set in a green-screen studio, where the interview is taking place between a cool-headed journalist and a politician. With writerJeff James, Jess and Morgs looked at a wealth of TV interviews, from Jeremy Paxman’s 1997 grilling of Michael Howard, wherehe asked the same question 12 times, to theformer prince Andrew’s disastrous turn on Newsnight. They also took inspiration from the current ultra-media-trained politicos who “continually and bombastically evade any questions at all”, says Wright.They liked the way the television interview is already a theatrical setup, says Wright. “I think there’s something fun about putting that on stage and asking the audience to engage with the theatricality as well.” It’s gladiatorial drama in smart tailoring. “It’s really high stakes; it’s win or lose for both of them,” adds Wright.In the show, the interview will be filmed live by four cameras – then, as well as seeing what’s happening in reality, the audience will watch another version on screen with background footage edited in. We’ll be privy to the fabrication of the image and a number of possible realities. There are also seven dancers in green-screen suits who manipulate the environment but will disappear in the edit.View image in fullscreenPrivy to the fabrication of the image … Deepfake.Photograph: ChewboyAs Runacre-Temple says, green screen can actually look quite lo-fi – “It’s got that slightly absurd, playful, silent movie quality about it” – and it’s ancient tech compared with the kind of AI deepfakes that are emerging today. “They look so hyper real,” says Runacre-Temple. “The danger of deepfakes is not only that people believe things that aren’t true to be real, but that they start to disbelieve things that are true, and this gap opens up of doubt and scepticism about everything.” Or, as in their story, someone who has been caught out doing something they shouldn’t can insist it’s a fake image. “It’s really about the strange shifting relationship with the landscape of truth.”I go to visit rehearsals on a day when there’s no tech in sight, bar a couple of laptops. “It’s good to go analogue to actually finish the choreography,” says Wright, wryly, counting the diminishing days to the premiere. All we have is an enormous studio and two incredible dancers: Rebecca Bassett-Graham, best known for dancing with Wayne McGregor’s company, who is playing the journalist; and as the politician, Kennedy Junior Muntanga, who has worked with Akram Khan.View image in fullscreen‘It’s got that slightly absurd, playful, silent movie quality about it’ … Deepfake.Photograph: ChewboyThe text plays in voiceover while the two dancers embody and expand on its meaning. Their quick-fire movements visualise all the dynamics of a charged conversation: charm, challenge, cooperation, accusation, entrapment, etc. The feel is freewheeling, but each movement is tightly mapped to the syllable, every flex of muscle is considered. In certain scenes with the green screen, dancers will have to hit exact marks and even eyelines on exact words “or the whole illusion collapses”, says Wright. They’re creating their own high-stakes environment for the performers, where “the dancers’ virtuosity is a metaphor for these very virtuosic performances in interviews”.Will this battle have a winner? Can we believe what we see? Jess and Morgs aren’t giving any spoilers. “Hopefully it will be surprising and mischievous,” says Runacre-Temple.Deepfake is atDanceEast, Ipswich, on 25 September and atSadler’s Wells East, London, 1-3 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDanceTheatreAI (artificial intelligence)DeepfakeComputingAkram KhanWayne McGregorinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Meet the real-life Pokémon professors, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battling | Games | The Guardian
description: They offer advice, referee card games and manage players’ tantrums – we caught up with some of the volunteer profs who keep the competitive game going at this year’s world championships
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: They offer advice, referee card games and manage players’ tantrums – we caught up with some of the volunteer profs who keep the competitive game going at this year’s world championships
Content: Let the battles begin … people attend the 2026 Pokemon world championships in San Francisco, California.Photograph: Frederic J Brown/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLet the battles begin … people attend the 2026 Pokemon world championships in San Francisco, California.Photograph: Frederic J Brown/AFP/Getty ImagesGamesMeet the real-life Pokémon professors, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battlingThey offer advice, referee card games and manage players’ tantrums – we caught up with some of the volunteer profs who keep the competitive game going at this year’s world championshipsAna DiazThu 24 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProfessors may be the most revered characters in the fictional world ofPokémon(apart from perhaps the Gym Leaders). In Pokémon Red and Blue, Professor Oak greets the player in a pixelated lab coat, and later provides trainers with their first battle partner; since then, each successive generation of games has introduced another professor to aid and guide trainers through their journeys. If you’ve ever played a Pokémon game, they are often the first people that you meet, apart from your in-game mom.But you may not know that there are also real-world Pokémon professors – volunteers who help organise the game’s competitive communities around the world. Instead of lab coats, they can be seen at events wearing red Pikachu-mascot shirts labelled “staff”, paired with black trousers and shoes.I spoke with several of these profs at the 2026 Pokémon world championships in San Francisco, California. Not only do they happily distribute their knowledge about Pokémon, but they also serve as vital staff at the tournament, working as referees and teachers, as well as event managers.Theofficial Pokémon websitedescribes the Pokémon Professor Program as a “global network of passionate and knowledgable fans” who volunteer their time to help run official Pokémon events. There were roughly 300 Pokémon professors present at the 2026 Pokémon world championships, according to a representative of the Pokémon Company International. A professor’s responsibilities depend on the game they work with and their assigned role at the event. A Pokémon professor officiating a game such as Pokémon Unite might be hyper-focused on wrangling players and providing technical support, whereas a judge for a trading card game tournament might provide competitors with hands-on guidance as they navigate their first live competitive event.View image in fullscreenThe OG Pokémon prof … Professor Oak in Pokémon: Let’s Go, Pikachu!Photograph: The Pokémon Company/NintendoGemma Byard, a head judge in charge of making the final call on any decisions or questions that arise, became a Pokémon professor after her son started competing in the trading card game. She says that she and the other professors help ensure the integrity of the tournament, describing what goes into the day-to-day work at worlds – such as ensuring that event officials record the results of competitions correctly.“We’ve got to make sure that all of the match slips have the correct results on them and are signed by the players to ensure, you know, that we get the right results,” Byard said. “We have to make sure that the venue is safe for everybody that’s around. We’re constantly looking out for anything that may be unsafe, or anybody that shouldn’t be in the venue. There’s a lot to think about on top of the rulings.”Professors often juggle multiple responsibilities on the competition floor and will travel across the world to staff an event such as the world championships. When asked about how the Pokémon Company International compensates its professors, however, most people I spoke to declined to disclose details. One Pokémon professor said that the European professors are compensated with goodies, such as a special staff kit with merchandise, whereas the professors at regional tournaments in the US are paid wages; the same professor said that the Pokémon Company International helped with travel, room and board for the event. (When asked for an official statement explaining how Pokémon professors are paid, a representative from the Pokémon Company International declined to comment.)Evelyne de Groot travelled from the Netherlands to staff this year’s championships. Like the other Pokémon professors I spoke to, de Groot worked her way up to staffing worlds after organising local competitions in her home region. Before we spoke, she was helping usher players out of the Moscone Center after the main convention hall closed for the evening. This year, she worked at a trading card game side event called Pokémon Sisterhood League, dedicated to giving women and non-binary people a chance to compete and connect.View image in fullscreenPassionate and knowledgeable …about 300 professors were working at this year’s Pokémon world championships in San Francisco.Photograph: San Francisco Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesFor her, a good Pokémon professor must balance enforcing the rules with giving competitors the tools they need to enjoy the game itself. She compared the position to working in “customer service”.“[Players] make friendships. You see them smile. You see them have a good time, but you’re part of that,” de Groot said. “If you’re not organising it properly, if you don’t give them clear instructions, then you see some failure […] You will sometimes get questions. You need to make sure you’re knowledgable regarding that. If you don’t know what you’re doing, if you don’t know how the card game works, then you can’t help them.”De Groot’s experience as a professor has been relatively relaxed.
