However, some professors must serve as referees and make contentious calls throughout the competition. For Byard, that means she sometimes needs to deal with upset players. At one point during the tournament, she had to manage a player who was upset with a ruling that didn’t go his way.“I got called over to the table, and I said to him: ‘Look, I need you just to keep your voice down and be respectful, and we’ll talk through what’s happened.’ And he was like: ‘I don’t need to talk to you. I need to talk to the head judge,’” Byard said, chuckling. “Well, buddy, you are talking to the head judge. That’s the kind of sass that we deal with a lot.”View image in fullscreenTough calls … a judge surveys the scene at a previous Pokémon event.Photograph: PokémonA difficult call can lead to controversy. Earlier this year, a ruling from a different judge at another tournament made headlines when a competitive Pokémon Go player who goes by the name Firestar73 was disqualified after winning the final at thePokémon Orlando regional championships. Many, including the competitor himself ina statement, conceded that the decision was a “good-faith mistake”.I asked Byard about what it’s like to make tough calls at the tournament. She said that the professors are often seen as “the bad guys”. What does she wish competitors and viewers understood about the role?“What they don’t understand is that they’re seeing a picture, but we’re getting the entire story, and we’re making the decisions based upon that story,” she said. “That can make a real difference. And we’re the ones putting ourselves out there to right a situation that’s been broken by players. We haven’t caused any distress. We’re there just to try and put it back together again.”Interviews for this feature took place at the Pokémon world championships in San Francisco. The writer’s travel and accommodation expenses were met bythe Pokémon Company.Explore more on these topicsGamesPokémonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I was arrested protesting Netanyahu’s New York visit. Here’s why we took a stand | Darializa Avila Chevalier | The Guardian
description: I refuse to play host to a man who has overseen the slaughter or injury of more than 64,000 children in Gaza with American taxpayer dollars. I refuse to be complicit in genocide
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I refuse to play host to a man who has overseen the slaughter or injury of more than 64,000 children in Gaza with American taxpayer dollars. I refuse to be complicit in genocide
Content: ‘That is why I was arrested today outside of the United Nations alongside hundreds of my fellow New Yorkers.’Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘That is why I was arrested today outside of the United Nations alongside hundreds of my fellow New Yorkers.’Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty ImagesOpinionBenjamin NetanyahuI was arrested protesting Netanyahu’s New York visit. Here’s why we took a standDarializa Avila ChevalierI refuse to play host to a man who has overseen the slaughter or injury of more than 64,000 children in Gaza with American taxpayer dollars. I refuse to be complicit in genocideThu 24 Sep 2026 17.20 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.27 EDTShareBenjamin Netanyahu belongs at The Hague; not in the streets of New York City, and certainly not before the United Nations general assembly. The international criminal court has a warrant out for his arrest for war crimes and crimes against humanity. The UN’s own commission of inquiry has found that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza and named Netanyahu as its chief architect.As the Democratic nominee for New York’s 13th congressional district, I refuse to allow a war criminal to roam the streets of our city unchallenged. I refuse to play host to a man who has overseen the slaughter or injury of more than64,000 children in Gazawith American taxpayer dollars. I refuse to be complicit in genocide.That is why I was arrested today outside of theUnited Nationsalongside hundreds of my fellow New Yorkers.Israel has killed more than73,000 people in Gaza. It has bombed hospitals, schools, places of worship, fishing boats, and refugee tents. It hascollectively starvedan entire population as a tool in its genocide.It has subjected men, women and children to systematic sexual torture and imprisonment. It hasthreatened to kill people for flying kites, killed more than1,000 people since its so-called ceasefire, andfired 335 bulletsinto a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab.And when it comes to consequences, world leaders offer carefully worded statements that don’t even amount to a slap on the wrist.Here in the US, establishmentDemocratsand Republicans alike have shielded Netanyahu from prosecution for his crimes and sent over$21bn of our tax dollarsin just two years to fund Israeli bombs.TheBidenandTrumpadministrations both obscured evidence, lied about what Israel was doing in Gaza, funded the carnage, and isolated and arrested people that spoke out against it. Just last week, the Trump administrationproposed a $2.8bn weapons saleto Israel including 2,000lb bombs.New Yorkers refuse to be silent. That’s why today’s civil disobedience, led by Jewish Voice for Peace, NYC-DSA, Sunrise Movement, CAAAV, Palestinian Youth Movement, Adalah Justice Project, the US Campaign for Palestinian Rights and more had 400 participants including more than 100 people arrested to demand an end to this injustice.Netanyahu’s speech at UN spurs protests in New York City: ‘Let Gaza live’Read moreAnd NY-13, and New York City, is with us. This summer, Harlem, Washington Heights, Inwood and the West Bronx unseated a five-term, Aipac-backed incumbent. Their message was clear: invest in their babies here at home, not in bombs dropped abroad.They made me their Democratic nominee with a mandate to pass legislation like theBlock the Bombs Actand fight back against our country’s insatiable war machine. Across this city, New Yorkers elected candidates to Congress and the state assembly who’ll fight to stop the bombs, divest from death, and invest in a politics of life.Families inPalestine, Lebanon and Iran are not our enemies.Our enemy is a system where billionaires get rich from stoking hatred and war while our own communities go without. Tonight, shelters across uptown and the Bronxwill be full. This past year, more than100,000 childrenin New York City’s public schools have experienced homelessness. And right now, families are feeling the physical toll of cuts to Snap and Medicaid, and New York City Housing Authority residents are once again forced to sleep in inadequate housing.I ran for Congress because I am done being told that there is never enough money for our communities while watching our government write blank checks to enact atrocities. Every dollar spent on slaughtering communities abroad is a dollar stolen from our communities here at home.In 1967, Dr Martin Luther King Jrstood at the pulpit of Riverside churchin my district and warned that a country that spends more on war than “on programs of social uplift is approaching spiritual death”.Members of Congress have a responsibility to act with courage in the face of grave injustice, not to continue funding it. Unfortunately, nearly 60 years later, not much has changed.Palestinians are facing unthinkable conditions every single day under an Israeli apartheid regime that that disappears men, women and children intomilitary prisons knownfor their physical, sexual and psychological torture.And here at home, families in my district have to endure their schools, clinics and food assistance being cut to pay for war, and ICE kidnapping our neighbors for speaking up for Palestinians, while nearly 40% of the babies in my district are growing up inpoverty.From NY-13 to Palestine, all children, and all people, deserve the safety and the resources to live dignified lives. That’s why I take to the streets, and that’s why I’m headed to Congress: to stop sending our tax dollars to arm genocide, to end senseless wars, and to build a government accountable to the working people of this country.Our communities deserve leaders with an unwavering moral compass, who understand that our shared humanity is sacred, and that fights to build a politics of life even when it is politically costly. If that requires my arrest, so be it.Darializa Avila Chevalier is the Democratic nominee for New York’s 13th congressional districtExplore more on these topicsBenjamin NetanyahuOpinionIsraelGazaMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineNew YorkUnited NationscommentShareReuse this content

title: In its push to subordinate women, the American right is embracing raunch | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: Conservatives long promoted a politics of sexual prohibition. Now such morals have been shed in favor of male domination
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: Conservatives long promoted a politics of sexual prohibition. Now such morals have been shed in favor of male domination
Content: Ad featuring Sydney Sweeney in Times Square, New York City.Photograph: Michael M Santiago/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAd featuring Sydney Sweeney in Times Square, New York City.Photograph: Michael M Santiago/Getty ImagesOpinionUS politicsIn its push to subordinate women, the American right is embracing raunchMoira DoneganConservatives long promoted a politics of sexual prohibition. Now such morals have been shed in favor of male dominationThu 24 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 07.29 EDTShareUnder Kash Patel, the FBIwill now hire youeven if you have a history of hiring prostitutes, or of having sex with animals. The rightwing Maha influencer Alex Clark had a guest on to hertalk showto discuss the idea that wives should provide sex for their husbands on demand. A new ad for a sports gambling website is being hailed as a victory for the political right, because it features a nudeSydney Sweeneyclutching footballs to her breasts. TheTate brothers, who encourage their male followers to pursue compulsive sexual conquest and who have beenaccused of sex trafficking and violencein the operation of their online cam porn business,have reportedly beenfriendly with members of Trump’s circle. A dizzying array of elites on both sides of the aisle – conservatives very much included – seem to have been socializing with apedophile financier, and were so unfazed by his constant coterie of underaged girl companions that one begins to wonder whether they were habituated to such scenes. A prominentconservative writer, best known for her opposition to gender transition care for children, has announced a new book claiming to tackle the problem of young women who are supposedly unwilling to have enough sex. And the women of the president’s members club, Mar-A-Lago, are so well known for their dramatic facelifts, and their lips so stuffed with filler that they cannot quite close their mouths, that their faces are nowa shorthandin the world of plastic surgery.Raunch, vulgarity, a boorish entitlement to women’s sexual service, and the aesthetics – and, indeed, the business – of pornography are being embraced by the right.For those old enough to remember the rise of Pat Buchanan and Phyllis Schlafly in the Reagan era, or even the earnest displays of Christian faith that characterized the George W Bush administration, this can all be a bit dizzying. For decades, it was the left that embraced public sexuality, taking the lead on comprehensive sex education, gay rights, and abortion access, and celebrating the sexual revolution that was ushered in by the advent of the birth control pill in the 1960s. It was liberals who embraced feminism, and worked to make women’s new freedom to delay marriage and childbearing enforcible in civil rights law. It was the left that retheorized family and marriage, reshaping the age-old institutions into ones that could better accommodate gay relationships and women’s equality. It was the progressives who embraced abortion as a means of sexual freedom and women’s self-determination, and who fought for birth control and sexually transmitted disease testing to be funded by the federal government. And it was the left that championed pornography as a free speech issue – shouting down the feminists in their own camp who critiqued the misogyny of its content, and making porn production and distribution into cornerstones of the liberal vision of the first amendment.Why are Democrats so quiet about the Tate brothers? | Moira DoneganRead moreThe right, meanwhile, was long married – pun intended – to a politics of sexual prohibition. When the Christian right was at the peak of its power, the Republican party had many of the same policies it does now: demanding bans on abortion, opposing gay rights, looking askance at birth control, pushing cuts to sexual health programs, rolling their eyes at civil rights protections meant to protect women workers from sexual harassment, and opposing comprehensive sex education, favoring instead abstinence-only models. But back then, when Evangelicism and the prim repression of the Protestant right were the dominant cultural force within the Republican party, these policies came packaged in a distinct style: one of sexual prohibition and shaming, that emphasized a kind of sexual self-discipline in the guise of decency. Back then, it really was a scandal when a pastor was caught cheating on his wife, even when his partner in infidelity was an adult woman. Sexual morality was a virtue that the right trumpeted in a very particular style: no sex until marriage, and even then, only the baby-making, heterosexual kind.Was this all a ruse? The sexual morals of the Christian right seem to have evaporated as soon as the nation heard Donald Trumputter the words“grab ‘em by the pussy.” Now, an ostentatious lasciviousness reigns. In today’s Republican party, raunch is the coin of the realm, a “locker room talk” style of sexual vulgarity is de rigeur, and positions of power in the Trump world sometimes seem to go hand in hand with sexual assault allegations for men, and very specific kinds of surgical enhancements for women. The preachers have retreated, and the perverts have taken over. In the Maga era, sexual domination is synonymous with manliness, and porn is the lingua franca.But is this really such a great change? After all, the transformation of the Republican party from a Christian culture that prioritized sexual prohibition to a pornified culture that celebrates sexual force has been a stylistic change, not a policy change: Republican politicians are still voting to make casual, premarital, non-procreative sex as dangerous, expensive, and risky as they can possibly make it – at least for women. If the left’s celebration of porn as a free speech issue always somewhat undermined their supposed commitment to women’s equality, the right’s onetime finger-wagging at pornography’s glorification of women’s sexual humiliation always clashed with the reality that the Christian right shared the same message and goal. Sexual prohibition and sexual force, after all, are just two different styles of what is ultimately a single project: the use of sex to subordinate women. At least now we can stop pretending that they’re not the same thing.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsUS politicsOpinionFeminismGendercommentShareReuse this content

title: It pays to be generous: there’s nothing more embarrassing than being bank-transferred the price of a coffee | Johanna Cosgrove | The Guardian
description: If something is under $15 and you buy it for me, I will do the same for you next time. This is called trust and this is called reciprocity
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: If something is under $15 and you buy it for me, I will do the same for you next time. This is called trust and this is called reciprocity
Content: ‘If you haven’t experienced a lack of anything, how can you understand that providing the thing another person needs will fulfill both of you?’Photograph: filadendron/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘If you haven’t experienced a lack of anything, how can you understand that providing the thing another person needs will fulfill both of you?’Photograph: filadendron/Getty ImagesOpinionFriendshipIt pays to be generous: there’s nothing more embarrassing than being bank-transferred the price of a coffeeJohanna CosgroveIf something is under $15 and you buy it for me, I will do the same for you next time. This is called trust and this is called reciprocityThu 24 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 19.09 EDTShareLike many women in their 30s, one of my true joys is meeting a friend for a beverage. However, after catching up for a green juice (healthy) with a dear colleague recently, I was on the train home when I got a message saying “Hey! Can you please transfer me $12.50? Thank you!” My response can only be described as … horrified.The reason that it stuck in my craw is because I firmly believe thatyou should not request repayment for anything under $15.If we are out together and I shout you a coffee I would rather commitseppukuthan be bank-transferred $4.50 ($6 if you are in the CBD, $9 if you are a matcha observant). For context, A$15 is roughly US$10, £8, €9, NZ$19 and 1,680 yen. In this (scary) global economy, that doesn’t stretch much further than a small beverage/snack/Boots meal deal.It’s time for all of us to get a grip and stop flaking on friends for no good reasonRead moreIf something is under $15 and you buy it for me, know that I will do the same for you next time. This is called trust and this is called reciprocity (look upSahlins’ typologyif you are feeling academic or in need of a more eloquent explanation). Generosity is an important skill! I think about my parents, uncles and grandfather almost getting into fistfights over who would pay the bill at a restaurant. To provide something for your loved ones was once seen as something to be proud of. A sign of respect and humility! While I don’t share a blood bond with my favourite work wife, the trust and care is still there. We don’t have Venmo in the southern hemisphere, but in Australia we have PayID (which is superior imo), and in New Zealand, my country of birth, we have nothing but bank transfer, so the whole process of repayment is clunky and time-consuming.You may argue there are cultural contexts in which recounting every penny is both socially encouraged and a sign of respect. My grandmother grew up in the Netherlands, potentially the biggest proponents of financial fairness (ever heard the phrase “going Dutch”?). In Dutch (and German), the word for debt isSchuld,which can also mean guilt or fault – no doubt fostering lingering aversions to owing money. Young people in the Netherlands use Tikkie – an app similar to Splitwise – to immediately request repayment for even tiny amounts. This is rooted in a strong cultural mindset of equality rather than miser behaviour (I have heard it’s not unusual for gifts to be refused because no one wants to owe anyone anything). But to my family and forefathers I say: absolutely not.Rudeness! Manners! Whatever happened to being polite?! | First Dog on the MoonRead moreIf you need to hold on to your $15 or are skint until payday (me every week, lol) then … don’t offer. We can drink whatever we have at home. The ironic thing is, it’s never my friends who earn the least who ask to be paid back. US comedian and actor Robby Hoffman said in a recentNew York Times interview, “the poor have much less but when you go to their house it’s like ‘Take! Take! Take! You want a coke?’” I would offer that, generally, those fortunate enough to grow up wealthy have a slightly different relationship to generosity. Because if you haven’t experienced a lack of anything, how can you understand that providing the thing another person needs will fulfill both of you? Not to mention that $15 is a comparative drop in the ocean to anyone earning over $150,000 a year.The reason my personal threshold is $15 (in the year of our lord 2026 amid a cost-of-living crisis) isn’t due to any market research; it’s based purely on vibes. Twenty dollars? You can absolutely ask for that back. A 20 is a note, it’s (potentially) a meal, it’s a clean, crisp, substantial sum. Anything under? Reconsider your stingy attitude.Ultimately, at this late stage (of capitalism) we can’t afford to nitpick at the cost of love and care. So please go forth, shout your friends a treat if you can, and remember that it actually always pays to be generous!Johanna Cosgrove is an award-winning actor, writer and comedianExplore more on these topicsFriendshipOpinionSocial etiquettecommentShareReuse this content

title: I love seeing pooches in pubs. But not everyone, human or canine, understands the etiquette | Paul Daley | The Guardian
description: Soon the hounds of Victoria could be formally allowed into watering holes, but brawlers and biters aren’t welcome – neither are misbehaved dogs
Author: Paul Daley
Headline: Soon the hounds of Victoria could be formally allowed into watering holes, but brawlers and biters aren’t welcome – neither are misbehaved dogs
Content: ‘I love seeing dogs in the pub. I always assume that their behaviour and training deems them fit to be there,’ Paul Daley writes.Photograph: Jonathan Hordle/PAView image in fullscreen‘I love seeing dogs in the pub. I always assume that their behaviour and training deems them fit to be there,’ Paul Daley writes.Photograph: Jonathan Hordle/PAOpinionDogsI love seeing pooches in pubs. But not everyone, human or canine, understands the etiquettePaul DaleySoon the hounds of Victoria could be formally allowed into watering holes, but brawlers and biters aren’t welcome – neither are misbehaved dogsThu 24 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 18.44 EDTShareNot every dog, just like not every person, should go to the pub.Obstreperous drunks should stay home along with incessant barkers. Brawlers and biters, human or canine – no way!Soon the dogs of Victoria could be formallyallowed into pubsif (and thisisa ferociously bigif) theCarroll Labor governmentis returned at the forthcoming state election. While my blue-heeler-collie-crossOlive– who lives in Sydney but hails from inner-city Melbourne – would, if she could, vote for this amendment to the Food Act 1984, she is also well aware that not every bloke or bitch of her species understands pub etiquette.Are pubs and pups a good mix? Dog owners delight as Victoria looks to follow Europe’s leadRead moreThere’s no place in her books for growlers and sniffers and frisky types that don’t understand “back off”. Or dogs that won’t get the message either.Olive can go anywhere. In pubs and restaurants in Sydney’s inner west, where she lives, she will sit contentedly at our feet. She is not food driven. She is not interested in the schnitty and chips at the next table. She’ll gratefully accept a pat but is wary of taking treats from strangers – as we should all perhaps be.She is well in control of her – ahem! – bodily functions in public places, at all times.Which is more than can be said for the occasional other dog. Or person.Recently I witnessed a considerable human fracas (that ultimately involved bouncers) at one of my regular watering holes when a small poodle-cross (accidentally, perhaps) relieved itself in the crowded dining room. It was a divisive episode among patrons.The dog seemed ashamed – more so than the humans we’ve all witnessed do far worse, with greater deliberation, at closing time.Paws, pints and 3am pubs in Victorian premier’s election promise – videoAs a dog person,I understand not everybody else wants to see our best friends treading the sticky red carpet down at the local. Some people are legitimatelyscared of dogs. Others don’t like them around kids on the grounds of safety (simple solution: ban children from pubs and allow in dogs) or hygiene (even though children with dogs may developbetter immunity).There are gentle and sweet dogs who’ve lived in my household who we would never take to the pub – or pretty much anywhere food was being served.RondaandNariwere labradors. This might sound like an explanation in itself as to why they couldn’t ever settle in public amid food aromas. Both could have competitively eaten for Australia. There was no end to the disgusting dead stuff they scavenged and consumed in various parks.Then again, potential admission to the pub should not be judged on breed alone. I’ve seen perfectly chilled labs in the pub. Even the odd beagle, a breed that detects a sumptuous ham sandwich at the merest whiff of your leather wallet, and may devour it if given half a chance.As an aside, I have a mate who had a much-loved black labrador with a sweet tooth. Well, a tooth for anything really.It once pounced on and atean entire cake at an alfresco birthday party at an (off-leash!) six-year-old’s birthday party. Bad dog! No – Tommy was never going to get to the pub.Pet hates: what’s it like to dislike dogs in a dog-loving country?Read moreOn a recent car trip to a (Victorian) wine district,Olive was well pleased to be given a list of dog-friendly wineries. There were usually water bowls. Dog beds. Even treats.But there were also signs making it clear that people were responsible for the behaviour of their animals.In any public place, that’s got to be the rule. I love seeing dogs in the pub. I always assume that their behaviour and training deems them fit to be there. I’ve rarely seen a problem.Last time we were in Melbourne, Olive and I went to several pubs in the inner north. Other dogs were there. Nobody barked. Nobody complained. So here’s the memo: it’s already happening and it might not, therefore, be a (human) vote-changer.Finally, there is of course a reason bouncers are often on the doors of the pubs we go to. And it’s mostly to do with the behaviour of people – not dogs.Paul Daley is a Guardian Australia columnistExplore more on these topicsDogsOpinionPetsVictoriaAnimalsPubsVictorian politicsAustralian lifestylecommentShareReuse this content

title: Tom Watson’s move to Palantir is the latest sign of how far the rot has spread in UK politics | Clive Lewis | The Guardian
description: When a former Labour deputy leader joins a firm built on surveillance and military targeting, it deepens public cynicism – and democracy depends on trust, says Labour MP Clive Lewis
Author: Clive Lewis
Headline: When a former Labour deputy leader joins a firm built on surveillance and military targeting, it deepens public cynicism – and democracy depends on trust, says Labour MP Clive Lewis
Content: ‘Palantir probably doesn’t hire a former deputy leader for his coding skills. But does it hire access?’ Tom Watson in London, January 2025.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Palantir probably doesn’t hire a former deputy leader for his coding skills. But does it hire access?’ Tom Watson in London, January 2025.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersOpinionPalantirTom Watson’s move to Palantir is the latest sign of how far the rot has spread in UK politicsClive LewisWhen a former Labour deputy leader joins a firm built on surveillance and military targeting, it deepens public cynicism – and democracy depends on trustThu 24 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 09.25 EDTShareWhatever is said about Tom Watson, the former deputy leader of the Labour party has a knack for landing headlines. In the past he did it at the expense of the rich and powerful – from News International,over phone hacking, to the Home Office,over its mass surveillance of our data. But his latest headline – that he has joined Palantir as a senior vice-president – has been at the expense of public confidence in the political class.Hisnew appointmentis more than just a private career choice. It sends yet another signal to a weary public about just how far the rot in our democracy has spread.Now, the former scourge of mass surveillance finds a surveillance company “the most interesting … on the planet”. It’s quite a journey, and one not many of us will want to take with him. Palantir does do work of real consequence. That’s rather the point. Watson says some criticism of Palantiris propaganda. Some of it is also true, which is the part he will find harder to square.Palantir is a company built on surveillance and military targeting. Its co-founder Peter Thielwrote in 2009that he no longer believed freedom and democracy were compatible. He sees technology as an alternative to politics, a way to change the world without having to persuade voters, andbacks private “startup cities”run by chief executives. This attitude runs through the company’s DNA. Palantir’s co-founder and chief executive, Alex Karp,has boastedthat its work is there “to scare enemies and on occasion kill them”. Its software is used totarget people for ICE raidsin the US, andcivilians in Gaza. This isn’t just another global corporation with some unsavoury corners to its business.I can’t parse Watson’s mind or motivation. Palantir probably doesn’t hire a former deputy leader for his coding skills. But does it hire access? Access to networks across party and government, and to the doors behind which Palantir would fight to keep a£330m NHS England contractand legally challengeSadiq Khan’s blockon a £50m Metropolitan police contract?Watson won’t be alone. He will joinmore than 30former UK officials at a company that Peter Mandelson’s former lobbying firm, Global Counsel, counted as a client. Mandelson accompanied Keir Starmerto Palantir’s Washington officein 2025, while still retaining a stake in Global Counsel.The MoD has since signed amajor partnershipwith Palantir. And none of this will have broken a single law. The rules on jobs for former ministers last only two years and have no legal force. Therein lies the problem.Whether it’s Tony Blair and his relationship with Oracle, Mandelson and Global Counsel or Nick Clegg and his time at Meta, the section of the political class meant to oppose vested interests and promote public service appears to have switched sides.According to the Institute for Public Policy Research’slatest findings, the main political parties, including Labour and the Liberal Democrats, have been accepting donations from wealthy individuals at an accelerating pace. The research found 72% of all £1m-plus donations from individuals since records began in 2001 had come since 2019. Sadly, none of this can be described as an aberration. Rather, it’s how the system increasingly works. Now politicians’ proximity to wealth and the “elites” who own it has fostered a growing public mistrust. One need only listen toDanny Dyer at a rally last week, calling for public ownership of water, to get a feel for that sentiment. These examples are all symptoms of the growing proximity between political power and the wealth it is supposed to hold to account.In the recentRobin Cook memorial lectureI gave, I termed this malaise the “integrity gap”: the widening gulf between what governments and politicians say and what people believe. Every flagrant act deepens public cynicism about politics, and about the democracy that depends on public trust. This is a fact of which those around Trump are well aware. They know every allegation of presidential corruption erodes people’s willingness to defend democracy.Thiel understands this implicitly. His vision for our society is simply not compatible with a progressive worldview. That is why a former Labour deputy leader lending his name toPalantirmatters so much.The integrity gap will not close with better messaging. It will close only when politicians show whose side they are on. That means revolving-door rules with the force of law, and a regulator with teeth. It means capping political donations and ending second jobs in the House of Commons, while abolishing the House of Lords altogether. And it means public ownership and democratic control of the things firms such as Palantir want to run, from our health data to our water.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThose who sell access to power have made their choice. Those who oppose Thiel’s vision need to make theirs, and act on it. It’s time to pick a side.Clive Lewis is theLabourMP for Norwich SouthDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: We’re in a crisis of loneliness – but is buying friends on an app likely to help solve it? | Elle Hunt | The Guardian
description: Shortcuts work against the rewards of friendship: authentic relationships can surely only be forged when you’re not expecting a return on your money, says journalist Elle Hunt
Author: Elle Hunt
Headline: Shortcuts work against the rewards of friendship: authentic relationships can surely only be forged when you’re not expecting a return on your money, says journalist Elle Hunt
Content: People meeting at a party.Photograph: Thomas Barwick/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople meeting at a party.Photograph: Thomas Barwick/Getty ImagesOpinionFriendshipWe’re in a crisis of loneliness – but is buying friends on an app likely to help solve it?Elle HuntShortcuts work against the rewards of friendship: authentic relationships can surely only be forged when you’re not expecting a return on your moneyThu 24 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 14.59 EDTShareWhat price would you put on friendship? In these hyper-capitalistic times, where nothing is beyond being given a monetary value, perhaps even Mastercard wouldn’t dare to claim that it’s priceless. AYouGov surveyfound that 15% of Britons say they have no close friends, while nearly one in 10 (8%) have no friends at all. The numbersare similarly dismalin the US. As we face this contemporary crisis of connection, it is little wonder that friendship, or at least the possibility of it, is increasingly being marketed for sale.There has been a striking increase in online platforms and apps that promise to introduce you – algorithmically, through social mixers or a combination – to your next BFF. There’sCliq,PLY, standing for “People Like You”, andRealRootswhich promises user satisfaction with the tagline: “Make new friends. Guaranteed”. Meanwhile,222boldly declares it is “not a friend-making service”, but a means to “explore serendipity” through social experiences with compatible people.And this new sweep of pay-to-play friendships doesn’t stop at apps and algorithmic matchmaking. It is accompanied by supper clubs, book clubs, running clubs and other opportunities for you to mingle with people in your area – for a fee, of course.CircleUp, for example, holds regular social mixers across the UK for paying members, so that you can “keep seeing the same faces”. Others cultivate a more exclusive crowd.Gathering Tableshosts dinners for a “curated mix of guests”, united by their willingness to pay £145 a head.These initiatives dangle community, but whether this trumps their commercial reason for being is debatable. The price of these apps and events is sometimes framed as a means of securing commitment, not just covering costs. “When you do things for free, people often don’t turn up,” PLY’s foundertold the Guardian. But the effort becomes less civic-minded when you consider the desire for friendship is what makes these services valuable in the first place. These friend-making apps and paid-for gatherings may well offer opportunities for social connection – they are at least a date in the diary. But make no mistake, they exist primarily to encourage investment in a brand and even create opportunities to spend. Of course it is possible to make genuine connections in commercial spaces – many of us have made close bonds at work – but paying for introductions feels antithetical to the spirit of true friendship.This new commercial interest in facilitating “gathering” speaks to the sense of collective untethering from community. Many of us understand we are lacking community, perhaps even more than friendship. It is unsettlingly common to hear people complaining of their current social network, as though a more suitable or nourishing one already exists, just waiting for you to slot into it. No wonder brands are attempting to package them up.Cliq claims the first step to “start your community” is to download its app. But real community is built, not bought (and certainly not downloaded). It takes time, shared investment and oftensome weathering on both sides. It is certainly possible that meaningful, enduring ties can begin at a paid-for meet-up. But while the payment can create the conditions for friendship, it can’t manufacture the friendship itself.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hill I will die on: Private karaoke is the death of socialism – only a pub singalong is good enough for the people | Kelli BlanchettRead moreTellingly, ease is often central to the offering: Cliq claims “finding your people shouldn’t be difficult”. Shouldn’t it? No matter how you meet, it takes time and effort to turn an acquaintance into a friend; that same process, multiplied and sustained, is what creates a community. Seeking shortcuts or higher-quality connections is not only beside the point, it works against the rewards: authentic relationships can only be forged without expectation of a return on investment.That’s not to say we don’t need more places and opportunities to meet new people; the very existence of these services at least demonstrates that we do. But before entrusting our need for greater intimacy and affection to a third party, we might ask ourselves if we could be doing more to put ourselves out there socially. Could we extend an invitation to friendly strangers, or introduce our mutuals and turn acquaintances into friends?The best community-building exercise I’ve heard of lately was before a performance of Austentatious – the Jane Austen comedy play – where all solo ticket-holders were invited to come early and mingle before the show. The event was free, organised around a preexisting commitment and people could opt in. There was the opportunity to meet people; the work, and potential reward, of making a new friend was left to you.Elle Hunt is a freelance journalistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: OpenAI’s Medicare hack is a bleak opportunity for Australia to address its security shortcomings post-haste | Van Badham | The Guardian
description: All Australians should demand independent means to protect ourselves from Dr Sam Altman Frankenstein and Daddy America
Author: Van Badham
Headline: All Australians should demand independent means to protect ourselves from Dr Sam Altman Frankenstein and Daddy America
Content: An AI agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare and three other systems in June.Photograph: Susie Dodds/AAPView image in fullscreenAn AI agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare and three other systems in June.Photograph: Susie Dodds/AAPOpinionOpenAIOpenAI’s Medicare hack is a bleak opportunity for Australia to address its security shortcomings post-hasteVan BadhamAll Australians should demand independent means to protect ourselves from Dr Sam Altman Frankenstein and Daddy AmericaThu 24 Sep 2026 03.27 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 03.28 EDTShareWhoopsie! DrSam AltmanFrankenstein regrets to inform you he’s lost control of his OpenAI monster.It’s roving around doing things that provokeinternational legal investigation, and Australia has found out in the worst possible way.The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, was obliged to announce from the United Nations summit on Thursday morning Australian time that an agentic AI from theOpenAIstable had gained unauthorised access to both public and non-public information from Australia’s Medicare website.An OpenAI agent infiltrated Medicare – and Australia only found out months later. Here’s what we know so farRead moreThe good news in this debacle is that so far it appears no personal information held in Medicare’s records was compromised. Pursuing “a benign task” of compiling some health statistics, the portal breach accessed non-sensitive data about spending.The good news, alas, ends here. OpenAI – a company worth US$852bn as per its last valuation – informed the government of the breach by … sending an email to its public email account three months after the hack occurred. Albanese revealed the date of Services Australia’s worst ever Inbox Zero was 10 September, and the Australian Cyber Security Centre was informed on 15 September.Albanese at the UN has proved a fairly nimble diplomat, much to the surprise of anyone who has been on the receiving end of his vengeance at home. One imagines that a desire to soften fierce Trumpian pushback to Labor’s attempts at “digital duty-of-care” regulations for – ha! – AI and social media inspired the PM’s epically cringeworthygrip-and-grin selfiewith the unpopular president. It was “photo diplomacy” wisely followed by a well-publicised hug with Volodymyr Zelenskyy.After a direct meeting with Altman, the PM described the “obviously unacceptable” incident and his government’s “extreme concern”. Announcing immediate taskforces and urgent reviews into the breach and its national security implications, Albanese said Altman was aware “the company had not done good enough”.“Aware” may actually be underselling it, because Altman has been making speeches of his own at the UN – to no less than theUN security council, alongside his supposed corporate rival, Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei – urging the governments of the world to collectively enforce regulations of the technology guided by democratic institutions.Begging the question: Dr Frankenstein, what the hell’s been going on in your lab?View image in fullscreenCEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, speaks at a United Nations security council meeting on artificial intelligence and international security on 23 September.Photograph: John Angelillo/UPI/ShutterstockOne longs for the tender innocence of last week when we could describe warnings from ex-Anthropic employees thatAI could destroy the world within 10 yearsas merely utterly terrifying – because the attitude of the security council member representing the world’s richest democracy is that the “only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT”.Here’s hoping one will turn up. In the unregulated, commercial AI environment where “crawler” AIs are autonomously finding their way around sovereign data protection systems to scrape information, the explanatory metaphor that leaps to mind is if nuclear weapons had been retailed and the world only found out about radioactive fallout once a 10-year-old playing with it in a back yard had permanently depopulated Baltimore.Is American laissez-faire fuckwittery to blame here? Yes – and Australians are right to be screaming that if OpenAI were a Chinese or Iranian company hacking into our systems ambassadors would be marching out of embassies with grand announcements and thundering speeches of condemnation.But they’d also be wise to remember that geographically isolated, distant middle power Australia has only been afforded grandiosity on the world stage because in the post-second world war, pre-Trump era, it had the umbrella protection of a meaningful alliance with Daddy America.double quotation markEvery one of us should back calls to regulate the living bejeezus out of all AI-capable foreign platforms seeking to operate hereAnd these days it’s Daddy America who’s a rules-free maniac whose sole political calculation is that money equals power and a literal “to the victor the spoils” foreign policy. To imagine Donald Trump’s US state department will be inspired into acts of responsibility due to Australian shaming it for data theft is some high genre alternate history. The man Trump pardoned who ran a stolen-data criminal marketplace spoke at the Republican convention in Dallas this year. Symbolic, no?Internationally, the realignment of powers in the wake of Trump’s thuggery advances, but what role Australia will be offered in that realignment is uncertain, and it is narcissistic to pretend otherwise.Locally, we’re not powerless. The Medicare breach is a bleak opportunity to address our revealed information security shortcomings post-haste, with full democratic transparency and accountability. All Australians should demand independent means to protect ourselves from the new front in the information war. If Albanese’s new taskforce determines that ministerial oversight failed to protect Medicare or any other comprised dataset, heads must – publicly – roll.The ACTUhas long been warningof US abrogation of AI security obligations, demanding the development of “sovereign AI” capacity to meet oncoming threats. Every one of us should back calls to regulate the living bejeezus out of all AI-capable foreign platforms seeking to operate here – or impose moratoriums on operations outright.I am not entrusted to represent Australia diplomatically, so let me say to Mr Altman what a prime minister on a diplomatic mission apparently can’t: if your creatures are thieving our data and you are too much of a coward to pick up the damn phone to tell us, your destruction may be individual, it may be collective – but it is ensured.Van Badham is a Guardian Australia columnistExplore more on these topicsOpenAIOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Medicare AustraliaSam AltmanHackingAustralian security and counter-terrorismAustralian politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Britain would not cut up the Bayeux tapestry. So seize this moment and reunite the Parthenon sculptures in Greece | Kyriakos Mitsotakis | The Guardian
description: Both Greek and British citizens think the sculptures should be returned. What’s needed now is political will and courage, says Kyriakos Mitsotakis, prime minister of Greece
Author: Kyriakos Mitsotakis
Headline: Both Greek and British citizens think the sculptures should be returned. What’s needed now is political will and courage, says Kyriakos Mitsotakis, prime minister of Greece
Content: Some of the Parthenon sculptures on view at the British Museum in London.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSome of the Parthenon sculptures on view at the British Museum in London.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianOpinionParthenon marblesBritain would not cut up the Bayeux tapestry. So seize this moment and reunite the Parthenon sculptures in GreeceKyriakos MitsotakisBoth Greek and British citizens think the sculptures should be returned. What’s needed now is political will and courageKyriakos Mitsotakis is the prime minister of GreeceThu 24 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 10.52 EDTShareFor the first time in nearly 1,000 years, the Bayeux tapestry isback in Britain. Its arrival is a significant cultural moment, and a reminder that, in an age of social media and ubiquitous screens, historic objects still capture the public imagination.TheBritish Museumdescribes the tapestry as one of the “wonders of the medieval world”. But the museum already houses many wonders, including one that is instantly recognisable: the Parthenon sculptures, chiselled away and illegally removed from Athens to be taken to Britain more than two centuries ago by Lord Elgin.There are striking similarities between the two pieces. Both were conceived as single works, intended to be seen and understood as a whole. In the case of the Parthenon sculptures, that relationship is also architectural: they were created as inseparable elements of the monument itself. Nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it. Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures. A single masterpiece was divided, and its surviving parts are now principally split between London and Athens.The sculptures tell a story of unique historical importance. Not only of gods and heroes, but also of ordinary civil life in ancient Athens. They gave a visual expression in stone to the religious, civic and political identity of fifth-century Athens. The Parthenon frieze, in particular, remains one of the world’s most compelling representations of the collective life of the city from which democracy emerged. It is a powerful celebration of Athenian democracy.Unlike the sculptures, the Bayeux tapestry survives as one continuous work, measuring nearly 70 metres. It too tells a story, from the events preceding the Norman Conquest to the battle of Hastings and the death of Harold. Its wonder lies not just in the individual scenes, but in the way they are experienced together as a whole.View image in fullscreenThe Parthenon gallery at the Acropolis Museum in Athens.Photograph: Louisa Gouliamaki/ReutersThe case for reunification is not an argument for emptying the world’s museums. The Parthenon constitutes a specific and exceptional case. The issue is not merely one of possession or legal title. It concerns the restoration of the physical, aesthetic and conceptual integrity of a dismembered monument of outstanding universal value.The surviving sculptures should be viewed together, at the same time, within sight of the monument for which they were created. TheAcropolis Museumwas designed specifically to make this possible.Greece cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum’s ownership of the sculptures,or a scheme that would mean we “borrow” parts of our own monument. And the British public is increasingly on Greece’s side. A nationally representative poll published last year found thata majority supportsthe return of the sculptures to Greece. More strikingly,72% agreedthat they are best understood as part of a single ensemble with the Parthenon.For decades, Greece has been in dialogue with Britain to achieve that goal. In recent years, my government has held detailed discussions with the leadership of the British Museum about how reunification might be achieved. I was, therefore, surprised at the recent suggestion from the Museum that the Bayeux tapestry loanmight provide a templatefor an agreement over the Parthenon sculptures. I do not believe it does.France has lent the artwork as an undivided whole, and that work will return to France as an undivided whole. The Parthenon presents the reverse situation: integral parts of the monument were forcibly removed and dispersed. Our objective is their permanent reunification. Unesco’s Intergovernmental Committee for the Return of Cultural Property to Countries of Origin has repeatedlycalled uponthe UK to engage with Greece on this matter ingood-faith dialogue.Reunification could become the foundation of a broad and enduring cultural partnership between our countries, creating new opportunities for exhibitions, scholarship, conservation and exchanges between Greek and British museums. Together we could create a new model of cultural cooperation between two democratic nations and allies with deeply shared values and ideals. That is the prize.In 2023, before becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham urged that the sculptures be sent back “no strings attached”, adding: “Let’s use culture to change how Britain is seen around the world.” I could not agree more.At a time when democratic principles are being challenged all over the world, restoring the unity of a monument so closely associated with the emergence of democracy itself would send a powerful signal.Greeceremains ready. What is needed now is the political will and courage to take the decisive step, to reunite the sculptures and transform a historic dispute into a unique act of cultural friendship.Kyriakos Mitsotakis is the prime minister of GreeceExplore more on these topicsParthenon marblesOpinionGreeceMuseumsExhibitionsBritish MuseumUnescoHeritagecommentShareReuse this content

title: Abandoned, dismissed and gaslighted: there is no excuse for the way ME sufferers have been betrayed | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: Changes in guidance and science seem to have little impact on millions of devastated lives. It’s a social crisis playing out behind closed doors, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: Changes in guidance and science seem to have little impact on millions of devastated lives. It’s a social crisis playing out behind closed doors, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: Illustration: Bill Bragg/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Bill Bragg/The GuardianOpinionME / Chronic fatigue syndromeAbandoned, dismissed and gaslighted: there is no excuse for the way ME sufferers have been betrayedGeorge MonbiotChanges in guidance and science seem to have little impact on millions of devastated lives. It’s a shocking social crisis playing out behind closed doorsThu 24 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTShareI’ve spent my working life covering neglected issues. But few are neglected like the devastating chronic condition ME/CFS (myalgic encephalomyelitis, or chronic fatigue syndrome). In severe cases, the illness shuts down people’s lives almost entirely, causing an extreme loss of energy and a wide range of physical and cognitive symptoms that can prevent patients from working, socialising and, sometimes, even moving or eating. Yet these people have been more or less airbrushed from our minds.To find out what this neglect looks like in practice, this week I putout a call on Blueskyasking people with ME/CFS about their recent experiences of treatment. I was immediately inundated with horrifying testimonies. “I’ve just been completely abandoned”; “a 10-year waiting list for treatment”; “we’ve given up seeking medical support”; “stuck in limbo”; “I just felt utterly unheard, invalidated”. I’ve been sent hundreds of shocking and heart-rending accounts.Exact numbers are hard to establish, but in the UK alone, anestimated 400,000 peoplelive with the condition.It affects women far more than men, by a ratio of about 4:1, according to a study in England. The number of people with long Covid, some of whom meet the diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS,was estimated in 2024at 2 million in England and Scotland.You might have imagined politicians and the media would be all over it. Instead, this great social crisis is met with silence or worse. Some outlets, despite the overwhelming weight of evidence, havemockedortrivialisedthese conditions.There’s along, dark history here, rooted in centuries of dismissal of predominantly female illnesses as “hysterical”, and amplified in recent decades by government attempts to reduce the benefits bill and insurers’ attempts to reduce payouts. If you can establish that a condition is caused by malingering, poor self-care or a negative attitude, you won’t have to cough up.Official guidance in many countries was informed by a series of deeply flawedstudiesthat purported to show these illnesses could be treated with cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), or graded exercise therapy (GET). In 2020, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice)foundthat the quality ofallthe research promoting these therapies as curative treatments for ME/CFS was either “low” or, in most cases, “very low”. In 2021,it stopped recommending these therapiesas primary treatments. We now know CBT cannot treat the condition (though it can sometimes help patients to come to terms with it), while GET is not only useless but actively dangerous, as exercise can trigger one of the most devastating ME/CFS symptoms: post-exertional malaise (PEM). PEM robs people of their remaining energy, rendering many patients bedbound, sometimes incapable of almost all movement.Since then, two other things have happened. At the inquest into the death of a young ME/CFS patient, thecoroner ruledthat provision in the health service for patients with severe ME “was and is nonexistent”. Something would have to be done. And a number of seemingscientific breakthroughs, somevery recent, havebegun inching towards identifyingpossible biological causes of both ME/CFS and long Covid. Now, or so we should hope, it’s undeniable.So what has changed as a result of these shifts? Alongside the horror and heartbreak in the testimonies of the people who emailed me, I was struck by the sense of sheer relief that someone, anyone, was asking the question.Many said they arestillbeing treated as if they have a psychological illness, andstillbeing pushed into GET and CBT. One patient told me: “I’ve gone from relatively mild to now mostly house- and bedbound, largely thanks to repeated attempts at graded exercise and ‘pushing through’.” A few days ago, anNHSclinic told another patient to undertake “graded exercise” and “simply to walk, despite the fact I’m a wheelchair user”.One mother told me “the consultant cardiologist recommended a graded exercise programme” and “a treadmill test” for her bedbound son. When she told him this contradicted Nice guidelines, he replied: “Well, what do you want me to do?” Another made the same challenge to her GP, but the doctor “denied this strongly and reiterated to my daughter that she should do the exercises”. This is very common: many doctors, I’m told, seem unaware of the new guidelines and react defensively when challenged. In many practices, GET has simply been rebranded as “building tolerance” or “pacing up” or “a little more activity each day”.Patients report being treated with “contempt and derision”. Loads are still being offered CBT. Some have been propelled by NHS doctors towards quack private “cures”, now offered by a growing industry that preys on people’s desperation.Others tell me they’ve not been pushed into inappropriate treatments, but “that’s only because I receive no treatment for it whatsoever”. Some have had to explain to their doctors what ME/CFS is. And it gets worse. I’ve been contacted by parents who have been accused of fabricating and inducing illness and even referred to social services, because doctors who seem to know nothing about ME/CFS believe they are making up their children’s symptoms.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt’s as if nothing has been learned. Perhaps that’s not surprising. A freedom of information requestto NHS Englandfound that, of the tens of thousands of practitioners who would benefit from it, after a year, only 74 had completed the new learning module on ME/CFS guidance. Meanwhile, as recently as last summer, the Department for Work and Pensions wasstill teaching its traineeselements of the old, discredited view of the condition. And, as the Liberal Democrat MP Tessa Munt, a hero of this story, tells me: “The piecemeal offerings in thegovernment’s final delivery planare not going to touch the system-wide failings.”It’s not only the UK. I’ve been contacted by patients from around the world. InSwedenandAustralia, official guidance still recommends GET and CBT. In Switzerland, I’m told, treatment is spiralling backwards, with a new wave of psychologisation. Norway, Finland and the Netherlands, despite their progressive medical reputations, sound like a waking nightmare for ME/CFS patients.Of course, as there is no effective treatment, it’s a difficult situation for doctors as well as patients. But even worse than no solutions is false solutions, and a dangerous, gaslighting, even punitive approach to a terrible disease.Across the decades, millions of people have been neglected, dismissed and mistreated, and still it goes on. We need to ask why so many patients have been abandoned, why discredited and dangerous treatments continue to be prescribed and why ignorance and neglect still dominate, in the health system and beyond. In other words, there has seldom been a stronger case for a public inquiry.George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsME / Chronic fatigue syndromeOpinionNHSHospitalsHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Coalition says it wants cheaper power, not ideology. But its evidence-free plan is all ideology | Adam Morton | The Guardian
description: The reheated plans to scrap renewable schemes, boost fossil fuels and revive nuclear are transparently Trumpian
Author: Adam Morton
Headline: The reheated plans to scrap renewable schemes, boost fossil fuels and revive nuclear are transparently Trumpian
Content: The Coalition would scrap Labor’s capacity investment program which backs solar, wind and battery schemes.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenThe Coalition would scrap Labor’s capacity investment program which backs solar, wind and battery schemes.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPClear airClimate crisisThe Coalition says it wants cheaper power, not ideology. But its evidence-free plan is all ideologyAdam MortonThe reheated plans to scrap renewable schemes, boost fossil fuels and revive nuclear are transparently TrumpianWant to get this in your inbox when it publishes?Sign up for the Clear Air Australia newsletter hereWed 23 Sep 2026 20.23 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 01.25 EDTShareGive the Coalition points for chutzpah, if nothing else. In a press release on Wednesday, first given to the Australian for a not exactly hard-won “exclusive”, it declared “Australians need cheaper power, not more ideology”.You don’t have to get far beyond that headline to find its position comes from a worldview that is ideology on steroids. That worldview says climate breakdown is not real, or at least not a real concern, and Australia should abolish nearly all plans to respond to or prepare the economy – and people’s lives – for the changes under way.Australia’s big polluters rely on carbon offsets for climate credibility. But the system looks like a house of cards | Adam MortonRead moreAs one campaigner put it, it is a plan to let climate change rip. Greenhouse gas emissions would be much higher than on the current trajectory.From a here-and-now consumer point of view, it is a plan that is based on the fallacy that the big jump in power bills in recent years is due to renewable energy and a legislated net zero emissions target. Evidence and most experts clearly say otherwise. But both are disregarded.Most of what the Coalition announced wasn’t actually new. The fresh bit is that it has promised to package up eight commitments in a new bill that would be introduced within 30 days if it was elected. Remarkably, at least half of those commitments are to abolish policies that were introduced under Coalition governments led by Scott Morrison, Tony Abbott and John Howard.Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletterAngus Taylor and Matt Canavan say they would tear up the safeguard mechanism, introduced under Abbott, ostensibly to put a limit on pollution from major industrial sites. They would abolish the mid-century net zero emissions goal brought in by Morrison and Barnaby Joyce and legislated under Labor. They would repeal the Howard-era ban on nuclear energy.Coalition and One Nation’s plan to ditch net zero would not lower power prices, CSIRO report findsRead moreThey say they would scrap Labor’s capacity investment scheme, which is meant to underwrite solar, wind and energy storage developments, and replace it with a scheme that could also use public money to encourage fossil fuels and nuclear generation.And they would abolish the vehicle efficiency standard that requires auto companies to lower the average emissions of their new car fleets – a policy that has belatedly seen a substantial increase in electric vehicle models available, including at the more affordable end, ending the farce in which Australians had far less opportunity to buy clean cars than any similar country.Bizarrely, the Coalition claims the latter policy has somehowreducedvehicle choice. Tell that tothe 25% of new car buyers who chose an EVlast month – a higher percentage than bought a petrol or diesel car – and who are now enjoying much lower running costs.Many of these policies are transparently Trumpian. They otherwise mostly fly in the face of global trends.For the first time, renewable energy – solar, wind and hydro – last year overtook coal-fired power as the leading source of electricity. Solar energy capacity expanded by 30% in one year. According to the International Renewable Energy Agency, 85% of new power capacity built last year was renewable, and 90% of the renewables built were cheaper than the lowest fossil fuel alternative. Global EV sales are up more than 10% this year and expected to account for nearly 30% of the global total, withChina leading the way.Clean solutions are rising due to governments taking some action to reduce emissions and limit an accelerating climate crisisthat is killing thousands of people. But cost is at least as big a factor, particularly in electricity generation.In Australia, that argument has been muddied by events. Aswe have pointed out before, power bills increased dramatically after Russia’s attack on Ukraine sent global gas prices skyrocketing four years ago.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When he publishesSign up toClear Air AustraliaAdam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAbout the same time, coal power prices were pushed up by flooding at east coast mines and outages at ageing generators. Combined, these issuespushed up the wholesale cost of electricity by about 20%not long after Labor had overconfidently suggested that bills would come down by $275.Despite claims to the contrary, renewable energy was not a major issue. Correlation is not causation. In fact, wholesale prices have fallen in some cases due to the influx of batteries that have allowed cheap excess solar power to be stored and used at night.That’s the good news. The more complicated news is that replacing an old coal-fired system is expensive, however you do it. A renewables-dominated power system may not bring prices down much, if at all. But there is clear evidence that it will be cheaper than other options.It will also cut heat-trapping pollution that is doing escalating damage and could allow an industrial shift that sets up Australians for a potential economic future as demand for fossil fuels falls.This is not to say the Albanese government is doing enough. The renewables transition isat risk of slowingand new coal and gas export developmentsare still being approved. The prime minister gavea keynote speech at climate weekin New Yorkin which he avoided saying fossil fuels are the problem.But Taylor goes further. On Wednesday, he implicitly dismissed climate change as a threat. He suggested all types of energy, dirty and clean, should be equally available. He claimed this would lower bills.Evidence? That’s not how this ideology works.Adam Morton is Guardian Australia’s climate and environment editorExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisClear airAustralian politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on a supersized El Niño: a natural phenomenon and human folly are a lethal combination | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Hundreds of thousands are expected to die, millions to go hungry. This is not just about weather patterns, but about injustice
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Hundreds of thousands are expected to die, millions to go hungry. This is not just about weather patterns, but about injustice
Content: A dried-up field in Jonggol, Indonesia. El Niño increases drought risk in a large swathe of the world.Photograph: Mast Irham/EPAView image in fullscreenA dried-up field in Jonggol, Indonesia. El Niño increases drought risk in a large swathe of the world.Photograph: Mast Irham/EPAOpinionEl Niño southern oscillationThe Guardian view on a supersized El Niño: a natural phenomenon and human folly are a lethal combinationEditorialHundreds of thousands are expected to die, millions to go hungry. This is not just about weather patterns, but about injusticeThu 24 Sep 2026 13.37 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTShareSome warnings are so grave that it is almost impossible to fully comprehend them. The descriptions ofa super-sized, “Godzilla-level” El Niñoalready heating our planet would sound hyperbolic were they not issuing from eminent scientists. They say that the weather pattern, which occurs roughly every two to seven years, may be the strongest in at least a millennium. With its peak yet to come, the temperature rise in the Pacific Ocean has already surpassed the previous high.The consequence will be huge amounts of heat in an atmosphere already experiencing frighteningly higher temperatures due to the human-caused climate crisis. Next year is almost certain to be the hottest on record globally, breaking this year’s record. The World Food Programme has warned that 50 million people are likely to bepushed into acute hunger. Others estimate that the extra heat from El Niño alone will cause thedeaths of 450,000 people by February, from Nigeria and Indonesia to the US. That extraordinary toll is in addition to those killed by the wildfires, droughts and floods it is likely to bring – and also to deaths caused by global heating.While the weather system develops in the Pacific Ocean, its knock-on effects will be felt far away. It increases drought risk in a large swathe of the world, while increasing rainfall elsewhere. Indiahas already experienceda 50% shortfall in essential monsoon rains this month, affecting crops. In Sri Lanka, reservoirs for drinking water are running dry. European countries may be indirectly affected, with a stormier autumn, but the primary impact for them islikely to be on food supplies.View image in fullscreenEd Miliband, the UK foreign secretary.Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/GettyWhile there is ongoing debate aboutthe impact of global heating on the pattern itself, a major study published last monthfoundthat strong El Niños in recent decades have been supercharged by the overheating of the planet due to fossil fuels. It is beyond doubt that the effects of this natural phenomenon are compounded by human-made folly and injustice. Domestically and internationally, the poorest will be worst hit, due to factors such as living conditions and underlying health, while being the least able to pay their way out of trouble. At the same time, the wealthy few will continue to enrich themselves from an economic system built on pumping out more emissions. Defenders of the status quo will continue to insist that we cannot afford to clean up our act. It is more than ever evident that we cannot afford not to do so.The UK foreign secretary’s warning to other countries at the UN on Wednesday that El Niño and the climate and nature crises threatentheir national security and defencewas welcome. Andy Burnham, as well as Ed Miliband, should be seizing the opportunity to make the political case for tough action on emissions, and accelerating efforts to prepare the UK for increasingly extreme weather. The Climate Change Committee, which advises the government, warned in alandmark report in Maythat the country is “built for a climate that no longer exists”.Globally, boosting the loss and damage fund to ensure support for developing countries, which have contributed the least to the climate crisis but are likely to suffer most, should be a priority. ThisunprecedentedEl Niño poses an immense threat. It could also be a spur to action against global heating and its associated injustices, which otherwise will only deepen.Explore more on these topicsEl Niño southern oscillationOpinionClimate Change CommitteeGreenhouse gas emissionsClimate crisisPovertyeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: George Bush, murder and nautical infidelity: the Chicks’ 20 greatest songs – ranked! | The Chicks | The Guardian
description: As the country trio once known as Dixie Chicks celebrate 20 years of their album Taking the Long Way, we count down the best of their catchy, sometimes controversial catalogue
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: As the country trio once known as Dixie Chicks celebrate 20 years of their album Taking the Long Way, we count down the best of their catchy, sometimes controversial catalogue
Content: The former Dixie Chicks …(from left)Martie Maguire, Natalie Maines and Emily Strayer in 2002.Photograph: Harry Langdon/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe former Dixie Chicks …(from left)Martie Maguire, Natalie Maines and Emily Strayer in 2002.Photograph: Harry Langdon/Getty ImagesRankedThe ChicksGeorge Bush, murder and nautical infidelity: the Chicks’ 20 greatest songs – ranked!As the country trio once known as Dixie Chicks celebrate 20 years of their album Taking the Long Way, we count down the best of their catchy, sometimes controversial catalogueAlexis PetridisThu 24 Sep 2026 08.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 09.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. If I Fall You’re Going Down With Me (2001)One of eight singles released from the album Fly. Amazement at the sheer number should be matched by astonishment at their consistency. If I Fall … is just great. Organ-driven rock lent a Nashville twang by the fiddle, it barrels along, rich with the confidence of a band who know they can’t put a foot wrong.19. Tights on My Boat (2020)You don’t want for dirt dished about Natalie Maines’ divorce on Gaslighter, the band’s eighth album, but this accusation of nautical infidelity stands out. It’s ferociously angry and very funny – plus its understated, live-in the-studio sound only compounds the sense that you’re eavesdropping on tea being spilled among friends.18. You Were Mine (1998)A great country weeper in its own right, You Were Mine is also part of the Chicks’ origin story. It was written by the sisters Emily Strayer and Martie Maguire about their parents’ divorce; they then invited Maines, the daughter of the producer Lloyd Maines, to sing on the demo, rather than the then Chicks vocalist Laura Lynch. A lineup change and vast success ensued.17. The Long Way Around (2006)The chief theme of the Taking the Long Way album – being celebrated soon with a 20th anniversary reissue and tour – was the Chicks’ war of words with President George W Bush and Nashville conservatives. The musically sweet-toned opening track suggests that attitude was par for the course – of a piece with a longstanding disinclination to “kiss all the asses” and “do it like everybody else”.View image in fullscreenThe Chicks performing in 2003.Photograph: Pictorial Press/Alamy16. Julianna Calm Down (2020)Over a soft organ backing and something approaching a dancefloor pulse, the Chicks offer hard-won advice to the recently dumped: “Put on your best shoes and strut the fuck around like you’ve got nothing to lose.” Its slow build to a euphoric climax – elevated by Maguire’s fiddle – is great.15. Ready to Run (1999)You could suggest the Celtic motifs on Ready to Run are an acknowledgment of Irish folk’s seminal influence on country; equally, they may have something to do with the Corrs’ late-90s success. Either way, Ready to Run’s breezy mood carries a witty lyric that offers a middle finger to marriage and commitment.View image in fullscreenThe band during their world tour in Cincinnati, Ohio, in June 2016.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for PMK14. Texas Man (2020)Marooned in California post-divorce, Maines pines for the more rough-hewn gents of her home county. But the beauty of Texas Man is really about the music’s experimental bent: a tight, close-miked, new-wave-leaning sound replete with fuzzed-out guitar that’s completely unlike anything the Chicks had released before, but still somehow sounds like them.13. Cold Day in July (1999)Five minutes of inconsolable misery. “The moon is full, and my arms are empty / All night long, I’ve pleaded and cried,” it opens, with Maines’ voice at its most angst-ridden. The guitar-driven arrangement is simple, but spot-on: it doesn’t need anything more to work its sob-inducing magic.12. Sin Wagon (1999)In the early 80s, there was talk of a subgenre called cowpunk. It never crossed over into the mainstream, but the title perfectly fits Sin Wagon, named after a line in Grease. A thrilling blend of speedy bluegrass with raw, growling energy, its lyrics are home to a splendid celebration of “mattress dancin”.11. Sleep at Night (2020)There’s a pleasing circularity about Sleep at Night, which bears the distinct influence of the noted Chicks fan Taylor Swift; you can almost hear her delivering the line: “My husband’s girlfriend’s husband just called me up – how messed up is that?” An extra point for the slapping rhythm track, the perfect accompaniment to the punches landed in the lyrics.10. Easy Silence (2006)The negative image of Taking the Long Way’s two-fisted lead single Not Ready to Make Nice, Easy Silence details the downside of being the centre of a media storm. It sounds utterly, affectingly weary – “everyone is running” it notes, before evincing a longing to “keep the world at bay”.9. There’s Your Trouble (1998)The Chicks’ biggest UK chart hit offers the perfect example of why their fourth album, Wide Open Spaces, catapulted the former bluegrass/western-swing combo to superstardom: beautifully turned songwriting, a fresh pop sheen that didn’t overwhelm their audible country bona fides, impressively tough and salty lyrics and – in their new vocalist Maines – the ideal voice to deliver them.8. Landslide (2002)This version of the Stevie Nicks song is bold – the original is a classic – and ahead of the curve, arriving years before Fleetwood Mac became a hip name for leftfield musicians to drop. Stripped down to country basics, in keeping with the rest of the album Home, the song shines, highlighting the trio’s impeccable harmonies.7. Long Time Gone (2002)The back-to-the-land saga of Darrell Scott’s Long Time Gone comes complete with a critique of modern Nashville – “they got money, but they don’t have Cash” – and the Chicks’ version is suitably old-fashioned, with no drums and a distinct bluegrass influence about the banjo and fiddle. The lyrics are biting, but it still sounds like a party.6. Gaslighter (2020)The title track of the first Chicks album in 14 years pulled no punches. Its subject, Natalie Maines’ ex-husband Adrian Pasdar, had reportedly been concerned that the group’s unreleased material would violate a confidentiality clause in their prenuptial agreement. Gaslighter was released after the couple finalised their divorce, but it is almost unsettlingly brutal in its frankness – and insanely catchy.5. Wide Open Spaces (1998)Wide Open Spaces started life as a student’s poem about returning to Texas from university in Montana and ended up a kind of Stetson-cladShe’s Leaving Home. A huge hit – and the kind of Chicks song that one suspects sunk in deep with the young Swift.View image in fullscreenStrayer, Maines and Maguire on the set of a video shoot for Goodbye Earl in 2000.Photograph: Paul Natkin/WireImage4. Travelin’ Soldier (2002)This is destined to be remembered as the track Maines was introducing in London when she criticised Bush, but the ensuing furore shouldn’t overshadow how fantastic Travelin’ Soldier is.
