Stark and moving, never mawkish, it isn’t a protest song so much as a heartbreaking story entwined with the Vietnam war.Big hits, massive ballads and titanic emotions: Céline Dion’s greatest songs – ranked!Read more3. Cowboy Take Me Away (1999)A song based on the slogan of a US advert – for Calgon bath and beauty products! – should be a novelty. Cowboy Take Me Away is anything but. Instead, it’s a wistful paean to escape, lent a tear-jerking quality by the sense said escape may never happen. Balanced between uplift and melancholy, the music fits perfectly.2. Not Ready to Make Nice (2006)The Chicks’ best-known musical response to the Bush incident is a thing of snarling, screw-the-lot-of-you wonder: “It’s too late to make it right / I probably wouldn’t if I could.” The ensuing album slightly belaboured the point, but as a short, sharp burst of bitterness and bile, Not Ready to Make Nice is a triumph.1. Goodbye Earl (1999)Long before controversy engulfed their career, the Chicks were entirely capable of causing it. Twenty country stations refused to play Goodbye Earl, apparently horrified by the lyric: high school friends Mary-Anne and Wanda successfully plot to murder Wanda’s abusive husband after he breaches a restraining order and leaves her in intensive care. It still sold a million copies – deservedly so. The chorus is a singalong monster, the lyric is gripping and superbly written and the Chicks’ reading of it is perfect. The vocals switch from cold rage to gleeful celebration over music that is taut and explosive. Tongues firmly in cheek, they stuck a cover of Stand By Your Man on the B-side.Listen to the playlist.SpotifyTaking the Long Way: 20th Anniversary Edition is released on 3 October via Legacy Recordings. The Chicks’ anniversary tour begins on 30 September, at Fox theatre, Detroit.Explore more on these topicsThe ChicksRankedPop and rockCountryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I get lost going to the bathroom’: John Hannah on world travel, stealing props and being ‘the Scottish Eminem’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Four Weddings and a Funeral actor answers your questions on inspiring Eminem, nicking props and having a new perspective after turning 60
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The Four Weddings and a Funeral actor answers your questions on inspiring Eminem, nicking props and having a new perspective after turning 60
Content: ‘It’s good if people think I’m Jimmy Nesbitt, because I can be rude and he gets the blame’ … John Hannah.Photograph: Valéry Hache/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It’s good if people think I’m Jimmy Nesbitt, because I can be rude and he gets the blame’ … John Hannah.Photograph: Valéry Hache/AFP/Getty ImagesFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesInterview‘I get lost going to the bathroom’: John Hannah on world travel, stealing props and being ‘the Scottish Eminem’As told toRich PelleyThe Four Weddings and a Funeral actor answers your questions on being confused with James Nesbitt, his own Sliding Doors moment and a new perspective since turning 60Thu 24 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow often do you get asked to recite thatWH Audenpoem fromFour Weddings and a Funeral, and can you do it from memory right now?mattyjjandsimoitNot for a long time. I could probably do the first couple of lines: Stop all the clocks, cut off the telephone / Prevent the dog from barking with a juicy bone / Turn out the lights? And with muffled drums / Something, something … let the mourners come. There you go. Terrible!View image in fullscreenHannah in Four Weddings and a Funeral, 1994.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyInSteve Coogan’s Paul Calf’s Video Diary, your character praisesOrson Welles’ The Trialfor its “tremendous energy”, while Paul says he would “rather watch Dave Lee Travis playing Macbeth”. What’s your actual opinion of The Trial [by Franz Kafka]?AdrianH1God, it’s a long time since I’ve read that. I read a lot of those books in my younger days, but probably, like a lot of people, even those who are graduates of English literature, I’d be hard pushed these days to tell you what it was about, other than the persecution of some minor character.As a popular jobbing actor, you have a massive list of credits. Has anyone ever come up to you to express their appreciation for a certain role and you had no idea what they were on about?KevcoeNo. It’s always heartwarming when somebody comes up and offers their congratulations on something a little bit lower down the pecking order. Fortunately, people rarely ever come up to tell me that they thought I was shit in something. I quite often get Paul Calf’s Video Diary, and that Macbeth line. To be frank, I can’t quite remember the context.ShouldEminembe thanking you forStan, rather thanDido, given that he first heard Thank You on the Sliding Doors soundtrack?vammypIt’s strange how Sliding Doors and Four Weddings have travelled the world. It’s certainly cool to think that somebody as far out of left field as Eminem has actually even seen something you’ve done. Although, the story I heard was he was so sickened by the sweetness that he decided to counterpoint it with an obsessed fan trying to murder his girlfriend.What’s your Sliding Doors moment?MurdomaniaIt’s interesting that “sliding doors” as an expression has become such common parlance, hasn’t it? I certainly don’t run for trains any more.View image in fullscreen‘I don’t run for trains any more’ … with Gwyneth Paltrow in Sliding Doors.Photograph: Alex Bailey/Paramount/Miramax/Intermedia/Kobal/REX/ShutterstockI was so traumatised by your characters inTruth or DareandCarnivàlethat whenever I see you in anything else, I think: “Oh no, it’s that horrible man.”Do you enjoy playing characters like that?FioreSebekThere you go: a prime example of something coming from left field. I do think that old cliche is true about bad guys always being more fun. I also get to play a lot of scientists or doctors, because for some reason, my Scottish accent makes me sound educated.Which was most fun: filmingCharlie Brooker’s police procedural parodyA Touch of Cloth, or appearing in an episode of Black Mirror?MrMustardA Touch of Cloth was great fun. We certainly had to do a lot of takes for all the laughing. Black Mirror felt more like a 1980s dark BBC late-night psychopath drama. Working with Charlie was quite high-concept in Black Mirror, but high camp in Cloth.Apparently, you nicked some props from The Mummy to decorate your then-new home. What have you pinched since?LuddersIt’s like the old joke: you shag one sheep … You nick one prop. It was this fibreglass, spray-painted gold, Egyptian dog head with arms all going in different directions. I had a tiny garden at the time, and thought it would be something to look at other than a wall. But Brendan [Fraser] took the piss out of me, and constantly said I nick stuff. I can imagine Ridley Scott’s allowed to steal Aliens and put them in his vineyard. Richard E Grant’s a bit of a klepto too – he’s got shitloads in his garden. And Alan Cumming is a bit sticky-fingered.If you took part in Celebrity Race Across the World, would you still narrate it in the third person?AngryTomatoWell, the bottom line is I wouldn’t be doing Race Across the World. I get lost going to the bathroom. I’ve missed planes, turned up on the wrong day, got off the train at the wrong stop … I’m no good at stuff. So I’d be terrible.Have you ever had more fun on a set than onSpartacus– thundering great big lines of fruity dialogue about “Thracianwhores” while lounging about in various states of distress withLucy Lawless?mikebhoyIt was pretty spectacular. As we mentioned earlier, it’s always fun playing the villain. You only got the scripts as you were shooting, so you never knew what was coming next. Some of the stuff, you could not believe. I think in episode two, I come into our chamber with Lucy Lawless. We’re about to have a bit of how’s-your-father, but it’s been a stressful day, so she gets one of the servants to get me going by fellating me, so I had to deliver all this dialogue, while pretending to be fellated. If I had to live in Roman times, I know where I’d like to be. I’d definitely want to be upstairs.View image in fullscreen‘Pretty spectacular’ … with Lucy Lawless in Spartacus.Photograph: AlamyDid the Co-op employ you to do their voiceovers becauseyou have the perfect Scottish accent to rhyme “good” with “food”?OnTheEdgeOfEuropeNo, I think that was one of those happy coincidences. I don’t think they realised that it could possibly rhyme. It’s like when Eminem rhymes all these things with “orange”. I’m the Scottish Eminem!InAgents of SHIELD, you created Life Model Decoys of people. If you could make one of anyone in real life, who would you choose?NotCEEFAUXhonestMy dad. He died 11 years ago. My mum, too. It’s funny, you still miss them. I wish I could phone them up and tell them what was happening, what was going on. As a parent, my kids are never off their phones, but you never hear from them unless they want money. I think back to when I left home at 16 and, if I wanted to phone my parents, I’d have to grab a handful of coins and head across the street to the phone box, which I probably did once a month. Recognising how things are now as a parent, I sort of wish I’d got to know my parents better. If you asked me who I could have dinner with, alive or dead, I’d speak to my mum and dad. I’d ask them all this shit I wish I could have asked them before.You’ve had a really diverse career, despite some people’s attempts to pigeonhole you as a Scottish mummy’s boy. What’s left on the bucket list?AmongstTheWavesWell, when I turned 60, I joked with my kids that I was retiring. What that meant was I felt comfortable with what I’d achieved. Maybe there were sort of gaps, maybe it wasn’t quite as great a career as I would have liked, but I was going to step back from trying tohavea career. I think I spent too long seeing jobs as a step to the next job, and didn’t really appreciate the moment. So turning 60 I thought: “Bollocks to this, I’m just going to do stuff that I like, that’s filming somewhere nice, or is especially well paid. If it’s got two out of three of those things, I’ll do it.”View image in fullscreen‘I’ve never been busier’ … in Bad Day at the Office.The reality is that I’ve probably never been busier. Stuff like Bad Day at the Office comes out of left field. After decades of complaining about playing cops and being a Scottish mummy’s boy it was nice to do something that was so ridiculous, strange and experimental that, at 64, you could never have imagined it.Do you andJames Nesbittever go out for a pint together just to watch the confusion on people’s faces?RobinGoodfellowWe used to play five-a-side back in the 90s. The last time I bumped into him was when his daughter and my son graduated from Manchester uni, last summer. It’s good if people think I’m Jimmy Nesbitt, because I can then swear at them and be rude and he gets the blame.When did you last use the expression“by Jupiter’s cock”?wellywearer2This morning, funnily enough.Bad Day at the Office is in UK and Irish cinemas from 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmFilm & Music reader interviewFour Weddings and a FuneralJames NesbittinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Kneebone review – who knew porcelain could be so edgy, nerve-wracking and marvellous? | Art | The Guardian
description: The British sculptor’s delicate, intimate and ready-to-pop creations feel right at home among Hertford House’s rococo masterpieces
Author: Chloë Ashby
Headline: The British sculptor’s delicate, intimate and ready-to-pop creations feel right at home among Hertford House’s rococo masterpieces
Content: Hanging in the balance … Pull, 2023.Photograph: White Cube (Theo Christelis)/© the artistView image in fullscreenHanging in the balance … Pull, 2023.Photograph: White Cube (Theo Christelis)/© the artistArtReviewRachel Kneebone review – who knew porcelain could be so edgy, nerve-wracking and marvellous?Wallace Collection, LondonThe British sculptor’s delicate, intimate and ready-to-pop creations feel right at home among Hertford House’s rococo masterpiecesChloë AshbyThu 24 Sep 2026 11.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaybe it was that wine glass I broke this morning while unloading the dishwasher, but seeing a Rachel Kneebone porcelain sculpture suspended makes me nervous. Can those skinny wires really hold the weight? Should there perhaps be a soft landing just in case? Emerging from a tangled clump of ribbons and roses are a couple of bone-white bubbles, ready to pop. This is art that quite literally hangs in the balance; a sense of peril is what makes it so marvellous.Born in 1973, the British sculptor is the latest contemporary artist to be invited to show her workat the Wallace Collection. Following in the footsteps of Damien Hirst, Flora Yukhnovich and Grayson Perry, Kneebone has positioned nine milky sculptures made between 2017 and 2026 throughout Hertford House. So this display, titled Metamorphoses, is an intervention – that’s the art world lingo. Except it feels different, like the contrast has been turned down. Sure, there are collisions as well as similarities, but seeing sculpted heaps of human and floral forms alongside the prized masterpieces for which the London gallery is best known feels … right.View image in fullscreenDecoration meets high drama … Temple, 2026.Photograph: White Cube (Theo Christelis)/© the artistKneebone was studying at the Royal College ofArtin 2004 when she started working with porcelain, a medium more commonly associated with the types of cups and saucers safely stowed away behind glass in Manchester Square. Instead, Kneebone gives us strangely intimate pileups that recall art historical sources from the sculptural fragments of Auguste Rodin to the erotic figures of Jake and Dinos Chapman. Among the fleshly folds are glimpses of Ovid and Dante. While distinctly modern, they also nod to classical friezes, baroque fountains and, as is about to become abundantly clear, rococo canvases.One of two works that have been created specially for the show, Temple, is presented on a plinth at the top of the stairs. Sandwiched between Boucher’sThe Rising of the Sun(1753) andThe Setting of the Sun(1752), it’s a lustrous, solid take on the churning waves the 18th-century French master conjures in paint. Emerging from the surf are three columns and a jumble of gnarly barnacles and tendrils, plus a gleaming scallop shell containing a pearl – a reference to Boucher’s bejewelled water nymphs. Just like those vast mythological scenes, it’s a mashup of decoration and high drama, pleasure and peril.Challenging preconceived notions of domesticity, Kneebone embraces instability, finding beauty in the blisters and cracks that can emerge when her chosen material is fired in the kiln. Look closely and you’ll notice distortions and fissures among her graceful twisting forms. In the billiards room, Dance (2017) is perfectly imperfect, a throng of protruding legs and toes – some pointed, others flexed – sprouting from a hulking mass with deep fractures at the base.Which is where the metamorphosis part comes in. Like heated clay, Kneebone’s figures are undergoing a transformation, their limbs buckling and splaying. They’re also playfully sensual. Either side of Boucher’sJupiter and Callisto(1769), Pearl IV (2025) and Pearl II (2025) lunge towards one another like lovers, just as the god disguised as Diana springs towards the nymph. Elsewhere, rounded porcelain forms might resemble bubbles and pearls, but here there’s no mistaking the resemblance to Callisto’s creamy breasts.View image in fullscreenRewards slow looking … Dance, 2017.Photograph: White Cube (Stephen White)/© the artistShape-shifting art rewards slow looking, and at the Wallace you can walk around it (as well as under it), watching it change and morph from different points of view. What makes the pairing of Kneebone’s contemporary creations and the treasures in the collection so delightful is that it makes you look at well-known works afresh, too.It’s only seeing Bower (2026) in front ofThe Swing(c1767-68) that I notice the silvery quality of Fragonard’s palette, complemented by the porcelain, a dazzling white. Guided by Kneebone’s twisting forms and knots, my eyes aren’t drawn to the young woman wearing the frothy pink frock, as is usually the case, but to the knotted rope wound around the bulky branches above. As for the cracks: well, they may be a fortuitous byproduct of the kiln, but they do provide a nice nod to the fractured relationship between the lady and her elderly husband, who’s playing tug of war with a much younger man.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSurrounded by amorous scenes and opulent paintings of fruit and flowers, you might expect porcelain to feel cold and austere. Instead, it’s titillating and decadent – just wait until you see the two pieces positioned at either end of the great gallery, seductively pale beside the red damask walls and flashy gilt frames. I’d wondered whether nine works – or eight, depending on the fate of that suspended one – would get lost among the infinite riches of the Wallace Collection. No chance. The beauty of even a single Kneebone sculpture is the way its parts merge and multiply before your eyes.At theWallace Collection, London, until 25 AprilExplore more on these topicsArtSculptureCeramicsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘My first screen kiss was in a cowshed!’ Lesley Manville on her greatest roles – and why sex scenes for over-50s are booming | Television | The Guardian
description: In the last 15 years, she has gone from respected actor to stratospheric, garlanded star. Now she is back on TV as a chic sleuth in a racy car – despite being terrible at guessing whodunnit
Author: Gabriel Tate
Headline: In the last 15 years, she has gone from respected actor to stratospheric, garlanded star. Now she is back on TV as a chic sleuth in a racy car – despite being terrible at guessing whodunnit
Content: ‘I’m glad I was never flavour of the month’ … Manville.Photograph: Clara Molden/Camera Press/TelegraphView image in fullscreen‘I’m glad I was never flavour of the month’ … Manville.Photograph: Clara Molden/Camera Press/TelegraphTelevisionInterview‘My first screen kiss was in a cowshed!’ Lesley Manville on her greatest roles – and why sex scenes for over-50s are boomingGabriel TateIn the last 15 years, she has gone from respected actor to stratospheric, garlanded star. Now she is back on TV as a chic sleuth in a racy car – despite being terrible at guessing whodunnitThu 24 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 04.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is high summer and, while Lesley Manville may be suffering a bit with hay fever and the heat (“I’m so white, all I do is burn”), she doesn’t do wilting. Soon to head outside to tend to the ailing garden of her London home, she is enjoying a rare period of rest after six almost unbroken months ofOedipuson Broadway and thenLes Liaisons Dangereusesat the National. She keeps, incidentally, the Tony she won for playing Jocasta in Oedipus on a shelf by the computer, “next to its friend, Larry Olivier” – an Olivier awarded for the same role.“You don’t go into a job thinking about awards,” she says, before grinning conspiratorially. “Listen, you don’t say to an Olympian, ‘Oh, is it OK that you didn’t win?’ Yes, you like to win!”double quotation markOedipus and Les Liaisons Dangereuses were both highly sexualised pieces of theatre and I love thatManville has done a fair bit of winning recently, and not before time. The last 15 years have seen her graduate from widely respected actor to garlanded star: since 2011 there has been that Tony, two Oliviers, an Oscar nomination for Paul Thomas Anderson’s Phantom Thread, Emmy and Golden Globe nominations and seven Bafta nominations. Her cinematic collaborators have included not only PTA but Luca Guadagnino, Alfonso Cuarón and Joel Coen. This relatively late blooming has come as a relief.View image in fullscreen‘You’d like to win!’ … Manville was Oscar-nominated for Phantom Thread, directed by Paul Thomas Anderson, in 2017.Photograph: Focus Features/Zuma Press/PA Images“I’m so glad I was never flavour of the month,” she says, “because it’s so hard to maintain. No one went to LA for pilot season when I was young – we were just interested in doing the work. But you’re right, there has been a shift. Winning the Olivier forIbsen’s Ghostsin 2014 took me somewhere else, theatre-wise. An Oscar nomination makes a difference. A whole sequence of high-profile television, not least The Crown, which obviously wasn’t all about Princess Margaret but boy did Peter Morgan write me two astonishing episodes. Mrs Harris Goes to Paris brought me to a new audience, andMumis the thing I still get stopped about most.”These are just some of the most recent projects from an amazing body of work, one of which Manville – whose combination of wry wit, warm intelligence and stern savvy keeps me on my toes throughout our conversation – is rightly proud. Marble Hall Murders, her new TV series, starting on BBC One this week, completes Anthony Horowitz’s trilogy of ingenious Susan Ryeland mysteries. It may be one of her lighter pieces, but it’s no less satisfying for that.Manville was willingly cajoled into returning as publisher-cum-crimebuster Ryeland by Horowitz, who offered to write a third book if she’d do a third series. Susan is back being single, back in London and back in publishing – albeit reluctantly – when a young writer proposes to conclude the bestselling saga of fictional detective Atticus Pünd. As before, many of the cast take dual roles as fact and fiction intertwine, and Pünd’s investigation into the murder of a publicly beloved, privately monstrous children’s author in Corfu is reflected by events in Susan’s world, where her sparring partners include Mark Bonnar and Rupert Penry Jones. If it is indeed the end, Manville will miss Susan immensely.“She feels closer to me than a lot of other parts I’ve played. I like to think I don’t conform to a received notion of how one should be when one reaches a certain age. I love the fact that she wears these fabulous clothes, drives an open-top red sports car – I used to drive an MG in my 20s, although it broke down all the time – and doesn’t put up with any shit. Like her, I’m very clear about who I am. I’ve found myself at this point in my life. And although I’m absolutely terrible at guessing whodunnit, I’ve caught out a few boyfriends in the past, so my detective work hasn’t been all bad.”Manville, now 70, grew up on a council estate in Hove, a seaside town in East Sussex, one of three daughters of lifelong Labour supporters. “Those principles stay with you. My early influences were very leftwing, working at the Royal Court with actors and playwrights who felt the same way.” These included Andrea Dunbar and Caryl Churchill. “I really want the Labour party to be everything it could be, and under Andy Burnham, we might have a glimmer of hope that happens. I’ve got a lot of time for him.”Manville was a gifted performer from a young age, albeit not in the art form she would go on to conquer. “I had a really good, classically trained voice when I was young,” she says. “I could have been an opera singer, but something about it felt formal and stiff, so my 15-year-old brain went, ‘OK, I’ll go and do musicals.’”View image in fullscreen‘Like an extreme sport’ … with Aidan Turner in a publicity shot for Les Liaisons Dangereuses.Photograph: Alexandre BlossardThanks to a council grant she commuted daily to London’sItalia Conti stage school, and, after O-levels, studied dance, singing and drama. “From my first job in a musical when I was 16 until I was 22, I did every job I was offered. I was a presenter. I did two pantomimes, a musical, a telly play, everything, but I never thought about playing characters. I just played me. Meeting Mike Leigh was the lightbulb moment, not just because he told me I was good but because I played someone a million miles from me. And I thought, ‘This is what I want to do.’”That was in 1979, and Manville has now worked with Leigh more than any other actor, their eight films together producing what were, for years, her defining screen roles. Lonely daytime drinker Mary inAnother Year, and the nervy, vulnerable breadwinner Penny inAll or Nothing, in particular, condensed so much of what makes her great: the precision of characterisation, the deep dredging of despair, the dogged resilience. She still values Leigh’s opinion more than almost anyone else’s.She even turned down an offer to joinArlene Phillips’dancing troupe Hot Gossip. When I suggest she could resurrect her dancing on Strictly, she gently corrects me, explaining that she never really let it die. I should have guessed from her enviably upright deportment. “I’ve spent every night of the last three months dancing with professionals in Les Liaisons Dangereuses,” she says. “It felt like an extreme sport and it’s been wonderful!”View image in fullscreen‘Meeting Mike Leigh was the lightbulb moment’ … Manville with David Bradley in Another Year.Photograph: Cinematic Collection/AlamyShe pauses before taking a brief, impassioned detour. “Thank God, just because we’re over 50, we don’t have to have walking sticks – or not be thought of as sexual any more. We are! Oedipus and Les Liaisons were both highly sexualised pieces of theatre and I love that. Anyway, if I’d been asked to do Strictly 15 years ago, I might have said yes. Now, I’m not available much.”She has been busy ever since her breakthrough TV role back in 1975, in ITV’s then new daytime soap Emmerdale Farm. “My first screen kiss was in a cowshed!” she says, hooting with laughter. “My character was younger and adored an older man. It was more affectionate than passionate. I’ve been kissed in more glamorous locations since.”As with so many actors, soap opera gave her an “amazing grounding” in the technique and discipline of screen acting. “But I knew it was time to go. I remember a lot of the cast saying, ‘Oh, you shouldn’t leave. It’s great money. You’ve got security.’ I just thought, ‘I know, I hear you, I’ve learned a lot, it’s been amazing. But I’m off.’”View image in fullscreen‘I learned a lot’ … Manville as Rosemary Kendall, with Frazer Hines as Joe Sugden, in Emmerdale Farm in 1975.Photograph: ITV/REX/ShutterstockAt times, her work rate frankly boggles the mind. For 10 weeks in 2018, for instance, she spent her days filming the costume drama Harlots in Watford and her evenings on the West End stage for Long Day’s Journey into Night. Where did this all come from?“I just want to keep going. You’re either that person or you’re not. I’m very good at looking after myself. Just crack on with it is very much my philosophy and not a lot fazes me. If there was an Olympic event for multitasking, I’d win! When I was a single mum, I went back to work because I had to.” Gary Oldman, her first husband, left her, and the UK, three months after their son Alfie was born in 1989. “When I had too much to do, a play to learn and a baby who needed feeding and bathing and stories, I allocated my time much better.”Alfie is now a father of three and a cameraman who has worked on projects with both his parents. “My friend Alan Rickman was on Harry Potter,” Manville remembers, “and he said, ‘Alfie, I’ll get you through the door [as a runner], but the rest is up to you,’ which was exactly right. Now if I see Alfie at work I’ll think, ‘What are you doing here?’ What a privilege. And he likes me. I like him. So it’s a win-win.”Manville’s work ethic and eye for quality endure: days after we speak, it is announced that she will star with Anna Maxwell Martin in a new production of the American tragicomedyAugust: Osage County, and she is currently filming a new Prime series called Escorted, playing a Manhattan nightclub singer opposite Brett Goldstein as her son. There will be no slowing down for this formidable performer.“I’ve got as much energy as all of those dancers I’ve just finished working with,” she says matter-of-factly. “I really am a bit like Susan Ryeland. I couldn’t give a fuck how old I am!”Marble Hall Murders is on BBC One on 26 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTelevisionLesley ManvilleActingTheatreDramaMike LeighThe CrownfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nicole Eisenman review – ICE-like goons clash with sublime stargazing as America’s magical magpie returns | Art | The Guardian
description: Abstract, humorous yet deeply unsettling, the painter’s dazzling exhibition sees her caught between distant skies and the ugly reality on the ground
Author: Ben Eastham
Headline: Abstract, humorous yet deeply unsettling, the painter’s dazzling exhibition sees her caught between distant skies and the ugly reality on the ground
Content: ‘Dazzling variety of tones and textures’ … The Waiter by Nicole Eisenman.Photograph: © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy the Artist and Sadie Coles HQ, LondonView image in fullscreen‘Dazzling variety of tones and textures’ … The Waiter by Nicole Eisenman.Photograph: © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy the Artist and Sadie Coles HQ, LondonArtReviewNicole Eisenman review – ICE-like goons clash with sublime stargazing as America’s magical magpie returnsSadie Coles HQ, LondonAbstract, humorous yet deeply unsettling, the painter’s dazzling exhibition sees her caught between distant skies and the ugly reality on the groundBen EasthamThu 24 Sep 2026 10.14 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 12.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNicole Eisenman’s2023 exhibition at the Whitechapel Gallerytook its title from Hillary Clinton’s account of the 2016 US presidential election: “What happened.” With its absurdist riffs on contemporary American life, the show confirmed that Eisenman is among the most important artists of her time and that “what happened” was a disaster. So her return to London might be thought of as a sequel, with the working title: “So what do we do now?”Eisenman is justly celebrated for her rambunctious, magpie and irreverent subversions of the conventional histories of art and society. A painter who has lately (and successfully) turned to sculpture, her work often places people in situations – ranging from crowded bars to town squares flooded with mud – that match broad humour to sharp technique in reflecting on how our identities are shaped by the company we keep. And yet my first thought on entering Sadie Coles’ gallery was the artist had turned her back on the world.View image in fullscreenNever allows the eye to settle … The Orgy.Photograph: © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy the Artist and Sadie Coles HQ, LondonThe ground floor is dominated by a vast painting of a solitary figure standing alone amid the ruins of Stonehenge. Identified by the title as The Waiter, he looks up to a night sky teeming with the wonders of the universe and holds a drum but does not play it. The painting is overwhelming, not only for its scale but also for its dazzling variety of tones and textures, from the schematic design of the planets to its impasto treatment of the moss on the stones, which blooms from the surface of the canvas in wild green clumps. The effect is sublime.Yet this image of a musician struck dumb by nature is also unsettling. Has Eisenman retreated from the public arena to wait things out in cosmic speculations? Is she the latest artist to join the flight from reason, seeking refuge in the dubious consolations of New Age mysticism? The neighbouring canvas shows an astronomer alone beneath a sky through which the Milky Way slices a star-studded diagonal. Behind her are low-rise apartments through the illuminated windows of which cartoon figures can be seen eating, embracing, squabbling. Again the impression is of a woman who has averted her gaze from the mess of humanity to make beautiful pictures of the more trustworthy heavens.View image in fullscreenBack to earth with Parking Lot of Violent Forces and Depressive Positions.Photograph: © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy the Artist and Sadie Coles HQ, LondonI was happy to be brought back to earth. In the upstairs gallery, Parking Lot of Violent Forces and Depressive Positions, the title of which saves me some descriptive labour, riffs onPhilip Guston’s 1969 painting City Limits. Where Guston shows his hooded clowns roaming around in an absurdly small car in search of somebody to lynch, Eisenman has replaced them with goons in the military fatigues and wraparound shades beloved of ICE agents, pimpled white arses riding up out of their trousers. If the comment on contemporary US society is clear, then British viewers might also be reminded of the recent images of paunchy men standing in ragged formation as some ex-private schoolboy exhorts them to avenge their feelings of inadequacy on those who cannot defend themselves.Set in an apocalyptic landscape overseen by a comic-book monster, the painting proposes righteous anger as an alternative response to “what happened”. Hedonism is another, and one long associated with the end of empire. Unfurling across six conjoined canvases, The Orgy is a remarkable compositional achievement, transforming a writhe of limbs, feet and breasts into interlocking planes of colour that never allow the eye to settle. Like a stubbornly physical take on the more lyrical visions of mid-century painters such as Lee Krasner, it conjures the momentary escape (from the world, from the self) that sexual ecstasy affords.Hands at the edges of this orgy clutch at the rippling bedsheet as if preparing to draw a veil over the scene, and it is notable that the only other direct depiction of human companionship (Me and G under the J) is also framed by a painted curtain. The device reminds the viewer that the artist retains the right to block their gaze into the lives of others. That feels consistent with a more general ambivalence about the function of images in a surveillance society, in which to be visible is to be vulnerable (a fact not lost on Eisenman, whosuffered a substantial backlashafter speaking out about Israel’s assault on Gaza).View image in fullscreen‘Bleakest and best form of comedy’ … Stack by Nicole Eisenman at the Royal Academy.Photograph: Peter Nicholls/Getty ImagesAnother response to the predicament, hinted at by two sculptural installations on the theme of dance and a jangling cubist portrait, is to embrace abstraction. There would be a certain irony if Eisenman, who emerged when socially conscious figurative painting was widely accepted to be dead, should take that path now that the wheel has turned. But abstraction might offer some relief from the market’s demand that artists today produce easily legible expressions of their own (and their communities’) identity, not to mention their ideological commitments. When artists are being blacklisted, you can understand the appeal.If this show finds the artist at a crossroads, uncertain of what road to take next, then who doesn’t feel that way? A couple of hundred yards down the street, a sculpture by Eisenman has been unveiled in the courtyard of the Royal Academy. It shows the bent-backed artist carrying the world on her shoulders. Unlike Atlas, however, her world comprises a gigantic barrel of wine, an oversized potato, the artist’s leaping cat and, on top of it all, the late British sculptor Phyllida Barlow. The artist staggers forward, one hand wrapped around a stick, the other holding out a glass in the faint hope of catching a drip of wine from the barrel. This is the bleakest and best form of comedy. The artist can’t go on, she’ll go on.Nicole Eisenman is at Sadie Coles HQ, Savile Row, London until 21 Novemberandthe courtyard of the Royal Academy until 5 FebruaryExplore more on these topicsArtRoyal Academy of ArtsSculpturePaintingExhibitionsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Price hikes, ads and lower quality: has ‘streamflation’ ruined the TV experience? | Television | The Guardian
description: US consumers are starting to opt out of the streaming world as several services raise prices without offering many perks
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: US consumers are starting to opt out of the streaming world as several services raise prices without offering many perks
Content: A still from Toy Story 5.Photograph: Disney/PAView image in fullscreenA still from Toy Story 5.Photograph: Disney/PATelevisionPrice hikes, ads and lower quality: has ‘streamflation’ ruined the TV experience?US consumers are starting to opt out of the streaming world as several services raise prices without offering many perksJesse HassengerThu 24 Sep 2026 10.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 10.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt may not be quite as politically buzzy as the price of gasoline or eggs, but another household expense is going up for millions of people. Disney has brought the price-gouging experience of its theme park home again by raising the prices of most iterations and bundles of its Disney+ and Hulu streaming services. Whether you pay to watch them with or without ads, separately or bundled together, you’re probably getting a price hike of a couple of bucks per month. The few bundles that will remain the same price feature ad-supported versions of both services (plus ESPN). Don’t worry, though; paying extra to avoid the ad-supported versions of those services won’t mean that you’re missing out on some cross-promotional opportunities. Disney’s terms of service note that they reserve the right to insert ads before and after programming on whatever subscription tier they want, regardless of what you’re paying for. True magic!Kim Kardashian’s Team Moms highlights the ridiculous excess of the US youth-sports industryRead moreThis particular magic isn’t reserved for Disney, though. Price hikes among streaming services have become so common that The Verge has adedicated pageaggregating the news of them, which tends to arrive every few months. Apple, apparently high on Emmy fumes, has raised its prices four times in four years, keeping pace with many of its competitors despite a vastly smaller dedicated catalog. Depending on which version of Peacock subscribers use, they’ve seen their bills padded by five or six dollars a month just since the summer of 2025, including another increase last month. Netflix, meanwhile, hasn’t gone up since March 2026. That’s not a reprieve; that’s a sign another hike must be around the corner.Consumers have noticed. Reportedlyan estimated 39% of Americanscanceled a streaming service in the past six months due to what’s been dubbed “streamflation”. Anothersurveyindicates that a majority of people subscribe to at least three such services, which is consistent with estimates of streaming households spending about $70 per month. Access to the six big streaming services (Netflix, Disney+/Hulu, HBO Max, Paramount+, Apple TV, Peacock) will boost that number somewhere in the neighborhood of $120, on top of which subscribers need broadband internet for the services to actually work. For the total price, you might as well call the whole thing Cable+, in that it’s like your old cable bill, only there’s more of it. No wonder cancellations are rampant.To retain subscribers without putting the screws directly to them, it might be viable for streaming companies to stabilize annual prices – typically a discounted lump-sum payment covering a full year of a service – even when raising monthly costs. Some, like Netflix, don’t offer this option. While those that do have kept annual subscriptions cheaper than the a year’s worth of month-to-month, companies don’t seem interested in maintaining bargain levels. The annual price for Disney+ at launch was $70. Now it’s $190, an increase of 170% – presumably to stay competitive with eggs. Amazon Prime, whose streaming service began as a perk for members already paying an annual membership fee for unlimited shipping and other benefits, has also risen while inserting more ads into its programming and downgrading the picture quality. You want higher resolution and fewer ads? That’s another $50 a year.View image in fullscreenMatthew Rhys in Widow’s Bay, a big hit for Apple.Photograph: Robert Clark/AppleThe reasons for all this shameless gauging are pretty simple: Wall Street doesn’t just demand profits (though those have sometimes been scarce in the streaming world) but endless growth, and some services don’t have all that much more room, realistically, to sign up more users any more. Netflix has 325 million subscribers worldwide. What’s their reach goal? 500 million? Three billion? What happens when everyone on Earth with an internet connection and a credit card already has Netflix?Not every service is so close to a saturation point (unless you count electricity as a streaming service). But it’s notable that even a supposedly lower-tier streamer like Peacock commands over 40 million monthly subscribers, equivalent to more than 10% of the United States population. (It’s a heavily US-skewing service, so unlike Netflix those users aren’t especially global.) By comparison, the biggest magazine in the US has a subscriber base of around half that (and that’s the AARP magazine, an outlier in that it’s distributed to paying members). The New York Times, considered an especially successful recent example of the subscription model, has 13 million subscribers. The AMC Stubs A-List program that allows moviegoers to see four films a week has about 1 million.That’s all to say that streaming has unprecedented reach, which means the only realistic way to boost profits is to either raise subscription prices, or make less stuff. The latter might sound ridiculous, especially given that we’ve been living in the post-boom age for streaming shows for a while now. Then again, that’s worked out well for the catalog-basedTubi, whose original works are lower-profile and lower-budget than its competitors. One of several free streaming services, Tubi outstrips some of those paid competitors in market share and turns a profit based only on its ads.Watching a movie or a show on a free service isn’t exactly an optimal experience; there are those ad breaks, sometimes the transfers aren’t top-notch, and the content churn tends to be a little faster than the subscription streamers. It’s definitely not a place where you can catch much of anything nominated for an Emmy in the past five or six years (though some Oscar movies or second-tier popular hits from that period might turn up). On the other hand, free streamers often manage to under-promise and over-deliver; at a time when paid subscriptions seem eager to offer less than ever, especially in the quite broad field of films made before 1995, Tubi, PlutoTV and their ilk always have at least a couple dozen stone-cold classics on hand that more than make up for not including the latest big-name time-wasters (looking at you,Matthew McConaughey/Woody Harrelson sitcomwhere they play themselves!). And the price always stays the same.View image in fullscreenTubi’s original works are lower-profile and lower-budget than its competitors.Photograph: TubiStill, some free streaming services with surprisingly robust and shifting catalogs aren’t exactly the dream of cord-cutting that was fed to consumers throughout the 2010s. The initial idea was to shed the bloat from all-or-nothing cable services that hold monopolies, or something close to it, in plenty of geographic areas. Competition for subscribers would keep good deals in the offing. Instead, what’s been happening over the past five years or so is a redistribution of that money from one set of giant companies to another. There’s slightly more consumer control over the size of the bills, in the sense that, yes, it’s possible to cancel a couple of services in a way that picking and choosing individual cable channels wasn’t possible outsidea few premium subscriptions. But there’s also far less clarity about how to catch the best shows and movies of any given year. For ages, it was mostly a simple formulation: have cable, add HBO. Now even the prestige of HBO seems a little more niche – a Game of Thrones spin-off; a well-liked Green Lantern show – than in the past.There’s also a strange sense that this scramble of greed isn’t paying off as well as it should; many streaming services feel like they’re in far more precarious financial positions than most cable companies or channels were at their peak. It’s a dystopian development: corporations still want consumers on the hook for endless subscription payments, but also seem to want them to share in the nervous stock-checking of a shareholder, without any particular upside. Each month, you check your streaming holdings and see if you’re about to be charged even more, and whether you need to pick one to divest (cancel, whether for good or for now). You can toggle some of them on and off timed to the occasional appearance of a major series like Severance or The Pitt, but the onus for keeping track of erratic streaming schedules is on the subscriber. None of these shows are as necessary as basic groceries. But the ability to relax and watch TV after a long day is still in danger of becoming another budget-related stressor – an unholy combination of cable bloat and the endless doomscroll.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionUS televisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Royal Philharmonic Orchestra at 80 review – birthday celebration champions bold creativity | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Julia Fischer, Pablo Ferrández and Jan Lisiecki brought poetry and virtuosity to Beethoven’s Triple Concerto tour de force and there was vision and cohesion in Strauss’s Ein Heldenleben; Errollyn Wallen’s energetic Flare opened a special evening
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Julia Fischer, Pablo Ferrández and Jan Lisiecki brought poetry and virtuosity to Beethoven’s Triple Concerto tour de force and there was vision and cohesion in Strauss’s Ein Heldenleben; Errollyn Wallen’s energetic Flare opened a special evening
Content: Orchestral joyride … Flare by Errollyn Wallen, centre, was performed at the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra at 80 concert, Royal Albert Hall, London.Photograph: Andy ParadiseView image in fullscreenOrchestral joyride … Flare by Errollyn Wallen, centre, was performed at the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra at 80 concert, Royal Albert Hall, London.Photograph: Andy ParadiseClassical musicReviewRoyal Philharmonic Orchestra at 80 review – birthday celebration champions bold creativityRoyal Albert Hall, LondonJulia Fischer, Pablo Ferrández and Jan Lisiecki brought poetry and virtuosity to Beethoven’s Triple Concerto tour de force and there was vision and cohesion in Strauss’s Ein Heldenleben; Errollyn Wallen’s energetic Flare opened a special eveningClive PagetThu 24 Sep 2026 09.36 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 09.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe year 1946 had its moments. The UN held its first meeting, Winston Churchill delivered his “iron curtain” speech and in London Sir Thomas Beecham founded theRoyal Philharmonic Orchestra. Over 80 years, few ensembles have been as inventive or chameleonlike, embracing everything from film soundtracks such as The Bridge on the River Kwai to pumped-up rock anthems in Hooked on Classics.This birthday celebration may have looked a little safe on paper, but each work represented a creative leap forward: in 1804, Beethoven’s Triple Concerto was the first to feature an entire piano trio as concertante soloist; in 1899, Richard Strauss’s Ein Heldenleben was the composer’s most colossally orchestrated score to date. Vasily Petrenko, the latest in a line of RPO music directors that includes Rudolf Kempe and André Previn, proved an obliging accompanist in the Beethoven before delivering an affectionate and spacious account of the Strauss.First, though, came the world premiere ofErrollyn Wallen’s Flare. A trio of whooping trumpets followed by a massive wallop on full orchestra and off it went, a two-minute orchestral joyride, all barefaced horns and effervescent strings.View image in fullscreenA lyrical threesome… Julia Fischer, Pablo Ferrández and Jan Lisiecki.Photograph: Andy ParadiseThe Triple Concerto was light on its feet, Petrenko spotlighting the poetic, almost flirtatious performances of cellist Pablo Ferrández and violinist Julia Fischer. Pianist Jan Lisiecki, rather awkwardly placed with his back to them, found moments to swivel around, cajoling the string duo into a lyrical threesome. Amid the collegiate C major sunshine, the scrupulously balanced trio still found room to pull virtuosic rabbits out of Beethoven’s musical hat.By way of contrast, Strauss’s tone poem got off to a determined start, the RPO strings chugging along with limber woodwind and rock-solid brass (nine horns – “quite the thing to express heroism,” the composer declared). The Hero’s Companion, a portrait of the composer’s tempestuous wife, was carried off with self-effacing virtuosity by leader Duncan Riddell. The strength of this performance, however, lay in its sense of vision and musical cohesion. The rip-roaring orchestral battle, with laser-focused offstage brass and the final retreat from the world with its soulful strings, saw Petrenko and the RPO emerge as the real heroes of the night.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicRoyal Philharmonic OrchestraErrollyn WallenreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m a writer but then nobody’s perfect’: how Billy Wilder conquered Hollywood | Movies | The Guardian
description: From émigré roots to a titan of modern cinema, penning classics such as Double Indemnity, Some Like It Hot and The Apartment, a new retrospective celebrates the father of film noir’s incredible career
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From émigré roots to a titan of modern cinema, penning classics such as Double Indemnity, Some Like It Hot and The Apartment, a new retrospective celebrates the father of film noir’s incredible career
Content: An inveterate self-mythologiser … Billy Wilder.Photograph: BFIView image in fullscreenAn inveterate self-mythologiser … Billy Wilder.Photograph: BFIMovies‘I’m a writer but then nobody’s perfect’: how Billy Wilder conquered HollywoodFrom émigré roots to a titan of modern cinema, penning classics such as Double Indemnity, Some Like It Hot and The Apartment, a new retrospective celebrates the father of film noir’s incredible careerDarren RichmanThu 24 Sep 2026 04.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 21.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLike all survivors,Billy Wildernever forgot where he came from or what he had left behind. He was born at the start of the 20th century in Austria-Hungary and died at the start of the 21st in California, the inscription on his gravestone a nod to his most famous line: “I’m a writer but then nobody’s perfect.” Wilder, though, had a habit of of making flawless films throughout his career, a point proved by Almost Perfect, a comprehensive retrospective of his work, running at the BFI Southbank from 19 October until the end of the year.Wilder was an inveterate self-mythologiser, a film-maker with a brand long before there were opportunities for promotion through Instagram accounts and chicken shop dates. He told a story of living in Berlin during his fledgling years in show business and being kept awake all night by “a toilet that was on the blink”.“I would lie there and listen to it, and since I was young and romantic, I’d imagine it was a beautiful waterfall – just to get my mind off the monotony of it and the thought of it being a can.”Most of us would have called a plumber but the aspiring young film-maker chose instead to use the incident as fuel for perhaps the greatest body of work in cinema’s golden age. This is the man who made Double Indemnity, the archetypal film noir and the genre’s zenith, a film often imitated but never equalled. He was responsible forSome Like It Hot, a movie routinely voted the greatest comedy ever made, while his Sunset Boulevard is generally acknowledged as the best film about show business. The Apartment, arguably his magnum opus, is rightly considered one of the greatest films in the history of the medium.View image in fullscreenFilm noir’s zenith … Barbara Stanwyck and Fred MacMurry in Double Indemnity.Photograph: BFILike Stanley Kubrick, Wilder mastered a variety of genres and displayed a range rarely seen in the profession. Ace in the Hole was a scathing satire of the newspaper industry, Witness for the Prosecution a hugely influential courtroom drama and The Lost Weekend dealt with alcoholism in a way that was unprecedented in the 1940s. Even a lesser work like The Seven Year Itch contains one of the century’s defining images: that of Marilyn Monroe standing on a subway grate as her dress is blown upwards. Wilder was undeniably an egotist but he had much to be egotistical about.He was born Samuel Wilder in 1906 to a Jewish family but the name change in this case was not an attempt at assimilation. His mother nicknamed the young Wilder “Billie”, having been inspired by Buffalo Bill’s Wild West shows, an entertainment she experienced during a brief spell living in New York. Wilder worked as journalist andtaxi dancerearly in his career, jobs that seem to foreshadow an almost pathological desire to observe people in all their complexity, as well as a love of the limelight.His screenwriting career began in Berlin during the silent era, most notably collaborating with Robert Siodmak and Edgar G Ulmer for People on Sunday. All three men would end up in Hollywood having fled their home countries due to the rise of nazism and are among the most significant players in shaping the film noir movement, the fatalism of the genre surely a byproduct of the fates of their families.View image in fullscreenA fatalism inspired by the fate of his family … Mauvaise Graine.Photograph: BFIWhen Adolf Hitler came to power, Wilder fled to France. With some understatement, he said: “It seemed like the wise thing for a Jew to do.” He made his directorial debut there in 1934 with Mauvaise Graine although nothing about that film suggested what was to come once he arrived in Hollywood later in the same year.Wilder teamed up with Charles Brackett and penned films for the great and the good of Hollywood, writing screenplays for the likes of Howard Hawks, Mitchell Leisen and Ernst Lubitsch. The last was Wilder’s hero and he hung a sign above his desk for ease of reference while working. It read simply: “What would Lubitsch do?”Wilder made a couple of minor American films beforeDouble Indemnity– but this was the movie that made his name, the most influential crime picture in the annals of cinema. The Holocaust hangs over Double Indemnity like the smoke from Phyllis Dietrichson’s cigarette and it is worth noting that Wilder was working on the project as his family perished in the camps thousands of miles away. It was as though he used all his creativity and negativity about the human condition to do something worthwhile with the survivor’s guilt. Tellingly, in an alternative ending that has never made its way out of the Paramount vaults, Fred MacMurray’s Walter is executed in a gas chamber.Early in those Hollywood days, Wilder was summoned to the consulate and it looked as though he might be deported. It was not just his febrile imagination that led Wilder to conclude he would ultimately end up “shipped off to Dachau” unless he could convince this interlocutor of his worth. The American on duty asked Wilder what he did for a living and the answer was succinct: “I write movies.” The official paced back and forth in the office before stamping the young man’s passport and saying: “Write some good ones.”View image in fullscreenWilder’s magnum opus … Shirley MacLaine and Jack Lemmon in The Apartment.Photograph: BFIHe certainly did that, from early gems such as an adaptation of Erich Kästner’s Emil and the Detectives in the Berlin years to underappreciated work at the end of his career such as the superlative The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes, via one of cinema’s great runs from the 1940s to the 1960s. He never forgot that interrogation and maintained, to the end, that he “did not want to disappoint that dear man in Mexicali”.Wilder’s final few films suggested a man out of time, although Fedora at least inspired Jonathan Coe’s terrific 2020 novel Mr Wilder & Me. The latter is being adapted for the screen by Christopher Hampton with Stephen Frears set to direct, yet raising the funds has proved difficult. This feels somewhat apt since Fedora concerns an ageing film star bemoaning the New Hollywood film-makers of the 1970s, dismissing them as “kids with beards”.Fluctuating between obscurity and acclaim feels right for a film-maker who expertly blended darkness with light. Twenty-five years after being kept awake by the toilet, Wilder made it to an Austrian spa and an actual waterfall, “the most beautiful in the world”.“There I am in bed, listening to the waterfall. And after all I have been through, all the trouble and all the money I’ve made, all the awards and everything else, there I am in that resort, and all I can think of is that goddamned toilet. That, like the man says, is the story of my life.”Almost Perfect: The Films of Billy Wilder is at theBFI Southbank, London, from 19 October until 31 DecemberExplore more on these topicsFilmBilly WilderFilm industryCrime filmsComedy filmsDrama filmsRomance filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: U2 announce new album Carnaval de Luz, featuring final recording by Dolly Parton | U2 | The Guardian
description: Irish rock legends’ 16th studio album, described by the Edge as ‘a messy, provocative, sacred collection of songs’, to arrive in November
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Irish rock legends’ 16th studio album, described by the Edge as ‘a messy, provocative, sacred collection of songs’, to arrive in November
Content: Riding the crest of an industrious spell … U2, who have announced new album Carnaval de Luz.Photograph: Viviane SassenView image in fullscreenRiding the crest of an industrious spell … U2, who have announced new album Carnaval de Luz.Photograph: Viviane SassenU2U2 announce new album Carnaval de Luz, featuring final recording by Dolly PartonIrish rock legends’ 16th studio album, described by the Edge as ‘a messy, provocative, sacred collection of songs’, to arrive in NovemberBen Beaumont-ThomasThu 24 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleU2 have officially announced their first album of new material in nearly a decade, entitled Carnaval de Luz, to be released on 13 November.Closing out the album’s 12 tracks is Torn, the final recorded performance byDolly Parton, who duets with Bono on a song described in press materials as “a tender country song detailing broken family ties, that holds wider resonances”. Parton died aged 80 on 25 August.Guitarist the Edge described Carnaval de Luz, U2’s 16th studio album, as “a messy, provocative, sacred collection of songs”, whileBonopromised “loud guitars, deep bass, some ecstatic rhythms … the same imagination that brings us our creativity can also bring us monsters. So we make the drums louder. We build a bigger fire. We make our stories wilder and funnier. We make the melodies sweeter and the songs, they better shine, because if the world is in darkness we better not be.”The album caps an industrious spell for the Irish rock legends, who have already released two EPs this year: Days of Ash and Easter Lily.Speaking as Days of Ash was released in February, Bono trailed the release of the new album, saying it would have “a carnival vibe … a more defiantly joyful feel” than the vexed political songwriting of that EP, which reflected on ICE, Iran, Ukraine and the Israel-Palestine conflict.Days of Ash was praised by the Guardian’s Alexis Petridis, who said the “zeal, purpose and belief” of the band’s peak years “has been recaptured here”.U2: Days of Ash review – six new tracks reaffirm the band as a vital political voiceRead moreThe new album announcement comes 50 years, to the week, after drummer Larry Mullen Jr, then aged 14, pinned a message to the noticeboard of Dublin’s Mount Temple Comprehensive School which read “drummer seeks musicians to form band”.The quartet, rounded out with bassist Adam Clayton, were all there from the very first meeting, and went on to become arguably the defining rock band of the late 20th century thanks to critically acclaimed and commercially successful albums such as The Joshua Tree and Achtung Baby.They extended their success into the new millennium, with a trio of back to back UK No 1 albums: All That You Can’t Leave Behind, How to Dismantle an Atomic Bomb and No Line on the Horizon. Their most recent albums are a loosely connected trilogy between 2014 and 2023: Songs of Innocence, Songs of Experience and Songs of Surrender, the latter a collection of reworked versions of material from their back catalogue.Carnaval de Luz reunites the band with Brian Eno and Daniel Lanois, the duo who produced The Unforgettable Fire, The Joshua Tree and Achtung Baby. Eno co-writes and plays synths on three tracks, while Lanois plays pedal steel on the Parton duet. More contemporary names also feature in the form of EDM megastar Martin Garrix, co-writer of Glorify, and pop star and producer Ryan Tedder, co-producer of Silencio.The latter track, a raucous rock’n’roll song, has been released alongside the album announcement. The first track from the album, Street of Dreams, was released in July.Explore more on these topicsU2Pop and rockIrelandDolly PartonBononewsShareReuse this content

title: Macklemore announces Free Palestine tour to benefit humanitarian aid organisations | Macklemore | The Guardian
description: The US rapper, removed from Ed Sheeran’s US stadium tour after voicing support of Palestine, has convened a charity show that will visit Dublin, Paris and London, with a North American run to be announced
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: The US rapper, removed from Ed Sheeran’s US stadium tour after voicing support of Palestine, has convened a charity show that will visit Dublin, Paris and London, with a North American run to be announced
Content: Macklemore performing in Switzerland in 2025.Photograph: Anthony Anex/Keystone/APView image in fullscreenMacklemore performing in Switzerland in 2025.Photograph: Anthony Anex/Keystone/APMacklemoreMacklemore announces Free Palestine tour to benefit humanitarian aid organisationsThe US rapper, removed from Ed Sheeran’s US stadium tour after voicing support of Palestine, has convened a charity show that will visit Dublin, Paris and London, with a North American run to be announcedLaura SnapesThu 24 Sep 2026 12.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 18.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMacklemore has announced a “Free Palestine” tour, a series of live shows that will feature the US rapper performing alongside musicians and friends to raise funds for humanitarian causes in Palestine.The news comes after Macklemore (AKA Benjamin Haggerty) was removed from Ed Sheeran’s US stadium tour after he called for a “free Palestine” onstage and said he wanted the people of Gaza and “the occupied West Bank” to know “we have not forgotten about them”.The speech, made on 4 September, prompted venue owners to refuse to allow any concerts featuring Macklemore to take place on their property.Sheeran respondedto the backlash over Macklemore’s removal with a written statement in which he declined responsibility for the decision and said: “I am not complicit.”View image in fullscreenA poster for the London date of Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour.All Sheeran’s remaining support acts subsequently dropped out of the tour – Irish songwriter Aaron Rowe, Billie Eilish’s older brother Finneas and Danish band Lukas Graham – alongside the Irish trad group Beoga, who were to accompany Sheeran for portions of the show.Macklemore posted on Instagram alongside his tour announcement: “If these last couple of weeks have shown us anything, it’s that something has shifted over the last three years. There has been a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now.“It’s 2026. Being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work anymore. People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community. To use the stage for more than entertainment. To push back when the call for a FreePalestineis met with attempts to silence it.“What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage. When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention.”On his solo return to the stage in Philadelphia on 19 September, Sheeran read an apology about “making mistakes” from a teleprompter. “I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet,” he said.Small groups of fans protested outside the venue, with some of them having sold their tickets in protest. Other concertgoers said they were sticking by the musician. A tearful Sheeran told the crowd: “Everyone is telling me to cancel, and I’m feeling all of my friends and family and people I know abandon me and I look at the end of the week and I see 50,000 people who haven’t abandoned.”In the days since the controversy kicked off, Sheeran is estimated to have lost almost half a million followers across social media, according todata from Social Blade reported by the Independent.3:09Ed Sheeran sorry for ‘mistakes’ as tour resumes – videoMacklemore’s statement continued: “So, as you all know, my schedule freed up a bit.” He said he had been using his time to contacts “artists who have shown up and used their stages to stand in solidarity with the Palestinian people, regardless of the consequences. Artists who understand that our platforms mean very little if we’re only willing to use them when it’s safe.”No further lineup details have yet been released for Macklemore’s tour.“Because of how quickly all of this has come together, a lot of the conversations, schedules and details are still being worked out,” he wrote. “But this is a moment of momentum, and there is work to be done.”Macklemore’s tour will begin in Dublin on 26 October. Two of Sheeran’s former support acts are Irish and many Irish musicians have been outspoken in their support for the Palestinian people, citing their own country’s history of occupation and oppression, asRowe did in his statementexplaining his departure from Sheeran’s tour:“As Irish people, we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation,” Rowe wrote. “I need to be true to myself and my ancestors who resisted colonisation, and fought for a freedom that I enjoy today in Ireland.”The list of organisations to benefit from the concerts has been shared: Anera, Glia, Gaza Soup Kitchen, Taawon, Heal Palestine, Palestinian Youth Movement, Middle East Children’s Alliance, Jewish Voice for Peace, Medical Aid for Palestinians. Institute for Middle East Understanding, Palestine Children’s Relief Fund and UNRWA USA.A press release said that these organisations “represent the array of work in support of Palestinian people. That includes medical care, humanitarian assistance, education, community support, advocacy, organising and media work connected to Palestinians.”Further dates in Paris (29 October) and London (30 October) have been announced, with North American dates to follow. Fans hoping to get tickets are encouraged to sign up for presale access at macklemore.com.Explore more on these topicsMacklemoreEd SheeranPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Pete Byrne, frontman of British new wave band Naked Eyes, dies aged 74 | Music | The Guardian
description: Duo had US hits with their cover of Always Something There to Remind Me as well as Promises, Promises and more
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Duo had US hits with their cover of Always Something There to Remind Me as well as Promises, Promises and more
Content: Pete Byrne performing in 2014.Photograph: Randy Miramontez/AlamyView image in fullscreenPete Byrne performing in 2014.Photograph: Randy Miramontez/AlamyMusicPete Byrne, frontman of British new wave band Naked Eyes, dies aged 74Duo had US hits with their cover of Always Something There to Remind Me as well as Promises, Promises and moreBen Beaumont-ThomasThu 24 Sep 2026 05.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 05.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePete Byrne, the frontman of British new wave group Naked Eyes who carried them to repeated chart successes in the US, has died aged 74.The news was announced on the band’s website and social media on Wednesday, stating that Byrne died peacefully in Los Angeles on 14 September after a brief illness.Byrne was part of the “second British invasion” when synthpop and new wave bands from the UK, powered in part by the rise of MTV, swept into the US, with peers including Duran Duran, A Flock of Seagulls and more.He formed Naked Eyes in the late 1970s after the failure of his groups Studio and Neon, with Neon featuring future Tears for Fears members Curt Smith and Roland Orzabal as well as his future Naked Eyes bandmate Rob Fisher and others. “Rob and I found that running a band was not as interesting as writing and recording,” Byrne said. “We decided to go back to square one.”View image in fullscreenNaked Eyes in 1983, with Byrne, left.Photograph: Ron Wolfson/Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesThey split off as a duo, renamed themselves and signed to EMI. Their debut single became their biggest hit: a cover of the Burt Bacharach-penned Always Something There to Remind Me, powered by Byrne’s earnest boyish croon, which reached the Top 10 in the US, Canada and Australia.Though Naked Eyes never hit the Top 40 in their native UK, they continued a run of US successes with three more Top 40 hits there: Promises, Promises (which reached No 11 and featured Madonna on unreleased remixes), When the Lights Go Out and (What) In the Name of Love (which was remixed by Arthur Baker).The group weren’t able to replicate their synth-heavy studio setup on tour, and they split after their second album, 1984’s Fuel for the Fire. Byrne later blamed the split on him and Fisher living in Los Angeles and London respectively, and on EMI losing faith in the project.Byrne retreated, writing and producing with other artists – later including a song for Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen – and recorded backing vocals for Stevie Wonder’s 1985 US No 1 Part-Time Lover. He released a solo album, The Real Illusion, in 2001, and began working with Fisher again, rebooting Naked Eyes as a solo project after Fisher’s death in 1999. Byrne released two further albums under that name and became a familiar face on 80s revue tours, alongside the likes of the Go-Go’s and the Human League.Speaking in 2017, Byrne said music has been “the main focus of my life since I was 18. Nothing has changed really. I still get up in the morning, make coffee, fiddle around on the guitar and scribble down some nonsense. And I eventually look back and say: ‘There might be something there.’”He is survived by three children, Merlin, Dylan and Chloe, from his marriage to ex-wife Elena, as well as his siblings Eileen, Sandy, Carol and Steve.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rocknewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Cracking auction, Gromit!’ Original Aardman puppets go under the hammer  | Aardman | The Guardian
description: Wallace and Gromit stop-motion models and other beloved creations raise money to train new generations of animators
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Wallace and Gromit stop-motion models and other beloved creations raise money to train new generations of animators
Content: Wallace and Gromit stop-motion puppets from the film Vengeance Most Fowl are displayed during a preview of the Propstore auction of Aardman memorabilia.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAView image in fullscreenWallace and Gromit stop-motion puppets from the film Vengeance Most Fowl are displayed during a preview of the Propstore auction of Aardman memorabilia.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAAardman‘Cracking auction, Gromit!’ Original Aardman puppets go under the hammerWallace and Gromit stop-motion models and other beloved creations raise money to train new generations of animatorsSteven MorrisThu 24 Sep 2026 17.41 EDTFirst published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWallace’s reaction as the auction got into full swing might have been a trademark “good grief!” – and the enthusiasm of some of the bidding could have caused even the phlegmatic Gromit to show surprise.Fans of Wallace and Gromit and other beloved creations of Aardman Animations seized the chance to grab souvenirs when more than 200 pieces – including Wallace, Gromit, Shaun the Sheep and Chicken Run puppets fromAardmanproductions – went under the hammeron Thursday.Wallace’s dog Gromit was nearly a cat, reveals creator as Aardman turns 50Read moreSought-after items included Wallace and Gromit stop-motion models from the Bristol studio’s hugely popular 2024 filmVengeance Most Fowl.Lot 216, for example, was Wallace in his traditional outfit of a knitted green tank top, red tie and brown trousers. The catalogue said he was in “smashing condition”, and gave details of his construction: “Wallace’s head is moulded from clay; while his body is made of silicone to facilitate smooth repositioning by the animators.“He has a skeleton, just like every salt-of-the-earth lad, it’s just that his happens to be made of metal. His teeth, shirt collar, tie, pen, and pencil are fast-cast resin and his eyes are plastic.” It sold for an eye-popping £50,400.A puppet of Gromit on all fours from the same film was “crafted over a fully jointed internal metal armature, allowing him to be held in his most natural pose”. It fetched £31,500.The catalogue made it clear these were not toys but pieces of art needing special packaging, shipping and careful handling. “Please also be aware that exposure to extreme temperatures may cause damage,” it said.View image in fullscreenFeathers McGraw alongside CI Mackintosh. A Feathers puppet, with the villain wearing his red rubber glove disguise, sold for almost £57,000.Photograph: Richard Gardner/ShutterstockAnother eye-catching lot was number 219 – Wallace and Gromit’s nemesis, Feathers McGraw, disguised as a nun. The catalogue reminded bidders of one of the best Wallace and Gromit lines: “Feathers McGraw? Don’t be ridiculous. That’s just an innocent nun, out for a pleasure cruise.”It went for more than £30,000 while a second Feathers puppet – with the villain wearing his red rubber glove disguise to make out he was a chicken rather than a sinister penguin – did even better, selling for almost £57,000. Crime, it appears, does pay.It was not only Wallace, Gromit and Feathers that proved popular.Aardmanaficionados snapped up pieces related to the studio’s early days, including clay puppets of Morph and his pal Chas.Every lot started at £100 but as bidding got under way at teatime in London, it was clear they were not going to stay low for long.The Morph and Chas puppets, made from plasticine by Aardman co-founder Peter Lord and accompanied by handwritten care instructions, one of the first lots to be auctioned, sold for £3,780.View image in fullscreenChas (left) and Morph sold for £3,780.Photograph: PropstoreMischievous Morph first appeared in 1977 as part of Take Hart, before starring in his own series of adventures. Another lot – lunch for six with Lord in Bristol – was bought by someone for more than £11,000. A stop-motion masterclass with an Aardman animator sold for just over £20,000.Storyboards fromWallace & Gromit: the Wrong Trouserssigned by another Aardman grandee, Nick Park, went for almost £4,000. A 9cm-tall clay rabbit that appeared inThe Curse of the Were-Rabbitcost almost £10,000.Bidders whose budget could not stretch to a Wallace or Gromit puppet could buy more modest souvenirs such as lot 89 – dry stone walls and gate from the Shaun the Sheep TV series. That came with “adhesive remnants from where the pieces were secured to the set”. It sold for a more affordable £567.The sale, run bythe memorabilia auction house Propstore, marked the 50th anniversary of the studio, with the profits to be used to train new generations of animators.Ngaio Harding-Hill, the director of attractions and live experiences and archive at Aardman, described it as an “unprecedented opportunity” to own a part of the studio’s 50-year history.Harding-Hill said the collection had been carefully curated by the Aardman team to make sure the studio’s five decades were reflected in the auction.She said: “Proceeds from the auction will be invested in talent development initiatives across Aardman, including bursaries at our world-class training facility, the Aardman Academy, meaning every sale is contributing to nurturing the next generation of animation talent.”Explore more on these topicsAardmanWallace & GromitAnimation on TVTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Global release announced for acclaimed Gaza documentary NAZA | NAZA | The Guardian
description: Theatrical rollout across 56 territories planned for documentary about Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza before film will stream on Guardian website
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: Theatrical rollout across 56 territories planned for documentary about Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza before film will stream on Guardian website
Content: ‘The death threats will not stop the film’ … a scene from NAZA.Photograph: The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The death threats will not stop the film’ … a scene from NAZA.Photograph: The GuardianNAZAGlobal release announced for acclaimed Gaza documentary NAZATheatrical rollout across 56 territories planned for documentary about Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza before film will stream on Guardian websiteCatherine ShoardandLorenzo TondoThu 24 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 17.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNAZA, the award-winning documentary from Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, is set to be released in cinemas inmore than 50 countries before a digital global release on theguardian.com.The film, which the Guardian produced, premiered at the Venice film festival earlier this month, where it was met with a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went onto win the special jury prize.‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligenceRead moreAfter screenings in Bologna and at the San Sebastián film festival, the film will receive its North American premiere on Saturday at the New York film festival before opening four days later at the IFC Center in New York City.
