On 9 October it will expand to Los Angeles and other key US cities before a national rollout.A theatrical release in partnership with MK2 Films is also planned in 55 other territories, including the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Canada, Hong Kong, Brazil, Turkey, Thailand, France, Spain, Germany, Turkey, Central America and the Middle East.After its run in cinemas, the film will stream in late November on the Guardian’s website, for free, as part of the news organisation’s commitment to the dissemination of independent journalism.“NAZA is grounded in rigorous journalism published over the past three years,” said Harry Davies, a Guardian investigations correspondent and one of NAZA’s producers. “But it is also a powerful piece of cinema that will soon be available on screens, large and small, around the world.”Documentary NAZA gets 25-minute standing ovation at Venice film festival premiere – videoA number of distributors and cinemas in Israel have been offered the film, and the Guardian is exploring ways by which NAZA can be seen in the occupied Palestinian territories.From ovations in Venice to death threats in Israel: the extreme responses to NAZA documentaryRead moreThe documentaryreveals the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. NAZA is a military acronym euphemistically used by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians that it expects will be killed in an airstrike.Shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, the film features interviews with 24 members of Israeli intelligence and military, granted on the condition of anonymity. The film builds on journalism first published by the Guardian, +972 Magazine, an Israeli-Palestinian publication, and Hebrew-language outlet Local Call between 2023 and 2025.In 2024, Abraham and Szorwon the best documentary Oscarfor No Other Land, along with their two Palestinian co-directors, Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal. Jonathan Glazer, the Oscar-winning film-maker of The Zone of Interest and Under the Skin, has executive produced, while his longtime collaborator, James Wilson of JW Films, also produced the film.The film won unanimously positive reviews at its premiere, but last week Benjamin Netanyahu and a number of senior military and far-right political figures called for the directors’ citizenship to be revoked, and accused them of“treason against the state”.The Israeli prime minister said he would seek new laws allowing the country to strip citizenship from people who “smear” Israeli soldiers and “defame” the state of Israel. Alongside the announcement,dozens of rightwing activists gathered outside Szor’s parents’ home.Police and border police officers were deployed at the scene. One protester called for the “death penalty for traitors” and demanded that the homes of the film-makers’ families be demolished.Speaking on Thursday, Abraham and Szor said: “We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israelis to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible.“The threats from the Israeli government to revoke our citizenship and the death threats do not change that and will not stop the film. We thank our colleagues for the solidarity and look forward to sharing NAZA all over the world very soon.”‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directorsRead moreLast week, 43 local human rights organisations issued ajoint statementurging Israeli authorities to stop what they described as incitement and threats against the film-makers, and not to prosecute either them or their sources.More than 1,500 Israeli film-makershave also signed a petition defending “freedom of expression and creation” and expressing solidarity with Szor and Abraham.Their sentiments have been echoed by a number of leading film-makers around the world, including Ken Loach, Joshua Oppenheimer, Paul Laverty, Laura Poitras, Nan Goldin, Richard Eyre and Hanif Kureishi. Oppenheimer, the US director of Oscar-nominated documentaries The Act of Killing and The Look of Silence, said, “The Israeli government is waging a full-scale intimidation campaign against film directors. I am appalled and enraged.”Explore more on these topicsNAZAFilm industryVenice film festivalGazaJonathan GlazerNo Other LandPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: The Real Rooneys review – at least Wayne and Coleen’s reality show proves they can laugh at themselves | Television | The Guardian
description: This trip into the celeb couple’s Cheshire mansion is nowhere as real as they’d like you to believe. But their self-deprecation is hard not to enjoy
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: This trip into the celeb couple’s Cheshire mansion is nowhere as real as they’d like you to believe. But their self-deprecation is hard not to enjoy
Content: Wayne and Coleen share some family time.Photograph: Disney+View image in fullscreenWayne and Coleen share some family time.Photograph: Disney+TV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Real Rooneys review – at least Wayne and Coleen’s reality show proves they can laugh at themselvesThis trip into the celeb couple’s  Cheshire mansion is nowhere as real as they’d like you to believe. But their self-deprecation is hard not to enjoyJack SealeThu 24 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 10.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘No one knows the real Rooneys,” saysColeen Rooneyat the start of her family’s new reality-TV series, The Real Rooneys. “This is a side of us we’ve never shown before.” Coleen and her husband, ex-footballer Wayne, have had their personalities dissected in the tabloids every week for the past two decades; now we’re promised the truth. But how real can The Real Rooneys be?There are two obvious problems here, the first being that the Rooneys’ lives feel like fiction: he was a generational sporting talent, a one-in-a-million player whose success has bought him and Coleen a ridiculous Cheshire mansion with a cinema, indoor pool and adjacent football pitch. To get back to the road you have to drive over a bridge across a lake. As we join them, Coleen is working out how to capitalise on a recent appearance on I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, while Wayne is plotting an uptick in his media appearances that he hopes will make him a regular on Match of the Day. Technically, the Rooneys exist on our Earth, but – as they both admit, recalling their working-class childhoods in Croxteth, Liverpool – they have left ordinary life behind.‘We’ve been on a good run lately. We’ve not had a row for weeks!’: Coleen and Wayne Rooney on marriage, mistakes and making reality TVRead moreEven if we accept that they are to some extent real people, the further problem is that if you want to get to know someone, watching a behind-the-scenes “at home with” reality show is not the way to do it. This is an established format that was initially shaped by the Kardashians and has now evolved to fit the specific needs of retired British sportsmen looking to relaunch themselves as media personalities. By design, the shows are anything but realistic, instead offering a carefully calibrated blend of fantastic luxury that viewers can escape into, and domestic rituals – breakfast, the school run – offered up in a half-hearted attempt to show that really, these famous folk are just like us.We are being sold a product that is fundamentally just the family brand, but is, these days, increasingly a commercial venture that the show happily advertises. So it is here, as episode one revolves around Coleen attending meetings with buyers and strategists at Primark, with a view to launching her debut fashion collection. We’re steered towards believing that the success of the line will be heavily dependent on Coleen herself, rather than Primark’s in-house experts dialling her input up or down to suit their purposes. The Primark bosses talk about Coleen being a good fit on account of how authentic, relatable and down-to-earth she is; that’s the commodity they’re buying.View image in fullscreenThe Rooneys at play.Photograph: Kerry Spicer/DisneyStill, it’s not as blatant as Michael Owen’s aggressively cynical recent series Meet the Owens, which quickly descended into one long promo for his racehorse trading business – and which failed in its secondary mission to dispel Owen’s reputation for being boring, because it involved footage of him talking. Here, Coleen comes across as honest, self-aware and, crucially, someone who doesn’t seamlessly fit into the role she has been given. When the producers hand her a tablet with a photo gallery charting the history of the questionable outfits she has worn in public, her self-deprecating reactions are endearingly genuine.Wayne Rooney, meanwhile, is a man who transcends the artifice of the celebrity reality documentary. The lazy tabloid caricature of him is that he’s not very bright, which doesn’t seem to be true at all: he’s not naturally as verbose as some of his peers and he’s certainly diffident in his dealings with Coleen and their four sons, but he shares his wife’s willingness to be the butt of a joke, particularly around the premature end of his coaching career after he left his role as manager of Plymouth Argyle by mutual agreement.We get a glimpse of the Rooney family’s bantering sense of humour in one of the otherwise heavily sanitised chats with the kids, as they bounce and fidget on a vast, pearl-coloured sofa, when second eldest son Klay wheels out a perfect parody of a nasal Mancunian football pundit droning on about what a great player his dad was. “Oh, top drawer, honestly. He was top drawer. Back in the day, the way he got the ball and travelled with it, he was tyyyyop draaaa-wer. The power he had at such a young age, oh my word … ” Coleen, approximately 25 yards away on a different part of the same settee, is in hysterics.Documentaries have a standard trick to make those sofa chats feel more natural, which is to let us hear the question being asked from somewhere behind the camera. This one takes that a step further by regularly spinning the camera around to show the interviewer and crew, as if to say: “Look how unfussy this programme is, it’s not like the others.” That’s only true up to a point, but the Rooneys are more real than most.The Real Rooneys is on Disney+ nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewWayne RooneyColeen RooneyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Big Little Truths by Liane Moriarty review – Big Little Lies sequel shoots for high drama but fails to deliver | Fiction | The Guardian
description: At 400-plus pages, Moriarty’s follow-up is too long and offers too little reward, with menopause, vaping teens and even a stalker failing to raise the stakes
Author: Bec Kavanagh
Headline: At 400-plus pages, Moriarty’s follow-up is too long and offers too little reward, with menopause, vaping teens and even a stalker failing to raise the stakes
Content: Liane Moriarty’s sequel Big Little Truths ‘is too long and offers too little reward’.Composite: Macmillan AustraliaView image in fullscreenLiane Moriarty’s sequel Big Little Truths ‘is too long and offers too little reward’.Composite: Macmillan AustraliaAustralian book reviewsFictionReviewBig Little Truths by Liane Moriarty review – Big Little Lies sequel shoots for high drama but fails to deliverAt 400-plus pages, Moriarty’s follow-up is too long and offers too little reward, with menopause, vaping teens and even a stalker failing to raise the stakesSupported byAbout this contentBec KavanaghThu 24 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLiane Moriarty’s Big Little Lies was such a runaway success – debuting at No 1 on the New York Times bestseller list andadapted for a television miniseriesstarring Reese Witherspoon, Nicole Kidman and Zoë Kravitz – that she always had her work cut out for her if she was to return the fluctuating narrative back to the page. Recognising this hurdle, Moriarty opens the sequel (her first) with a note to readers that details the way the new novel both responds to its TV adaptation – by making Laura Dern’s Renata and Meryl Streep’s Mary-Louise more central characters – and returns readers to the original landscape, the fictional Pirriwee Peninsula along Sydney’s northern beaches.Liane Moriarty: ‘I was wondering, “How is everyone on this plane going to die?”’Read moreMoriarty immediately situates the reader back in Australia: a magpie swoops “like a missile” at an unsuspecting cyclist against a backdrop of “bright yellow native wattle” and “lush-purple” jacarandas. Time has passed, in both the real and fictional world. It has been 12 years since the 2014 publication ofBig Little Lies, and the sweet kindergarteners at the heart of the original are teenagers now, with mothers in the midst of menopause. The idyllic setting is shattered when a severed human finger is posted to the local high school, setting the scene for a sequel packed with all the intrigue, drama and suspense of the first.Sadly, for the most part, Big Little Truths fails to deliver. In the first book, the death of a major character brings an urgency that alleviates the heft of the novel (both are more than 400 pages). A key figure in the community has died – who? And which of the melodramatic but mostly unremarkable Pirriwee parents is responsible? This tension is mirrored in the kindergarten cohort where Ziggy, son of newcomer Jane, has been accused of choking one of the other girls on his first day. Themes of abuse and toxic masculinity offer a moral underpinning, while romance and tensions between the mothers provide drama that the Real Housewives would envy. Whatever it lacked in nuance, Big Little Lies made up for in thrills and intrigue.Big Little Truths, however, has lost this edge. United by their shared experience in the first book, the Pirriwee mums – Renata, Jane, Bonnie, Madeline and Celeste – have become each other’s ride or dies. In the midst of “the menopause”, the women carry each other through the various crises of middle-age – health scares, ageing parents and increasingly alienated teenagers. The only thing that threatens this equilibrium is the discovery that their kids are vaping, and this low-level drama doesn’t rock the boat for long.The children, who are rehashing the central events of the novel to a counsellor in the polyvocal chorus that will be familiar to readers of the first novel, also seem to live relatively uncomplicated lives. There are hints at lingering trauma from the events of their childhood, but no lasting scars. They are, for the most part, totally normal, occasionally obnoxious, earnest, endearing teenagers. The stakes of the first novel have lowered, replaced by these more immediate, intimate dramas.The realism of these scenes sits uncomfortably against its melodrama, although this too feels flat. There’s a mysterious, stalker figure whose presence is so obviously signalled throughout the first half of the novel that it’s hard to find him genuinely alarming, and the severed finger of the opening pages is, for the most part, relegated to the background. For a large part of the narrative it feels as if the novel’s dramatic tension is too far away to really ignite.Time Travel for Beginners by Jaclyn Moriarty review – an imaginative tale of turning back timeRead moreAs much as it’s a relief to see women united rather than in cruel competition, and to witness some genuinely touching moments between them as they rediscover themselves and each other during a period so like adolescence – fragile, hilarious and full of emotion – it’s not enough to carry the novel. These moments of true connection and vulnerability are small punctuations in a novel that still shoots for high drama and falls short. When we finally get to Moriarty’s trademark reveal it feels overly contrived and the heavy-handedness of the moral lesson cheapens the subtle, but infinitely more powerful, moments between the women.This isn’t to suggest there’s no fun to be had here. There’s enough happening in the first half of the novel to keep things moving, and the return of familiar faces feels like putting on a beach cardigan. But for its 400-plus pages, Big Little Truths is too long and offers too little reward.Big Little Truths by Liane Moriarty is out now (via Pan Macmillan in Australia, Penguin Random House in the UK, and Crown in the US)Explore more on these topicsFictionAustralian book reviewsBig Little LiesThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Yellow Dog by Martin Amis review – Bill Nighy has a ball  | Martin Amis | The Guardian
description: From spoof monarch to porn tycoon, the actor narrator goes to town on the larger-than-life characters in this Booker-nominated satire
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: From spoof monarch to porn tycoon, the actor narrator goes to town on the larger-than-life characters in this Booker-nominated satire
Content: Narrator Bill Nighy.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for BFIView image in fullscreenNarrator Bill Nighy.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for BFIAudiobook of the weekMartin AmisReviewYellow Dog by Martin Amis review – Bill Nighy has a ballFrom spoof monarch to porn tycoon, the actor narrator goes to town on the larger-than-life characters in this Booker-nominated satireFiona SturgesThu 24 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 10.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the 2003 novel Yellow Dog, Xan Meo is set upon by two men in a pub who cosh him over the head: “Like the statue of a fallen tyrant, he crashed sideways into the damp paving, and lay still.” Meo is a writer and actor whose late father was a dangerous gangster; the attack is in revenge for Meo naming an old associate of his father in print. Meo survives, though the injury leaves him with an altered personality. Where he was previously a conscientious husband and father, now he is a chip off the old block.While Meo languishes in hospital, King Henry IX – who is struggling to conceal his boredom with the job – is informed that images of his 15-year-old daughter in the bath are in circulation. And Clint Smoker, star reporter and gossip peddler at the tabloid newspaper the Morning Lark, gets an unexpected tipoff.Yellow Dog is the Booker-nominated satirical novel byMartin Amiswhich, through a trio of interconnected comic narratives, explores the baser instincts of men. It is one of several Amis titles being released on audio this year; others include Money, London Fields, Night Train and The Rachel Papers.Bill Nighy is The Yellow Dog’s narrator, and he has a ball voicing Amis’s larger-than-life protagonists. Along with Meo, Smoker and King Henry, a suitably eccentric supporting cast includes Russia, Xan’s long-suffering wife; gruff bodyguard Mal Bale; pornography tycoon Cora Susan; and mercurial football striker and tabloid darling Ainsley Car. Though some of these characters veer into caricature on the page, Nighy succeeds not only in making them believable but great fun to be around.Available via Vintage Digital, 11hr 54minFurther listeningLove LanePatrick Gale, Tinder, 7hr 53minGale’s follow-up to his 2015 novel A Place in Winter finds his elderly protagonist Harry Cane sailing home to a radically different England and trying to reconnect with the family he abandoned. Read by the author.HonouredNaz Shah, Weidenfeld & Nicolson, 7hr 13minThe Labour MP for Bradford West narrates her memoir recalling her traumatic childhood and teen years – she witnessed domestic violence against her mother and was forced into marriage at the age of 15 – and her eventual path into politics.Explore more on these topicsMartin AmisAudiobook of the weekAudiobooksreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Exit Party by Emily St John Mandel review – alternate visions of post-crisis America | Science fiction books | The Guardian
description: Is the price of stability necessarily the loss of freedom? Two possible future worlds are linked in the new novel from the author of Station Eleven
Author: Nina Allan
Headline: Is the price of stability necessarily the loss of freedom? Two possible future worlds are linked in the new novel from the author of Station Eleven
Content: Superlative storytelling … Emily St John Mandel.Photograph: Laura Barisonzi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSuperlative storytelling … Emily St John Mandel.Photograph: Laura Barisonzi/The GuardianBook of the dayScience fiction booksReviewExit Party by Emily St John Mandel review – alternate visions of post-crisis AmericaIs the price of stability necessarily the loss of freedom? Two possible future worlds are linked in the new novel from the author of Station ElevenNina AllanThu 24 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 02.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn her second novel, 2009’s The Singer’s Gun, Emily St John Mandel tells the story of Anton Waker, a young man desperate to make a break from his criminal family. His plans are thwarted by his cousin Ari, whose hard-nosed talent for operating outside the law has become a way of life. A decade later inThe Glass Hotel, a painting called Swan Dive that hangs in the lobby of the luxury retreat stands as a symbol of escape from a trap that is closing. You will not need to have read either of these earlier novels to enjoy Mandel’s seventh, Exit Party, though their loose intertwining of narrative threads will provide extra pleasure and a sense of homecoming for those who have. It is also interesting to observe Mandel’s evolution from a writer of quirky tales of offbeat protagonists to a novelist whose world-spanning, politically resonant narratives now attract a wide and devoted following.Exit Party begins five years into our future, in 2031. Ari Waker has just come out of prison after serving an 18-year sentence for the attempted murder by contract killing of her cousin Anton. Much has changed while she has been inside: a second civil war has devastated lives and blighted the economy, and the United States as such has ceased to exist.As the novel opens, the newly inaugurated independent State of California is celebrating the end of violence and the lifting of curfews. Ari and her flatmate Gloria have been invited to a party at the home of Gloria’s friend, Kareem. Ari has the feeling that she is meant to be there; she has experienced such premonitions before, and learned to trust them. Arriving at Kareem’s home, she has the sense that something strange is happening. A woman she’s never met before addresses her as Ibari – the name that is legally hers but never used. A painting disappears from the wall. Someone else talks of “extra people” and of the party being “a door that swings both ways”. “There’s something wrong with this party,” mumbles Kareem, before stepping out into the night and walking away.double quotation markMandel’s landscapes are intricately constructed, an elegant dance in which plot, character and idea appear effortlessly matchedKareem never returns. But Ari does not have time to dwell on the incident. Forced back on her own resources, she spends the next few years working menial jobs, all the time with the underlying sense that there is a different future waiting for her, if she can only reach it: “It wasn’t that she thought she deserved more than what she had … it was just that she’d once had a considerable amount of money, her own business, and a beautiful apartment in a tower in New York City”. Old habits die hard, and it is not long before Ari falls back into criminal company. She is offered a surveillance job – she has always been attracted to detective work – but when the woman she is spying on turns out to be the doppelganger of Gloria, her former flatmate, Ari can no longer ignore the sense of deja vu that has begun to plague her life.Ari’s world is fractious and chaotic, characterised by scarcity, systemic instability and the ravages of climate change. While her ability to adapt to every situation has enabled her to survive, it has also prevented her from making lasting attachments, a fact she recognises but cannot bring herself to regret. Gloria’s doppelganger Nico speaks of a different world, in which Ari’s own doppelganger Ibari is a high-ranking detective in a government secret police force known as Service.In this other world, Nico was a physicist, part of a team conducting experiments into teleportation. She was also a dissident. In the novel’s second half, B-Side, we enter a United States where environmental catastrophe has been averted and resources are equitably distributed. It is also a society ruled by universal surveillance, in which the presidency is passed from father to son and where anyone veering from the established order is quietly disappeared.This is a peaceful dystopia, its glittering streetscapes and self-styled progressivism more reminiscent of Huxley’s Brave New World than Orwell’s concrete-and-jackboots Nineteen Eighty-Four. It is an eerie place, nonetheless. “I studied History before I came to Service,” Ibari says when asked why she decided to serve the lawmakers. “It made me terrified of discord.” While Ibari – reticent, calculating, a loyal arm of Service – might seem to be the polar opposite of the fiercely driven, anarchic Ari, the two women ultimately prove themselves capable of similar acts of recklessness and similar loyalty.Is the price of stability necessarily the loss of freedom? The question plays out daily in our political reality, its fictional possibilities providing inspiration for writers from Plato’s time onwards. The “upbeat-downbeat” ending Mandel chooses for her novel is not new in science fiction; indeed, it bears comparison to her own earlier take on the post-catastrophe novel, the 2014 blockbusterStation Eleven. What makes Exit Party a superlative example of the form is its structural cohesiveness, its expert play of signs and symbols, its psychological realism. Mandel’s imaginative landscapes have from the first been intricately constructed, an elegant dance in which plot, character and idea appear effortlessly matched. In Exit Party, her ability to handle a complex array of material while never once allowing her focus to drift from the human story reaches new heights.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat does the stolen painting Swan Dive represent? Freedom? Risk? A doomed plunge towards self-destruction? In one particular, irrecoverable moment, Mandel memorably demonstrates how by the end of this extraordinary novel it will have come to mean all three.Exit Party by Emily St John Mandel is published by Picador (£18.99). title: Forgotten Island review – best friends forever trapped in frantic DreamWorks animation | Movies | The Guardian
description: This over-controlled adventure never takes a breath or a moment to let its characters come to life
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: This over-controlled adventure never takes a breath or a moment to let its characters come to life
Content: Rare moments of silence … Jo, voiced by R&B star HER, left, and Raissa, voiced by Liza Soberano in Forgotten Island.Photograph: DreamWorks Animation/Universal Pictures/APView image in fullscreenRare moments of silence … Jo, voiced by R&B star HER, left, and Raissa, voiced by Liza Soberano in Forgotten Island.Photograph: DreamWorks Animation/Universal Pictures/APMoviesReviewForgotten Island review – best friends forever trapped in frantic DreamWorks animationThis over-controlled adventure never takes a breath or a moment to let its characters come to lifePeter BradshawThu 24 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrantically and even stroboscopically over-energised, this big new movie from DreamWorks about best friends for ever seems to me another example of exhausting AI-type content production in animation. You could make the same argument against plenty of live-action films of course, but it is in animation that this kind of soulless blitzkrieg tends to predominate. Forgotten Island is over-controlled and over-determined, a movie that never, or hardly ever, takes its pedal from the metal, never takes a breath or a moment to let its characters come to life. At times it seems to be aping the world of Japanese anime, but without its sense of character or capacity for calm.The story, weirdly reminiscent of The Hangover of all things, is set in thePhilippinesin the pre-social media 90s. Jo, voiced by R&B star HER, is a lonely and super-imaginative teen always in trouble at school; like Moana she has a wise grandma who guides her to her ancestral destiny and has captivated Jo with stories of her culture and identity – stories of the forgotten island of Nakali. Jo makes friends with similarly lonely Raissa (Liza Soberano) who like Jo is smart but with a much more focused sense of academic discipline.Their alliance is pledged and a friendship bracelet woven, but as the years go by, poor Jo winds up with a loser’s job in a fast food joint, whereas Raissa feels guilty about leaving Jo behind as she heads for college at Caltech in the glamorous world of America. (The moment when she tells Jo she is leaving – effectively breaking up with her – is a rare moment of silence in which real emotions emerge and something is recognisably at stake.) But it is now that Jo discovers a mystical portal into the magical forgotten island of Nakali and semi-accidentally makes Raissa tumble down through this portal with her; they awaken 12 hours later to discover they have already done things here of which they have no memory and need to find out what. They also need to discover the portal which will take them back.This Hangover-style amnesia facilitates a quest narrative, in the course of which they meet a goofy pal in the form of a wacky shapeshifting dog called Raww (Dave Franco) and a scary batibat, or memory demon, resembling Jabba the Hutt called Batiba (Jenny Slate) to whom they may have to surrender precious memories in return for freedom. They also encounter the terrifying figure of Manang (Lea Salonga) who, like Batiba may have relatable vulnerabilities that we don’t yet appreciate. And so it continues, developing and resolving with algorithmic efficiency. It leaves you with a strange sense of emptiness.Forgotten Island is out on 17 September in Australia, 25 September in the US, and 16 October in the UKExplore more on these topicsFilmAnimation in filmScience fiction and fantasy filmsHERPhilippinesAsia PacificreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘This gap opens up of doubt and scepticism about everything’: Jess and Morgs confront the politics of deepfakes | Dance | The Guardian
description: In the choreographers’ new work, virtuosic movement and some green-screen magic unfurl the theatricality of high-stakes television interviews
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: In the choreographers’ new work, virtuosic movement and some green-screen magic unfurl the theatricality of high-stakes television interviews
Content: ‘It’s really about the strange shifting relationship with the landscape of truth’ … Morgann Runacre-Temple and Jessica Wright.Photograph: Yonathan KellermanView image in fullscreen‘It’s really about the strange shifting relationship with the landscape of truth’ … Morgann Runacre-Temple and Jessica Wright.Photograph: Yonathan KellermanDanceInterview‘This gap opens up of doubt and scepticism about everything’: Jess and Morgs confront the politics of deepfakesLyndsey WinshipIn the choreographers’ new work, virtuosic movement and some green-screen magic unfurl the theatricality of high-stakes television interviewsThu 24 Sep 2026 05.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 09.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt appears the interviewer has got him on the ropes. “For the record, I did not take part in a pagan ceremony with minor members of the royal family in which we daubed ourselves in paint,” states the beleaguered politician, caught outside Buckingham Palace with his flies undone and forced to defend himself. This is a fabrication, of course – I’m watching the scene play out in an east London dance studio – but it doesn’t feel miles away from something that could be true. And how do we know what’s the truth anyway? That’s the question inDeepfake, the latest piece from award-winning dance duo Jessica Wright and Morgann Runacre-Temple, AKAJess and Morgs.The pair tell modern stories with ambitious tech – film and live camera work – and often techy themes, too. “We’ve always been drawn to where there’s a crossover between the theme and the form,” says Runacre-Temple. “What gets us excited is seeing the contemporary world reflected back.” The pair scored a massive hit with their 2022 pieceCoppélia, made for Scottish Ballet, which turned a twee 19th-century ballet about a dancing doll into a cautionary tale of AI automatons and unrestrained tech bro egos. Definitely not one-hit wonders, earlier this year theymade their debut at the highly esteemed Paris Opera Ballet.View image in fullscreenGladiatorial drama in smart tailoring … Deepfake.Photograph: ChewboyDeepfake is set in a green-screen studio, where the interview is taking place between a cool-headed journalist and a politician. With writerJeff James, Jess and Morgs looked at a wealth of TV interviews, from Jeremy Paxman’s 1997 grilling of Michael Howard, wherehe asked the same question 12 times, to theformer prince Andrew’s disastrous turn on Newsnight. They also took inspiration from the current ultra-media-trained politicos who “continually and bombastically evade any questions at all”, says Wright.They liked the way the television interview is already a theatrical setup, says Wright. “I think there’s something fun about putting that on stage and asking the audience to engage with the theatricality as well.” It’s gladiatorial drama in smart tailoring. “It’s really high stakes; it’s win or lose for both of them,” adds Wright.In the show, the interview will be filmed live by four cameras – then, as well as seeing what’s happening in reality, the audience will watch another version on screen with background footage edited in. We’ll be privy to the fabrication of the image and a number of possible realities. There are also seven dancers in green-screen suits who manipulate the environment but will disappear in the edit.View image in fullscreenPrivy to the fabrication of the image … Deepfake.Photograph: ChewboyAs Runacre-Temple says, green screen can actually look quite lo-fi – “It’s got that slightly absurd, playful, silent movie quality about it” – and it’s ancient tech compared with the kind of AI deepfakes that are emerging today. “They look so hyper real,” says Runacre-Temple. “The danger of deepfakes is not only that people believe things that aren’t true to be real, but that they start to disbelieve things that are true, and this gap opens up of doubt and scepticism about everything.” Or, as in their story, someone who has been caught out doing something they shouldn’t can insist it’s a fake image. “It’s really about the strange shifting relationship with the landscape of truth.”I go to visit rehearsals on a day when there’s no tech in sight, bar a couple of laptops. “It’s good to go analogue to actually finish the choreography,” says Wright, wryly, counting the diminishing days to the premiere. All we have is an enormous studio and two incredible dancers: Rebecca Bassett-Graham, best known for dancing with Wayne McGregor’s company, who is playing the journalist; and as the politician, Kennedy Junior Muntanga, who has worked with Akram Khan.View image in fullscreen‘It’s got that slightly absurd, playful, silent movie quality about it’ … Deepfake.Photograph: ChewboyThe text plays in voiceover while the two dancers embody and expand on its meaning. Their quick-fire movements visualise all the dynamics of a charged conversation: charm, challenge, cooperation, accusation, entrapment, etc. The feel is freewheeling, but each movement is tightly mapped to the syllable, every flex of muscle is considered. In certain scenes with the green screen, dancers will have to hit exact marks and even eyelines on exact words “or the whole illusion collapses”, says Wright. They’re creating their own high-stakes environment for the performers, where “the dancers’ virtuosity is a metaphor for these very virtuosic performances in interviews”.Will this battle have a winner? Can we believe what we see? Jess and Morgs aren’t giving any spoilers. “Hopefully it will be surprising and mischievous,” says Runacre-Temple.Deepfake is atDanceEast, Ipswich, on 25 September and atSadler’s Wells East, London, 1-3 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDanceTheatreAI (artificial intelligence)DeepfakeComputingAkram KhanWayne McGregorinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Three Men in a Boat review – quirky novella makes for perky, fun-forward theatre | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A rag puppet Montmorency, a fake moustache and an aria for reeking cheese add to the mischief of Jerome K Jerome’s very English story
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: A rag puppet Montmorency, a fake moustache and an aria for reeking cheese add to the mischief of Jerome K Jerome’s very English story
Content: Slapstick … Jonny Weldon, Bronté Barbé and Richard David-Caine in Three Men in a Boat.Photograph: Helen MurrayView image in fullscreenSlapstick … Jonny Weldon, Bronté Barbé and Richard David-Caine in Three Men in a Boat.Photograph: Helen MurrayTheatreReviewThree Men in a Boat review – quirky novella makes for perky, fun-forward theatreRose theatre, Kingston upon ThamesA rag puppet Montmorency, a fake moustache and an aria for reeking cheese add to the mischief of Jerome K Jerome’s very English storyMark LawsonThu 24 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBack from Lib Dem conference, Ed Davey watched this adaptation in his Kingston constituency ofJerome K Jerome’s novellaabout a trio of late Victorian gents rowing the Thames accompanied by fox terrier Montmorency. Might the up-for-fun politician suddenly drop on to the stage in a Scooby-Doo suit?He didn’t, although Christopher Haydon’s perky production features one actor making an applause-winning entrance from an improbable location. This version is also certainly more liberal and democratic than the 1889 text whose language has often dated in meaning or propriety.View image in fullscreenMind your ankles … Calum Donald-Bruce with Montmorency.Photograph: Helen MurrayBronté Barbé plays, with false moustache and lower voice notes, the eccentric Harris who, with lugubrious George (Richard David-Caine), joins pompous hypochondriac Jerome (Jonny Weldon) on a river trip that starts from Kingston. As with all quirky, discursive books, the challenge of adaptation is imposing momentum and tension. Al Smith’s dramatisation neatly juggles chronology (the sixth chapter is his first scene) and anchors the book’s best set pieces (swan attack, putrid cheese, a murder investigation) in a new narrative where the blokes are heading to Oxford for Harris’s wedding, his choice of best man a bugbear.Three Men in a Boat has come to represent an idyllic, witty lost England.Tom Stoppard, an immigrant ecstatic to have landed here, wrote a 1975 BBC adaptation in that spirit. But the book has darker meditations on religion, society and death. Smith makes George, originally a bachelor banker, a doctor who has been recently widowed, with a boldly bleak monologue about bereavement that is presumably a tonal surrogate for an incident in the original, not dramatised, where the boaters spot a floating corpse.Otherwise, the show foregrounds jauntiness. Montmorency, a menace to ankles, cats and other dogs in the book, is here a charming puppy rag puppet (animated by Calum Donald-Bruce), a theatrical device now so familiar that it prompts in-jokes: “We’ll have to eat the puppeteer!”View image in fullscreenJaunty … Three Men in a Boat.Photograph: Helen MurrayThe 135-minute show is punctuated by eight musical numbers and, though it is now almost obligatory for classic literature to be sung and danced (the most recent victimJane Eyre), this is a logical candidate. The book includes references to Gilbert and Sullivan, opera, music hall, banjos, bagpipes and accordions. Grant Olding’s songs incorporate all, including a biographical patter number about Jerome, an Italianate aria for the reeking cheese and a Tchaikovsky ballet pastiche (choreographed by Simon Hardwick) when the journey reaches swan river.That sequence and others justify the poster for the show which, referencing Magritte and Dalí, suggests the story is surrealist. But slapstick dominates in an engaging evening that smooths the jagged oddness of the book.AtRose theatre, Kingston upon Thames, until 10 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)MusicalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Julia Jacklin: The Gem review – tender, emotional storytelling of hope and hopelessness  | Australian music | The Guardian
description: The Australian musician’s fourth album blends mystery and intimacy with luscious pop-rock, bright, upbeat jangle and stripped-back acoustics
Author: Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen
Headline: The Australian musician’s fourth album blends mystery and intimacy with luscious pop-rock, bright, upbeat jangle and stripped-back acoustics
Content: Julia Jacklin: her ‘gentle, startlingly controlled voice is her superpower’.Photograph: Izzie AustinView image in fullscreenJulia Jacklin: her ‘gentle, startlingly controlled voice is her superpower’.Photograph: Izzie AustinAustralian musicReviewJulia Jacklin: The Gem review – tender, emotional storytelling of hope and hopelessness(4AD/Remote Control Records)The Australian musician’s fourth album blends mystery and intimacy with luscious pop-rock, bright, upbeat jangle and stripped-back acousticsGiselle Au-Nhien NguyenThu 24 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJulia Jacklin is an artist of dualities. Over her decade-plus career, the Melbourne singer-songwriter has examined the question of how to be both vulnerable but protected, spiritual but grounded.Her second studio album and commercial breakthrough, 2019’sCrushing, introduced her to an international audience as an introspective storyteller. Rich in detail, Crushing delivered tales of heartbreak and betrayal with a kind of quiet impassivity, setting the scene for her own duality as an artist – at once open and reserved.In 2022 Jacklin turned even more inward withPre Pleasure, examining the impact of childhood religion on her sexuality. The sound often contrasted these complicated ponderings: these were big, bold songs more obviously influenced by modern pop, chimes and all.Gang of Youths are back: ‘Does it sound like a cynical gesture towards pop radio stardom?’Read moreThe musician’s fourth album, The Gem, finds its place between these musical and thematic worlds. God is, again, a recurring theme – Jacklin grapples with the tension of “how to feel free with someone watching over me”, as she sings on track five, Angel Vision. She shifts the perspective by imagining herself, or a loved one, in the almighty role.The second track on the 10-song album, God Sometimes, describes the necessity of taking control of your own destiny, whereas If I Had the Hand of God takes the opposite approach, with Jacklin wondering if being all-knowing would actually change anything at all. Hope and hopelessness blur into a singular kind of surrender.View image in fullscreen‘The Gem offers a window into the contradictions and confusions of Jacklin’s smart, sensitive mind.’Photograph: John McDermott/James J RobinsonJacklin’s eye remains sharply observational throughout, as she imbues life’s ordinary scenes with contemplative weight – whether watching a neighbour eat a peach over their kitchen sink, calling her dad or forgetting to water a friend’s plants. “Can’t afford to have an inner life,” she sings on the album opener, Brand New – but everyday moments do seem to awaken her rich internal monologue across the record.Julia Jacklin finds the light: ‘I’ve wasted a lot of energy in my life trying to be cool’Read moreSonically, The Gem balances luscious pop-rock (God Sometimes, The Hardest Thing) with bright, upbeat jangle – such as in the lead single, Get Away From Me (I Think I’ll Love You Soon) – and stripped-back acoustics (Angel Vision, the piano-led You Turned On the Tap). At the album’s halfway mark, Real Life finely straddles the line between lo-fi and more dense arrangements, beginning with a tinny drum machine before building to something more quietly complex.Jacklin’s gentle, startlingly controlled voice is her superpower, bringing stories to life with tenderness and emotion. She accompanies herself on Brand New, singing the title phrase over and over as it’s layered with a defiant statement: “I’m free now, let me be brand new.” Elsewhere, sumptuous harmonies come courtesy of her bandmate and collaborator Jacob Diamond; the album closer, I Wish, features the Melbourne folk duo the Maes, bringing to mind another Melbourne band, Folk Bitch Trio, and their melting three-part harmonies.The vocals are especially affecting on Walk On Me, which sounds as though it could be a cut from Crushing. Downbeat guitar and drums back a vignette of a doomed, unequal relationship: “When the band begins to play / I say, ‘I know this song’ / you say, ‘Everyone knows this one’ / so why am I the only person singing along?” Jacklin sings plaintively, before the music takes over. Her voice transforms into an instrument for the rest of the song, soaring over thick sonic layers. There are no words but the pained strength in her vocalisations says it all.Blending mystery and intimacy, The Gem offers a window into the contradictions and confusions of Jacklin’s smart, sensitive mind. The album cover shows a triptych of lockets, all containing Jacklin’s face: in two circular frames, she smiles, but in a rectangular one, her expression is inscrutable. It’s an apt visualisation of Jacklin’s genius duality, continuing her trajectory as one of Australia’s finest contemporary songwriters.The Gem is out nowExplore more on these topicsAustralian musicPop and rockFolk musicIndiealbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Himari: Debut album review – teenage prodigy’s playing has depth and feeling | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The programme feels a little safe but the 15-year-old Japanese violinist impresses in her debut recording of works by Wieniawski, Chopin, Godowsky and Sibelius
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: The programme feels a little safe but the 15-year-old Japanese violinist impresses in her debut recording of works by Wieniawski, Chopin, Godowsky and Sibelius
Content: Easy lyricism … Himari.Photograph: Naruyasu NabeshimaView image in fullscreenEasy lyricism … Himari.Photograph: Naruyasu NabeshimaClassical musicReviewHimari: Debut album review – teenage prodigy’s playing has depth and feelingHimari/Berlin Philharmonic/Weigle/Wang(Decca)The programme feels a little safe but the 15-year-old Japanese violinist impresses in her debut recording of works by Wieniawski, Chopin, Godowsky and SibeliusClive PagetThu 24 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen 13-year-old Himari Yoshimura took to the stage with the Berlin Philharmonic in March 2025, she became the youngest Asian soloist to appear with the orchestra in a subscription concert. A subsequent contract with Decca made her the label’s youngest-ever female signing. Her debut album features that Berlin performance of Wieniawski’s Violin Concerto No 1, alongside studio recordings of music by Chopin, Godowsky and Sibelius.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Himari: DebutPhotograph: Naruyasu NabeshimaWhat is immediately apparent is the technical security of her playing, combined with an easy lyricism across the instrument’s full range. The fearsome double stopping in the Wieniawski is impressive, with some supple dynamic phrasing in the upper register. Occasionally a leap to a high note comes up a hair’s breadth short, something absent from the studio recordings, but this is nevertheless a significant performance. She’s not entirely helped by Sebastian Weigle’s smooth but staid accompaniments. It’s not the greatest concerto and needs a lighter touch to give it some lift (compare Michael Rabin and Adrian Boult).The rest of the programme is safe, old-school even, including Heifetz and Milstein arrangements of Chopin Nocturnes, a suitably toothsome reading of Godowsky’s Alt Wien and a lithe-limbed account of the Mazurka from Sibelius’s Five Pieces for Violin and Piano. The playing exhibits depth and feeling, ably supported by pianist Chelsea Wang. The finale, Wieniawski’s Fantasia on Themes from Gounod’s Faust, reveals a keen instinct for musical storytelling amid the fireworks.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: Beverly Buchanan review – ramshackle mini barns and shanties bursting with brutal history  | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Inspired by the shacks and sheds of the American south, Buchanan’s exceptional sculptures combine folk art and minimalism to memorialise the survival of enslaved people
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: Inspired by the shacks and sheds of the American south, Buchanan’s exceptional sculptures combine folk art and minimalism to memorialise the survival of enslaved people
Content: The weathering effect of injustice … Miss Flossie's Shack, 1989.Photograph: Andrew Judd/collection of Lorenzo Legarda Leviste and Fahad MayetView image in fullscreenThe weathering effect of injustice … Miss Flossie's Shack, 1989.Photograph: Andrew Judd/collection of Lorenzo Legarda Leviste and Fahad MayetArt and designReviewBeverly Buchanan review – ramshackle mini barns and shanties bursting with brutal historySpike Island, BristolInspired by the shacks and sheds of the American south, Buchanan’s exceptional sculptures combine folk art and minimalism to memorialise the survival of enslaved peopleEddy FrankelThu 24 Sep 2026 10.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 10.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen she was a kid, Beverly Buchanan visited tenant farmers and sharecroppers across the American south-east with her dad. There in the fields she saw shacks and sheds, shanties and shotgun houses. More than 100 years after the abolition of slavery, she saw in this rough improvised architecture a symbol of survival and perseverance, of a people making their own way against the odds.Buchanan spent the rest of her life – a life marked by multiple chronic illnesses before she died in 2015 – translating that architectural heft into art. This show at Spike Island is filled with ramshackle, half-broken, semi-dilapidated little sculptures, each one based on the buildings of the south. There are houses made of scrap wood, churches made of cardboard, tiny barns hammered together and splashed with paint or covered with buttons. The one large sculpture here is great, a shed seemingly on the verge of collapse, but Buchanan’s physical condition forced her to work on a smaller scale as she was often stuck at home for long periods.They’re improvised sculptures, just like the shacks of the south are improvised buildings. And each one is filled to the brim with history, bursting at the seams with the past. In every shack sculpture you see an echo of slavery, a memorial to the people who survived it, a paean to the endurance of the enslaved.View image in fullscreenArchitecture as a symbol of perseverance … Lamar County. CA, 2003.Photograph: courtesy of the Estate of Beverly Buchanan and Andrew Edlin Gallery, New YorkThe sculptures sit neatly between folk art and minimalism. You can see them as modernist geometric forms or slapdash DIY craft; both are true, and that’s what makes them so compelling. But Buchanan was keen to reject any idea that her art was nostalgic. She saw her work as an attempt to make sure these symbols of grim history weren’t erased. Lots of her best stuff remains in the fields and marshes where it was installed, almost as much a part of nature as the trees and tide. She experimented with concrete and tabby, a material made from oyster shells, sand and ash historically formed into bricks by the enslaved people of the deep south. Buchanan made her own tabby bricks – a filthy, dangerous process – then stacked them up and left them outside where they could be eroded slowly by nature.This idea of weathering is everywhere in Buchanan’s work, symbolising the way people, bodies, could be worn away by injustice. A handful of these works – which she called Frustulas – sit on plinths here, pockmarked and weather-beaten, like someone left a modernist sculpture out in the rain. Each one, again, is a fragment of a violent past, an object weighed down by the history implied in its material, its shape.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLike modernist sculptures left out in the rain … Untitled (Maquette), c1970s.Photograph: Andrew Judd/collection of Lorenzo Legarda Leviste and Fahad MayetNot everything here is that emotionally heavy. A lot of Buchanan’s work is serious and formal and societal, but plenty of it is more personal too. She spent a lot of time in her local pharmacy, a place she could get her meds, but also one where she could meet friends, have some lunch. She made the pharmacy a promo T-shirt, drew out her favourite lunch menu. They’re fun objects that show you a lighter side to Buchanan but they’re not particularly interesting as artworks. The same goes for a lot of her drawings of flowers and chickens and angels, though her self-portraits tell a bit more of a story.The show is also a bit hamstrung by some overthought curation, which pulls the work into a bunch of barely discernible thematic groupings. And there’s no part of me that understands the inclusion of new work by young English artist Phoebe Collings-James – a sound piece and a film of her cousins playing with a sculpture – which has zero relation to Buchanan or her work.But the good stuff here – the shacks and Frustulas – is exceptional. It’s not just morose memorialising of brutal history: it’s a joyful celebration of ingenuity and survival in a world of inequality. As rickety as they look, these shacks tell a story that’s built to endure.AtSpike Island, Bristol, 26 September-31 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designSculptureArtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Taking a deep dive in Helsinki’s subterranean city | Helsinki holidays | The Guardian
description: Under the Finnish capital lies a world of swimming pools, go-karting tracks, playgrounds – and even an art gallery
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Under the Finnish capital lies a world of swimming pools, go-karting tracks, playgrounds – and even an art gallery
Content: Itäkeskus swimming hall, excavated from granite bedrock, could accommodate almost 4,000 people in an emergency.Photograph: Maarit HohteriView image in fullscreenItäkeskus swimming hall, excavated from granite bedrock, could accommodate almost 4,000 people in an emergency.Photograph: Maarit HohteriHelsinki holidaysTaking a deep dive in Helsinki’s subterranean cityUnder the Finnish capital lies a world of swimming pools, go-karting tracks, playgrounds – and even an art galleryGabriella BennettThu 24 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 02.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe moon is an impostor.Swimmingbackstroke beneath its surface, I look up at craggy hollows in close relief. White rock undulates in all directions, a forest of peaks rising next to a desert of craters. Every time I trick myself into thinking I’m somewhere celestial, the sound of children splashing brings me back to earth.This is no lunar landscape but Helsinki’s underground swimming hall, excavated from granite bedrock and officially opened in 1993. These days,Itäkeskusuimahalliis one of the Finnish capital’s most visited leisure facilities, welcoming 400,000 people a year. Local people mingle with tourists, I will discover, during a week exploring Helsinki’s subterranean metropolis.My visit was one of 12 research trips I made over three years to better understand how cities are being reimagined. It turned into a book,How to Build a City, for which I travelled to locations that are testing the frontiers of urban living in response to an increasingly uncertain world.Many global cities feature a version below ground, but Helsinki’s is thought to be the only one transformed for peace. As urbanisation increased the population, a more efficient solution was needed for heating plants and telecoms cables. You could scatter them around in expensive pockets of land, digging up the streets and sacrificing parks. Or you could tuck them away beneath ground level, by adding to bomb shelters first carved out during the second world war.And that’s what Helsinki did. By 2010, its city council approved the world’s first officially masterplanned underground city, home to hundreds of vast human-made caves and tunnels up to 90 metres deep. Itäkeskus pool was opened 17 years before this space allocation plan was approved.In peacetime, the caves function as shopping malls, playgrounds, a go-karting track and subway stations, all connected by almost 200 miles (293km) of tunnels. In the event of war, however, each can be transformed into a bomb shelter, part of a network capable of accommodating 900,000 Finns.View image in fullscreenTourists explore the roof of Helsinki’s underground art museum, Amos Rex.Photograph: Paavo Turtiainen/AlamyItäkeskus swimming hall alone could house almost 4,000 people. In less than 48 hours it can be drained and fitted with decontamination showers. For the rest of the time, there are no clues as to its defence nature. Only the comforting hallmarks of the public pool: the tang of chlorine in my nose and the warmth that cloaked my skin.I arrived in Helsinki on the morning of the spring solstice, although the ground was still dusted with greying snow and I was grateful for the heated carriages on my 25-minute Metro ride from the city centre. At Itäkeskus station, past a school surrounded by Soviet-style tower blocks, silver birches trailed bare branches over cars. From the outside, a municipal glass building gave an uninspiring welcome, but inside, I found a different world entirely.A broad staircase swept me down steeply, framed by rocky, whitewashed walls. After paying (entry to all four of Helsinki’s public swimming halls is €6 for adults and €3.30 for children, making it popular with families as well as budget-conscious travellers), I disrobed in changing rooms spun off from a cathedral-tall granite core. Signs were in Finnish, but the space was easy for non-natives to navigate. Staff spoke excellent English.double quotation markA postmodern dreamscape was revealed, a large pool lined in lavender, canary yellow and burgundy tilesAt one side of the colossal hangar, men grimaced as they lowered themselves into a triangle of freezing water. On the other, a postmodern dreamscape was revealed, a large pool lined in lavender, canary yellow and burgundy tiles, with huge plastic triangles in cerulean and lilac suspended overhead. The only windows were set into a lifeguard’s tower next to a waterfall that filled the air with the roar of water in motion.Swimming under the ersatz moon was an otherworldly experience. After 50 lengths, I’d earned my reward. Included in the entry fee is access to a gym, which I did not visit, plus a hot tub, steam room and two saunas, which I did. A graphic on the door showed a swimming costume crossed out in red and I gingerly removed mine, sliding into place on the bench and reminding myself that prudishness is a uniquely British affliction. Inside, it was so dark I could barely make out other bodies. The low light created the effect of a confession booth.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenTemppeliaukio church is half-buried in the Töölö neighbourhood.Photograph: Danny Lehman/Getty ImagesAround me, conversations bubbled in Finnish, American English and German. The quotidian details of living emerged. I joined in, asking a stranger for dinner recommendations and whether I should brave the plunge pool. If you don’t dwell on it, you could forget the true purpose of this place.It was something I kept returning to over the following days as I wandered through experimental installations at Helsinki’s underground art museumAmos Rex(from €20; children go free), whose antennae-like skylights popped up on concrete stalks from the pavement near the chichi shopping district of Kluuvi. And in the Töölö neighbourhood’s exquisiteTemppeliaukio church(€8; children go free), half-buried in a giant mound of rock.All were examples of a supremely responsive city. All were bomb shelters, too. Evidence that you can design for the future with verve and beauty. Helsinki shows it is possible to do it all.How to Build a City: Journeys into the Urban Future by Gabriella Bennettis published byHeadline(£25). To support the Guardian buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com.
